    • Environments: The bundled plugins are a Browser validator (real Chrome via agent-browser) and an iOS Simulator validator (via xcrun simctl). Custom ones implement src/validators/validator-plugin.ts.
    • Scanners: It uses Claude Code (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, Bedrock or Vertex) or Codex (OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY). It reads .env from the working directory.
    • Output: Markdown, HTML and JSON reports with reproduction steps and evidence go to ~/.redai/runs/<runId>/. REDAI_HOME overrides the location.
    • Setup: Install with bun install -g @kpolley/redai, then run redai. It needs Bun 1.2 or later, and validators need their skill directory in .agents/skills/ inside the target workspace.
    • Demo: examples/webapp is a deliberately vulnerable app on localhost:3000, with an iOS counterpart in examples/iosapp.
    • Caveats: Use it only on systems you are authorized to test. Findings may be wrong, environments need manual login and setup, and ~/.redai/ may hold credentials and transcripts.

    Takeaway: Try RedAI on internal apps to cut false positives from AI scanners through live PoC validation. Run it only in isolated test environments, and treat ~/.redai/ as sensitive data.

  • Google Agent Skills: Reusable Skills for AI Agents to Interact with Google Cloud Services
    summary

    TL;DR: google/skills is Google’s Apache-2.0 collection of Markdown Agent Skills and plugins for Google Cloud and other Google products. Coding agents can load it to work with GKE, BigQuery, IAM, SecOps and more.

    • What it is: Markdown skill files that agent harnesses load. They are not standalone tools.
    • Install: Run npx skills add google/skills, then pick skills, target agents and project or global scope. Update with npx skills update.
    • Plugins: Bundles of skills plus MCP servers. For Claude Code, run claude plugin marketplace add google/skills, then claude plugin install <plugin>@google-plugins. Codex and Antigravity CLI are also supported.
    • Infrastructure coverage: A large GKE set (autoscaler, networking, upgrades, multi-tenancy, workload troubleshooting), Cloud Storage, Filestore, load balancers and TPU/GPU troubleshooting.
    • Security coverage: GKE workload security, Workload Identity Federation troubleshooting, Security Command Center, Google SecOps (triage, detection engineering, threat hunting), IAM Policy Simulator and Privileged Access Manager.
    • Observability coverage: A Cloud Monitoring PromQL generator, Logging Query Language queries, Cloud Trace, SLO alert setup and GKE cost analysis.
    • Other: Well-Architected Framework pillar skills, BigQuery, Spanner, AlloyDB, Cloud SQL, the gcloud CLI skill, and a migrate-legacy-codebases-to-safe-Rust skill.
    • Caveats: Some skills are in Public Preview or carry renamed products. Some live in external repos outside this update flow, and only collaborators can open PRs.

    Takeaway: Install only the GKE, IAM and observability skills your agents need, at project scope. Review the Markdown before trusting it, because these are instructions your agent will follow.

  • GPT-5.5: Mythos-Like Hacking, Open to All
    summary

    TL;DR: XBOW reports that GPT-5.5 is a step change for automated pentesting. It misses 10% of known vulnerabilities on XBOW’s benchmark, and XBOW calls it comparable to Anthropic’s restricted Mythos but more widely available.

    • Method: Models run inside XBOW’s full agent workflows against open-source apps frozen at known-vulnerable versions. The main metric is miss rate.
    • Numbers: Combined blackbox and whitebox miss rates were 40% for GPT-5, 18% for Opus 4.6 and 10% for GPT-5.5.
    • Blackbox: GPT-5.5 without source code beats GPT-5 with source code.
    • Whitebox: Gains were large enough that XBOW says the whitebox benchmark is saturated, or “killed”.
    • Behavior: GPT-5.4 found vulnerabilities in fewer actions, while GPT-5.5 found more of them. XBOW describes this as going further, not just faster.
    • Computer use: GPT-5.5 scored 97.5% on visual acuity, within the margin of the best result (Opus 4.7). It logs in with about half the iterations of the next-best model.
    • Persistence: It still sometimes keeps going when it should give up, but about half as often as earlier GPT versions or Opus.
    • Caveats: This is a vendor self-evaluation after a few weeks of early access, with no sample sizes or CVEs. The Mythos comparison is based on reports, not on XBOW’s own testing.

    Takeaway: Assume broadly available models can now find most known vulnerability classes in your apps, even blackbox. Shorten patch windows and run AI-assisted testing on your own services before attackers do.

  • CTFs in the AI Era: How AI Is Changing Capture the Flag Competitions
    summary

    TL;DR: Include Security argues that frontier LLM agents now solve most easy-to-medium CTF challenges, as BSidesSF 2026 showed. Professional pentesting still needs human judgment that CTFs never test.

    • Evidence: At BSidesSF 2026, 16 teams solved every challenge and every challenge had at least 25 solves. Claude Code and Codex solved everything except a few OSINT challenges.
    • Contrast: In 2025, ChatGPT handled only easy challenges. The author placed 5th solo in 2025 and estimates he would have placed about 75th in 2026 without LLM help.
    • Setup: A Debian VM with Conda, Playwright and Ghidra plus a Ghidra MCP server. It ran Claude Code on Opus 4.6 at max effort, one tmux session per scraped CTFd challenge.
    • Team pipelines: Top teams watched for new challenges, ran several agents per challenge and auto-submitted flags. A coordinator LLM shared discoveries between fast and deep-reasoning models.
    • Cost: The Claude Max 5x plan ($100/month) weekly token limit just covered the whole event.
    • Why CTFs suit LLMs: Single flag goal, verifiable success, small self-contained targets, no reporting, and low consequences for mistakes.
    • Why pentesting differs: It needs business context for false positives, large systems you cannot run locally, scope discipline, reporting and client communication.
    • Caveats: Evidence is mostly one event plus second-hand anecdotes. The setup skips permission prompts, which is safe only inside an isolated VM.

    Takeaway: Use LLM agents to speed up bounded and verifiable security tasks. Keep humans responsible for scope, impact and false-positive triage, and run permissionless agents only in disposable VMs.

  • DeepSec: Agent-Powered Vulnerability Scanner for Large Codebases
    summary

    TL;DR: deepsec from Vercel Labs is an Apache-2.0 agent-powered vulnerability scanner that runs on your own infrastructure. It is built to find long-hidden bugs across large existing repos.

    • How it works: scan uses regex matchers to find candidate sites quickly and without AI. process has an AI agent investigate them. An optional revalidate pass re-checks findings and looks for fixes in git history.
    • PR mode: process --diff investigates only the files changed in a diff.
    • Other commands: triage (P0/P1/P2 with a cheaper model), enrich (committer and owner info), report, export, metrics, status.
    • Setup: Run npx deepsec init at the repo root. It adds only a .deepsec/ folder, and later runs use pnpm deepsec scan and pnpm deepsec process from inside it.
    • Models: Defaults to the strongest models at maximum thinking, tunable with --thinking-level. Calls go through Vercel AI Gateway unless you pass --model-auth direct with your own key’s environment variable name.
    • Scale: deepsec sandbox process --sandboxes 10 fans work out to Vercel Sandbox microVMs. Interrupted runs resume and skip files already analyzed.
    • Cost: The README warns that large codebases can cost thousands or tens of thousands of dollars. Cap spend with --max-cost-usd and --max-duration.
    • Security model: Treat it like a coding agent with full shell access. Prompt injection from vendored or external code is a known concern, and sandbox egress is limited to agent hosts.

    Takeaway: Pilot deepsec on one critical repo with --max-cost-usd set, and run it in sandbox mode. Then wire process --diff into PR checks for ongoing coverage.

  • Warp: Agentic Development Environment with AI-Powered Coding and Terminal
    summary

    TL;DR: Warp has open-sourced the client code of its terminal-born agentic development environment. It ships a built-in coding agent and also runs external CLI agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI.

    • What it is: An agentic development environment that grew out of the Warp terminal, covering code, agents, terminal and Drive.
    • License: The UI framework crates warpui_core and warpui are MIT. The rest of the code is AGPL v3.
    • Agents: Use Warp’s own coding agent or bring your own CLI agent.
    • Build: ./script/bootstrap sets up the platform, ./script/run builds and runs Warp, and ./script/presubmit runs fmt, clippy and tests. AGENTS.md is the engineering guide.
    • Contributing: File an issue first. Maintainers add ready-to-spec or ready-to-implement labels before code PRs are welcome, and report vulnerabilities privately per CONTRIBUTING.md.
    • Automation: build.warp.dev shows agents triaging issues, writing specs, implementing changes and reviewing PRs.
    • Caveats: OpenAI is the founding sponsor, and the agent workflows run on GPT models. Warp Factories and build.warp.dev are early access, and experimental features ship in a Preview build.
    • Numbers: The repo page showed about 65.7k stars, 5.7k forks and 4k open issues at fetch time.

    Takeaway: Check that AGPL v3 is acceptable before you fork or embed Warp code. Review how its agent integrations handle your shell credentials before rolling it out to a team.

  • Practical Package Security: The Unofficial Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz gives a practical guide to defending against package supply-chain compromises like Axios and trivy-action. It uses cooldowns, lockfiles, install-script blocking, registry proxies and canary credentials to cut exposure and blast radius.

    • Pattern: An attacker takes over a maintainer account or build system and pushes a malicious version. Hours to days of exposure is enough, as with Axios 1.14.1/0.30.4, live about 3 hours with about 100M monthly downloads.
    • Incidents: TeamPCP force-pushed 75 of 76 trivy-action tags to steal CI secrets, which then led to PyPI compromises including LiteLLM.
    • Cooldowns: Delay new versions with Renovate minimum release age, Dependabot minimum package age, pnpm update delays or uv exclude-newer. Wiz claims seven days would have stopped 90+% of recent attacks.
    • Lockfiles: Use npm ci in CI, because npm install can rewrite the lockfile. Lockfile adoption is about 50% in npm and about 99.7% in Go.
    • Install scripts: Disable them with npm ignore-scripts or pnpm onlyBuiltDependencies. Roll out by denying by default and allowlisting exceptions.
    • Environments: Run installs in remote dev environments, away from laptop credentials. Aim for zero-touch production with no standing developer prod credentials, and use isolated browsers against cookie theft.
    • Registries: Start with a pull-through proxy (Artifactory, Nexus, CodeArtifact) for visibility. Then move critical paths to curated registries.
    • Detection: Plant canary credentials in CI environment variables. At Grafana, an AWS key canary exposed a compromised Action within minutes.
    • Caveats: Cooldowns delay security patches, and wrapper scanners rely on lagging OSSF malware data. Lockfiles do not control transitive dependencies in common ecosystems.

    Takeaway: Add a 7-day cooldown in Renovate or Dependabot and switch CI to npm ci. Disable install scripts by default, and plant AWS canary tokens in CI secrets today.

  • CloudSec Tidbits: The Danger of Multi-SSO AWS Cognito User Pools
    summary

    TL;DR: Doyensec shows how multi-tenant SaaS apps that let tenants add their own OIDC/SAML IdPs to one AWS Cognito User Pool can suffer ghost identities, account takeover and login-routing hijacks.

    • Setup at risk: One Cognito User Pool where tenants self-register external IdPs through CreateIdentityProvider, with identity logic in Lambda triggers.
    • Ghost identities: If PreSignUp_ExternalProvider lacks a domain check, Cognito saves the attacker’s user. A later rejection in PostConfirmation leaves the record, which can then be used through password reset or impersonation.
    • Trigger gaps: First federated login and later logins run different trigger chains that share only TokenGeneration. Checks placed only on PreAuthentication_Authentication miss first login.
    • Sub-splitting: Federated usernames have the form <ProviderName>_<sub>. ProviderName cannot contain _, but sub can, so a guard and a JIT consumer can parse the same username differently.
    • Homoglyphs: Provider names with Cyrillic lookalike letters pass Cognito’s byte-level uniqueness check but look identical in the Hosted UI and logs.
    • Routing hijack: Cognito does not verify ownership of IdpIdentifiers. An attacker IdP can claim an unclaimed domain such as gmail.com and receive every login for that domain.
    • Attribute abuse: AttributeMapping values from a malicious IdP are attacker-controlled. WriteAttributes does not stop Lambdas calling AdminUpdateUserAttributes on custom:tenantID or custom:role.
    • Fixes: Branch PreSignUp on triggerSource, and parse usernames everywhere with one helper using maxsplit=1. Derive tenant and role server-side, and require domain-ownership proof before accepting an IdpIdentifiers claim.
    • Caveats: These are attack patterns, with no CVE or named vendor. Exposure depends on each platform’s trigger logic, and a Terraform lab plus the maSSO malicious-IdP tool are provided.

    Takeaway: If you run self-service SSO on Cognito, audit every Lambda triggerSource path. Treat all IdP claims, including sub, as untrusted input, and never let tenants claim IdpIdentifiers domains they have not verified.

  • How to Harden GitHub Actions: An Updated Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz updated its GitHub Actions hardening cheat sheet for 2026 after the tj-actions, trivy-action and Axios incidents. It covers org settings, secrets, workflow authoring, third-party actions and runners.

    • Threat pattern: A compromised workflow or action leaks credentials, and the attacker then moves laterally. In tj-actions (March 2025), a vulnerable workflow leaked PATs that were used to poison actions across thousands of repos.
    • Org settings: Make the default GITHUB_TOKEN read-only, since orgs created before February 2023 may still default to read-write. Turn on SHA pinning enforcement (August 2025) and block actions during incidents with a ! prefix.
    • PPE vectors: Pwn Requests through pull_request_target or workflow_run, script injection from issue titles or branch names into run:, GITHUB_ENV/GITHUB_PATH abuse (for example LD_PRELOAD), and living-off-the-pipeline tools.
    • Workflow authoring: Set permissions: {} at the top and grant per job. Use persist-credentials: false on actions/checkout, and pass untrusted values through env, never inline interpolation.
    • Secrets: Scope secrets to step-level env. Avoid toJson(secrets) and secrets: inherit, prefer OIDC, and keep release credentials in GitHub Apps.
    • Third-party actions: Pin to commit SHA, because tags can be force-pushed. Add a 7-14 day cooldown with pinact --min-age 7 or Renovate minimumReleaseAge.
    • Branch protection: Dismiss stale approvals on new commits, and require approval from someone other than the last pusher to stop PR hijacking.
    • Runners: Never attach self-hosted runners to public repos. Use ephemeral runners with default-deny egress.
    • Tools: zizmor for static analysis, octoscan, OpenSSF allstar, and trajan/Gato-X for self-testing. GitHub’s roadmap adds a workflow dependencies: lockfile that pins transitive actions.

    Takeaway: Run zizmor across all workflows and enforce SHA pinning at org level. Set read-only default tokens and permissions: {}, then replace long-lived cloud secrets with OIDC.

  • The Insecurity Landscape of AI-Powered GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz found bypasses of the access gates in Anthropic, OpenAI and Google AI GitHub Actions, plus ways to leak credentials from them. Its rule is that whoever controls the prompt input will achieve injection, so limit both input and blast radius.

    • Thesis: AI actions take free-form input and give nondeterministic output, and prompt injection has no complete fix. Security depends on who can supply input and what the agent can reach.
    • Bot gate bypass: anthropics/claude-code-action and openai/codex-action trust any actor whose name ends in [bot]. With allowed_bots: "*", any attacker-created GitHub App can trigger them.
    • Dangling apps: With a named bot allowlist, an attacker can register an unclaimed app with the trusted name. Wiz compares this to dangling domains.
    • Dependabot confused deputy: @dependabot recreate or @dependabot show makes Dependabot the github.actor. That bypasses allowlists that trust Dependabot.
    • Credential files: Auth actions such as google-github-actions/auth@v2 write GCP, AWS, Azure, Docker or SSH credential files. In a demo, an issue prompt got Gemini to print GCP credentials into the workflow log.
    • Verbose leaks: show_full_output: true in claude-code-action and gemini_debug: true in run-gemini-cli expose every file the agent reads in public logs.
    • Numbers: claude-code-action appears in 12K+ public workflows and run-gemini-cli in 1K+. Misconfigured repos total 200,000+ combined stars.
    • Vendor response: OpenAI added allow-bot-users and stopped trusting Dependabot. Anthropic updated its docs. claude-code-security-review, qodo-ai/pr-agent and coderabbitai/ai-pr-reviewer have no built-in access control.
    • Fixes: Drop allow-bots/allowed_bots wildcards and check author association (OWNER, MEMBER, COLLABORATOR) on comment triggers. Never pair AI actions with credential-generating auth steps or debug output in public repos.

    Takeaway: Search your org for AI actions that use bot wildcards, comment triggers without author-association checks, or cloud auth steps in the same job. Lock those down before an issue comment exfiltrates credentials.

  • distil AI Slop Detector: Chrome Extension That Detects AI-Generated Text Locally
    summary

    TL;DR: Distil Labs’ AI Slop Detector is a Chrome extension that runs a fine-tuned Gemma 3 270M model locally via WebAssembly. It labels pasted text ai_generated or human_written without sending it anywhere.

    • Model: Gemma 3 270M with a LoRA fine-tune for 4 epochs, quantized to Q4_K_M at about 242 MB. The model downloads from HuggingFace on first use.
    • Training: GPT OSS 120B acted as teacher. About 50 hand-written seeds were expanded to about 10,000 synthetic examples, based on a Kaggle AI-generated essays dataset.
    • Runtime: Runs on CPU through Wllama (WebAssembly) in an offscreen document. Each query takes about 0.5-2 seconds on consumer CPUs.
    • Accuracy: The tuned model scored 100%, the Q4 quantized model about 95% (19/20 on the extended suite), and the base model about 40%.
    • Real-world samples: ChatGPT outputs 98% (50 samples), human tweets 94% (50), Reddit comments about 92% (100+), formal emails 88% (30).
    • Size trade-off: Full precision is about 1.1 GB at 100%. Q4_K_M cuts size by about 78% for about 95% accuracy.
    • Setup: Load the unzipped repo unpacked at chrome://extensions/ in Developer mode. You can train your own with the Distil CLI and the distil-cli-skill Claude skill.
    • Limits: About 1 in 20 predictions may be wrong, and formal human writing gets false positives. Test sets are tiny (20 examples), and “slop” is defined by one dataset.

    Takeaway: Use this as a reference pattern for private, on-device small-model classifiers distilled from a large teacher. Do not use its verdicts to make decisions about people.

  • below: Interactive Tool to View and Record Historical Linux System Data
    summary

    TL;DR: below is Meta’s Apache-2.0 Linux resource monitor, a cgroup2-aware alternative to atop. It can show live data, record history continuously, and replay what the system looked like at a past point in time.

    • What it is: An interactive tool to view and record historical system data. Its name reflects rejecting many of atop’s design choices.
    • Data: Hardware utilization, the cgroup hierarchy, per-cgroup and per-process stats, and Pressure Stall Information (PSI).
    • Modes: below live for a live view and below replay -t "3m ago" for history. Recording runs as a daemon through etc/below.service and systemctl start below.
    • Export: below dump writes JSON, CSV or OpenMetrics for scripts. below snapshot creates a replayable file to share.
    • Install: dnf install below on Fedora 34+ and Amazon Linux 2023.9, apk add below on Alpine 3.17+, emerge sys-process/below on Gentoo, or cargo install below.
    • Docker: Images are published as below/below on Docker Hub.
    • Limits: No cgroup1 support. Prometheus and Grafana integration is basic and goes through dump (contrib/grafana/).
    • Caveats: The README does not state kernel or BPF requirements, and its examples use sudo.

    Takeaway: Enable the below recording service on cgroup2 hosts. After an incident, below replay shows which cgroup caused CPU, memory or IO pressure at the moment it happened.

  • boring: Lightweight CLI Tool for Managing SSH Tunnels
    summary

    TL;DR: boring is a small MIT-licensed CLI for managing SSH tunnels. It defines local, remote and SOCKS5 forwards in a TOML file and opens or closes them by name, glob or group, with automatic reconnection.

    • Features: Local, remote, socks and socks-remote forwarding, Unix sockets, keep-alives and auto-reconnect. It works with ~/.ssh/config and ssh-agent.
    • Config path: ~/.boring.toml on macOS and Windows, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/boring/.boring.toml on Linux. $BORING_CONFIG overrides both.
    • Format: Each tunnel is a [[tunnels]] table with name, local, remote, host, mode and optional user, identity, port, group.
    • Port ranges: local and remote accept lists and ranges such as 8000-8010,8080, paired by position.
    • Keep-alive: keep_alive defaults to 120 seconds and can be set globally or per tunnel.
    • Commands: boring list, boring open <patterns> (or -a for all, -g for a group), boring close and boring edit.
    • Daemon: Logs go to /tmp/boringd.log and the control socket is /tmp/boringd.sock. Override them with $BORING_LOG_FILE and $BORING_SOCK, and set $DEBUG for verbose logs.
    • Install: brew install boring, a release binary, or make from source. Windows needs a source build with Go 1.25+ via build_win.bat.

    Takeaway: Replace ad-hoc ssh -L commands for bastion and database access with grouped boring tunnels. This keeps forwards reproducible and auto-reconnecting while reusing your existing SSH config and agent.

  • CodeBurn: CLI Tool Tracking Token Usage, Cost, and Performance Across AI Coding Tools
    summary

    TL;DR: CodeBurn is a free, local, MIT-licensed tool that reads AI coding agents’ session files to break down token usage and API-equivalent cost by tool, model, project and task.

    • How it works: Parses session files your agents already write on disk; no account, API key or proxy; prices come from LiteLLM, cached 24 hours.
    • Coverage: README body lists 42 integrations (About blurb says 37), including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Cline, Kiro, OpenCode, Goose.
    • Views: Terminal dashboard, codeburn web, desktop app, menu bar/tray, plus breakdowns by git branch and 13 rule-based task categories.
    • Optimize: codeburn optimize scans 30 days for waste like re-read files, unused MCP servers, oversized CLAUDE.md; grades A to F; --apply fixes with undo.
    • Guard: Opt-in Claude Code hooks via codeburn guard install warn at $5 and stop a session at $15, both configurable.
    • Agent access: MCP server (claude mcp add codeburn -- npx -y codeburn mcp) exposes get_usage and get_savings.
    • Setup: npx codeburn, npm install -g codeburn or brew install codeburn; needs Node.js 22.13+.
    • Caveats: Dollars are estimates, not invoices; Cursor, Kiro and some Copilot tokens are estimated; can undercount versus Claude Code’s own counter.
    • Privacy: CLI sends nothing; desktop app telemetry defaults off in EU/EEA/UK/Switzerland but on elsewhere; Cursor sync disabled with CODEBURN_CURSOR_SYNC=0.

    Takeaway: Run npx codeburn to see where agent spend goes, use optimize to trim context waste, and turn off desktop telemetry if outside the EU default.

01.04.2026

  • claude-code-config: Trail of Bits Claude Code Configuration Guide and Sandboxing Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: Trail of Bits’ opinionated Claude Code setup covering sandboxing, deny rules, blocking hooks, MCP, local models and workflows, installable via /trailofbits:config.

    • Settings: Sets DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING, enableAllProjectMcpServers: false and cleanupPeriodDays: 365; avoids CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC because it kills auto-updates.
    • Sandboxing: Use /sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) plus Read/Edit deny rules for ~/.aws, ~/.kube, SSH/GPG keys, registry tokens, keychain.
    • Why both: Deny rules alone cover only built-in tools; with /sandbox they also apply to Bash at the OS level.
    • Hooks: Two PreToolUse Bash hooks block rm -rf (suggest trash) and direct pushes to main/master, exiting with code 2.
    • Caveat: Hooks are guardrails, not a security boundary; prompt injection can route around them.
    • Rules: Path-scoped ~/.claude/rules/*.md are not re-injected after auto-compaction, so must-hold rules go in CLAUDE.md or hooks.
    • Worktree gotcha: A blocked worktree helper can make the agent silently fall back to git checkout -b in the shared directory.
    • Local models: LM Studio with Qwen3-Coder-Next (about 45GB, MLX 4-bit) needs 64GB+ unified memory, context at least 25K.
    • Usage: Prefer /clear over /compact, rewind after two failed corrections, and enable /fast (2x cost) only at session start.

    Takeaway: Copy the deny rules, sandbox config and blocking hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json, and only run --dangerously-skip-permissions when both sandbox and deny rules are active.

  • skills: Trail of Bits Claude Code Skills for Security Research and Audit Workflows
    summary

    TL;DR: Trail of Bits’ public marketplace of skills and plugins for AI-assisted security analysis, auditing, verification and development, usable from Claude Code, Codex and ChatGPT workspaces.

    • Code auditing: Largest group, including differential-review, insecure-defaults, sharp-edges, static-analysis, semgrep-rule-creator, variant-analysis, supply-chain-risk-auditor, agentic-actions-auditor.
    • Verification: constant-time-analysis, mutation-testing, property-based-testing, spec-to-code-compliance, zeroize-audit, writing-lean-proofs.
    • Other security: Smart contracts (building-secure-contracts), malware (yara-authoring), reverse engineering (dwarf-expert), mobile (firebase-apk-scanner).
    • Development: modern-python, modern-cpp, gh-cli, devcontainer-setup, second-opinion, git-cleanup, open-sourcing.
    • Install (Claude Code): /plugin marketplace add trailofbits/skills, then /plugin menu.
    • Install (Codex): codex plugin marketplace add trailofbits/skills, then codex plugin add <plugin-name>@trailofbits.
    • Trophy case: The constant-time-analysis skill found a timing side-channel in ML-DSA signing.
    • Caveats: Local add must run from the repo’s parent directory; ChatGPT import needs interface.display_name in agents/openai.yaml.
    • License: CC-BY-SA-4.0; contributors run make check, which covers most but not all of CI.

  • claude-code-devcontainer: Sandboxed Devcontainer for Safely Running Claude Code with Unrestricted Permissions
    summary

    TL;DR: Trail of Bits devcontainer that runs Claude Code in bypassPermissions mode inside a disposable container, limiting it to the project directory for audits and untrusted repo review.

    • Problem: bypassPermissions on the host lets Claude run any command unconfirmed; the container confines it to /workspace and disposable state.
    • Setup: Needs Docker Desktop, OrbStack or Colima plus @devcontainers/cli; clone to ~/.claude-devcontainer and run install.sh self-install.
    • Commands: devc ., up, down, rebuild, destroy, shell, exec, mount, cp, and sync to copy session logs for /insights.
    • Patterns: Per-project containers for one-off reviews, or a shared workspace with several repos for client engagements.
    • Network: Full egress by default; optional iptables/ipset allowlist for api.anthropic.com, GitHub, npm and PyPI, dropping the rest.
    • Network limits: Per-IP filtering leaks across shared CDNs, DNS stays open, IPv6 is unfiltered, rules vanish on restart.
    • Not protected: Container escape, files planted in shared .git for later host execution, VS Code “Reopen in Container” RPC, rule changes via NET_ADMIN and sudo.
    • Exposure: Forwarded SSH agent lets container code authenticate as you; ~/.gitconfig mounted read-only; Docker socket not mounted.
    • Image: Ubuntu 24.04, Node.js 24, Python 3.13 with uv, user vscode with passwordless sudo.

    Takeaway: Use devc for untrusted repos from the terminal, not VS Code, enable the egress allowlist, and avoid forwarding your SSH agent or mounting $HOME.

  • load-secrets-action: Load Secrets from 1Password into GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: Official 1Password GitHub Action that loads secrets from 1Password vaults into workflow jobs as step outputs or environment variables, with log masking.

    • How it works: Declare env vars whose values are op://vault/item/field references; the action resolves them at runtime.
    • Auth: service account: Set OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN from a GitHub secret.
    • Auth: Connect: 1Password Connect is supported as an alternative backend.
    • Auth: Workload Identity: Public preview; exchanges the job’s OIDC token for short-lived access using OP_WORKLOAD_ID, OP_ENVIRONMENT_ID, OP_INTEGRATION_KEY and id-token: write.
    • Workload Identity scope: Loads every variable in the configured 1Password environment, so scope that environment tightly.
    • Output modes: Default exposes secrets as step outputs via steps.<id>.outputs.<NAME>; export-env: true exports them as env vars.
    • Extras: OP_ENV_FILE points to a .env template; ?ssh-format=openssh selects SSH key format.
    • Masking: Loaded values are masked in job logs.
    • Caveats: Mixing Workload Identity with service account or Connect variables, or setting only some of its three, causes a config error.

    Takeaway: Prefer step outputs over export-env to limit secret exposure to later steps, and evaluate Workload Identity to drop long-lived service account tokens.

  • Infrastructure Agents Guide: How to Design, Build, and Operate AI Agents for Infrastructure Teams
    summary

    TL;DR: Cloudgeni’s open design guide for building and running AI agents that change infrastructure safely, covering runtime, sandboxing, credentials, GitOps, guardrails and audit across 13 chapters.

    • Problem: Agents that can terraform apply can also destroy, agents reading configs can leak secrets, and looping agents run up cost.
    • Core rule: Agents produce diffs, not deployments; every change lands via pull request, with direct execution only as a separate break-glass path.
    • Least privilege: Credentials are short-lived, scoped, time-limited and auditable to control blast radius.
    • Fail-safe: When uncertain the agent stops and asks a human; timeouts and policy gates are structural, not advisory.
    • Equal treatment: Agent changes pass the same review, CI and deployment pipelines as human changes.
    • Mental model: Four layers: policy plane, agent runtime, change control, and observability tracing every tool call and credential request.
    • Alternatives: Compares Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph; sandboxes like E2B, Modal, Daytona, AgentCore; Vault, Atlantis, Spacelift, OpenTelemetry.
    • Hardening: Chapter on trajectory tests, prompt-injection defense and security benchmarks, plus go-live checklists and compliance mapping.
    • License: Text under CC BY 4.0, code snippets under MIT; vendor-authored by Cloudgeni.

    Takeaway: Before giving an agent cloud access, restrict it to opening PRs with short-lived scoped credentials and full tool-call tracing, using the guide’s go-live checklist.

  • NotebookLM: AI Is Eating Security — BSidesSF, RSA, Claude Finds Firefox 0-Days
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

  • Google Workspace CLI: Unified Command-Line Tool for Drive, Gmail, Calendar, and Admin APIs
    summary

    TL;DR: gws is an unofficial Rust CLI for Google Workspace that builds its commands at runtime from Google’s Discovery Service, with JSON output aimed at people and AI agents.

    • How it works: Reads the service name, fetches its Discovery Document (cached 24 hours), builds a clap command tree, then authenticates and calls the API.
    • Coverage: Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Chat, Admin and more; new endpoints appear without a release.
    • Features: --dry-run, --page-all NDJSON pagination, gws schema <method>, --upload, and helpers like +send, +agenda, +append.
    • Auth order: GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_TOKEN, then a credentials file, then gws auth login storage encrypted with AES-256-GCM, then plaintext ~/.config/gws/credentials.json.
    • Scope limit: Unverified testing-mode apps allow about 25 scopes, so pick services like -s drive,gmail,sheets instead of the 85+ scope preset.
    • Agent skills: Ships 100+ SKILL.md skills (README tagline says 40+) and 50 recipes.
    • Prompt injection: --sanitize uses Model Armor to scan API responses in warn or block mode.
    • Install: GitHub release binaries, npm @googleworkspace/cli, cargo install, Nix or Homebrew.
    • Caveats: Not an official Google product; breaking changes expected before v1.0.

    Takeaway: Use gws with narrowly scoped OAuth and --sanitize when handing Workspace access to agents, and avoid the plaintext credentials fallback.

  • zeroboot: Sub-Millisecond VM Sandboxes for AI Agents via Copy-on-Write Forking
    summary

    TL;DR: Zeroboot is a prototype that spawns KVM VM sandboxes for AI agent code in under a millisecond by copy-on-write forking a pre-snapshotted Firecracker VM.

    • How it works: Firecracker boots a template once and snapshots memory and CPU state; each fork maps memory with mmap(MAP_PRIVATE) and restores CPU state.
    • Isolation: Every fork is a separate KVM VM with hardware-enforced memory isolation.
    • Numbers (claimed): Spawn p50 0.79ms, p99 1.74ms, about 265KB per sandbox, Python fork plus exec about 8ms, 1000 concurrent forks in 815ms.
    • Comparison (claimed): E2B about 150ms p50, Daytona about 27ms, microsandbox about 200ms.
    • API: POST /v1/exec with code and a Bearer token; Python and TypeScript (@zeroboot/sdk) SDKs; self-host on any Linux box with KVM.
    • Security caveat: Forks inherit CSPRNG state; the kernel pool is reseeded via RNDADDENTROPY, but userspace PRNGs like OpenSSL and numpy need manual reseeding.
    • Limits: One vCPU per fork, no networking (serial I/O only), and template changes need a full re-snapshot of about 15 seconds.
    • Status: Described as a working prototype, not production-hardened.

    Takeaway: Worth tracking for fast agent sandboxes, but reseed userspace RNGs per fork before generating keys or tokens, and do not run it in production yet.

  • Building a Cloud-Native Detection Engineering Lab with Terraform and AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: A walkthrough moving a RAM-hungry local detection engineering lab to AWS, with Terraform deploying Kali, Windows and an Elastic SIEM via one terraform apply.

    • Problem: A course lab of Kali, Windows, Ubuntu and ELK VMs needed more RAM than the author’s laptop had.
    • Architecture: Three EC2 instances: Kali attacker (t2.medium), Windows Server target (t2.medium), Ubuntu Elasticsearch plus Kibana (t2.large).
    • Bootstrap: user_data installs Elastic 8.x on Ubuntu and Sysmon with the SwiftOnSecurity config plus Winlogbeat on Windows.
    • Ordering: depends_on makes Windows wait for the Elastic instance before shipping logs.
    • Insecure defaults: Opens 22, 3389, 5601 and 9200, and sets xpack.security.enabled: false; the author flags this as lab-only.
    • Detection example: Elastic query rule for process.name:nmap, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1046 Network Service Discovery.
    • Workflow: Lab is online in about 10 minutes; hunt with winlogbeat-* index; terraform destroy tears it down.
    • Tooling note: Built with help from Clawdbot, which the author later uninstalled over unknown security implications.
    • Next steps: Atomic Red Team, Sigma-to-Elastic conversion, and detection-as-code synced via GitHub Actions.

    Takeaway: Reuse the pattern for a throwaway lab, but lock the security group to your IP and enable Elastic security before exposing ports 9200 and 5601.

  • claudetop: Real-Time Cost Tracking and Analytics for Claude Code Sessions
    summary

    TL;DR: claudetop is an MIT-licensed “htop for Claude Code” status line showing live session cost, burn rate, cache efficiency, context use and plan limits.

    • Problem: Claude Code hides spend; the author cites a $10 estimate versus a $65 bill, blaming compaction for hidden token use.
    • Features: Session cost, hourly burn rate, monthly forecast, what-if pricing on Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and cache hit ratio.
    • Alerts: BURN RATE over $15/hr, LOW CACHE under 20% after 5 minutes, COMPACT SOON over 80% context, SPINNING? for spend without code.
    • Plan windows: Shows 5-hour, 7-day and per-model limits for Pro, Max and Team subscribers only.
    • How it works: Reads Claude Code’s status line JSON; claudetop-usage polls the /usage endpoint at most once a minute using the stored OAuth credential.
    • Analytics: claudetop-engine loads all JSONL sessions into SQLite with a dashboard on localhost:8080; claudetop-stats reports by day, tag or month.
    • Config: CLAUDETOP_THEME, CLAUDETOP_DAILY_BUDGET, CLAUDETOP_TAG; plugins are executables in ~/.claude/claudetop.d/.
    • Install: ./install.sh from source, or claude plugin marketplace add liorwn/claudetop; needs jq, bc, curl.
    • Caveats: Costs are estimates from a repo-maintained pricing.json; several features such as iTerm2 integration are macOS-oriented.

    Takeaway: Install from source after reading the scripts, since it reads your Claude OAuth credential, and set a daily budget to catch runaway subagent loops.

  • IronCurtain: A Personal AI Assistant Built Secure from the Ground Up
    summary

    TL;DR: Niels Provos introduces IronCurtain, a research-prototype personal AI assistant that forces every agent action through a trusted MCP proxy enforcing a plain-English policy compiled into deterministic rules.

    • Problem: Cites 40,000+ exposed OpenClaw instances leaking API keys and history, plus prompt injection that can turn agents against owners.
    • Chokepoint: A trusted process acts as MCP proxy; its policy engine returns allow, deny or escalate for each call; each MCP server runs in its own OS sandbox.
    • Code Mode: The LLM writes TypeScript against a typed API, run in a V8 isolate with no filesystem, network or env access via one execute_code tool.
    • Docker Mode: Agents like Claude Code run with --network=none; only exits are a Unix socket to the proxy and a TLS MITM proxy for LLM calls.
    • Credentials: The container gets a fake API key; the MITM proxy swaps in the real key, which never enters the sandbox.
    • Policy: A natural-language “constitution” compiles into rules like allow-git-local-read-ops and escalate-git-remote-ops for git_push.
    • Auto-approver: Opt-in; approves only explicitly requested actions, sees only the user prompt and sanitized details, and escalates vague replies like “go ahead”.
    • Limits: Prompt injection and model drift remain unsolved; IronCurtain limits blast radius rather than preventing them; Claude Code integration is rough.
    • Try it: npx @provos/ironcurtain; supports filesystem, git, web fetch, Brave and SerpAPI search, and Signal.

    Takeaway: Apply the pattern to your own agents: enforce policy outside the model at a single proxy, deny network by default, and keep real credentials out of the sandbox.

  • AWS Security Agent On-Demand Penetration Testing Now Generally Available
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Agent’s on-demand penetration testing is now GA: AI agents find, exploit and validate vulnerabilities across AWS, other clouds and on-prem, at $50 per task-hour.

    • How it works: Agents discover issues, then attempt exploitation with targeted payloads and multi-step chains to confirm each finding and cut false positives.
    • Context: Combines SAST, DAST and pen testing, ingesting source code, IaC, OpenAPI specs, architecture docs and threat models.
    • Chaining: Links lower-severity issues into critical paths, for example stored XSS to session hijack to exposed admin config leaking DB credentials.
    • Setup: Create an agent space per app, prove domain ownership via DNS TXT or file, then target public URLs or private endpoints through a VPC.
    • Auth testing: Multiple credential sets including privileged and MFA accounts; LLM-based sign-in handles OAuth, SAML and Okta.

    • Numbers: 92.5% on CVE Bench v2.0; average test about 24 task-hours, roughly $1,200; customers report 70 to 90% savings.

  • Session Policies for Amazon EKS Pod Identity
    summary

    TL;DR: EKS Pod Identity associations now accept an inline IAM session policy that narrows a role’s permissions per service account, avoiding one IAM role per permission variant.

    • Problem: Least privilege per workload means many roles, pressing against the 5,000-role account quota.
    • How it works: Effective permissions are the intersection of the role’s policies and the session policy; it can only restrict, never expand.
    • API: New policy field on CreatePodIdentityAssociation and UpdatePodIdentityAssociation, up to 2,048 characters of JSON.
    • Hard requirement: disableSessionTags must be true when policy is set, otherwise the call fails with PackedPolicyTooLarge.
    • Cross-account: With targetRoleArn, the policy applies at the target-role hop; the source role needs sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession.
    • Validation: JSON, allowed characters, size, IAM schema via STS dry-run, and packed size after compression.
    • Propagation: Changes take about 10 seconds; running pods keep old credentials until refresh, so recreate pods for immediate effect.
    • Use cases: Multi-tenant SaaS, multiple environments in one cluster, and per-job S3 or DynamoDB subsets.
    • Tooling: Supported in the AWS CLI, EKS API, CloudFormation and eksctl across Commercial, China and GovCloud Regions.

    Takeaway: Use session policies to scope shared roles per namespace, but note that losing session tags breaks any ABAC conditions on them, and watch CloudTrail during rollout.

  • Leveling Up Secure Code Reviews with Claude Code
    summary

    TL;DR: SpecterOps consultant shows how he uses Claude Code as a comprehension aid during secure code reviews, not as an autonomous bug finder, using a tuned system prompt.

    • Thesis: Claude Code speeds up understanding unfamiliar codebases; asking it directly for vulnerabilities produced many false positives.
    • System prompt: Loaded via --system-prompt-file, with a red-team persona, confidence levels, a data-flow checklist and source/sink categories.
    • Teach mode: A [TeachMe] token switches on explanations for unfamiliar languages or frameworks, e.g. ANTLR grammars and AST parsing.
    • Output rules: Line-numbered snippets, parent function names, full paths, VS Code links and curl test examples.
    • BloodHound CE case: Traced POST /api/v2/graphs/cypher through cypherquery.go; Cypher is ANTLR-tokenized and filtered before PostgreSQL translation, limiting SQL injection.
    • Open questions: Whether read-only Cypher controls can be bypassed, and whether LOAD FROM CSV reaches local files.
    • BadWindowsService case: Claude mapped untrusted-input features (named pipes, file system, secrets) and wrote a PowerShell PoC, but output was not exhaustive.
    • Caveats: Factual errors happen (claimed BloodHound uses Neo4j); verify against code and correct its memory.
    • OPSEC: Don’t send client code to public Claude.ai; use local models or Amazon Bedrock with client approval.

    Takeaway: Use an LLM to map data flows and entry points in code you review, keep a reusable system prompt, and validate every claim yourself before reporting it.

  • scion: Multi-Agent Orchestration Testbed for Running Isolated Concurrent AI Agents
    summary

    TL;DR: Scion is a pre-1.0 Apache-2.0 platform from GoogleCloudPlatform for orchestrating teams of AI coding agents, each isolated in its own container with its own credentials.

    • How it works: A Hub control plane handles state, identity and dispatch; a Runtime Broker provisions agent containers.
    • Harnesses: Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex and OpenCode, with per-agent models and credentials.
    • Runtimes: Docker, Podman, Apple Container, Kubernetes and Cloud Run; auto-detected, overridable in .scion/settings.yaml.
    • Templates: A system prompt plus skills; agents delegate via CLI, message each other, and notify on completion.
    • Workspaces: Shared directories, Git worktrees or separate clones; add .scion/agents to .gitignore to avoid nested worktree issues.
    • Interfaces: Web chat plus Telegram, Discord, Slack, Google Chat and Microsoft Teams; MCP config, lifecycle hooks, A2A bridge, Skill Bank.
    • Setup: brew install homebrew-scion/scion/scion, scion server start, then scion init and scion start my-agent "task".
    • Modes: Local CLI, Workstation, single-node hosted, and HA hosted with Postgres and shared storage; hosted adds roles and scoped secrets.
    • Caveats: Not an officially supported Google product; APIs and config may change between releases.

    Takeaway: If you run several coding agents in parallel, Scion gives per-agent container isolation and scoped credentials; pin versions given its pre-1.0 churn.

  • Enforcing AI Governance Across AWS Organizations Using Bedrock Guardrails
    summary

    TL;DR: Sonrai shows how to enforce AI governance org-wide on AWS using SCPs and Bedrock Policies: block MCP-driven API calls, enforce guardrails, restrict regions, models and long-term Bedrock API keys.

    • Managed MCP servers: aws__call_aws can make arbitrary API calls; deny all actions when aws:ViaAWSMCPService is true (or target servers via aws:CalledViaAWSMCP).
    • MCP caveat: Agents like Claude Code or Kiro running the local AWS CLI bypass this control entirely.
    • Bedrock Policies: Org-level policy type BEDROCK_POLICY applies shared guardrails (e.g. PROMPT_ATTACK filter) to all models, even when callers specify none.
    • Guardrail gotchas: Guardrails are regional; sharing needs a resource policy allowing bedrock:ApplyGuardrail by aws:PrincipalOrgID; input_tags: honor lets direct callers bypass.
    • Region lock: SCP denying bedrock:* and bedrock-mantle:* outside allowed regions via aws:RequestedRegion; check cross-region inference profiles first.
    • Model control: Deny foundation-model ARNs like arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/deepseek* plus bedrock-mantle:Model; allow-listing is awkward.
    • Service kill switch: Deny bedrock-agentcore:*, exempting security or break-glass roles via aws:PrincipalArn.
    • API keys: Deny bedrock:CallWithBearerToken when BearerTokenType is LONG_TERM, and deny iam:CreateServiceSpecificCredential.
    • Caveats: Account-level PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration is easier to tamper with; test every control in a sandbox org first.

    Takeaway: Add SCPs blocking long-term Bedrock keys, unapproved regions and MCP-originated calls, and enforce a baseline prompt-attack guardrail via Bedrock Policies from the management account.

  • npm Security Best Practices: A Curated Collection of Package Manager Security Guidelines
    summary

    TL;DR: Liran Tal’s curated list of npm supply-chain hardening practices, with concrete config for npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun covering install scripts, cooldowns, lockfiles and publishing.

    • Install scripts: npm config set ignore-scripts true; pnpm 10+ and Bun block them by default with allowBuilds / trustedDependencies allowlists.
    • Cooldown: min-release-age (npm), minimumReleaseAge (pnpm, Bun), npmMinimalAgeGate (Yarn); Dependabot cooldown and Renovate minimumReleaseAge for PRs.
    • Git deps: npm config set allow-git none (npm 11.10.0+); pnpm blockExoticSubdeps: true restricts git/tarball sources to direct deps.
    • Trust downgrade: pnpm 10.21+ trustPolicy: no-downgrade rejects versions with weaker provenance than earlier releases.
    • Deterministic installs: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, yarn install --immutable; validate lockfiles with lockfile-lint.
    • Install-time tools: npq and Socket Firewall (sfw npm install) vet packages before install.
    • npx hardening: Pre-install MCP servers into a locked workspace and run with --no --offline.
    • Publishing: Enable 2FA, use npm publish --provenance and OIDC trusted publishing to drop long-lived tokens.
    • Other: Scoped names plus .npmrc registry routing against dependency confusion; inspect tarballs with npm pack --dry-run; secrets via op run.

    Takeaway: Set ignore-scripts, a release-age cooldown and allow-git none in CI and dev machines today, and move package publishing to OIDC trusted publishing.

  • Anthropic Mythos Preview: Advanced Cybersecurity Capabilities and Vulnerability Discovery
    summary

    TL;DR: Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team reports that Claude Mythos Preview autonomously finds and exploits zero-days across major OSes and browsers, so access is restricted via Project Glasswing.

    • Claim: Security skills emerged from general coding and agentic gains, not targeted training; it finds bugs in every major OS and browser.
    • Firefox benchmark: 181 working JS-engine exploits versus 2 for Opus 4.6, though the harness lacked the browser sandbox.
    • OpenBSD: 27-year-old SACK bug allowing remote crash; ~1,000 scaffold runs cost under $20,000.
    • FreeBSD: CVE-2026-4747, a 17-year-old unauthenticated NFS RPCSEC_GSS RCE to root, exploited fully autonomously.
    • Other finds: 16-year-old FFmpeg H.264 bug, Linux kernel LPE chains of 2-4 bugs, Botan certificate-auth bypass, web auth bypasses.
    • Method: Isolated containers running Claude Code, per-file agents ranked by likelihood, AddressSanitizer as the oracle, a final filter agent.
    • Validation: Of 198 human-reviewed reports, 89% matched severity exactly, 98% within one level.
    • Access: No general release; Project Glasswing gives partners and OSS maintainers access; a Cyber Verification Program is planned.
    • Caveats: Under 1% of findings are patched, so most claims are unverifiable; vendor-authored; costs framed with hindsight.

    Takeaway: Expect a surge of AI-found CVEs and faster exploitation; shorten patch cycles and start running LLM-driven security review on your own code now.

  • GitHub Actions 2026 Security Roadmap: Deterministic Dependencies and Policy Controls
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub’s 2026 Actions security roadmap adds dependency locking, workflow execution policies, scoped secrets, telemetry streaming and a native egress firewall in response to CI supply-chain attacks.

    • Motivation: Attacks like tj-actions/changed-files, Nx and trivy-action exploited mutable refs, over-permissioned tokens and open egress.
    • Dependency locking: New dependencies: workflow section pins direct and transitive actions to SHAs, like go.sum; hash mismatch stops the run.
    • Execution policies: Ruleset-based actor and event rules, e.g. ban pull_request_target or limit workflow_dispatch to maintainers.
    • Evaluate mode: Policies log would-be blocks in policy insights before enforcement.
    • Scoped secrets: Bind secrets to repos, branches, environments or workflow paths; no implicit inheritance in reusable workflows.
    • Permission change: Write access no longer grants secret management; it moves to a dedicated custom role.
    • Actions Data Stream: Near real-time run telemetry to Amazon S3 or Azure Event Hub, at-least-once delivery.
    • Egress firewall: Layer 7, outside the runner VM, monitor and enforce modes; GitHub-hosted runners only.
    • Timeline: Most previews in 3-6 months, GA at 6-9 months from March 2026; targets, not commitments.

    Takeaway: Pin actions to SHAs, remove pull_request_target where possible, and plan to adopt lockfiles, scoped secrets and egress monitor mode as they reach preview.

  • How AI-Powered “Solve by Default” Transforms Staff+ Engineering Impact
    summary

    TL;DR: Staff security engineer Scott Behrens describes “solve by default”: using AI agents to fix problems himself instead of filing tickets in other teams’ backlogs.

    • Problem: Small fixes sat 6-12 weeks in other teams’ queues; learning their codebases himself took days.
    • Example: Go services lacked proxy support; Claude learned the repo, fixed, tested, linted, documented and opened a PR, merged in about an hour.
    • Ops work too: Tailored security agents run assessments and build dashboards, with him validating results.
    • Practice: Treat human time as the scarce resource and offload the rest to agents.
    • Parallelism: Run at least 2 agent tasks at once to reduce idle time.
    • Validation: Use linters, tests, Playwright screenshots, packet captures and LLM-as-judge; humans own requirements and architecture.
    • Inputs: Turn meeting notes and memos into PRD requirements and working code.
    • Caveats: Cross-functional work still needs humans; agents miss macro architecture; broken workflows can cost a day or two.
    • Trap: Avoid the “automator’s trap” of spending a week to save ten minutes a year.

    Takeaway: Next time you’d file a ticket for another team’s small bug, try having an agent produce a tested PR, and keep validation evidence attached.

  • clawsec: Complete Security Skill Suite for AI Agents with Drift Detection and Integrity Verification
    summary

    TL;DR: ClawSec from Prompt Security is an AGPL collection of security skills and signed advisory feeds for OpenClaw-family agent runtimes, gating risky skill installs and detecting drift.

    • Platforms: OpenClaw, NanoClaw, Hermes and Picoclaw, each with its own skill package.
    • Signed intelligence: Advisory feed and checksum manifest verified via detached Ed25519 signature and pinned key before matching installed skills.
    • Guarded installs: Advisory matches halt installs and need a second explicit confirmation to proceed.
    • Drift detection: Baselines critical files, config, attestations and release artifacts, flagging changes to protected agent files.
    • Packages: clawsec-suite, clawsec-nanoclaw, hermes-attestation-guardian, picoclaw-security-guardian; picoclaw-self-pen-testing is opt-in.
    • Install: npx skills add prompt-security/clawsec --skill clawsec-suite -a openclaw --global -y, then scripts/setup_advisory_hook.mjs.
    • Design: It recommends and gates; destructive removals and overrides stay approval-controlled.
    • Caveats: *-traffic-guardian dirs are specs, not shipped proxies; feed may include advisories without CVE IDs.
    • Config impact: The advisory hook changes persistent OpenClaw config, so review before enabling.

    Takeaway: If you run OpenClaw-style agents, add signed advisory checks and install gating for third-party skills, treating skills as supply-chain artifacts.

  • The AI Vulnerability Storm: Building Mythos-ready Security Program
    summary

    TL;DR: CSA, SANS and OWASP GenAI CISO briefing (v0.95, April 2026) on preparing security programs for a wave of AI-discovered vulnerabilities after Anthropic’s Mythos and Project Glasswing.

    • Thesis: AI sharply increases attacker vulnerability discovery and exploitation; defenders face asymmetric burden because patching is slow.
    • Context cited: Mythos produced 181 Firefox exploits versus 2 for Opus 4.6; Zero Day Clock shows time-to-exploit under one day.
    • Prior signals: XBOW topping HackerOne, DARPA AIxCC finding 54 vulns, AISLE’s 12 OpenSSL zero-days, Linux kernel reports rising from 2 to 10 per week.
    • Risk register: 13 draft risks mapped to OWASP LLM/Agentic Top 10, MITRE ATLAS and NIST CSF 2.0, e.g. unmanaged agent attack surface.
    • Priority actions: 11 actions, from LLM security review of all code before merge to standing up a VulnOps function within 12 months.
    • Tools named: Claude Code Security, Codex Security, Knostic OpenAnt, raptor, Trail of Bits agentic skills.
    • Basics: Egress filtering, segmentation, phishing-resistant MFA, SBOMs, software minimization, deception and canaries.
    • People: Plan for burnout, reserve capacity and simultaneous high-severity incidents in one week.
    • Caveats: Aggressive timelines may be unrealistic; supply-chain cooldowns conflict with faster patching.

    Takeaway: Start LLM-driven code review in CI now, verify egress filtering and segmentation, and prepare triage capacity for a flood of vendor patches.

01.03.2026

  • Security as a Platform: Codifying Scans, Signals, and Guardrails
    summary

    TL;DR: Plaid describes rebuilding fragmented per-repo security scanning into a shared platform with one-line Terraform onboarding, dynamic pipelines and unified vulnerability management.

    • Problem: Hundreds of services across GitHub orgs, per-language analyzers, thousands of mostly unexploitable CVE alerts, patchy secret detection.
    • Onboarding: A one-line Terraform change enables PR scans, daily full scans, status checks, PR comments and tracking.
    • Dynamic pipelines: Steps chosen by changed files, e.g. IaC analysis only when .tf files change; PR scans are incremental.
    • Domains: SAST with curated rules, reachability-aware SCA, IaC, privacy, supply chain, and AI-based business logic scans.
    • Execution: Pinned scanner containers run on Plaid-managed agents inside its AWS VPC; control plane is hosted.
    • Unified findings: Normalized data model, auto-resolution on fix, team attribution via code ownership and cloud metadata.
    • Guardrails from incidents: Bug bounty SameSite cookie report became a rule flagging values other than Lax or Strict.
    • Rollout: Small high-confidence ruleset first, new controls in soft-fail mode to tune false positives before blocking.
    • Caveats: No quantified outcomes; roadmap items like AI auto-fixes are not delivered; only sub-5-minute PR feedback is cited.

    Takeaway: Make security scanning opt-in by one line of IaC, launch new rules soft-fail, and use reachability to cut SCA noise.

  • Amazon EKS Introduces Enhanced Network Security Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Amazon EKS added cluster-wide network policies and DNS-based egress filtering, extending VPC CNI NetworkPolicy support beyond namespace-level pod segmentation.

    • ClusterNetworkPolicy: Centrally enforces network access filters across the whole cluster, not just per namespace.
    • FQDN egress: DNS-based policies filter outbound traffic to external endpoints by domain name.
    • Builds on: Existing Kubernetes NetworkPolicy support in the VPC CNI plugin.
    • Version: Requires Kubernetes 1.29 or later for new clusters.
    • CNI: ClusterNetworkPolicy needs VPC CNI v1.21.1+, in all EKS launch modes.
    • Limit: DNS-based policies work only on EC2 instances launched by EKS Auto Mode.
    • Existing clusters: Support was announced as coming “in the coming weeks”.
    • Regions: All commercial AWS Regions; pricing not mentioned.

    Takeaway: Upgrade VPC CNI to v1.21.1+ and use ClusterNetworkPolicy for baseline deny rules; consider Auto Mode if you need FQDN egress allowlists.

  • Announcing Amazon EKS Capabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: Amazon EKS Capabilities, GA since November 30, 2025, are AWS-managed Argo CD, ACK and kro running outside your clusters on AWS-owned infrastructure.

    • Argo CD: Managed GitOps continuous deployment.
    • ACK: AWS Controllers for Kubernetes manage AWS resources from Kubernetes manifests.
    • kro: Kube Resource Orchestrator composes and orchestrates Kubernetes resources.
    • Hosting: Runs on AWS-owned infrastructure separate from your clusters.
    • Operations: AWS handles scaling, patching and upgrades.
    • Enablement: New or existing clusters via EKS API, CLI, eksctl, console or IaC.
    • Regions: All AWS Regions except GovCloud (US) and China.
    • Gaps: The announcement lists no pricing, quotas or supported versions.

    Takeaway: Evaluate managed Argo CD, ACK and kro to drop self-hosted controllers, after checking pricing and quotas on the EKS pages.

  • Amazon EKS and ECS Announce Fully Managed MCP Servers in Preview
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS previewed fully managed, cloud-hosted MCP servers for Amazon EKS and ECS on November 21, 2025, giving AI assistants live cluster context with IAM and CloudTrail.

    • What: Remote MCP servers for EKS and ECS hosted by AWS; nothing to install locally.
    • Maintenance: Automatic updates and patching.
    • Security: Access controlled through AWS IAM.
    • Audit: Calls logged in AWS CloudTrail.
    • Developer use: Guided workflows, code generation and context-aware debugging in AI coding assistants.
    • Operator use: Knowledge base of best practices and troubleshooting guidance.
    • Clients: Kiro CLI, Cursor and Cline are named.
    • Gaps: Exposed tools, IAM setup, pricing and regions are not in the announcement.

    Takeaway: Grant these MCP servers least-privilege IAM, monitor their CloudTrail activity, and consider SCP condition keys to block MCP-originated calls where unwanted.

  • Deep Dive: Streamlining GitOps with Amazon EKS Capability for Argo CD
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS deep dive on the managed EKS Argo CD capability in a hub-and-spoke setup, using IAM Identity Center, EKS Access Entries, CodeConnections and ECR OCI Helm charts.

    • Architecture: Hub cluster hosts the capability for management only; spokes can be cross-account, cross-region or private.
    • Spoke access: EKS Access Entries grant the capability role API access, removing VPC peering, Transit Gateway or role chaining.
    • SSO: IAM Identity Center groups map to Argo CD ADMIN and VIEWER roles.
    • Git auth: repo-creds secrets, Secrets Manager secretArn references, or CodeConnections OAuth for GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps.
    • ECR: Native auth with no token-refresh CronJobs; Helm charts via oci:// (Argo CD v3.1+).
    • Deployment: ApplicationSets with cluster generator; dev auto-syncs one replica, prod manual sync with three.
    • CI promotion: Project-scoped JWT for a ci-pipeline role, then argocd app sync and argocd app wait --health.
    • Caveats: No controller logs, only events and status; demo grants AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy, replace with least privilege.
    • Tokens: Project tokens last up to 365 days; global tokens expire after 12 hours.

    Takeaway: For multi-account EKS fleets, managed Argo CD with Access Entries removes network plumbing; scope spoke permissions and rotate project tokens.

  • prek: A Git Hook Manager Written in Rust, Drop-In Alternative to pre-commit
    summary

    TL;DR: prek is a Rust rewrite of pre-commit: a single dependency-free binary that runs your existing hook configs faster, with monorepo support and supply-chain safeguards.

    • What it is: A framework that runs hooks before commit, on demand or in CI, and manages the toolchains those hooks need.
    • Compatibility: Drop-in replacement; reads existing .pre-commit-config.yaml and hooks unchanged, plus a native prek.toml format (prek util yaml-to-toml migrates).
    • Speed: Shares hook environments across repos, fetches and sets up in parallel, uses uv for Python venvs; claims multiple times faster than pre-commit.
    • Built-in hooks: Rust-native fast path for common pre-commit-hooks entries, and offline repo: builtin hooks like deny-pattern and require-pattern.
    • Monorepos: Workspace mode keeps per-project configs, runs from one command, and runs independent same-depth projects concurrently.
    • Workflow: Hook groups with --group/--no-group, --glob/--directory/--files targeting, --dry-run preview, and honors core.hooksPath.
    • Security: Verifies checksums of downloaded toolchains; prek update supports --cooldown-days, SHA freezing, and impostor-commit detection for pinned revisions.
    • Adoption: Used by CPython, Apache Airflow and FastAPI; installs via standalone script, uv, Homebrew, mise, Cargo, npm, Nix and others.

    Takeaway: Swap pre-commit for prek in CI and dev machines to drop the Python dependency, and use prek update --cooldown-days plus SHA freezing with --check in CI to harden hook supply chains.

  • mactop: Terminal-Based Monitoring Tool for Apple Silicon Chips
    summary

    TL;DR: mactop is a Go top-style terminal monitor for Apple Silicon Macs showing CPU, GPU, ANE, power, temperature and bandwidth metrics without needing sudo.

    • Scope: Apple Silicon (ARM64) only, macOS Monterey 12.3+; written in Go with CGO by Carsen Klock.
    • How it works: Reads native Apple APIs (SMC, IOReport, IOKit, IOHIDEventSystemClient, Mach kernel API), so no root is needed for monitoring.
    • Metrics: Per-core E/P/S-core usage (M5 S-cores included), GPU frequency, ANE and DRAM power, DRAM read/write bandwidth, temperatures, fans, battery, network, disk I/O.
    • Extras: Thunderbolt bandwidth and device tree, RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 detection, memory pressure via kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level, listening ports layout.
    • UI: 22 layouts, themes (Dracula, Catppuccin, hex colors), htop-style process list with filter and kill (F9), vim-like navigation, 20 languages.
    • Automation: --headless outputs JSON, YAML, XML, CSV or TOON; --count and --pretty for scripting; --menubar runs as a menu bar item.
    • Prometheus: Optional exporter via -p <port> with CPU/GPU/ANE usage, power, bandwidth, fans, temperatures and thermal state.
    • Caveats: --fan-control writes SMC keys and requires sudo; per-process GPU usage is experimental; M5+ DRAM bandwidth is an estimate.

    Takeaway: Install with brew install mactop and use mactop --headless --count 1 or the -p Prometheus exporter to feed Apple Silicon build hosts or CI runners into existing monitoring.

  • memlab: Framework for Finding JavaScript Memory Leaks and Analyzing Heap Snapshots
    summary

    TL;DR: MemLab is Meta’s open-source framework for finding JavaScript memory leaks by driving browsers with Puppeteer and diffing heap snapshots, plus CLI, APIs and an MCP server for analysis.

    • How it works: A scenario file defines url, action and back; memlab run --scenario replays it, compares heap snapshots and filters leaked objects.
    • Output: Clusters leaks and prints one retainer trace per cluster, the reference chain from GC root that keeps the object alive.
    • Custom detectors: Add a leakFilter(node, heap) callback to flag objects using your own logic over the heap graph.
    • Heap analysis: memlab analyze unbound-object finds growing objects; memlab view-heap and memlab trace --node-id inspect snapshots interactively.
    • Runtimes: Works with snapshots from Chromium browsers, Node.js, Electron and Hermes; Node programs can assert on their own memory in tests.
    • MCP server: @memlab/mcp-server lets AI assistants load snapshots, find largest retainers, detached DOM nodes, closures and duplicated strings.
    • Caveats: Readable traces need non-minified code or preserved names; the example MCP config sets --max-old-space-size=8192 for large snapshots.

    Takeaway: Add memlab run scenarios for key user flows to CI to catch frontend or Electron leaks before release, and use memlab analyze on Node service heap dumps during memory incidents.

  • zerobrew: A 5-20x Faster Experimental Homebrew Alternative
    summary

    TL;DR: zerobrew is an experimental, uv-style Homebrew client for macOS and Linux that installs the same Homebrew bottles several times faster via a content-addressed store and in-process relocation.

    • What it is: A zb CLI that uses homebrew-core formulae, bottles and metadata; it compiles nothing and maintains no formulae.
    • How it works: Relocates binaries in-process and links from a content-addressed store with APFS clonefiles, instead of Ruby evaluation plus install_name_tool and re-signing per binary.
    • Numbers: 100-package benchmark: 782s vs 216s cold (3.6x) and 650s vs 27.7s warm (23x); median package 4.8x cold, 52x warm.
    • Bottlenecks: Cold installs are bandwidth bound; ca-certificates post-install (~5s) sets the cold floor; fontconfig’s fc-cache is not cached yet.
    • Commands: zb install, zb bundle (Brewfile), zb outdated, zb upgrade, zb gc, zb reset, and zbx to run without linking.
    • Brew compat: zb install-alias brew adds a brew shim for common subcommands; search, services, tap and --cask are not supported.
    • CI guardrails: Parity workflow compares installed prefixes byte for byte with Homebrew; nightly timing fails below 1.5x cold or 3x warm speedup.
    • Caveats: Warm speed costs extra disk (bottle plus unpacked keg kept); maintainers advise running alongside Homebrew, not replacing it.

    Takeaway: Try zb bundle against your Brewfile to speed up laptop or macOS CI runner provisioning, but keep real Homebrew installed for casks, taps and services.

  • aws-config-d: Manage Multiple AWS SSO Organizations with Separate Config Files
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-config-d is a dependency-free shell tool that splits ~/.aws/config into per-organization files under ~/.aws/config.d/ and rebuilds the real config on shell start.

    • Problem: Multi-org consultants end up with one huge ~/.aws/config; the AWS CLI has no native config.d/ support (feature request open since March 2022).
    • How it works: A shell hook runs aws-config-d auto; if any part is newer than ~/.aws/config, it concatenates all parts in lexicographic order.
    • Disabling: Suffix a file with .off or move it to disabled/; aws-config-d enable, disable, list and rm manage this.
    • Drift detection: A SHA-256 of the last generated file catches outside edits (e.g. aws configure sso) and warns instead of silently overwriting.
    • Setup: install.sh creates config.d/, migrates the existing config to 01-migrated-config, installs to ~/.local/bin, and hooks bash, zsh or fish.
    • Testing: 42 tests across bash, zsh and fish in isolated Docker containers.
    • Limits: Pure concatenation workaround; aws configure sso still edits the generated file; ~/.aws/credentials is not managed.

    Takeaway: If you juggle several AWS organizations, keep one file per client in ~/.aws/config.d/ and disable finished engagements, so stale SSO profiles stop leaking into daily work.

  • Presidio: Open-Source Framework for Detecting and Anonymizing Sensitive Data
    summary

    TL;DR: Presidio is an MIT-licensed SDK for detecting and anonymizing PII in text, images and structured data, now community-governed under the Data Privacy Stack organization.

    • What it is: Identification and anonymization modules for entities like credit cards, names, locations, SSNs, bitcoin wallets, phone numbers and financial data.
    • Components: presidio-analyzer, presidio-anonymizer, presidio-image-redactor and presidio-structured, published on PyPI.
    • How it works: Predefined or custom recognizers combine NER, regular expressions, rule-based logic and checksums with surrounding context, in multiple languages.
    • Extensibility: Can call external PII detection models and customize both detection and de-identification logic.
    • Deployment: Runs from Python or PySpark, Docker, or Kubernetes; image redactor handles standard images and DICOM medical images.
    • Project move: Transitioned from Microsoft to the community data-privacy-stack GitHub org with a Technical Steering Committee; APIs unchanged.
    • Images: New Docker images ship on GHCR; mcr.microsoft.com/presidio-* images are frozen, so switch to ghcr.io/data-privacy-stack/presidio-*.
    • Caveat: Automated detection gives no guarantee of finding all sensitive data; the project says to add other protections.

    Takeaway: Use Presidio to scrub PII from logs or LLM prompts before they leave your boundary, and update any mcr.microsoft.com/presidio-* image references to GHCR.

  • Top 10 Web Hacking Techniques of 2025
    summary

    TL;DR: PortSwigger’s annual community-nominated, panel-ranked list of the ten most novel web attack techniques published in 2025, with side-channels as the dominant theme.

    • Process: 63 community nominations (down from 121), community vote to 15 finalists, then a panel including James Kettle, Soroush Dalili and LiveOverflow ranked the top 10.
    • #1: “Successful Errors” by Vladislav Korchagin: error-based techniques for blind SSTI and code injection, polyglot detection, open-source toolkit.
    • #2: “ORM Leaking More Than You Joined For” by Alex Brown: a generic method to exploit search and filter features via ORM leaks.
    • #3: Novel SSRF via HTTP redirect loops by @shubs, turning blind SSRF into visible response data.
    • #4-5: Unicode normalization exploitation (Ryan and Isabella Barnett, ActiveScan++ updates) and SOAPwn: .NET HttpWebClientProtocol proxy and WSDL abuse to RCE (Piotr Bazydło).
    • #6-8: Cross-Site ETag Length Leak (Takeshi Kaneko), Next.js internal cache poisoning (Rachid Allam), XSS-Leak via Chrome connection-pool prioritisation (Salvatore Abello).
    • #9-10: HTTP/2 CONNECT abuse for internal port scanning (flomb) and parser differentials across languages and frameworks (joernchen).
    • Themes: Side-channels became a core exploitation primitive; Kettle speculates vibe-coding may revive older weak coding practices.
    • Also noted: Kettle’s “HTTP/1.1 Must Die” was shortlisted but excluded by his own rules; malformed-chunk desync and SAML auth bypass nominations missed the cut.

    Takeaway: Use the list as a 2026 testing checklist: probe for parser differentials, blind SSTI via errors, ORM filter leaks, redirect-loop SSRF and cache poisoning in your own apps and Next.js deployments.

  • Skill Scanner: Security Scanner for AI Agent Skills
    summary

    TL;DR: Cisco AI Defense’s Skill Scanner is a best-effort open-source scanner that flags prompt injection, data exfiltration and malicious code in AI agent skills before you install them.

    • How it works: Combines YAML and YARA-X signatures, AST and dataflow analysis, an optional LLM-as-a-judge, and a bounded CEL decision layer (cel-go v0.32.0).
    • Formats: Agent Skills spec (OpenAI Codex, Cursor); --lenient also scans Claude Code .claude/commands/*.md and flat markdown skill repos.
    • Numbers: On MaliciousSkillBench held-out split (839 malicious, 545 harmless), rules alone catch 7.7% at HIGH with 4.0% FPR.
    • With LLM judge: Gemma 4 26B on balanced sends 66.7% to review at MEDIUM+ (15.4% FPR) and blocks 33.7% at HIGH (6.4% FPR).
    • Presets: balanced, low-noise and quiet policies trade recall for false positives; a local model keeps everything on the machine.
    • CI/CD: SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning, reusable GitHub Actions workflow, pre-commit hook, REST API and --fail-on-severity exit codes.
    • Setup: uv tool install cisco-ai-skill-scanner (CPython 3.11-3.14); extras for Bedrock, Gemini, Vertex and Azure OpenAI judges.
    • Limits: No findings does not mean safe; false positives and negatives occur, and the authors say human review remains essential.

    Takeaway: Gate third-party agent skills with skill-scanner scan --use-llm --policy balanced --fail-on-severity high in CI, but treat it as triage, since rules alone miss over 90% of malicious skills.

  • AI-Assisted Cloud Intrusion Achieves Admin Access in 8 Minutes
    summary

    TL;DR: Sysdig documents an apparently LLM-assisted AWS intrusion that went from credentials leaked in a public S3 bucket to admin via Lambda code injection in about 8 minutes, then abused Bedrock and GPUs.

    • Initial access: IAM user keys found in public S3 buckets holding RAG data, named with common AI tool conventions; the user had Lambda read/write plus ReadOnlyAccess.
    • Privilege escalation: Used UpdateFunctionCode and UpdateFunctionConfiguration on EC2-init, which had an admin execution role, to mint access keys for admin user frick.
    • Technique detail: Injected code returned new keys in the function response, with no reverse shell; timeout raised from 3 to 30 seconds; path matches pathfinding.cloud lambda-004.
    • Persistence and spread: Created backdoor-admin with AdministratorAccess; 19 principals, 6 roles over 14 sessions, 5 users taken over; tried OrganizationAccountAccessRole across accounts.
    • AI indicators: Fast, heavily exception-handled code with Serbian comments, hallucinated account IDs, and a nonexistent anthropic/training-scripts GitHub repo.
    • LLMjacking: Confirmed Bedrock invocation logging was off, then invoked Claude, DeepSeek R1, Llama 4 Scout, Nova and Titan models, accepting Marketplace agreements as needed.
    • GPU abuse: p5.48xlarge launches failed on capacity; a p4d.24xlarge ($32.77/hour) ran 5 minutes with public JupyterLab on port 8888 and all TCP ports open.
    • Evasion: IP rotator per request, role chaining across many principals; Sysdig publishes IP and naming IOCs such as stevan-gpu-key.
    • Defenses: Short-lived role credentials, private RAG buckets, restrict Lambda update and PassRole, Lambda versioning, Bedrock invocation logging, SCPs limiting models and instance types.

    Takeaway: Audit who can call lambda:UpdateFunctionCode on functions with privileged roles, enable Bedrock invocation logging, and use SCPs to block unapproved models and GPU instance types.

  • OpenClaw Security Engineer’s Cheat Sheet
    summary

    TL;DR: Semgrep’s cheat sheet for security teams on OpenClaw (Clawdbot/Moltbot), the popular local LLM agent: its risks, how to find it on your fleet, and how to harden or contain it.

    • What it is: An LLM orchestrator (about 160k GitHub stars) whose model output becomes tool calls on the host, likely already on employee laptops.
    • Core risk: Data becomes code; any processed web page, email or document can carry prompt injection, and blast radius grows with connected capabilities.
    • Credentials: Secrets are stored unencrypted in a known location; prompt-injected exfiltration has been publicly demonstrated.
    • Skills supply chain: About 12% of audited ClawHub skills were malicious (386 or 341 of 2,857); 26% of 31,132 ecosystem skills had a vulnerability.
    • Malware tactics: ClickFix lures, typosquatting, reputation washing, gamed popularity, curl | bash, base64 commands and xattr -d com.apple.quarantine.
    • Detection: Look for openclaw/moltbot/clawdbot binaries and npm packages, ~/.openclaw config dirs, gateway port 18789, and domains like clawhub.com.
    • Hardening: Dedicated VM, container sandbox, allowInsecureAuth false, dmPolicy pairing, groupPolicy allowlist, OPENCLAW_DISABLE_BONJOUR=1, run openclaw audit.
