    • GCP: Admin Activity logs on by default, kept 400 days, but writes only; enable Data Access ADMIN_READ for reads. Config changes show in DATA_WRITE, off by default.
    • Workspace: Admin, Login, SAML, OAuth and Groups logs on by default for 6 months; streaming to GCP is free. Only the Login category includes error logs.
    • Detections: Unusual sign-in locations, brute force, persistence via new users, roles or VMs, enumeration, and data destruction.

    Takeaway: Check each default against what you would need in an incident: turn on GCP ADMIN_READ, S3 data events where it matters, and longer Azure retention before you need them.

  • Mitigating Attack Vectors in GitHub Workflows
    summary

    TL;DR: Joyce Brum of Google’s Open Source Security Team (OpenSSF blog, August 12, 2024) lists the main GitHub Actions attack vectors and concrete mitigations for each.

    • pull_request_target: Checking out and running PR head code with secrets lets an attacker print them; base32 encoding bypasses log redaction.
    • workflow_run artifacts: A privileged workflow that downloads artifacts from an unprivileged PR run can be fed attacker-controlled code.
    • Script injection: ${{ github.event.comment.body }} or issue titles in run: execute as shell; writing untrusted data to $GITHUB_ENV injects variables.
    • Cache and Actions: Untrusted code in the default-branch context can poison caches; tag pins can be moved; imposter commits from forks can look legitimate.
    • Mitigations: permissions: {} or contents: read by default; pass untrusted data via env:; split unprivileged and privileged workflows; pin Actions to full SHAs and check for the fork warning; no caching in release workflows.
    • Tools: OpenSSF Scorecard CLI and Scorecard Action, plus Dependabot or Renovate (monthly suggested).

    Takeaway: A compact hardening checklist for any repo with Actions. Run Scorecard and grep your workflows for pull_request_target and inline ${{ }} in run steps first.

  • AWS: VPC Flow Logs, NAT Gateways, and Kubernetes Pods, a Detailed Overview
    summary

    TL;DR: Arseny Zinchenko (RTFM, May 2024) uses VPC Flow Logs with a custom format and CloudWatch Logs Insights to find which EKS pods drive NAT Gateway data-processing costs.

    • Cost: NAT Gateway is $0.045/hour (about $32/month) plus $0.045/GB processed in both directions.
    • Log format: Custom fields including pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr, pkt-src-aws-service, flow-direction, traffic-path, interface-id; srcaddr/dstaddr are the hop, pkt-* the original endpoints.
    • Terraform: terraform-aws-modules/vpc ~> 5.5.2 with flow_log_max_aggregation_interval = 60 and flow_log_log_format (escape ${...} as $${...}).
    • Queries: Logs Insights parse @message over 19 fields, then sum(bytes) by NAT ENI, source EC2 or pod IP.
    • Pod visibility: By default the VPC CNI SNATs pod IPs to the node IP, hiding pods. Setting AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_EXTERNALSNAT=true on aws-node makes pkt_srcaddr show the pod IP. hostNetwork: true also works but is discouraged.
    • Findings: One outbound flow via NAT yields three records (EC2 ENI egress, NAT ENI ingress and egress); NAT ENI records have an empty instance-id. CloudWatch storage of flow logs got expensive even for a small VPC.
    • Source caveat: The itnext.io page returned 403; summary is based on the author’s identical post on setevoy.substack.com.

    Takeaway: If NAT costs are high on EKS, enable custom-format flow logs and external SNAT temporarily to attribute traffic to pods, then fix the top talkers (often S3 or DynamoDB that should use VPC endpoints).

  • How to Build a Secure Recon Network Using Tailscale
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami Tawil (Bugcrowd, September 17, 2024) shows bug bounty hunters how to put a recon VPS behind Tailscale, with no public inbound access, an exit node, Taildrive file sharing and Tailscale SSH.

    • Architecture: Ubuntu 24.04 VPS running Amass, a Windows 11 PC and an Android phone joined in one tailnet.
    • Lockdown: sudo ufw default deny incoming, sudo ufw allow in on tailscale0, then reconnect via the Tailscale hostname.
    • Exit node: Enable IP forwarding in /etc/sysctl.d/99-tailscale.conf, sudo tailscale up --advertise-exit-node, approve in the admin console.
    • Taildrive: ACL nodeAttrs granting drive:share and drive:access, a tailscale.com/cap/drive grant, tailscale drive share reconbox ~/, mapped on Windows at http://100.100.100.100:8080.
    • SSH: sudo tailscale up --ssh --advertise-exit-node (add --accept-risk=lose-ssh if warned), then browser SSH from the admin console.
    • Caveat: The example Taildrive grant uses * sources and destinations with read-write access.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to keep recon infrastructure and its data off the internet. Tighten the example ACLs to specific users and devices before relying on it.

  • AWS and Kubecost Collaborate to Deliver Kubecost 2.0 for Amazon EKS Users
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post (September 30, 2024) announcing Kubecost 2.0 features for EKS users at no cost, in the EKS-optimized bundle that has been free since August 2022.

    • Network costs: Near real-time network cost by pod, namespace, cluster and cloud service, including cross-AZ and cross-region traffic.
    • Actions: Automated request right-sizing and scheduled cluster or namespace turndown (nights, weekends), configured in UI or YAML.
    • Forecasting: ML forecasts in Allocations, Assets and Cloud Cost dashboards, plus anomaly detection.
    • Performance: New API backend claims 100x faster at scale, 3x better resource efficiency, and up to three years of history.
    • Install: Helm from oci://public.ecr.aws/kubecost/cost-analyzer with the EKS values file (example pins 2.4.1), the EKS add-on, or AWS Marketplace. Bundles Prometheus and kube-state-metrics by default.
    • Prereqs: Helm 3.9+; EBS CSI driver on 1.23+; configure a StorageClass on 1.30+, which has none by default. Do not expose the UI without an auth layer.

    Takeaway: A free way to get per-pod and network cost visibility on EKS. Port-forward the UI for a quick look and use the network view to find cross-AZ chatter.

  • Managing AWS EKS Access Entries with Terraform and OpenTofu
    summary

    TL;DR: Saifeddine Rajhi (AWS Community Builders, October 14, 2024) explains EKS access entries as the replacement for the aws-auth ConfigMap and shows how to manage them with the terraform-aws-modules/eks module in Terraform or OpenTofu.

    • Why: aws-auth is a manual, hard-to-audit YAML map where one mistake can lock users out. Access entries go through the EKS API and also remove the hidden default cluster creator.
    • Modes: CONFIG_MAP, API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, API. Switching is one-way: aws eks update-cluster-config --access-config authenticationMode=API.
    • Terraform: Module ~> 20.0 with enable_cluster_creator_admin_permissions = true and access_entries taking principal_arn, kubernetes_groups and policy_associations (each a policy_arn and access_scope of cluster or namespace).
    • Policies: AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy, AmazonEKSAdminPolicy, AmazonEKSEditPolicy, AmazonEKSViewPolicy; the example scopes View to the default namespace.
    • RBAC mix: Map entries to kubernetes_groups such as eks-admins and bind them with a ClusterRoleBinding.
    • Verify: aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name <name>.

    Takeaway: Move to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP first, recreate aws-auth mappings as access entries in code, verify, then switch to API. Remember there is no way back.

  • Cloud-Native Incident Response in AWS: Part II
    summary

    TL;DR: Part II of Invictus Incident Response’s AWS cloud-native IR series (October 4, 2024) is a practical guide to using Amazon Athena to query logs during an investigation.

    • Model: Athena does not index data; it queries it in place in S3, with Glue holding the schema. The post warns against treating it as a SIEM.
    • Partitioning: Partition by region, year, month, day and hour to reduce scanned data, cost and query time.
    • Log sources: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, ELB, S3 access and CloudFront logs.
    • Loading: You need the S3 location and a DDL statement; the example creates an elb_logs table by changing LOCATION.
    • Query tips: Use LIMIT to cap cost; result reuse (60 minutes to 7 days) misses recent events; use dot notation for STRUCT fields and json_extract_scalar for STRING JSON, for example roleSessionName from AssumeRole events.
    • Extra: A downloadable Athena cheatsheet on GitHub.

    Takeaway: Pre-create partitioned Athena tables for CloudTrail and flow logs before an incident, so responders can query in minutes instead of writing DDL under pressure.

  • s3cme: Template Go Repo with Supply Chain Security Pipelines (ko SBOM, cosign, SLSA Provenance)
    summary

    TL;DR: s3cme by Mark Chmarny is an Apache-2.0 template Go repo with GitHub Actions pipelines built for software supply chain security: scan, build with ko, sign with cosign, and attach SLSA provenance.

    • On push: Trivy code vulnerability scan and CodeQL SARIF results into repo security alerts.
    • On tag: ko image build and push with SBOM, Trivy image scan with a max-severity gate, cosign signing and attestation, SLSA provenance via slsa-github-generator, verified with slsa-verifier and a CUE policy.
    • Schedule: CodeQL analysis every 4 hours.
    • Release: Version lives in .version; make tag tags and pushes; images go to ghcr.io with .sig, .att and SPDX 2.3 .sbom artifacts.
    • Verify: cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance with a certificate identity regexp, GitHub OIDC issuer and policy/provenance.cue.
    • Cluster enforcement: Sigstore policy-controller with policy/slsa.yaml and namespace label policy.sigstore.dev/include=true.

    Takeaway: A working reference for wiring SBOM, signing and SLSA provenance into a Go release pipeline. Copy the workflows and admission policy rather than designing from scratch.

  • Terraform Stacks Part 1: An Introduction
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Guy (October 23, 2024) introduces HCP Terraform Stacks, a public-preview feature for deploying the same set of modules across many environments without custom pipelines, with an Azure walkthrough.

    • Files: .tfstack.hcl for components, providers, variables and outputs; .tfdeploy.hcl for deployments, identity and orchestration.
    • Components: component blocks reference modules; providers get labels such as provider "azurerm" "this".
    • Deployments: Instances of the stack, for example dev, stg, prd, each with its own subscription and inputs.
    • Orchestration: orchestrate blocks with check conditions; the example auto-approves only dev when the plan is applyable. Other actions (deferral_replan, replan, converged) listed but not explored.
    • Limits: Public preview, not for production; 20 deployments per stack, 500 stack resources per org; VCS integration required; the demo needed Terraform 1.10.0-alpha20240926 and the tfstacks CLI. An identity_token variable had to be ephemeral.

    Takeaway: Worth tracking if you maintain workspace-per-environment sprawl in HCP Terraform, but it is HCP-only and preview, so do not migrate production yet.

  • zizmor: Static Analysis Tool for GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: zizmor is an MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions (and Dependabot and pre-commit configs) that finds security issues in CI/CD definitions. The repo now lives at github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor.

    • Audits: Template injection leading to code execution, accidental credential persistence and leakage, excessive permission scopes, imposter commits and confusable git refs; the full list is at docs.zizmor.sh/audits/.
    • Scope: GitHub Actions workflows and actions, Dependabot and pre-commit configurations.
    • Build: Repo contains Cargo.toml and pyproject.toml, indicating Rust with Python packaging (inference from files, not stated).
    • Docs: Install, quickstart and usage recipes are at docs.zizmor.sh, not in the README.
    • Maintainer: Sponsor links point to woodruffw (William Woodruff).

    Takeaway: Run zizmor in CI over .github/workflows to catch injection and over-permissioned tokens before attackers do. It pairs well with OpenSSF Scorecard.

  • AWS Security Guardrails and Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Naman Sogani built two Python scripts that use Claude 3.5 Sonnet on AWS Bedrock to generate AWS security requirements and secure-by-default Terraform modules per service.

    • Requirements Generator: requirements-generator.py merges and enhances requirements from Checkov and Prowler into JSON (ID, name, description, provider, domain).
    • Terraform Creator: terraform-creator.py writes main.tf, variables.tf and notes.md per service, with requirement traceability and coverage notes.
    • Assumptions: Hub-and-spoke via Transit Gateway, Identity Center SSO, no IAM user keys, CloudTrail and flow logs on, private-only resources.
    • Prompt rules: Do not create supporting resources (KMS keys, buckets, SGs); one resource block per resource; most secure defaults.
    • Services: Examples include S3, SageMaker, MSK, RDS, ALB, ECS, EKS, API Gateway, Kinesis, MWAA and KMS.
    • Repo: github.com/naman16/AWS-Security-Guardrails-TF.
    • Limits: AI output needs review; no measured accuracy given, only ‘a few hours’ with ‘reasonable accuracy’; some requirements cannot be expressed in Terraform.

    Takeaway: A useful starting point for a secure module library, not a finished one. Review each generated module against your own environment before use.

  • safer-scps: Safer AWS SCP Deployments via Real-Time Monitoring
    summary

    TL;DR: safer-scps by Matthew Fuller is a pair of CloudFormation stacks that stream SCP-caused AccessDenied events from every member account to a central place in near real time, so you can watch for breakage while rolling out a Service Control Policy.

    • Problem: SCPs have no dry-run mode and CloudTrail delivery can lag more than 15 minutes.
    • Flow: In each member account, an EventBridge rule matches AccessDenied events whose message ends in ‘deny in a service control policy’ and forwards them to a management-account event bus, then CloudWatch Logs.
    • Metrics: A metric filter splits by Account and Action for an ‘ScpErrors’ dashboard (30 s period) or Live Tail.
    • Deploy: bus.yml in the management account with your Org ID; rules.yml via StackSets with the EventBusArn output.
    • Cost: Cross-account events about $1 per million, logs about $0.50/GB; near zero unless error volume is high. Stop Live Tail when done.
    • Limits: Per-region deployment, relies on exact AWS error text, data events untested; log group name is inconsistent in the README.

    Takeaway: Deploy it before your next SCP change and keep the dashboard open during rollout, so a bad deny shows up in seconds instead of in a support ticket.

  • How AWS Enforcement Code Logic Evaluates Requests to Allow or Deny Access
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS IAM User Guide page describing the order in which AWS enforcement code evaluates policies to reach Allow or Deny.

    • Defaults: Everything is implicitly denied except the root user; an explicit deny anywhere overrides any allow.
    • Order: Explicit deny across all policies, then RCPs, then SCPs, then resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permissions boundaries, and session policies.
    • RCPs and SCPs: Each must contain an applicable Allow or the request is denied. RCPFullAWSAccess is attached automatically and cannot be detached.
    • Resource policies: Within one account, an Allow to an IAM user, role session or federated user ARN can grant access despite an implicit deny in identity policies, boundaries or session policies. An Allow to a role ARN is still limited by boundaries and session policies.
    • Exceptions: IAM role trust policies and KMS key policies must explicitly allow the principal.
    • Sessions: Non-session principals end at Allow; if a session policy is passed and does not allow the action, the request is denied.

    Takeaway: Keep this page open when debugging AccessDenied. The subtle bit is same-account resource policies granting directly to sessions, which can bypass permission boundaries.

  • aws-gate: Better AWS SSM Session Manager CLI Client
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-gate by xen0l is a BSD-licensed Python CLI wrapper around AWS SSM Session Manager that lets you connect to EC2 instances by name, tag, IP, DNS or ASG instead of only instance ID, and adds SSH over SSM.

    • Lookup: Instance ID, DNS or private DNS, IP, Name:value tag, instance name, or asg:name.
    • Config: Host aliases with profile and region in ~/.aws-gate/config and ~/.aws-gate/config.d.
    • Commands: aws-gate session <id>, aws-gate ssh <id> [command] with local port forwarding (for example to RDS), aws-gate ssh-config to generate ~/.ssh/config, and ssh-proxy used as ProxyCommand.
    • SSH keys: Ephemeral keys pushed via EC2 Instance Connect; scp works but can be slow.
    • Requirements: Python 3.5+, session-manager-plugin, SSM Agent 2.3.68.0+, suitable instance profile IAM.
    • Install: pip install aws-gate, Homebrew tap xen0l/homebrew-taps, or Docker. Debug with GATE_DEBUG.

    Takeaway: Makes SSM a practical SSH replacement so you can close port 22. Check recent commit activity before standardizing, since maintenance status is not stated.

  • Pinniped: The Easy, Secure Way to Log in to Your Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Pinniped is an Apache 2.0 project from VMware Tanzu that provides identity services for Kubernetes: it plugs external identity providers into clusters for one login experience across on-prem and managed cloud clusters.

    • Purpose: Authentication for Kubernetes using externally managed identities instead of shared credentials.
    • Single sign-on: Users log in once to reach all their clusters.
    • Tooling: Works with native tools such as kubectl.
    • Install: Described as easy to install on almost any Kubernetes cluster, including managed cloud environments.
    • IdPs: Repo topics list OIDC, LDAP and Active Directory; integrates with an enterprise IdP over standard protocols.
    • Numbers: About 742 stars and 5,000+ commits at fetch time.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted option for replacing static kubeconfigs and cloud-specific auth with one SSO flow across mixed clusters. See pinniped.dev for the component architecture before deploying.

  • The Dark Side of Domain-Specific Languages: Uncovering New Attack Techniques in OPA and Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Shelly Raban (Tenable, November 18, 2024, from her fwd:cloudsec Europe talk) shows how OPA Rego policies and Terraform code can be abused to execute code and exfiltrate secrets in pipelines.

    • OPA setup: An attacker with write access to the bucket OPA loads policies from uploads malicious Rego that runs at evaluation.
    • OPA exfil: opa.runtime().env plus http.send leaks environment variables; a Rego chain queries IMDSv2 for instance role credentials; net.lookup_ip_addr tunnels data via DNS even when http.send is blocked.
    • Terraform plan-time: PR pipelines running terraform plan (for example setup-terraform) execute data sources, so any PR author can run code on the runner.
    • Data sources: external runs a local program; http leaks secrets in URLs (IMDSv2 unreachable since it needs PUT); dns_a_record_set exfiltrates a Secrets Manager value via DNS.
    • Provisioners: local-exec (example pipes /etc/passwd to netcat) and remote-exec (coin miner on new EC2).
    • Mitigations: Separate plan and apply roles, vetted modules and providers, OPA capabilities.json allow_net, logging, and custom scanning before plan.

    Takeaway: Treat terraform plan on untrusted PRs as code execution. Give plan jobs minimal credentials and restrict network egress for OPA and Terraform runners.

  • AWS Application Load Balancer Announces CloudFront Integration with Built-In WAF
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS (November 15, 2024) added a one-click option in the ALB console that puts a CloudFront distribution with a preconfigured AWS WAF web ACL in front of an Application Load Balancer.

    • What it does: Creates and configures ALB, CloudFront and WAF together, replacing a manual multi-service setup.
    • Protection: Preconfigured WAF web ACL with basic protections against common web threats.
    • Origin lock-down: Optional security group allowing only CloudFront IPs; if it is the only inbound rule, all requests pass through CloudFront and WAF.
    • Caching: CloudFront caches HTML, CSS/JS and images per the app’s Cache-Control headers.
    • Pricing and regions: Standard ALB, CloudFront and WAF pricing; all commercial regions; new and existing ALBs.

    Takeaway: The fastest way to get edge WAF and origin lock-down for an ALB app. Review the default WAF rules and make sure the ALB is not still reachable directly.

  • Updated Whitepaper: Architecting for PCI DSS Segmentation and Scoping on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Assurance Services (Abdul Javid, Padmakar Bhosale, Ted Tanner, November 15, 2024) announce an updated whitepaper on PCI DSS 4.0 segmentation and scoping on AWS.

    • Alignment: Follows the PCI Council’s information supplement on scoping and network segmentation, updated for PCI DSS 4.0.
    • New content: Reference architectures for account structure with AWS Organizations OUs, network-layer design patterns, firewall rule examples mapped to PCI requirements, and more hands-on segmentation scenarios.
    • Topics: Defining boundaries between in-scope and out-of-scope resources, east-west and north-south traffic flows, and account and network structure as the base of segmentation.
    • Key point: Software-defined networking and service choice can shrink the cardholder data environment compared with on-prem.
    • Audience: Engineers, QSAs and internal security assessors.

    Takeaway: If you run card data on AWS, use the whitepaper’s account and OU patterns to isolate the CDE early; account-level separation is the cheapest scope reduction.

  • Amazon EKS Now Supports Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)
    summary

    TL;DR: Since October 22, 2024, Amazon EKS supports Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) zonal shift and zonal autoshift to move in-cluster traffic away from an impaired Availability Zone.

    • Zonal shift: You trigger moving in-cluster network traffic for multi-AZ apps from an impaired AZ to healthy ones.
    • Zonal autoshift: AWS performs the shift for you when it detects AZ impairment.
    • Practice runs: Configurable tests to confirm the cluster runs with one less AZ.
    • Enable: EKS console, AWS CLI, CloudFormation or eksctl; then manage shifts via the ARC console, CLI or Zonal Shift APIs.
    • Regions: All commercial regions except GovCloud (US). Pricing is not mentioned.

    Takeaway: Enable it on multi-AZ clusters and run a practice shift; it exposes workloads that cannot survive losing an AZ (single replicas, zonal volumes, tight PDBs).

  • Hands-On Security Tips for Centralized Root Access in AWS (AssumeRoot)
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Medium post by oraspir with hands-on tips for AWS Organizations centralized root access and sts:AssumeRoot, including notes for CSPM and CDR tooling.

    • Feature: Centralized root access lets the management account (or a delegated admin) manage member account root credentials and run task-scoped root sessions instead of logging in as root.
    • Enable: Two features from the management account: root sessions (enables sts:AssumeRoot) and root credentials management (remove member root credentials).
    • AssumeRoot rules: Must be called with management or delegated-admin credentials, not root, and against a regional STS endpoint; the global endpoint is not supported. Sessions are visible in CloudTrail.
    • Hardening: Delegate to a dedicated security account, limit sts:AssumeRoot to who needs it, and narrow tasks with the sts:TaskPolicyArn condition key.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; this summary is based on the post title, search snippets and AWS documentation, not the article’s specific tips.

    Takeaway: Enable centralized root access, delete member root credentials, and alert on AssumeRoot events in CloudTrail. Read the original post for its specific detection tips.

  • AWS Application Load Balancer Introduces Header Modification for Traffic Control and Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Since November 21, 2024, AWS Application Load Balancer can rename its TLS headers, insert response headers, and drop its Server header.

    • Rename: All ALB-generated TLS headers: the six mTLS headers and the two TLS version and cipher headers, so existing backends can keep their expected names.
    • Insert: Custom response headers such as CORS and security headers like HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security).
    • Remove: Disable the ALB-generated Server response header to reduce fingerprinting.
    • Regions: All commercial, GovCloud (US) and China regions. Pricing not mentioned.

    Takeaway: Set HSTS and strip the Server header at the ALB instead of in every app, and use header renaming to ease migrating mTLS backends.

  • Secure Root User Access for Member Accounts in AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (Jonathan VanKim, Sowjanya Rajavaram, November 22, 2024) on centrally managing root access for AWS Organizations member accounts: removing root credentials and running short, task-scoped root sessions.

    • Root credentials management: Centrally view, delete and block recovery of member root passwords, access keys, signing certs and MFA.
    • Privileged root actions: Task-scoped root sessions of up to 15 minutes, started only from the management or delegated admin account with sts:AssumeRoot.
    • Enable (CLI): aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal iam.amazonaws.com, register-delegated-administrator, aws iam enable-organizations-root-sessions, aws iam enable-organizations-root-credentials-management.
    • Task policies: IAMDeleteRootUserCredentials, IAMCreateRootUserPassword, IAMAuditRootUserCredentials, S3UnlockBucketPolicy, SQSUnlockQueuePolicy under arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/.
    • Example: aws sts assume-root --target-principal <acct> --task-policy-arn arn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/S3UnlockBucketPolicy, then aws s3api delete-bucket-policy.
    • Caveats: New accounts get no root password; SCPs and VPC endpoint policies still apply to root sessions; restrict with sts:TaskPolicyArn.

    Takeaway: Turn this on, delegate to a security account, and delete member root credentials. It removes the need to vault dozens of root passwords and MFA devices.

  • How to Use AWS Resource Control Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Scott Piper (Wiz, November 28, 2024) explains AWS Resource Control Policies (RCPs), the resource-side counterpart to SCPs, with practical example policies.

    • What: Org-wide guardrails on who can access your resources, including principals outside the Organization; they only restrict and never grant.
    • Services: S3, STS, SQS, Secrets Manager and KMS at launch.
    • Examples: Enforce TLS (1.3) on S3 org-wide; data perimeter statements; deny sts:AssumeRole unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches or the caller is an approved vendor; restrict sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to a GitHub sub like repo:octo-org/*; block S3 deletes even from external accounts.
    • vs SCPs: SCPs do not apply to external principals, RCPs do; RCPs do not travel with an account that moves OU or Org.
    • Pain points: Denials return a generic AccessDenied that does not name the RCP; no dry-run, so review with Access Analyzer and CloudTrail and roll out sandbox-first.

    Takeaway: RCPs make data perimeter and OIDC trust restrictions enforceable in one place. Start with the GitHub OIDC and org-only AssumeRole examples, rolled out gradually.

  • Securely Share AWS Resources Across VPC and Account Boundaries with PrivateLink, VPC Lattice, EventBridge, and Step Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: Jeff Barr (AWS News Blog, December 1, 2024) introduces Resource Gateways and Resource Configurations, built on VPC Lattice and PrivateLink, to share private resources across VPCs and accounts and call them from EventBridge and Step Functions.

    • Resource Gateway: Ingress point into a VPC: choose VPC, private subnets (fixed after creation), IP type and up to five security groups.
    • Resource Configuration: Defines reachable resources by IP, DNS name or ARN: HTTPS endpoints, databases, EC2, EKS services, or on-prem systems over VPN or Direct Connect.
    • Sharing: Via AWS RAM for cross-account; consumers add it to a service network with a VPC endpoint or create an endpoint directly.
    • EventBridge and Step Functions: A ‘Private’ connection references the shared configuration so HTTP tasks and API destinations can call private APIs.
    • Pricing: Existing Step Functions, EventBridge, PrivateLink and VPC Lattice pricing, including per-GB data into the VPC.
    • Availability: 21 regions at launch; private hosted zone support planned.

    Takeaway: Removes Lambda-in-VPC and SQS workarounds for calling private services from serverless workflows. Scope RAM shares and gateway security groups tightly.

  • Use Your On-Premises Infrastructure in Amazon EKS Clusters with Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes
    summary

    TL;DR: Channy Yun (AWS News Blog, December 1, 2024) introduces EKS Hybrid Nodes: on-prem and edge machines join an EKS cluster whose control plane AWS runs.

    • Networking: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect or other VPN; node and pod CIDRs must be non-overlapping RFC 1918 IPv4; a pod CIDR is needed for webhooks on nodes or a CNI that does not NAT.
    • OS: Amazon Linux 2023, Ubuntu 20.04/22.04/24.04, RHEL 8 and 9; AWS supports the EKS integration, not the OS.
    • CNI: Cilium or Calico must be installed before nodes become Ready; kube-proxy and CoreDNS are installed automatically.
    • Bootstrap: nodeadm install and nodeadm init with a node config file.
    • Credentials: SSM hybrid activations or IAM Roles Anywhere; cluster must use API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP with an access entry for the hybrid nodes role.
    • Pricing and regions: Cluster hourly rate plus an hourly fee per hybrid node vCPU; all regions except GovCloud (US) and China.

    Takeaway: A managed control plane for on-prem capacity, but you own hardware, OS and node upgrades. Plan CIDRs and the CNI before the first node.

  • Exploiting Public AWS Resources: CLI Attack Playbook
    summary

    TL;DR: Eduard Agavriloae’s Hacking The Cloud playbook gives AWS CLI commands for exploiting 12 resource types made public through misconfigured resource-based policies.

    • Black-box discoverable: S3 buckets (three variants), AMIs, EBS snapshots, RDS snapshots, IAM roles, SSM documents, CloudFront.
    • Not black-box discoverable: SNS topics, SQS queues, private API Gateways, Lambda functions, ECR repositories.
    • S3: aws --no-sign-request s3 ls s3://BUCKET then s3 cp.
    • SNS and SQS: sns list-subscriptions-by-topic, sns subscribe, sns publish; sqs send-message, receive-message, purge-queue.
    • Lambda and ECR: aws lambda invoke --function-name <full ARN> cross-account; aws ecr-public get-login-password into docker login, then inspect image history for secrets.
    • Roles and private APIs: sts assume-role against misconfigured trust policies; private API Gateways tested from EC2 with an execute-api interface endpoint.
    • Tools: CloudShovel (scan AMIs for secrets) and coldsnap (EBS snapshots).

    Takeaway: Run the same commands against your own accounts, or use IAM Access Analyzer, to find public snapshots, AMIs and over-permissive SNS, SQS and Lambda policies.

  • AWS re:Invent 2024 Security Talks
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A 63-video YouTube playlist by the AWS Security Digest channel collecting AWS re:Invent 2024 security session recordings (uploaded by AWS Events).

    • Size: 63 videos, about 7,156 views at fetch time.
    • Identity and root: SEC232 ‘Secure by design: Enhancing the posture of root with central control’, SEC221 identity security, SEC346 application authorization, SEC207 Cedar policies.
    • Detection and IR: SEC219 GuardDuty threats, SEC321 detection and response innovations, SEC313 ‘Responding to cloud incidents: Tales from the front lines’, SEC360 AWS Security Incident Response.
    • Secrets and network: SEC204 and SEC234 secrets management, SEC322 least-privilege egress controls, SEC358 Verified Access for non-HTTP protocols, SEC341 enterprise PKI.
    • Platform: KUB315 securing EKS workloads, DOP203 governance with IaC, DEV344 S3 red team vs blue team, DEV401 security invariants, CDN303 ‘I didn’t know AWS WAF did this’.
    • AI: SEC323 AWS approach to secure generative AI, SEC403 generative AI for security, AIM360 Bedrock security and privacy.
    • Source caveat: Based on the playlist page’s title and video list only; no transcripts were read.

    Takeaway: Pick by session code rather than watching in order. SEC313, SEC322, DEV401 and KUB315 are the most hands-on for cloud security engineers.

  • Announcing Amazon EKS Auto Mode
    summary

    TL;DR: Announced December 1, 2024 at re:Invent, EKS Auto Mode has AWS manage compute, networking and storage for EKS clusters, including instance selection, scaling and OS patching.

    • Compute: AWS picks EC2 instances for workloads and scales them with demand.
    • Operations: AWS provisions, operates and upgrades the instances in your account with AWS-controlled access and lifecycle, including OS patches.
    • Security: Nodes are described as ephemeral to limit risk; maximum node lifetime is not stated on the page.
    • Pricing: No upfront fee; a management charge on provisioned compute on top of normal EC2 cost (rate not stated).
    • Requirements: Kubernetes 1.29+, via EKS API, console or IaC.
    • Regions: All except GovCloud (US) and China.

    Takeaway: Removes most node and add-on operations for teams that do not want to run Karpenter, CNI and CSI themselves. Compare the management fee against your current ops effort before migrating.

  • Announcing Node Health Monitoring and Auto-Repair for Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: Since December 16, 2024, EKS offers a node monitoring agent that detects Kubernetes-specific node health problems and node auto-repair that replaces unhealthy nodes.

    • Monitoring: The agent continuously checks EC2 worker nodes for Kubernetes-specific health issues (specific checks not listed on the page).
    • Auto-repair: EKS acts on unhealthy nodes, including replacing them.
    • Enable: Install the node monitoring agent add-on; enable auto-repair in managed node group APIs or console; both are on by default in EKS Auto Mode.
    • Cost: No additional charge.
    • Regions: All except GovCloud (US) and China.

    Takeaway: Free and low effort; enable it on managed node groups. Ensure PDBs and replica counts let workloads survive an automatic node replacement.

  • Kubernetes v1.32: Penelope
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes v1.32 ‘Penelope’, released December 11, 2024, ships 44 enhancements: 13 stable, 12 beta and 19 alpha.

    • Name: From Penelope in the Odyssey, who wove by day and unpicked by night, like releases adding and removing features; also marks the end of Kubernetes’ tenth year.
    • Stable: Structured Authorization Configuration, bound service account token improvements, Custom Resource field selectors, sizing memory-backed volumes, auto-removing StatefulSet PVCs, Memory Manager, status.hostIPs, custom profiles in kubectl debug.
    • Beta: Job managedBy (for Kueue), anonymous auth limited to endpoints like /healthz, /livez, /readyz, recovery from volume expansion failure, VolumeGroupSnapshot, DRA structured parameters, label and field selector authorization.
    • Alpha: Async scheduler preemption, CEL-based Mutating Admission Policies, pod-level resource specs, zero-second PreStop sleep, /statusz and /flagz endpoints.
    • Removals: Old DRA implementation (KEP 3063) withdrawn; flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta3 removed, use v1 (available since 1.29).

    Takeaway: Before upgrading, migrate any FlowSchema or PriorityLevelConfiguration manifests to v1. Consider the beta option to restrict anonymous auth to health endpoints as a quick hardening win.

26.06.2024

  • Docs as Code Is a Broken Promise
    summary

    TL;DR: Sarah Moir argues that docs-as-code is usually adopted as a toolset without the processes behind it, so the promised quality and collaboration benefits rarely arrive.

    • Tooling drift: Writers can use any editor or the GitHub UI, so spell checks and style linting run unevenly.
    • Git burden: Git is complex for writers; mistakes can leave a clone or branch broken and force a fresh start.
    • Unenforced process: Nothing stops contributors ignoring publishing and Git practices; the author’s squash-merge setting was silently changed by GitHub and cluttered main for weeks.
    • Checks: Merge gates and builds need engineering time docs teams rarely have; doc PRs can wait on unrelated product tests.
    • Review: Reviewers see raw markup, not rendered pages, leading to confused comments.
    • Alternatives: No full fix; suggests choosing how much of the practice to adopt, newer CMSes (ReadMe, Heretto, Paligo), and a writer-efficiency community.

    Takeaway: If you run docs in Git, invest in the guardrails (linting, preview builds, branch protection), not just the repo. Otherwise you get developer overhead without the benefits.

  • Who Touched My GCP Project? Understanding the Principal Part in Cloud Audit Logs, Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Gavriel Fried (Mitiga, April 9, 2024) explains how GCP Cloud Audit Logs record who performed an action, across principal types and impersonation chains, for incident responders.

    • Fields: authenticationInfo.principalEmail (may be redacted), principalSubject (often principal://iam.googleapis.com/...), serviceAccountKeyName (key used), serviceAccountDelegationInfo[] (delegation history), thirdPartyPrincipal, authoritySelector.
    • Principals: Users; user-managed service accounts (up to 10 keys), built-in ones like the Default Compute Engine SA, Google-managed ones; service agents such as <project_number>@cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com; workload identities.
    • Key activation: gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=... shows the SA in principalEmail with serviceAccountKeyName set.
    • Impersonation: GenerateAccessToken with Token Creator permissions creates no key; chains like --impersonate-service-account=SA1,SA2,SA3 appear under serviceAccountDelegationInfo and metadata.identityDelegationChain.
    • Permissions: iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken for one hop, iam.serviceAccounts.implicitDelegation for longer chains.
    • VMs: Activity from a VM shows the attached SA, with the Default Compute Engine account in delegation info.

    Takeaway: When investigating GCP, walk the delegation chain back to the original human or external principal; principalEmail alone often names only the last service account.

  • IAM Is the Worst
    summary

    TL;DR: Mat Duggan (March 15, 2024) argues cloud IAM in AWS and especially GCP has become too complex for anyone to know what access exists, and proposes usage-based right-sizing instead of guessing least privilege up front.

    • AWS complaints: Effective access depends on many overlapping layers; role names mislead; working setups end up as custom roles full of unused permissions.
    • GCP complaints: Basic roles are too broad, while 1,600+ predefined roles change constantly and carry launch-stage labels; custom roles cannot combine predefined roles.
    • Examples: roles/datastore.viewer vs roles/datastore.keyVisualizerViewer; whether roles/datastore.backupsAdmin needs roles/datastore.backupSchedulesAdmin; custom roles where about 90% of permissions go unused.
    • Proposal: Start broad, record used permissions, then automatically remove unused ones every 30 to 90 days with GCP role recommendations or AWS Access Advisor.
    • Elevation: Temporary, expiring permissions on request or via on-call status.

    Takeaway: A useful argument for data-driven least privilege. Use Access Advisor or IAM Recommender output to prune roles on a schedule instead of hand-crafting policies.

  • Leveraging Nuclei Templates to Identify Risks and Threats in Critical Cloud Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: Ofir Yakobi (Orca Security, April 3, 2024) shows how Orca used Nuclei templates, some AI-generated, to detect risks in two deliberately vulnerable cloud test environments, and how the templates feed Orca’s external scanning.

    • SSRF case: An Azure-hosted app behind Application Gateway; setting X-Forwarded-Host to 169.254.169.254 reached the instance metadata endpoint. The template matches ‘compute’ and ‘resourceGroupName’ in the response.
    • TeamCity case: CVE-2024-27198 auth bypass on a TeamCity server older than 2023.11.4 on EC2, where a crafted jsp parameter created an admin account. The template fetches /login.html and regex-matches the version, not the bypass itself.
    • AI: Templates generated from text prompts with Nuclei’s AI platform.
    • Integration: Orca runs AI-generated and manual templates in external scans, combined with asset inventory and prioritized by exposure, privileged identities and sensitive data access.
    • Limits: Only two example templates; no template count given.

    Takeaway: Version-check templates are cheap but only flag likely exposure. Pair external Nuclei scans with patching and metadata-endpoint protections such as IMDSv2.

  • Terraform 1.8 Provider Functions for AWS, Google Cloud, and Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp blog post (April 2024) announcing that provider-defined functions, new in Terraform 1.8, are generally available in the AWS, Google Cloud and Kubernetes providers.

    • Requirements: required_version >= 1.8.0 and the provider declared in required_providers.
    • Syntax: provider::<local_name>::<function>(), e.g. provider::aws::arn_parse(arn).
    • AWS (v5.40): arn_parse returns an object of ARN components (.account_id, region); arn_build(partition, service, region, account, resource) assembles an ARN string.
    • Google Cloud (v5.23): name_from_id, location_from_id, project_from_id parse resource IDs; region_from_zone("us-west1-a") returns us-west1.
    • Kubernetes (v2.28): manifest_decode turns YAML into an object for kubernetes_manifest; manifest_decode_multi decodes multi-document YAML into a list for for_each.
    • Use cases: Transforming and parsing combined data, building identifiers and simplifying variable validation.

    Takeaway: Replace split()/regex hacks on ARNs, GCP IDs and YAML with provider functions once you are on Terraform 1.8 and the listed provider versions.

  • Private, Secure, and Seamless Connectivity to Cloud SQL Using Private Service Connect
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog post on using Private Service Connect (PSC) to reach Cloud SQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL and now GA for SQL Server) privately, as an alternative to VPC-peering-based Private Service Access.

    • Setup: Create a Cloud SQL instance with PSC enabled, create a PSC endpoint in your VPC pointing at the instance’s service attachment URI, optionally allowlist consumer projects, then connect via internal IP, DNS, Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or Language Connectors.
    • Patterns: One endpoint per VPC; read replicas are separate instances and each needs its own endpoint; on-prem via Interconnect/VPN; PSC global access for cross-region within a VPC.
    • IP usage: One IP per endpoint, versus PSA reserving a whole subnet range per region.
    • Firewalling: PSC allows granular rules; PSA needs a whole range allowlisted.
    • Quotas: VPC peering quotas that limit PSA scaling do not apply to PSC.
    • Multi-tenant: The same instance can be exposed into different VPCs with different endpoints, useful for SaaS.

    Takeaway: For multi-VPC or multi-project access to Cloud SQL, PSC avoids peering sprawl and wide firewall ranges. Remember replicas need their own endpoints.

  • Go Performance from Version 1.0 to 1.22
    summary

    TL;DR: Ben Hoyt (April 2024) benchmarks his GoAWK interpreter compiled with every Go release from 1.0 to 1.22, following his earlier 1.2-to-1.18 comparison.

    • Benchmarks: countwords (word frequency over a 10x King James Bible, string and I/O heavy) and sumloop (10 million-iteration tight loop); best of three runs on an x86-64 Linux laptop.
    • Overall gain: countwords is about 8x faster on Go 1.22 than 1.0; sumloop about 24x faster.
    • Big jumps: Largest gains in Go 1.3, 1.5, 1.7 and 1.12; later releases bring smaller incremental speedups.
    • Regression: Go 1.2 slowed countwords (7.5s in 1.1 to 25.5s in 1.2), likely the stack hot-split issue; 1.3 fixed it with contiguous stacks (2.8s).
    • PGO: Profile-guided optimisation (Go 1.20+) gave about 2% on countwords and 7% on sumloop on 1.22, with binaries about 5% larger.
    • Binary size: Fairly stable apart from the jump in 1.2.

    Takeaway: Upgrading Go is a nearly free performance win, and PGO is worth a try for a few percent at a small size cost.

  • Redka: Redis Re-Implemented with SQLite
    summary

    TL;DR: Redka by nalgeon is a re-implementation of core Redis on top of SQL storage (SQLite or PostgreSQL), compatible with the Redis API and the RESP wire protocol. BSD-3-Clause.

    • Data types: Strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets, plus key management, server/connection and transaction commands.
    • Modes: Standalone Redis-compatible server, or a Go module used in-process (also as an in-process server for tests).
    • Storage: SQLite or PostgreSQL backends; data is not limited to RAM.
    • Extras: ACID transactions and SQL views over the data for analysis and reporting.
    • Performance: The README says tens of thousands of operations per second and states it is not about raw performance; benchmarks live in a separate doc.
    • Status: In maintenance mode with no new features planned; described as ready for testing and non-critical production.

    Takeaway: Handy as a Redis stand-in for tests or small apps where you want durable, SQL-queryable data. Do not use it where Redis latency or throughput matters.

  • index_advisor: PostgreSQL Index Advisor
    summary

    TL;DR: index_advisor from Supabase is a PostgreSQL extension that takes a query and recommends indexes that would lower its estimated cost.

    • Install: Requires the hypopg extension; sudo make install, then create extension if not exists index_advisor cascade;.
    • Usage: select * from index_advisor('select book.id from book where title = $1'); returns e.g. CREATE INDEX ON public.book USING btree (title).
    • Output: startup_cost_before/after, total_cost_before/after (jsonb), index_statements (text[]) and errors (text[]).
    • Features: Handles generic parameters ($1, $2), materialized views, and resolves tables and columns hidden behind views; join queries can yield several suggestions.
    • Tests: make install; make installcheck.
    • Limits: Costs are planner estimates, so suggested indexes are not guaranteed to speed up real execution; write and storage overhead are not considered.

    Takeaway: A quick way to sanity-check slow queries from pg_stat_statements. Validate suggestions with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before creating them in production.

  • State of DevSecOps
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog’s State of DevSecOps report, built from telemetry across its customers’ applications, cloud workloads and CI pipelines. The page now carries a newer edition than the one linked in 2024; figures below are from the current page.

    • Exploitable vulns: 87% of organisations have at least one exploitable vulnerability, affecting 40% of services; Java services are most affected (59%).
    • EOL runtimes: 10% of services run an end-of-life language or runtime version; those had exploitable vulns 50% of the time versus 37% otherwise.
    • Dependency lag: The median dependency is 278 days behind its latest major version (Java 492, Ruby 357); services deployed less than monthly lag 295 days versus 172 for daily deploys.
    • Too-fast updates: 50% of organisations adopt third-party libraries within a day of release; 1.6% of npm-using orgs used at least one malicious dependency in the past year.
    • GitHub Actions: Only 4% pin all Marketplace actions to hashes, 71% never pin, and 2% run a previously compromised action unpinned.
    • Prioritisation: Only 18% of critical dependency vulns stay critical after runtime-context severity adjustment.
    • Source caveat: The report edition has changed since the link was saved; numbers may differ from the 2024 version.

    Takeaway: Pin Actions by commit SHA, keep dependencies current but with a short cooling-off period, and use runtime context to triage CVEs instead of paging on CVSS.

  • The End of GitHub PATs: You Can’t Leak What You Don’t Have
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Moore (Chainguard CTO, April 2024) introduces Octo STS, a GitHub App that acts as a Security Token Service so workloads trade OIDC tokens for short-lived GitHub tokens instead of using PATs.

    • Problem: Cross-repo access, PRs that must trigger Actions, org-level changes and automation outside Actions forced long-lived PATs, deploy keys or App private keys, which get reused and over-scoped.
    • Design: Modeled on AWS STS and GCP federation; trust policies live in the target repo at .github/chainguard/{name}.sts.yaml, or in the org .github repo for org-wide policies.
    • Policy fields: Identity rules on issuer/subject, claim_pattern to match claims such as workflow_ref, and a repository list for org-level policies.
    • Flow: Caller gets an OIDC token (GitHub Actions or another IdP like a Google service account), sends it to Octo STS, which checks the policy and returns a short-lived scoped token.
    • Limits: The App holds a superset of permissions it can hand out; its signing key is long-lived but kept in KMS for signing only; only listed permissions can be federated.

    Takeaway: If your CI still carries GitHub PATs, Octo STS (or the same pattern) removes the static secret entirely. Lock down who can edit the policy files, since they now grant access.

  • NSA Publishes Guidance for Strengthening AI System Security
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NSA press release (15 April 2024) announcing the AI Security Center’s first joint Cybersecurity Information Sheet, Deploying AI Systems Securely, written with CISA, FBI and Five Eyes partners.

    • Co-authors: NSA AISC with CISA, FBI, Australia’s ACSC, Canada’s Cyber Centre, New Zealand’s NCSC and the UK NCSC.
    • Audience: Organisations deploying and operating AI systems built by someone else, not AI developers.
    • Goals: Protect confidentiality, integrity and availability of AI systems, mitigate known vulnerabilities, and provide controls to detect and respond to malicious activity.
    • Structure: Three areas: secure the deployment environment, continuously protect the AI system, and secure AI operation and maintenance.
    • Example controls: Strict access controls, regular audits and penetration tests, logging and monitoring, patching, user training, high availability and disaster recovery planning.
    • Related: Builds on the earlier joint Guidelines for Secure AI System Development and Engaging with Artificial Intelligence; aligns with CISA CPGs and NIST CSF.
    • Source caveat: nsa.gov returned 403; summary based on CISA’s alert and news coverage found via search.

    Takeaway: A reasonable checklist when putting a third-party model or LLM service into production. Treat the model like any other high-value workload: harden the environment, control access, and log everything.

  • Copilot-For-Security: Community Repository for Microsoft Security Copilot
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft’s community repository for Security Copilot (formerly Copilot for Security), the generative-AI assistant for security and IT operations. It holds samples, not the product itself. The repo now redirects to Azure/Security-Copilot.

    • Contents: Plugin samples, Logic Apps, promptbook samples, sample prompts, monitoring assets, customer guides and technical workshops.
    • Docs: Official product documentation is linked from the README, not hosted in the repo.
    • Contributing: Fork, branch, PR; a CLA bot checks each pull request and automated checks run before review.
    • License: MIT.
    • Activity: At capture, about 1,217 commits, 649 stars, 280 forks and 45 open pull requests.

    Takeaway: Useful if you run Security Copilot and want ready-made plugins and promptbooks to adapt. Review community plugins before connecting them to production data sources.

  • Integrate Kubernetes Policy-as-Code Solutions into Security Hub
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post (Joaquin Manuel Rinaudo, April 2024) with a sample solution that pushes Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper policy violations from EKS clusters into AWS Security Hub.

    • Architecture: A scheduled Lambda runs every 10 minutes, authenticates to each EKS cluster with its IAM role via the Kubernetes Python client, reads policy reports or Gatekeeper constraint status, and sends active violations to Security Hub.
    • Lifecycle: Findings that are resolved in the cluster are archived in Security Hub.
    • Access: kube-setup.sh creates a read-only ClusterRole bound to read-only-group, mapped via EKS access entries (default) or aws-auth.
    • Deploy: Configure parameters.json (policy type, clusters, optional subnet and security group), run deploy.sh from the delegated admin account; cleanup.sh removes it.
    • Demo: Kyverno policy requiring a namespace label plus a noncompliant namespace to generate a finding.
    • Limits: Gatekeeper output is capped by the constraint violations limit (raise with --constraint-violations-limit); private API endpoints need subnet and SG settings; it is a sample, not a supported product.

    Takeaway: A simple way to get Kubernetes admission and audit findings into the same place as the rest of your AWS findings. Fine as a starting point for multi-account EKS fleets.

  • From Ground Zero to Production: Go’s Journey at Google
    summary

    TL;DR: Yves Junqueira, a former Google SRE and early Go adopter, recounts (March 2024) how Go went from an experiment to a production platform inside Google.

    • First tools: A crawler gathering performance stats from thousands of servers to monitor Bigtable health for Google+.
    • Core libraries: Go support for internal RPC (Stubby), auth (LOAS), naming (Chubby) and Blaze build rules.
    • Automation: A Bigtable drain system that shifts traffic away from unhealthy clusters through the global load balancer, using a Chubby-based master election library.
    • First user-facing service: A JID conversion service at hundreds of thousands of QPS; versus Java it used more CPU but had much shorter GC pauses.
    • Server toolkit: An internal library (not a framework) adding logging, load shedding and traffic management without changing how code looks.
    • Adoption: Social SRE moved tooling from Python to Go, and SRE leadership later recommended Go over Python for production work.
    • Lessons: Typed, compiled code eases long-lived tool maintenance; automated draining can cascade; health checks that are too strict spread outages; Hyrum’s law.

    Takeaway: A first-hand history plus practical SRE lessons on automation failure modes. Worth reading if you build control-plane tooling.

  • The Kubenomicon: Offensive Kubernetes Attack Techniques and Mitigations
    summary

    TL;DR: The Kubenomicon is an open, offensive-focused knowledge base of Kubernetes attack techniques, each paired with guidance on how to defend against it.

    • Structure: ATT&CK-style matrix inspired by Microsoft’s Kubernetes Threat Matrix, adding the exploitation and remediation detail that matrix lacks.
    • Tactics: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection and Impact.
    • Fundamentals: Background pages on nodes, RBAC, etcd, secrets and other components.
    • Contributing: Community pull requests to the GitHub repo; a contributing page is linked.
    • Related: Credits Microsoft’s matrix, the RedGuard Kubernetes threat matrix and HackTricks Kubernetes.

    Takeaway: A good map for Kubernetes threat modelling or red-team prep. Use the per-technique defences as a hardening checklist.

  • Our Journey Migrating to AWS IMDSv2
    summary

    TL;DR: Archie Gunasekara (Slack Cloud Foundations, December 2023) describes how Slack moved roughly 60,000 EC2 instances across 17 regions and hundreds of accounts from IMDSv1 to IMDSv2.

    • Discovery: CloudWatch MetadataNoToken metric joined with account, owner and Chef role data by an imds-cw-metric-collector app, fed to Prometheus dashboards to chase service owners.
    • Finding callers: AWS ImdsPacketAnalyzer packaged as a .deb in Slack’s APT repo; Ubuntu 18.04 hosts needed lsof and nethogs instead.
    • Client fixes: Updated bash scripts, AWS CLI and SDKs so they use tokens.
    • Terraform: Shared modules default http_tokens = "required" unless the account is on an accounts_using_imdsv1 exclusion list.
    • SCPs: Deny ec2:RunInstances without MetadataHttpTokens = required and deny ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions, with listed exemptions.
    • Enforcement: EventBridge plus Lambda Slack alerts on IMDSv1 launches; an EKS-hosted IMDSv1 Terminator flips existing instances to IMDSv2 via a cross-account role.
    • Gotchas: SCPs do not apply to the management account or service-linked roles (e.g. Auto Scaling); launch templates cannot be gated on ec2:Attribute/HttpTokens; some dev instances broke when v1 was turned off.

    Takeaway: A practical playbook for IMDSv2 at fleet scale: measure with MetadataNoToken, fix clients, default in IaC, then enforce with SCPs and auto-remediation.

  • AWS Monitoring with EventBridge
    summary

    TL;DR: Andreas Wittig (cloudonaut, March 2023) lists AWS events worth alerting on via EventBridge rules routed to SNS, with Terraform examples.

    • Security: Root user console sign-ins (via CloudTrail).
    • Platform: AWS Health events for outages and breaking changes.
    • Compute: EC2 Auto Scaling failed launches/terminations and instance refreshes; ECS tasks stopped with non-zero exit codes.
    • Data: Failed EBS snapshots; failed AWS Backup backup, copy and restore jobs.
    • Ops: SSM Automation executions that fail or time out; Elastic Beanstalk warning/error status changes.
    • Supply chain/certs: ECR scan findings (critical/high/medium/undefined); ACM certificates nearing expiry.
    • Routing: Service emits event, EventBridge rule pattern-matches, target is an SNS topic that emails, texts or calls HTTPS endpoints.
    • Tooling: aws_cloudwatch_event_rule examples from the open-source marbot-io/terraform-aws-marbot-monitoring-basic module; marbot is the author’s commercial product.

    Takeaway: A cheap baseline alerting layer most accounts lack. Copy the event patterns, especially root sign-in and AWS Health.

  • Statusnook: Deploy a Status Page and Start Monitoring Endpoints in Minutes
    summary

    TL;DR: Statusnook (goksan) is a self-hosted status page with built-in endpoint monitoring, written in Go with htmx and SQLite. MIT licensed.

    • Install: curl -fsSL https://get.statusnook.com | sudo bash for standalone with managed TLS (needs ports 80/443); add -- -port 8000 behind a reverse proxy.
    • Docker: docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 -v statusnook-data:/app/statusnook-data --restart always goksan/statusnook, or the provided compose.yaml.
    • Hosting templates: DigitalOcean, Vultr, Railway and Zeabur one-click deploys; prebuilt amd64/arm64 Linux binaries.
    • Config: Web UI or YAML, editable in settings or pushed via GitHub.
    • Features: Status page, monitors with logs, notifications view; the README does not list check types or notification channels.
    • Maturity: Small project (22 commits on main at capture, about 988 stars).

    Takeaway: A lightweight option for a status page plus uptime checks on one box. Host it outside the infrastructure it monitors.

  • Cognito Scanner: Script Implementing Cognito Attacks Such as Account Oracle and Privilege Escalation
    summary

    TL;DR: Cognito Scanner from Padok is a Python CLI that tests AWS Cognito user pools and identity pools for common misconfigurations. Apache-2.0.

    • Unwanted account creation: Signs up users when self-registration should be disabled: cognito-scanner account-creation --region=... --client_id=... --username=... --password=... --user_attributes=....
    • Account oracle: Enumerates existing usernames from response differences: cognito-scanner account-oracle --client_id=... --region=... --file=usernames.txt.
    • Identity pool escalation: Uses user and identity pool IDs to obtain temporary AWS credentials with more privilege than intended.
    • Inputs: App client ID (all attacks), user pool ID and identity pool ID (escalation), region and test credentials.
    • Install: pip install cognito-scanner or build from source; Python 3.

    Takeaway: Run it against your own Cognito-backed apps: disable public sign-up if unused, enable user-existence error prevention, and scope authenticated and unauthenticated identity pool roles tightly.

  • Exploit Education: Resources for Learning Vulnerability Analysis and Exploit Development
    summary

    TL;DR: Exploit Education, by Andrew Griffiths, offers free downloadable VMs for learning vulnerability analysis, exploit development, debugging and binary analysis.

    • Nebula: Beginner Linux privilege escalation, scripting-language bugs and file system race conditions (levels 00-19).
    • Phoenix: Stack, format string, heap, network and final levels on old Linux without modern mitigations; 32- and 64-bit, x86 and ARM. Successor to Protostar.
    • Fusion: Advanced memory corruption, format string and heap challenges against modern protections (levels 00-14).
    • Main Sequence: The Ruxcon 2012 CTF: tooling, binary analysis, basic crypto, client-side exploits, password cracking and web.
    • Protostar: Archived; replaced by Phoenix.
    • Downloads: VM images are linked from the site’s downloads page.

    Takeaway: A classic progression for learning memory corruption: start with Nebula, then Phoenix, then Fusion.

  • aws-scps-for-sandbox-and-training-accounts: Example SCPs for Sandbox and Training Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: A small collection of example AWS Service Control Policies from welldone-cloud for locking down sandbox and training accounts. MIT licensed.

    • Account baseline: scp-deny-changing-account-baseline-configuration.json blocks changes to baseline settings such as contacts, billing and tax.
    • Financial commitments: scp-deny-making-agreements-purchases-and-reservations.json blocks agreements, purchases and reservations with long-term cost.
    • Central IAM: scp-deny-modifying-central-iam-resources.json protects centrally managed IAM resources.
    • Regions: scp-deny-using-other-regions.json restricts activity to allow-listed regions.
    • Services: scp-deny-using-other-services.json restricts to an allow-listed set of services.
    • Caveats: Starting points only; adapt before attaching in AWS Organizations. The README suggests aws-nuke for resetting accounts and links further SCP examples (AWS docs, Wiz posts).

    Takeaway: Attach region, service and purchase guardrails to any sandbox OU before handing out accounts; pair with periodic aws-nuke cleanup.

  • docker-phobia: Analyze Docker Image Size
    summary

    TL;DR: docker-phobia by remorses is a Go CLI that analyses a Docker image and shows its contents as a treemap so you can see what makes it large.

    • How it works: Uses dive’s internal API to pull and analyse the image, writes a JSON of file sizes, starts a local server on port 8080 and opens docker-phobia.vercel.app to render it.
    • Visualisation: Rectangles are files and folders sized by bytes; colours indicate layers, similar shades mean nearby layers.
    • Install: curl -sf https://goblin.run/github.com/remorses/docker-phobia | sh or go install github.com/remorses/docker-phobia@latest.
    • Usage: docker-phobia for an interactive image picker, or docker-phobia node:18-slim.
    • Roadmap: Hover tooltips, versioned releases, shareable treemaps by image SHA.

    Takeaway: Faster than scrolling dive’s tree when hunting for bloat. Note the rendering happens on a hosted web page, so check what data leaves your machine.

  • octo-sts: GitHub App That Acts as a Security Token Service for the GitHub API
    summary

    TL;DR: octo-sts is a GitHub App (started by Chainguard) that works as a Security Token Service: OIDC-bearing workloads exchange their token for a short-lived, policy-scoped GitHub token, removing the need for PATs.

    • Trust policies: .github/chainguard/{name}.sts.yaml in the target repo, or in the org .github repo for org-wide policies; directory configurable via OCTOSTS_POLICY_DIR.
    • Policy fields: issuer, subject or subject_pattern, claim_pattern, permissions (e.g. contents: read), repositories/repository_ids for org policies, optional app/app_pattern. Regexes match the whole value.
    • In Actions: Use octo-sts/action with id-token: write, inputs scope (e.g. my-org/my-repo) and identity (policy name); output token for GH_TOKEN.
    • Permissions: The App requests a superset; issued tokens carry only the policy’s scopes.
    • Org controls: trusted-token-issuers.yaml allowlist with enforce or audit mode; protect the policy repo with branch protection and CODEOWNERS.
    • Self-hosting: Signed images ghcr.io/octo-sts/app and ghcr.io/octo-sts/webhook; settings for GHES (GITHUB_BASE_URL), OCTOSTS_ALLOWED_ISSUERS and multi-App routing.

    Takeaway: The cleanest current answer to cross-repo automation without PATs. Treat the policy files as privileged config and review changes to them.

  • AWS CloudQuarry: Digging for Secrets in Public AMIs
    summary

    TL;DR: Eduard Agavriloae and Matei Josephs (Security Cafe, May 2024) scanned tens of thousands of public AWS AMIs for secrets and found over a hundred valid AWS access keys, including root keys.

    • Scope: 3,173,232 public AMIs from 27 regions, filtered (no Marketplace, no AWS-owned, no instance-store, owners with at most 50 AMIs, small volumes) to 26,778 targets.
    • Method: Launch instance from AMI, stop, detach root volume, terminate, attach to a scanner instance, then find for .aws, .ssh, .env, .git, web.config and run gitleaks over 400+ GB of repos (about 48 hours).
    • Effort and cost: About 6 months of work and 14+ days of scanning; cost estimated at under $1.2k (conclusion cites a $500+ bill).
    • Findings: 121 valid unique AWS key pairs including 20 root keys (the post also says 120+ and 18 elsewhere), 10+ live Stripe keys, 10+ GitHub/GitLab tokens, SSH keys, DB strings and JWT secrets.
    • Disclosure: Few accounts had usable contacts; about 5 of 70+ companies replied in 90 days. AWS then notified customers; two weeks later 58 keys were still valid.
    • Impact proven: A test Stripe refund and read access to a FinTech’s private GitLab repos.

    Takeaway: Scan images for credentials before making any AMI public, set account security contacts, and rotate anything that ever touched a shared image.

  • cdncheck: Detect the CDN, Cloud or WAF Behind an IP Address
    summary

    TL;DR: cdncheck from ProjectDiscovery is a Go CLI and library that identifies the CDN, cloud provider or WAF behind an IP address or DNS name.

    • Install: go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/cdncheck/cmd/cdncheck@latest.
    • Input and output: -i for IPs/hosts; -resp shows provider names, -j JSONL, -o file, -silent.
    • Categories: -cdn, -cloud, -waf limit output; -mcdn/-mcloud/-mwaf match and -fcdn/-fcloud/-fwaf filter specific providers.
    • Library: cdncheck.New() then CheckCDN, CheckCloud or CheckWAF, each returning match flag, provider and error.
    • Data: Providers defined in provider.yaml from URLs, ASNs or static CIDRs, compiled into sources_data.json; CNAME and Wappalyzer mappings in other.go.
    • Examples: CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai, Cloudflare, Incapsula, Sucuri, AWS, Google, Oracle.

    Takeaway: Useful in recon pipelines to drop CDN/WAF IPs before port scanning, or to find origin hosts that sit outside the WAF.

  • actionlint: Static Checker for GitHub Actions Workflow Files
    summary

    TL;DR: actionlint by rhysd is a static checker for GitHub Actions workflow files that catches syntax, type and security mistakes before you push. MIT licensed.

    • Syntax: Unknown or missing keys, invalid needs: dependencies, runner labels, cron syntax and glob patterns.
    • Expressions: Type-checks ${{ }} expressions, flagging nonexistent properties and type mismatches.
    • Actions and reusable workflows: Validates with: inputs, steps.<id>.outputs, and reusable workflow inputs, outputs and secrets.
    • Security: Detects script injection from untrusted inputs and hard-coded credentials.
    • Script linting: Runs shellcheck and pyflakes on run: steps when installed.
    • Install: Release binaries, Homebrew, go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest, Docker, or a download script for CI; WebAssembly playground online.
    • Usage: Run actionlint at the repo root; workflows are found automatically.

    Takeaway: Add it to pre-commit and CI for every repo with workflows; the injection check alone justifies it.

  • Cap: Open-Source Loom Alternative for Instant Screen Sharing
    summary

    TL;DR: Cap is an open-source Loom alternative for recording, editing and sharing screen recordings, with desktop apps for macOS and Windows and a web dashboard.

    • Instant Mode: Uploads while recording so a share link is ready when you stop.
    • Studio Mode: Records locally and opens an editor for backgrounds, zooms, trimming, captions and export.
    • Features: AI titles, summaries, chapters and transcripts; password/private sharing; custom domains; comments and viewer analytics; Loom import.
    • Storage: Cap Cloud, your own S3-compatible bucket, local-only, or full self-hosting.
    • Self-host: docker compose up -d starts Cap Web on localhost:3000; Railway and Coolify supported; replace default secrets for production.
    • Stack: Rust, TypeScript, Tauri v2, SolidStart, Next.js, Drizzle, MySQL, Tailwind; analytics on Tinybird.
    • License: AGPLv3, with some crates (cap-camera*, scap-*) MIT.

    Takeaway: A credible self-hostable replacement for Loom when recordings must stay in your own bucket.

  • Linux Maintainers Were Infected for 2 Years by SSH-Dwelling Backdoor with Huge Reach
    summary

    TL;DR: Ars Technica (Dan Goodin, May 2024) covers ESET’s 47-page report on Ebury, an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer that has compromised over 400,000 servers since 2009, including kernel.org infrastructure.

    • kernel.org: Ebury ran on at least four Linux Foundation servers between 2009 and 2011, two years earlier than thought; attackers held /etc/shadow data for 551 users and cleartext passwords for 275 (50%).
    • Separate incidents: The 2011 Phalanx compromise of kernel.org appears to be an unrelated group; no sign the kernel source was tampered with.
    • Scale: 400,000+ compromises over almost 15 years, mostly Linux plus about 400 FreeBSD and a few OpenBSD, SunOS and one Mac; about 40,000 live at any measurement, rising to 110,000 in 2023.
    • Spread: Originally via stolen SSH credentials from backdoored OpenSSH; ESET found five newer methods, including adversary-in-the-middle attacks from inside compromised data centres.
    • Hosting providers: In 2019 a US registrar/host was hit (about 2,500 physical and 60,000 virtual servers); in 2023, 70,000 servers at another provider. An ESET honeypot there was infected within a week of one SSH login.
    • Monetisation: Credential and crypto-wallet theft, card data, spam and traffic redirection via Apache and kernel modules.

    Takeaway: If you rely on hosting providers, assume SSH password logins can be harvested. Use keys with MFA or certificates, and check against ESET’s published Ebury IoCs.

  • Building a GitOps CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions (SOC 2)
    summary

    TL;DR: Mathieu Larose (April 2024) walks through a GitOps CI/CD design on GitHub Actions built to satisfy SOC 2 change-management expectations, with an app repo and an infra repo.

    • Repos: App repo builds artifacts tagged by commit SHA; infra repo holds desired state per environment as envs/dev.json, staging.json, prod.json. Trunk-based, single main branch.
    • Publish flow: PR, required tests, second-developer approval, merge, build and publish; a bot opens and merges an infra PR to update dev.
    • Deploy flow: Infra PRs with tests and peer review; promotion is copying a version config (dev to staging) via PR; rollback is a revert PR.
    • Hotfixes: Manually triggered workflow makes the bot cut hotfixes/<name> from a chosen commit; same PR process applies.
    • Controls: Rulesets block direct pushes, force-pushes and deletion on main, enforce linear history, required checks and at least one approval.
    • Caveat: The bot uses bypass permissions (gh pr merge --admin) for automated infra PRs, so those skip human approval.

    Takeaway: A good template for audit-friendly delivery: every change is a reviewed PR with SHA-tagged artifacts. Scope the bot’s bypass tightly, since it is the exception auditors will ask about.

  • XZ Utils Made Me Paranoid
    summary

    TL;DR: Kevin Haubris (TrustedSec, May 2024) built VerifyELF, a scanner that detects function hooks in running Linux processes, prompted by the XZ Utils backdoor.

    • Section comparison: Reads loaded shared library sections from process memory via ptrace (root required) and compares them to on-disk ELF files after applying relocations.
    • GOT check: For a target PID, resolves imported symbols and compares the Global Offset Table with memory; covers only functions the binary calls directly.
    • Validation: Detected the XZ backdoor (which hooks RSA_public_decrypt) on a Debian testing ISO and a proof-of-concept hook on accept.
    • Triage: nm -D maps a reported offset to a function; objdump -x shows if it is in headers (likely false positive).
    • False positives: Duplicate library copies (e.g. a second libnghttp2 in NetworkManager), Nvidia/OpenGL writable text sections, RPATH/RUNPATH copies, symbol version mismatches.
    • Limits: dlopen/dlsym loads are hard to attribute; Snap binaries skipped; container processes may false-positive.
    • Code: github.com/trustedsec/VerifyELF.

    Takeaway: Memory-versus-disk integrity checks are a practical way to hunt for XZ-style implants on critical hosts like sshd servers.

  • Everything I Learned to Negotiate Your Salary
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A 15-minute video (November 2021) by Chloe Shih, a tech product manager, sharing the negotiation tactics she used when moving to a PM role at Discord.

    • Format: Personal brain dump of tactics, framed as a starting point rather than a complete guide.
    • Structure: Intro, negotiation prep (4:13), tips 1-5 (5:56), tips 6-10 (9:45), upcoming plans (13:32).
    • Context: Made after announcing her move to Discord as a PM; channel covers PM careers in tech.
    • Sponsor: Sponsored by CASETiFY.
    • Source caveat: No transcript available; based only on the YouTube title, description and chapter list. The ten tips themselves are not described here.

    Takeaway: A short, personal take on offer negotiation from a tech PM. Watch the two tips chapters before an offer call.

  • Hello GPT-4o
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: OpenAI’s 13 May 2024 announcement of GPT-4o (o for omni), a single model that reasons across text, audio and vision in real time and was made available to free ChatGPT users.

    • Model: One natively multimodal model for text, audio and image input and output, rather than chained separate models.
    • Availability: Free in ChatGPT at launch, with higher usage limits for paid tiers; also offered through the API.
    • Benchmarks: MMLU 88.7 versus 86.5 for GPT-4 (per Wikipedia).
    • Languages: Over 50 languages at release.
    • API price (current, per Wikipedia): $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
    • Voice: Advanced Voice Mode was delayed and reached Plus and Team users in September 2024; the Realtime API followed on 1 October 2024.
    • Source caveat: openai.com returned 403; summary based on Wikipedia and press coverage, so latency and launch-day pricing claims from the original page are omitted.

    Takeaway: The release that made fast multimodal models the default tier. Mainly of historical interest now; check current model docs for pricing and limits.

  • A Step-by-Step Guide to Securely Upgrading Your EKS Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Stevie Caldwell (Fairwinds, republished on the CNCF blog May 2024) gives a step-by-step EKS upgrade process and the tools that make it safer.

    • Order: Read release notes, upgrade add-ons and controllers, fix deprecated APIs, align node groups (max one minor of skew), back up, upgrade control plane, then data plane, then kubectl; roll dev, staging (1-2 week soak), prod.
    • Tools: Pluto and kubepug for deprecated APIs, eksup for upgrade playbooks, GoNoGo for Helm add-on readiness, Nova for outdated charts and images, Velero for backups.
    • Pre-checks: Enough free subnet IPs (up to five), control plane IAM role and security group present, KMS key access if secret encryption is enabled.
    • Add-ons: VPC CNI, kube-proxy and CoreDNS are not auto-upgraded and move one minor at a time; Cluster Autoscaler and AWS Load Balancer Controller must match the cluster version.
    • Availability: Use PodDisruptionBudgets and topologySpreadConstraints during node rotation.
    • Constraints: No downgrades; in-place upgrades are one minor at a time; consider blue/green for multi-version jumps; extended support costs extra and ends with forced upgrades.

    Takeaway: EKS does not check your deprecated APIs or add-ons for you. Run Pluto/kubepug in CI and script this sequence so upgrades become routine.

  • Monitoring Your EKS Clusters’ Audit Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: Falco blog post (Thomas Labarussias, May 2023 update) on the k8saudit-eks plugin, which lets Falco evaluate EKS Kubernetes audit logs pulled from CloudWatch Logs.

    • Mechanism: Polls the cluster’s audit log stream in /aws/eks/<CLUSTER_NAME>/cluster using AWS SDK sessions (pull model).
    • IAM: Read-only logs:Describe*, logs:FilterLogEvents, logs:Get*, logs:List* scoped to that log group.
    • Local install: falcoctl installs k8saudit-eks, json and k8saudit-rules; run Falco with --disable-source syscall.
    • Helm install: IRSA annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn, driver.enabled=false, collectors.enabled=false, controller as a single-replica Deployment.
    • Config: region, profile, use_async, polling_interval (default 5s), shift (default 1s), buffer_size (default 200), and the cluster name in open_params.
    • Rules: Reuses the standard k8saudit ruleset, e.g. K8s Serviceaccount Created, Attach/Exec Pod.
