    • Limits: Only assigned Intune apps are documented; component coverage is still growing; custom app registration is in a separate doc.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to snapshot M365/Intune config as JSON for change tracking or handover docs; schedule it with an app registration and diff the output.

  • More Powerful Go Execution Traces
    summary

    TL;DR: Go blog post (March 2024, Michael Knyszek) on the overhauled runtime/trace execution tracer: much lower overhead, scalable traces, flight recording and a programmatic reader.

    • Overhead: Before Go 1.21 tracing cost about 10-20% CPU; frame-pointer unwinding and other work brought it to roughly 1-2% for many apps.
    • Scalability: Go 1.22 rewrote traces so they can be split into self-contained segments.
    • Flight recording: Experimental FlightRecorder in golang.org/x/exp/trace keeps a rolling buffer and snapshots when something slow happens, e.g. an HTTP request over 300 ms.
    • Reader API: Experimental trace.NewReader / ReadEvent for analyzing traces in code, e.g. how often goroutines block on network I/O.
    • Viewing: go tool trace or the open-source gotraceui.
    • Limits: Flight recorder and reader are experimental; go tool trace still loads the whole trace into memory.

    Takeaway: Tracing is now cheap enough to leave on in production; a flight recorder triggered on slow requests is a practical way to catch tail-latency issues.

  • Measuring Your System’s Performance Using Software (Go Edition)
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Lemire (March 2024) shows how small Go benchmarks can reveal hardware and runtime behavior: allocations, inlining, cache lines, latency and branch prediction.

    • Benchmarks: BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B) run with go test -bench .; b.N grows until a run lasts at least one second.
    • Allocations: b.ReportAllocs(); a 100,001-element slice allocated 802,816 bytes/op while small data stayed on the stack.
    • Inlining: -gcflags=-m reports it, //go:noinline disables it; inlined loop about 295 ns/op vs 865 ns/op.
    • Cache: A strided copy suggests a 128-byte cache line; a shuffle test suggests about 16 MB of cache.
    • Dependencies: Prefix sum 142.8 ns/op vs 30.04 ns/op for successive differences; linked lists are latency-bound.
    • Branches: Random data: branchy copy 19,518 ns/op vs branchless 7,124 ns/op.
    • Caveats: Results vary by hardware and are noisy; microbenchmarks alone do not justify optimizations; branchless can lose when branches are predictable.

    Takeaway: Good template for writing your own probes; measure on your target hardware before trusting any of these numbers.

  • For Loops and More in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Miki Tebeka (Ardan Labs, March 2024) surveys Go loop forms and the bugs each can introduce, including Go 1.22 additions.

    • Assembly: go build -gcflags=-S shows a loop as jumps (JMP, INCQ, CMPQ, JLT); lensm for visual reading.
    • Multiple variables: Init/post clauses can update several vars, but i++, j-- is invalid Go; use i, j = i+1, j-1.
    • Labeled break: A plain break inside switch exits only the switch and can cause an infinite loop; use break loop. goto also shown.
    • Range copies: for _, a := range iterates over copies, so edits are lost; index or read/modify/write (acts[i] = a). Map values need read/modify/write too.
    • Go 1.22: for i := range 3 over integers and for range b.N in benchmarks.
    • Trivia: About 657 goto uses in the Go 1.22 standard library (rough count).
    • Limits: Range-over-func deferred to a later post; no performance data.

    Takeaway: Quick refresher on the range-copy and break-in-switch traps that still catch experienced Go developers.

  • How to Write a 4000 Stars GitHub README for Your Project
    summary

    TL;DR: Daytona CEO Ivan Burazin (March 2024) describes the README structure Daytona used at its open-source launch, when the repo reached nearly 4,000 stars in its first week.

    • Header: Logo, health badges, one-line pitch plus subtitle, visuals (GIFs via LiceCap), feature highlights, and a quickstart with as few commands as possible.
    • Body: Purpose, backstory, detailed getting-started steps; keep it concise and move depth into a docs folder.
    • Hygiene: Contributing guide, license, code of conduct (Contributor Covenant), advising git add <file1> <file2> over git add ..
    • Checklist: Remove empty sections, fix broken links, open labeled issues for missing content.
    • Beyond README: SECURITY.md, a filled About section, Releases, custom labels, “good first issue” tags, issue templates.
    • Caveats: Based on one project’s experience; no data linking README quality to stars.

    Takeaway: A reasonable checklist for launching an internal or open-source tool; the quickstart and SECURITY.md items are the cheapest wins.

  • Using GitHub Actions to Add Go Binaries to a Release
    summary

    TL;DR: Rob Allen (February 2024) shows the GitHub Actions workflow that builds Go binaries for his Flickr uploader Rodeo and attaches them to a GitHub Release automatically.

    • Trigger: on: release with type created.
    • Job: Single build job on ubuntu-latest, actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-go@v1 with Go 1.20.
    • Build: build-executables.sh <tag> cross-compiles all platforms into ./release.
    • Upload: svenstaro/upload-release-action@v2 with GITHUB_TOKEN, file_glob: true and rodeo-* to upload everything in one step.
    • Design choice: No matrix, since one Go container can cross-compile every target instead of spinning up a runner per platform.
    • Limits: Build script is covered in a separate post; a commenter suggests GoReleaser, not evaluated.

    Takeaway: Fine for small tools; pin action versions to SHAs and consider GoReleaser if you need checksums, SBOMs or signing.

  • How I Built My Own Go Package Index
    summary

    TL;DR: Ozan Sazak (March 2024) explains how he built go.sazak.io, a vanity import path index for his Go packages, from a GitHub sync tool plus a static Next.js site.

    • Mechanism: go get fetches HTML go-import meta tags (import path, VCS, repo URL); optional go-source links source.
    • Sync tool: sync-github-repos lists public repos via the GitHub API, keeps those whose go.mod starts with module go.sazak.io/, and writes metadata (stars, latest tag, packages) to JSON.
    • Flags: HasCLIApp from a cli topic tag; AlphaRelease for pre-releases or versions below v1.0.0.
    • Frontend: Next.js, Shadcn UI, deployed on Vercel.
    • Automation: Pre-commit hook runs --username ozansz --hostname go.sazak.io --out ui/src/repos.json --force-authenticated; each push redeploys.
    • Limits: Single static page; data refreshes only at commit time.

    Takeaway: Vanity import paths decouple your module names from GitHub; this is a small, copyable pattern if you want that for a personal or company namespace.

  • Retina: eBPF Distributed Networking Observability Tool for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Retina is Microsoft’s MIT-licensed, cloud-agnostic eBPF network observability platform for Kubernetes, providing Prometheus metrics and on-demand packet captures.

    • Metrics: Prometheus format, exportable to Prometheus or Azure Monitor, visualized in Grafana or Log Analytics.
    • Plugins: dropreason, packetforward, linuxutil, dns; packetparser for advanced metrics and CRD captures.
    • Captures: kubectl krew install retina then kubectl retina capture create --pod-selectors <app=my-app>.
    • Platforms: Linux, Windows and Azure Linux nodes; Windows Server 2019 no longer supported, use 2022.
    • Supply chain: Images verifiable with cosign against the GitHub OIDC issuer.
    • Limits: packetparser advanced mode may perform poorly on 32+ core nodes under heavy load; use basic mode there.

    Takeaway: Worth trying for packet drops and DNS issues in clusters without a full service mesh; start in basic mode on large nodes.

  • Keep Hackers Out of Your Cluster with These 5 Simple Tricks
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2024 talk by Datadog’s Christophe Tafani-Dereeper and Frederic Baguelin giving a threat-informed, data-driven list of Kubernetes controls, based on honeypots and real container-escape exploitation.

    • Data: Public honeypots imitating the Docker API, Kubernetes API server and Kubelet API, plus a review of exploited container-escape CVEs; attacker goals grouped as deploy malicious workloads, backdoor the cluster, escape containers.
    • Control plane: Use managed Kubernetes, never disable API server auth, keep the API server off the internet (e.g. IAP for private GKE).
    • IMDS: GKE Workload Identity; on EKS/AKS block metadata with NetworkPolicy. On EKS, IMDSv2 alone is not enough; set hop limit to 1 on worker nodes.
    • Cloud privileges: Map pods to cloud roles with Datadog’s Managed Kubernetes Auditing Toolkit (MKAT).
    • Admission control: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or Pod Security Admission; allow only vetted registries, block privileged pods and host mounts; audit first, then enforce.
    • Exploit resistance: securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true breaks many automated payloads.
    • Source caveat: No video transcript retrieved; based on the Datadog Security Labs abstract and the companion tl;dr sec guest post.

    Takeaway: A short, prioritized EKS/GKE hardening list; the IMDS hop-limit and read-only root FS items are cheap and high value.

  • Introducing TrailDiscover: Simplifying Access to Security Insights About CloudTrail Events
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Adan Alvarez introduces TrailDiscover, an open catalog of AWS CloudTrail events documenting which ones attackers have abused, what they enable and what logs they produce, with a searchable site at traildiscover.cloud.

    • Structure: One JSON file per event grouped by AWS service, with event name, source, description, MITRE ATT&CK tactics/techniques, real-world-use evidence links, related research and security implications.
    • Site: Searchable Events pages and an Insights page breaking down incident sources, ATT&CK mappings and services.
    • Extras: The repo now also offers an MCP server for AI assistants and a Datadog dashboard generator.
    • Contributing: PRs for new events; run build.py in tools to regenerate site output; reuse the same URL/title when one report covers several events.
    • Caveats: Author says it is early and may contain mistakes; ATT&CK mappings are best guesses; some implications were AI-generated then reviewed.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; summary based on the project’s GitHub README (adanalvarez/TrailDiscover).

    Takeaway: Good reference when writing CloudTrail detections or triaging an unfamiliar event name during an incident.

  • NamespaceHound: Protecting Multi-Tenant Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz (Shay Berkovich, Megan Moore, March 2024) releases NamespaceHound, an open-source Python CLI that assesses namespace-crossing and anonymous-access risk in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters.

    • Checks: 22 crossing types, e.g. RBAC_SECRETS_STEALING and RBAC_WORKLOAD_CREATION (both High), plus anonymous access.
    • Usage: -n NAMESPACE to scope, -c to include kube-system, -o table/json/csv/html, --kubeconfig, -v.
    • Permissions: Needs read on all resource types (admin, cluster-admin or system:masters also works).
    • Design: Stores no cluster data locally and builds no graph.
    • Framework: Extends Wiz’s PEACH tenant-isolation model to Kubernetes, with hardening advice on RBAC, storage reclaim policies and disabling token automount.
    • Limits: Risk assessment only, not enforcement; Kubernetes has no native way to monitor namespace crossing.

    Takeaway: Run it against any cluster where namespaces are your tenant boundary; findings usually point at over-broad RBAC.

  • bincapz (malcontent): Enumerate Binary Capabilities, Including Malicious Behaviors
    summary

    TL;DR: bincapz, now renamed malcontent, is Chainguard’s Apache 2.0 Go tool that enumerates program capabilities with YARA to detect supply-chain compromises, especially by diffing versions.

    • Rules: YARA-X with over 14,500 rules; third-party sets (Elastic, Mandiant, etc.) only with --third-party.
    • Targets: ELF, Mach-O and PE binaries, scripts in many languages, archives and OCI images.
    • Modes: analyze lists all capabilities, diff compares versions by risk, scan filters by threshold (default HIGH).
    • Settings: --min-risk (default low), --jobs 12, --max-depth 32, --sensitivity 5; registry auth via --oci-auth and MALCONTENT_REGISTRY_* env vars.
    • Run: cgr.dev/chainguard/malcontent:latest or make install-yara-x and make out/mal.
    • Limits: Best on Linux, weaker on macOS, weakest on Windows; analyze is noisy by design; AV may flag it due to embedded YARA strings.

    Takeaway: The diff mode is the useful part: run it between dependency or image versions in CI to spot newly added network, exec or persistence behavior.

  • Fixing Security Vulnerabilities with AI
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub engineering post (Tiferet Gazit, February 2024) on how code scanning autofix, now Copilot Autofix, uses an LLM to propose fixes for CodeQL alerts and how they evaluated it.

    • Prompt: CodeQL query help, the alert message and line-numbered snippets along the data flow; asks for instructions, before/after code blocks and any new dependencies, without changing functionality.
    • No raw diffs: Models struggle with line-number arithmetic, so edits are expressed as code blocks.
    • Post-processing: Fuzzy matching, syntax parsing, name/type checks; suggested packages verified against registries and screened for vulnerabilities or malware.
    • Evaluation: Harness over 1,400+ JS/TS alerts from 63 CodeQL queries; success means alert gone, no new alerts, no syntax errors, test results unchanged.
    • Numbers: Iteration tripled success rate and cut LLM compute by a factor of six.
    • Limits: Initial release JS/TS only; prompt size limited visible files; edits confined to included code.

    Takeaway: The evaluation criteria are a good model for any AI-fix pipeline: re-run the scanner and tests, never trust the patch alone.

  • OPA 1.0 Is Coming: Here’s What You Need to Know
    summary

    TL;DR: Anders Eknert’s March 2024 OPA blog post on preparing Rego policies for OPA 1.0’s backward-incompatible changes.

    • Keywords: import future.keywords becomes a no-op; if and contains become mandatory in rule heads.
    • Strictness: Several strict-mode checks become default, e.g. duplicate imports and deprecated built-ins are rejected.
    • Reserved names: input and data can no longer be used as identifiers.
    • Server binding: Defaults to localhost instead of all interfaces; use opa run --server --addr 0.0.0.0:8181 to expose it.
    • Migration (v0.59.0+): Add import rego.v1, rewrite with opa fmt --rego-v1, verify with opa check --rego-v1, run with --v1-compatible.
    • Caveat: Change list described as non-comprehensive and subject to change.

    Takeaway: Run opa fmt --rego-v1 and opa check --rego-v1 across your policy repos and check any deployments that relied on OPA listening on all interfaces.

  • weAudit: Collaborative Code Auditing Extension for VS Code
    summary

    TL;DR: weAudit is Trail of Bits’ free VS Code extension for collaborative code review: bookmark findings and notes, track which files are reviewed, and export results.

    • Findings/notes: Create from a selection (default cmd+3 finding, cmd+4 note); shown in a sidebar list and highlighted inline; can span multiple regions.
    • Review tracking: Mark files reviewed (cmd+7) or regions partially reviewed (cmd+shift+7); cmd+0 jumps between partial regions.
    • Export: Markdown export, GitHub/GitLab issue creation and permalinks.
    • Sharing: Each auditor’s data lives in .vscode/$USERNAME.weaudit, which teammates can share and toggle per user.
    • Settings: Tree view mode, GitHub org, username, permalink separator, highlight colors.
    • Limits: Sharing is file-based, not real-time sync.

    Takeaway: Useful for security reviews or large PR audits where you need to prove coverage; commit or share the .weaudit files to coordinate.

  • Learning Go in 2024: From Beginner to Senior
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Boyle’s ByteSizeGo guide (March 2024) organizes Go learning resources into Beginner, Junior, Mid-level and Senior tiers, each with books, talks, podcasts and a suggested project.

    • Beginner: Standard-library-only CLI that reads a birth date and prints age, run with go run.
    • Junior: HTTP exchange-rate server (/exchange/GBP/USD) with a naive buy signal vs the 7-day average, using table-driven tests.
    • Mid-level: Web scraper with pagination, DB storage and email alerts; concurrency primitives, pipelines, execution traces.
    • Senior: Distributed-systems framework (service discovery, load balancing, fault tolerance, consistent hashing) inspired by go-kit; Go memory model, Kubernetes memory limits.
    • Caveats: Non-exhaustive; many resources paid; some books from 2015-2016; promotes the author’s own products; a newer edition exists.

    Takeaway: The project ladder is the useful part for structuring your own or a team’s Go upskilling.

  • The Case of a Leaky Goroutine
    summary

    TL;DR: Wouter Groeneveld (Brain Baking, March 2024) walks through finding a goroutine leak that caused OOM restarts of Kubernetes pods in a Go service.

    • Detection: Grafana showed goroutine memory climbing; Pyroscope (docker run -it -p 4040:4040 grafana/pyroscope) showed goroutines parked in runtime.gopark inside pipeline functions.
    • Profiling: _ "net/http/pprof" exposes /debug/pprof/; go tool pprof with diff_base compares dumps against a baseline.
    • Root cause: A helper ToDoneInterface closed the wrong channel in defer, and the context was not derived (e.g. WithCancel), so goroutines in a long-running job never exited.
    • Testing: defer goleak.VerifyNone(t) from Uber’s goleak catches leftover goroutines.
    • Production: Uber’s LeakProf mentioned as the systematic option.
    • Fix: Do not convert channels; use derived contexts.

    Takeaway: Add goleak to tests of any code that spawns goroutines, and expose pprof so leaks can be diffed in a running pod.

  • threatcl: Threat Modeling as Code with HCL
    summary

    TL;DR: threatcl (formerly hcltm) is an MIT-licensed CLI for writing threat models as HCL files so they can live in version control and be validated in CI.

    • Format: HCL2 spec (separate repo); JSON also accepted but without imports and variables.
    • Validate: validate, with -invariants to enforce org-wide rules.
    • Outputs: export to JSON, OTM or HCL; dashboard to Markdown with custom templates; dfd renders data flow diagrams as PNG or DOT.
    • Terraform: terraform converts terraform show -json output into information_asset blocks.
    • Extras: server/query for GraphQL, beta mcp, and lsp.
    • Install: Release binaries, Homebrew, ghcr.io/threatcl/threatcl; releases have SLSA provenance verifiable with gh attestation verify.

    Takeaway: Good fit for threat-modeling-as-code: keep models next to the service, validate in PRs, and generate DFDs from the same source.

  • IAMGraph: Mapping Cross-Account Attack Paths in AWS Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: IAMGraph from WithSecure Labs (now under ReversecLabs) models AWS IAM role trust and assume-role paths across many accounts in Neo4j to find cross-account attack paths.

    • Input: Output of aws iam get-account-authorization-details for each account; permissions evaluated with WithSecure’s IAMSpy.
    • Run: iamgraph --db-uri bolt://localhost:7687 run --input-dir ./input/; model and analyse stages can run separately.
    • Database: Neo4j in Docker/Podman; NEO4J_AUTH=none for local use, else --db-user with password prompt.
    • Graph: Account, IAMUser, IAMRole, IdentityProvider, IAMPrincipal nodes with IN, TRUSTS and CAN_ASSUME edges.
    • Queries: Example Cypher for roles trusting *, roles trusting identity providers, and cross-account assume paths.
    • Limits: Accounts IAMSpy cannot load are skipped (e.g. managed policies used only as permission boundaries); large graphs overwhelm the Neo4j browser.

    Takeaway: Run it across an AWS Organization to spot unexpected cross-account trust, especially wildcard principals and third-party roles.

  • Using Tailscale for Persistence
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune (raesene, March 2024) demonstrates how an attacker with brief cluster-admin access can use Tailscale for stealthy persistence on Kubernetes nodes, forming a small controllable “botnet”.

    • Tailnet design: ACL tags so controllers reach bots but bots cannot reach controllers or each other; tags must exist in the ACL policy before use.
    • Enrollment: Reusable auth key that auto-applies the bots tag.
    • Egress: Falls back to DERP over 443/TCP, so it works anywhere outbound 443 is open.
    • Hiding: containerd ctr runs the container in namespace sys_net_mon with --net-host and host root mounted read-only at /host; binaries renamed systemd_net_mon_server / systemd_net_mon_client; client run with --ssh.
    • Alternative: Static pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests so kubelet keeps it running.
    • Limits: ctr needs direct node access (e.g. SSH); post does not cover detection.

    Takeaway: Watch for unexpected containerd namespaces, static pod manifests, renamed binaries and outbound Tailscale/DERP traffic from nodes.

  • cleanowners: GitHub Action to Remove Non-Organization Members from CODEOWNERS
    summary

    TL;DR: cleanowners is an MIT-licensed GitHub Action from GitHub’s OSPO that opens PRs removing users who are no longer organization members from CODEOWNERS files.

    • Behavior: Also opens a PR adding a placeholder if CODEOWNERS is missing or empty.
    • Auth: GitHub App (GH_APP_ID, GH_APP_INSTALLATION_ID, GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY) preferred over GH_TOKEN; classic PAT needs repo and read:org.
    • App permissions: Contents and Pull requests read/write, Metadata read, Organization Members read.
    • Settings: ORGANIZATION or REPOSITORY, EXEMPT_REPOS, DRY_RUN, ISSUE_REPORT, GH_ENTERPRISE_URL.
    • Workflow: github-community-projects/cleanowners@v2 on a cron (example "3 2 1 * *", monthly).
    • Limits: Community support only, no GitHub SLA; App must be installed on each scanned repo.

    Takeaway: Stale CODEOWNERS silently break required-review rules; run this monthly with DRY_RUN first.

  • Small Language Models for Application Security: Beyond ChatGPT
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Conference talk by Louis Barrett on using small language models, rather than large hosted models like ChatGPT, for application security tasks.

    • Topic: Applying small, self-hostable language models to AppSec work as an alternative to general-purpose chatbots.
    • Likely themes: A related Loco Moco Security Conference session (“Small Language Models for Application Security II”, July 2024) describes using small off-the-shelf models, training them, scoping projects, and keeping company data inside the organization. It is not confirmed to be the same talk or speaker.
    • Context: Related public work (e.g. Wiz fine-tuning a small model for secret detection) argues small models give privacy and latency benefits when run on-premises.
    • Source caveat: The YouTube page returned no description or transcript; summary is based on the video title and web search results only, so specifics of the talk are unknown.

    Takeaway: Watch it if you are weighing self-hosted small models for code review or secret detection where sending source code to a third-party LLM is not acceptable.

  • Ultimate Guide to Secrets in Lambda
    summary

    TL;DR: AJ Stuyvenberg (March 2024) compares four ways to give AWS Lambda functions secrets, environment variables, SSM Parameter Store, Secrets Manager and KMS, on cost, latency, auditability, rotation and size.

    • Env vars: Encrypted at rest, exposed via GetFunctionConfiguration; 4 KB total limit; about 25 ms added to cold start; poor per-secret auditing.
    • Parameter Store: Standard params free, 4 KB, 10,000 per region; advanced $0.05/month, 8 KB, TTL policies; above 40 RPS costs $0.05 per 10,000. About 217 ms cold, 39.3 ms warm.
    • Secrets Manager: $0.40/secret/month, 65 KB, rotation and cross-region replication. About 177 ms cold, 29.4 ms warm.
    • KMS: $1/key/month, $0.03 per 10,000 requests, 4 KB per encrypt; decrypt about 64.4 ms cold, 6.45 ms warm. Envelope encryption suits about 100 KB of secrets.
    • Extension: Criticizes the closed-source AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension; prefers SDK calls or Powertools.
    • Recommendations: Env vars for low-blast-radius keys, SecureString parameters for larger secrets, Secrets Manager when compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) requires rotation.

    Takeaway: Whatever you pick, lock down lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration and kms:Decrypt, since anyone with the former can read env-var secrets in plaintext.

  • Access: Discord’s Centralized Portal to Discover, Request and Manage Internal Access
    summary

    TL;DR: Access is Discord’s Apache 2.0 open-source portal where employees discover, request and manage access to internal systems, built on top of Okta groups.

    • Stack: React/TypeScript SPA with a FastAPI backend; PostgreSQL 14+ in production, SQLite for development; OIDC or Cloudflare Access for login.
    • Okta token: Needs Group Admin and Application Admin; managing groups that grant Okta admin needs Super Admin.
    • Jobs: access sync, access notify, access sync-app-groups, plus repair commands with --dry-run.
    • Expiry: Pending requests expire after one week by default (MAX_ACCESS_REQUEST_AGE_SECONDS=604800), or never.
    • Plugins: pluggy-based hooks (async) for notifications, conditional access, metrics and app-group lifecycle.
    • MCP: Optional ENABLE_MCP=true lets LLM clients browse and file requests but not approve them.
    • Limits: Okta is the source of truth and authoritative sync can push changes back; lifecycle hook delivery is not guaranteed.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted alternative to commercial access-request tools if you already run Okta; treat its Okta token as highly privileged.

  • AzurEnum: Enumerate Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) Fast
    summary

    TL;DR: AzurEnum, from SySS Research (Enrique Hernandez, Domenik Jockers), is an MIT-licensed Python tool for fast enumeration of a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) tenant’s security-relevant configuration.

    • Tenant info: User, group and app counts, Entra ID license, tenant ID.
    • Settings: Group creation, consent policy, guest access, named locations, conditional access policies and their enforcement.
    • Privilege: Admin roles, PIM assignments (including group-based), administrative units, dynamic groups, sync and MFA status of admins.
    • Secrets: Flags credentials stored in object attributes.
    • Setup: Python 3 and pipx; Linux recommended; username/password auth, tenant ID, text or JSON output.
    • Limits: Output depends on the user’s rights; Global Reader gives the most complete results.

    Takeaway: Quick first-pass audit for pentests or your own tenant review; run it as Global Reader and look first at admin MFA, guest settings and credentials in attributes.

  • CloudSecDocs: Engineering Decisions Reading List
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lancini’s CloudSecDocs “Engineering Decisions” page is a curated, annotated reading list on how teams document, design and operate software and cloud infrastructure.

    • Documentation: Design docs, RFCs, PRDs, ADRs and technical writing resources.
    • Infrastructure: Architectures, AWS/GCP implementations, Kubernetes and microservices.
    • Dev environments and CI: Deployment pipelines and cloud development environments.
    • Software engineering: Build vs buy, modularization, platform engineering pitfalls.
    • Notable links: monday.com multi-region architecture, Uber’s Crane and Superuser Gateway, Square on VPC endpoints, Lambda mTLS and secrets infrastructure, “Multicloud failover is almost always a terrible idea”, Stripe’s ledger.

    Takeaway: A good bookmark when you need prior art for a design doc or ADR, especially on privileged access and multi-region architecture.

  • Building an Interactive Shell in Golang
    summary

    TL;DR: DoltHub’s Zach Musgrave explains how to build interactive shells in Go with the abiosoft/ishell package, using Dolt’s SQL shell as the worked example.

    • Commands: Each ishell.Cmd has Name, Help and Func; start with shell.Run().
    • Free-form REPL: Needs DoltHub’s fork with ishell.UninterpretedConfig (LineTerminator: ";", QuitKeywords) and a shell.Uninterpreted handler.
    • Exit handling: EOF handler calls c.Stop() on Ctrl-D; first Ctrl-C warns, second quits.
    • History: HistoryFile in readline.Config, shell.AddHistory(), Ctrl-R search.
    • Completion: shell.CustomCompleter() suggesting SQL keywords, tables and columns.
    • Libraries: readline, fatih/color, shlex.
    • Limits: ishell is no longer actively developed (though stable); for non-interactive CLIs use cobra, gum or kingpin.

    Takeaway: Good starting point if your Go tool needs a REPL with history and completion; expect to fork or vendor ishell.

  • The Copenhagen Book: A Basic Guideline on Implementing Auth for the Web
    summary

    TL;DR: The Copenhagen Book by pilcrowOnPaper is a free, MIT-licensed, community-maintained guide to implementing authentication in web apps.

    • Chapters: Server-side tokens, sessions, password authentication, email verification, password reset, generating random values, OAuth, MFA, WebAuthn, CSRF, open redirect, plus an ECDSA cryptography section.
    • Stance: Self-described as opinionated and sometimes incomplete; recommends pairing it with the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series.
    • Status: Repository archived June 2026 and read-only; replaced by auth.pilcrowonpaper.com.
    • Popularity: About 2.1k stars on GitHub.
    • Caveat: The landing pages fetched list topics only; per-chapter specifics (hashing parameters, token sizes) were not reviewed here.

    Takeaway: Useful plain-language reference for rolling your own sessions or password reset; check the successor site for current guidance since the original is unmaintained.

  • Leveraging AWS SSO (Identity Center) with Google Workspace
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris (PrimeHarbor, May 2023) walks through using Google Workspace or Cloud Identity as the external IdP for AWS IAM Identity Center, with group sync via AWS’s ssosync.

    • Switch source: Change the Identity Center identity source to an external IdP, doing it as an IAM user to avoid lockout.
    • SAML app: Custom SAML app in Google Admin with AWS’s ACS and issuer URLs, Name ID format EMAIL; upload Google IdP metadata to AWS.
    • Provisioning: Google does not support SCIM to AWS natively, so deploy ssosync (Go, runs as Lambda from the Serverless Application Repository).
    • ssosync setup: GCP project with Admin SDK, service account JSON key, domain-wide delegation with read-only directory scopes; can sync only groups with a prefix such as “AWS”.
    • Access: Assign synced groups to accounts through permission sets.
    • Gotchas: Existing Identity Center users/groups may be deleted if they do not match Google; Cloud Identity free tier works, no Workspace license needed.

    Takeaway: Workable SSO pattern for Google shops; protect the ssosync service account key, since it can read your whole directory.

  • CloudFox: Automating Situational Awareness for Cloud Penetration Tests
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudFox is Bishop Fox’s open-source Go CLI that automates situational awareness during cloud penetration tests, finding exploitable attack paths in AWS, Azure and GCP.

    • Coverage: AWS (34 commands), Azure (4), GCP (60); Kubernetes planned.
    • AWS: cloudfox aws --profile <name> all-checks; modules like instances, secrets, permissions, iam-simulator, eks.
    • Azure/GCP: whoami, rbac, vms; GCP privesc, hidden-admins, storage-enum.
    • Design: Read-only principal, no exploitation, no compliance findings; in black-box use failed checks fail silently, so any output means you had access.
    • Install: Binary release, Homebrew or go install.
    • Limits: Use v1.17.0+ (AWS service mapping change); some checks need SecurityAudit plus a custom policy; cape needs pmapper data; GCP APIs must be enabled per project.

    Takeaway: Run it with a SecurityAudit-style role against your own accounts to see what an attacker with those creds would find first.

  • Tsunami: Google’s Extensible Network Security Scanner for High-Severity Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: Tsunami is Google’s Apache 2.0 general-purpose network security scanner with a plugin system focused on detecting high-severity vulnerabilities with high confidence.

    • Plugins: Detection logic lives in plugins; public ones are in google/tsunami-security-scanner-plugins.
    • Layout: common, main, plugin, plugin_server/py, proto, workflow directories; Gradle and Go modules plus a Python plugin server.
    • Packaging: Docker images (core, devel, full) and tsunami.yaml / tsunami_tcs.yaml configs.
    • Status: About 8.6k stars; README says it is “not an official Google product” despite the Google org.
    • Reuse: Its detectors are used by other tools, e.g. Ostorlab KEV.
    • Limits: The README itself has no run commands or requirements; see the linked build docs.

    Takeaway: Good for low-noise external checks of critical CVEs and exposed admin interfaces; pair with a broader scanner for coverage.

  • Terraform CI/CD and Testing on AWS with the New Terraform Test Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS DevOps blog (April 2024, Kevon Mayers and Welly Siauw) on testing Terraform modules with the native terraform test framework and running those tests in an AWS CodePipeline.

    • Framework: *.tftest.hcl files with run blocks that plan or apply and check assert conditions; requires Terraform CLI 1.6+.
    • Negative tests: expect_failures checks invalid inputs are rejected, e.g. a CodeCommit repo name over 100 characters.
    • Helpers: Setup modules in tests/setup create dependencies (e.g. KMS keys) whose outputs feed later runs.
    • Cleanup: Test resources are destroyed whether tests pass or fail; warnings for resources that cannot be destroyed.
    • Pipeline: CodeCommit, CodeBuild and CodePipeline running terraform init/validate/plan/apply/test.
    • Limits: Tests run sequentially; the pipeline example is tied to CodeCommit.

    Takeaway: terraform test with expect_failures on variable validation is a cheap win for shared modules; the CI pattern ports to any runner.

  • 15 Must-Attend Security Sessions at Next ‘24
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog (April 2024, Ruchika Mishra) listing 15 recommended security sessions at Google Cloud Next ‘24 in Las Vegas.

    • Scale: The Security Professionals track had more than 40 breakouts plus demos and lightning talks.
    • AI for security: Sessions on AI in SecOps; one cites early feedback that AI cuts triage time for complex cases sevenfold.
    • Securing AI: Google SAIF (Secure AI Framework) and privacy-first generative AI.
    • Network and data: Cloud NGFW, Secure Web Proxy, Cloud Armor, VPC Service Controls and Organization Restrictions for exfiltration prevention.
    • Threat management: Security Command Center Enterprise, multicloud detection, Mandiant’s 2023 cloud compromise lessons.
    • Other: IAM best practices, security foundations, Chrome Enterprise DLP, customer talks (TD, Charles Schwab, Mayo Clinic, Verizon).

    Takeaway: Mostly useful as a pointer to recorded sessions; the VPC Service Controls and Mandiant cloud compromise talks are the most practical for GCP defenders.

  • awesome-secure-defaults: Secure-by-Default Libraries to Eliminate Bug Classes
    summary

    TL;DR: awesome-secure-defaults, maintained by the tl;dr sec organization, is a curated list of secure-by-default libraries that eliminate whole bug classes instead of relying on developers to get things right.

    • Categories: Headers, SSRF, cryptography, HTML sanitization (XSS), regex, deserialization, CSRF, open redirect, path traversal, templating, SQL injection, prompt injection.
    • Examples: helmet (Express headers), google/tink (misuse-resistant crypto), DOMPurify (XSS), gorilla/csrf and nosurf (Go CSRF), google/re2 (no catastrophic backtracking), google/safearchive (path traversal and symlinks).
    • Infrastructure: Hardened OSes, distroless images, harden-runner for GitHub Actions egress filtering.
    • Format: Each entry lists language, category and activity badges.

    Takeaway: Use it to pick paved-road libraries; standardizing on one of these per bug class beats repeated code review findings.

  • libnuke: Common Go Packages for the Cloud Nuke Tools
    summary

    TL;DR: libnuke by Erik Kristensen (ekristen) is an MIT-licensed Go library holding the shared scanning, filtering and deletion framework behind his maintained fork of aws-nuke and sibling cloud-nuke tools.

    • Origin: Much code comes from rebuy-de’s aws-nuke, consolidated from ekristen’s aws-nuke and azure-nuke forks.
    • Packages: config (YAML), filter, nuke (scan and removal ordering), queue (generic retry queue), resource, settings (e.g. overriding EC2 deletion protection), plus log/errors/types/utils.
    • Consumers: aws-nuke, azure-nuke, gcp-nuke, oci-nuke, stackit-nuke.
    • Design note: Retries alone do not solve resource deletion ordering; dependency management is acknowledged as a gap in the original code.
    • Limits: “Initial Development”, 0.y.z versions, breaking API changes possible.

    Takeaway: Mostly relevant if you build your own nuke tool; for users, it signals that ekristen’s aws-nuke is the actively maintained line.

  • AWS Organization Migration Notes
    summary

    TL;DR: Gist by houey with notes from migrating a large enterprise’s AWS Organization off a legacy management account that also ran workloads, plus an updated guide covering newer AWS features.

    • Core constraint: You cannot change an organization’s management account, so build a new org and move accounts; account IDs stay, the org ID changes.
    • Plan: Inventory dependencies and export billing data; build a hardened new management account with OUs including Incoming and Suspended; deploy the security baseline.
    • Cutover: Decommission Control Tower and legacy StackSets, move accounts in waves, move the old management account last, then remove old org IDs from policies.
    • Gotchas: Discounts may revert to list price unless agreements are updated first; default account quota is 10; policies referencing the old org ID break; StackSet role ARNs change; Identity Center access is lost at transfer; delegated admins block account departure.
    • Coverage: SCPs, Resource Control Policies, Declarative Policies, centralized root access, Control Tower Landing Zone 4.0.
    • Services touched: Organizations, IAM Identity Center, CloudTrail, Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, S3, KMS, RAM, Billing, Savings Plans.

    Takeaway: Grep every resource policy for the old org ID and line up billing and delegated-admin changes before moving the first account.

  • Incident Responder Interview Questions
    summary

    TL;DR: LetsDefend blog post (Berkay Soylu, February 2024) with 27 incident responder interview questions and sample answers, plus brief interview prep tips.

    • Sections: General IR, network-related IR, event log analysis, and DFIR.
    • Topics: NIST IR lifecycle, incident vs event, IOCs vs IOAs, root cause analysis, packet analysis, C2, IDS, honeypots.
    • Logs and forensics: Windows event log analysis, log correlation, forensic timelines, triage, imaging, Windows artifacts, volatile data collection, order of volatility.
    • Examples: “What is an incident?”; “Explain the concept of ‘Order of Volatility’”.
    • Prep advice: Research the role and company; avoid sharing salary expectations early.

    Takeaway: Entry-level question bank; useful for interviewers building a baseline screen or for juniors preparing for SOC/IR roles.

  • GoAlert: Open-Source On-Call Scheduling, Escalations and Notifications
    summary

    TL;DR: GoAlert is Target’s Apache 2.0 open-source on-call platform for scheduling, automated escalations and SMS/voice notifications, shipped as a single binary.

    • Features: On-call schedules, escalation policies, SMS and voice alerts, web UI.
    • Integrations: Grafana, Prometheus Alertmanager, Site24x7, Mailgun and a generic API.
    • Demo: docker run -it --rm -p 8081:8081 goalert/demo, log in at localhost:8081 as admin/admin123; SKIP_SEED=1 skips seed data.
    • Images: Docker Hub latest for releases, nightly for master.
    • Dev: make start serves on localhost:3030.
    • Limits: README states no scale limits; production setup is in the docs folder’s getting-started guide.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted PagerDuty/Opsgenie alternative worth evaluating for cost or data-residency reasons; try the demo image first.

10.04.2024

  • Ostorlab KEV: One Command to Detect Remotely Exploitable Known Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: Ostorlab KEV is an Apache 2.0 agent group for the ostorlab scanner that runs one command to detect remotely exploitable known vulnerabilities, sourced from CISA KEV, Google Tsunami, Ostorlab Asteroid and bug bounty findings.

    • Agents: agent_group.yaml runs Nuclei, Tsunami, Nmap, Asteroid and Metasploit; add Subfinder and dnsx for subdomains.
    • Install: pip install -U ostorlab; needs Python 3.9+ and Docker.
    • Scan: ostorlab scan run --install -g agent_group.yaml ip 8.8.8.8 (also domain-name, link).
    • Results: ostorlab scan list, ostorlab vulnz list -s <scan-id>, ostorlab vulnz describe -v <vuln-id>.
    • Limits: Intrusive templates excluded; many KEV CVEs are not covered because they need local access, auth or user interaction; Interactsh checks need target egress to the callback server.

    Takeaway: Cheap way to check your external attack surface against CISA KEV; a clean result does not mean KEV-clean, since coverage is partial.

  • A Recipe for Scaling Security
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: David Dworken’s January 2024 Google Bug Hunters post on how Google rolls out security features across many existing services, using the multi-year Strict CSP rollout as the case study.

    • Focus: Retrofitting protections into existing services rather than greenfield design.
    • Ingredients: Tooling to push code changes at scale, compile-time checks, and experiment systems for safe rollout.
    • Data: Precision-focused data spanning the infrastructure, plus measuring adoption over time.
    • Developer experience: Treated as a core ingredient so teams adopt the control.
    • Related: Companion example on eliminating debug log leakage by construction, monitored with static analysis and runtime checks.
    • Source caveat: The page is JavaScript-rendered and could not be read; summary is based on search results and the tl;dr sec #216 description.

    Takeaway: The point applies beyond Google: secure-by-default frameworks plus automated migration and adoption metrics scale better than per-team reviews.

  • Azure Attack Paths
    summary

    TL;DR: Fabian Bader’s (Cloudbrothers) living reference of Azure and Entra ID attack paths, first published March 2022 and updated since, each with diagram, detection guidance and KQL/PowerShell hunting queries.

    • Partner access: Azure Lighthouse malicious delegations and abuse of delegated administrative privileges (DAP).
    • Graph and roles: API permissions such as Application.ReadWrite.All leading to Global Admin; Privileged Authentication Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator abuse.
    • Subscription takeover: Global Admin toggling “Access management for Azure resources” to gain root-scope control.
    • Compute: VM Run Command, over-privileged managed identities, DSC, Guest Configuration, Hybrid Runbook Workers.
    • Hybrid identity: Entra Connect MSOL_ account password resets and Golden SAML via stolen ADFS signing keys.
    • Tools: Az and Microsoft.Graph PowerShell, AADInternals, BloodHound, ADFSpoof.
    • Mitigations: Move to granular DAP, least privilege for identities and app permissions, monitor role changes and Run Command in Sentinel, treat Entra Connect as Tier 0.

    Takeaway: Use it as a checklist for Entra/Azure hardening and to seed Sentinel hunting queries.

  • Kubernetes Scheduling and Secure Design
    summary

    TL;DR: Doyensec (Francesco Lacerenza, Lorenzo Stella, January 2024) argues Kubernetes pod scheduling is a security control: placing critical workloads on separate nodes limits blast radius when a pod is compromised.

    • Mechanisms: nodeSelector (AND of labels), node affinity/anti-affinity, inter-pod affinity/anti-affinity, taints and tolerations, nodeName.
    • Key point: Only hard (required...) rules give security guarantees; a toleration permits placement but does not force it.
    • Attacks: Editing node labels or taints to attract sensitive pods to an attacker node; submitting pod specs that steer onto critical nodes; label combinations that block legit scheduling.
    • Mitigations: Dedicated node pools for critical namespaces, hard rules, restricted RBAC on node label/taint updates, NodeRestriction admission plugin so kubelets cannot set protected labels.
    • Trade-offs: From isolated node pools up to fully separate clusters.
    • Tools: kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins and custom schedulers.

    Takeaway: Pair taints (to keep others out) with hard node affinity (to keep critical pods in), and lock down who can patch nodes.

  • Microsoft’s Dangerous Addiction to Security Revenue
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Stamos (January 2024, LinkedIn) argues Microsoft’s Midnight Blizzard disclosure understated the breach and that Microsoft treats security as an upsell profit center, which he calls “morally indefensible”.

    • Disclosure: He reads Microsoft’s post as revealing other organizations using Microsoft cloud identity and email were also compromised.
    • Attack: A “legacy” test OAuth app with elevated access let the attacker reach corporate mailboxes via the Exchange Online full_access_as_app role; he calls the legacy label a dodge.
    • Identity complexity: Azure AD/Entra is overly complex and hybrid setups combine cloud and on-prem weaknesses.
    • Upselling: Cites paid features like Entra ID Protection and Purview Audit (Premium) being needed to detect such attacks; compares it to charging for seat belts.
    • Context: Reports of at least ten breached companies (Washington Post) and about 200 organizations targeted in the SolarWinds-linked SVR campaign.
    • Disclosure of interest: Stamos worked at SentinelOne, a Microsoft competitor.

    Takeaway: Audit OAuth apps and service principals with app-only Exchange or Graph permissions, especially in test tenants, and budget for the logging tiers you need to detect abuse.

  • Salary Negotiation in 30 Seconds
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Crittenden’s January 2024 post compresses salary negotiation into a short checklist: never name a number first, let the employer make the offer, then counter in writing.

    • Current salary: Do not disclose it. Saying you would rather not say is an acceptable answer.
    • Requirements: Do not state a target. Say it depends on other offers, or decline.
    • Offer call: Wait for their number, thank them, say you will consider it, end the call.
    • Counter: Reply by email asking 10-20% above the offer. Expect a counter, then make one final ask a few thousand higher.
    • Fixed band: Negotiate title (a higher level means a higher band) or a signing bonus, which is often more flexible and typically 5-20% of annual compensation.
    • Risk: Companies have sunk time and approvals into you, so hard negotiation rarely gets an offer pulled.
    • Further reading: Recommends the book Fearless Salary Negotiation.

    Takeaway: Keep it as a pre-call checklist: no first number, counter by email, and fall back to title or signing bonus when base is capped.

  • GPTs: Collection of Leaked GPT System Prompts
    summary

    TL;DR: linexjlin/GPTs is a GitHub collection of leaked system prompts from custom ChatGPT GPTs, one file per GPT, with roughly 32k stars.

    • Sources: Most prompts came from one linked X post, others from contributor pull requests, some extracted by the maintainer.
    • Size: The README index lists more than 200 GPTs, each with its credited author or source.
    • Layout: A prompts/ folder with one file per GPT, an index in the README, links to open-source GPT repos with actions and knowledge files, and a prompt-analysis link.
    • Languages: Entries span English, Chinese, Japanese and others.
    • License: No license is stated on the page.

    Takeaway: Useful as a corpus of real-world system prompts and as proof that GPT instructions are trivially extractable. Never put secrets or proprietary logic in a GPT or agent system prompt.

  • The Curious Case of DangerDev@protonmail.me
    summary

    TL;DR: Invictus IR walks through a month-long AWS account takeover that started with one leaked long-term access key for an admin IAM user and ended in SES phishing, GPU cryptomining attempts and lookalike domain registration.

    • Initial access: An exposed access key for an IAM user with AdministratorAccess. Early activity was only SES recon (GetSendQuota, ListIdentities) and later ListUsers.
    • Persistence: Created IAM user DangerDev@protonmail.me with CreateLoginProfile and AttachUserPolicy (AdministratorAccess), a user named ses mimicking SES SMTP users, and new access keys for existing users.
    • Backdoor roles: Two roles trusting external accounts with lookalike names (AWSLanding-Zones-ConfigRecorderRoles, AWSeservedSSO vs AWSReservedSSO), then AttachRolePolicy with AdministratorAccess and AssumeRole from the attacker’s own account.
    • Compute abuse: Opened RDP/SSH, launched a t2.micro test, then tried three p3.16xlarge instances; one hit account limits, one ran about an hour. After eviction, a short-lived LightSail instance from another identity.
    • SES and domains: CreateEmailIdentity for several domains, spam and phishing aimed at crypto exchange credentials, a sending-quota increase request, and four PayPal-lookalike domains via RegisterDomain.
    • Evasion: Deleted users, policies and keys, and read GuardDuty findings (ListFindings, GetFindings).
    • IOCs: AWS account IDs 265857590823 and 671050157472, mostly Indonesian IPs. Discovery came from an AWS Trust and Safety SES support case.
    • Gaps: Missing VPC flow logs hindered the investigation.

    Takeaway: Alert on IAM user and role creation with external trust, admin policy attachment, SES quota requests and GPU launches, and kill long-term admin access keys.

  • Scanning Git for Secrets: The 2024 Comprehensive Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Truffle Security’s guide to finding hardcoded credentials in git repositories, built around their open-source TruffleHog scanner and its per-platform commands.

    • Scale: Cites GitHub’s figure of over 1.7 million leaked secrets detected in 2022, and Truffle’s own research of about 1,800 public pushes per day leaking live keys and passwords.
    • Where secrets live: Code and config files, plus issues, PR comments and other content outside the repo tree.
    • Tool: TruffleHog detects 800+ secret types and verifies hits against provider APIs to cut false positives.
    • Git commands: trufflehog git <url>, trufflehog git file://<path>, with --only-verified, --branch and --since-commit.
    • Platform commands: trufflehog github --repo=<url> --issue-comments --pr-comments, trufflehog github --org=<name> --token=<PAT>, trufflehog gitlab --repo=<url> --token=<token> with --endpoint for self-hosted.
    • Other hosts: Bitbucket, CodeCommit, Gitea and Gerrit use the generic git mode.
    • CI: Runs in GitHub Actions, CircleCI and Travis CI to scan new commits.

    Takeaway: Run an org-wide trufflehog github --org sweep with --only-verified once, then wire --since-commit scans into CI.

  • action-tmate: Debug GitHub Actions via SSH with tmate
    summary

    TL;DR: action-tmate is a GitHub Action by mxschmitt that opens a tmate SSH or web terminal session into a running Actions runner so you can debug a workflow interactively.

    • Status: The public ssh.tmate.io servers shut down in July 2025, so default settings no longer work. Self-host a tmate server and set tmate-server-host, tmate-server-port and the fingerprint inputs.
    • Usage: Add uses: mxschmitt/action-tmate@v3 as a step, optionally gated by if: ${{ failure() }} or a workflow_dispatch input. Create a file named continue to resume the job.
    • Detached mode: detached: true prints connection info, lets later steps run and exposes ssh-command, ssh-address and web-url outputs.
    • Access control: If the triggering user has SSH keys on GitHub only those keys can connect; otherwise anybody with the connection string can. limit-access-to-actor: true enforces keys.
    • Exposure: The connection string is printed to the logs every 5 seconds, so anyone with log access sees it.
    • Other inputs: sudo: false, install-dependencies: false for self-hosted runners, msys2-location on Windows. Set step timeout-minutes to cap sessions.
    • Platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows runners.

    Takeaway: Handy for hard CI bugs, but always set limit-access-to-actor: true and a timeout, and never use it in public repos where secrets are in scope.

  • github-to-aws: Set Up GitHub Actions to Deploy to AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: github-to-aws is a small MIT-licensed CLI by Matthieu Napoli that sets up GitHub Actions OIDC deployment to AWS through a CloudFormation stack, removing long-lived access keys.

    • What it creates: An OIDC trust and an IAM role via cloudformation.yml, assumable only by workflows from the repo you name.
    • Run: npx github-to-aws --repo=your-org/your-repo, optional --profile and --region. It asks before changing anything and prints the role ARN.
    • Workflow side: Add permissions: id-token: write (and contents: read), then aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with role-to-assume and aws-region.
    • Permissions: The role gets AdministratorAccess. The author suggests forking the template to narrow it.
    • Removal: Delete the CloudFormation stack.

    Takeaway: A quick way to get keyless GitHub-to-AWS auth, but replace AdministratorAccess with a scoped policy and restrict the trust to specific branches or environments before production use.

  • Amazon EKS Introduces Upgrade Insights
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announced Amazon EKS upgrade insights on December 20, 2023: EKS automatically scans clusters for issues that could break an upgrade to a newer Kubernetes version and gives remediation advice.

    • Checks: Scans against an AWS-maintained list of upgrade-impacting issues, updated as Kubernetes and EKS change. The announcement does not list individual checks.
    • Access: Results are viewable any time in the EKS console or via the EKS APIs, evaluated against all future EKS-supported versions.
    • Remediation: Each insight comes with recommended fixes.
    • Regions: All regions except AWS GovCloud (US) and China (Beijing, Ningxia).
    • Cost: Not mentioned in the announcement.

    Takeaway: Check cluster insights (for example deprecated API usage) before every EKS version bump instead of relying only on manual tools like pluto or kubent.

  • Amazon EKS Pod Identity: A New Way for Applications on EKS to Obtain IAM Credentials
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS’s launch post for EKS Pod Identity, a simpler alternative to IRSA that maps IAM roles to Kubernetes service accounts through an EKS API instead of a per-cluster OIDC provider.

    • Trust policy: Roles trust pods.eks.amazonaws.com for sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, optionally conditioned on account or cluster.
    • Mechanism: CreatePodIdentityAssociation links role to service account. An EKS webhook injects env vars and a projected token; the eks-pod-identity-agent DaemonSet calls AssumeRoleForPodIdentity to return credentials.
    • Session tags: Credentials carry namespace, service account, cluster ARN/name and pod name/UID tags, so one ABAC policy can cover many workloads.
    • Vs IRSA: No OIDC provider or trust-policy edits per cluster, one role can serve many clusters, avoids trust-policy size limits. IRSA still needed for EKS Anywhere, ROSA and self-managed clusters; both can coexist.
    • Limits: EKS 1.24+. Associations cannot move between clusters, namespaces or service accounts; UpdatePodIdentityAssociation only changes the role.
    • Setup: eksctl v0.165.0+, add the agent add-on, then eksctl create podidentityassociation. Apps need a recent AWS SDK that supports the container credential provider.

    Takeaway: Prefer Pod Identity for new EKS workloads, and use session-tag conditions in policies to scope access per namespace.

  • Image Filesystem: Configuring Kubernetes to Store Containers on a Separate Filesystem
    summary

    TL;DR: Kevin Hannon (Red Hat) explains on the Kubernetes blog how to put the container runtime’s image and writable-layer storage on its own disk and how the kubelet’s eviction and garbage collection react.

    • Terms: imagefs is the runtime filesystem (image layers and writable layers); nodefs is usually /var/lib/kubelet (ephemeral storage, logs).
    • CRI-O: Set graphroot and runroot in /etc/containers/storage.conf. On SELinux, relabel with semanage fcontext -a -e /var/lib/containers/storage <path> and restorecon -R -v <path>.
    • containerd: Set root (default /var/lib/containerd) and state (default /run/containerd) in /etc/containerd/config.toml.
    • Kubelet: Detects the split automatically. GC removes unused images from imagefs and dead pods/containers from nodefs.
    • Eviction defaults: memory.available<100Mi, nodefs.available<10%, imagefs.available<15%, nodefs.inodesFree<5%. Setting evictionHard replaces all defaults, so list every signal.
    • Pitfalls: Ephemeral storage accounting stays on nodefs even when writable layers live on imagefs; filesystem-backed emptyDir uses nodefs.
    • Future: KEP-4191 would split the writable layer from images.

    Takeaway: When moving runtime storage to a dedicated disk, re-check imagefs eviction thresholds and remember ephemeral-storage limits are still measured on nodefs.

  • Profile Guided Optimisation (PGO) in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Andrew Phillips explains Go’s Profile Guided Optimisation: feed a production CPU profile back to the compiler so it inlines, devirtualizes and lays out hot code better.

    • Optimizations: Larger inline budget for hot functions, hot-call-site-only inlining for big functions, devirtualization of interface calls that usually hit one type, and hot-path block and function layout.
    • Workflow: Build normally, capture a pprof CPU profile under real load, save it as default.pgo in the main package directory, rebuild, and repeat as code changes.
    • Profile hygiene: Commit the profile to version control, do not profile benchmarks, and use per-OS/arch profiles for platform-specific code.
    • Robustness: Small edits keep profiles useful; big renames of hot functions invalidate them. Resolution is line-level, so dense one-liners hurt.
    • Costs: Profiling adds overhead and PGO builds are slower. A bad profile can in theory slow code down.
    • Numbers: The post gives no measured speedups; its 10% CPU figure is illustrative.
    • Advice: Do not hand-devirtualize code; let PGO do it.

    Takeaway: For CPU-bound Go services, commit a representative default.pgo and refresh it periodically; it is close to free performance.

  • Context Control in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: A Go post on using context.Context for control flow, built around a worker design that the author got wrong by storing a context and then fixed by making the call blocking.

    • Two roles: Context carries cancellation signals across API boundaries and request-scoped data.
    • Rule 1: Only entry points (main(), TestXxx()) create root contexts with context.Background(); mid-chain code derives children.
    • Rule 2: Pass the context down; use context.TODO() as a marker where the real one is not plumbed yet.
    • Rule 3: Do not store contexts or use them after the function returns, since the caller may cancel.
    • Example: A poll-and-publish-to-PubSub worker. A Start() that spawned a goroutine with the caller’s context broke rule 3; the fix made Start() block and rely on ctx.Done() instead of a custom Stop() and quit channel.
    • Design advice: Keep library work synchronous and let callers choose concurrency; use context.WithTimeout per unit of work.

    Takeaway: Replace bespoke Stop methods and quit channels with a blocking Run(ctx) and let the caller own the goroutine and cancellation.

  • Do You Know if All Your Repositories Have Up-to-Date Dependencies?
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub’s OSPO introduces Evergreen, a GitHub Action that finds repositories in an organization without Dependabot version updates configured and opens PRs to enable them.

    • Problem: Dependabot version updates need a dependabot.yml per repo, making central rollout and consistency hard.
    • Scope: Targets version updates, which are separate from Dependabot alerts and security updates for known vulnerabilities.
    • How it works: Runs on a schedule or manually, checks each repo for a Dependabot config, and opens a pull request adding one where missing.
    • Numbers: GitHub’s internal rollout found hundreds of private repos needing Dependabot enabled.
    • Details: Configuration options live in the linked github/evergreen repository.

    Takeaway: If you run many repos, schedule Evergreen org-wide to get baseline dependency update coverage without hand-editing each repo.

  • terraform-aws-atlantis: Terraform Module to Deploy Atlantis on AWS Fargate
    summary

    TL;DR: The community terraform-aws-modules module that deploys Atlantis (Terraform pull-request automation) on ECS Fargate behind an ALB.

    • Resources: ACM certificate (optional Route53 validation), ALB with listeners and security groups, ECS cluster and Fargate service, optional EFS for plan persistence, plus IAM roles and CloudWatch logs.
    • Patterns: examples/github-complete builds everything; examples/github-separate reuses an existing cluster and ALB via create_cluster = false and create_alb = false.
    • GitHub wiring: ATLANTIS_GH_USER, ATLANTIS_REPO_ALLOWLIST, and ATLANTIS_GH_TOKEN and ATLANTIS_GH_WEBHOOK_SECRET from Secrets Manager ARNs.
    • Server config: Pass atlantis.yaml via ATLANTIS_REPO_CONFIG_JSON.
    • Defaults: Image ghcr.io/runatlantis/atlantis:latest, port 4141, 2048 CPU and 4096 MiB.
    • Permissions: Examples attach AdministratorAccess to the task role.
    • Requirements: Terraform >= 1.10 and AWS provider >= 6.28 (current README).

    Takeaway: Fast path to self-hosted Atlantis; pin the image tag, scope the task role, and read the Atlantis security docs before exposing the webhook.

  • kubeconform: Fast Kubernetes Manifests Validator with Custom Resource Support
    summary

    TL;DR: kubeconform by Yann Hamon is a fast Kubernetes manifest validator inspired by kubeval, with concurrent validation, flexible schema sources and CRD support.

    • Speed: README benchmark of about 50,700 resources in 35,100 files on a 4-core laptop: about 6.7 s with -n 8 versus about 35.3 s for kubeval.
    • Schemas: Defaults to a self-updating fork of kubernetes-json-schema; -schema-location takes multiple URLs or paths, with Go-template variables like ResourceKind and ResourceAPIVersion.
    • CRDs: Add the Datree CRDs-catalog as a schema location, or convert CRDs with the bundled openapi2jsonschema script.
    • Flags: -strict, -summary, -output json|junit|tap|pretty|text, -kubernetes-version, -skip, -reject, -ignore-missing-schemas, -cache.
    • Install: brew install kubeconform, go install github.com/yannh/kubeconform/cmd/kubeconform@latest, or ghcr.io/yannh/kubeconform images for CI.
    • Limits: Schema validation only; use kubectl --dry-run=server for server-side checks.

    Takeaway: Drop-in replacement for kubeval in CI; run with -strict -summary and add the CRDs-catalog so custom resources are not silently skipped.

  • Start with the Go Standard Library
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Matthew Sanabria’s post argues that Go developers should reach for the standard library first and only add third-party dependencies when stdlib genuinely falls short.

    • Source caveat: The site returned HTTP 522 on repeated attempts and the archive was not reachable; this summary is based on the title and URL only.
    • Core point: Per the title, start new Go work with standard library packages before adopting frameworks or libraries.
    • Context: Published around Go 1.22, which added method and wildcard routing to net/http, a common reason cited for dropping external routers; not verified against this article.

    Takeaway: Before adding a dependency to a Go project, check whether a stdlib package (for example net/http, log/slog, testing) already covers the need.

  • errcheck: Check for Unchecked Errors in Go Code
    summary

    TL;DR: errcheck by Kamil Kisiel is a classic Go linter that reports returned errors that are silently ignored.

    • Scope: Flags error return values that are neither assigned nor explicitly discarded with _. Analysis of assigned-but-unused errors is left to staticcheck.
    • Install: go install github.com/kisielk/errcheck@latest (current README requires Go 1.25+).
    • Usage: errcheck ./... or a package path; errcheck all for everything in GOPATH and GOROOT.
    • Flags: -blank (also flag _ =), -asserts (unchecked type assertions), -exclude <file>, -ignoretests, -ignoregenerated, -tags, -abspath, -excludeonly.
    • Exclude file: One function per line, pkg.Func or (*pkg.Type).Method, optional first-argument type suffix such as (os.Stdout); merged with a built-in list of stdlib calls that never error.
    • Exit codes: 1 when issues are found, 2 on other failures.
    • Integrations: Emacs go-errcheck.el and vim-go :GoErrCheck; it also exposes a go/analysis analyzer.

    Takeaway: Run it in CI (it is also bundled in golangci-lint as errcheck) and consider -blank to catch lazy _ = discards.

  • secator: The Pentester’s Swiss Knife
    summary

    TL;DR: secator from FreeLabz is a Python task and workflow runner that wraps around 45 offensive security tools behind one CLI with unified inputs and output schema.

    • Tools: nmap, naabu, httpx, katana, ffuf, feroxbuster, nuclei, trivy, subfinder, gitleaks, trufflehog, wpscan and more, grouped by category.
    • Commands: secator x <tool> runs a task, secator w <workflow> a workflow (for example url_crawl), secator s <scan> a scan (for example host).
    • Install: pipx install secator, pip, an install script, Docker (freelabz/secator) or Docker Compose. Tools auto-install on first use unless security.autoinstall_commands is false; or run secator install tools.
    • Distributed: Optional Celery-based distributed execution.
    • Results: -o/-f output options, secator query to search past reports, and a MongoDB addon.
    • Extras: Shell completion for bash, zsh and fish; usable as a library. BSD-style license.

    Takeaway: Good for standardizing recon pipelines across a team; run it in a container since it installs many third-party binaries on demand.

  • (Almost) Every Infrastructure Decision I Endorse or Regret After 4 Years Running Infrastructure at a Startup
    summary

    TL;DR: Jack Lindamood (February 2024) reviews four years of infrastructure choices at a startup (apparently Cresta), grading each AWS, Kubernetes and SaaS decision as endorsed or regretted.

    • Endorsed AWS: AWS over GCP, EKS, RDS (data loss is company-ending), ElastiCache Redis, ECR over quay.io, AWS VPN with Okta, Control Tower Account Factory for Terraform.
    • Endorsed K8s stack: Karpenter, Helm v3, Flux GitOps, ExternalSecrets, ExternalDNS, cert-manager, Nginx ingress.
    • Endorsed tooling: Terraform over CloudFormation, Atlantis over Terraform Cloud, Renovate over Dependabot, PagerDuty, Notion, Linear, Slack, Go for services.
    • Caveats: GitHub Actions is good but self-hosted runners are buggy; pg-diff migrations work but schema changes stay risky; Bazel is likely overkill for Go.
    • Regrets: EKS managed add-ons (switched to Helm), AWS premium support (costs about an engineer), Datadog pricing for K8s and GPU, shared databases across apps, Google Workspace as IdP instead of Okta early, SealedSecrets, Bottlerocket, not adopting OpenTelemetry early, not using Lambda more.
    • Process: Post-mortem nudges via Slack bot, biweekly alert reviews, monthly cost meetings.

    Takeaway: A practical shortlist for small platform teams: managed data stores, Karpenter, GitOps, External Secrets, and OpenTelemetry from day one to avoid vendor lock-in.

  • How to Be IR Prepared in AWS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Cado Security’s February 2024 guide on which AWS logs to enable ahead of time so incident responders have evidence when a breach happens.

    • Source caveat: The URL now redirects to a Darktrace product page (Darktrace acquired Cado) and the archive was unreachable; this is based on the tl;dr sec 219 summary and Cado blog listings.
    • Premise: Shift from whether a breach happens to when, and prepare logging before it.
    • Services covered: CloudTrail, EC2, Amazon VPC (flow logs), Lambda, CloudFront, RDS and CloudWatch.
    • Per service: What each log records, where it is delivered, how to enable it, and how to access it.
    • Series: Companion posts cover Azure and Google Cloud.

    Takeaway: Audit your accounts now for CloudTrail (including data events where needed), VPC flow logs and service logs, since they cannot be recovered after an incident.

  • How to Be IR Prepared in Azure
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Cado Security’s February 2024 companion guide on preparing Azure logging for incident response, explaining which logs to enable and how.

    • Source caveat: The Cado blog now redirects to Darktrace after the acquisition and the archive was unreachable; this is based on Cado’s own description and related cheat-sheet pages.
    • Goal: Demystify Azure’s sometimes complicated logging methods.
    • Content: Which logs should be enabled and how to enable them, plus how to access and export them per Cado’s Azure IR cheat sheet.
    • Series: Part of a set with AWS and Google Cloud editions.

    Takeaway: Verify that Azure Activity logs, Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, and resource diagnostic logs are retained and exported before you need them.

  • Images as Code: The Pursuit of Declarative Image Builds
    summary

    TL;DR: Chainguard CTO Matt Moore (creator of distroless and Bazel rules_docker) argues for declarative Images as Code builds and explains how that led to apko and Chainguard Images.

    • Problem: Dockerfile RUN is imperative and arbitrary, which breaks reproducibility claims and complicates multi-tenant and multi-arch builds.
    • History: Bazel rules_docker offered every Dockerfile directive except RUN and produced the first generally reproducible image builds.
    • apko: Declaratively assembles an image from scratch from a list of APK packages, using a pure Go apk-tools library so it runs on any host; used with Wolfi.
    • SBOM angle: Images built with curl, tar or bash are invisible to SCA tools; distroless needed a package database added to be scannable.
    • Supply chain: cosign signing plus SBOM and SLSA attestations.
    • Ecosystem: Last-mile builders ko, jib, buildpacks; Terraform providers for ko, apko, cosign and OCI.
    • Claim: 100% of Chainguard Images are now built declaratively.

    Takeaway: Prefer declarative builders (ko, apko, jib) over RUN-heavy Dockerfiles to get reproducible, scannable images with accurate SBOMs.

  • Fargate Is Not Firecracker
    summary

    TL;DR: Former AWS EKS team member Justin Garrison argues that AWS Fargate does not run tasks in Firecracker microVMs, contrary to common belief, and relies on EC2-style virtualization.

    • Evidence: Firecracker docs only say it was built to improve services like Lambda and Fargate; Lambda historically used per-customer EC2 instances for isolation.
    • 2020 blog: AWS’s Fargate post was mostly about moving from Docker to containerd and only said Fargate can use a Firecracker runtime by swapping the containerd plugin.
    • Why not: The author attributes it more to organizational politics at AWS scale than technical difficulty.
    • Insider note: He worked on AWS containers and EKS from April 2020 to January 2024 and says staff avoided correcting the Firecracker assumption.
    • Isolation: Customer isolation is EC2 hardware virtualization; Fargate does not remove noisy neighbors or give per-container hardware isolation.
    • Ops tradeoff: Fargate shifts work elsewhere, such as EBS or GPU attachment, daemons as sidecars, and higher cost than EC2.
    • Source caveat: The architecture claim is the author’s inference, not an AWS document.

    Takeaway: Do not base threat models on Fargate being a microVM per task; treat it as managed EC2 isolation and weigh its cost and operational limits honestly.

  • The Attacker’s Guide to Azure AD Conditional Access
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Daniel Chronlund’s January 2022 post looks at Azure AD (Entra ID) Conditional Access from an attacker’s viewpoint, warning that a poorly understood policy set gives a false sense of security.

    • Source caveat: The page renders client-side and returned only the blog title; this is based on the title and secondary references found by web search.
    • Quoted theme: If you do not understand how Conditional Access works, it might bring you a false sense of security.
    • Attack surface cited secondhand: Legacy authentication that bypasses MFA when not blocked, and excluded users and apps that fall outside policies.
    • Author: Microsoft security MVP known for a Conditional Access policy design baseline and PowerShell/Graph deployment scripts on GitHub.

    Takeaway: Regularly audit Conditional Access for exclusions, unblocked legacy auth and uncovered apps or platforms, since attackers look for exactly those gaps.

  • The Two-Headed SIEM Monster
    summary

    TL;DR: Omer Singer (February 2024) argues that many enterprises now run two SIEMs, the incumbent Splunk plus a side SIEM from an XDR or cloud vendor, and that this split hurts security operations.

    • New heads: XDR vendors (CrowdStrike bought Humio for about $400M, SentinelOne bought Scalyr for under $200M) and cloud providers, notably Microsoft Sentinel with subsidized Azure and O365 ingestion.
    • Why Splunk stays: Shared use by IT and DevOps, fraud and compliance use cases, mature analytics, leadership dashboards, egress costs, long-tail integrations, SPL skills.
    • Detection risk: Attacks span email, endpoint, cloud and network, so each SIEM sees only part.
    • Content sprawl: Rules in separate repos and languages; confirming zero-day coverage is manual.
    • Ops cost: Duplicate data models and retention, swivel-chair investigations, playbooks and ML that do not port.
    • Advice: Talk to peers running multiple SIEMs and weigh savings against fidelity, rule management, data quality and automation impact.

    Takeaway: Before adopting a cheap bundled side SIEM, model the cost of split detections and investigations, not just ingestion pricing.

  • How to Enforce Creation of Roles in a Specific Path: Use IAM Role Naming in Hierarchy Models
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post showing how to use IAM role paths (for example /security/, /D1/) to separate central IT roles from developer roles and enforce guardrails by path instead of by name.

    • Protected paths: Central roles live under /iam/, /security/, /network/.
    • SCP 1: Denies iam:CreateRole, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary and other writes on those paths, exempting callers via ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalArn for /iam/. New roles in the path are covered automatically.
    • SCP 2: Denies s3:* on a sensitive bucket unless the caller ARN is under /security/.
    • Self-service: Dev teams may create roles only in their path (for example arn:aws:iam::...:role/D1/*) and only with iam:PermissionsBoundary set to an approved boundary.
    • Detection: CloudTrail Lake query and an EventBridge rule on CreateRole in /iam/ with SNS alerting.
    • Limits: A role’s path cannot be changed after creation, role names must be unique across paths, and deep hierarchies get hard to maintain.

    Takeaway: Plan a role path scheme early; path-based SCPs and boundaries scale better than name-pattern guardrails, but migrating existing roles means recreating them.

  • Hidden GitHub Commits and How to Reveal Them
    summary

    TL;DR: Neodyme shows that force-pushed commits are not deleted on GitHub and can be recovered through the public Events API, exposing secrets developers thought they had removed.

    • Problem: git reset --hard HEAD^ plus git push -f hides a commit from branch history, but GitHub keeps it and it stays reachable by SHA.
    • Method: The repo events endpoint /repos/{owner}/{repo}/events lists PushEvents including the pre-force-push SHA, which can be opened directly by URL.
    • Private to public: These events persist when a private repo is made public.
    • Short SHAs: The post notes commits can sometimes be found by brute-forcing the first four hash characters.
    • Demo: neodyme-labs/github-secrets-demo shows a commit absent from the UI but recoverable.
    • Tool: Released github-secrets to scan public repos for dangling commits.
    • Mitigation: Treat any pushed secret as compromised and rotate; full removal including caches requires GitHub Support.

    Takeaway: Force-pushing is not secret removal. Rotate the credential immediately and scan your own public repos for dangling commits.

  • github-secrets: Find Secrets in Dangling or Force-Pushed GitHub Commits
    summary

    TL;DR: Neodyme’s github-secrets is a Python 3 script that scans GitHub repositories for dangling or force-pushed commits that may contain secrets, companion to their hidden-commits blog post.

    • Requirements: Python 3 and requests; clone and run.
    • Token: Optional fine-grained PAT with no permissions, exported as GITHUB_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, to raise API rate limits.
    • Single repo: python3 github_scanner.py <user/repo>.
    • Bulk: -u <user> for all user repos, -o <org> for an organization, -t [N] for trending repos (default 100).
    • Rate limits: README includes curl commands to check remaining API quota.
    • Limits: The README does not document detection logic or output format; the method (Events API PushEvents) is described in the blog post.

    Takeaway: Run it against your own org with -o to find secrets left in force-pushed commits, then rotate anything it surfaces.

  • Security Playbook for Compromised AWS Account Credentials
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Samples incident response playbook for compromised IAM credentials, structured by NIST-style phases from preparation through post-incident review.
