    • Preparation: Open an AWS Support security case with timeline and suspected ARNs, notify the account team, verify the alternate security contact.
    • Detection: GuardDuty IAM findings (for example UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/ConsoleLoginSuccess.B, Stealth:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled), billing spikes, the IAM credential report, unfamiliar roles and trust policies, the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV2 policy, IAM Access Analyzer findings.
    • Analysis: CloudTrail Event history by event name (ConsoleLogin, AssumeRole, GetFederationToken), by resource, and by access key ID; IAM Access Advisor; Detective and Security Hub. No Athena queries are included.
    • Containment: Disable console access and deactivate keys, revoke role sessions, swap EC2 security groups to an isolation group, block IPs in bucket policies. For Identity Center, disable the user and add deny policies using identitystore:userId and aws:TokenIssueTime, or an SCP.
    • Eradication: Remove attacker resources in all regions (EC2 including stopped, AMIs, EBS snapshots, Lambda functions and layers) after backing up evidence; scan with Inspector.
    • Recovery: Restore from clean snapshots and S3 versions, rebuild from trusted sources, possibly in a new account; patch via SSM Patch Manager.

    Takeaway: Adapt it into your own runbook now, especially the Identity Center session-revocation deny policy, which is easy to get wrong under pressure.

  • AWSZeroTrustPolicy: Auto-Generate Least-Privilege Policies from User Activity
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudDefense.AI’s AWSZeroTrustPolicy is a work-in-progress FastAPI service that reads CloudTrail logs from S3 and generates least-privilege IAM policies from observed activity.

    • Input: CloudTrail logs in per-region S3 buckets, a days lookback, and AWS credentials or a role ARN with external ID.
    • Stack: Python 3.6+, FastAPI, Uvicorn and a running Redis server (apparently for caching service-action mappings).
    • Run: redis-server, then uvicorn app:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0, then POST to http://localhost:8000/run with accountType, accessKey, secretKey, roleArn, accountId, days, bucketData.
    • Output: The API returns time taken; the README does not document the policy format or storage.
    • Caveats: Marked work in progress, README contains copy-pasted Falco text, and the example sends long-lived keys in a request body to an endpoint bound on 0.0.0.0.

    Takeaway: An interesting idea but immature; IAM Access Analyzer policy generation does the same job natively and is safer to start with.

  • New EKS Access Management and Pod Identity Features: A Security Analysis
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz analyses the late-2023 EKS access entries (cloud-to-cluster) and Pod Identity (cluster-to-cloud) features, concluding they help but add new attack surface and audit blind spots.

    • Access complexity: In API_AND_CONFIG_MAP mode, effective permissions are the union of aws-auth mappings, access entries and attached access policies, so Kubernetes RBAC alone does not show who is admin.
    • Token theft: A pod with sensitive hostPath mounts or read access to /var/lib/kubelet/pods can steal another pod’s Pod Identity token and call the agent for STS credentials.
    • Default SA risk: Associating a Pod Identity with a default service account hands credentials to any pod that omits a service account.
    • Component surface: The eks-pod-identity-agent DaemonSet uses hostNetwork with open ports and a privileged init container.
    • Blind spots: Admission controllers and kube-audit logs do not see access entry creation or policy association; these appear only in CloudTrail.
    • Recommendations: Treat access-entry permissions as high privilege, avoid identities on default SAs, set automountServiceAccountToken: false, block /var/lib/kubelet mounts via admission policy, separate risky workloads by node, and correlate CloudTrail with K8s audit logs.

    Takeaway: Add CloudTrail detections for CreateAccessEntry and AssociateAccessPolicy, and enforce admission rules against kubelet hostPath mounts before rolling out Pod Identity.

  • Engineering a SIEM Part 1: Why Did We Need to Build Our Own SIEM?
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of Rippling’s series explains why its security team built an in-house SIEM on a security data lakehouse after evaluating Panther and Sumo Logic.

    • Vendor gap: A multi-week Panther PoC showed they would still need many custom integrations and detections for Rippling’s in-house tools.
    • Cost problem: License-driven SIEMs push teams to drop log sources, creating blind spots and slower investigations.
    • Scale targets: 2-3 TB of logs per day, detection latency under 10 minutes, retention well beyond the typical 30-180 days.
    • Engineering targets: Everything as code with CI/CD, SQL instead of a proprietary language, semi-structured JSON queries without reindexing, RBAC and tamper-resistant logs.
    • Operations: Onboard any new log source in 3 days, spend about 3-5 hours per week on ops, alert on pipeline failures.
    • Reuse: Leverage the data engineering team’s existing lakehouse instead of re-ingesting product data.
    • Architecture: Deferred to part 2.

    Takeaway: A useful requirements checklist for anyone weighing build vs buy for a SIEM; the decisive factors were custom log sources and volume-based cost.

  • AI Monitoring Employees for ‘Thought Crimes’ in Apps Like Slack and Zoom
    summary

    TL;DR: 9to5Mac reports on Aware, an AI vendor whose models analyze employee messages in Slack, Teams and Zoom for sentiment and policy violations, and on the privacy concerns it raises.

    • What it does: Analyzes text and images for sentiment, and flags bullying, harassment, discrimination, noncompliance, pornography and nudity.
    • Modes: Aggregate sentiment reporting that Aware says is anonymous, plus a tool that can flag individual posters.
    • Customers: Reported users include Chevron, Delta, Starbucks, T-Mobile and Walmart.
    • Scale: Aware claims more than 20 billion interactions analyzed across over three million employees.
    • Critics: Jutta Williams (Humane Intelligence) calls it thought crime; Amba Kak (AI Now Institute) warns of a chilling effect and notes FTC, DOJ and EEOC concerns.
    • Privacy risk: Aggregated data can be de-anonymized when sliced by age, location, division or tenure.

    Takeaway: Assume workplace chat is monitored and analyzed; security teams deploying such tools should scope them tightly and involve legal and privacy review.

  • SiCat: The Useful Exploit Finder
    summary

    TL;DR: SiCat by justakazh is a Python exploit finder that searches multiple public exploit and vulnerability sources by keyword or from Nmap results.

    • Sources: Exploit-DB, NVD, CVE.org, GitHub PoCs, Nuclei templates, Wordfence CVE templates, Metasploit modules and Nmap NSE scripts.
    • Input: -k <keyword>, -nmap <target> for a live scan, -nmap-file <file> for existing Nmap XML, -web <url> for Wappalyzer tech detection.
    • Source selection: -edb, -nvd, -cve, -nuclei, -wcve, -gh, -msf, -nse; -l caps results per module (default 25).
    • Output: -o <file> -ot text|json, or -r for a sortable HTML report; --web-interface starts a GUI on port 5000.
    • Install: install.sh or install.bat, Docker build, or pip install .. A GitHub token in ~/.sicat/config.json avoids rate limits.

    Takeaway: Handy for quickly mapping Nmap service versions to known public exploits during authorized assessments.

  • Offensive Lab Environments (Without the Suck)
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Travis Kaun (TrustedSec, February 2024) describes building disposable Active Directory lab environments quickly and cheaply for testing payloads and simulating attacks.

    • Source caveat: The fetch tool refused the page; this is based on web search snippets and TrustedSec’s top-blogs listing.
    • Hardware: A small workstation costing about $300.
    • Stack: Hyper-V on Windows 11 with the AutomatedLab tool handling deployment.
    • Goal: Dynamic, repeatable AD labs that can be rebuilt instead of hand-maintained.
    • Reception: Ranked sixth in TrustedSec’s most-read blogs of 2024; also given as a talk at Wild West Hackin’ Fest Deadwood 2024.

    Takeaway: If your test lab is a fragile hand-built VM set, AutomatedLab on Hyper-V is a low-cost way to make AD environments reproducible.

  • AI for Security: Eight Areas of Opportunity
    summary

    TL;DR: Menlo Ventures (Venky Ganesan, Rama Sekhar, Sam Borja, February 2024) lists eight security areas where they see generative AI creating startup opportunities, with example companies.

    • Vendor risk and compliance: Auto-filling security questionnaires (Dialect).
    • Security training: Dynamic, threat-realistic training (Immersive Labs, Riot), citing the MGM and Caesars breaches.
    • Pentesting: AI-assisted scanning, exploitation and reporting (Run Sybil, BugBase Pentest Copilot).
    • Anomaly detection: Telemetry-monitoring agents (Abnormal Security), with false positives still high.
    • Synthetic content: Detecting AI-generated identities (Deduce, DeepTrust); 76% of companies believe they extended credit to synthetic customers.
    • Code review: Making SAST shift-left practical (Semgrep, Mobb).
    • Dependencies: Supply chain risk (Socket, 70+ risk signals); 96% of codebases contain open source per Synopsys.
    • SOAR: Autonomous alert triage and investigation (Dropzone AI).

    Takeaway: A VC market map rather than technical guidance; useful for scanning which AI security product categories exist.

  • LLM Agents Can Autonomously Hack Websites
    summary

    TL;DR: Paper by Richard Fang, Rohan Bindu, Akul Gupta, Qiusi Zhan and Daniel Kang (UIUC, February 2024) showing GPT-4-based agents can autonomously exploit website vulnerabilities without prior knowledge of the bug.

    • Capability: Agents performed blind database schema extraction and SQL injection with no human feedback.
    • Models: GPT-4 succeeded; the abstract states existing open-source models were not capable.
    • No prior knowledge: The agent did not need to be told the vulnerability in advance.
    • Real world: GPT-4 found vulnerabilities in live websites in the wild.
    • Method: Agents with tool use (browser/API access, documents, planning), per the paper.
    • Source caveat: Success rates and cost figures are in the full paper, not the abstract page read here.

    Takeaway: Autonomous exploitation of common web bugs by frontier LLMs is real; basic input-validation flaws will be found faster and cheaper than before.

  • Detecting Manual AWS Actions: An Update!
    summary

    TL;DR: Arkadiy Tetelman updates his 2019 ClickOps detection: instead of matching console user agents, alert on any mutating CloudTrail event from a human session identified by an email-based role session name.

    • Invariant: Humans reach AWS only via Okta and AssumeRoleWithSAML, no IAM users; Okta sets the role session name to the employee email.
    • Trigger: Alert when session name ends in the company domain, readOnly is false, and the event is not on a filter list. Covers console and CLI.
    • Bypass detection: Alert on AssumeRole where an email session name is swapped for something else (role chaining or self-assumption).
    • Why changed: The 2019 user-agent approach was misguided; readOnly replaces List/Get/Describe prefix matching.
    • Filter list: Hardcoded events mislabeled as mutating or too noisy (for example glue:StartJobRun); some like signin:ConsoleLogin and sts:AssumeRole deserve their own alerts.
    • Caveats: readOnly is sometimes wrong, the list is environment-specific, older roles may still allow self-assumption, and the invariant needs company-wide workflow buy-in.

    Takeaway: If you federate through an IdP, enforce email session names and alert on human write actions to keep production IaC-only.

  • Detecting AWS Canaries Without Detonating Them
    summary

    TL;DR: Truffle Security shows that AWS canary tokens (such as Thinkst Canarytokens) can be identified offline from the access key ID alone, without calling AWS and triggering the alert.

    • Old method: GetCallerIdentity reveals the account but fires the canary and logs to CloudTrail.
    • Offline decode: Building on Tal Be’ery’s research, strip the key prefix, base32-decode and bitmask to recover the AWS account ID, then compare against known canary accounts.
    • Dataset: Sampled about 500 canaries from public GitHub, found roughly six unique accounts; example code lists seven account IDs.
    • TruffleHog: Canary detection is now built in, so scans flag canaries without verifying them; check a file with trufflehog filesystem <file>.
    • Limits: Older Thinkst accounts and Thinkst paid offerings may not be covered; new accounts appear over time.

    Takeaway: Attackers can skip free canary keys, so defenders should not rely on public canary services alone; self-hosted canaries in your own accounts are harder to fingerprint.

  • Terracognita: Reverse Terraform, Generate IaC from Existing Cloud Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Terracognita by Cycloid is an MIT-licensed reverse-Terraform tool that reads existing cloud resources and generates Terraform HCL and state.

    • Providers: AWS (provider v4.9.0), AzureRM (v3.20.0), Google (v4.9.0) and vSphere (v2.2.0); built against Terraform v1.1.9.
    • Usage: terracognita aws --hcl out.tf --tfstate out.tfstate, then terraform init and terraform plan to verify.
    • Filtering: --include and --exclude by resource type (for example aws_instance).
    • Modules: --module <path> generates a module, --module-variables picks attributes to expose as variables; the target path is overwritten after confirmation.
    • Install: Release binaries, brew install terracognita, AUR, make install (Go 1.17+), or the cycloid/terracognita Docker image.
    • Status: About 2.4k stars and 84 open issues; pinned, aging provider versions suggest limited recent maintenance.

    Takeaway: Useful for a one-off import of ClickOps infrastructure, but expect to clean up output; for current providers consider Terraform 1.5+ import blocks with -generate-config-out.

  • Best Practices for Managing Terraform State Files in AWS CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS DevOps Blog walkthrough of storing Terraform state in S3 with DynamoDB locking and running plan and apply from CodeBuild, using a sample Lambda deployment.

    • Why remote: Local state is hard to share, stores secrets in plain text, and can be lost or corrupted.
    • Backend: S3 bucket with versioning, server-side encryption (AES256 or SSE-KMS) and restrictive IAM or bucket policies.
    • Locking: DynamoDB table with a LockID primary key.
    • Layout: One bucket per account, prefixes per environment and project.
    • Pipeline: CodeCommit repo, two CodeBuild projects (plan and apply) with buildspecs, Lambda as the sample app.
    • Sample names: Bucket tfbackend-bucket, key terraform.tfstate, region eu-central-1, lock table tfstate-lock.
    • Steps: Clone the aws-samples repo, terraform init/plan/apply the bootstrap, set backend.tf, run the CodeBuild projects, verify state and lock, terraform destroy to clean up.

    Takeaway: Standard baseline; note that Terraform 1.10+ supports native S3 locking (use_lockfile), which can replace the DynamoDB table.

  • How to Automate Rule Management for AWS Network Firewall
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post presenting anfw-automate, a solution where spoke accounts define their own AWS Network Firewall rules in S3 config files and a central account validates and applies them.

    • Spoke side: S3 bucket with one config file per region; S3 events and VPC deletion events from CloudTrail go via EventBridge to the central account.
    • Central side: EventBridge custom bus triggers a RuleCollect Lambda that validates config and converts it to Suricata rules, an SQS FIFO queue (with DLQ), then a RuleExecute Lambda that updates the firewall policy, rule groups and IP sets.
    • Validation: VPC must exist, S3 object version must be latest, no TLD-only rules, no any destinations, pass rules only, CIDRs mapped to IP set variables.
    • Reserved keywords: sid, priority and metadata are reserved for admins and the solution.
    • Deployment: CDK bootstrapping of resource, central and delegated admin accounts; CodePipeline deploys LambdaStack, ServerlessStack and a StackSet to spokes.
    • Limits: One config file per region per account, back-off for ThrottlingException, firewall needed in every region and AZ used by spokes, VPCs must attach to Transit Gateway.
    • Claim: Rule updates go from minutes to seconds.

    Takeaway: A reference design for self-service egress allowlisting in a centralized inspection VPC; the validation rules are worth copying even if you build your own.

  • Wrangle Your Alerts with Open-Source Falco and the gcpaudit Plugin
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog (February 2024) introducing Falco’s gcpaudit plugin, which turns GCP audit logs into Falco events so you can write Falco rules for cloud control-plane threats.

    • Pipeline: A Cloud Logging sink sends critical audit events to a Pub/Sub topic; the plugin subscribes, filters and enriches them for Falco rules.
    • Services covered: Compute Engine, KMS, Cloud Armor, IAM, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Pub/Sub, Cloud Logging and Cloud Functions.
    • Rules: Built around MITRE ATT&CK, for example alerting on VM deletion or database backup removal.
    • Outputs: stdout, syslog, HTTP(S), gRPC by default; FalcoSidekick adds 60+ destinations including SIEMs like Chronicle.
    • Deployment: Run one plugin instance per environment, on a VM or as a GKE pod, not per node. Falco cannot run on GKE Autopilot.
    • Setup: Detailed steps in the falcosecurity/plugins gcpaudit/walkthrough.md.

    Takeaway: If you already run Falco, gcpaudit gives cheap GCP audit-log detections in the same rule language without a full SIEM.

  • podinfo: Go Microservice Template for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: podinfo by Stefan Prodan is a tiny Go web app that demonstrates Kubernetes microservice best practices and is used by Flux and Flagger for end-to-end tests and workshops.

    • Runtime features: Readiness and liveness probes, graceful shutdown, file watching for secrets and configmaps, structured logging with zap, viper config.
    • Observability: Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing.
    • Testing aids: Fault injection (random errors and latency), delay, status, echo, panic endpoints over HTTP and gRPC, plus JWT, Redis cache and WebSocket endpoints.
    • Security: SPIFFE mTLS with X.509 SVIDs, cosign-signed multi-arch images with SBOM and SLSA provenance, govulncheck scanning.
    • Install: Helm (GitHub Pages or OCI on ghcr.io), kubectl apply -k Kustomize, Timoni OCI module, or docker run.

    Takeaway: The go-to dummy workload for testing GitOps, service mesh, autoscaling or progressive delivery setups, and a clean reference for a production-ready Go service.

  • Go Enums Suck
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A zarl.dev post arguing that Go lacks real enums, since iota constants are just integers, and proposing a generated, type-safe pattern that later became the goenums code generator.

    • Source caveat: The page is JavaScript-rendered and returned no text; this is based on search snippets, aggregator pages and the goenums project.
    • Problem: iota-based constants are plain integers underneath, with no exhaustiveness, validation or rich behavior.
    • First proposal: JSON marshalling plus a container struct to make values behave like enums in other languages, driven by a config file.
    • Follow-up: In Go Enums Still Suck, after Hacker News and Lobsters feedback (for example that stringer covers part of this), the author replaced the config with go/ast parsing and extra properties in comments.
    • Tool: goenums generates type-safe enum implementations from simple constant declarations; docs at zarldev.github.io/goenums.

    Takeaway: If you want stronger enums in Go, try stringer for basics or goenums for validation, parsing and JSON support generated from constants.

31.01.2024

  • errtrace: An Alternative to Stack Traces for Your Go Errors
    summary

    TL;DR: errtrace from bracesdev is an experimental Go library, inspired by Zig, that records an error’s return trace (the path back up through callers) instead of a creation-time stack trace.

    • Concept: The trace is built incrementally at each return, so it works across goroutines and channels where stack traces mislead.
    • API: Call errtrace.Wrap(err) at each return site; print with errtrace.FormatString(err) or %+v.
    • Auto-instrumentation: errtrace -w ./... rewrites source, usable as an editor formatter; experimental go build -toolexec=errtrace. Opt out with //errtrace:skip.
    • Caveats: Wrapping breaks == comparisons and direct type assertions; use errors.Is and errors.As.
    • Performance: About 14.7 ns/op with 0 allocs for Wrap (198.5 ns/op with the safe tag) vs about 103.5 ns/op for fmt.Errorf; about 188 ns vs 717 ns for pkg/errors at 10 frames.
    • Platform: Uses assembly on amd64 and arm64; other architectures fall back to safe mode.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to get actionable error paths in Go services; try it via the rewriting tool on one package before committing project-wide.

  • Gorse: Open-Source Recommender System Engine
    summary

    TL;DR: Gorse is an Apache-2.0 open-source recommender system engine in Go that trains on users, items and feedback and serves recommendations over REST.

    • Sources: Latest items, user-to-user and item-to-item similarity, collaborative filtering.
    • Multimodal: Text, image and video via embeddings; supports reranker and decision APIs.
    • Architecture: Master node (training, non-personalized recs, config, membership), worker nodes (offline per-user recs), server nodes (REST API, real-time recs).
    • Storage: MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB or Postgres for data; Redis, MySQL, MongoDB or Postgres for cache.
    • Ops: GUI dashboard on the master for pipeline editing, monitoring and import/export.
    • Quick start: docker run -p 8088:8088 zhenghaoz/gorse-in-one --playground loads a GitHub-repos demo at localhost:8088.

    Takeaway: A self-hostable alternative to building recommendations from scratch or buying a SaaS; the playground image is a quick way to evaluate it.

  • 2023 Global DevSecOps Report Series
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: GitLab’s 2023 Global DevSecOps Report series surveyed developers, security and operations staff on security practices and AI adoption; the landing page now shows a newer edition.

    • Source caveat: The URL now hosts the 2026 report, so 2023 figures come from GitLab press releases and coverage found via web search.
    • April 2023 (Security Without Sacrifices): More than 5,000 respondents surveyed in March 2023; 71% of security pros said developers catch a quarter or more of vulnerabilities, up from 53% in 2022.
    • AI in testing: 62% of developers used AI/ML to check code (51% in 2022) and 53% used bots in testing (39% in 2022).
    • September 2023 (State of AI): Over 1,000 respondents in June 2023; 83% said AI adoption is essential, 79% worried about AI tools accessing private data or IP.
    • Security and AI: 40% cited security as an AI benefit; 40% of security pros feared AI code generation would add to their workload; 81% wanted more AI training.

    Takeaway: Useful benchmark numbers for shift-left and AI adoption discussions; pull the full PDFs for methodology before quoting them.

  • re:Invent 2023 Recap
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris’s opinionated security-focused recap of AWS re:Invent 2023, covering what he finds useful, risky or overhyped.

    • Security Hub: Central configuration and customizable controls fix multi-account pain; worries that cyber insurers may adopt AWS-defined best practices blindly.
    • GuardDuty and Inspector: ECS on Fargate runtime monitoring matters since sidecars are hard there; agentless Inspector EC2 scanning will surface old non-SSM instances.
    • IAM Access Analyzer: New paid unused-access findings at $0.20 per role or user per month, worth it if it works; custom policy checks too.
    • Identity and data: EKS Pod Identity is a significant new credential path teams will adopt without understanding; S3 Access Grants changes data access models; ALB mTLS welcomed.
    • Governance: AWS Config still lacks good delegated admin and cross-region management; dislikes Control Tower for small companies; interested in Data Exports, CloudTrail Lake and CloudWatch Logs Infrequent Access.
    • GenAI: Calls Amazon Q an omnipotent practical joker, suggests blocking Q and possibly Bedrock IAM prefixes via SCP, cites OWASP Excessive Agency for Bedrock Agents.
    • Snark: Console-to-Code hallucinated CloudFormation types.

    Takeaway: Prioritize Security Hub central config, Access Analyzer unused access and a Pod Identity review, and decide on an SCP stance for Amazon Q and Bedrock.

  • Bolstering Security and Automating Management of Target Australia’s EKS Clusters
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Gazal Gafoor (GitHub @gazal-k) describes how Target Australia runs its Amazon EKS clusters, with Bottlerocket nodes for security and Karpenter in place of Cluster Autoscaler for node management.

    • Node OS: Bottlerocket, the container-focused AWS OS, chosen for its security benefits.
    • Autoscaling: A move from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter, described as more cost-effective and flexible.
    • Adoption: Karpenter’s ADOPTERS.md lists Target Australia using Karpenter to scale and auto-update the EKS compute behind much of the Target Online platform.
    • Scope: An operator’s experience report on running EKS at scale, not a vendor tutorial.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403. This summary uses the Learn Kubernetes Weekly issue 53 blurb and the Karpenter adopters list, not the article body.

    Takeaway: Bottlerocket plus Karpenter is a common EKS baseline for a smaller node attack surface and automated node updates. Read the original for Target’s exact configuration.

  • Deep Dive into the New Amazon EKS Pod Identity Feature
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper (Datadog Security Labs) reverse-engineers EKS Pod Identity, the November 2023 alternative to IRSA for giving pods AWS credentials, and looks at its security implications.

    • Mechanism: Associations map a service account to an IAM role via aws eks create-pod-identity-association. An admission webhook injects container credential provider env vars into pods.
    • Agent: The eks-pod-identity-agent DaemonSet in kube-system runs with host networking and CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, listening on 169.254.170.23:80.
    • Research method: Agent binary pulled with crane and analysed with Ghidra and redress, since it was initially closed source. AWS open-sourced it in mid-2024 and the findings held.
    • Risk: If the worker node role has eks-auth:AssumeRoleForPodIdentity, an attacker on the node can request credentials for any pod’s role.
    • Auditability: Listing associations (list-pod-identity-associations) is simpler than parsing IRSA trust policies. Datadog’s MKAT tool was extended to map these relationships.
    • Update (June 2025): Cross-account access via targetRoleArn with role chaining, which needs specific trust relationships.

    Takeaway: Treat node compromise as compromise of every pod role on that node, and use association listing to audit pod-to-role mappings. IRSA is not going away, so expect to audit both.

  • IceKube: Finding Complex Attack Paths in Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: IceKube is a WithSecure Labs tool that finds attack paths in a Kubernetes cluster, from a low-privileged starting point to targets such as cluster-admin, using a Neo4j graph.

    • Model: Cluster resources go into Neo4j and are explored with Cypher. Attack-path relationships carry attack_path = 1 so queries can filter for them.
    • Commands: enumerate (collect resources), attack-path (build attack relationships), run (both), purge, plus download and load for offline analysis.
    • Setup: Start Neo4j with docker-compose or Docker, install via Poetry or pip, and point kubectl at the cluster with a cluster-admin account.
    • Data handling: Needs read access to secrets. It strips secret data on ingest but keeps types and annotations. Events and componentstatuses are skipped by default.
    • Usage tip: Disable ‘Connect result nodes’ in the Neo4j browser to avoid rendering every relationship.
    • Source caveat: The labs.withsecure.com page now redirects to a generic WithSecure hub. This summary is based on the WithSecureLabs/IceKube GitHub README.

    Takeaway: Useful for RBAC reviews and pentests where privilege chains span service accounts, pods and secrets. Run it from a trusted host, since it needs near-admin read access.

  • Security Architect and Principal Security Engineer Interview Questions
    summary

    TL;DR: Tad Whitaker’s GitHub list of Glassdoor-sourced interview questions for senior IC security roles, Security Architect and Principal Security Engineer. It is a companion to his 2016 Security Engineer list.

    • Motivation: The earlier list did not separate career levels. This one targets the top of the non-manager ladder (L6).
    • Source: Questions pasted from Glassdoor into one Markdown file. No total count is stated.
    • Mix: About 7.8 Security Architect questions for every Principal Security Engineer question.
    • Companies: Includes Netflix, Morgan Stanley, 7-Eleven, Airbus, Alcoa and Wiz. Small startups are absent, likely because they lack these roles.
    • Categories: Technical, Behavioral/Influential, and Frameworks/Design/Threat Modeling.
    • Finding: The author saw no clear difference between the two roles’ question sets.

    Takeaway: A practical prep list for senior security interviews, weighted towards architecture and threat-modeling discussion. Pair it with real design exercises, since the questions are lightly curated.

  • Awesome Roadmaps
    summary

    TL;DR: Awesome Roadmaps (liuchong) is a curated GitHub list of learning roadmaps, mostly for software development, with about 7.4k stars.

    • Categories: Programming Language, Web, Mobile, Infrastructure/Operations, Game Development, AI/ML/Data Science, Security, Miscellaneous, Tools & Resources, Articles & Books.
    • Anchor entry: The interactive Developer Roadmap project.
    • Language and web: C++, Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Angular, React, Vue and Frontend roadmaps.
    • Ops: DevOps Roadmap and Platform Engineering Roadmap.
    • AI: Microsoft AI for Beginners, Hugging Face Agents Course, LLM Course, and Anthropic’s ‘Building Effective Agents’ article.
    • Contributing: Pull requests or issues.

    Takeaway: A starting index for building a study plan in an unfamiliar area. Check each linked roadmap for freshness before you follow it.

  • Nord Stream: Extract Secrets from CI/CD Environments by Deploying Malicious Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: Nord Stream, from Synacktiv, extracts secrets from CI/CD platforms by deploying malicious pipelines. It supports Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab.

    • Azure DevOps: Dumps variable groups, secure files and service connections (AzureRM, GitHub, AWS, SonarQube, SSH). It lists orgs from a token and can generate self-hosted runner YAML for SSH connections.
    • GitHub: Extracts repo, environment and org secrets. It can list and disable branch protections (admin needed), obtain Azure or AWS OIDC credentials via workflows, and GPG-sign commits to satisfy signature rules.
    • GitLab: Lists and extracts CI/CD variables and secure files. Listing needs admin, but a low-privilege user with write access can exfiltrate via a pipeline.
    • Flags: --token, --org, --repo, --project, --env, --yaml, --build-yaml, --list-secrets, --list-protections, --describe-token, --no-clean, --clean-logs, --force, --output-dir.
    • Opsec: It cleans pipeline traces by default (--no-clean keeps them). GitLab activity-tab pipeline logs cannot be deleted.
    • Install: pipx from the Git repo. Requires git in PATH.

    Takeaway: Anyone with push rights to a pipeline can read its secrets. Scope tokens tightly, use environment protections and OIDC, and alert on unexpected pipeline runs and branch-protection changes.

  • CI/CD Secrets Extraction: Tips and Tricks
    summary

    TL;DR: Hugo Vincent and Théo Louis-Tisserand (Synacktiv, March 2023) explain how a red team pulled CI/CD secrets from Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions and GitLab, then pivoted into Azure and GitHub. This is the write-up behind the Nord Stream tool.

    • Cleartext leaks: Repo history checked for committed secrets with TruffleHog and Gitleaks.
    • Azure DevOps: Pipelines print variable-group secrets, secure files and service-connection credentials (ARM, GitHub). Output is encoded to dodge log masking.
    • GitHub: Workflows dump repo and environment secrets and request OIDC tokens from federated trusts.
    • GitLab: Admins read CI/CD variables via API. Lower-privileged users run pipelines that print env vars.
    • Bypasses: GitHub environment rules (reviewers, branch policies), branch protections and GitLab protected branches can be changed or removed by admin tokens. Developer push to a protected branch can expose protected secrets.
    • Defences: Rotate any leaked secret, stream audit and deployment logs to a SIEM, enforce signed commits, apply least privilege, scan continuously, and prefer short-lived OIDC.

    Takeaway: CI/CD masking is not a security boundary. Assume anyone who can edit a pipeline can read every secret it gets, and design permissions around that.

  • Avoid Accidental Exposure of Authenticated Amazon API Gateway Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Mark Wolfe (November 2023) shows how API Gateway APIs meant to use IAM auth can expose resources publicly, and how to layer defences with AWS SAM.

    • Misconfiguration: The API uses AWS_IAM, but no default authorizer is set. Any resource that omits an auth method is public.
    • Fix 1: Set a default authorizer (DefaultAuthorizer: AWS_IAM) so unconfigured resources are protected.
    • Fix 2: Set auth on every resource, for example with the x-amazon-apigateway-auth OpenAPI extension.
    • Fix 3: Attach a resource policy that requires IAM and limits callers to listed accounts (ResourcePolicy with AwsAccountWhitelist).
    • Verification: With the default authorizer, an unauthenticated call returns ‘Missing Authentication Token’. With only the resource policy, the call is denied for lacking execute-api:Invoke.

    Takeaway: Do not rely on per-route auth alone. Set a default authorizer and a resource policy so one forgotten route does not become public.

  • terraform-null-label: The Why and How It Should Be Used
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Gowie (Masterpoint, October 2023) explains Cloud Posse’s terraform-null-label module, which generates consistent resource names and tags so naming conventions do not depend on people reading docs.

    • Inputs: namespace (2-4 letter org code), tenant, environment (region shorthand such as uw2), stage (dev/stage/prod), name (component, such as rds) and attributes (extra descriptors).
    • Outputs: id for resource names and tags for tagging any resource or module.
    • Chaining: A second label inherits through the first module’s context output and overrides only what differs, for example private vs public load balancers.
    • Customisation: Delimiter and label order are configurable.
    • context.tf: Simplifies passing context through root and child modules and workspaces. Advanced use is deferred to a follow-up post.
    • Caveats: ‘stage’ naming is legacy, and ’environment’ means region, the inverse of common usage. Examples are simplified.

    Takeaway: Use null-label (or context.tf) early in a Terraform codebase to get uniform names and tags. Agree on what environment and stage mean before you roll it out.

  • Kubernetes Security Fundamentals: API Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 2 of Rory McCune’s Kubernetes security fundamentals series (Datadog Security Labs, December 2023). It maps which ports and endpoints each Kubernetes component exposes, and what needs authentication, on kubeadm and managed clusters.

    • etcd: 2379/2380 need client certs. 2381 serves metrics on localhost with no auth or TLS.
    • kube-apiserver: 6443 on all interfaces. /version and /healthz are allowed unauthenticated.
    • Control plane: Controller manager (10257) and scheduler (10259) bind to localhost and need auth except for health checks.
    • Node: Kubelet 10250 needs credentials except at root. kube-proxy has unauthenticated metrics on 10249 and health on 10256.
    • Managed services: EKS/AKS/GKE API endpoints may be internet-exposed by default. AKS requires auth for all apiserver access. GKE exposes the read-only kubelet port 10255. AKS and EKS expose kube-proxy metrics on all interfaces.
    • Recommendations: Restrict the API server with IP allowlists, private endpoints or firewalls. Keep etcd, scheduler and controller manager local or firewalled, and encrypt in transit.

    Takeaway: A handy port reference for firewall rules and exposure reviews. Check whether your managed cluster’s API endpoint is public by default.

  • Zonal Autoshift: Automatically Shift Traffic Away from Availability Zones with Potential Issues
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS (Sébastien Stormacq, November 2023) launched zonal autoshift in Route 53 Application Recovery Controller. AWS shifts your load balancer traffic away from an Availability Zone when its internal monitoring detects a problem, then shifts it back.

    • Trigger: AWS-initiated only. There is no API to start an autoshift.
    • Practice runs: A weekly 30-minute rehearsal on enabled resources. You can block UTC windows, and two CloudWatch alarms act as circuit breakers (one blocks start, one aborts on health).
    • Supported: ALBs and NLBs with cross-zone load balancing disabled.
    • Requirements: Enable per resource and keep spare capacity in the remaining AZs. Pre-scaling is advised, since Auto Scaling may react slowly.
    • Limits: One AZ at a time. You cannot trigger it for testing, but a manual zonal shift behaves the same.
    • Cost: No extra charge, in all Regions except China and GovCloud.

    Takeaway: Cheap AZ-failure resilience if you already run static stability with spare capacity. Wire up the practice-run alarms before you enable it.

  • Moving Away from CDK
    summary

    TL;DR: SST (January 2024) explains why it is dropping AWS CDK and CloudFormation for Ion. Ion defines components with Terraform providers and deploys them through an embedded Pulumi engine, and it will become SST v3.

    • Core complaint: CDK only generates CloudFormation, and ‘CloudFormation is a black box that does not run locally’.
    • Listed problems: Cyclical dependencies when linking resources, ‘Export in use’ errors, swallowed errors, custom-resource workarounds, rollback failures, double builds, orphan stacks, hard imports and slow deploys.
    • Limits: CloudFormation caps a stack at 500 resources, and one Next.js site creates about 68.
    • State: Ion stores deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user’s account.
    • Roadmap: SST v2 gets updates but no new constructs, and Ion becomes v3 once stable.

    Takeaway: A concrete list of CloudFormation pain points to weigh when choosing IaC. If you have hit the same issues, Terraform or Pulumi-based tooling avoids them.

  • Three New Capabilities for Amazon Inspector Broaden Vulnerability Scanning for Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS (Sébastien Stormacq, November 2023) added three Amazon Inspector capabilities: build-time container scanning, agentless EC2 scanning, and generative-AI code fixes for Lambda.

    • CI/CD scanning: Jenkins and TeamCity plugins, an API and a CLI generate an SBOM, send it to Inspector and return near-real-time results to gate builds. You do not need to enable Inspector.
    • Agentless EC2 (preview): Snapshots EBS volumes, scans them, then deletes the snapshots. Hybrid mode combines this with SSM-agent scanning. Preview in us-east-1, us-west-2 and eu-west-1.
    • Lambda code remediation: Generative AI plus automated reasoning flags injection, data leaks, weak crypto and missing encryption, and suggests patches inline. Available in 10 Regions at no extra cost.
    • Pricing: On demand, per EC2 instance or per image scan. The build-time API is in 21 Regions.

    Takeaway: Agentless mode covers EC2 instances without SSM, and the CI plugin moves image scanning before deployment. Review AI-suggested patches like any other PR.

  • How to Improve Cross-Account Access for SaaS Applications Accessing Customer Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: Ashwin Phadke (AWS Security Blog, November 2023) gives SaaS providers patterns for accessing customer AWS accounts without long-term access keys and without confused-deputy risk.

    • Anti-pattern: Asking customers for IAM user access keys, which need manual rotation.
    • Technique 1: A customer-created cross-account role whose trust policy requires a unique sts:ExternalId that the provider passes in every AssumeRole call.
    • Technique 2: Least-privilege roles per product component, reached through one integration role via role chaining (A to B to C) with optional session policies. Chained sessions are capped at 1 hour.
    • Technique 3: ABAC with role tags as trust-policy conditions, and transitive session tags for better CloudTrail attribution.
    • Recommendations: Generate unique external IDs, scope roles narrowly, ship integration guides, and plan for hourly session refresh.

    Takeaway: If you build or buy SaaS that touches AWS accounts, require role assumption with a per-customer external ID and refuse long-lived keys.

  • Optimize AWS Administration with IAM Paths
    summary

    TL;DR: David Rowe and Valentine Reid (AWS Security Blog, November 2023) show how IAM paths group roles and policies by team or function, so you can scope permissions and guardrails with wildcard ARNs.

    • Concept: A path is a prefix such as /developer/ in arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/developer/S3Access. The default is /, and paths can nest.
    • Reserved: Service-linked roles live in /aws-service-role/.
    • Scoping: Grant management over role/teamA/* only. Deny principals outside a path with aws:PrincipalArn plus ArnNotLike.
    • Other keys: iam:PolicyARN limits which managed policies can be attached, and iam:PassRole limits which roles can be passed.
    • Guardrails: SCPs can block changes to roles and policies in sensitive paths such as /security/.
    • Limit: Role names must be unique in an account regardless of path.

    Takeaway: Paths let you delegate IAM administration per team without listing every role ARN. Plan them early, because the path is part of the ARN that policies match on.

  • Use IAM Roles Anywhere to Improve Security in On-Premises Container Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: Ulrich Hinze and Alex Paramonov (AWS Security Blog, November 2023) walk through replacing static IAM user keys in on-premises containers with temporary credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere and X.509 certificates.

    • Role: bucket-lister, trusted only by rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com for certificates with CN myContainer, granting s3:ListAllMyBuckets.
    • Trust anchor: myPrivateCA, created from the CA certificate to trust the on-prem PKI.
    • Profile: bucket-lister, linked to the role ARN.
    • Flow: The container signs a CreateSession request with its private key and gets temporary credentials. The demo then runs aws s3 ls.
    • Cert checks: OpenSSL is used to verify the CA and end-entity certificates meet Roles Anywhere requirements.
    • Caveat: The demo CA is a 3-year OpenSSL CA, called ’not suitable’ for production. Use existing PKI or AWS Private CA with short-lived, auto-rotated certs.

    Takeaway: For workloads outside AWS, Roles Anywhere removes long-lived keys if you already run PKI. Certificate issuance, rotation and revocation become the real security control.

  • go-recipes: Tools for Go Projects
    summary

    TL;DR: go-recipes by Nikolay Dubina is an MIT-licensed catalogue (about 4.8k stars) of commands and tools for Go projects. Each entry is a short recipe with the command to run.

    • Testing: Coverage browsing and treemaps (go-cover-treemap, gocov-html, gocovsh), PR coverage comments, shuffled, parallel and fuzz tests, and goroutine-leak checks (goleak).
    • Test output: tparse, gotestsum (slowest tests, reruns, JUnit), richgo, gotestdox.
    • Mutation testing: ooze and several go-mutesting forks.
    • Dependencies: Upgrade checks, module Go versions, go-libyear, graphs with modgraphviz, import-graph and goda, and licence scraping with go-licenses.
    • Other areas: Repo topics also list benchmarking, code generation, code visualisation, compilers, profiling and static analysis.
    • Source caveat: This summary is based on the README section headings and repo topics, not a full read.

    Takeaway: Bookmark it as a lookup table when you need a Go tool for coverage, flaky tests or dependency audits.

  • Sign in with GitHub in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Eli Bendersky (December 2023) implements ‘Sign in with GitHub’ in Go using GitHub’s OAuth web application flow, for authentication only.

    • Flow: Redirect to GitHub, receive a temporary code on the callback, exchange it with client ID and secret for a token, then call the user API. No extra scopes are requested.
    • Three variants: Standard library only, golang.org/x/oauth2, and the gologin middleware package (StateHandler, CallbackHandler).
    • CSRF: A random state cookie that expires after 1 hour.
    • Routes: / (login link), /login/ (redirect) and /github/callback/ (validate state, exchange code, fetch user).
    • Caveats: No real session layer. Credentials come from env vars, error handling uses panic and log.Fatal, and the gologin debug cookie config is for non-TLS dev only.

    Takeaway: A clear reference for the OAuth code-exchange mechanics. Add proper sessions, error handling and secure cookies before you use it in production.

  • aws-summarize-account-activity: Summarize Recently Active IAM Principals, API Calls and Regions from CloudTrail
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-summarize-account-activity (welldone-cloud) is a Python script that reads an AWS account’s CloudTrail event history and summarises active IAM principals, their API calls, regions, source IPs and user agents.

    • Output: A JSON file of summaries by principal, region, error code, IP and user agent. Optional PNG charts with --plot-results.
    • Flags: --activity-type (ALL, SUCCESSFUL or FAILED), --past-hours (default 336, max 2160 = 90 days), --dump-raw-cloudtrail-data (JSONL), --profile.
    • Permissions: Only ec2:DescribeRegions and cloudtrail:LookupEvents.
    • No setup: Uses the default 90-day event history via LookupEvents, so no trail is required.
    • Limits: LookupEvents is throttled to 2 requests/second, so large accounts are slow. Management events only, and not every service logs to CloudTrail.
    • Requirements: Python 3.10+.

    Takeaway: A quick first look in incident response or account inheritance to see who is active and from where. For bigger windows or data events, use Athena over a trail.

  • Considerations for Keeping Images Up to Date
    summary

    TL;DR: A Chainguard Academy guide on balancing security patches against stability when you update container images. Chainguard rebuilds its images daily.

    • Versioning: Explains semver (X.Y.Z) and image references ([host]/[repository][image_name][:tag]).
    • Tags: Mutable. ’latest’ is only a convention, and pinning to a major or minor tag can bring unexpected version jumps.
    • Digests: Immutable content hashes that guarantee reproducibility but are hard to read.
    • Automation tools: Watchtower, FluxCD, Argo CD Image Updater, Renovate, Dependabot and Chainguard’s Digestabot GitHub Action.
    • Recommendation: Pin by digest and keep digests current with automated PRs. Chainguard requires human approval before deploy.
    • Caveat: Fully automate only as far as your test suite and risk appetite allow. ‘There is no one-size-fits-all approach’.

    Takeaway: Digest pinning plus a bot that opens update PRs (Digestabot or Renovate) gives you reproducibility and fresh patches. Gate merges on tests.

  • AWS Security Services Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS-maintained, open-source guide (aws/aws-security-services-best-practices on GitHub) on deploying and running AWS security services well. It is explicitly not a general AWS security best-practices guide.

    • Services: GuardDuty, Security Hub (including CSPM), Inspector, Macie, Detective, Security Lake, WAF, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, certificate services, and more.
    • Structure: Per-service guides that go from pre-deployment considerations through post-enablement to full operationalisation. Some have subpages, for example WAF managed rules, custom rules, bot control and logging.
    • Approach: Use-case and design-factor driven, not a numbered checklist.
    • Extras: A network security fundamentals section, and links to sibling guides for EKS, ELB, observability and networking.
    • Languages: English, Korean and Japanese. Outside contributions are welcome.

    Takeaway: Read the relevant section before you enable a service org-wide. It covers the delegated-admin, multi-account and tuning decisions that console defaults skip.

  • Migrate from Service Account Keys in Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud IAM documentation on moving an organisation off service account keys in three phases: Assess, Plan and Deploy.

    • Assess: Use service account usage insights to find keys, recent key use and accounts unused for 90 days. A reference architecture exports this to a BigQuery table, sa_key_usage. Role recommendations flag excess permissions.
    • Plan: Define scope, find quick wins (keys on inactive resources), choose enforcement points, design an exceptions process and talk to workload owners.
    • Enforce: The iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation org policy, with tag-based exemptions. It does not affect existing keys.
    • Alternatives: Workload Identity Federation for GKE, attached service accounts, user credentials for dev, service account impersonation, and Workload Identity Federation for on-prem or other clouds.
    • Rollout: Disable keys before deleting them so you can roll back. A key exposure response constraint can auto-disable leaked keys.
    • Exceptions: Some third-party products still need an uploaded key.

    Takeaway: Block new key creation first, then work through existing keys by usage data. Federation and attached identities cover most cases.

  • Atuin: Shell History in SQLite with Context and Sync
    summary

    TL;DR: Atuin replaces shell history with a SQLite database that records context for each command, and can sync history across machines with end-to-end encryption.

    • Context stored: Exit code, working directory, hostname, session and duration.
    • UI: Rebinds ctrl-r and up-arrow to a full-screen search. Filter modes cover session, directory or global. Alt- jumps to an entry, Enter runs and Tab edits.
    • Sync: Optional and fully encrypted, so the server cannot read history. Use the hosted server, self-host, or run offline.
    • Shells: zsh, bash, fish, nushell, xonsh, PowerShell.
    • Setup: Run the installer from setup.atuin.sh, then atuin register -u <USERNAME> -e <EMAIL>, atuin import auto, atuin sync.
    • Extras: Stats such as most-used commands. Your old history file is left in place.
    • Caveat: Bash support depends on bash-preexec, which has limitations.

    Takeaway: A big upgrade for anyone who works across several hosts. Self-host the sync server, or keep it offline if shell history might hold secrets.

  • Flowpipe: Cloud Scripting Engine for Workflows as Code
    summary

    TL;DR: Flowpipe, from Turbot, is an AGPL-3.0 ‘cloud scripting engine’ for workflows as code. Pipelines are written in HCL and connect cloud APIs, people and systems.

    • Pipelines: Ordered HCL steps that make HTTP calls, request human input, send messages, run queries or call other pipelines.
    • Triggers: Webhook, query or schedule.
    • Mods: Library mods for AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub, Jira, Okta, PagerDuty, Slack, Teams and others, plus sample mods on the Flowpipe hub.
    • Ecosystem: Works with Steampipe (data access) and Powerpipe (dashboards). Turbot Pipes is the hosted team offering.
    • Install: Homebrew on macOS, or a shell script on Linux and WSL. Build from source with make.
    • Commands: flowpipe pipeline list --mod-location <path>, flowpipe pipeline run --mod-location <path> <pipeline>.

    Takeaway: An option for version-controlled cloud remediation and ChatOps-style approvals if you already use Steampipe. Note the AGPL licence before embedding it.

  • Setting Secure Defaults on AWS and Avoiding Misconfigurations
    summary

    TL;DR: Scott Piper (Wiz, December 2023) lists account-level AWS settings and SCPs that set secure defaults, block risky features and stop those guardrails from being undone.

    • S3: Block Public Access (aws s3control put-public-access-block) plus Bucket owner enforced (put-bucket-ownership-controls) to disable ACLs, each locked with an SCP.
    • Sharing: EC2 AMI block public access (deny ec2:DisableImageBlockPublicAccess), SSM public document sharing disabled per region (aws ssm update-service-setting), and RAM sharing to external principals denied.
    • Lambda: An SCP requires AWS_IAM auth on function URLs.
    • IAM: An SCP denies creating IAM users, access keys and login profiles. Use roles instead.
    • EC2: Require IMDSv2 via MetadataHttpTokens and limit hop count. Run aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default in every region (existing volumes are not affected).
    • Network and admin: Block IGW, peering and Global Accelerator changes in workload accounts, and pin an admin role to a source IP.
    • Caveat: Review CloudTrail and Access Advisor first, since restrictions can break workloads. EC2 APIs still default to allowing IMDSv1.

    Takeaway: A ready-made checklist for a new AWS Organization baseline. Apply the settings, then lock each one with an SCP.

  • How to Use Dockerfiles with wolfi-base Images
    summary

    TL;DR: Adrian Mouat (Chainguard, September 2023) shows how to keep normal Dockerfile workflows while building on Wolfi and Chainguard images.

    • static image: For statically compiled binaries in multi-stage builds. A Distroless replacement.
    • glibc-dynamic: For software that needs common shared libraries. JDK and JRE images cover Java.
    • wolfi-base: Includes apk and a shell, for when you need specific packages or versions.
    • Examples: Tailscale golink pins a Go compiler on wolfi-base with a shell-less final image. A Python build pins 3.11 with apk’s ~ syntax. A network debug image is about 50 MB.
    • Caveat: Wolfi is rolling and ships only ’latest’. Final images built on wolfi-base keep a shell and package manager.

    Takeaway: Build in wolfi-base and copy artefacts into a minimal Chainguard runtime image to keep the attack surface small. Pin package versions, because Wolfi rolls forward.

  • vscode-terraform-live-graph: Live Terraform Graph in VS Code as You Code
    summary

    TL;DR: An MIT-licensed VS Code extension by adamiBs that renders a live Terraform resource graph beside your editor as you type.

    • Requirements: Terraform CLI on PATH, Graphviz, and VS Code 1.75.1 or later.
    • Usage: Open a .tf file and run ‘Terraform Graph View’ from the Command Palette. The graph appears on the right and updates on edit.
    • Under the hood: Relies on Terraform’s graph output rendered through Graphviz.
    • Limits: Files must be valid Terraform. The README does not document behaviour on large configs.

    Takeaway: Handy for seeing dependencies while you write modules. Do not expect it to stay readable on big root modules.

  • aws2tf: Import Existing AWS Resources into Terraform and Generate HCL
    summary

    TL;DR: aws2tf (aws-samples) is a Python tool that imports existing AWS resources into Terraform state and writes matching HCL, aiming for a clean terraform plan afterwards.

    • Behaviour: Replaces hardcoded values with references, follows and imports dependencies, swaps account and region literals for data sources, then runs terraform plan to confirm there are no changes.
    • Coverage: About 1,600 resource types (the README cites 1,582 and 1,612 in different places).
    • Flags: -t (types), -i (ID), -m (merge), -s (stack), -f (experimental multithreading), -tv (provider version), plus data-source switches -dnet, -dsgs, -dkms, -dkey, -ec2tag.
    • Requirements: macOS or Linux, Python 3.12+, boto3, AWS CLI v2, Terraform 1.12+ and jq. Use the v5 branch for provider 5.x.
    • Limits: Whole-account scans are ‘Not recommended’ (slow). State is local only, and test coverage is 25%.

    Takeaway: Useful for bringing click-ops resources under Terraform. Import by type or ID, review the generated code, then move state to a remote backend.

  • The Uber Go Style Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Uber’s Go Style Guide (Apache-2.0, about 17.8k stars) documents the Go conventions used at Uber, in one style.md, with 17 community translations.

    • Guidelines: Verify interface compliance at compile time, copy slices and maps at boundaries, keep channel size one or none, start enums at one, and use time for time.
    • Safety rules: Handle type-assertion failures, don’t panic, avoid mutable globals and init(), exit only in main, and don’t fire-and-forget goroutines.
    • Errors: A dedicated section on error types, wrapping and naming.
    • Performance: Prefer strconv over fmt, avoid repeated string-to-byte conversions, and preallocate container capacity.
    • Style: Import grouping, reduced nesting, no unnecessary else, _ prefix for unexported globals, and no naked parameters.
    • Patterns: Table-driven tests and functional options.
    • Linting: Recommends lint runners. The repo ships a .golangci.yml.

    Takeaway: A sensible default Go style for a team. Adopt it wholesale and enforce it with golangci-lint instead of writing your own.

  • Kamal: Deploy Web Apps Anywhere
    summary

    TL;DR: Kamal, from Basecamp (MIT), deploys containerised web apps to bare-metal or cloud VMs over SSH, with zero-downtime switching. It started with Rails but works with any app packaged in Docker.

    • Execution: Runs commands on hosts over SSH via SSHKit. Works across one or many servers.
    • Routing: kamal-proxy moves traffic between old and new containers to give zero-downtime deploys.
    • Scope: Any Docker-packaged web app.
    • Docs: Install, config and command reference are at kamal-deploy.org, not in the README.
    • Source caveat: The README is brief. Details beyond the above come from the linked docs site, which was not read.

    Takeaway: A simpler option than Kubernetes for running a few apps on your own servers. Lock down the SSH access it relies on.

  • AWS Account Security Onboarding Mind Map
    summary

    TL;DR: Artem Marusov (LinkedIn, January 2024) shares a mind map that works as a checklist for the minimum security setup when you add a new account to an existing AWS Organization.

    • Approach: AWS-first, with no commercial or open-source third-party tools.
    • Exclusions: Leaves out some services, including Control Tower, which he says AWS Organizations already covers.
    • Formats: Editable XMind file, plus PNG and PDF exports.
    • Related reading: Scott Piper’s AWS Security Maturity Roadmap, the AWS Security Maturity Model, and zoph.me’s AWS Security Survival Kit (CloudTrail alerts).
    • Automation: A commenter notes Prowler 3.13 can automate the checks.
    • Source caveat: The mind map image’s branches were not readable from the page text. This summary covers the article framing only.

    Takeaway: Use it as an onboarding checklist for new accounts, and automate the checks with Prowler or SCPs instead of re-doing them by hand.

  • SSH-Snake: Self-Propagating Script for SSH Private Key and Host Discovery
    summary

    TL;DR: SSH-Snake, by Joshua Rogers (GPL-3.0, now archived), is a self-propagating Bash script that finds SSH private keys and reachable hosts, then recursively uses them to map a network’s SSH trust paths.

    • Loop: Find keys, derive user@host targets, try SSH, and repeat on each new host. The traversal is depth-first and skips hosts already visited.
    • Discovery sources: .bash_history, common key paths, known_hosts, SSH config, last-login records and IP ranges. Strategies can be toggled, except find_ssh_keys.
    • Fileless: Passed to remote bash via stdin over SSH, so nothing is written to disk. Snake.nocomments.sh stays under the size at which bash writes a temp file.
    • Analysis: Python tools for forward and reverse lookup and shortest path between hosts. Graphs via Cytoscape, Gephi or Graphviz.
    • Detection: The README notes the process tree and the many failed SSH attempts as evidence.
    • Limits: IPv4 only, port 22 assumed, GNU coreutils needed, and no SSH agent socket support.

    Takeaway: It shows how far one unprotected private key can reach. Alert on SSH fan-out and failed-auth bursts, and replace static keys with SSH certificates or passphrase-protected keys.

  • EvilSlackbot: Slack Bot Phishing Framework for Red Teaming Exercises
    summary

    TL;DR: EvilSlackbot (Drew-Sec) is a Python 3 framework for authorised red-team and phishing simulations inside Slack workspaces, driven by a stolen or issued bot or user token.

    • Tokens: Needs an xoxb or xoxp token. Run -c to check which attacks that token’s permissions allow.
    • Attacks: -sP spoofed messages with custom bot name and icon, -m phishing links as the bot, -a with -f for file attachments.
    • Recon: -s keyword-searches Slack for leaked secrets (xoxp only). -cL lists public channels.
    • Targeting: -e single email, -eL email list file, -cH channel name. -o writes output to a file.
    • Requirements: Python 3 and slackclient.
    • Limits: Secret search does not work with bot tokens, channel listing is public channels only, and OAuth scopes are not documented.

    Takeaway: Leaked Slack tokens allow convincing internal phishing. Restrict app installs, rotate tokens and train users that bots can be spoofed.

  • Kubernetes Deep Health Checks
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Boyle (Encore, January 2024) explains how readiness probes that check downstream dependencies (‘deep health checks’) can turn one failing service into a full outage.

    • Scenario: A payments backend’s readiness endpoint checks auth, balance, Kafka and the DB, and returns 500 if any fails. When auth goes down, every dependent pod leaves the load balancer at once.
    • Symptom: Users see ‘upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection failure’, and pod metrics go quiet, which slows diagnosis.
    • Probe roles: Liveness restarts stuck containers, readiness removes pods from load balancing, and startup holds off the other probes for slow starters.
    • Principle: A service is ready if it can serve a response, even an error.
    • Instead: Retry with exponential backoff, count failures, return 5xx, and alert on SLOs. Reduce coupling with caching, circuit breakers and stateless design.

    Takeaway: Keep readiness probes local to the pod. Handle dependency failures in the app and in alerting, not by pulling every replica out of service.

  • vulnerable-code-snippets: Intentionally Vulnerable Code Snippets for Review Practice
    summary

    TL;DR: YesWeHack’s collection of intentionally vulnerable code snippets for code-review practice. They first appeared as weekly Friday posts on its Twitter account.

    • Languages: PHP, Python, Go, Java, JavaScript and C, plus supporting SQL, HTML and CSS.
    • Vuln classes: 22 classes mapped to CWEs, including SQLi, XSS, SSRF, insecure deserialisation and buffer overflow.
    • Count: The README table lists 43 snippets, each with a short flaw description.
    • Running: Each snippet folder has a docker-compose.yml. Start with docker compose up --build in an isolated environment.
    • Audience: All skill levels.

    Takeaway: Good bite-sized drills for secure code review training or interview prep. Run them only in isolated containers.

  • better-commits: CLI for Better Conventional Commits
    summary

    TL;DR: better-commits (Everduin94) is a Node CLI that prompts you through writing Conventional Commits messages, previews them, then runs native git commit.

    • Install: npm install -g better-commits (Node 20+).
    • Config: A global .better-commits.jsonc in your home directory is created on first run. better-commits-init creates a per-repo config.
    • Inference: Ticket, type and scope are inferred from the branch name.
    • Branches: better-branch creates a branch or worktree from the same naming segments (user, version, type, ticket, scope, description).
    • Hooks: Pre- and post- shell commands such as branch_pre_commands and worktree_post_commands, with templates like {{TICKET}}.
    • Scripting: --no-interactive and --dry-run for agents and automation. Also interactive git status/add and per-type emoji.

    Takeaway: A low-friction way to standardise commit and branch naming in a team that uses Conventional Commits for changelogs or semantic-release.

  • How to Introduce Semgrep to Your Organization
    summary

    TL;DR: Maciej Domański (Trail of Bits, January 2024) gives a seven-step plan for rolling out Semgrep static analysis in an organisation.

    • 1-2 Fit and explore: Check language support (30+), then run semgrep --config auto on a small project.
    • 3 Rulesets: p/default, p/owasp-top-ten, p/cwe-top-25 and language packs. Start high-confidence with --severity ERROR.
    • 4 Tune: Add non-security rules, suppress with justified nosemgrep comments, and use .semgrepignore.
    • 5 Custom rules: An internal rules repo with README, inventory, contribution checklist and peer review. Metadata (CWE, confidence, impact) and fix: autofixes. Trail of Bits rules are available as p/trailofbits.
    • 6 Evangelise: Train developers with Learn Semgrep and the Playground, and open discussion channels.
    • 7 CI/CD: Pilot one repo, run scheduled full scans on main and diff-aware scans on PRs, then block PRs on findings.
    • Privacy: --config auto sends metrics. Disable with --metrics=off or SEMGREP_SEND_METRICS.

    Takeaway: Introduce SAST gradually, starting with low noise and blocking only once trusted. The custom-rules repo is where most of the long-term value comes from.

  • aws-scps-for-sandbox-and-training-accounts: Example SCPs for Sandbox and Training Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: welldone-cloud’s example Service Control Policies for AWS sandbox and training accounts. They block baseline changes, long-term financial commitments and use outside allow-listed regions and services.

    • Account baseline: scp-deny-changing-account-baseline-configuration.json covers contacts, billing and tax settings.
    • Money: scp-deny-making-agreements-purchases-and-reservations.json blocks agreements, purchases and reservations.
    • Central IAM: scp-deny-modifying-central-iam-resources.json.
    • Allow-lists: scp-deny-using-other-regions.json and scp-deny-using-other-services.json.
    • Cleanup: The author suggests aws-nuke to reset accounts to a known-good state.
    • Caveat: A ‘starting point’ that needs adapting. File behaviour here is inferred from file names and README text, and no deployment steps are given.

    Takeaway: Attach these to a sandbox OU so learners cannot buy reservations or wander into unused regions. Pair them with scheduled aws-nuke runs.

  • The Final Answer: AWS Account IDs Are Secrets
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Grzelak (Plerion, January 2024) argues that AWS account IDs should be kept confidential for practical reasons. AWS’s official position is that they are not sensitive.

    • AWS stance: Cites AWS’s Steven Armstrong (‘Account IDs are not considered sensitive’), AWS docs and Eric Brandwine.
    • Why IDs matter: Most AWS attacks need a target identifier (role ARN, queue URL), so an unknown account ID acts as an unintended control.
    • Attacks cited: Unauthenticated principal enumeration (for example, confirming workspaces_DefaultRole exists), ECR-based lateral movement and ACM-PCA privilege escalation.
    • Number: Plerion data shows about 55% of AWS accounts have an unexempted publicly exposed resource, rarely exploited partly because the IDs are unknown.
    • Advice: Pass IDs via environment variables rather than hardcoding them, publish artefacts from dedicated accounts, and avoid default principal and resource names.
    • Context: A vendor opinion piece. A February 2024 follow-up covers how IDs leak, and Truffle Security showed IDs can be decoded from access key IDs.

    Takeaway: Do not build security on hiding account IDs, but don’t publish them carelessly either. Fix the public resources that a known ID would let an attacker find.

  • A Recipe for Scaling Security
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: David Dworken (Google Bug Hunters blog, 22 January 2024) describes how Google scales security across a large product portfolio by building protections into the platform rather than fixing bugs one by one.

    • Case study: The rollout of Strict Content Security Policy (CSP) across Google web apps, which began around 2016.
    • Approach: ‘Safe coding’ and secure-by-default frameworks, so whole bug classes such as XSS are prevented centrally.
    • Blueprint: The post promises a recipe other companies can adopt.
    • Related talks: A July 2024 keynote, ‘A Recipe for Scaling (Web) Security: Lessons from Google’s Frontlines’, covers safe coding and legacy code. A ‘Security Signals’ talk covers tracking CSP adoption at scale.
    • Source caveat: The page is JS-rendered and its body could not be read. This summary is based on search snippets and related talk abstracts, so specific steps and numbers are not included.

    Takeaway: Invest in secure-by-default frameworks and policies such as Strict CSP, and measure their adoption, rather than relying on bug-by-bug remediation.

  • Azure Attack Paths
    summary

    TL;DR: Fabian Bader (Cloudbrothers, March 2022, updated February 2025) catalogues Azure and Entra ID attack paths to Global Admin or subscription control, with detection queries and mitigations.

    • Delegation abuse: Malicious Azure Lighthouse offers, and over-broad partner delegated admin rights (GDAP was introduced to limit these).
    • App permissions: App registrations with high-risk Graph permissions such as Application.ReadWrite.All can lead to Global Admin.
    • Entra roles: Privileged Authentication Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator can reach Global Admin. ‘Access management for Azure resources’ grants User Access Administrator at root scope.
    • Compute paths: VM Run Command, managed identities, DSC, Guest Configuration, and hybrid runbook workers with Run As certificates.
    • Hybrid identity: Password reset via the Entra Connect sync account, and Golden SAML via ADFS.
    • Tooling: AADInternals, BloodHound, PowerShell snippets, and KQL hunting queries for Sentinel and Log Analytics.
    • Mitigations: Prune partner and API permissions, scope managed identities, monitor role changes and Run Command, and ’treat your Entra ID connect server as you would a domain controller’.

    Takeaway: A good checklist for Entra and Azure privilege reviews. Start by auditing Graph app permissions and the Connect server, the paths most often missed.

  • Mastering Kubernetes Security: Safeguarding Your Container Kingdom
    summary

    TL;DR: Madhav Nakar (detection engineer, January 2024) gives security analysts an overview of the Kubernetes security model and threat landscape. It is organised around the 4Cs: Code, Container, Cluster, Cloud.

    • Components: API server, etcd, kubelet and kubectl. Managed clusters lack direct host telemetry.
    • Threats: Vulnerable apps, malicious or typosquatted images, secrets in image layers, permissive RBAC, risky security contexts, exposed kubelet API, metadata credential theft, anonymous API access, and exposed etcd or Dashboard.
    • RBAC: Restrict service account permissions, disable automatic token mounting and standardise RBAC objects.
    • Admission: Review pod creation requests and use static tools such as kubesec.
    • Network: NetworkPolicies to limit pod-to-pod traffic.
    • Detection gap: Kubelet activity is not in Kubernetes audit logs, so extra telemetry is needed. Treat admin activity inside short-lived containers as suspicious.
    • Source caveat: The Red Canary URL now redirects to a Zscaler blog copy with the same topic. This summary is based on that page.

    Takeaway: A solid primer for SOC staff new to Kubernetes. Note the kubelet audit gap and add runtime or EDR telemetry on nodes.

  • Kubernetes Scheduling and Secure Design
    summary

    TL;DR: Francesco Lacerenza and Lorenzo Stella (Doyensec, January 2024) argue that Kubernetes scheduling is an overlooked security control. Isolating critical workloads on separate nodes limits lateral movement from a compromised pod.

    • Mechanisms: nodeSelector (AND of labels), nodeName (hard pin), node affinity and anti-affinity, inter-pod affinity, taints and tolerations, topology spread and custom schedulers.
    • Key rule: Only hard (required...) rules give security guarantees. Soft (preferred...) rules are for performance only.
    • Attacks: Editing node labels or taints to attract sensitive pods, users setting scheduling fields to land on critical nodes, label combinations that block scheduling, and a compromised kubelet relabelling its own node.
    • Defences: Enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin and restrict who can modify node metadata. Review user-controlled scheduling fields.
    • Design: Group workloads by trust, data sensitivity, exposure and privilege. Use dedicated node pools for critical namespaces, or separate clusters for the most sensitive.

    Takeaway: Put sensitive workloads on dedicated, tainted node pools with required affinity, and lock down node label and taint edits. Otherwise a pod escape anywhere reaches everything.

  • Memos: Privacy-First, Lightweight Note-Taking Service
    summary

    TL;DR: Memos is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted, privacy-first note-taking app that keeps short notes on a personal timeline.

    • Features: Markdown with LaTeX, checklists, attachments, links between memos, pinning, reactions and comments, and calendar, map, tag and search views.
    • Sharing: Per-memo visibility. New memos are private by default.
    • APIs: REST and gRPC, plus a Web Clipper.
    • Self-host: docker run -d --name memos -p 5230:5230 -v ~/.memos/:/var/opt/memos neosmemo/memos:stable. Compose, native binary, Kubernetes and source builds are also offered.
    • Storage: SQLite by default, with MySQL and PostgreSQL supported.
    • Privacy: The site states it sends no usage data or analytics.

    Takeaway: A lightweight self-hosted alternative to cloud note apps. Put it behind auth and TLS and back up the data volume.

03.01.2023

  • Fourteen Years of Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Russ Cox’s Go team post for Go’s 14th open source birthday (10 November 2023), reviewing the year’s Go 1.20 and 1.21 releases and what came next.

    • PGO: Profile-guided optimization, previewed in 1.20 and released in 1.21, typically gives 2% to 7% CPU improvement.
    • Coverage: Go 1.20 added coverage profiles for binaries built with go build, so integration tests can collect coverage.
    • Compatibility: Go 1.21 expanded GODEBUG conventions and added built-in toolchain management per module.
    • Tooling: On-disk indexes in gopls cut startup latency and memory 3-5x; update with go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest.
    • Std library: New generic cmp, maps, slices packages, structured logging in log/slog, and WASI preview 1 support.
    • Security: Govulncheck 1.0 shipped in July 2023, with VS Code and GitHub Action integration; 1.21 toolchain builds are reproducible.
    • Next: Go 1.22 changes for loop variable semantics to remove accidental aliasing bugs.

    Takeaway: A compact changelog of the Go 1.20/1.21 era. Use it to check whether you have adopted PGO, slog and govulncheck yet.

  • inshellisense: IDE-Style Command Line Autocomplete
    summary

    TL;DR: inshellisense is Microsoft’s terminal-native runtime that gives IDE-style autocomplete in the shell, using the Fig autocomplete specs for 600+ CLI tools.

    • Platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS; shells include bash, zsh, fish, pwsh, powershell, xonsh and nushell.
    • Install: npm install -g @microsoft/inshellisense or Homebrew tap, then is init; check with is doctor.
    • Usage: is starts a session, exit stops it, is -c checks if you are inside one.
    • Shell plugin: is init zsh >> ~/.zshrc (and equivalents) starts it with every shell; it must be the last line in the config.
    • Keys: Suggestions are accepted with tab; keybindings are configurable and only captured when suggestions are visible.
    • Status: Repo is active (about 10.7k stars, pushed October 2026).

    Takeaway: A quick way to get Fig-style completion back without Fig. Try it if you want discoverable flags for unfamiliar CLIs.

  • arsenal: Quick Inventory and Launcher for Hacking Programs
    summary

    TL;DR: Arsenal, from Orange Cyberdefense, is a Python inventory and launcher for pentest commands: search a cheatsheet, pick a command, and it is prefilled in your terminal.

    • Mechanism: Emulates real user input via TTY/IOCTL, so it works with any shell and commands land in history.
    • Variables: Global variables prefill arguments, e.g. >set ip=10.10.10.10.
    • Install: python3 -m pip install arsenal-cli, then run arsenal (suggested alias a); also on the AUR.
    • tmux: ./run -t sends the command to another pane; -t -e executes it there directly.
    • Cheatsheets: Reads .md and .rst cheats from my_cheats, ~/.cheats or paths in config.py; supports <argument|default_value>.
    • Origin: Inspired by navi, rewritten because the bash original was hard to extend.

    Takeaway: Useful for keeping hard-to-remember offensive commands one search away. Add your own cheats so it reflects your workflow.

  • Session-Hijacking-Visual-Exploitation: Visual Session Hijacking Demo
    summary

    TL;DR: Session Hijacking Visual Exploitation (SHVE) by Doyensec is a tool that hijacks user sessions by injecting malicious JavaScript, letting the operator visually drive the victim’s browser session.

    • Architecture: A Node.js server plus Electron client apps (prebuilt in Releases or built with npm run pack).
    • Requirements: Node.js 19.0.0 recommended due to compatibility issues with newer versions; nvm suggested.
    • Setup: cd server && npm install && npm start; first start runs an interactive configuration that creates a user.
    • Client: Log in with the created user and download/install a certificate from the client.
