    • Status: About 218 stars; last push March 2024.

    Takeaway: A demonstration tool for showing the real impact of XSS beyond alert(). Use it in authorized tests to make session-hijack risk concrete for stakeholders.

  • Key Takeaways from the Wiz 2023 Kubernetes Security Report
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz’s summary of its 2023 Kubernetes Security Report, based on scans of over 200,000 cloud accounts, which finds low container security maturity and proposes a “Zone Defense” strategy.

    • Time to first scan: New EKS clusters got malicious scans in 22 minutes; AKS in 2 hours 13 minutes; GKE in under three hours.
    • Exposure trend: Shodan data shows rising numbers of public K8s API servers and exposed kubelet endpoints.
    • Attacks: Cryptomining with XMRig, CCMiner and XMR-Stak-RX; examples PyLoose, newhello, and RBAC Buster, which pivots from anonymous API access to stealing AWS credentials.
    • Low adoption: Only 9% of clusters use network policies; Wiz says the problem is lack of adoption, not lack of controls.
    • Attack chain view: Control plane initial access is less likely than data plane; after initial access, lateral movement and privilege escalation are easy; cloud pivot is a growing impact path.
    • Zone Defense: Proactively cover the most vulnerable points rather than pairing a control to every attack vector.

    Takeaway: Network policies, admission control and cloud-pivot hardening are under-used. Prioritize turning on existing controls over buying new ones.

  • aws-ml-opt-out: Terraform Module to Opt Out of All AWS AI/ML Data Harvesting
    summary

    TL;DR: A small MIT-licensed Terraform module by gblues that applies an AWS Organizations AI services opt-out policy, so AWS AI/ML services do not retain and use your content.

    • Requirements: Terraform 0.13+ and Python with boto3.
    • Modes: Create a new organization (create_organization = true) or modify an existing one (create_organization = false).
    • Policy types: AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY is always enabled; extra types via additional_enable_policy_types.
    • Mechanism: For existing orgs, a Python boto3 script enables the policy types; interpreter set with python_interpreter.
    • Troubleshooting: “NO-ORGANIZATION-FOUND” means you need create_organization = true.
    • Caveat: Author asks production users to fork it; last push January 2024, about 29 stars.

    Takeaway: The opt-out is a single org policy and easy to forget. Apply it at the org root, whether via this module or your own aws_organizations_policy resource.

  • Awesome-GPT-Agents: Curated List of GPT Agents for Cybersecurity
    summary

    TL;DR: A community-curated list by fr0gger of custom ChatGPT GPTs (agents) for offensive and defensive cybersecurity.

    • Examples: MagicUnprotect (Unprotect DB of malware evasion techniques), GP(en)T(ester), Threat Intel Bot, Vulnerability Bot, SourceCodeAnalysis, Web Hacking Wizard, CyberGPT.
    • Usage tips: Keywords such as “Retrieve”, “Based on your knowledge” and “Generate” trigger knowledge retrieval or the code interpreter.
    • Disclaimer: Users should evaluate agents before use; some are experimental.
    • Status: About 6.6k stars; last push July 2024.

    Takeaway: A catalog, not a vetted toolset. Treat listed GPTs as third-party services and do not paste sensitive data into them.

  • State of Cloud Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog’s recurring State of Cloud Security research, analyzing posture data from thousands of organizations on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. The URL now shows the October 2025 edition, not the 2023 one originally linked.

    • Page changed: Content is the 2025 update, building on the October 2024 edition.
    • Multi-account: At least 84% of organizations use more than one AWS account; 86% use AWS Organizations; 14% do not use it at all.
    • Guardrails: Among AWS Organizations users, 40% use SCPs and 6% use resource control policies (RCPs).
    • Data perimeters: Adoption is growing but most organizations lack centralized control.
    • Credentials: Long-lived cloud credentials remain pervasive and are the most common cause of publicly documented cloud breaches.

    Takeaway: Useful benchmark numbers for arguing for SCPs/RCPs and removing long-lived keys. Check which year’s edition you cite.

  • Bolstering Security and Automating Management of Target Australia’s EKS Clusters
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Gazal Gafoor (GitHub @gazal-k) describes how Target Australia runs its Amazon EKS clusters, with Bottlerocket nodes for security and Karpenter in place of Cluster Autoscaler for node management.

    • Node OS: Bottlerocket, the container-focused AWS OS, chosen for its security benefits.
    • Autoscaling: A move from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter, described as more cost-effective and flexible.
    • Adoption: Karpenter’s ADOPTERS.md lists Target Australia using Karpenter to scale and auto-update the EKS compute behind much of the Target Online platform.
    • Scope: An operator’s experience report on running EKS at scale, not a vendor tutorial.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403. This summary uses the Learn Kubernetes Weekly issue 53 blurb and the Karpenter adopters list, not the article body.

    Takeaway: Bottlerocket plus Karpenter is a common EKS baseline for a smaller node attack surface and automated node updates. Read the original for Target’s exact configuration.

  • Latio Security Tools List: Find Your Next Security Tool
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Latio’s security tools list is a directory by Latio Tech (James Berthoty) for comparing cybersecurity tools and vendors by category.

    • Page title: Now “Compare Cybersecurity Tools & Vendor Reviews | Latio”.
    • Purpose: Helps buyers find and compare security products in categories such as cloud and application security.
    • Source caveat: The page is a JavaScript app; only the title was retrievable, so this is based on the title and URL.

    Takeaway: A starting point for vendor discovery. Verify claims with vendor docs and your own trials.

  • Kubernetes Removals, Deprecations, and Major Changes in Kubernetes 1.29
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post (16 November 2023) listing removals, deprecations and major changes ahead of Kubernetes v1.29.

    • Policy recap: GA APIs cannot be removed within a major version; beta APIs are supported for 3 releases after deprecation; alpha can go anytime.
    • Registries: Traffic to k8s.gcr.io redirects to registry.k8s.io; legacy apt.kubernetes.io/yum.kubernetes.io were frozen on 13 September 2023 in favor of pkgs.k8s.io.
    • Cloud providers: DisableCloudProviders and DisableKubeletCloudCredentialProviders default to true; in-tree Azure, GCE and vSphere users must run an external cloud controller manager with --cloud-provider=external.
    • Flow control: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta2 is no longer served; move to v1beta3 (field assuredConcurrencyShares renamed nominalConcurrencyShares).
    • Node field: .status.nodeInfo.kubeProxyVersion is deprecated because kubelet does not actually know the kube-proxy version.

    Takeaway: Before upgrading to 1.29, check for in-tree cloud provider use and v1beta2 FlowSchema manifests.

  • org-kickstart: Kickstart and Manage Your AWS Organization via Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: org-kickstart is PrimeHarbor’s opinionated Terraform landing zone for AWS Organizations, pitched as an alternative to Control Tower “for the rest of us”.

    • Why: Authors say Control Tower is heavy, hard to adjust, lags best practice and is expensive for small orgs due to AWS Config.
    • Security account: Creates one with delegated admin for GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Security Hub, SSO and CloudFormation, enabled in every default region.
    • Logging and OUs: Organization CloudTrail to a bucket in the Security account; default OUs Workloads, Governance, Sandbox, Suspended.
    • Policies: Default AI opt-out policy on root; manages and templates SCPs, RCPs and declarative policies.
    • Access and billing: Audit role via StackSet; AdministratorAccess permission set and group in Identity Center; CUR bucket for Athena.
    • Usage: Manual bootstrap (BOOTSTRAP.md), then copy examples/local-deploy; pin releases with ?ref=0.3.0. Docs at aws-kickstart.org.

    Takeaway: A readable baseline for a new AWS org without Control Tower. Pin a tagged release, since the default branch latest moves.

  • New: Multi-Account Search in AWS Resource Explorer
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS News Blog post announcing that AWS Resource Explorer can search resources across accounts in an AWS Organization or OU, not just across Regions.

    • Access points: Resource Explorer console, unified console search bar, AWS CLI, SDKs and AWS Chatbot.
    • Setup: Enable trusted access for AWS Account Management, configure Resource Explorer in each account (e.g. via Systems Manager Quick Setup or CloudFormation), optionally use a delegated admin, then create a multi-account view.
    • Views: Organization-wide visibility, in the Region holding the aggregator index; optional filters and tag attributes; access controlled by granting view access.
    • Example query: elasticache:* redis3.2 finds old Redis versions across accounts and Regions.
    • Limits: Only resources in your own account get direct console links; available in a listed set of Regions.

    Takeaway: Handy for incident response and cost hunts across many accounts. Set up the aggregator index and a delegated admin view once.

  • 12 Personal Go Tricks That Transformed My Productivity
    summary

    TL;DR: Phuong Le’s Devtrovert article (August 2023) sharing utility snippets and language tricks from his team’s Go utilities library.

    • Timing: defer TrackTime(time.Now()) or defer TrackTime()() to log elapsed time.
    • Two-stage defer: A function returns a teardown closure, defer setupTeardown()(); best for tests since errors are not handled gracefully.
    • Slices: Pre-allocate with make([]int, 0, 10) and append to avoid index bugs; Go 1.20 allows [3]int(a[0:3]).
    • Imports: _ import runs init(); dot import exposes identifiers without the package name.
    • Errors: Go 1.20 errors.Join combines errors and works with errors.Is.
    • Interface check: var _ Buffer = (*StringBuffer)(nil) catches missing methods at compile time.
    • Others: Method chaining via pointer receivers, a generic ternary helper (author says avoid), and avoiding naked parameters.

    Takeaway: The compile-time interface assertion and errors.Join are the most broadly useful. Treat dot imports and the ternary helper with caution.

  • OMGCICD: Attacking GitLab CI/CD via Shared Runners
    summary

    TL;DR: Pulse Security article (November 2023) showing how any GitLab user can compromise a shared, privileged docker-in-docker runner and steal secrets from other projects’ pipelines, including production deploys.

    • Poisoned pipeline: A developer edits .gitlab-ci.yml and dumps env with env | gzip -c | base64 -w0 to bypass variable masking (OWASP CICD-SEC-04).
    • GitLab default: Variables are now available only to protected branches by default, but new runners run on all branches.
    • Shared runner attack: An instance-level runner is usable by any project, so the attacker creates a personal repo and runs a reverse shell pipeline.
    • Escape: DIND and Kubernetes runners seen in the wild ran Privileged; the attacker mounts the host block device and drops an SSH key for root.
    • Harvest: From the host, the attacker waits for a high-value pipeline and steals its environment variables and keys, here leading to root on production.
    • Scope: Not GitLab-specific; the authors saw the same problem in most CI/CD platforms that use one runner for all pipelines.

    Takeaway: Never share a runner between untrusted projects and production deploys. Use dedicated, non-privileged runners scoped to protected branches for sensitive jobs.

  • Post-Exploiting a Compromised etcd: Full Control over the Cluster and Its Nodes
    summary

    TL;DR: NCC Group research by Luis Toro Puig (7 November 2023) showing that root on the etcd host gives full cluster control, not only secret theft, by writing protobuf-encoded resources directly into etcd.

    • URL moved: The old research.nccgroup.com link redirects to a research index; the article now lives at nccgroup.com/research-blog/.
    • Tooling: Uses auger (Joe Betz, Google) to (de)serialize Kubernetes protobuf in etcd; NCC built the kubetcd wrapper PoC with kubectl-like syntax.
    • Requirements: Root on the etcd host to read /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key; existing resources as templates; self-managed clusters only, not managed control planes.
    • Tampering: Change a pod’s creation timestamp, e.g. kubetcd create pod nginx -t nginx --time 2000-01-31T00:00:00Z makes it look 23 years old.
    • Persistence: Mismatch the pod name and etcd path (-p randomentry) so kubectl delete returns NotFound.
    • Hiding: --fake-ns injects pods under a namespace path that does not match the manifest, making them semi-hidden.

    Takeaway: Protect etcd certificates and control plane hosts as cluster-admin equivalents. Monitor etcd for writes that bypass the API server.

  • Security Best Practices for Authors of GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub Blog post (16 November 2023) with minimum security practices for people who publish GitHub Actions, since a compromised action affects every workflow that uses it.

    • Context: 169% increase in Actions minutes on public repos; over 20,000 actions in the Marketplace.
    • Dependabot: Enable it on the action’s source repo to catch vulnerable dependencies.
    • Code scanning: Enable CodeQL or a third-party tool that outputs SARIF.
    • Triage: Have a process to resolve critical alerts promptly.
    • Disclosure: Add a SECURITY.md so issues are reported privately, not in public Issues.
    • Accounts: Require MFA for maintainers; get the verified creator badge via the Technology Partner Program.

    Takeaway: If you publish actions, these are low-effort basics. Consumers should still pin actions to commit SHAs.

  • Terrareg: Open Source Terraform Module Registry with UI and Git Integration
    summary

    TL;DR: Terrareg by MatthewJohn is an open source, self-hosted Terraform module registry with a web UI, Git integration and module analysis.

    • API: Fully implements the Terraform modules API; everything is API driven.
    • Sources: Host modules internally or index them from external Git; SCM hooks auto-index new versions.
    • Analysis: Shows README, inputs, outputs, providers and resources; security alerts and cost estimation per example.
    • UI: Interactive usage builder; example code with rewritten source arguments.
    • Auth: SSO via OpenID Connect, SAML2 and GitHub; provider support in early alpha.
    • Run: docker run ... ghcr.io/matthewjohn/terrareg:latest with SECRET_KEY and ADMIN_AUTHENTICATION_TOKEN; a valid TLS cert is needed for Terraform to treat it as a registry.
    • Warning: It downloads and analyses modules, so untrusted modules or providers can allow arbitrary code execution.

    Takeaway: A practical private registry if you want versioned module discovery without Terraform Cloud. Only index modules you trust.

  • Amazon S3 Now Supports Enabling S3 Object Lock on Existing Buckets
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS What’s New (20 November 2023): S3 Object Lock can now be enabled on existing buckets, and S3 Replication now works for buckets with Object Lock.

    • Before: Object Lock had to be enabled at bucket creation.
    • Modes: Retain Until Date for fixed-time immutability, or Legal Hold for indefinite.
    • Existing objects: Set retention per object or use S3 Batch Operations for tens to billions of objects; new objects get the default retention.
    • Replication: Create immutable copies in the same or another account or Region.
    • Compliance: Assessed by Cohasset Associates for SEC 17a-4(f), FINRA 4511 and CFTC 1.31.
    • Availability: All Regions including GovCloud; console, API, SDK or CLI.

    Takeaway: You can now add ransomware-resistant immutability to existing backup buckets without migrating data. Remember that default retention only covers new objects.

  • AWS IAM Identity Center Now Provides New APIs to Automate Access to Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS What’s New (17 November 2023): IAM Identity Center added APIs to manage user and group assignments to supported AWS and cloud applications.

    • Before: Application access was managed in the Identity Center console and each application’s console.
    • Now: Workflows can programmatically assign application access, alongside existing account access APIs.
    • Cost: Identity Center has no additional charge.
    • Availability: All Regions where IAM Identity Center is supported; documented in the API reference.

    Takeaway: Application assignments can now live in code with account assignments. Fold them into your IaC or access automation.

  • How to Use Multiple Instances of AWS IAM Identity Center
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post (updated through February 2024) explaining organization instances versus the new account instances of IAM Identity Center, and how to control and audit them.

    • Organization instance: One per organization in the management account (or delegated admin); full features including permission sets and SAML 2.0 apps; the recommended pattern.
    • Account instance: Subset of features, bound to one account and Region; one per account; initially only Amazon CodeCatalyst assignments; no permission sets or customer managed SAML apps.
    • Enablement: If Identity Center was enabled before 15 November 2023 in a default Region, account instance creation must be enabled from the management account.
    • Opt-in Region: An org instance in an opt-in Region prevents account instances.
    • Patterns: Five deployment cases; case 1 (org instance only, account instances disabled) is recommended.
    • Use cases: Temporary trials of AWS managed apps, or when an org-wide deployment is impossible.

    Takeaway: Decide deliberately whether member accounts may create account instances. Block them with policy if you want one identity source.

  • Rapidly Scaling for Breaking News with Karpenter and KEDA
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon talk by Mel Cone and Deepak Goel of The New York Times on scaling multi-tenant EKS clusters for breaking news with Karpenter and KEDA.

    • Requirement: NYT may need to double cluster node count in under two minutes.
    • Traffic shape: Breaking news spikes come without warning, last minutes, and peak above 100k requests per second.
    • Tools: Karpenter for node provisioning, KEDA for event-driven pod autoscaling.
    • Bottleneck: Traffic to the unified HTTP ingress is often the biggest constraint.
    • Design focus: Trade-offs between flexibility, maintainability and cost savings.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video description only.

    Takeaway: A real-world case for pairing Karpenter with KEDA. Watch it if your spikes are short and sharp, and check your ingress first.

  • Ambient Mesh Architecture
    summary

    TL;DR: Istio documentation on ambient mode architecture, the sidecar-less data plane. The old URL now leads to an index page linking sub-pages on the control plane, data plane, HBONE and ztunnel traffic redirection.

    • Page changed: Content has moved under /docs/ambient/architecture/; the summary uses the current data plane page.
    • ztunnel: A per-node L4 proxy run as a DaemonSet that intercepts mesh traffic and enforces L4 policy.
    • Waypoint: An optional L7 proxy, usually per namespace, for L7 policy; enabled with the istio.io/use-waypoint label.
    • Enrollment: Pods join the mesh with the istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient label.
    • HBONE: Traffic between mesh-capable endpoints is upgraded to an encrypted HTTP-based overlay tunnel.
    • Routing: Otherwise traffic follows normal Kubernetes service routing.

    Takeaway: Ambient splits L4 (ztunnel) from L7 (waypoint), so you pay for L7 only where needed. Read the current docs, since paths and features changed after 2023.

  • Istio: The Past, Present and Future of the Project and Community
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon talk by Louis Ryan (solo.io) and John Howard (Google) on Istio’s project health, recent features and roadmap after its CNCF graduation.

    • Topics: Project and community health and new features in recent releases.
    • Ambient: Progress on the sidecar-less ambient data plane mode.
    • Gateway API: Status of Gateway API support.
    • Future: Roadmap and community-building plans, plus how to contribute.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video description only.

    Takeaway: A late-2023 snapshot of Istio’s direction. Watch it for context on why ambient and Gateway API became the focus.

  • Node Size Matters: Running K8s as Cheaply as Possible
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon talk by Alex Meijer and Michael Dresser (Stackwatch) on Kubernetes node system overhead as a hidden cost, and how node choice affects it.

    • Problem: Overhead is the reserved, unusable part of every node; poor node selection can leave much less capacity than expected.
    • Study: Overheads measured across major cloud providers’ node families.
    • Tooling: Demo of new overhead measurement features in OpenCost (CNCF Sandbox).
    • Output: Actionable recommendations and methods for sizing clusters.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video description only.

    Takeaway: Small nodes waste a larger share on reserved overhead. Measure allocatable versus capacity before picking instance sizes.

  • flan: A Pretty Sweet Vulnerability Scanner
    summary

    TL;DR: Flan Scan is Cloudflare’s lightweight network vulnerability scanner: a container wrapper around Nmap and the vulners NSE script that maps detected service versions to CVEs.

    • Status: The repository is archived (read-only).
    • Workflow: Put IPs or CIDRs in shared/ips.txt, run make build then make start.
    • Default scan: nmap -sV -oX /shared/xml_files -oN - -v1 $@ --script=vulners/vulners.nse <ip>; extra Nmap flags (UDP, IPv6) can be passed to docker run.
    • Reports: LaTeX by default; also md, html and json (e.g. make html); raw XML kept in shared/xml_files.
    • Cloud upload: Push reports to S3 or GCS with upload=aws|gcp and bucket= env vars.
    • Kubernetes: Can be deployed as a scanner on Kubernetes.

    Takeaway: A simple pattern for scheduled version-based CVE scanning. Since it is archived, use it as a reference or fork rather than a maintained tool.

  • Cilicon: Self-Hosted Ephemeral macOS CI on Apple Silicon
    summary

    TL;DR: Cilicon, by Trade Republic, is a macOS app that uses Apple’s Virtualization Framework to run ephemeral macOS CI VMs on Apple Silicon with near-native performance.

    • CI support: GitHub Actions, Buildkite Agent, GitLab Runner and arbitrary scripts.
    • Cycle: Each job gets a fresh VM, which is discarded afterwards.
    • Version 2.0: Runs commands over a built-in SSH client instead of a Login Item script; partly adopts the tart image format.
    • Images: Integrated OCI client pulls prebuilt tart images; Cirrus Labs macos-sonoma-xcode images are recommended.
    • Migration: Rename vmBundlePath to source; 1.0 images can be auto-converted (default SSH admin:admin).
    • Known issue: swift-nio SSH problems on macOS 15.0-15.3; use 15.4+.

    Takeaway: A low-cost way to get clean, ephemeral macOS runners on your own Macs. Change default VM credentials before use.

  • awskillswitch: Lambda Function to Contain an AWS Account Compromise
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Kill Switch, by secengjeff, is a Go Lambda function and PoC client deployed in a dedicated Security account to quickly contain an AWS account compromise.

    • Actions: apply_scp freezes a target account with an SCP; detach_policies strips a role; revoke_sessions revokes sessions on one role or ALL customer managed roles; delete_role.
    • Roles: Needs assumable roles from the Security account into the management account (for apply_scp) and into target accounts; StackSets suggested.
    • Permissions: Documented per action, e.g. organizations:CreatePolicy and organizations:AttachPolicy for apply_scp.
    • Anti-tamper: Example SCP denies modifying security-role (iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, iam:DetachRolePolicy, etc.) so attackers cannot disable it.
    • Warning: Default apply_scp restricts most IAM actions and may break applications; review switch.conf first.
    • Build: Tested on go1.21.3 arm64; last push December 2023.

    Takeaway: Pre-stage containment actions before an incident, not during one. Even if you skip the tool, copy the role-protection SCP pattern.

  • AWS pre:Invent 2023
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris’s annual “pre:Invent” roundup (22 November 2023) of security and governance relevant AWS announcements made between 1 October and re:Invent 2023, with his commentary.

    • Volume: 511 announcements since 1 October; 17 November had the most.
    • SCPs in China: Service control policies now work in the AWS China (Beijing and Ningxia) Regions.
    • AMIs: EC2 AMIs can be set to disabled, which makes them private and blocks new launches.
    • SSM: Default Host Management Configuration (DHMC) enables Systems Manager for all EC2 instances in an organization; he notes SSM is needed for Inspector v2.
    • Other items: AWS Config added 19 resource types; multi-VPC ENI attachments went GA.
    • Sections: Security, Backup & Recovery, Governance and FinOps, Serverless, and services adding new security features.

    Takeaway: A curated filter over hundreds of launches. Skim the security and governance sections when you plan your next guardrail changes.

  • How to Create an AMI Hardening Pipeline and Automate Updates to Your ECS Instance Fleet
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog walkthrough that hardens ECS-optimized AMIs against the CIS Docker Benchmark with EC2 Image Builder and automatically rolls them out to ECS container instances.

    • Scope: Covers CIS Docker Benchmark sections 1-3 (host, Docker daemon, daemon files), but not every control in them.
    • Build: Image Builder pipeline runs an Ansible playbook from S3, validates benchmarks, writes results to S3, and triggers an Amazon Inspector scan.
    • Rollout: An SNS message starts a Lambda that kicks off a Step Functions state machine; it creates a new launch template version and starts an ASG instance refresh.
    • Targeting: Cluster tags set at CloudFormation deploy time choose which ECS clusters are refreshed.
    • Notifications: Instance refresh results go to an SNS topic; a weekly Lambda warns when a newer ECS-optimized base AMI exists.
    • Prerequisites: Existing ECS cluster with EC2 capacity providers, AWS CLI, Inspector for EC2 enabled.

    Takeaway: A reusable build-scan-refresh loop for EC2-backed ECS. The weekly base-AMI check still needs a human to update the recipe.

  • Preventing Accidental Internet-Exposure of AWS Resources (Part 1: VPC)
    summary

    TL;DR: Kevin Hock’s Part 1 of a series on preventing accidental internet exposure in AWS, focused on VPC resources: ban Internet Gateways in sub-accounts via SCP and provide centralized egress.

    • Core control: Deny ec2:CreateInternetGateway in sub-accounts; every VPC internet exposure path needs an IGW.
    • Problem: AWS couples egress and ingress, since both need an IGW, so private accounts need a paved egress path.
    • Option 1 (recommended): Centralized egress via Transit Gateway, with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a TGW in another account.
    • Cost: By his graph, at 20 VPCs you need over 55 TB before centralized egress costs more; 1 PB breaks even at 324 VPCs.
    • Other options: PrivateLink or peering with a proxy (mostly non-options because of source/destination checks), GWLB with a firewall, VPC Sharing, IPv6 for egress.
    • Reference: SummitRoute/aws_exposable_resources lists resources that can be made public.

    Takeaway: One SCP removes a whole class of accidental exposure. Build the central egress path first so teams do not need an IGW.

  • Deep Dive into the New Amazon EKS Pod Identity Feature
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper’s Datadog Security Labs deep dive into EKS Pod Identity, launched at re:Invent 2023 as an alternative to IRSA for giving pods AWS credentials.

    • Setup: aws eks create-pod-identity-association maps a namespace and service account to a role that trusts pods.eks.amazonaws.com (sts:AssumeRole, sts:TagSession).
    • Visibility: eks:ListPodIdentityAssociations and DescribePodIdentityAssociation show which pods get which roles.
    • Agent: The eks-pod-identity-agent add-on runs as a DaemonSet with hostNetwork: true, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE and a privileged init container.
    • Mechanism: The agent serves 169.254.170.23/v1/credentials, takes the service account token and calls eks-auth:AssumeRoleForPodIdentity.
    • SDK pickup: A webhook injects AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI and AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE, the existing container credential provider used by ECS.
    • Method: Black-box reverse engineering of the binary with crane, Ghidra and redress; later confirmed against source released mid-2024.

    Takeaway: Pod Identity moves pod-to-role mapping into the EKS API, which is easier to audit than IRSA trust policies. Note that node credentials can also call the assume API.

  • What Is GitOps and Why Is It (Almost) Useless? Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of Andrii Chepik’s HackerNoon critique (August 2023) arguing that GitOps, as promoted by Weaveworks since 2017, is not a silver bullet and brings hidden complexity, using Flux with Helm as the example.

    • Background: Immutable infrastructure splits stateless and stateful parts; CI/CD automates delivery; configuration drift is the IaC problem GitOps targets.
    • Flux and Helm: Walks through HelmRelease custom resources and how Flux reconciles them.
    • Checklist: GitOps needs image build scripts, an infrastructure repo, a HelmRelease generator, a Helm repo, and several CI and Flux accounts.
    • Single source of truth: Git is not the only source; the HelmRelease depends on a Helm chart and a Docker image stored elsewhere.
    • Next: Part 2 covers multiple environments, secrets, CI Ops vs GitOps, rollback and multiple clusters.

    Takeaway: A useful counterpoint before adopting Flux-style GitOps. List the extra repos, accounts and controllers you will need.

  • What Is GitOps and Why Is It (Almost) Useless? Part 2
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 2 of Andrii Chepik’s HackerNoon GitOps critique (August 2023), covering multi-environment, secrets and multi-cluster problems, and naming who actually benefits from GitOps.

    • Environments: Promoting by merging dev to stage breaks when HelmRelease values differ; valuesFiles does not merge well either.
    • valuesFrom advice: Keep a single value in the ConfigMap, the environment name, and do the rest with Helm templating; otherwise config spreads across 4 repos and 2 deploy systems.
    • Secrets: Plain-text passwords in Git are a no-go; options include random in-environment secrets, Mozilla SOPS or Bitnami Sealed Secrets.
    • Multi-cluster: A HelmRelease alone does not say where the app came from, its build logs, or which clusters pull it.
    • Who needs it: Teams without a working CI/CD, as one security layer, for large multi-component platforms, or where pull beats push (e.g. canary).
    • Definition: Author’s formula: GitOps = Continuous Delivery minus Continuous Deployment.

    Takeaway: Decide whether pull-based delivery solves a real problem for you. If not, a well-built CI/CD push pipeline may be simpler.

  • cloudtrail2sightings: Convert CloudTrail Data to MITRE ATT&CK Sightings
    summary

    TL;DR: cloudtrail2sightings, by zmallen, converts CloudTrail logs from incidents or simulated attacks into MITRE ATT&CK Sightings JSON using a Vector pipeline.

    • Input: CloudTrail JSON with a top-level Records key (check with jq -r 'has("Records")'); a sample cloudtrail.zip is included.
    • Data sources: Suggests stratus-red-team or the public flaws.cloud CloudTrail dataset.
    • Run: Set the include path, then vector --config vector.toml; output goes to sightings.json.
    • Queries: jq examples list software_name (userAgent) and map eventName to technique_id, and filter for stratus-red-team activity.
    • Status: Small project (about 84 stars), last push July 2022.

    Takeaway: A quick way to tag known-bad CloudTrail events with ATT&CK technique IDs. Run it on stratus-red-team output to validate detections.

  • azurechat: Azure Chat Solution Accelerator Powered by Azure OpenAI Service
    summary

    TL;DR: Azure Chat is Microsoft’s solution accelerator for deploying a private ChatGPT-style chat tenant in your own Azure subscription on Azure OpenAI, with chat over your files and data.

    • Status: The repository is now archived.
    • Benefits claimed: Private to your tenant, network isolation and enterprise authentication, plug-in internal data sources and services.
    • 2025 updates: Managed identity deployment that removes almost all keys, Entra ID app registration helper scripts (appreg_setup.sh/.ps1), private endpoints and ESLZ-compliant deployment.
    • Deploy: Azure Developer CLI or Deploy to Azure button; an identity provider and admin user are required.
    • Features: Chat over files, personas, extensions; GitHub Actions deploy docs.

    Takeaway: A reference design for an internal LLM chat on Azure. Since it is archived, use it for patterns, not as a maintained product.

  • IceKube: Find Attack Paths Within a Kubernetes Cluster from Low Privilege to Cluster-Admin
    summary

    TL;DR: IceKube, from WithSecure Labs, enumerates a Kubernetes cluster into Neo4j and computes attack paths from low-privilege identities to targets such as cluster-admin.

    • Setup: docker-compose up -d for Neo4j (localhost:7474), then pip install icekube or Poetry.
    • Access needed: A kubectl context with broad read access including secrets; secret data fields are deleted on ingestion.
    • Commands: icekube enumerate, icekube attack-path, icekube run (both), icekube purge.
    • Querying: Cypher queries in Neo4j; attack edges have attack_path: 1; disable “Connect result nodes” in the browser.
    • Offline: icekube download or the Rust tool freezer, then icekube load.
    • Filtering: -i to ignore resource types; events and componentstatuses are ignored by default.

    Takeaway: BloodHound-style path analysis for Kubernetes RBAC. Run it on your own clusters to find service accounts with unexpected escalation routes.

  • How to Use the PassRole Permission with IAM Roles
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog deep dive on iam:PassRole: what it is, when it is checked, and best practices to prevent privilege escalation.

    • What it is: A permission, not an API call, checked when a resource such as a Lambda function or EC2 instance is created or updated with a service role.
    • Three conditions: The caller has iam:PassRole on that role with no denies; the role trusts the service principal; the role and caller are in the same account.
    • Avoid wildcards: Resource: "*" with iam:PassRole lets someone pass any role, including admin ones.
    • Separate statements: Keep iam:PassRole in its own policy statement so its resource can be scoped.
    • Paths and naming: Allow passing only roles under a path such as /application_role/, combined with permissions boundaries for developer-created roles.
    • Governance: PassRole is still subject to SCPs, VPC endpoint policies, session policies and permissions boundaries.

    Takeaway: Audit policies for iam:PassRole on *. Scope it to a role path, which gives developers freedom without an escalation path.

  • Introducing IAM Access Analyzer Custom Policy Checks
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog launch post for IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks, which use automated reasoning to check IAM policies for critical permissions or increased permissiveness before deployment.

    • Problem: Manual reviews of developer-written IAM policies slow delivery.
    • CheckNoNewAccess: Compares a new policy with an existing one and reports if it grants more access.
    • CheckAccessNotGranted: Checks that a policy does not allow listed sensitive actions, e.g. cloudtrail:StopLogging or cloudtrail:DeleteTrail.
    • July 2024 update: Added CheckNoPublicAccess for resource policies; CheckAccessNotGranted can also check specific resources.
    • Workflow: Run from the CLI locally or embed in CI/CD; samples use the AWS CLI and CDK, with a GitHub repo.

    Takeaway: Put these checks in the pipeline as a gate on IAM changes. A short deny-list of critical actions catches the worst mistakes cheaply.

  • Self-Study DevOps Projects
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Self-study DevOps Projects by Tomasz Cholewa (cloudowski) is a set of graded hands-on tasks; Task 1 is building, containerizing and running a simple web app on Kubernetes.

    • Level 1: Write a small app (e.g. Go, Python) that shows hostname and version, with a Dockerfile.
    • Image goals: Multistage or scratch builds, as small as possible, for both amd64 and arm64, pushed to a private registry.
    • Run: Multiple instances on a cluster with probes and resource requests/limits.
    • Level 2: Automate builds on every git push and ensure no critical vulnerabilities in each image.
    • Structure: The site lists Tasks 1-5.
    • Source caveat: The live page returned empty content; this is based on a Wayback Machine snapshot from April 2025.

    Takeaway: A good practical syllabus for juniors. Use Task 1 as an onboarding exercise covering images, multi-arch and probes.

  • Learn and Test DMARC
    summary

    TL;DR: Learn and Test DMARC is an interactive web tool that visualizes how a receiving mail server validates SPF, DKIM and DMARC for an email you send to its test address.

    • Tester: Send a mail to the given @dmarctester.com address and watch SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks step by step.
    • Results shown: Source IP and hostname, SPF domain and result, DKIM domain, selector and algorithm, alignment, p= policy and final verdict.
    • Header analysis: Paste email headers or source for a visual explanation.
    • Quiz: A ten-question DMARC quiz with explanations.
    • Notes: Best viewed on desktop; results can be anonymized; sponsored by a DMARC monitoring vendor.

    Takeaway: The fastest way to see why a domain’s mail fails alignment. Use it when setting up or debugging SPF, DKIM and DMARC records.

  • Breaking DRM in Polish Trains
    summary

    TL;DR: 37C3 talk by Redford, q3k and MrTick on reverse-engineering Polish EMU trains that stopped working after servicing by an “unauthorized” company, revealing deliberate lock-out logic.

    • Story: Trains from a series of Polish EMUs refused to move a few days after arriving at an independent service company; the manufacturer blamed interference with a security system.
    • Technical content: How modern EMUs and the Train Control & Monitoring System work, and how to analyze TriCore machine code.
    • Finding: The “security” systems found inside, with the punchline of running unlock.py on a dozen trains.
    • Format: 61 minutes, 27 December 2023, with translated audio tracks and English subtitles; link starts at 13:09.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk page abstract only.

    Takeaway: A strong right-to-repair case study. It shows why firmware in critical infrastructure needs independent scrutiny.

  • Amazon EKS Introduces Upgrade Insights
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announced Amazon EKS upgrade insights on December 20, 2023: EKS automatically scans clusters for issues that could break an upgrade to a newer Kubernetes version and gives remediation advice.

    • Checks: Scans against an AWS-maintained list of upgrade-impacting issues, updated as Kubernetes and EKS change. The announcement does not list individual checks.
    • Access: Results are viewable any time in the EKS console or via the EKS APIs, evaluated against all future EKS-supported versions.
    • Remediation: Each insight comes with recommended fixes.
    • Regions: All regions except AWS GovCloud (US) and China (Beijing, Ningxia).
    • Cost: Not mentioned in the announcement.

    Takeaway: Check cluster insights (for example deprecated API usage) before every EKS version bump instead of relying only on manual tools like pluto or kubent.

  • Top Announcements of AWS re:Invent 2023
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS News Blog recap of the major re:Invent 2023 launches, grouped by category, last updated 14 December 2023.

    • Generative AI: Amazon Q across services (e.g. Generative SQL in Redshift, Q in QuickSight), plus SageMaker Studio and inference updates.
    • Zero-ETL: Previews for Aurora PostgreSQL, RDS for MySQL and DynamoDB into Redshift, and OpenSearch with S3.
    • Compute: Graviton4-powered R8g instances in preview and high-memory U7i instances.
    • Containers: EKS Pod Identity simplifies IAM permissions for EKS applications.
    • Storage: S3 Express One Zone (up to 10x S3 Standard performance), EBS Snapshots Archive in AWS Backup, Backup restore testing, EFS Archive, EFS up to 250,000 read IOPS.
    • Ops: CloudWatch Logs pattern analytics and anomaly detection; SQS FIFO throughput increase and DLQ redrive.

    Takeaway: A one-page index of the year’s launches. For security, look at Pod Identity, Backup restore testing and the Security, Identity and Compliance section.

13.11.2023

  • Gosh: Writing Go at the Command Line
    summary

    TL;DR: Nick Wells’s talk at September Gophers about gosh, a tool he wrote so Go code can be written and run directly at the command line, as other languages allow.

    • Gap filled: Go has no built-in way to execute code inline from the shell; gosh adds one.
    • Content: How gosh works internally and examples of what you can do with it.
    • Source caveat: Based only on the short video description; tool flags and implementation details are not covered here.

    Takeaway: Worth a look if you reach for Python or awk one-liners but would rather stay in Go.

  • go-openai: OpenAI ChatGPT, GPT-3, GPT-4, DALL·E, Whisper API Wrapper for Go
    summary

    TL;DR: go-openai by sashabaranov is a popular unofficial, zero-dependency Go client for the OpenAI API (about 10.8k stars).

    • Page changed: The README now targets the 2026 API surface and recommends the Responses API, not the 2023 ChatGPT/GPT-4/DALL-E focus in the title.
    • Install: go get github.com/sashabaranov/go-openai; requires Go 1.18+.
    • Responses API: client.CreateResponse with Instructions and Input; PreviousResponseID continues a conversation; CreateResponseStream streams deltas.
    • Chat Completions: Still available for existing integrations.
    • Coverage: Embeddings, images, audio, moderation, files, fine-tuning, batches, vector stores and legacy Assistants.

    Takeaway: The de facto Go OpenAI client. Pin a version, because model constants and recommended APIs have changed a lot since 2023.

  • Following Attackers’ (Cloud)trail in AWS: Methodology and Findings in the Wild
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog Security Labs (Martin McCloskey, Christophe Tafani-Dereeper, Frederic Baguelin) describe hypothesis-driven threat hunting in AWS CloudTrail and share attacker behaviors and IOCs seen in the wild.

    • Hypotheses: Attackers create IAM users for persistence, abuse SES for spam, create or import EC2 key pairs and change security groups, and enumerate stolen permissions.
    • Backdoor users: Observed names include root, ses-admin, sesadminsmtp, ampIify-dev and EmperorsToolsShops32; root is likely chosen to blend in.
    • Signals: Bursts of AccessDenied, CreateUser from EC2 role sessions (i-...), the same user name tried across environments, and typo-like names.
    • Check before persist: GetUser probes for names such as admindvelop; DescribeInstances filtered on key name xg1 before CreateKeyPair.
    • Security groups: Attempts to create a group named Java_Ghost in several environments.
    • Enumeration: Common first calls include sts:GetCallerIdentity, ses:GetAccount, ses:GetSendQuota, ses:ListIdentities, sns:GetSMSAttributes and iam:ListUsers.
    • Actor link: One user name ties to the “Emperors Tools” toolkit sold online, whose upload script itself has an arbitrary file upload bug.

    Takeaway: SES and IAM user creation are top abuse paths after key leaks. Turn these IOCs and AccessDenied patterns into CloudTrail detections.

  • Attacking AWS Cognito with Pacu (Part 1)
    summary

    TL;DR: Rhino Security Labs Part 1 by David Kutz-Marks on common AWS Cognito misconfigurations seen in pentests, introducing two new Pacu modules.

    • Components: App client, user pool (like an OIDC IdP) and identity pool (issues temporary AWS credentials).
    • Enumeration: Client, user pool and identity pool IDs leak in HTTP responses.
    • Open sign-up: Self-registration is on by default, so attackers can register with leaked IDs even without a login page.
    • Escalation: User-modifiable custom attributes used for RBAC; case-sensitive email changes can enable account takeover.
    • Pivot: The ID token can list extra IAM roles the user can assume.
    • Tooling: cognito__enum (needs IAM creds with Cognito read) and cognito__attack (needs at least one resource ID); details in Part 2.

    Takeaway: Check Cognito for open sign-up, writable attributes used in authorization, and over-permissive identity pool roles.

  • former2: Generate CloudFormation / Terraform / Troposphere Templates from Existing AWS Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Former2 by Ian Mckay generates infrastructure-as-code from existing AWS resources by scanning your account with the AWS JavaScript SDK in the browser.

    • Outputs: CloudFormation, Terraform, Troposphere, CDK v1/v2 (TypeScript, Python, Java, C#), CDK for Terraform, Pulumi, and draw.io diagrams.
    • Coverage: Badges show about 84% of CloudFormation and 49% of Terraform resource types.
    • Helper extension: Needed for services without CORS such as S3 and IAM; available for Chrome, Firefox and Edge.
    • Credentials: Use an IAM key pair, ideally with ReadOnlyAccess unless you use the Import feature.
    • Usage: Run at former2.com or self-host; a limited CLI is also available.

    Takeaway: Fast way to codify click-ops resources. Use read-only keys and review the output, since generated code mirrors whatever drift exists.

  • waf-btk: WAF Bypass PoC
    summary

    TL;DR: waf-btk by Ghost Security is a PoC HTTP/HTTPS proxy that bypasses cloud WAF rules by padding request bodies beyond the size those WAFs inspect.

    • Status: Archived; last push October 2023.
    • Inspection limits listed: AWS WAF 8k, Cloudflare 128k, Google Armor 8k, Azure WAF 128k.
    • Run: make run listens on 127.0.0.1:8888.
    • Usage: Add header waf-btk-padding: <KB> (stripped before forwarding); use 8 or more for AWS WAF and 128 or more for Cloudflare.
    • Demo: A JSON body with SELECT * FROM is blocked normally and passes once padded.
    • Mitigation: Block or drop requests larger than the inspection limit, where practical.

    Takeaway: WAF body inspection limits are a real gap. Add a size-constraint rule for oversized bodies on endpoints that do not need them.

  • CloudFlair: Find Origin Servers of Websites Behind CloudFlare Using Censys Scan Data
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudFlair by Christophe Tafani-Dereeper finds origin servers of sites behind Cloudflare (or CloudFront) by matching the site’s TLS certificates against Censys internet-wide scan data.

    • Important caveat: Since late 2024 Censys no longer gives API access to free accounts, so CloudFlair no longer works with free accounts.
    • Method: Find certificates for the domain, find IPv4 hosts presenting them, then compare each candidate’s HTML with the real homepage.
    • Setup: Set CENSYS_API_ID and CENSYS_API_SECRET, create a venv and pip install -r requirements.txt.
    • Run: python cloudflair.py myvulnerable.site; add --cloudfront for CloudFront targets.
    • Root cause: Origins that do not restrict access to the CDN’s IP ranges.

    Takeaway: If your origin answers on the internet, the CDN is not protecting it. Allow-list CDN ranges or use authenticated origin pulls.

  • endoflife.date: Find EOL Dates
    summary

    TL;DR: endoflife.date is a community site that documents end-of-life dates and support lifecycles for software, devices and services in one consistent format.

    • Scale: Tracks 486 products as of the fetch.
    • Coverage: Languages (Python, Java, Node.js), databases (PostgreSQL, Redis), OSes, frameworks, servers (Nginx, Kubernetes) and cloud services (EKS, GKE, AKS).
    • API: Data is available through an API and iCalendar feeds.
    • Ecosystem: Tools such as norwegianblue, end_of_life and cicada use the API.
    • Contributing: Open to new products and corrections; offers guidance for vendors publishing EOL data.

    Takeaway: Use the API in CI or inventory scripts to flag runtimes and clusters nearing EOL before they become a finding.

  • PCI DSS v4.0 on AWS Compliance Guide Now Available
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Assurance Services announces the PCI DSS v4.0 on AWS Compliance Guide, which collects common questions on building PCI DSS compliant workloads on AWS.

    • Audience: Payment application developers, compliance teams, internal assessors and PCI QSAs.
    • Shared responsibility: How the model maps to PCI DSS requirements and what AWS’s Level 1 Service Provider status means.
    • Scoping: Guidance on scoping the cardholder data environment.
    • Diagrams: Examples of diagrams required for assessments.
    • Detail: Requirement-by-requirement guidance with references to AWS documentation for evidence.

    Takeaway: A starting point for v4.0 assessments on AWS. Pair it with your QSA early to agree on scope.

  • Delegating Permission Set Management and Account Assignment in AWS IAM Identity Center
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post showing three IAM policy patterns for delegating IAM Identity Center permission set management and account assignment to teams, without giving them full Identity Center admin.

    • Distinction: This is not Identity Center delegated administration; it works whether Identity Center lives in the management account or a delegated member account.
    • Scenario: Red, Blue and Yellow teams, each in its own OU, with Identity Center delegated to an Identity account.
    • Accounts-based (Red): Assign existing, centrally managed permission sets to accounts in the team’s OU.
    • Permission-based (Blue): Edit and use one specific permission set on the team’s single account.
    • Tag-based (Yellow): Create and edit permission sets tagged Team: Yellow and assign them across the OU.
    • Update: January 2024 fix lets use case 3 use sso:CreateAccountAssignment and sso:ProvisionPermissionSet on permissionSet resources; the console needs extra permissions.

    Takeaway: Tag- or OU-scoped delegation lets teams self-serve access safely. Start with the accounts-based model, which keeps permission set content central.

  • Only One Label to Improve Your Kubernetes Security Posture, with the Pod Security Admission (PSA): Just Do It!
    summary

    TL;DR: CNCF community post by Mathieu Benoit arguing that one namespace label enabling Pod Security Admission is a cheap, built-in security win, and showing how to enforce that label cluster-wide.

    • Background: PSA is stable in Kubernetes 1.25 (beta in 1.23) and replaces PodSecurityPolicy; levels are privileged, baseline, restricted.
    • Enable: kubectl label ns psa-tests pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.
    • Effect: An insecure nginx Deployment is created but its pods are rejected for allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities, runAsNonRoot and seccompProfile.
    • Secure example: Non-root UID 65532, drop: [ALL], readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, RuntimeDefault seccomp, nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged.
    • Enforce the label: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (beta in 1.28) denies namespaces without enforce=restricted; Kyverno is an alternative.
    • Managed: GKE Autopilot applies baseline with usability changes.

    Takeaway: Label namespaces restricted and make the label mandatory with an admission policy. Use warn or audit mode first to find breaking workloads.

  • Bootstrap an Air Gapped Cluster with Kubeadm
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post by Rob Mengert (Defense Unicorns, 12 October 2023) walking through bootstrapping a kubeadm cluster in a simulated air-gapped Fedora VM.

    • Lab: Fedora 37, Kubernetes v1.27.3, CNI plugins v1.3.0, Flannel v0.22.0; the air gap is a default route to a dummy interface, with scp from the host acting as the transfer.
    • Artifacts: Docker (for an internal registry), containerd, libcgroup, socat, conntrack-tools, CNI plugins, crictl, kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl, k9s, systemd units, kubeadm config and all images.
    • Discovery: He found dependencies by attempting install and fixing each error; each real crossing can cost 20 minutes to weeks.
    • Node prep: sysctl and module config (overlay, br_netfilter), legacy iptables, swap off; firewalld, systemd-resolved and SELinux disabled for the demo only.
    • Packages: Notes that OS packages now come from pkgs.k8s.io.
    • Caveats: Real setups may use data diodes, and artifacts here were not scanned before crossing.

    Takeaway: Build and test a complete artifact manifest before the real crossing. Every missed dependency is another trip.

  • ssh-audit: SSH Server and Client Security Auditing
    summary

    TL;DR: ssh-audit, maintained by Joe Testa (fork of arthepsy/ssh-audit), audits SSH server and client configuration: banners, key exchange, host keys, ciphers, MACs and compression.

    • Analysis: Flags algorithms as unsafe, weak or legacy and gives add/remove recommendations based on the detected software version.
    • History: Uses version history for OpenSSH, Dropbear SSH and libssh to judge compatibility.
    • Policy scans: Check against built-in or custom hardened policies (-P, -M custom_policy.txt).
    • Platform: Linux and Windows, Python 3.10-3.14, no dependencies; PyPI, Homebrew, Docker and Snap packages.
    • Extras: Hardening guides and a web front-end.
    • Status: Actively maintained (about 4.3k stars, pushed October 2026).

    Takeaway: Run it against your bastions and in CI with a policy file to keep SSH crypto settings from drifting.

  • sshlog: SSH Session Monitoring Daemon
    summary

    TL;DR: SSHLog is a free, open source C++/Python Linux daemon that passively monitors OpenSSH servers via eBPF, recording sessions and triggering actions on activity.

    • Recording: Logs all SSH session commands and output for every user.
    • Session sharing: Attach to another user’s session read-only or interactively with sshlog attach [TTY ID].
    • Actions: Slack messages or arbitrary commands on events, remote syslog forwarding, statsd metrics, plug-in architecture.
    • No replacement: Works with the existing OpenSSH daemon.
    • Deploy: Runs as a privileged Docker container (ghcr.io/sshlog/agent:1.1.0) with --net=host --pid=host; diagnostic mode exposes a web UI on port 5000.
    • CLI: sshlog sessions and sshlog watch for live activity.

    Takeaway: Useful for bastion auditing without changing sshd. Lock it down, because session injection and a privileged container are powerful features for attackers too.

  • Vulnerability Management: You Should Know About EPSS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Ryan McGeehan’s Starting Up Security post (9 October 2023) explaining FIRST’s Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and why its probabilistic, accountable scores help prioritize large CVE backlogs.

    • What it is: EPSS gives the probability that a CVE is exploited in the wild within the next 30 days.
    • Example: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) scored about 97.5%; before in-the-wild exploitation was seen it was 95.2%, and exploitation followed within 30 days.
    • Lookup: https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-2019-0708&pretty=true returns epss and percentile.
    • Versus CVSS: CVSS is an ordinal, hand-crafted score with no measurable error; EPSS is statistical, changes daily and can be scored (e.g. Brier scores); FIRSTCON 2023 data shows it is close to calibrated.
    • Limits: CVE-only, so first-party bugs without CVEs get no score; unusual cases like Log4j are hard (Log4j started at 35%).
    • Role: Scores help triage until human analysis happens; they do not replace it.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; based on a Wayback Machine copy of the article.

    Takeaway: Add EPSS as a second sort key on top of CVSS when triaging scanner output. Fetch it from the free FIRST API.

  • SSH-Harvester: Harvest Passwords Automatically from OpenSSH Server
    summary

    TL;DR: SSH-Harvester by jm33-m0 is a post-exploitation PoC that injects a shared library into a running OpenSSH sshd and captures passwords as users log in.

    • Tested on: OpenSSH portable 8.2p1 and 9.3p1.
    • Demo: sudo ./start_sshd.sh, then ./inject.sh, then ssh -p2222 user@localhost.
    • Injection: Per the author’s blog, uses __libc_dlopen_mode via GDB (echo 'print __libc_dlopen_mode("/path/lib.so", 2)' | gdb -p <PID>), so sshd need not restart; root is assumed.
    • Harvesting: The library forks a monitor that PTRACE_ATTACHes to sshd children, breakpoints auth_password, and reads the password from RSI.
    • Weaponized version: The author recommends the emp3r0r framework; last push May 2023.

    Takeaway: Root on an SSH server means password logins can be silently harvested. Prefer key-based auth and alert on ptrace or gdb attaching to sshd.

  • marvin: CLI Tool That Scans a K8s Cluster with CEL Expressions for Issues and Misconfigurations
    summary

    TL;DR: Marvin, by Undistro, is a CLI that scans a Kubernetes cluster using CEL (Common Expression Language) checks to report misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and best-practice gaps.

    • Run: marvin scan against the current kubeconfig context; output lists severity, check ID, status and failed/passed counts.
    • Built-in checks: e.g. M-101 host namespaces, M-102 privileged container, M-104 hostPath, M-201 credentials in config, M-113 running as root, M-402/M-403 probes, M-405 to M-407 requests and limits.
    • Custom checks: Write your own CEL checks and run marvin scan --disable-builtin --checks ./examples/.
    • Install: GitHub release binaries, install script, Krew (kubectl plugin) or from source.
    • Ecosystem: Used as a plugin in Zora; supports skipping resources and documents required RBAC.

    Takeaway: A light, scriptable posture scanner. CEL custom checks make it easy to encode your own cluster policies.

  • Terraform AWS Provider: Everything You Need to Know About Multi-Account Authentication and Configuration
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Hector Reyes Aleman’s Medium guide (14 October 2023) to authenticating the Terraform AWS provider across multiple AWS accounts, from SSO profiles to state layout, workspaces and provider aliases.

    • Scenario: AWS Organizations with Identity Center; Identity, Shared-Services, Dev, Test and Prod accounts; deploy an S3 bucket per environment.
    • Precedence: Provider parameters, then env vars, shared credentials, shared config, container credentials, instance profile, matching the AWS CLI and SDKs.
    • SSO users: aws configure sso creates named profiles using a “Terraform” permission set; no static keys needed.
    • IAM users: Avoid scattering IAM users; keep them in one monitored Identity account and assume roles into others.
    • State: Partial backend configuration, either per workload account or centralized in Shared-Services with profile = "shared-services" in the S3 backend.
    • Workspaces and aliases: Map terraform.workspace to account IDs; use provider alias for cross-account resources such as Route 53 delegation.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Pick one entry point (SSO profiles locally, OIDC in CI) and assume roles from there. Keep state in a separate, locked-down account.

  • Amazon EC2 Now Supports Setting AMIs to a Disabled State
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS What’s New (13 October 2023): EC2 AMIs can now be set to a disabled state, which keeps them but blocks new launches.

    • Effect: A disabled AMI becomes private if it was shared, and no new instances can launch from it.
    • Why: Deregistering was not always allowed for regulatory, compliance or governance reasons, so obsolete AMIs piled up.
    • Discovery: Disabled AMIs are hidden from DescribeImages by default.
    • Reversible: Re-enable with a simple API call.
    • Availability: All Regions, including GovCloud and China.

    Takeaway: Disable outdated or vulnerable golden images instead of deleting them. That keeps audit history while stopping new launches.

  • viddy: A Modern Watch Command
    summary

    TL;DR: Viddy, by sachaos, is a modern replacement for watch. It runs a command periodically and adds history you can rewind.

    • Basics: Runs a command at an interval with colour output and diff highlighting.
    • Time machine: Rewind through earlier outputs “like video”. History can be saved and loaded.
    • Navigation: Output in a pager, Vim-like keymaps, text search, and suspend or restart of execution.
    • Customisation: Keymaps and colours. Supports shell aliases.
    • Install: cargo install viddy, brew install viddy, release tarballs, and community packages (APT via pkg.haus, MacPorts, Scoop, AUR).
    • Status: Not archived. The current README gives a Cargo install, which shows the tool is now distributed as a Rust crate.

    Takeaway: Drop it in wherever you use watch, e.g. viddy kubectl get pods. Rewinding means you can still see a short-lived state after it has passed.

  • Oh-Auth: Abusing OAuth to Take over Millions of Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: Salt Labs research by Aviad Carmel (24 October 2023), third in an OAuth series, showing account takeover on Grammarly, Vidio and Bukalapak because they did not verify that social-login access tokens were issued for their own app.

    • Flaw: Sites accepted a Facebook (or similar) access token without checking its App ID, e.g. via graph.facebook.com/debug_token.
    • Attack: An attacker runs a lure site (“YourTimePlanner.com”) with social login, collects users’ tokens for its own App ID, then replays them to the vulnerable site.
    • Impact: Full account takeover for users whose email matched; Vidio alone has 100M monthly active users.
    • Scope: Applies to implicit and explicit flows and PostMessage-based flows; Google, Apple and others work similarly.
    • Status: All three companies fixed the issues; Salt expects thousands of other sites are vulnerable.
    • Series: Earlier posts covered Booking.com and Expo.

    Takeaway: Always verify the token audience (App ID or client ID) server-side before trusting a social login. The fix is about one line.

  • Azure Security Best Practices and Patterns
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft Learn index page of Azure security best practices for designing, deploying and managing Azure solutions, aimed at IT pros. The page has been updated since 2023 to reference newer benchmarks.

    • Topics: Secrets, databases, data encryption, identity and access, network, operational security, AI, PaaS, Service Fabric, IaaS, hybrid networks, IoT, App Service and Storage.
    • Benchmark: Points to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) as the main set of prescriptive controls.
    • MCSB v2 (preview): Adds an AI security domain with seven recommendations and grows Azure Policy measurements from over 220 to over 420.
    • Implementation: Track compliance in the Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard and enforce baselines with Azure Policy.
    • SFI: Also references Microsoft’s Secure Future Initiative and its six Zero Trust-aligned pillars.

    Takeaway: Treat this as a map of Azure security guidance. MCSB in Defender for Cloud and Azure Policy is the practical place to start.

  • nebula: AI-Powered Ethical Hacking Assistant
    summary

    TL;DR: Nebula by Beryllium Security started as an AI-powered ethical hacking assistant; the repository now describes itself as a “cybersecurity harness built around the operator”.

    • Page changed: The current README describes a much newer product than the 2023 assistant in the title.
    • Projects: One project per engagement holding assets, browser sessions, Kali terminals, code, notes, findings and reports.
    • Testing tools: Security browser with interception, Repeater and Intruder; Kali tools in Docker or Podman with optional OpenVPN egress.
    • AI features: Add SKILL.md skills; the “Butler” assistant can review chats, start work and manage approvals; optional OpenAI voice.
    • Controls: Operator-set scope, approvals and budgets; hashed evidence and provenance linked to findings and reports.
    • Warning: Use only on systems you own or are authorized to test.

    Takeaway: Now more of an engagement workspace than a chat helper. Evaluate the current version, not the 2023 one.

  • tabby: Self-Hosted AI Coding Assistant
    summary

    TL;DR: Tabby by TabbyML is a self-hosted, open source AI coding assistant offered as an on-premises alternative to GitHub Copilot (about 33.9k stars).

    • Self-contained: No external DBMS or cloud service needed.
    • Integration: OpenAPI interface for cloud IDEs and existing infrastructure.
    • Hardware: Runs on consumer-grade GPUs.
    • Recent releases: v0.27 to v0.30 (2025) added a richer @ menu, shareable Answer Engine pages, docs via REST API and GitLab merge request indexing; LDAP auth arrived in v0.24.
    • Agent: TabbyML’s Pochi links GitHub issues to tasks and PRs.
    • Deploy: Docker images (tabbyml/tabby) and a live demo.

    Takeaway: A solid option when code cannot leave your network. Budget GPU capacity and pin a release.

  • cve: Gather and Update All Available and Newest CVEs with Their PoC
    summary

    TL;DR: trickest/cve is an automatically updated repository collecting almost every publicly available proof-of-concept for CVEs, organized by year (about 8.2k stars).

    • Source data: CVE details from the CVE Project’s cvelist.
    • Reference mining: Checks each CVE’s references for PoCs using ffuf with the regex (?i)[^a-z0-9]+(poc|proof of concept|proof[-_]of[-_]concept)[^a-z0-9]+.
    • GitHub search: find-gh-poc finds repos mentioning the CVE ID; HackerOne video PoCs are included too.
    • Hygiene: Merges new results without overwriting manual edits; false positives filtered via blacklist.txt.
    • Extras: Per-CVE markdown pages, version badges, and a hot CVE list (hot_cves.csv).
    • Automation: Built on Trickest workflows.

    Takeaway: Quick way to check whether a CVE has public exploit code, which matters for prioritization. Treat PoC repos as untrusted code.

  • Slack Attack: A Phisher’s Guide to Initial Access
    summary

    TL;DR: Push Security post by Luke Jennings (24 October 2023) showing how external attackers can phish employees via Slack Connect, using IM phishing (SAT1018) and IM user spoofing (SAT1019) from Push’s SaaS attack matrix.

    • Why IM: Users trust IM more than email, it feels urgent, and it lacks email-style gateways and controls such as SPF.
    • External invites: Slack Connect invites carry attacker-chosen user and org names; the hidden first message tempts targets to accept.
    • Internal spoofing: Once in a shared channel, an external user can mimic an internal employee and DM members without a new invite.
    • Chameleon attack: After a benign first connection, the attacker later renames themselves (e.g. to the CEO) and messages again; useful for CEO fraud against finance staff.
    • Link previews: Link forging and unfurled previews can hide the real destination, with weaker analysis than email gateways.
    • Context: Slack Connect launched June 2020 and Teams external access January 2022; similar attacks may apply to other IM apps.

    Takeaway: Restrict Slack Connect to approved organizations and train staff that external display names can change at any time.

  • A Short Note on AWS KEY ID: Decode to AWS Account Number
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Tal Be’ery’s Medium note (24 October 2023) showing how to decode the AWS account ID from an access key ID, refining earlier work by Scott Piper and Aidan Steele.

    • Structure: The first four characters (e.g. AKIA, ASIA) are a documented key-type prefix.
    • Encoding: The remaining 16 characters are Base32, giving 80 bits (10 bytes).
    • Trick: The account ID sits in the first bytes but is shifted by one bit: take the first 6 bytes, mask 0x7fffffffff80, shift right by 7.
    • Example: ASIAY34FZKBOKMUTVV7A decodes to account 609629065308; a Python function and an online demo are provided.
    • Updates: Bitmask bug fixed 25 October 2023; older keys starting with I/J appear to use different logic (January 2024).
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: A leaked key ID alone reveals which account it belongs to, even offline. Use it in triage of leaked keys without calling AWS APIs.

  • local-ai-stack: Starter Kit to Build Local-Only AI Apps That Cost $0 to Run
    summary

    TL;DR: local-ai-stack by ykhli is a JavaScript starter kit for document Q&A apps that run 100% locally at no cost, based on a16z’s AI Starter Kit.

    • Inference: Ollama.
    • Vector DB: Supabase pgvector, run locally with supabase start.
    • Orchestration: Langchain.js; app logic in Next.js.
    • Embeddings: Transformers.js with all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
    • Steps: npm install, set SUPABASE_PRIVATE_KEY from supabase status, run node src/scripts/indexBlogLocal.mjs, then npm run dev on localhost:3000.
    • Status: Last push January 2024.

    Takeaway: A small, readable RAG reference that keeps data on your machine. Expect to update dependencies, since it has not changed since early 2024.

  • Use Shared VPC Subnets in Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog walkthrough of running EKS clusters in subnets shared from a central network account via AWS RAM, so a network team owns the VPC and a platform team owns the cluster.

    • Model: The owner (network) account shares subnets with participant (application) accounts in the same AWS Organization.
    • Lab: aws-samples/eks-shared-subnets; a CloudFormation VPC with nine subnets over three AZs (control plane, worker nodes, public load balancers), shared via Resource Access Manager.
    • Network team scope: IP allocation, routes, IGWs, NAT gateways, peering and on-prem connectivity.
    • Considerations: Cluster and nodes should sit in shared subnets of the same VPC; EKS does not support clusters across multiple VPCs.
    • Security groups: Cluster, node and pod security groups must be created in the participant account.
    • Tooling: AWS CLI with credentials for both accounts and eksctl.

    Takeaway: Shared VPCs centralize network control without giving app teams VPC admin. Plan IP space and security group ownership up front.

  • How to Upgrade Amazon EKS Worker Nodes with Karpenter Drift
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog post (updated May 2024 for the Karpenter v1beta1 API) on patching and upgrading EKS worker nodes continuously using Karpenter’s Drift feature.

    • Drift: Nodes that no longer match their NodePool or EC2NodeClass are replaced by provisioning new nodes, cordoning and evicting pods, then terminating old ones.
    • Timing: Drift checks run every 5 minutes, and immediately when a NodePool or EC2NodeClass changes.
    • AMI families: AL2, AL2023, Bottlerocket, Ubuntu, Windows2019, Windows2022 and Custom (which needs amiSelectorTerms).
    • Pinned AMIs: Set AMI IDs, names or tags in the EC2NodeClass to promote AMIs through environments; if several match, the latest is used.
    • Auto AMIs: With EKS-optimized AMIs, new releases or a control plane upgrade trigger drift automatically.
    • Safeguards: Karpenter respects PodDisruptionBudgets with backoff; karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true" protects sensitive pods.

    Takeaway: Drift turns node patching into a continuous process. Pin AMIs if you need staged promotion, and set PDBs before turning it on.

  • Operating Resilient Workloads on Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog post on designing resilient workloads on EKS by spreading replicas across more failure domains: nodes, AZs, clusters and Regions.

    • Principles: High availability, fault tolerance, auto scaling, self-healing, safer upgrades (blue/green, canary) and easy rollbacks.
    • Shared responsibility: AWS runs the EKS control plane across multiple AZs and replaces unhealthy instances; customers own workload resilience.
    • Kubernetes features: Replicas, health checks and self-healing, resource quotas and limits for fault isolation, rolling updates and rollbacks.
    • Patterns: Multi-node, multi-AZ, multi-cluster and multi-Region deployments.
    • Trade-off: Each extra failure domain adds cost and operational overhead, so match it to workload criticality.

    Takeaway: Start with multi-AZ replicas, topology spread and probes. Go multi-cluster or multi-Region only when the business impact justifies the cost.

  • kor: Golang Tool to Discover Unused Kubernetes Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Kor by yonahd is a Go tool that finds unused (orphaned) Kubernetes resources so you can clean up clusters.

    • Resource types: ConfigMaps, Secrets, Services, ServiceAccounts, Deployments, StatefulSets, Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, HPAs, PVCs, PVs, Ingresses, PDBs, CRDs, Jobs, ReplicaSets, DaemonSets, StorageClasses, NetworkPolicies and more.
    • Install: Release binaries, brew install kor, go install github.com/yonahd/kor@latest, Docker (yonahdissen/kor), Krew (kubectl krew install kor) or Helm.
    • Cluster mode: Can run as a CronJob in the cluster via Helm.
    • Output: Shows the reason each resource is considered unused.
    • Commercial: KorPro adds cost analysis and multi-cluster management.
    • Status: Active, about 1.9k stars.

    Takeaway: Run kor all before cleanup sprints; unused Secrets and ServiceAccounts are security debt, not just clutter. Verify before deleting.

  • InfoSecMap: Mapping Out the Best InfoSec Events and Groups!
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: InfoSecMap is a free, community-run directory and map of InfoSec events and groups, from major conferences to CTFs and local meetups.

    • Filtering: Find listings by geography, type and topic, with list and map views for events and groups.
    • Extra pages: Calls for papers, sponsors, trainers and volunteers.
    • Hubs: Organization hubs for DEF CON, 2600, LATAM, OWASP and Security BSides; a DEF CON Groups map at infosecmap.com/defcon.
    • Curation: Automated tools plus manual review of submissions.
    • Support: OWASP lists it as a corporate supporter; free to use.
    • Source caveat: The site returned a Cloudflare challenge; based on web search results from its own pages and OWASP.

    Takeaway: Handy for finding local meetups and open CFPs. Confirm dates on the event’s own site.

  • Gsec: Web Security Scanner
    summary

    TL;DR: Gsec by gotr00t0day is a Python web security scanner and exploitation tool combining custom scanners with Nuclei.

    • Passive scan: Shodan assets, RapidDNS and crt.sh subdomains, DNS enumeration, Wayback URLs, related domains.
    • Active scan: Ports, server info, security headers, CMS checks, tech and language detection, path traversal, crawling, OS detection, Nuclei.
    • Vuln checks: SSRF, XSS, host header injection, CORS, session management and SSL/TLS analysis.
    • Newer suites: README now covers v3.8 with API testing (BOLA/IDOR, mass assignment), cloud misconfiguration, request smuggling and GraphQL tests, so it has grown since 2023.
    • Comparison: The README’s table comparing it to Nikto, ZAP and Burp is the author’s own claim.
    • Requirements: Python 3.11.3 badge; API keys for some services.

    Takeaway: A one-shot recon and scan wrapper for authorized tests. Validate findings by hand, since it wraps many tools of mixed precision.

  • raven: Risk Analysis and Vulnerability Enumeration for CI/CD
    summary

    TL;DR: Raven (Risk Analysis and Vulnerability Enumeration for CI/CD) is an Apache 2.0 tool from Cycode Labs that mass-downloads GitHub Actions workflows, loads them into a Neo4j graph and runs queries to find insecure CI patterns.

    • Components: A downloader (per org/user or top public repos by star count), an indexer into Neo4j, a predefined query library and a reporter that can run in PR CI.
    • Install: pip3 install raven-cycode, plus a local Redis server and Neo4j database (Docker examples in the README).
    • Track record: Cycode says it used Raven to find and report issues in FreeCodeCamp, Storybook and Microsoft Fluent UI, and keeps a hall of fame of disclosed findings.
    • Attack classes: The research behind it covers workflow injection, branch-name injection, third-party integration risk and artifact poisoning.
    • Uses: Scanning your own org, bug bounty scanning of named orgs, and research.
    • Status: The repo is still active (pushes in 2026).

    Takeaway: Useful for auditing many GitHub Actions workflows at once instead of reading YAML by hand. Run it against your own org and review the injection and artifact findings first.

  • Announcing the EKS Cluster Games
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz Research announced The EKS Cluster Games, a free online cloud security CTF in which players act as attackers against common Amazon EKS misconfigurations.

    • Format: Five scenarios, each focused on one possible EKS security issue. Wiz says it has seen some of them in its own research engagements.
    • Participation: Individual completion is tracked, but teams may discuss strategies.
    • Rewards: Registered finishers appear on a live leaderboard and receive a certificate. KubeCon 2023 attendees could claim a prize at the Wiz booth.
    • Access: The challenge runs in the browser from anywhere. Questions go to research@wiz.io.
    • Context: It follows Wiz’s earlier cloud CTFs and targets Kubernetes-on-AWS identity and access issues.

    Takeaway: A low-cost way for a team to practise EKS attack paths hands-on. Use it as a training exercise before reviewing your own cluster configuration.

  • osquery-defense-kit: Production-Ready Detection and Response Queries for osquery
    summary

    TL;DR: osquery-defense-kit (ODK) from Chainguard is an Apache 2.0 set of 250+ osquery queries for detection and incident response on Linux and macOS.

    • Design rule: Detection queries are written to return zero rows during normal behaviour, so any returned row can raise an alert.
    • Layout: detection/ (grouped by MITRE ATT&CK tactic), policy/ and incident_response/ for periodic evidence collection.
    • Requirements: osquery 5.7.0 or later, macOS or Linux, and Go 1.20+ for the osqtool helper if developing locally.
