    • Commands: make detect (point-in-time), make collect (IR snapshot), make packs and make verify. Released query packs plug into the packs stanza of osquery.conf.
    • Case studies: The README maps real malware such as Shikitega (Linux, 2022) to queries that would have fired, e.g. execution/tiny-executable.sql and execution/unexpected-shell-parents.sql.

    Takeaway: A ready-made starting set if you already run osquery fleet-wide. Expect to tune exceptions for your environment before alerting on every row.

  • GOAD: Pentest Active Directory Lab Project
    summary

    TL;DR: GOAD (Game Of Active Directory) from Orange Cyberdefense is a GPL-3.0 project that builds a deliberately vulnerable Active Directory lab for pentest practice.

    • Labs: GOAD full (5 VMs, 2 forests, 3 domains), GOAD-Light (3 VMs, 1 forest, 2 domains), MINILAB (1 DC on Windows Server 2019 plus 1 Windows 10 workstation), SCCM (4 VMs with Configuration Manager), and challenge labs NHA and DRACARYS with no schema given.
    • Licensing: Uses free 180-day Windows evaluation VMs. After that, license each server or rebuild.
    • Version: Now at GOAD v3 with documentation at orange-cyberdefense.github.io/GOAD.
    • Warning: The authors say the lab is extremely vulnerable. Do not reuse its recipes for real environments or expose it to the internet without isolation.
    • Status: Actively maintained, about 8.5k stars.

    Takeaway: One of the most complete free AD attack labs. Run it on an isolated host network and plan for the 180-day rebuild cycle.

  • tetragon: eBPF-Based Security Observability and Runtime Enforcement
    summary

    TL;DR: Tetragon is the Cilium project’s eBPF-based tool for security observability and runtime enforcement on Linux hosts and Kubernetes.

    • Events: Process execution and exit (process_exec, process_exit by default), system call activity, and file and network I/O.
    • Kubernetes-aware: Events are enriched with namespace and pod identity, so detection can be scoped per workload.
    • Generic tracing: process_kprobe, process_tracepoint and process_uprobe events, configured through TracingPolicy resources.
    • Use cases: Network observability, filename access, credential monitoring and privileged execution.
    • Tooling: Install guides for Kubernetes and plain Linux (Docker), plus the tetra CLI. Docs live at tetragon.io.
    • License: Apache 2.0 for user space, with BSD/GPL for eBPF code.

    Takeaway: Worth evaluating as a Falco-style runtime sensor if you already run Cilium. Start with process lifecycle events, then add TracingPolicies for sensitive files.

  • Go, Containers, and the Linux Scheduler
    summary

    TL;DR: River Phillips explains (Nov 2023) why Go services in CPU-limited containers can see long garbage collection pauses, and fixes it by setting GOMAXPROCS to the CPU quota.

    • Cause: The Go runtime creates one OS thread per host core and ignores cgroup CPU limits, so on a 16-core host it expects 16 CPU-seconds per second.
    • Scheduler: Under the Linux CFS quota, threads stop being scheduled once the container uses its quota, which stretches GC stop-the-world phases.
    • Measurement: With docker run --cpus=4 and no limit set, a GC cycle took just under 2.5 ms with almost 10% in stop-the-world, per go tool trace.
    • Fix: With -e GOMAXPROCS=4, the cycle dropped under 1 ms and stop-the-world was 26 μs, about one tenth.
    • Rule: GOMAXPROCS=max(1, floor(CPUs)), or use Uber’s automaxprocs library to read the value from cgroups.
    • Note: The post mentions CFS was the default until Linux 6.6 and an open Go issue to make this automatic.

    Takeaway: If you run Go with CPU limits, set GOMAXPROCS or import automaxprocs. Check your Go version first, since newer runtimes may handle this themselves.

  • goleak: Goroutine Leak Detector
    summary

    TL;DR: goleak is Uber’s MIT-licensed Go library that fails tests when goroutines are still running at the end of a test or test package.

    • Install: go get -u go.uber.org/goleak. It supports only the two most recent Go minor versions.
    • Per test: defer goleak.VerifyNone(t) at the start of a test.
    • Per package: goleak.VerifyTestMain(m) inside TestMain, which also suits tests using t.Parallel().
    • Limitation: With t.Parallel, per-test checks cannot tell a leak from a test that has not finished.
    • Finding the culprit: Build with go test -c -o tests, then run each test from go test -list . individually to see which one leaks.
    • Stability: v1 with strict SemVer.

    Takeaway: Adding VerifyTestMain to packages with background workers is cheap and catches leaks early in CI.

  • tailspin: A Log File Highlighter
    summary

    TL;DR: tailspin (tspin) is an MIT-licensed Rust log viewer by Ben Sadeh that highlights dates, numbers, IPs, UUIDs, URLs and more in any log format with no configuration.

    • How: Runs a set of pattern matchers on each line and makes no assumption about log format.
    • Usage: tspin application.log (opens in less), kubectl logs pod --follow | tspin, or tspin --exec='kubectl logs -f pod_name'.
    • Highlight groups: Dates, durations, keywords (severities, booleans, null, HTTP methods), URLs, numbers, UUIDs, key-value pairs, pointers and Unix processes. Toggle with --enable and --disable.
    • Extras: --extras ipv6 or jvm-stack-trace, or set TAILSPIN_EXTRAS.
    • Theming: ~/.config/tailspin/theme.toml.
    • Install: brew install tailspin, cargo install tailspin, and packages for Arch, Nix, FreeBSD, NetBSD and Windows (scoop).

    Takeaway: A drop-in improvement for reading raw logs in a terminal. Pipe kubectl logs through it when you do not have a log UI to hand.

  • sshx: Fast, Collaborative Live Terminal Sharing over the Web
    summary

    TL;DR: sshx by Eric Zhang is an MIT-licensed tool that shares a terminal over the web with one command, on a collaborative infinite canvas.

    • Features: Multiple movable windows, live cursors, a global server mesh, automatic reconnection, latency estimates and Mosh-style predictive echo.
    • Encryption: End-to-end with Argon2 and AES.
    • Install: curl -sSf https://sshx.io/get | sh, or ... | sh -s run to run without installing, or brew install sshx.
    • CI debugging: Add the run command as a step to get a live shell in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and others. The author warns that anyone can see the session URL in public CI logs.
    • Hosting: The servers run on Fly.io and Redis Cloud. Self-hosting is not supported.

    Takeaway: Handy for pairing and CI debugging, but it relies on a third-party hosted service. Do not use it in public repos or on systems where an external relay is not allowed.

  • Security Considerations for Running Containers on Amazon ECS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (Mutaz Hajeer, Ibtissam Liedri, Temi Adebambo, Nov 2023, updated through 2025) sets out the customer’s security responsibilities on Amazon ECS and a list of best practices.

    • Shared responsibility: On EC2 and External instances there is no task isolation, and containers can reach agent data and other tasks’ credentials. Each Fargate task runs in its own VM.
    • IAM: Least-privilege resource-level permissions, a scoped task role per task definition, deploys through CI/CD pipelines, and CloudTrail auditing of ECS API access.
    • Network: awsvpc mode (the only mode with per-task security groups), TLS in transit, separate VPCs for strict isolation, and PrivateLink endpoints for ECS, ECR, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch.
    • Secrets: Secrets Manager or encrypted SSM Parameter Store with KMS. ECS does not support versioned Parameter Store parameters.
    • Runtime: Amazon Inspector scanning of ECR images, ECR tag immutability, non-root USER, no privileged mode (Security Hub control ECS.4), no ECS Exec in production, and dropped Linux capabilities.
    • Updates: Jan 2024 added GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for ECS. Mid-2025 updates clarified container and instance security boundaries.

    Takeaway: A good checklist for an ECS review. Prefer Fargate where you need task isolation, and treat co-located EC2 tasks as one trust zone.

  • websec-answers: In-Depth Answers for Websec Interview Questions by tib3rius
    summary

    TL;DR: websec-answers by x1trap is a community repo with in-depth answers to Tib3rius’s web security interview questions (tib3rius.com/interview-questions).

    • Content: The author tries to answer every question and has also added a LinkedIn Q&A section.
    • Caveat: The author warns that answers may contain mistakes or gaps.
    • Format: A short README links to the answer documents. There is no license.
    • Activity: The last push was in November 2023, so the repo appears unmaintained since then.

    Takeaway: Useful revision material for AppSec or pentest interviews. Check answers against primary sources such as PortSwigger before relying on them.

  • OffensiveGo: Golang Weaponization for Red Teamers
    summary

    TL;DR: OffensiveGo by @RistBS, @Enelg and @dreamkinn collects examples of offensive tooling rewritten in Go for red team engagements, in the style of OffensiveRust and OffensiveNim.

    • Why Go: Simple syntax, garbage collection, easy cross-compilation and goroutines.
    • OPSEC caveat: Static linking makes binaries large, about 1.9 MB for Hello World versus 54 KB in C.
    • Build tips: go build -ldflags="-s -w" strips symbols (about 30% smaller). -ldflags -H=windowsgui hides the console window.
    • Topics: Workspace setup with go mod, Plan 9 assembly in Go, obfuscating builds and Go binary internals.
    • Examples: A set of offensive utilities plus a list of other notable Go security tools.
    • Status: Last push January 2024, no license.

    Takeaway: A reference for red teamers moving tooling to Go. Defenders can use it to understand how Go implants are built and stripped.

  • Terraform Security Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: Nigel Douglas of Sysdig (Mar 2023) lists Terraform security best practices, centred on scanning manifests and keeping secrets out of code and state.

    • Scan manifests: Terrascan, Checkov and KICS, e.g. terrascan scan -f /path/to/terraform/code. The post links this to the SCARLETEEL incident, where keys in S3 aided lateral movement.
    • Credentials: No hardcoded secrets. Use TF_VAR_ env vars or -var, Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, frequent rotation and least-privilege IAM.
    • Modules: Review what third-party modules create, always terraform plan before apply, and update with terraform get -update.
    • State: Remote, encrypted state (S3 with encrypt = true plus DynamoDB locking). Never edit state by hand; use terraform import.
    • Process: Git version control, GPG signing of manifests (Terraform has no built-in signing), and CI/CD with validate, fmt -check and plan -out.
    • Other: Do not put secrets in outputs. Use prevent_destroy = true for critical resources.

    Takeaway: A baseline checklist. The most useful items are a scanner in CI and an encrypted remote state backend.

  • A Comprehensive Guide to Testing in Terraform: Keep Your Tests, Validations, Checks, and Policies in Order
    summary

    TL;DR: A guide on mattias.engineer covers every layer of Terraform validation, from terraform validate to custom conditions, terraform test, check blocks and Sentinel policies, and says when to use each.

    • CLI: terraform validate and terraform fmt during development and in the pipeline.
    • Custom conditions: Variable validation blocks, lifecycle precondition/postcondition that halt an apply, and output preconditions.
    • terraform test (1.6+): .tftest.hcl files with run blocks, command = plan or apply (default apply), assert and expect_failures. Mainly for module producers.
    • check blocks (1.5+): A scoped data source plus assert. Failures are warnings, not blockers, and suit continuous validation, e.g. an http check on a website.
    • Policies: OPA/Rego or Sentinel. The local workflow is terraform plan -out=tfplan, terraform show -json, then sentinel apply. Policies belong to the organisation, not inside modules.
    • Samples: A local provider module with four tests, and an azurerm consumer with a check and storage policies.
    • Source caveat: The URL now redirects to mattias.engineer/blog/2023/terraform-testing-and-validation/.

    Takeaway: A clear map of which Terraform mechanism to use for which failure. Use tests for module interfaces, conditions for blocking failures and checks for monitoring.

  • kube-audit-rest: Kubernetes Audit Logging When You Don’t Control the Control Plane
    summary

    TL;DR: kube-audit-rest by Richard Tweed is an Apache 2.0 service that captures Kubernetes create and mutation API calls through a validating admission webhook, for clusters where you cannot configure API server audit logging (EKS, GKE, AKS).

    • Motivation: Managed audit logs bill per call and cannot be filtered at ingestion. The author says this can avoid thousands of dollars per cluster per year.
    • Scope: A logger only. Filtering, redaction and forwarding are left to other tools (Elasticsearch examples provided).
    • Requirements: Permission to create a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration, a CA and TLS certificate, a reachable endpoint and disk space (default /tmp).
    • Fallback: A MutatingAdmissionWebhook also works, but a subverted binary could then enable cluster takeover and may not log the final object.
    • Images: Distroless (default) and Alpine variants for amd64 and arm64. Deployment examples are in ./k8s and testing/setup.sh.
    • Advice: If you control the API server, use built-in audit logging instead.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to get filterable change logs from managed clusters. Note it only sees writes that pass admission, not reads.

  • sso-sync-to-amazon-rds: Sync SSO Users from AWS IAM Identity Center to Amazon RDS Databases
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Samples CDK solution that syncs users from AWS IAM Identity Center groups into PostgreSQL or MySQL RDS databases, so they log in with IAM authentication and temporary AWS credentials.

    • Flow: An Identity Center user event goes to EventBridge, which triggers a Lambda that adds the username. The event is forwarded cross-account to a custom bus, where a Lambda creates or deletes the DB user and records the mapping in DynamoDB.
    • Stacks: EventBridgeSSOLambda (Identity Center account), EventBridgeLambdaRDS (database account) and Outputs (reads existing DB endpoint and VPC details). It does not create databases.
    • Group filter: IAM_IDC_GROUP_NAMES, e.g. "DBA,Analytics". Group names must match pre-created database role names.
    • Design: Built for multi-account and multi-region setups, since RDS rarely sits in the Identity Center account.

    Takeaway: A pattern for removing static database passwords for humans. Review the Lambda’s DB privileges before deploying, since it can create users.

  • MTKPI: Multi Tool Kubernetes Pentest Image
    summary

    TL;DR: MTKPI (Multi Tool Kubernetes Pentest Image) by r0binak is an MIT-licensed container image bundling common Kubernetes pentest tools, for clusters where you cannot download tools into a pod.

    • Base: Built on ttyd, so you get a web shell through port-forward when your service account lacks pods/exec.
    • Tools: botb, kubeletctl, kubesploit agent, CDK, peirates, traitor, ctrsploit, kdigger, kubectl, deepce, helm, kube-hunter, kube-bench, DDexec and kubetcd.
    • Coverage: The author says it covers most of the Microsoft Threat Matrix for Kubernetes.
    • Evasion: Renames binaries (kubectl to k, curl to kurl) to dodge signature-based rules in Falco or Tracee.
    • Deploy: kubectl apply -f .../deploy/mtkpi.yaml (image r0binak/mtkpi:v1, port 7681, read-only root filesystem).
    • Warning: Some tools can damage the cluster. Test in environments such as KIND.

    Takeaway: Useful for authorised assessments. Defenders should note that renaming binaries defeats name-based detection rules.

02.10.2023

  • Chrome Extensions Can Steal Plaintext Passwords from Websites
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (Bill Toulas, Sep 2023) reports University of Wisconsin-Madison research showing Chrome extensions can read plaintext passwords from web pages, and a proof-of-concept extension passed Chrome Web Store review.

    • Flaw: Extensions get broad DOM access, and Manifest V3 adds no security boundary between extensions and page content, so input values can be read as the user types.
    • Scale: About 17,300 extensions (12.5% of the store) have the needed permissions, and 190 already read password fields into variables.
    • Websites: Of the top 10,000 sites, about 1,100 store passwords in plaintext in the DOM and about 7,300 allow direct extraction of input values.
    • Examples: gmail.com and cloudflare.com (plaintext passwords in source), facebook.com and citibank.com (DOM extraction), irs.gov and capitalone.com (SSNs), amazon.com (card details).
    • Ethics: The PoC was approved but kept unpublished, then removed, and no data was collected.
    • Responses: Google said it was looking into it and pointed to its FAQ, which does not treat password-field access with proper permissions as a security issue.

    Takeaway: Treat every browser extension with page access as able to read credentials. Limit extensions on admin workstations with an allowlist policy.

  • llm-opstower: DevOps AI Assistant CLI for AWS Services, CloudWatch Metrics, and Billing
    summary

    TL;DR: llm-opstower is an MIT-licensed plugin for the llm CLI from OpsTower.ai that answers natural-language questions about AWS resources, CloudWatch metrics and billing.

    • Install: pip install llm, then llm install from the GitHub zip, llm keys set opstower --value demo, and llm models default opstower.
    • Examples: llm "list each ec2 instance id, name, state, last restart, image, and size" and CloudWatch CPU averages.
    • Access: A demo key uses a live demo AWS account. The docs describe creating a read-only IAM user for your own account.
    • Claims: The vendor says it leads its own DevOps AI Assistant Open Leaderboard for AWS services, metrics and billing. These are self-run evaluations.
    • Status: Described as of October 2023. The last push was August 2024, so the project appears inactive.

    Takeaway: An early example of LLM agents over cloud APIs. If you try something like it, give it only a read-only IAM role.

  • Strategies for the Integration of Software Supply Chain Security in DevSecOps CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NIST SP 800-204D (initial public draft, August 2023) by Ramaswamy Chandramouli (NIST), Frederick Kautz and Santiago Torres-Arias sets out strategies for integrating software supply chain security into DevSecOps CI/CD pipelines for cloud-native applications.

    • Scope: Microservice-based cloud-native apps, often with a service mesh, built through CI/CD pipelines that move code through build, test, package and deploy.
    • Key terms: Actors, artifacts, attestations, provenance, repositories, SBOM, SDLC and SLSA.
    • Driver: Executive Order 14028 on improving the nation’s cybersecurity.
    • Final version: NIST published the final SP 800-204D in February 2024 (doi 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-204D), so this link is to the superseded draft.
    • Source caveat: The PDF could not be text-extracted here. This summary is based on the NIST CSRC publication page (abstract, authors, keywords, dates), not the document body.

    Takeaway: Read the final February 2024 version rather than this draft. It is a useful reference when mapping SLSA, SBOM and attestation controls onto your pipeline.

  • Certified-Kubernetes-Security-Specialist: Curated Resources to Prepare for the CKS Exam
    summary

    TL;DR: Walid Shaari’s CC-BY-SA-4.0 repo curates study resources for the CNCF/Linux Foundation Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) exam, cross-referenced to the documentation allowed during the exam.

    • Exam facts (per README): 2 hours, 15-20 hands-on tasks, 67% to pass, valid 2 years, requires a valid CKA, $375 with one free retake within a year.
    • Allowed sites: kubernetes.io/docs, github.com/kubernetes and kubernetes.io/blog, plus the listed third-party tool docs.
    • Legend: Icons mark resources usable in the exam, external resources not allowed in the exam, and items still to verify.
    • Structure: Organised by the official CKS curriculum domains, with links to docs, blogs and videos.
    • Version note: Advises picking the right Kubernetes docs version (e.g. v1.26 as of January 2023). Exam details may have changed since.
    • Status: About 2.1k stars, still updated in 2026.

    Takeaway: A solid study map for CKS. Check the current Linux Foundation exam page for price, version and rules before booking.

  • pht-awsbackup-management: Scripts and IaC for a Ransomware-Resilient AWS Backup System
    summary

    TL;DR: PrimeHarbor’s pht-awsbackup-management provides scripts and CloudFormation for a ransomware-resilient, organisation-wide AWS Backup setup driven by resource tags.

    • Tag-driven tiers: aws_backup_bcp_tier = tier1 (hourly, copied to a second region, 180 days), tier2 (hourly, 180 days), tier3 (daily, 90 days), tier4 (daily, 45 days), or none.
    • Prerequisites: CloudFormation delegated admin, Backup Policies and SCPs enabled in Organizations, an AWS Backup delegated administrator with cross-account monitoring, and resource types opted in per region.
    • Vaults: Deployed to every account and region through an Organizations StackSet, preferably from us-east-1. The stack also creates CentralAWSBackupRole.
    • Setup: Get the root OU ID with aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[0].Id' --output text.
    • Status: Small repo (about 16 stars), last push September 2023, no license file.

    Takeaway: A practical pattern of tag-based tiers plus central vaults and SCP guardrails. Adapt it rather than deploy as-is, and test restores, not just backups.

  • aws-list-resources: List Resources in an AWS Account and Regions via the Cloud Control API
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-list-resources from welldone-cloud is a Python script that uses the AWS Cloud Control API to list resources in an account across regions and writes them to a JSON file.

    • Versus Resource Explorer: Cloud Control supports more resource types, needs only read access (no index or view creation), and returns global resources such as IAM roles in each region.
    • Usage: python aws_list_resources.py --regions us-east-1,eu-central-1, or --regions ALL --include-resource-types AWS::EC2::*,AWS::DynamoDB::*.
    • Options: --exclude-resource-types, --include-resource-types (wildcards), --only-store-counts and --profile.
    • Requirements: Python 3.11+ and configured AWS credentials.
    • Limits: Only finds types supported by Cloud Control’s List operation. It filters out AWS default resources, but new defaults may slip through.

    Takeaway: A quick read-only inventory for an unfamiliar or inherited account. Run it on the primary region first, since global resources appear there too.

  • Discover the Benefits of AWS WAF Advanced Rate-Based Rules
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (Rodrigo Ferroni, Maksim Akifev, Sep 2023) explains AWS WAF rate-based rules with custom aggregation keys, added in May 2023, which can count requests by attributes other than source IP.

    • Keys: Header, cookie, query parameter, query string, HTTP method, URI path, label namespace, source IP and forwarded IP. Up to five can be combined into one composite key.
    • Count all: Rate-limits all requests matching a required scope-down statement.
    • Use cases: Layer 7 DDoS by User-Agent or session cookie plus IP (for users behind NAT), and API limits by method plus Authorization header with a custom HTTP 429 and Retry-After: 900.
    • Tenancy: Different limits for free and paid tenants via a tenant-id header, or for mutating and read requests.
    • Advice: Keep a blanket IP-based rule as well, since bots can send random or no cookies.
    • Cost: No extra charge. Capacity is 2 WCUs base plus 30 WCUs per custom key (e.g. IP plus cookie = 62 WCUs). Logs gain limitKey and customValues fields.

    Takeaway: If you rate-limit only by IP, add a key per session or API token for authenticated endpoints, and keep the IP rule as a backstop.

  • The Beginner’s Guide to Cybersecurity
    summary

    TL;DR: A Software Analyst Cyber Research (SACR) Substack guide (Sep 2023, by Francis Odum per reader comments) maps the cybersecurity market for newcomers by what an enterprise must protect.

    • Model: Hardware, software, network, people, and data/governance/risk/compliance, each broken into product segments with example vendors.
    • Segments: EDR/XDR, UEM, IoT/OT, enterprise browsers, SAST/DAST/IAST, supply chain, CSPM/CWPP/CIEM/CASB, firewalls, SWG, SASE, identity, SIEM/SOAR, MDR, DLP, email security, DSPM and vulnerability management.
    • Market figures cited: About $200B growing over 11% a year (Gartner), 3,500+ vendors (Momentum Cyber), and the largest pure-play vendor holding about 4% share.
    • Other figures cited: About 40% of ransomware enters via email (Gartner), and ransomware-as-a-service can cost about $40 a month.
    • Argument: Frameworks like CIA and NIST have not stopped rising attacks, so the author argues for returning to fundamentals and expects continued consolidation.
    • Note: Includes promotion for the author’s bootcamp.

    Takeaway: A useful taxonomy if you need to explain security product categories to non-specialists or place a vendor quickly. The market numbers are second-hand and from 2023.

  • Profile-Guided Optimization in Go 1.21
    summary

    TL;DR: Michael Pratt’s Go blog post (Sep 2023) announces that profile-guided optimisation (PGO) is production-ready in Go 1.21 and walks through using it on a sample service.

    • Gains: Workloads typically see 2-7% lower CPU usage in Go 1.21.
    • Usage: Collect a CPU profile (e.g. from net/http/pprof /debug/pprof/profile) and save it as default.pgo in the main package directory. The toolchain then uses it automatically, or you can pass -pgo=<file> to go build.
    • Practice: Commit default.pgo for reproducible builds. Slightly stale profiles still work but should be refreshed. Confirm with go version -m <binary>.
    • Example: A Markdown-to-HTML service improved from about 374.5 µs to 360.2 µs per op (3.83%), and total CPU fell about 3%.
    • Mechanisms: Hot-function inlining (here mdurl.Parse, which also removed heap allocations via escape analysis) and profile-based devirtualisation of interface calls.

    Takeaway: A near-free CPU win for Go services you can profile in production. Add a profile-refresh step to your release process.

  • CloudSec 360 Series: AI and Cybersecurity with tl;dr sec Clint Gibler
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Wiz-hosted webinar registration page in which Clint Gibler (tl;dr sec, then Head of Security Research at Semgrep) reviewed how AI is being applied across cybersecurity.

    • Content (per Wiz listings): A survey of AI-in-security work across cloud, web, AppSec and offensive security, the current landscape, open problems and future direction, with links and tools to try.
    • Date: Wiz’s event page lists 22 September 2023. A later ISF listing describes a pre-recorded version on 13 December 2023.
    • Series: Search results show Gibler as a CloudSec 360 speaker, but one listing treats the AI webinar as a separate Wiz event. The title here may conflate the two.
    • Source caveat: The Goldcast registration page returned no content (JavaScript-only or expired). This summary is based on Wiz and ISF event listings found by web search, not the recording.

    Takeaway: The registration link is probably dead. Look for the recording on Wiz’s events pages or Gibler’s tl;dr sec newsletter, which covers the same AI-in-security material.

  • Static Taint Analysis for Go
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Kent Gruber (picatz) wrote about static taint analysis for Go, implemented in his open-source taint library, which traces data from sources such as *net/http.Request to sinks such as database/sql queries.

    • Approach: Builds an SSA call graph rooted at main (callgraphutil.NewGraph), then taint.Check(cg, sources, sinks) returns paths from sources to sinks.
    • SQL injection example: Sinks are (*database/sql.DB).Query, QueryContext, QueryRow and the Tx variants. A finding is reported when the query argument is not an *ssa.Const, i.e. not a constant prepared statement.
    • Sources: HTTP requests and gRPC proto.Message types in the example.
    • Explainability: taint.CheckDetailed with taint.WithSanitizers("html.EscapeString") returns ordered evidence of propagation and sanitiser decisions.
    • Current state: The repo is still maintained and now needs Go 1.26+.
    • Source caveat: The blog is a JavaScript single-page app and the post did not load. This summary is based on the picatz/taint GitHub README, which may have changed since the 2023 post.

    Takeaway: A good starting point if you want custom Go taint rules beyond what gosec or CodeQL give you. Expect to model your own sources, sinks and sanitisers.

  • Container Security Fundamentals Part 6: seccomp
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 6 of Rory McCune’s Container Security Fundamentals series for Datadog Security Labs (Sep 2023) explains seccomp, the syscall filter that acts as a last line of defence for containers.

    • Mechanism: BPF-based filters that allow or deny Linux syscalls. Syscall tables differ by architecture, so profiles must account for that.
    • Docker default: Applied to every container. It is an allowlist, so new kernel syscalls are blocked by default.
    • Real CVE: The default profile blocks CVE-2022-0185, a container escape via unshare. The demo shows unshare failing by default and working with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined.
    • Custom profiles: JSON with defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO. The author copies Docker’s default and removes io_uring_enter, io_uring_register and io_uring_setup, citing their role in kernel bugs.
    • Applying: docker run --security-opt seccomp=<profile>.json. Inspektor Gadget can record an app’s syscalls to build a least-privilege profile.
    • Scope: Kubernetes seccomp settings are left for a later series.

    Takeaway: Never run with seccomp=unconfined without a reason. In Kubernetes, make sure workloads use RuntimeDefault and consider blocking io_uring.

  • Introduction to Azure DevOps Workload Identity Federation (OIDC) with Terraform
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Jared Holgate (Microsoft, Sep 2023) introduces workload identity federation (OIDC) for Azure DevOps service connections and shows how to configure it with Terraform for credential-free deployments to Azure.

    • Trust setup: A federated credential on an App Registration or user-assigned managed identity, with issuer https://vstoken.dev.azure.com/<organisation-id>, subject sc://<org>/<project>/<service-connection> and audience api://AzureADTokenExchange.
    • Terraform: hashicorp/azurerm >= 3.0.0 and microsoft/azuredevops >= 0.9.0. Use azuredevops_serviceendpoint_azurerm with service_endpoint_authentication_scheme = "WorkloadIdentityFederation", and feed its issuer and subject outputs into azurerm_federated_identity_credential.
    • Pipelines: The DevLabs TerraformTaskV4@4 and Jason Johnson’s Terraform tasks detect the connection type and set auth env vars. The backend uses ARM_USE_AZUREAD: true.
    • Status: Public preview at the time, on by default, scoped to service connections.
    • Source caveat: The techcommunity URL now redirects to a Microsoft login. The summary is based on the same post on devblogs.microsoft.com/devops.

    Takeaway: Moving Azure DevOps Terraform pipelines to workload identity federation removes long-lived service principal secrets. It is worth doing for every service connection.

  • Introducing Infrastructure Manager: Provision Google Cloud Resources with HashiCorp Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud (Danny Hammo, Vlad Ouzienko, Sep 2023) announced Infrastructure Manager, a generally available managed service that runs Terraform plan and apply for Google Cloud resources.

    • What it does: Runs the Terraform plan/apply workflow for you, so you do not need to build your own pipelines.
    • Content: Works with Google’s pre-packaged Terraform modules, providers and Jump Start Solutions for Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, GKE and more.
    • Integration: Cloud Logging for troubleshooting and Cloud IAM for access control.
    • Positioning: An on-ramp to IaC aligned with Google’s Terraform on Google Cloud maturity model.
    • Docs: cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs.
    • Missing details: The post gives no pricing, state-management details or limits.

    Takeaway: A managed alternative to running Terraform in your own CI for GCP-only estates. Compare state handling, policy checks and cost with your existing pipeline before switching.

  • AWS SCP Evaluation
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS Organizations guide explains how service control policies (SCPs) are evaluated across the root, OUs and accounts, with seven worked scenarios.

    • Allow rule: An action is allowed only if an explicit Allow exists at every level from the root, through each OU, to the account. This is why FullAWSAccess is attached everywhere by default.
    • Deny rule: An explicit Deny at any level in the path denies the action for everything below, regardless of lower-level allows.
    • Pitfall: Removing FullAWSAccess at any level without a replacement blocks all actions below it. A deny-only SCP at the root therefore blocks everything.
    • Allowlist strategy: Replace FullAWSAccess with a service allowlist (e.g. ec2:*, cloudwatch:*) at the root or per OU, so new services stay blocked until approved.
    • Combined example: An allowlist plus Deny organizations:LeaveOrganization.
    • Tip: Use IAM service last accessed data to decide which services to allow.
    • Scope: Does not apply to declarative policy types such as backup or tag policies.

    Takeaway: When an SCP change has an unexpected effect, check that an Allow exists at every level of the path. Prefer deny statements for broad guardrails.

  • Access Accounts with AWS Management Console Private Access
    summary

    TL;DR: Suresh Samuel (AWS, Sep 2023, updated Dec 2023) shows how AWS Management Console Private Access restricts console sign-in from your network to a known set of AWS accounts or organisations.

    • Mechanism: PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints for the console and sign-in, with endpoint policies that allow or deny by account, organisation or OU.
    • Routing: Requires Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN, a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint, a private hosted zone, and conditional forwarding of aws.amazon.com DNS from on-premises.
    • Regions: Start in us-east-1, then add endpoints and records such as <region>.console.aws.amazon.com per region. CloudFormation templates are provided.
    • Related control: The aws:SourceVpc condition key can restrict IAM actions to traffic from the VPC.
    • Limits: Devices off the corporate network can still reach the public console. Docs, health and status subdomains are not supported.
    • Cost: The author estimates about $212.20 a month for two AZs, before usage charges.

    Takeaway: Useful for regulated environments that must stop staff signing into personal or unknown AWS accounts from corporate networks. Pair it with endpoint controls, since it does nothing off-network.

  • Policy Management in Kubernetes Is Changing
    summary

    TL;DR: Emin Alemdar (CNCF Ambassador) argues on the CNCF blog (Sep 2023) that native ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL expressions will change Kubernetes policy management, which today relies on Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper webhooks.

    • Feature: Policy rules written as Common Expression Language (CEL) inside the Kubernetes API. They can be parameterised and scoped, with no external webhook.
    • Maturity: Alpha in Kubernetes 1.26, beta in 1.28. It was off by default then, needing the feature gate and the admissionregistration.k8s.io v1alpha1 or v1beta1 API.
    • Resources: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy plus a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding that applies it, e.g. to a namespace.
    • Demo: On 1.27 with v1alpha1, it blocks Deployments with more than five replicas in namespaces labelled environment=demo.
    • Opinion: The author expects Kyverno and Gatekeeper to adapt rather than disappear, and expects native policies to become standard once on by default.

    Takeaway: For simple validation rules, native CEL policies remove a webhook dependency. Keep Kyverno or Gatekeeper for mutation, generation and richer reporting.

  • AWS Identity and Access Management Provides Action Last Accessed Information for More Than 140 Services
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (14 Sep 2023) says IAM now shows action-level last accessed information for more than 140 services, to help trim unused permissions from roles.

    • What: For each role, you can see which specific actions were used, for services such as CloudWatch, KMS and ELB, not just whether the service was used.
    • Use: Part of periodic access reviews: find unused actions and narrow policies to what the role actually calls.
    • Where: The Access Advisor tab on any IAM resource in the console. A full list of supported services and actions is in the IAM docs.
    • Availability: All regions where the corresponding services are supported.

    Takeaway: Use action last accessed data to right-size roles that were granted service:* during development, after a representative observation period.

  • Amazon CloudWatch Adds Amazon EKS Control Plane Logs as Vended Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (5 Sep 2023) says Amazon EKS control plane logs are now classed as CloudWatch Vended Logs, which get volume-based tiered pricing.

    • Log types covered: Kubernetes API server, audit, AWS IAM authenticator, controller manager and scheduler logs.
    • Effect: These logs now qualify for the discounted, tiered Vended Logs ingestion pricing instead of standard custom-log pricing.
    • Purpose: Lower cost for publishing control plane logs to CloudWatch to detect and respond to cluster events.
    • Missing details: The post gives no prices. It points to the CloudWatch pricing page.

    Takeaway: If you disabled EKS audit logs because of CloudWatch cost, re-check the numbers under Vended Logs pricing. Audit logs are the main source for Kubernetes incident response.

  • AWS Community: Share and Learn with Our Community of Cloud Enthusiasts
    summary

    TL;DR: community.aws was AWS’s community site for articles and posts by builders and AWS staff. It now 301-redirects to AWS Builder Center (builder.aws.com).

    • Status: The original community.aws content has moved. The link now lands on Builder Center’s home page.
    • Builder Center features: Community articles and spotlights, topic spaces, hackathons, free AWS Workshops with sandbox environments, and a Wishlist to propose and vote on AWS feature requests.
    • Trending topics now: Agentic AI, Amazon Bedrock, Lambda, serverless and DevOps.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the current Builder Center page. The 2023 community.aws page could not be viewed.

    Takeaway: Update the bookmark to builder.aws.com. The free workshop sandboxes are the most practically useful part.

  • Build Your OCI Images with ko While Still Using GoReleaser!
    summary

    TL;DR: GoReleaser’s docs describe its kos: integration, which builds and publishes Go container images with ko instead of a Dockerfile, reusing the builds settings.

    • Config: A kos: list with repositories (default $KO_DOCKER_REPO; extra repos are copied with crane), tags (default latest, templated) and platforms (default linux/amd64).
    • SBOM: sbom: spdx by default, or none.
    • Base image: base_image defaults to cgr.dev/chainguard/static.
    • Other options: bare, preserve_import_paths, ldflags, env, labels, annotations, user and linux_capabilities.
    • Signing: Manifests are added to artifacts, so docker_signs with artifacts: manifests can sign them.
    • Behaviour: --snapshot publishes to goreleaser.ko.local, and normal runs build only in the publish phase. You must docker login first.
    • Limit: ko does not evaluate per-target env, so .Os and .Arch are unavailable in ko env templates.

    Takeaway: For pure Go services this drops the Dockerfile and gives small distroless images with an SBOM. Pin base_image explicitly so it does not change underneath you.

  • tartufo: Search Git Repositories for High Entropy Strings and Secrets in Commit History
    summary

    TL;DR: tartufo is GoDaddy’s GPL-2.0 Python tool that scans git repositories, across full history and all branches, for secrets using regexes and entropy checks. It is no longer maintained.

    • Status: The README says it is not actively maintained, and the GitHub page shows the repository archived (read-only) on 29 Sep 2026.
    • Detection: High-signal regexes plus Shannon entropy on base64 and hex strings longer than 20 characters in each diff.
    • Modes: Full history scan, or pre-commit mode to screen changes before commit.
    • Options: --entropy/--no-entropy, --regex/--no-regex, --scan-filenames and --output-format json|compact|text|report.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt it for new work. Use a maintained scanner such as gitleaks or TruffleHog for history scans and pre-commit hooks.

  • cloudgoat: Rhino Security Labs’ Vulnerable by Design AWS Deployment Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudGoat is Rhino Security Labs’ BSD-3-Clause vulnerable-by-design cloud lab that deploys capture-the-flag scenarios into your own AWS (and now Azure) account.

    • Scenarios: Easy (e.g. iam_privesc_by_rollback, lambda_privesc), medium (e.g. ec2_ssrf, ecs_takeover, rds_snapshot, bedrock_agent_hijacking) and hard (e.g. rce_web_app, codebuild_secrets, detection_evasion).
    • Install: pipx install cloudgoat, then cloudgoat config aws and cloudgoat config whitelist --auto.
    • Run: cloudgoat create <scenario>, plus list and destroy. Each scenario starts, resets and stops independently.
    • Requirements: Linux or macOS, Python 3.9+, Terraform 1.5.0+, AWS CLI (Azure CLI for Azure scenarios) and jq.
    • Warnings: Never deploy it in production or near sensitive resources. destroy only removes what CloudGoat created.
    • Status: Still maintained by the CloudGoat community. The scenario list has grown since 2023 (now includes AI and Bedrock scenarios).

    Takeaway: A good hands-on AWS attack lab. Use a dedicated throwaway account, keep the IP whitelist on, and destroy scenarios when done.

  • 38TB of Data Accidentally Exposed by Microsoft AI Researchers
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz Research (Hillai Ben-Sasson, Ronny Greenberg, Sep 2023) found that Microsoft AI researchers exposed 38 TB of internal data through an over-permissive Azure SAS token in a public GitHub repo.

    • Exposure: Disk backups of two employees’ workstations, passwords to Microsoft services, secret keys, and 30,000+ Teams messages from 359 employees.
    • Root cause: robust-models-transfer linked to an Account SAS token scoped to the whole storage account, with full control (not read-only).
    • Expiry: The token’s expiry was extended from 2021 to 6 Oct 2051.
    • Supply chain risk: The models were pickle files, so write access could have allowed code injection into models users downloaded.
    • Timeline: Token committed 20 Jul 2020, reported to MSRC 22 Jun 2023, revoked 24 Jun 2023, disclosed 18 Sep 2023.
    • Advice: Avoid Account SAS for external sharing. Prefer Service SAS with a stored access policy or User Delegation SAS (max 7 days), use dedicated storage accounts for sharing, enable logs, and scan repos for tokens.

    Takeaway: SAS tokens are bearer credentials that are hard to inventory or revoke. Scan your repositories for them and restrict Account SAS at the storage account level.

  • go-exploit: A Go-Based Exploit Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: go-exploit from VulnCheck is a Go framework for writing small, self-contained, consistent exploits suited to large-scale scanning and integration with other tools.

    • Phases: Target verification, version scanning, exploitation, and command and control. They can be chained or run independently.
    • Networking: SSL/TLS auto-detection, per-exploit SSL requirements, full proxy support, and SMB/NetBIOS and other protocol helpers.
    • Payloads: Java gadgets, LDAP and serialiser infrastructure, .NET serialisers, and reverse shell, bind shell and dropper examples.
    • C2: A built-in C2 for catching shells or hosting implants, plus integration with Metasploit and Sliver.
    • Output: Key-value or JSON. Targets can come from lists, files or VulnCheck IP-Intel.
    • Examples: Implementations for CVE-2023-22527 (Confluence) and CVE-2025-0364 (BigAnt). The project is active with newer CVEs added.

    Takeaway: Useful for teams that need reproducible, scriptable exploit checks for vulnerability validation. Run it only against systems you are authorised to test.

  • openrisk: Generate a Risk Score from Nuclei Scan Results
    summary

    TL;DR: openrisk is an experimental ProjectDiscovery Research tool that reads Nuclei scan output and asks an OpenAI model to produce a 0-10 risk score for a single host.

    • Input: Nuclei results as text, markdown or JSON, for one target at a time.
    • Model: The current README says GPT-4o and requires OPENAI_API_KEY.
    • Install: go install -v github.com/projectdiscovery/openrisk@latest. The current README needs a very recent Go toolchain.
    • Run: openrisk -f nuclei_scan_result.txt. The example output gives a score of 10 citing Pantheon, AWS and Netlify takeover findings.
    • Library: It can be embedded via the Options, OpenRisk and IssueProcessor types and GetScore.
    • Caveat: ProjectDiscovery labels it experimental and less tested than its main tools.

    Takeaway: A demo of LLM triage on scanner output, not a calibrated risk model. Note that it sends findings to OpenAI, and do not use the score for prioritisation without human review.

  • How to Rotate: Open-Source Collection of API Key Rotation Tutorials
    summary

    TL;DR: How To Rotate, sponsored by Truffle Security (makers of TruffleHog), is an open-source collection of step-by-step tutorials for rotating leaked API keys for common SaaS providers.

    • Method: Each tutorial covers three steps: generate a new key, replace the compromised one, and revoke the old key.
    • Coverage: AWS, GCP, Azure (DevOps, Functions, Search, Storage), GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Mailgun, MongoDB, NPM, OpenAI, Tailscale, Square and more.
    • Selection: Tutorials target the keys Truffle Security sees leaked most often.
    • Extras: A Key Rotation 101 section, and contributions via PR following the CONTRIBUTING guide.

    Takeaway: Link it from your secret-leak runbook so responders can rotate a provider’s key without searching vendor docs mid-incident.

  • Source Code Management Platform Configuration Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: The OpenSSF Best Practices Working Group (Aug 2023, with contributors from Microsoft, IBM, F5, Snyk, Legit Security and the Linux Foundation) published configuration best practices for GitHub and GitLab.

    • Categories: CI/CD, enterprise, members and access control, repository, and operations.
    • Identity controls: Enforce 2FA and SSO, and keep fewer than three owners or admins per org or repo.
    • Workflow controls: A read-only default workflow token and restrictions on which actions may run.
    • Repo controls: Require code review with two reviewers on the default branch, block force pushes and deletion, enable secret scanning, and use SSL plus a secret on webhooks.
    • Operations: Annual policy reviews, incident response plans, audits and alerts.
    • Tooling: Legit Security’s Legitify (the guide says it detects all listed policies), OpenSSF Allstar and Scorecard.
    • Labels: Each control is tagged with the platform(s) it applies to.

    Takeaway: A concrete baseline for hardening your GitHub or GitLab org. Run Legitify or Scorecard against it to find gaps quickly.

  • When MFA Isn’t Actually MFA
    summary

    TL;DR: Retool’s Snir Kodesh (Sep 2023) describes a social engineering breach that hit 27 cloud customers, all in crypto, and blames Google Authenticator’s cloud sync for turning MFA into effectively single-factor.

    • Phishing: On 27 Aug 2023, SMS phishing about open enrollment led an employee to a fake Okta-style page where they entered credentials and an MFA code.
    • Vishing: The attacker then called with a deepfaked voice posing as IT and got one more code. They used it to add their own device to the employee’s Okta account.
    • Pivot: The Google account session exposed all OTP seeds synced by Google Authenticator, which gave access to the VPN and internal admin tools.
    • Impact: On 29 Aug Retool notified 27 cloud customers. The attacker changed emails and reset passwords. On-prem deployments were not affected.
    • Criticism: Sync is on by default through what Retool calls dark patterns, and admins cannot disable it centrally in Google Workspace.
    • Recommendations: FIDO2 hardware keys, defence in depth, human approval for high-impact actions, and minimal trust between products.

    Takeaway: TOTP codes and synced authenticators can be phished or harvested. Move admin and SSO access to phishing-resistant FIDO2 or passkeys.

  • iamlive: Generate an IAM Policy from AWS, Azure, or GCP Calls Using Client-Side Monitoring or Proxy
    summary

    TL;DR: iamlive (iann0036) generates an IAM policy from the API calls your CLI or SDK actually makes, by listening through AWS client-side monitoring (CSM) or an embedded proxy.

    • Providers: AWS by default. Azure and GCP are in preview and the README warns they may produce incorrect output.
    • Usage: Run iamlive in a separate terminal while you run your CLI, SDK or Terraform commands, then press Ctrl+C to finish.
    • Flags: --provider aws|azure|gcp, --set-ini (temporarily rewrites .aws/config for CSM or the CA bundle), --profile, --fails-only (CSM mode) and --output-file.
    • Install: Release binaries, brew install iann0036/iamlive/iamlive, or go install (Go 1.16+).
    • Other modes: A Lambda extension, Docker, a GitHub Action with Terraform, and LocalStack.

    Takeaway: A quick way to draft least-privilege policies for a Terraform module or script. Review the output, since it only reflects the calls made during that run.

  • dockle: Container Image Linter for Security and Best-Practice Docker Images
    summary

    TL;DR: Dockle from goodwithtech is a container image linter that checks built images against CIS Docker benchmark items and its own best-practice rules.

    • Checkpoints: CIS-DI-0001 to 0011 (e.g. 0001 non-root user, 0009 COPY over ADD), DKL-DI-0001 to 0006 (e.g. clear apt caches, avoid latest) and DKL-LI-0001 to 0003 (e.g. no empty passwords).
    • Run: brew install goodwithtech/r/dockle, then dockle <image>. It can also scan an image tarball.
    • Output: Text, -f json or -f sarif, with -o to save.
    • CI gating: It exits 0 by default. Use --exit-code and --exit-level info|warn|fatal, and skip rules with --ignore, DOCKLE_IGNORES or .dockleignore.
    • Positioning: Unlike Hadolint (Dockerfile lint) and Docker Bench (host and daemon audit), Dockle inspects the built image.
    • License: The repo page is inconsistent (Apache-2.0 in the sidebar, AGPL badge in the README).

    Takeaway: Cheap to add after docker build in CI alongside a CVE scanner. Set --exit-code or it will never fail a build.

  • aws-customer-playbook-framework: Sample Security Playbook Templates for AWS Scenarios
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Samples repository of incident response playbook templates for common AWS attack scenarios, meant as a starting point for your own runbooks.

    • 100-200 level: Compromised IAM credentials, DoS/DDoS, CodeCommit exposure, public S3 and RDS resources, SES compromise, unauthorised network changes, and Bedrock and Amazon Q security events.
    • 300-400 level: Cryptojacking, ransom response for EC2 Linux, EC2 Windows, RDS and S3, and SageMaker security events.
    • Supporting docs: A playbook development guide and creation process, a resource glossary, getting help from AWS, VPC Flow Log analysis with Athena, and EC2 forensics.
    • Languages: English plus machine-translated German, Spanish, French, Japanese and Chinese, which AWS says have not been human-reviewed.
    • License: Docs under Creative Commons (the page is inconsistent on CC BY vs CC BY-SA). Sample code is MIT-0.
    • Growth: The repo has expanded since 2023 with AI-service playbooks and an Amazon Q playbook-assistant guide.

    Takeaway: Fork the scenarios that match your threat model, fill in your own contacts, tools and log sources, then test them in tabletop exercises.

  • CloudRecon: Finding Assets from Certificates
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudRecon by Gunnar Andrews and Jason Haddix, presented at DEF CON 31, finds an organisation’s hidden cloud assets by scanning IP ranges and reading the CN and SAN fields of their TLS certificates.

    • Why: Dev sites and product portals often sit on cloud IPs outside the target’s ASN, sometimes with no domain, but still serve HTTPS certificates naming the org.
    • scrape: Live scan of IPs or CIDRs, matching a keyword in certificate fields.
    • store: Downloads certificate orgs, CNs and SANs into your own crt.sh-style database.
    • retr: Searches the stored certificates by keyword.
    • Example: Download merged cloud IPv4 ranges, then CloudRecon scrape -i ipv4_merged.txt -j | tee -a certdb.json, run inside tmux or screen.
    • Install: go install github.com/g0ldencybersec/CloudRecon@latest. Needs CGO and gcc.

    Takeaway: Useful for bug bounty and external attack surface work. Defenders can run the same search for their own org name to find forgotten cloud hosts.

  • AWS Console Session Traceability: How Attackers Obfuscate Identity Through the AWS Console
    summary

    TL;DR: A Gem Security post, now on the Wiz blog after Gem’s acquisition, shows how an attacker with stolen IAM user keys can assume a role and open a federated console session that hides who they are in CloudTrail.

    • Technique (“Console Conceal”): Stolen user key, then AssumeRole, then convert the role session into a console session.
    • Spoofed name: The role session name is free-form and unverified, so the attacker can set it to an innocent user’s email.
    • Broken link: CLI actions carry the temporary key ID from the AssumeRole response, but console actions use a different key ID. Console events also often show internal AWS source IPs.
    • Defence: Require SourceIdentity in role trust policies, set to the caller’s IAM username. It then appears in userIdentity for all later actions.
    • Investigation: Without SourceIdentity, correlate the session name in principalId, the role name and sessionContext.creationDate with the AssumeRole event (up to 1 second earlier). Use ConsoleLogin events for external IPs.
    • Source caveat: The URL redirects to wiz.io/blog, where the post is dated 22 Aug 2024 and credited to Itay Harel. The 2023 Gem original may have differed.

    Takeaway: Enforce sts:SourceIdentity on roles that humans assume. Without it, console activity from assumed roles is hard to attribute.

  • The Dark Side of Tech Culture
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Lettuce Work blog post on Medium titled “The Dark Side of Tech Culture”, about the downsides of tech company culture. Its content could not be retrieved.

    • Status: The page is on Medium’s custom-domain hosting and returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare block). No mirror or archived copy could be fetched.
    • Topic: Based on the title only, a critique of tech workplace culture. The specific arguments, examples and author are unknown.
    • Source caveat: Web searches for the title and publication found no copies or citations. This summary rests on the title and URL alone.

    Takeaway: Open the original in a browser to decide whether it is worth keeping. Nothing here should be taken as the author’s position.

  • Day-1 Skills That Cybersecurity Hiring Managers Are Looking For
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Miessler argues that entry-level security candidates get hired by showing they can be useful on day one, and lists the practical skills hiring managers want.

    • Technical skills: Product selection, ad-hoc security assessments, preparing for and handling an audit, integrating a new security product, and building a new tool.
    • Meta-skills: Excellent writing, fast learning and mentorship.
    • Reasoning: Unlike the military, most companies lack the time to grow junior talent, so they hire people who can already do the work.
    • Advantages: Programming experience, bug bounty work and active GitHub projects.
    • Goal: Be able to take on a project within about a week of starting.
    • Date: The page is dated 31 August 2019, so it predates when it was bookmarked.
    • Evidence: No survey data. It is opinion with references to Momentum Cyber’s CYBERscape and Michael Coates.

    Takeaway: For hiring or mentoring juniors, build portfolio items around these tasks (e.g. a written product evaluation or a small tool) rather than collecting more certifications.

  • A Simple, Yet Effective Cost Optimization Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Julian, CEO of The Duckbill Group (Sep 2023), describes the six-step order he and Corey Quinn follow when cutting a client’s AWS bill.

    • 1. Turn off unused resources.
    • 2. Store less data: Keep less, and move what remains to cheaper tiers, thinking in terms of the whole data lifecycle.
    • 3. Move less data: Data transfer is expensive, and compressing before transit reduces it.
    • 4. Cloud-ify workloads: Move along the “cloudiness continuum” towards serverless to cut compute time.
    • 5. Pre-pay: Reserved Instances, Savings Plans or private pricing come last because they lock in architecture.
    • 6. Repeat: Environments change, so revisit regularly.
    • Source caveat: The URL now redirects to duckbillhq.com.

    Takeaway: Buy commitments only after cleanup and architecture changes, or you will pre-pay for waste.

  • wazuh: Open Source Security Platform with Unified XDR and SIEM
    summary

    TL;DR: Wazuh is a free, open-source security platform combining XDR and SIEM, with endpoint agents that report to a central manager and an indexer and dashboard for analysis.

    • Architecture: Agents on monitored systems, a management server that analyses collected data, and the Wazuh Indexer for search and visualisation.
    • Intrusion detection: Agents look for malware, rootkits, hidden files, cloaked processes and unregistered listeners. The server applies signature rules to logs.
    • Log analysis: Agents forward OS and application logs. Agentless devices can send via syslog.
    • Other capabilities: File integrity monitoring, vulnerability detection, configuration assessment, incident response, regulatory compliance, and cloud and container security.
    • Scope: On-premises, virtualised, containerised and cloud workloads.

    Takeaway: A capable self-hosted SIEM/XDR if you have the staff to run and tune it. Budget time for rule tuning and indexer sizing.

  • Amazon VPC CNI Now Supports Kubernetes Network Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Srinivas Jasti and Sheetal Joshi (AWS, Aug 2023) announced native Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement in the Amazon VPC CNI using eBPF, removing the need for Calico or other add-ons on EKS.

    • Components: A Network Policy controller (managed on EKS), a node agent (aws-eks-nodeagent in the aws-node DaemonSet), and an eBPF SDK CLI (/opt/cni/bin/aws-eks-na-cli ebpf progs).
    • Requirements: VPC CNI 1.14.0+, EKS 1.25+, kernel 5.10+ (EKS Amazon Linux, Bottlerocket and Ubuntu AMIs qualify).
    • Enable: Off by default. Set enableNetworkPolicy: "true" in the VPC CNI add-on configurationValues.
    • Behaviour: New pods run with default allow until reconciled against existing policies.
    • Migration: No in-place migration from third-party plugins. Run only one policy engine, test on a separate cluster, and recycle nodes to clear old iptables and eBPF state.
    • Pairing: Can be combined with security groups for pods (IPv4).

    Takeaway: On EKS this is the simplest route to enforced NetworkPolicies. Note the brief default-allow window for new pods when designing strict isolation.

  • On Amazon EKS and Kyverno
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Medium post by micheldirk on running the Kyverno policy engine on Amazon EKS. Its content could not be retrieved.

    • Status: Medium returned HTTP 403 to all fetch attempts, and no archived copy could be retrieved.
    • Topic: From the title, using Kyverno admission policies on EKS. Specific policies, setup steps and findings are unknown.
    • Related material (not this post): Nirmata and the AWS Containers blog have published guides on EKS best-practice and Pod Security policies with Kyverno. Nirmata notes that Kyverno image verification does not work out of the box with images in Amazon ECR.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the title, URL and unrelated search results on the same topic. Nothing here is from the author.

    Takeaway: Open the original in a browser if needed. For the topic itself, the Kyverno and Nirmata EKS guides are maintained alternatives.

  • logging-operator: Logging Operator for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: The Logging operator (kube-logging, a CNCF Sandbox project) automates deploying and configuring a Kubernetes log pipeline: Fluent Bit collectors on each node feeding a Fluentd or syslog-ng forwarder.

    • Pipeline: A Fluent Bit DaemonSet collects container logs and adds pod metadata from the Kubernetes API, then a forwarder filters and transforms them and ships to outputs.
    • Forwarders: Fluentd or syslog-ng.
    • Model: Flows and outputs are custom resources, so apps can declare their logging in their own Helm charts.
    • Features: Namespace isolation, label selectors, TLS between components, configuration validation, and multiple flows, outputs and logging systems.
    • Outputs: S3, GCS, Elasticsearch, Loki and others.

    Takeaway: Useful when many teams share a cluster and each needs its own log routing. Keep an eye on forwarder resource use as the number of flows grows.

  • My Preferred Go Stack
    summary

    TL;DR: JT Archie (Sep 2023) lists the Go libraries he reaches for by default, with brief reasons for each.

    • CLI: kong, which parses arguments into structs, passes state to commands and supports global flags.
    • HTTP client: req, for less boilerplate, middleware, retries, default timeouts and a debug mode.
    • Web: echo, with documented routing and middleware, similar to Ruby’s Sinatra.
    • Concurrency: His own worker package for goroutine pools.
    • Data: go-sqlite3 (CGO, with full-text search) and lo for generic collection helpers.
    • Testing and lint: ginkgo with gomega for BDD-style tests, and golangci-lint with most linters on, valuing errcheck.
    • Logging: The standard library’s log/slog.

    Takeaway: A reasonable default stack for small Go services and CLIs. Note the CGO dependency of go-sqlite3 if you need static cross-compiled builds.

  • harden-runner: Runtime Security for GitHub-Hosted and Self-Hosted Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: Harden-Runner from StepSecurity is a CI/CD security agent that works like an EDR for GitHub Actions runners, monitoring network egress, file integrity and process activity during each job.

    • Problem: Ephemeral CI runners hold cloud secrets and build production artifacts, but rarely have security monitoring. The README cites SolarWinds and Codecov.
    • Usage: Add the step-security/harden-runner action as a step in each workflow job. See the docs for policy options.
    • Detections claimed: The tj-actions/changed-files compromise (CVE-2025-30066), the NX build system and Trivy release compromises, a malicious axios npm package, and supply chain attacks in Google Flank and Microsoft’s Azure Karpenter provider.
    • Scale claim: The vendor says it secures over 25 million workflow runs a week.
    • Tiers: Community is free for public repos on GitHub-hosted runners. Private repos, self-hosted runners (including ARC) and advanced features need Enterprise.
    • Platforms: Linux, Windows and macOS runners.

    Takeaway: Adding it to public-repo workflows costs little and shows what your builds contact. Egress blocking is the control that limits secret exfiltration.

  • Introducing pgroll: Zero-Downtime, Reversible Schema Migrations for Postgres
    summary

    TL;DR: Xata introduced pgroll, an open-source CLI for zero-downtime, reversible Postgres schema migrations using the expand/contract pattern, with old and new schema versions served at the same time.

    • Versioned schemas: Old and new versions are exposed as virtual schemas made of views over the physical tables, so old and new app versions can run side by side.
    • Example (NOT NULL): Adds a new column, adds the constraint NOT VALID, backfills in batches, and keeps old and new columns in sync with triggers.
    • Commands: pgroll start <file> begins a migration and pgroll complete removes the old column and triggers. Rollback works because the old schema stays live until completion.
    • Format: JSON with name and operations, e.g. alter_column with up and down SQL expressions for transforming values.
    • Operations mentioned: Set NOT NULL, rename column, add or remove constraints, and UNIQUE.
    • Missing details: The post names no license, author or supported Postgres versions, and calls this a first version.

    Takeaway: Worth evaluating if Postgres migrations force downtime or lockstep deploys. Check the project’s current status and limits before relying on it in production.

  • Software Supply Chain Vendor Landscape
    summary

    TL;DR: Francis Odum (guest author) and Clint Gibler map the software supply chain security vendor market for tl;dr sec (Oct 2023), covering 20+ vendors by category.

    • Categories: Legacy AppSec (Veracode, Checkmarx, Synopsys), modern platforms (Snyk), source code layer (Arnica, Jit), SCA, malicious package detection (Socket, Phylum, GuardDog), CI/CD security (OX, Cycode, Cider), containers (Chainguard, Aqua, Rapidfort), and SBOM and signing.
    • Drivers: The 2021 US executive order and a 2022 OMB memo on SBOMs and attestations. It cites NightDragon data that over 96% of CISOs are using or considering supply chain tools.
    • Reachability: Checking whether vulnerable functions are actually called may cut SCA alerts by over 90%. The authors say only Semgrep and Endor Labs meaningfully pursue it.
    • Market: Highly fragmented with 30+ startups and consolidation under way (Palo Alto bought Cider, Snyk bought Enso).
    • Standards: Many vendors build on SLSA, NIST SSDF and OpenSSF Scorecard.

    Takeaway: A useful map when shortlisting tools. Ask vendors specifically about reachability and malicious-package detection, the areas the authors see as differentiators.

  • KubeHound: Identifying Attack Paths in Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog’s adversary simulation team (Jeremy Fox, Julien Terriac, Edouard Schweisguth, Oct 2023) released KubeHound, an open-source tool that builds a graph of Kubernetes attack paths from a live cluster.

    • Architecture: A Go collector pulls objects from the API server, MongoDB holds intermediate data, and the graph is stored in JanusGraph, explorable with a client such as G.V().
    • Attacks modelled: Most known Kubernetes techniques from container escape to lateral movement, each with a reference page (e.g. CE_NSENTER, TOKEN_BRUTEFORCE).
    • Queries: Gremlin, plus a KubeHound DSL for common questions.
    • Results: From one compromised pod, the candidate set in a 300-container cluster dropped to 14. Blocking TOKEN_BRUTEFORCE removed 16 of 18 critical paths from one public service. Only 6 of 846 services had a path to a critical asset (shortest 4 hops).
    • Run: ./kubehound.sh backend-up, select a cluster with kubectx or KUBECONFIG, then ./kubehound.sh run.

    Takeaway: Graph-based path analysis helps prioritise which Kubernetes fixes remove the most risk. Run it on a staging cluster first to learn the queries.

  • 25 Hard-Hitting Lessons from 17 Years in Cybersecurity
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Privette of Return on Security (Sep 2023) shares 25 opinionated lessons from 17 years in cybersecurity, mostly about business alignment, careers and vendors.

    • Business: Budget reveals real risk tolerance. Understand how the company makes money. Many firms fund security mainly to avoid fines. Security supports the business and is not the main act.
    • Practice: Unpatched systems and weak response cause more harm than exotic zero-days. Security is mostly people and negotiation. Conversations assess risk better than spreadsheets.
    • Careers: Entry is a catch-22. Certifications get past HR but experience gets results. Changing employers is the fastest way to advance. Your network matters more than what you know.
    • Culture: Elitism often masks insecurity, and echo chambers are real.
    • Vendors: The more buzzwords, the less likely a product solves your problem. Conferences are better for networking than tool evaluation.
    • GRC: Often criticised, but it coordinates the whole security effort.

    Takeaway: A good prompt for reflection or mentoring talks. It is opinion, not data, but the patching and business-alignment points apply to most teams.

  • Overhauling AWS Account Access with Terraform, Granted, and GitOps
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Julian, with a guest section by Chris Farris (Sep 2023), describes how The Duckbill Group rebuilt consultant access to client AWS accounts using IAM Identity Center, Terraform, CodePipeline and Common Fate’s Granted CLI.

    • Before: Cross-account roles with ReadOnly, later ViewOnly, a two-page manual setup checklist for contractors, and CLI config files passed between staff.
    • Identity: Google Workspace as the source of truth with SCIM to Identity Center (Google Groups were not supported).
    • Terraform: Per client, it pulls account details from the CRM via Lambda and creates a group, a permission set (allowed to assume DuckbillGroupRole only with the matching external ID) and an assignment.
    • Pipeline: CodePipeline runs plan in CodeBuild, waits for human approval, then applies. It was chosen over GitHub Actions to keep IAM trust inside AWS.
    • Granted: Profiles generated from CRM data and published to a Granted profile registry in GitHub, so no config files change hands.
    • Permissions: Explicitly deny sensitive IAM actions rather than enumerate allows, since ReadOnly (261 services) and ViewOnly (150) each have gaps. Sessions last 6 hours.
    • Source caveat: The URL now redirects to duckbillhq.com.

    Takeaway: A good reference design for consultancies or platform teams managing access to many accounts. The deny list of sensitive read actions is the reusable piece.

  • Security Hub Gives Me Imposter Syndrome
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris (Oct 2023) critiques AWS Security Hub. It is cheap, easy and organisation-wide, but its scoring and controls measure compliance rather than risk and demoralise engineers.

    • Positives: Delegated admin, cross-region aggregation, the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard, and consolidation of Inspector, GuardDuty and Macie findings.
    • Cost: The advertised price covers only the delegated admin account. With AWS Config, the author’s bill exceeded 1% of total AWS spend.
    • Misleading scores: The Security Score (31%) and standard score (33%) disagreed. 1,699 criticals included Inspector findings, and 14,650 failed resources spanned 137 finding types while 82% of resources were compliant.
    • Noisy controls: A root hardware MFA check produced 289 critical findings across regions, and disabling it meant visiting each account and region.
    • Other issues: Fixes took nearly a day to show, and prioritisation was weak.
    • Workarounds: Use it mainly as an aggregator with most controls off and forward findings to a SIEM. AWS later added multi-account disable scripts and CloudFormation support.

    Takeaway: Do not use the Security Hub score as a KPI. Curate the enabled controls to match your actual risks before showing dashboards to engineering.

  • PCI v4 Is Coming. Are You Ready?
    summary

    TL;DR: Kamaria Harvey of Pen Test Partners (Sep 2023) summarises what changes in PCI DSS v4.0, released March 2022, ahead of v3.2.1’s retirement.

    • Approaches: The Defined Approach, or the new Customised Approach, which needs a formal risk assessment and Appendix E documentation. The article counts 64 changes that affect all entities.
    • Dates: Some requirements apply at once to v4.0 audits. Others become mandatory on 31 March 2025.
    • Data: Disk-level encryption is no longer enough except on removable media, and hashing must be keyed (HMAC or CMAC).
    • Authentication: Minimum password length rises from 7 to 12 characters, and MFA is needed for all CDE access, not just remote.
    • Web: A WAF is required for internet-facing apps from March 2025. Payment page scripts must be inventoried, and payment pages need change and tamper detection.
    • Operations: Automated log review replaces manual, internal vulnerability scans must be authenticated, scoping is documented yearly, and anti-phishing controls are required.

    Takeaway: The March 2025 dates have passed, so these are now mandatory. Check payment-page script controls and authenticated internal scanning, which teams often miss.

  • How to Traceroute Kubernetes Pod-to-Pod Traffic
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Globant engineering post on Medium about tracing the network path of Kubernetes pod-to-pod traffic. Its content could not be retrieved.

    • Status: Medium returned HTTP 403 to all fetch attempts, and no archived copy could be fetched.
    • Topic: From the title, running traceroute-style diagnostics between pods. The CNI, tools and commands it used are unknown.
    • Related approaches (not from this post): Running traceroute from a source pod to a destination pod IP, TCP traceroute when ICMP or UDP is blocked, and CNI-specific tracers such as Antrea Traceflow or ovnkube-trace.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the title and unrelated search results on the same topic.

    Takeaway: Open the original in a browser if needed. For live debugging, use your CNI’s own trace tooling, which shows policy and overlay hops that plain traceroute misses.

  • ZAP Is Joining the Software Security Project
    summary

    TL;DR: Simon Bennetts announced (1 Aug 2023) that ZAP was leaving OWASP to become a founding project of the Linux Foundation’s new Software Security Project (SSP), and dropping the OWASP prefix.

    • Reason: A project can belong to only one foundation. The author said OWASP struggled to invest in large projects, and ZAP needs more investment to compete with commercial scanners.
    • Name: “OWASP ZAP” becomes “ZAP”, with UI rebranding in the next full release.
    • Funding: The SSP would fund Simon Bennetts and Ricardo (thc202) to work on ZAP full time.
    • User impact: ZAP stays open source. Docker Hub images move to a new organisation (update pull URLs), but GHCR images are unaffected.
    • Later update: The page is now marked historical. ZAP is supported by Checkmarx and is no longer part of any foundation.

    Takeaway: If your pipelines still pull ZAP images from the old OWASP Docker Hub organisation, switch to the current official ZAP images.

  • Terraform 1.6 Adds a Test Framework for Enhanced Code Validation
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp announced Terraform 1.6 (GA 4 Oct 2023) with a native terraform test framework, plus config-driven import, Terraform Cloud CLI and S3 backend improvements.

    • Testing: Tests are written in HCL in .tftest.hcl files as sequences of run blocks with assertions, optionally using helper modules for setup.
    • Lifecycle: terraform test provisions real infrastructure per run, evaluates assertions, then destroys it. It replaces the experimental test feature from 0.15.
    • Import: The id in import blocks now accepts expressions and interpolation, e.g. a bucket name combined with the account ID.
    • Terraform Cloud: The cloud block accepts project. Saved plans work via terraform plan -out <file> and terraform apply <file>, storing only a reference to the remote run locally.
    • S3 backend: Config aligned with the AWS SDK and provider, with attributes moved into nested blocks. Old configs work but warn about deprecations.

    Takeaway: Module authors can now test without Terratest. Expect S3 backend deprecation warnings on upgrade and plan the config change.

  • nord-stream: Extract Secrets from CI/CD Environments by Deploying Malicious Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: Nord Stream from Synacktiv extracts secrets from CI/CD platforms (Azure DevOps, GitHub, GitLab) by pushing temporary malicious pipelines that print the secrets, then cleaning up.

    • Install: pipx install git+https://github.com/synacktiv/nord-stream. Requires git.
    • GitHub flow: nord-stream github --token "$GHP" --org org --repo repo --list-secrets to enumerate, then run without --list-secrets to exfiltrate repo and environment secrets.
    • Protections: It can list and disable branch protections (with --force) and abuse Azure and AWS OIDC trust.
    • Azure DevOps: Extracts service connection credentials and SSH secrets, and lists orgs.
    • GitLab: Lists secrets and protections, and deploys custom YAML.
    • OPSEC: Cleans workflow logs and can sign commits. Background is in Synacktiv’s CI/CD secrets extraction blog post.

    Takeaway: It shows that anyone who can push a pipeline can read its secrets. Restrict who can modify workflows, use environment protection rules, and scope OIDC trust tightly.

  • Announcing Updates to the AWS Well-Architected Framework Guidance
    summary

    TL;DR: Haleh Najafzadeh (AWS, Oct 2023) announced updates to 90 AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices across all six pillars.

    • Operational Excellence (26): A new observability design principle, all of OPS05 updated, and 28 practices consolidated into 16.
    • Security (8): SEC10 incident response aligned with the AWS Security Incident Response Guide, one new practice added, and better data-at-rest and in-transit guidance (SEC08, SEC09).
    • Reliability (7): REL06 and REL11 updates on monitoring, failover, remediation and multi-Region resilience.
    • Performance Efficiency (32): Restructured with 10 fewer practices and three fewer questions. New practices on caching and hardware acceleration.
    • Cost Optimization (10) and Sustainability (7): More prescriptive guidance, and updated risk levels for Sustainability.
    • Context: This follows 151 practices improved earlier in 2023. AWS says over 73% of practices were updated in the year.
