    Takeaway: If you ran Well-Architected reviews before late 2023, re-run the Security and Operational Excellence pillars against the updated guidance in the Well-Architected Tool.

  • mods: AI on the Command Line
    summary

    TL;DR: Mods from Charmbracelet is a CLI that pipes command output into an LLM and returns Markdown, JSON or other text, built for shell pipelines. It has since been sunset.

    • Status: Charm announced it sunset Mods and archived the repo on 9 March 2026 to focus on Crush. Much of the functionality is in crush run.
    • Backends: OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Cohere, Groq, and local models via LocalAI.
    • Install: brew install charmbracelet/tap/mods, winget install charmbracelet.mods, AUR, Nix, or Charm’s apt repo.
    • License: Remains open source. Charm invites forks.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt it for new work. Use Crush’s non-interactive mode or another maintained CLI, and avoid piping secrets into hosted models.

  • Autometrics: Easily Add Metrics to Your Code to Spot and Debug Production Issues
    summary

    TL;DR: Autometrics is an open-source observability micro-framework that instruments functions with request rate, error rate and latency metrics, built on Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. This link is the GitHub org.

    • Languages: autometrics-rs (Rust), autometrics-go, autometrics-ts, autometrics-py, and community-maintained C#/.NET and Java ports (with an IntelliJ plugin).
    • Generated queries: Builds Prometheus queries from instrumented function names, so you do not write PromQL by hand.
    • Doc links: Adds links to live charts in function doc comments.
    • Alerting: SLO-based alerts can be defined in source code. Software version info is correlated with metric anomalies.
    • Tooling: am, a companion CLI, shared dashboards, docs, and diff-metrics, a GitHub Action that comments on PRs about metric impact.
    • Status: The org page did not show whether the repos are still active, so check each repo before adopting.

    Takeaway: A low-effort way to get RED metrics per function with consistent naming. Confirm the language library is still maintained before building on it.

  • glide: Automate Permissions to Your Cloud and Critical Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: Glide is Common Fate’s open source privileged access management framework for requesting and approving temporary access to cloud and SaaS roles.

    • Status: The README says Glide was sunset and the repository archived on May 16, 2024; it is now read-only.
    • Access rules: Admins define rules for who can request access to what, and which resource owners approve it.
    • Access Providers: Pluggable providers provision access to SaaS services and cloud providers.
    • Approvals: Requests and approvals integrate with team chat tools such as Slack.
    • License: AGPL-3.0, with a commercial license available on request.

    Takeaway: Useful as a reference design for just-in-time access with approval workflows. Do not adopt it for new deployments, since it is archived.

  • NSA and CISA Red and Blue Teams Share Top Ten Cybersecurity Misconfigurations
    summary

    TL;DR: Joint NSA and CISA advisory AA23-278A (October 5, 2023) lists the ten most common misconfigurations their red, blue, hunt and incident response teams find in large organizations.

    • The ten: Default configurations; poor user/admin privilege separation; insufficient internal network monitoring; lack of network segmentation; poor patch management; bypass of system access controls; weak or misconfigured MFA; insufficient ACLs on network shares and services; poor credential hygiene; unrestricted code execution.
    • Finding: These weaknesses appear even in organizations with mature security postures, which the agencies call a systemic trend.
    • Defender actions: Remove default credentials and harden configs, disable unused services, automate patching with priority on known exploited vulnerabilities, and reduce, restrict, audit and monitor admin accounts.
    • Vendor ask: Software manufacturers are urged to adopt secure-by-design and secure-by-default practices so customers carry less of the burden.
    • Format: Each misconfiguration maps to attacker TTPs and to mitigations in the advisory.

    Takeaway: A practical audit checklist for any large environment. Walk through the ten items against your own estate and use the mitigations section as the fix list.

  • New ‘HTTP/2 Rapid Reset’ Zero-Day Attack Breaks DDoS Records
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (Bill Toulas, October 10, 2023) reports on HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, a DDoS technique tracked as CVE-2023-44487 that was exploited as a zero-day from late August 2023.

    • Record sizes: AWS, Cloudflare and Google reported mitigating attacks of 155 million, 201 million and 398 million requests per second respectively.
    • Small botnet: Cloudflare’s peak was three times its February 2023 record of 71 million rps and came from a botnet of about 20,000 machines.
    • Technique: Attackers open HTTP/2 streams and immediately cancel them with RST_STREAM frames, so the server keeps doing work while the concurrent-stream limit never triggers.
    • Impact: Proxies and load balancers are especially exposed; Cloudflare saw more 502 errors for customers.
    • Mitigation: There is no protocol-level fix; vendors add rate controls, and Cloudflare extended its “IP Jail” system to bar offending IPs from HTTP/2.
    • Disclosure: Cloudflare held the details for over a month so vendors could prepare patches.

    Takeaway: Patch every HTTP/2-terminating component (proxies, load balancers, web servers, language runtimes) for CVE-2023-44487, and confirm your edge has HTTP flood protection.

07.09.2023

  • Amazon EKS Makes It Easier to Configure and Use Amazon EFS for Persistent Shared File Storage
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (August 2, 2023) that the Amazon EFS CSI driver is now available as a managed Amazon EKS add-on.

    • What changed: The EFS CSI driver can be installed, configured and updated from the EKS console, AWS CLI, EKS API or IaC tools.
    • No manual install: It removes the need to deploy the driver yourself with kubectl or helm.
    • Maintenance: Add-ons get the latest security patches and bug fixes and are validated by AWS against EKS.
    • Use case: Attach persistent, elastic shared EFS file storage to pods.
    • Regions: All regions that support EFS except the two AWS China regions (Beijing and Ningxia).

    Takeaway: If you run the EFS CSI driver from a Helm chart, consider moving it to the managed add-on so AWS handles version compatibility.

  • AWS Announces Public IP Insights, a New Feature of VPC IP Address Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (July 28, 2023) of Public IP Insights, a free VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) feature that shows every public IPv4 address in an account.

    • Visibility: One view of public IPv4 usage across AWS services, with the resources each address is attached to.
    • Cleanup: Helps identify and release public IPv4 addresses not in use.
    • Security group insights: Flags inefficient use, such as EC2 instances with a public IP whose security group only allows SSH on port 22, and suggests EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint instead.
    • Cost: Free, in all commercial and GovCloud (US) regions.

    Takeaway: Use it to inventory public IPv4 addresses, both to shrink attack surface and to prepare for AWS charging for public IPv4.

  • Automating Custom Networking to Solve IPv4 Exhaustion in Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post showing how to automate VPC CNI custom networking with CDK EKS Blueprints to stop pods from exhausting a VPC’s IPv4 space.

    • Problem: The VPC CNI gives pods IPs from the node’s primary subnet, which can run out on large clusters; IPv6 is the long-term fix but many organizations are not ready.
    • Custom networking: Pods get IPs from secondary ENIs in subnets defined by the ENIConfig custom resource, carved from a secondary VPC CIDR; nodes keep primary-subnet IPs.
    • Pain point: Enabling it on an existing cluster means reconfiguring the add-on and cordoning and draining nodes; only new nodes pick it up.
    • Blueprint pattern: The cdk-eks-blueprints-patterns repo creates the secondary subnets, the VPC CNI add-on and ENIConfig, with options for prefix delegation, WARM_IP_TARGET and WARM_ENI_TARGET.
    • Prerequisites: AWS CLI v2, kubectl, AWS CDK 2.83.0+, npm 9.6.0+, yq and make.

    Takeaway: If pod IPs are the scaling limit, add a secondary CIDR and put it into code with a blueprint, so new clusters start with custom networking.

  • How H2O.ai Optimized and Secured Their AI/ML Infrastructure with Karpenter and Bottlerocket
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post co-written with H2O.ai about replacing Cluster Autoscaler and Amazon Linux 2 with Karpenter and Bottlerocket on EKS for ML workloads.

    • Before: Cluster Autoscaler with many node groups was slow and error-prone; provisioning new ML workloads often took 15 minutes or more, partly due to pulling large images.
    • Result: The post claims a 100-fold improvement in compute provisioning and configuration time.
    • Image prefetch: stargz and SOCI were considered but rejected as hard to use; they used Bottlerocket with pre-baked data volumes that already contain the container images.
    • Weighted provisioners: Several Karpenter provisioners, with a higher-weight one (weight: 2) restricted to GPU instance categories so GPU nodes are tried first without depending on availability.
    • Security: Bottlerocket’s minimal, container-only OS reduces the host attack surface since they never SSH in or install host software.

    Takeaway: For large ML images, pre-baked Bottlerocket volumes plus Karpenter are worth testing before reaching for lazy-loading snapshotters.

  • Scaling Kubernetes with Karpenter: Advanced Scheduling with Pod Affinity and Volume Topology Awareness
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post co-written by Lukonde Mwila showing how Karpenter provisions nodes that satisfy pod affinity, anti-affinity and volume topology constraints.

    • Affinity rules: Covers podAffinity and podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution and preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.
    • Use cases: Affinity co-locates interdependent pods in one AZ or node to cut latency; anti-affinity spreads pods across nodes or AZs for HA, as CoreDNS does with a hostname topologyKey.
    • Karpenter behavior: It watches unschedulable pods and launches compute that meets their affinity rules, with no extra node groups.
    • Walkthrough: Uses a karpenter.sh/v1alpha5 Provisioner on EKS, provisioned with Terraform EKS Blueprints.
    • Volume topology: The post’s second half covers volume topology awareness, meaning node placement that respects where a pod’s persistent volume lives.
    • Version note: The examples use the old v1alpha5 Provisioner API, which later Karpenter releases replaced with NodePools.

    Takeaway: Karpenter honours standard scheduling constraints, so keep them in pod specs rather than encoding placement in node groups. Translate the examples to current Karpenter APIs.

  • Kubernetes Audit Logs: The Unsung Hero of the Kube-verse
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeStory newsletter post by Stephane Karagulmez (August 5, 2023) explaining what Kubernetes audit logs capture, how to enable them and how to use them.

    • Captured data: Request URI, verb, user and groups, source IP, object reference, response status and optionally request and response bodies.
    • Stages: RequestReceived, ResponseStarted, ResponseComplete and Panic.
    • Enabling: kube-apiserver flags such as --audit-log-path, --audit-log-maxage=30, --audit-log-maxbackup=3, --audit-log-maxsize=100, plus an audit policy that sets levels.
    • Managed clusters: Notes how EKS (CloudWatch and CloudTrail integration) and GKE (Cloud Operations) expose audit logs.
    • Uses: Debugging, incident response and compliance, with log management and visualization tools.

    Takeaway: Turn on audit logging with a tuned policy before you need it; without it you cannot answer who did what in a cluster during an incident.

  • helm-dashboard: The Missing UI for Helm to Visualize Your Releases
    summary

    TL;DR: Helm Dashboard is an open source web UI from Komodor for viewing installed Helm releases, their history and their Kubernetes resources. It is not an official Helm project.

    • Features: Lists installed charts with revision history, shows manifest diffs between revisions and browses the resources each chart created.
    • Actions: Roll back or upgrade a release, with a manifest diff shown first.
    • Scanners: Integrates with popular problem scanners.
    • Multi-cluster: Switches between kube contexts; runs locally or inside a cluster.
    • Install: Since 1.0 it ships as a standalone binary that needs neither helm nor kubectl; it can also be installed as a Helm plugin.

    Takeaway: Handy for reviewing release history and diffs without memorising helm history and helm get manifest. Limit its cluster permissions if you install it in-cluster.

  • awesome-kubernetes-threat-detection: Awesome Kubernetes (K8s) Threat Detection
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated awesome-list by jatrost of resources on detecting threats in and defending Kubernetes.

    • Books: Including Hacking Kubernetes, Security Observability with eBPF, Container Security (Liz Rice), and relevant Gray Hat Hacking chapters.
    • Talks: A YouTube playlist of detection talks, such as Falco-based threat hunting across thousands of clusters.
    • Sections: Conferences, blogs and articles, TTPs and attack matrices, tools, detection rules and analytics, and people to follow.
    • Focus: Detection and defense rather than general hardening.

    Takeaway: A good starting reading list for building Kubernetes detection, especially the attack-matrix and detection-rule sections.

  • terraform-tui: Terraform Textual UI for State
    summary

    TL;DR: TFTUI by Ido Avrah is a terminal UI, written in Python, for browsing and working with Terraform state.

    • State tree: Shows the full state with modules nested, searchable by resource name and definition.
    • Resource view: Shows single resources with HCL highlighting and reveals sensitive values on demand.
    • Actions: Taint, untaint or remove resources or whole modules; create targeted and destroy plans and apply them.
    • Compatibility: Works with Terraform, OpenTofu and wrappers such as Terragrunt; switches workspaces without restarting.
    • Install: brew install idoavrah/homebrew/tftui, pipx install tftui or uv tool install tftui; needs Python 3.10+ and run as tftui in a project directory.

    Takeaway: Faster than chaining terraform state list and state show when exploring big states. Be careful with the remove and apply actions on shared state.

  • Understanding and Automating Credential Stuffing Testing with Nuclei
    summary

    TL;DR: ProjectDiscovery blog post by Parth Malhotra (June 8, 2023) on using Nuclei templates to test whether leaked or known credentials work on cloud and self-hosted services.

    • Context: Credential stuffing reuses leaked username and password pairs; the post cites a figure that only 35% of users use a different password for every login.
    • Cloud templates: Self-contained templates with fixed login endpoints, for example a Datadog login check that extracts a CSRF token and matches a Set-Cookie: dogweb= header plus HTTP 302.
    • Self-hosted templates: Need a target host, for example a Jira check against /rest/gadget/1.0/login.
    • Usage: Credentials are passed as variables, for example nuclei -var username=... -var password=... -t <template>.yaml.
    • Defense: Closes with detection and prevention strategies against stuffing.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to projectdiscovery.io/blog.

    Takeaway: Useful for authorised testing of credential reuse across an org’s SaaS and self-hosted logins. Run it only on accounts and systems you are allowed to test.

  • MITRE ATLAS for AI and ML
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) is MITRE’s knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and real-world case studies against AI and ML systems, modelled on ATT&CK.

    • Structure: Uses ATT&CK’s matrix layout: tactics are adversary goals, techniques are methods, case studies are documented incidents.
    • Example techniques: Data poisoning of training or fine-tuning data and prompt injection.
    • Mitigations: Technique entries link to case studies and mitigations.
    • Navigator: An adapted ATT&CK Navigator includes a heat map of the techniques most often referenced in case studies.
    • Counts vary: Third-party sources give different tactic and technique counts for different releases, so check the site for current numbers.
    • Source caveat: The site is a JavaScript app that returned only its title; this summary is based on web search results describing ATLAS.

    Takeaway: Use ATLAS for ML threat modelling and red-team planning just as you would use ATT&CK for conventional systems.

  • How to Build a Globally Distributed, Multi-Region Identity and Access Platform
    summary

    TL;DR: Ory blog post by founder and CTO Aeneas Rekkas (August 7, 2023) explaining why and how Ory built Ory Network as a multi-region identity and access platform.

    • Scale claim: Ory says it handles about 3 billion API requests a day across more than 11,000 production environments.
    • Stack: Built on open source plus Kubernetes, ArgoCD, Crossplane, Grafana and CockroachDB.
    • AZ vs region: Availability zones are not regions; it cites the fire that took down all three zones of GCP’s europe-west9.
    • Single-region risks: Downtime, data loss, limited disaster recovery, latency for distant users and exposure to network failures.
    • Copy-per-region anti-pattern: Running a separate stack per region causes data fragmentation and multiplies management overhead.
    • Title note: The archive title mentions Go, but the post focuses on architecture and infrastructure tooling. The URL now redirects to ory.com.

    Takeaway: A clear argument for a single logical multi-region system over independent regional copies; useful background before choosing a globally replicated database.

  • postgres_lsp: A Language Server for Postgres
    summary

    TL;DR: postgres-language-server (formerly Supabase’s postgres_lsp) is a Language Server Protocol implementation and toolchain for Postgres SQL, built on Postgres’s own parser.

    • Moved: The repo now lives at supabase-community/postgres-language-server; the old URL redirects.
    • Parser: Uses libpg_query for full compatibility with Postgres syntax.
    • Features: Autocompletion, hover, inlay hints, syntax diagnostics, type checking, formatting, migration linting, database linting and PL/pgSQL support.
    • Interfaces: LSP, a CLI, HTTP APIs and a WebAssembly module.
    • Editors: VS Code, Cursor, Neovim (nvim-lspconfig), Zed and Sublime Text.

    Takeaway: Worth adding to your editor if you write a lot of raw SQL or migrations; the CLI’s migration linting can also run in CI.

  • noir: Attack Surface Detector from Source Code
    summary

    TL;DR: Noir, by hahwul (now under the OWASP Noir project), reads source code to list an application’s endpoints and attack surface, then feeds them to DAST tools.

    • Purpose: Finds shadow APIs, deprecated endpoints and hidden routes from code instead of relying on documentation or proxy captures.
    • SAST-to-DAST bridge: Sends discovered endpoints to ZAP, Burp Suite, Caido and similar tools for more complete dynamic scans.
    • AI mode: The current README adds LLM-based analysis to detect endpoints in languages and frameworks it does not support natively.
    • Output: JSON, YAML, TOML, OpenAPI and other formats; noir -b <path> runs it on a codebase, and there is a GitHub Action.
    • Evolution: It began in 2023 as a white-box helper; the README has grown since, with news items into late 2025.

    Takeaway: Run Noir in CI before DAST so scanners test the routes that exist in code, not only those the crawler finds.

  • navgix: Multi-Threaded Golang Tool to Check for nginx Alias Traversal Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: navgix, from Hakai Offensive Security, is a multi-threaded Go tool that checks web servers for nginx alias traversal (“off-by-slash”) misconfigurations.

    • Bug class: An nginx location without a trailing slash combined with an alias lets requests like /static../ reach the parent directory.
    • Heuristic mode: Fetches the page, pulls directory paths from src attributes and tests each level (for example /static/, /static/img/).
    • Brute-force mode: Also tries a short list of directories that commonly have the issue, then confirms.
    • Install: git clone, then go build.
    • Credits: Based on Orange Tsai’s Black Hat 2018 “Breaking Parser Logic” research and bayotop’s off-by-slash.

    Takeaway: Grep your own nginx configs for location blocks with alias and no trailing slash, and use navgix to confirm on external hosts you are authorised to test.

  • AWS Security Monitoring in 2023: Untangle the Chaos
    summary

    TL;DR: Michael Wittig of cloudonaut (August 4, 2023) groups the overlapping AWS security services into three groups and gives a minimal setup for monitoring and alerting.

    • Three groups: Sources of information (CloudTrail, Config, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 DNS logs, Inspector, Macie, ECR scanning), best-practice and anomaly checks (Config rules, Trusted Advisor, GuardDuty, Access Analyzer), and aggregation (Security Hub, Security Lake, Detective, Audit Manager).
    • Overlap problem: Turning everything on means paying for the same check several times and getting several findings for one issue, such as a public S3 bucket.
    • Recommended set: In a delegated admin security account, enable AWS Config with 1-year retention and Security Hub with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard in every used region; GuardDuty and Inspector are optional.
    • Central hub: GuardDuty and Inspector send findings to Security Hub by default, so it becomes the single place to work findings (NEW, NOTIFIED, SUPPRESSED, RESOLVED).
    • Tuning: Disable Security Hub controls you disagree with so the finding count stays low.
    • Alerting: Security Hub publishes finding events to EventBridge, which routes them to whoever is responsible.

    Takeaway: A sensible minimal AWS security monitoring baseline: Config plus Security Hub org-wide, routed through EventBridge, instead of enabling every service.

  • Application Architecture as Code
    summary

    TL;DR: Gregor Hohpe (The Architect Elevator, August 2023) argues that cloud automation is moving from infrastructure towards applications and should be judged on several dimensions, not as one tool war.

    • History: CloudFormation (2011), Terraform (2014), Pulumi (2018), AWS CDK (2019), CDK v2 (late 2021), CDKTF GA (2022), Cue, and CloudFormation ForEach (July 2023).
    • Infrastructure from Code: The 2023 trend of deriving cloud resources from application code, which can make a separate automation language unnecessary.
    • Four dimensions: Provision resources, deploy application artifacts, compose connections between components, and specify settings.
    • Factions: Infrastructure teams tend to prefer Terraform; serverless application teams lean towards CDK or IfC; each side tends to judge the other by a different task.
    • Composition focus: Wiring components together (references, ARNs) is becoming the main concern, which he links to architecture as boxes and lines.

    Takeaway: When teams argue about Terraform versus CDK, split the discussion by which automation task each tool is serving.

  • VS Code’s Token Security: Keeping Your Secrets… Not So Secretly
    summary

    TL;DR: Cycode researcher Oreen Livni shows that a malicious VS Code extension can read tokens that other extensions, and VS Code’s own GitHub and Microsoft login, keep in VS Code’s “secure” secret storage.

    • Expectation: VS Code’s SecretStorage API is meant to isolate each extension’s secrets in the OS keychain.
    • Naive approach: Patching another extension’s code (CircleCI’s in the demo) to print its token works but needs per-extension, per-version effort.
    • Scalable attack: By studying VS Code’s open source code, they built a PoC extension that retrieves other extensions’ secrets without modifying them, including GitHub and Microsoft account sync tokens.
    • Extra bug: The post says they found an additional bug along the way.
    • Org risk: Stolen tokens often belong to organisation accounts, so one bad extension can expose company systems.
    • Page note: The post was last updated August 2025 and sits on a vendor marketing page.

    Takeaway: Treat every VS Code extension as able to read all IDE-stored tokens. Allowlist extensions on developer machines and prefer short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens.

  • Mountpoint for Amazon S3: Generally Available and Ready for Production Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS News Blog post (Jeff Barr, August 2023) announcing general availability of Mountpoint for Amazon S3, an open source file client that mounts S3 buckets on Linux.

    • Scope: Aimed at large, read-heavy workloads such as data lakes, ML training, rendering, autonomous vehicle simulation and ETL.
    • Semantics: Supports sequential and random reads and sequential, append-only writes; it does not aim for full POSIX semantics.
    • Mechanics: Linux VFS calls become S3 LIST, GET and PUT requests; it is tuned to use network bandwidth well.
    • Install: RPM for Amazon Linux, then mount-s3 <bucket> <dir>; the demo builds a time-lapse GIF from webcam images with ffmpeg.
    • Update: A September 2023 update adds how to enable file deletion.
    • Not for: The post says not to use it for things like Git repositories.

    Takeaway: Good for letting file-based tools read large S3 datasets without rewriting them for the SDK. Check the write and POSIX limits against your workload first.

  • AWS Observability Accelerator for Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Docs page from AWS Observability Accelerator for Terraform on setting up distributed tracing on Amazon EKS with an OpenTelemetry Collector that exports to AWS X-Ray.

    • Current content: The page now describes v3 of the eks-monitoring module, which is newer than when the link was saved.
    • Profiles: self-managed-amp supports traces (toggle with enable_tracing), cloudwatch-otlp always enables them, and managed-metrics is metrics only.
    • Collector: Receives OTLP on gRPC port 4317 and HTTP port 4318, then exports to X-Ray.
    • Instrumentation: Point apps at the collector with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector.otel-collector.svc.cluster.local:4317.
    • Example: Builds and pushes the go-sample-app from aws-otel-community to ECR and deploys it to EKS.

    Takeaway: A quick path to X-Ray tracing on EKS if you already use the accelerator’s Terraform modules; check which collector profile you run.

  • Using SBOM to Find Vulnerable Container Images Running on Amazon EKS Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post on generating SBOMs for every ECR image and querying them to find which EKS workloads run a newly disclosed vulnerable package.

    • Motivation: Cites Synopsys OSSRA 2023 (96% of commercial codebases contain open source; 48% had high-risk vulnerabilities) and Sonatype’s reported 742% average annual increase in supply chain attacks.
    • Generation: An EventBridge rule on ECR PUSH events triggers AWS CodeBuild, which runs Syft to create an SPDX JSON SBOM.
    • Storage: SBOMs go into an S3 bucket for analysis, mirroring how Amazon Inspector’s own SBOM export works.
    • Zero-day use: When a vulnerability like Log4Shell lands, query the SBOM inventory to find affected images and the clusters running them.
    • Scanning: Mentions Grype can scan SBOMs directly, and notes ECR events on EventBridge are best-effort.

    Takeaway: Generate and store SBOMs at push time so a zero-day becomes a query rather than a rescan of every image.

  • Hacking GitHub AWS Integrations Again
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Grzelak (August 3, 2023) shows how to find, at scale, AWS IAM roles that trust GitHub Actions OIDC without restricting which repository may assume them.

    • Misconfiguration: Trust policies that check only token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud and omit the :sub repo condition let any GitHub repo assume the role.
    • Lab: Steps to create the OIDC provider and a deliberately weak role, plus a workflow using aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials and aws sts get-caller-identity.
    • Validator: A GitHub Actions matrix job that tries to assume each ARN listed in target-role-list.json.
    • Finding roles: GitHub code search gave 15 hits and Sourcegraph over a thousand; for full coverage he parses GH Archive PushEvents and commit patches to .github/workflows for role ARNs.
    • Tooling: Includes a Python “Github AWS OIDC Firehose” script that watches the GitHub events API.
    • Mitigation noted: Enterprise-scoped issuer URLs limit exposure to one organisation, but this is not the default. Bitbucket, CircleCI and GitLab use similar org-scoped OIDC setups.

    Takeaway: Audit every IAM role trusting GitHub OIDC and require a sub condition pinned to specific repos and branches.

  • What’s New for Security in Kubernetes 1.28
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog Security Labs post by Rory McCune (August 15, 2023) on the security-relevant changes in Kubernetes 1.28, mainly Validating Admission Policy reaching beta.

    • Validating Admission Policy: Built-in admission control written in CEL, introduced in 1.26 and beta in 1.28; the alternative without third-party tools had been the less flexible Pod Security Admission.
    • Try it: Create a kind cluster with the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy feature gate and admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1 enabled in runtimeConfig.
    • Verify: kubectl api-resources --api-group=admissionregistration.k8s.io -o name should list validatingadmissionpolicies and validatingadmissionpolicybindings.
    • Example: A sample policy and binding that blocks privileged containers in the default namespace.
    • Self-subject review: An API that lets users see their own identity and attributes graduates to stable.

    Takeaway: Validating Admission Policy can replace simple Kyverno or Gatekeeper rules without a webhook. Test policies in a kind cluster first.

  • ansible-role-hardening: Ansible Role to Apply a Security Baseline, Systemd Edition
    summary

    TL;DR: konstruktoid’s Ansible role applies a systemd-focused security baseline to AlmaLinux, Debian and Ubuntu servers.

    • Status: The README says the role has moved to the konstruktoid/ansible-collection-hardening collection, which is recommended for continued updates.
    • Supported OS (current README): AlmaLinux 10, Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04; needs Ansible 2.18+.
    • Options: Examples include kernel_lockdown, sshd_admin_net, sshd_allow_groups, per-user sshd_match_users rules and ufw_rate_limit.
    • Docs: All defaults are in defaults/main.yml and meta/argument_specs.yml; ansible-doc -t role shows them.
    • Images: Hardened Ubuntu AMIs and Azure images built with Packer and this role live in konstruktoid/hardened-images.
    • Supply chain: Provides a SLSA provenance artifact; the README warns to test in a non-production environment first.

    Takeaway: A solid starting baseline for Linux hardening in Ansible. Use the collection instead of the role and review the SSH and firewall defaults before rollout.

  • Network Load Balancers Now Support Security Groups
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post on the August 10, 2023 launch of security groups for Network Load Balancers and how the AWS Load Balancer Controller uses them on EKS.

    • Feature: You can attach one or more security groups to an NLB to filter which traffic it accepts and forwards.
    • Old pain: Access was controlled with rules on instance security groups, which counted against per-instance quotas and limited how many NLBs you could run.
    • Controller support: AWS Load Balancer Controller 2.6.0+ creates and applies security groups to NLBs, instances and pods that use Security Groups for Pods.
    • Benefits: Backend ingress rules can reference the NLB’s security group, and the controller keeps a constant number of rules per cluster.
    • Walkthrough: Shows how EKS Service objects of type LoadBalancer get NLB security groups.

    Takeaway: Upgrade to Load Balancer Controller 2.6.0+ and use NLB security groups so backends only accept traffic from the load balancer.

  • Measure Cluster Performance Impact of Amazon GuardDuty EKS Agent
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post on how the GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring eBPF agent works and how to measure its overhead on your cluster.

    • Coverage: Runtime Monitoring (from March 30, 2023) adds over 30 findings from process, file and network activity inside containers and hosts.
    • Agent: Packaged as an EKS add-on and run as a DaemonSet that loads an eBPF probe; events are enriched with pod, namespace and cluster names.
    • Limits: The agent is capped at 1000m CPU and 1 GB memory.
    • Measurement: With Inspektor Gadget’s top ebpf gadget, a 4-second trace showed the agent called 525 times with just over 1 ms of runtime; kubectl top also shows usage.
    • Findings: Filter by resource type EKSCluster in the GuardDuty console; automate response with EventBridge or Security Hub custom actions.

    Takeaway: Before rolling the agent out fleet-wide, measure it on a representative node with Inspektor Gadget, since the post notes results depend on workload.

  • How Chick-fil-A Provides Observability for 2,800+ K8s Clusters
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Brian Chambers and Alex Crane (Chick-fil-A Tech, August 2023) describe how Chick-fil-A collects metrics and logs from edge Kubernetes clusters in about 2,800 restaurants.

    • Fleet: One edge Kubernetes cluster per restaurant runs business-critical workloads without depending on the internet, plus hundreds of thousands of IoT devices (fryers, grills, tablets) sending billions of MQTT messages a month.
    • Constraints: Too many logs to ship everything to the cloud. Early verbose logging used up store bandwidth and even hurt credit card processing. Metric cardinality across 2,800 sites gets expensive.
    • Metrics first: They push teams from log-derived metrics towards “first-class metrics”, which give health context with less data. HTTP status metrics matter less because most apps speak MQTT.
    • Pipeline: Prometheus scrapes pod /metrics endpoints and an edge Vector instance forwards the data to a cloud Vector instance, which routes it to each team’s chosen tools.
    • Mixed streams: Where tools combine logs and metrics, a sidecar scrapes metric tags from logs and forwards them to Vector.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetches; this summary is based on a Wayback Machine snapshot of the article, of which only the first part, through metrics and the start of the logs section, was read.

    Takeaway: At the edge, bandwidth and cardinality are hard limits. A routing pipeline such as Vector plus a metrics-first policy keeps observability from competing with production traffic.

  • EKS Node Autoscaling with Large Container Images and a Warm Pool
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Matt Kornfield (Better Programming, August 2023) describes trying to speed up EKS autoscaling for GPU workloads with 3-4 GB CUDA images by using an ASG warm pool.

    • Problem: Pulling a 3-4 GB image from private ECR took a minute or two, and with EC2 start time nodes needed 2-3 minutes to be ready.
    • Part 1, pull in warm pool: Pre-pulling images in user-data (with crictl) when instances enter the warm pool had previously caused corrupted images and widespread failures, so the team would not turn it back on.
    • Part 2, reuse on scale-in: Enabling the ASG “reuse on scale in” setting (supported in the Terraform provider) had no effect, because Cluster Autoscaler does not support warm pools and terminates nodes instead.
    • Part 3: The article goes on to the SOCI snapshotter as an alternative; that section is behind the Medium member paywall.
    • Source caveat: Direct fetches were blocked; this is based on the public, pre-paywall portion of a Wayback Machine snapshot.

    Takeaway: Warm pools do not work with Cluster Autoscaler on EKS. For large images, look at lazy-loading (SOCI) or pre-baked volumes instead.

  • An Introduction to Deploying Your Database on Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: An introductory Hashnode post explaining the Kubernetes basics for running a database: persistent storage and StatefulSets.

    • Deployments: Suited to stateless apps; pods get random names and share storage, which causes inconsistency if several database replicas write to the same storage.
    • Storage: Explains StorageClass, PersistentVolume (cluster-wide) and PersistentVolumeClaim (namespaced) so data outlives pods.
    • StatefulSet: Gives each pod a stable ordinal name (podname-0, -1) and its own PVC and PV.
    • Ordering: Pods start one after another, and each new replica syncs from the previous one.
    • Primary/replica: Describes one read-write primary pod and read-only replicas to avoid write conflicts.

    Takeaway: A beginner primer. For production databases, use an operator that handles replication, failover and backups rather than a bare StatefulSet.

  • Architecting Kubernetes Clusters: Choosing a Worker Node Size
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniele Polencic (Learnk8s, now LearnKube, updated August 2023) weighs fewer large worker nodes against many small ones for a Kubernetes cluster of the same total capacity.

    • Reserved resources: Kubelet and OS reservations shrink as a share on larger nodes, for example 6% of the first core and 25% of the first 4 GB of memory, plus a 100 MB eviction threshold.
    • Worked example: On an 8 GB, 2 vCPU node only about 75% of memory is left for pods; a 4 vCPU, 32 GB node fits 13 replicas of a 300m/2 GB pod (CPU-bound).
    • Efficiency: Large nodes waste less to reservations and fragmentation; per-node DaemonSets (kube-proxy, log agents, CSI drivers) are a fixed cost on every node.
    • Resilience: Few nodes limit how widely replicas can spread, and losing one large node has a bigger blast radius.
    • Other factors: Scaling increments and lead time, image pulls, kubelet and API server load, and per-node pod and volume limits.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to learnkube.com.

    Takeaway: There is no single right size. Medium-to-large nodes are usually more efficient, but keep enough nodes for replica spread and acceptable failure impact.

  • komoplane: Crossplane Troubleshooting Tool by Komodor
    summary

    TL;DR: komoplane is an experimental open source tool from Komodor that visualizes Crossplane resources to help with troubleshooting.

    • Goal: Show the structure of control plane resources (claims, composite resources, managed resources) to speed up debugging.
    • Install: Helm chart from https://helm-charts.komodor.io, via helm upgrade --install komoplane komodorio/komoplane.
    • Access: Web UI on port 8090 (configurable through extraArgs); port-forward to the pod.
    • Local mode: A standalone binary runs against your kubeconfig; set KUBECONTEXT to choose the context.
    • Related: Sibling of Komodor’s Helm Dashboard and validkube.

    Takeaway: Useful when Crossplane composition trees get hard to follow with kubectl. Treat it as an experiment, not a supported product.

  • wrongsecrets: Vulnerable App with Examples Showing How Not to Use Secrets
    summary

    TL;DR: OWASP WrongSecrets is a deliberately vulnerable application whose challenges teach how secrets leak and how not to manage them.

    • Content: Real and fake secrets hidden in code, configuration, Docker images and cloud deployments; each challenge shows a different leak path.
    • Quick start: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8090:8090 jeroenwillemsen/wrongsecrets:latest-no-vault, then open localhost:8080; a Heroku demo also exists.
    • Advanced tracks: Kubernetes and Minikube, HashiCorp Vault exercises, and cloud challenges on AWS, GCP and Azure.
    • Learning goals: Common secrets management mistakes, finding exposed credentials, secret detection tools and best practices.
    • Hosting: Can also run on Render and Railway.

    Takeaway: Good for team training or for testing whether your secret scanners catch realistic leaks. Run it in isolated environments only.

  • Google Workspace Will Require Two Admins to Sign Off on Critical Changes
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (Sergiu Gatlan, August 23, 2023) reports new Google Workspace controls against social engineering and account takeover, led by multi-party approval for sensitive admin actions.

    • Multi-party approval: A sensitive change by one admin must be confirmed by another; at launch it covered only 2-Step Verification settings changes, with preview planned in the following months.
    • Mandatory 2SV: Select admin accounts at resellers and the largest enterprise customers will have to use 2SV in a phased rollout; Google cites a 50% drop in compromised accounts with 2SV.
    • Gmail AI defenses: Extended to sensitive actions such as filter creation and forwarding, in preview.
    • Chronicle export: A faster path for exporting Workspace logs to Google’s Chronicle security operations suite.

    Takeaway: Turn on multi-party approval and enforce 2SV on all Workspace admins, since a compromised admin account has outsized impact.

  • Shipping RDS IAM Authentication (with a Bastion Host and SSM)
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy documents how he set up RDS IAM database authentication for a private RDS instance reached through a bastion host and SSM Session Manager port forwarding.

    • Steps: Enable IAM DB auth, create IAM roles with rds-db:connect plus port-forwarding permissions, add IAM-enabled database users, and document the connection commands.
    • Zero downtime: Enabling it via Terraform’s iam_database_authentication_enabled was zero-downtime; CPU rose from about 10% to 20% for under 5 minutes in his test.
    • Expected warnings: max_wal_senders and rds.logical_replication parameter messages after restart are normal.
    • IAM policy: A sample Terraform policy scopes ssm:StartSession to the bastion and the AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost document, and limits terminate and resume to the caller’s own sessions.
    • DB user: CREATE USER db_userx; GRANT rds_iam TO db_userx;
    • Connect: Get the endpoint, start an SSM port-forwarding session, generate an auth token and connect with psql (using aws-vault).

    Takeaway: A copyable recipe for passwordless, IAM-controlled access to private databases with no SSH or public endpoint.

  • basti: Securely Connect to RDS and Other AWS Resources in a VPC with No Idle Cost
    summary

    TL;DR: Basti is a CLI that gives you SSM Session Manager port forwarding to RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache and other private VPC resources, and manages the bastion EC2 instance for you.

    • Moved: The repository now lives at basti-app/basti.
    • How it works: Creates a small bastion instance in the target’s VPC, uses Session Manager port forwarding, and stops the instance when idle, so the cost is mostly a stopped instance.
    • Security: No SSH keys and no inbound internet access; access is fully controlled by IAM.
    • Usage: basti init (once per target), basti connect, then use localhost:<port>, for example psql -h localhost -p 5432; basti cleanup removes the resources.
    • Install: brew install basti or npm install --global basti.
    • Teams: Shared config files, automatic mode for CI, IaC support, minimal IAM permission docs and usage auditing.

    Takeaway: An easy way to drop SSH bastions and VPNs for occasional database access; pair it with IAM DB auth for keyless access end to end.

  • Kubernetes Validating Admission Policies: A Practical Example
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post by Craig Box and Ben Hirschberg of ARMO (March 30, 2023) showing how Kubescape ported its controls to CEL-based ValidatingAdmissionPolicies.

    • Webhook problems: Webhooks must run as a production service, must fail open or closed, and add latency to admission.
    • VAP: Introduced as alpha in 1.26, Validating Admission Policies are declarative, run in the API server and use CEL, which is sandboxed and runs in microseconds.
    • Kubescape: Its controls were written in Rego for OPA; the team ported them to CEL so findings can be enforced at admission.
    • Example: Control C-0017 denies containers without readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, with separate expressions for Pods, workload templates and CronJob jobTemplates.
    • Version safety: matchConstraints converts requests to the matched API version, so new API versions cannot bypass the rule.
    • Age note: The page carries Kubernetes’ “more than one year old” warning; the example uses the v1alpha1 API.

    Takeaway: Kubescape’s library is a ready set of CEL policies; adapt them to the GA admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 API on current clusters.

  • Pivoting Clouds in AWS Organizations Part 2: Examining AWS Security Features and Tools for Enumeration
    summary

    TL;DR: NetSPI’s Scott Weston (March 7, 2023), in part 2 of a series on pentesting AWS Organizations, covers organization features that attackers can abuse after compromising one account, plus a Pacu enumeration module.

    • Account Management phishing: With trusted access for AWS Account Management enabled, a compromised management account can change member accounts’ contact details to support social engineering.
    • Delegated policies: A November 27, 2022 feature lets delegated administrators manage Organizations policies; if granted too broadly, they could remove restrictive SCPs from their own or other accounts.
    • Pacu module: He added AWS Organizations support to Pacu and an organizations__enum module (PRs 326 and 335); view results with data organizations, including a graph.
    • Member accounts: Without delegation, the module still shows the basic organization description.
    • Defense: None of this is a zero-day; the root cause is misconfiguration of trusted access and delegation.

    Takeaway: Audit which services have trusted access and what delegated admins can change; treat the management account and its delegates as tier 0.

  • Building Docker Images Smaller, Rootless and Non-Shell for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Robert Nemet (DEV, April 2023) walks through shrinking a Go service image and making it run as non-root with no shell, for Kubernetes.

    • Starting point: A multi-stage build on debian:buster produced a 133 MB image running as root with a shell available.
    • Scratch: Moving the final stage to FROM scratch breaks the app until it is built static with CGO_ENABLED=0.
    • Strip: -ldflags="-s -w" removes debug info; the image went from 133 MB to 19.1 MB and then 13 MB.
    • Non-root: Run useradd -u 10001 appuser in the builder, copy /etc/passwd into scratch, set USER appuser and COPY --chown.
    • Trade-offs: Explains when cgo is needed and when a distroless or similar base is a better fit than scratch.
    • Build caching: Uses docker buildx with registry --cache-to and --cache-from.

    Takeaway: For Go services, a static binary on scratch or distroless, running as a fixed UID, is easy and shrinks the attack surface.

  • Methods to Backdoor an AWS Account
    summary

    TL;DR: Fawaz Masood Qureshi (Mystic0x1, August 20, 2023) lists ways an attacker with admin access can keep persistence in an AWS account.

    • Access keys: Add a second key to an existing privileged user with iam:CreateAccessKey (users can have two active keys), or create a new admin user.
    • Temporary credentials: aws sts get-session-token --duration-seconds 129600 gives 36-hour credentials that keep working after the long-term key is revoked.
    • AssumeRole: Create or modify a role whose trust policy allows assumption from an external, attacker-controlled account.
    • Security groups: Open inbound rules to keep network access.
    • EC2: Use user data scripts and SSM send-command to run code on instances.
    • Context: Follows the author’s two-part AWS privilege escalation series.

    Takeaway: Use it as a detection checklist. Alert on new access keys, GetSessionToken with long durations, trust policy changes to external accounts, user data edits and unexpected SSM commands.

  • Container Security Fundamentals Part 5: AppArmor and SELinux
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 5 of Rory McCune’s container security fundamentals series at Datadog Security Labs covers AppArmor and SELinux as mandatory access control layers for containers.

    • MAC vs DAC: MAC rules apply even to root (unless root disables MAC entirely); Debian-family systems default to AppArmor, Red Hat-family to SELinux.
    • AppArmor: sudo aa-status shows profiles; Docker applies docker-default, which is compatible but not tight.
    • Custom profile: A profile with deny /etc/** wl, loaded via apparmor_parser -r and applied with --security-opt "apparmor=docker-block-etc" blocks writes to /etc even as root.
    • SELinux: Covers targeted vs mls policy, enforcing/permissive/disabled modes and viewing labels with -Z (for example container_runtime_t).
    • Container policy: Under SELinux, a container with a bind-mounted home directory cannot write to it even as root; --security-opt label:disable removes that protection.

    Takeaway: Leave the default profiles on, never disable labels to “fix” permissions, and write custom profiles for high-risk workloads.

  • Backward Compatibility, Go 1.21, and Go 2
    summary

    TL;DR: Russ Cox’s Go blog post (August 14, 2023) explains how Go keeps its Go 1 compatibility promise, the GODEBUG mechanism formalized in Go 1.21, and that a breaking Go 2 will never happen.

    • API checking: Exported APIs are recorded in files such as go/api/go1.21.txt, and a test fails on any unrecorded change.
    • Testing: Development Go builds are tested against all of Google’s internal Go code before becoming its production toolchain.
    • Subtle breaks: Examples include untagged struct literals breaking when net.TCPAddr gained Zone, and nanosecond time.Now precision breaking round-trip tests, plus output, input and protocol changes.
    • GODEBUG: Behaviour changes that may break programs get a GODEBUG opt-out, kept for at least two years (four releases), with /godebug/non-default-behavior/<name>:events runtime metrics.
    • Go 2: “There will not be a Go 2 that breaks Go 1 programs”; the Go team will keep prioritizing compatibility.

    Takeaway: Upgrade Go toolchains with confidence, use tagged struct literals (go vet warns), and reach for GODEBUG settings when a new release changes behaviour.

  • RIP AWS Go Lambda Runtime
    summary

    TL;DR: Mark Wolfe (August 9, 2023) criticizes AWS’s deprecation of the go1.x Lambda runtime, then scheduled for December 31, 2023, in favour of the provided.al2 custom runtime.

    • Migration: No automated path; each function must be repackaged by hand.
    • Gotcha 1: The custom runtime ignores the Handler setting but still requires it; the binary must be named bootstrap in the zip root.
    • Gotcha 2: Lambda does not check that bootstrap exists at deploy time, so you get Runtime.InvalidEntrypoint “Couldn’t find valid bootstrap(s)” at invoke time.
    • Visibility: Go disappears as a named runtime in the console and becomes indistinguishable from Rust or other custom runtimes; old samples stop working.
    • Suggestions: AWS could ship a go1.al2 runtime like java8.al2, and validate packages for bootstrap on deploy.

    Takeaway: Build Go Lambdas as bootstrap for provided.al2 or provided.al2023, and add a CI check that the zip contains it.

  • Avoiding Pitfalls in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: DoltHub blog post (August 16, 2023) on Go pitfalls the Dolt team hit, aimed at programmers coming from C++ or Java.

    • Range: for v := range slice gives the index, not the element; with an []int this compiles silently and prints 0..n-1.
    • Multiple returns: They are not tuples; you cannot store, index or mostly pass them as a value, and mixing := and = on the left-hand side causes subtle shadowing bugs.
    • Type embedding: Embedding is not inheritance, which leads to surprises with method resolution.
    • Value receivers: Methods with value receivers operate on copies, so mutations are lost.
    • Nil: Covers nil pitfalls, including interfaces holding typed nil values.
    • Source: Every example is one the author says they personally hit.

    Takeaway: A short list to share with engineers new to Go. Most of these bugs compile cleanly, so linters and reviews need to watch for them.

  • Advanced Go Concurrency
    summary

    TL;DR: Encore blog post by André Eriksson (February 18, 2020) on the higher-level concurrency primitives in golang.org/x/sync and related patterns.

    • Basics recap: Goroutines, channels, context for cancellation, and sync and sync/atomic.
    • singleflight: group.Do(key, fn) collapses concurrent calls for the same key into one, for example one DB query shared by many requests for the same city’s weather; the third return value says whether the result was shared.
    • errgroup: Like sync.WaitGroup but returns the first error from tasks started with group.Go, then group.Wait().
    • Bounded concurrency: Uses semaphores, including the weighted semaphore package, to cap how many goroutines run at once.
    • Date note: Saved in 2023, but the post is from 2020; the packages it covers are still current.

    Takeaway: Reach for singleflight against cache stampedes and errgroup for fan-out with error handling before writing your own WaitGroup and channel code.

  • How to Develop a Great CLI with Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Ellis (actuated, August 22, 2023) shares lessons from building Go CLIs such as faas-cli, arkade, k3sup, actions-usage and actuated-cli.

    • Start small: faas-cli began with Go’s built-in flag package and moved to Cobra once it needed sub-commands like faas-cli secret list/create/delete.
    • Less typing: actuated-cli dropped the --owner flag by working out which enrolled organizations the user is authorized for, and takes the host as a positional argument.
    • Auth: Instead of hand-made PAT files, actuated-cli auth obtains and stores a token as gh auth does; Cobra’s Changed() lets explicit --token flags override the default.
    • JSON output: A --json flag for piping into jq that also exposes fields the table output hides.
    • SSH debugging: Covers the CLI’s support for actuated’s SSH gateway to debug CI jobs.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to actuated.com.

    Takeaway: Ship an MVP, add sensible defaults that remove flags, store auth once, and always offer --json.

  • Getting into AWS Cloud Security Research as a n00bcake
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Grzelak (August 29, 2023) gathers advice from AWS security researchers on how to start doing AWS cloud security research.

    • Process: Build things in AWS before breaking them and debug what fails (Christophe Tafani-Dereeper); script your manual work (Scott Piper’s CloudMapper and Parliament started this way); avoid the web console.
    • Practice targets: flAWS, flAWS 2 (attacker and defender paths), Rhino Security Labs’ CloudGoat and Bishop Fox’s CloudFoxable.
    • Write: He traces his advisory work, speaking and later roles back to three 2016 blog posts on hacking AWS.
    • Habits: Learn from experts, befriend engineers, stay ethical and get the reps in.
    • Focus areas: Trawl AWS docs, decompose Boto3 and other SDKs, look for API discrepancies and undocumented APIs, target AWS open source, probe shared responsibility, monitor changes and enumerate.

    Takeaway: A practical roadmap for newcomers: practise in deliberately vulnerable labs, then mine SDK definitions and docs for inconsistencies, and publish what you find.

  • Web AppSec Interview Questions
    summary

    TL;DR: Tib3rius’s page collects 61 web application security interview questions with hidden answers, originally posted as a social media series.

    • Format: Answers are hidden by default so you can practise; the author notes they are his answers, not complete ones.
    • Difficulty: Most questions are deliberately hard and focus on web app hacking.
    • Examples: Web cache deception vs poisoning; the two conditions for session fixation; Base64 vs Base64URL; five or more XSS types; boolean error-based blind SQLi.
    • More topics: Same-Origin Policy, TE.TE request smuggling, JWK vs JKU in JWTs, Sec-WebSocket-Key, CSP unsafe-inline, and CRLF injection.
    • Detail: Answers include payload examples such as CASE expressions with divide-by-zero to force errors.

    Takeaway: Good interview prep and a self-check for pentesters; also usable as a question bank when hiring AppSec engineers.

  • Early Retirement: Some Reflections Two Years In
    summary

    TL;DR: Jason Chan reflects two years after retiring in 2021 at age 45, sharing resources on deciding to retire, adjusting mindset and handling finances.

    • Deciding: He retired at peak earning power; he points to research on happiness, such as Laurie Santos’s Science of Well-Being and Arthur Brooks’s podcast, and the “hedonic treadmill”.
    • Grounding reads: Tolstoy’s “How Much Land Does a Man Need?” and Ishiguro’s “The Remains of the Day”.
    • Mindset: For the first time he controls his own time; you are “retiring to” a new life, not only “retiring from” a job, and must replace a work identity.
    • Books: Fritz Gilbert’s Keys to a Successful Retirement and Casey Weade’s Job Optional.
    • Now: Volunteering, hobbies, advising security startups and mentoring, especially people from underrepresented groups.
    • Finances: The shift from accumulating to drawing down; resources include r/financialindependence, the Bogleheads forum and Morningstar.

    Takeaway: A non-technical read for security leaders weighing an exit. Plan what you will retire to as carefully as the finances.

  • What I’m Doing and How It’s Going: How I Went from a $350K FTE to $700K+ Doing My Own Thing
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Miessler (August 19, 2023) explains leaving corporate security jobs (IOActive, Apple, Robinhood) to go independent, and how he now makes about $700K a year versus a $350K salary.

    • Why he left: Leadership that could not decide, articulate or execute; endless planning and Zoom calls; work he felt did not improve the world enough.
    • Structure: Unsupervised Learning is the parent company for building a product, consulting and advising, and the newsletter and podcast.
    • Consulting: A custom security assessment combining technical vulnerabilities and business resilience, plus advice on security, AI strategy and go-to-market.
    • Income streams: Newsletter and podcast sponsors, consulting, advisory equity, and speaking at $7.5K-$25K per talk (about $100K a year estimated); courses and books are not yet a factor.
    • Honesty: He says it is not all figured out and is still stressful.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to danielmiessler.com/blog.

    Takeaway: A concrete breakdown of independent security career income. The model rests on an audience built over years, so start publishing early.

  • Authorizing Cross-Account KMS Access with Aliases
    summary

    TL;DR: Luc van Donkersgoed (August 25, 2023) explains why an IAM policy that names a KMS alias ARN fails for cross-account access, and how to do it correctly.

    • Scenario: A Lambda in account A writes to an S3 bucket in account B whose policy requires a specific KMS key; the Lambda knows only the alias.
    • Failure: Naming arn:aws:kms:<region>:<account-b>:alias/... as the resource gives AccessDenied ... not authorized to perform: kms:GenerateDataKey.
    • Why: AWS docs say IAM policy statements must name the key ARN, not a key ID, alias name or alias ARN.
    • Fix: Set Resource to arn:aws:kms:<region>:<account-b>:key/* with a condition "kms:RequestAlias": "alias/my-example-kms-key-alias" (or use kms:ResourceAliases).
    • Safety: This is safe because alias names are unique per account and region; only wildcards in the alias need care.

    Takeaway: For alias-based KMS permissions, always use the kms:RequestAlias or kms:ResourceAliases condition keys instead of alias ARNs.

  • Falco-bypasses: Techniques to Bypass the Default Falco Ruleset
    summary

    TL;DR: BlackBerry research repo documenting techniques that evade the default Falco ruleset (as of Falco v0.28.1), with a test image and C “fuber” snippets.

    • Status: The repository is archived, and the research targets an old Falco version.
    • Skipped syscalls: Falco ignores many high-volume system calls (for example read, mmap, futex), which is itself a bypass vector.
    • Techniques: Bypasses via symlinks, executable naming, parent and ancestor naming, reverse-shell detection gaps, command-argument manipulation, sensitive mounts, crypto-mining detection and privileged container detection.
    • Sudo: A special case of the “Sudo Potential Privilege Escalation” rule tested with CVE-2021-3156.
    • DoS: Discusses CVE-2019-8339 and Falco denial of service on a host, Docker, kubeadm, Minikube and GKE.
    • Artifacts: The sshayb/fuber:latest image ships docker and kubectl under renamed binaries to avoid triggering rules; ends with a full attack simulation and recommendations.

    Takeaway: Rule-based runtime detection keyed on process names and paths is easy to evade. Test your Falco rules against these techniques and add behaviour-based checks.

  • Verifying Images in a Private Amazon ECR with Kyverno and IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
    summary

    TL;DR: CNCF community post by Kyverno maintainer Shuting Zhao (August 29, 2023) showing how to let Kyverno verify image signatures in private Amazon ECR using IRSA instead of registry secrets.

    • Problem: Passing ECR credentials to Kyverno as secrets is hard to manage across many clusters.
    • IRSA: Create the cluster’s IAM OIDC provider, then an IAM role bound to the Kyverno service account so it can pull from ECR with AWS SDK credentials.
    • Install: helm upgrade --install kyverno kyverno/kyverno --namespace kyverno --create-namespace.
    • Hardening: Pods can still inherit the node’s instance profile, so require IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 (aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1).
    • Verification: A Kyverno verifyImages rule checks signatures of images in the private ECR repo.

    Takeaway: Use IRSA (or EKS Pod Identity) for Kyverno’s registry access and block node metadata access, so signature verification needs no long-lived credentials.

  • power-pwn: Offensive and Defensive Security Toolset for Microsoft 365 Power Platform
    summary

    TL;DR: Power Pwn, by Michael Bargury, is an offensive and defensive security toolset that began with Microsoft 365 Power Platform and now also covers AI agents and services.

    • Scope change: The repo now describes itself as a toolset for discovery, recon and assessment of AI agents, beyond the Power Platform focus in the archive title.
    • Power Platform modules: PowerDump (tenant scanning and data collection), BackDoor (persistent backdoor flows), NoCodeMalware, PowerPhishing and Power Pages leak detection for Dataverse tables.
    • AI modules: Copilot Studio Hunter, Custom GPT Hunter, Agent Builder Hunter, LLM Hound (finds exposed MCP servers and AI middleware through Shodan) and Copilot M365 data retrieval tests.
    • Talks: Presented at DEF CON 30, Black Hat USA 2023 and 2024, and SecTor 2023.
    • Install: pip install powerpwn; some modules need ffuf, subfinder or Node.js with Puppeteer.

    Takeaway: Useful for assessing low-code and Copilot exposure in M365 tenants. Run it only with authorization, and check your tenant’s guest access and connector settings.

  • Improve Your Security Investigations with Detective Finding Groups Visualizations
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post on using Amazon Detective finding groups, and their visualizations, to combine related GuardDuty, Inspector and Security Hub findings into one security event.

    • Problem: More security coverage brings alert fatigue; finding groups cut noise by clustering related findings.
    • Services: GuardDuty (including RDS Protection, EKS Runtime Monitoring and Lambda Protection), Inspector, Security Hub, and Detective’s behaviour graph built from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and more.
    • Setup: Enable the services across accounts from an AWS Organizations delegated administrator; EKS Runtime Monitoring is a two-step enable that includes managing the agent automatically.
    • RDS Protection: Analyses Aurora login activity for suspicious behaviour, then you pivot in Detective.
    • Visualization: An interactive graph shows how the findings, resources and entities in a group relate.

    Takeaway: If you already pay for GuardDuty and Security Hub, Detective finding groups can speed up triage by showing an incident as one connected event.

  • OpenAI-Based Open Source Tools for Kubernetes AIOps
    summary

    TL;DR: Palark co-founder Dmitry Shurupov reviews open source tools that use OpenAI and ChatGPT for Kubernetes operations; first published August 23, 2023, rewritten January 18, 2024.

    • K8sGPT: The leading tool; k8sgpt analyze runs per-resource analyzers and --explain asks the LLM for fixes with ready-to-run kubectl commands; it has anonymization and Trivy and Prometheus integrations, and became a CNCF Sandbox project in December 2023.
    • Other tools: Kubernetes ChatGPT bot, kubectl-ai, kube-copilot, plus kubectl-gpt, mico, kopilot and kopylot, which the post marks as no longer active.
    • Usage: Most tools are CLIs or kubectl plugins.
    • Stats: Gives GitHub stars, commit counts, licenses and languages for each tool as of the rewrite.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to palark.com/blog.

    Takeaway: K8sGPT is the one to try first. Use anonymization or a local model before sending cluster details to an external LLM.

  • iambic: Version Control for IAM, Kept in Git
    summary

    TL;DR: IAMbic, from Noq, is “version control for IAM”: it keeps a human-readable, two-way representation of cloud and identity provider IAM in Git.

    • Sources: AWS, Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace, stored as YAML “IAMbic templates”.
    • Audit trail: Any IAM change, whether made through Terraform, CDK, CloudFormation or the console, becomes a git commit with timestamp and actor.
    • Two-way: It can also apply changes from Git to the cloud through a pull request flow in CI/CD, and prevent drift on chosen resources.
    • Temporary access: Declare expiring permissions and IAMbic removes them after the set time.
    • IaC coexistence: Designed to work alongside Terraform and other IaC tools.

    Takeaway: Useful even in read-only mode as an IAM change log in Git. Check that the project is still maintained before relying on its write-back mode.

  • Autostrada: The Perfect Start to Your New Go Project
    summary

    TL;DR: Autostrada is a web-based code generator that creates a ready-to-run scaffold for a new Go web application or JSON API, customised by the options you pick.

    • Output: Plain, idiomatic Go code you own (MIT licensed), not a framework you import.
    • Choices: App type (server-rendered web app or JSON API), database (none, SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL) with optional migrations, and router (http.ServeMux, Flow, Chi, Gorilla Mux, HttpRouter).
    • Config and logs: Flags or environment variables; plaintext, JSON or colorized logs; request logging middleware.
    • Free extras: Basic auth, Git-derived versioning, signed and encrypted cookies, and server-side sessions via SCS.
    • Paid (Autostrada Plus, $29 one-time): Automatic HTTPS via Let’s Encrypt, custom error pages, email helpers, error notifications and more.

    Takeaway: A quick way to start a Go service with sensible structure and no framework lock-in. Review the generated code once and treat it as your own.

  • climate: Autogenerate CLIs from Go Structs and Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: climate (“CLI Mate”) by avamsi generates Go CLIs from structs and functions, in the spirit of python-fire, on top of Cobra.

    • Idea: Define options as struct fields and commands as functions or methods; climate builds the flags and sub-commands.
    • Features: Nested sub-commands, global and local flags, generated help, typo suggestions and shell completion from Cobra.
    • Example: A greet command with --greeting (default Hello), --name (default World) and --times flags generated from a struct.
    • Sub-commands demo: A mock jj (Jujutsu VCS) CLI with git, init, squash and util sub-commands and global -R/--repository flags.

    Takeaway: Handy for small internal Go tools where hand-written Cobra boilerplate outweighs the logic. For large CLIs, plain Cobra gives more control.

  • Logging in Go: A Comparison of the Top 8 Libraries
    summary

    TL;DR: Better Stack guide by Ayooluwa Isaiah comparing Go logging libraries, now including the standard library’s log/slog from Go 1.21.

    • Title drift: Saved as “Top 8”, the page now covers 9 libraries (Zerolog, Zap, Slog, Phuslu/log, Logrus, Log15, Logf, Apex/log, Logr) and was updated January 22, 2026.
    • Benchmarks (author’s machine): Phuslu/log 27 ns/op and Zerolog 30 ns/op with 0 allocations; Zap 71 ns/op; Slog 174 ns/op; Logrus 2231 ns/op with 23 allocations; Log15 21997 ns/op.
    • Zerolog: The fastest structured JSON logger with zero allocations, CBOR option and ConsoleWriter for development.
    • Slog: A Logger frontend, Record type and swappable Handler backends (TextHandler for logfmt, JSONHandler); it can also use Zap as a backend.
    • Vendor note: The guide promotes Better Stack’s log service.

    Takeaway: Default to log/slog for new code for its standard API, and swap in a faster handler only if profiling shows logging matters.

  • dnscontrol: Synchronize Your DNS to Multiple Providers from a Simple DSL
    summary

    TL;DR: DNSControl, originally from Stack Exchange, is infrastructure as code for DNS: a JavaScript-compatible DSL that pushes the same records to one or more DNS providers.

    • Moved: The project now lives in the DNSControl/dnscontrol organization.
    • Config: dnsconfig.js declares registrars, providers and records, such as D("example.com", REG, DnsProvider(DSP), A("@","1.2.3.4"), CNAME("www","@")).
    • Workflow: dnscontrol preview shows the changes and dnscontrol push applies them.
    • Providers: The README lists 77 DNS providers and registrars, including Route 53, Cloudflare, Azure DNS and Gandi.
    • Start: dnscontrol init is an interactive wizard that writes creds.json and dnsconfig.js with your existing records; a Docker image ghcr.io/dnscontrol/dnscontrol is available.
    • GitOps: A dns-config starter repo shows the full Git-driven workflow.

    Takeaway: A good fit for multi-provider DNS or redundancy across providers. Run preview in CI on every PR and push only from the main branch.

  • kdash: Simple and Fast Dashboard for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: KDash, by Deepu K Sasidharan, is a fast terminal dashboard for Kubernetes written in Rust.

    • Version 2.0 actions: Delete (Ctrl-d), edit in $EDITOR (e), rollout restart (r), previous container logs (p), scale workloads, cordon nodes and suspend or trigger CronJobs from an action menu (m), with confirmation prompts.
    • Port-forward: Press f on a pod or service; Shift+F lists and stops forwards.
    • Logs: Toggle timestamps (t) and line wrap (w).
    • Themes: Catppuccin, Gruvbox Dark, Solarized Dark, Mono and custom themes, switchable at runtime.
    • Install: brew install kdash, Scoop, Chocolatey, AUR, crates.io or Docker.

    Takeaway: A lighter alternative to k9s for browsing clusters. Note that version 2 adds destructive actions, so use read-only credentials where that matters.

  • OpenTF Announces Fork of Terraform
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The OpenTF initiative’s August 25, 2023 announcement that it had forked Terraform from its last MPL-licensed version, after HashiCorp moved Terraform to the Business Source License on August 10, 2023.

    • Background: The OpenTF manifesto called on HashiCorp to revert to the MPL and said a fork would follow if it did not; the announcement says no reversal came.
    • Principles: Truly open source, community-driven with a public RFC process, impartial, modular and layered, and backward-compatible.
    • Foundation: The group said it had completed the documents needed to join the Linux Foundation, with the goal of entering the CNCF.
    • Status at the time: More than 10 engineers from several companies, repo rename nearly done, initial steering committee chosen, CI and end-to-end tests green.
    • Plans: Publish the repo within 1-2 weeks as a drop-in replacement compatible with existing providers and modules; first release 1.6.0-alpha.
    • Source caveat: opentf.org only shows a redirect notice to opentofu.org/announcement, which did not render; this is based on Spacelift’s cross-post of the announcement and news coverage. The project was later renamed OpenTofu under the Linux Foundation.

    Takeaway: This is the origin of OpenTofu, now the open source Terraform fork. Use it if BSL terms concern you, and test provider and state compatibility before switching.

  • netbird: WireGuard-Based Mesh Network with SSO/MFA and Simple Access Controls
    summary

    TL;DR: NetBird is an open source, WireGuard-based peer-to-peer overlay network with central, identity-based access control, usable self-hosted or as a cloud service.

    • Connect: Machines join an encrypted mesh with automatic peer discovery, NAT traversal and relay fallback, with no open ports or VPN gateways.
    • Access control: SSO and MFA, IdP integrations, groups and rules, device posture checks, periodic re-authentication and activity logging.
    • Networking: Routes to external networks, exit nodes, private and custom DNS zones, IPv6 dual stack, and newer features such as browser SSH and RDP and a reverse proxy with auto-TLS.
    • Automation: Public API, setup keys for bulk enrolment, a Terraform provider and an Ansible collection.
    • Platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS, TVs, FreeBSD, pfSense, OPNsense, MikroTik, OpenWRT, Synology, TrueNAS and Proxmox.
    • Growth: The README now also advertises a beta “Agent Network” for AI agent access.

    Takeaway: A strong self-hostable alternative to Tailscale-style mesh VPNs. Plan your IdP integration and access policies before rollout.

  • firezone: WireGuard-Based VPN Server and Firewall
    summary

    TL;DR: Firezone is a WireGuard-based remote access platform with identity-based policies, device trust and audit logs; its focus has changed since it was saved as a self-hosted VPN server and firewall.

    • Current model: A managed control plane; you run Gateways in your own networks near the resources, and users connect with Clients.
    • Self-hosting: The README says the licenses allow self-hosting but production self-hosting is not officially supported, and published clients are only guaranteed to work with the managed service.
    • Policies: Least-privilege access to specific resources by group, optionally requiring device attestation with X.509 certificates from MDM or enterprise PKI.
    • Identity: Google Workspace, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID or generic OIDC, with directory sync.
    • Audit: Configuration, session, API and flow logs with 90-day retention, exportable to a SIEM.
    • Performance: A shared Rust data plane; the README reports tested throughput of 2+ Gbps on mobile, 5+ Gbps on desktop and up to 10+ Gbps on tuned Linux.

    Takeaway: Evaluate it as a managed zero-trust access product, not as the self-hosted VPN the archive title describes. Self-hosters should look at NetBird or plain WireGuard.

  • Amazon VPC CNI Now Supports Kubernetes NetworkPolicy Enforcement
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (August 29, 2023) that the Amazon VPC CNI plugin can enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy natively.

    • What: The same VPC CNI that handles pod networking now enforces NetworkPolicy, so you no longer need a separate engine such as Calico for policy alone.
    • Rules: Allow or deny traffic between pods by label selectors, namespaces, IP blocks and ports.
    • Defense in depth: Works alongside security groups and network ACLs.
    • Troubleshooting: Policies can be traced at cluster and node level with the VPC CNI.
    • Requirements: VPC CNI v1.14+ on new clusters running Kubernetes 1.25+; off by default at launch.

    Takeaway: On EKS, enable the CNI’s NetworkPolicy support and start with default-deny policies per namespace, without another CNI add-on.

03.08.2023

  • Kubernetes Logging Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: CNCF community post by Selvam R (July 3, 2023; winner of the KCD Chennai Blogathon) on how Kubernetes logging works and general best practices.

    • Pipeline: Logs from the API server, kubelet, container runtime and apps are gathered by an agent pod, most commonly Fluentd, or Fluent Bit or Logstash, and shipped to Elasticsearch, Splunk, Kafka and similar backends.
    • Practices: Centralize logs, configure rotation, use structured JSON logging, and do not log secrets.
    • Context: Add timestamps, hostnames and request IDs for correlation; mask PII and sensitive values.
    • Levels: Use DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL to filter.
    • CLI tools: Mentions kubetail and other tools for tailing many pods beyond kubectl logs.

    Takeaway: An introductory checklist. Structured logs plus a node-level agent (Fluent Bit) and request IDs give the most value for the effort.

  • Securing CI/CD Pipelines with 1Password Service Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: 1Password blog post by Michael Carey (June 27, 2023) announcing general availability of 1Password Service Accounts for giving CI/CD and infrastructure programmatic access to secrets.

    • What: A service account token grants programmatic, vault-scoped access with control over permitted actions; the post says no additional infrastructure is needed.
    • GitHub Actions: Store the token as OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, then use 1password/load-secrets-action@v1 with export-env: true.
    • Secret references: Environment variables point to items as op://vault/item/field; values are masked in logs.
    • Other CI: Pre-built integrations for CircleCI and Jenkins.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to 1password.com/blog.

    Takeaway: If your team already uses 1Password, this removes copied CI secrets. Scope each service account to a single CI vault.

  • onepassword-operator: Integrate Kubernetes Secrets with 1Password
    summary

    TL;DR: The 1Password Connect Kubernetes Operator syncs 1Password items into Kubernetes Secrets and can restart deployments when items change.

    • Install: The 1password/connect Helm chart with --set operator.create=true, a Connect credentials file and an operator token.
