    Takeaway: Code Suggestions has been folded into GitLab Duo. Check current GitLab Duo docs, tiers and data handling before enabling it.

  • kbom: Kubernetes Bill of Materials
    summary

    TL;DR: KBOM (Kubernetes Bill of Materials) is an Apache 2.0 spec and CLI from KSOC that inventories a Kubernetes cluster’s components, similar to an SBOM for clusters. The repo has moved to rad-security/kbom.

    • Move: The ksoclabs/kbom README says the repo moved to rad-security/kbom after KSOC became RAD Security; the new repo was still active in 2026.
    • Spec: An initial JSON specification designed to extend across cloud providers and DIY Kubernetes.
    • Install: brew install rad-security/tap/kbom or make build.
    • Usage: kbom generate with --format json|yaml|cyclonedx-json|cyclonedx-xml, --output stdout|file, --out-path and --short.
    • Compatibility: Tested with Kubernetes newer than v1.19 on Azure, AWS and Google Cloud; some metadata may be missing on other clusters.

    Takeaway: A quick way to snapshot what runs in a cluster in CycloneDX format. Use the rad-security repo URL.

  • New StackRot Linux Kernel Flaw Allows Privilege Escalation
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (July 2023) reports StackRot, CVE-2023-3269, a Linux kernel use-after-free in memory management that allows local privilege escalation on kernels 6.1 through 6.4.

    • Discoverer: Security researcher Ruihan Li reported it on 15 June 2023; Linus Torvalds led the fix, which took almost two weeks.
    • Root cause: Stack expansion in the “maple tree” VMA structure (introduced in 6.1, replacing red-black trees) could replace a node without the mm write lock; the old node freed after the RCU grace period can be used after free.
    • Exploitability: Triggerable with minimal capabilities; Li called it possibly the first theoretically exploitable use-after-free-by-RCU bug.
    • Fixed versions: Backported to stable 6.1.37, 6.3.11 and 6.4.1 on 1 July 2023.
    • Distros: Debian 12 shipped 6.1 (affected unless patched); Ubuntu 22.04.2 shipped 5.19 (not in the affected range).
    • Exploit: Full details and PoC exploit were promised for the end of July 2023.

    Takeaway: Confirm any 6.1-6.4 kernels are at or above the fixed stable versions, especially on multi-tenant or container hosts.

13.06.2023

  • AWS IAM Actions
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: AWS IAM Actions is a web tool, with Cooper Walbrun named as author in the page metadata, for browsing and searching AWS IAM actions. The site returned only a “Request Blocked” page to automated requests.

    • Purpose (from title): A lookup of AWS IAM actions across services, to help write and review IAM policies.
    • Author: The page’s author meta tag names Cooper Walbrun.
    • Official equivalent: AWS’s Service Authorization Reference lists every service’s actions, resource types and condition keys.
    • Related data: The PyPI package iam-actions publishes a nightly scrape of AWS IAM services, actions and resource types as JSON; it is not confirmed to be related to this site.
    • Source caveat: Based on the page title, HTML metadata and web search results; the tool’s content and features could not be seen.

    Takeaway: Fine for quick lookups if it loads in your browser. For authoritative answers, use the AWS Service Authorization Reference.

  • Awesome-CloudSec-Labs: Awesome Cloud Security Labs
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated table by GitHub user iknowjason of free cloud-native security learning labs: CTFs, self-hosted workshops, guided vulnerability labs and research labs.

    • Size: About 47 entries; by technology roughly 19 AWS, 9 Azure, 6 Kubernetes and 4 GCP, plus container, CI/CD and Terraform labs.
    • Columns: Name, technology, category (author-hosted vs self-hosted CTF, guided lab), author and notes.
    • Examples: Wiz’s Big IAM Challenge, Cloud Hunting Games and Ultimate Cloud Security Championship; Bishop Fox CloudFoxable; Pwned Labs; Doyensec CloudSec Tidbits; AWS Well-Architected Security and AWS CIRT workshops.
    • Status: About 2,200 stars; last updated October 2025; no license file.

    Takeaway: One of the better starting points for hands-on cloud security practice. Prefer author-hosted labs if you do not want to pay for or clean up your own cloud resources.

  • mayfly: Operator to Manage Ephemeral Kubernetes Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Mayfly, from Namecheap (NCCloud), is an Apache 2.0 Kubernetes operator that deletes resources after an expiration time and can create resources on a schedule.

    • Expiration: Annotate resources with mayfly.cloud.namecheap.com/expire using a duration (from creation time) or an exact date.
    • Scope: The RESOURCES env var lists watched kinds as {ApiVersion};{Kind}, e.g. v1;Secret,test.com/v1alpha;MyCRD.
    • Scheduling: A ScheduleResource CRD creates resources after a delay (10s), at an exact time, or on a cron expression such as */20 * * * * *; can be combined with expiration.
    • Install: helm install mayfly nccloud/mayfly --set "env[0].name=RESOURCES" --set "env[0].value=v1;Secret".
    • Use cases: Temporary resources, temporary access grants and keeping clusters tidy.
    • Status: About 340 stars; active in 2026.

    Takeaway: Useful for time-boxed access (e.g. expiring RoleBindings or Secrets) and ephemeral test resources. Limit which kinds it watches.

  • Privilege Escalation in AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service
    summary

    TL;DR: Calif researchers show that any pod on a default EKS node can steal the node’s IAM credentials from IMDS, exchange them for a system:node Kubernetes token, and mint service account tokens for other pods on the same node, up to cluster-admin.

    • Step 1: From a low-privilege pod, get the EC2 instance role credentials from the metadata service, then run aws eks get-token --cluster-name=... to get a system:node identity.
    • Step 2: NodeRestriction still lets a node act on pods bound to it. kubectl create token -n ns1 sa-priv --bound-object-kind=Pod --bound-object-name=... --bound-object-uid=... returns a token for a privileged pod’s service account.
    • Test setup: EKS v1.25.7, one node, an alpine pod plus a pod using a cluster-admin service account.
    • Persistence: With admin rights, adding a record to the aws-auth ConfigMap keeps access even after the EC2 role’s permissions are revoked.
    • Mitigations: IMDSv2 with http_put_response_hop_limit set to 1, or iptables rules blocking IMDS. Isolate untrusted workloads on separate nodes and restrict public access to the API endpoint.
    • Update (Nov 2023): cert-manager’s service account has full pod permissions, which opens another escalation path.

    Takeaway: On EKS, treat every pod as having its node’s privileges until IMDS is blocked. Keep privileged service accounts off nodes that run untrusted workloads.

  • ebpf-beginners: The Beginner’s Guide to eBPF
    summary

    TL;DR: Liz Rice’s repository of code, slides and recordings for her “Beginner’s Guide to eBPF Programming” talks, plus pointers to her eBPF books.

    • Origin: Code from her eBPF Summit 2020 talk; ebpf.py is the Python (BCC) code written live, with slides and a YouTube recording.
    • Other talks: A Go version with libbpfgo, an eBPF load balancer from scratch in C (eBPF Summit 2021), eBPF networking examples, and “eBPF Superpowers” at DockerCon.
    • Books: “What is eBPF?” and “Learning eBPF”, downloadable from Isovalent or on O’Reilly; code for the latter lives in lizrice/learning-ebpf.
    • Status: Apache 2.0, about 1,700 stars; last updated May 2023.

    Takeaway: A good first stop for learning eBPF. For deeper, current examples go to the learning-ebpf repo.

  • go-callvis: Visualize Call Graph of a Go Program Using Graphviz
    summary

    TL;DR: go-callvis, by Ondrej Fabry, is a Go development tool that builds the call graph of a Go program and shows it as an interactive, package-focused view rendered through Graphviz dot output.

    • How it works: Runs pointer analysis to build the call graph, then emits dot output that Graphviz renders.
    • Install: go install github.com/ofabry/go-callvis@latest; needs Go 1.19+, Graphviz only with the -graphviz flag.
    • Interactive mode: go-callvis <target package> starts a web server on :7878 serving SVGs; click a package to switch focus.
    • Static output: -file=<path> with -format=svg|png|jpg.
    • Filtering: -focus, -group pkg,type, -limit, -include, -ignore, -nostd, -nointer, -tests; -algo static|cha|rta|vta picks the analyzer.
    • Legend: Colours mark focused/stdlib/other packages; dashed lines are dynamic calls, circle arrows concurrent calls, diamond arrows deferred calls.

    Takeaway: Useful for getting a map of an unfamiliar Go codebase. Narrow it with -focus and -nostd or the graph gets unreadable on large projects.

  • Move Over, Dockerfiles! the New Way to Craft Containers
    summary

    TL;DR: Chainguard engineers Jason Hall and Zachary Newman (April 2023) argue Dockerfiles are non-hermetic and bloated, and compare declarative alternatives: ko, Bazel rules_oci, Nix and apko.

    • Dockerfile problems: Implicit online dependencies make builds non-hermetic and non-reproducible; base images pull in unused software and vulnerabilities; build commands land in image metadata and can leak secrets; SBOMs miss dependencies.
    • ko: CNCF tool for pure-Go apps, ko build, no Docker needed, reproducible images with SBOMs by default; Jib (Java) and dotnet publish are similar but equally limited.
    • Bazel rules_oci: Fast, cached and reproducible, but practical only if the code already builds in Bazel.
    • Nix: dockerTools gives bit-for-bit reproducible images with shared layers; steep learning curve.
    • apko: Chainguard’s tool for base images where all content must come from APK packages; used for Chainguard Images.
    • Guidance: Use your existing Bazel/Nix ecosystem, use ko/Jib/dotnet publish where they fit, consider apko for minimal images with SBOMs, otherwise keep Dockerfiles on good base images.

    Takeaway: For Go services, ko is the cheapest win. Elsewhere, pick a minimal base image even if you keep Dockerfiles.

  • So Long Passwords, Thanks for All the Phish: Passkeys for Google Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Security Blog post by Arnar Birgisson and Diana K Smetters (May 3, 2023) announcing passkeys for personal Google Accounts; signing in with a passkey skips both the password and 2-Step Verification.

    • What it is: A private key stored on the device, unlocked by fingerprint, face or PIN; the public key goes to Google, which verifies a signed challenge.
    • Phishing resistance: The device only shares signatures with Google sites and apps, not phishing intermediaries; biometrics never leave the device.
    • Strength: Treated as stronger than most 2SV methods; can stand in for security keys in the Advanced Protection Program.
    • Fallbacks: Passwords still work for devices without passkey support; Google says it will increasingly scrutinize password fallbacks.
    • Cross-device: Passkeys may sync (e.g. via iCloud), and a phone passkey can approve a one-time sign-in on another device via proximity.
    • Caveats: Do not create passkeys on shared devices; revoke lost-device passkeys in account settings. Setup at g.co/passkeys.

    Takeaway: Enabling a passkey removes phishable password and SMS codes from the normal sign-in path. Keep recovery phone and email set.

  • azure-cost-cli: CLI Tool to Perform Cost Analysis on Your Azure Subscription
    summary

    TL;DR: azure-cost-cli, by Michiel van Oudheusden, is a .NET global tool that queries the Azure Cost Management API and prints subscription costs to console, text, CSV, Markdown or JSON, for use in scripts and pipelines.

    • Install: dotnet tool install --global azure-cost-cli; needs .NET 8.0 or 10.0 and az login or an identity with Cost Management Reader.
    • Commands: accumulatedCost, costByResource, dailyCosts --dimension MeterCategory, diff, plus budgets listing.
    • Analysis: Detects anomalies and trends in cost for automated reporting.
    • Output: -o json|text|csv|markdown so it can feed later workflow steps.
    • Limits: Not all subscription types (e.g. sponsored) are supported by the Cost Management API.
    • Current state: The README now references .NET 10, so it has been maintained past 2023.

    Takeaway: A quick way to post Azure spend into a PR comment or chat from CI. Check your subscription type is supported first.

  • AWS Verified Access Is Now Generally Available
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (April 28, 2023) that AWS Verified Access is generally available: VPN-less access to corporate applications, with each request checked in real time against identity and device posture.

    • Model: Built on AWS Zero Trust principles; fine-grained policies, e.g. only certain groups, only from compliant devices.
    • WAF: GA adds AWS WAF support to filter SQL injection, XSS and other web threats.
    • Signed identity context: Passes signed user context (login alias, role, department) to the app, which can reject unsigned requests or personalize content.
    • Regions at GA: 10, including US East (Ohio, N. Virginia), US West (N. California, Oregon), Sydney, Canada Central, Frankfurt, Ireland, London and Sao Paulo.
    • Resources: Links to the Verified Access page, networking blog, console and pricing.

    Takeaway: An option for replacing a VPN for internal web apps on AWS. Have the app verify the signed identity header so traffic cannot bypass the gateway.

  • Get Details on Security Finding Changes with the New Finding History Feature in Security Hub
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post by Nicholas Jaeger and Shachar Hirshberg (May 4, 2023) introducing Finding History in AWS Security Hub, an immutable record of every change to a finding.

    • What is tracked: Before and after values of changed fields, who or what changed them, and when.
    • Sources of change: Providers updating via BatchImportFindings; users, ticketing, SIEM or remediation tools via BatchUpdateFindings or the console.
    • Where: Security Hub console, select a finding, History tab; also available through the Security Hub APIs.
    • Cost: No additional charge, in all Regions where Security Hub runs; on by default for new or updated findings.
    • Use case: See actions already taken (workflow status, notes) during an investigation without separate tooling.

    Takeaway: Use the History tab as the audit trail when triaging or handing off findings, instead of tracking status changes elsewhere.

  • ATT&CK v13 Enters the Room: Pseudocode, Swifter Search, and Mobile Data Sources
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: MITRE’s Medium announcement of ATT&CK v13 (April 2023), written by Amy L. Robertson, covering CAR pseudocode in detections, faster site search and new Mobile data sources.

    • Pseudocode: CAR-derived pseudocode added to a number of data components, as a starting template for custom detections and a guide to what to collect.
    • Detection guidance: Detailed detection guidance added to some Enterprise techniques.
    • Mobile data sources: New in v13: Application Vetting, Command, Network Traffic, Process, Sensor Health, User Interface.
    • Enterprise counts: 14 tactics, 196 techniques, 411 sub-techniques, 138 groups, 22 campaigns, 740 software entries.
    • Changelogs: Human-readable detailed changelog and machine-readable JSON changelog added.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked the fetch (403); based on the official ATT&CK April 2023 update page and Industrial Cyber coverage found via search.

    Takeaway: If you map detections to ATT&CK, the v13 pseudocode is a starting point for writing your own rules. Use the JSON changelog to track what moved between versions.

  • Manage Multiple Terraform Projects in Monorepo
    summary

    TL;DR: A janik6n.net post (April 13, 2023) describes a Terraform monorepo layout with many projects and versioned modules, deployed through GitHub Actions without extra tools like Terragrunt and without branch-per-environment.

    • Rules: One project equals one state; modules use semantic versioning; main always reflects every live environment; only dev may be applied from a laptop.
    • Layout: live/<env>/<project>/ (e.g. api, data_processor, tf_state) and modules/<name>/v1.1.0/ folders, one directory per module version.
    • State: Per-target backends: S3 plus DynamoDB locking for AWS, Storage Account for Azure.
    • Pipelines: pr-to-main.yml validates and plans; deploy-main.yml deploys after plan review; shared logic in composite actions (prepare-plan, deploy).
    • Pros: Single source of truth, easy cross-env comparison, one auth setup per target, no submodules.
    • Cons: Overwhelming for newcomers, no git-tag module versioning, slower CI, higher mix-up risk.

    Takeaway: Version-by-folder modules are a simple alternative to a module registry. It works for in-house setups but costs disk duplication and CI time.

  • Start Pods Faster by Prefetching Images
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post by Elamaran Shanmugam, Naveen Kumar Bathula and Re Alvarez-Parmar (May 3, 2023) on cutting EKS Pod startup for large images by pre-pulling them onto nodes with EventBridge and Systems Manager.

    • Problem: Images of hundreds of MB to tens of GB take minutes to pull; node caching only helps after the first pull.
    • Push trigger: An ECR push event fires an EventBridge rule that runs SSM Run Command (AWS-RunShellScript) to pull the image on existing worker nodes.
    • New nodes: An SSM State Manager association, targeted by node tags, prefetches images on nodes as they join.
    • No in-cluster parts: Avoids DaemonSet or CronJob pullers such as kubernetes-image-puller.
    • Verification: sudo ctr -n k8s.io images ls on the node via SSM session; code in aws-samples/containers-blog-maelstrom.
    • Alternative: Mentions SOCI lazy loading, which needs an index built at image build time.
    • Result: Authors say startup drops to a few seconds even for large images.

    Takeaway: Worth it for ML or build images that are GBs in size. Watch that pre-pulled images fill node disk.

  • mirrord: Connect Your Local Process and Your Cloud Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: mirrord, by MetalBear, runs a local process as if it were inside a live Kubernetes pod: traffic, file access and environment variables are routed through a chosen target pod, so you can test against real cluster services without deploying.

    • Interfaces: VS Code extension, IntelliJ plugin and CLI (mirrord exec ... --target pod/my-pod); uses your default kubeconfig.
    • Mechanism: Starts an agent pod on the target’s node that mirrors incoming traffic to your process and routes outgoing traffic, file reads/writes and env vars through the target.
    • Capabilities needed: CAP_NET_ADMIN (iptables redirection), CAP_SYS_PTRACE (access via /proc), CAP_SYS_ADMIN (join the network namespace); can be reduced with agent.disabled_capabilities.
    • Non-disruptive: Mirrors rather than steals traffic by default, so others using the cluster are not affected.
    • Current README: Now also pitches use by AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) and lists adopters such as monday.com and SurveyMonkey.
    • License: MIT.

    Takeaway: Shortens the dev loop for services that depend on many in-cluster dependencies. The agent needs privileged capabilities, so limit it to dev or staging clusters.

  • edge-mc: KubeStellar, Multicluster Configuration Management for Edge, Multi-Cloud, and Hybrid Cloud
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The kcp-dev/edge-mc repo is now just a “We’ve Moved” pointer to kubestellar/kubestellar. KubeStellar is a CNCF Sandbox project for deploying and configuring workloads across many Kubernetes clusters as if they were one.

    • Status: The original edge-mc repo only contains a move notice; development continues at github.com/kubestellar/kubestellar.
    • Core idea: Define a binding policy between clusters and Kubernetes objects; KubeStellar then propagates them using ordinary single-cluster tooling, without changing existing resources.
    • Use cases: Separate environments, team isolation, compliance, cross-cloud resiliency, and edge sites, including disconnected ones.
    • Components: Core engine with BindingPolicy, WDS, ITS and WEC concepts; the newer ecosystem adds a web console and an MCP server.
    • Source caveat: Based on the move notice and the current KubeStellar README, which has changed a lot since the 2023 edge-mc era.

    Takeaway: Follow the KubeStellar repo, not edge-mc. Evaluate it if you are moving from one cluster to many and want to keep your existing manifests.

  • kube-green: K8s Operator to Reduce CO2 Footprint of Your Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: kube-green is a Kubernetes add-on and operator that scales down dev or preview workloads outside working hours to save resources, money and CO2. It is configured with a SleepInfo CRD.

    • CRD: kube-green.com/v1alpha1 SleepInfo with weekdays, sleepAt, wakeUpAt and timeZone (IANA, default UTC).
    • Options: suspendCronJobs: true; excludeRef to keep specific Deployments (e.g. api-gateway) running.
    • Sleep only: Omit wakeUpAt to put pods to sleep each night without automatic restore.
    • Install: Docs at kube-green.dev; Helm or kustomize; dev builds deploy with ko into KinD (make local-run).
    • Tests: make test for unit tests, make e2e-test / make e2e-test-kustomize for integration tests.
    • Project: MIT license, listed in the CNCF Landscape, has an adopters list.

    Takeaway: A cheap win for non-production namespaces that idle on nights and weekends. Exclude shared dependencies so wake-ups do not break other teams.

  • Platform Engineering: The Global Home for Platform Engineers
    summary

    TL;DR: platformengineering.org is the community hub behind PlatformCon and the Platform Weekly newsletter, with a Slack, events, jobs, a tooling landscape and courses for platform engineers.

    • Community size (current page): 280,000+ members, 25,000+ active Slack members, 4,000+ certified platform engineers.
    • Learning: “Learn with Luca” 101 content on Internal Developer Platforms, platform as a product, and DevOps versus platform engineering.
    • Certifications: Practitioner and Architect certifications plus free courses through Platform Engineering University.
    • Resources: Platform tooling landscape, industry reports, blog, salary benchmark, job board.
    • Current state: The homepage has grown since 2023 and now promotes agentic development platforms and paid enterprise training.

    Takeaway: A good place to start on IDP concepts and the tooling landscape. Treat the vendor-sponsored content and certifications as marketing.

  • Go Programming: Golang Course with Bonus Projects
    summary

    TL;DR: A freeCodeCamp full-length beginner Go course, about 9 hours, created by Lane Wagner of Boot.dev. It covers the language basics, then builds an RSS aggregator backend.

    • Language chapters: Why Go, variables, functions, structs, interfaces, errors, loops, slices, maps, advanced functions, pointers, local development, channels and concurrency, mutexes, generics, quiz.
    • Project: RSS aggregator using the go-chi/chi router, Postgres, pressly/goose migrations, API key authentication, many-to-many relationships, and a background aggregation worker.
    • Materials: Code at github.com/bootdotdev/fcc-learn-golang-assets; an interactive version is on Boot.dev.
    • Length: Project section starts at 6:43:13; last chapter at 9:05:28.

    Takeaway: A structured start for Go newcomers. Skip to the project half if you already know the syntax and want an idiomatic HTTP and Postgres example.

  • Tunnel via Cloudflare to Any TCP Service
    summary

    TL;DR: THC article on exposing any TCP service (such as SSH) through a free Cloudflare cloudflared tunnel by wrapping TCP in WebSockets on both ends, since Cloudflare tunnels normally carry only HTTP-style traffic.

    • Tools: websocat, cloudflared, gost; a 2024 update recommends DarkFlare, a single binary that combines websocat and cloudflared.
    • SSH example: Server: websocat -E -b ws-l:127.0.0.1:40008 tcp:127.0.0.1:22 plus cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:40008; client: websocat tcp-l:127.0.0.1:2222 ws://<url>.trycloudflare.com, then ssh -p 2222.
    • SOCKS example: gost -L mws://:40009 on the server, gost -L :1080 -F 'mwss://<url>:443' on the client, then proxychains for SSH or nmap -sT through the tunnel.
    • Multiplexing: mws/mwss carry all TCP connections over one WebSocket.
    • Caveats: Free tier limits connections; TLS ends at Cloudflare, so the tunnel is never end-to-end encrypted.

    Takeaway: Shows how a firewall-bypassing reverse tunnel needs only outbound HTTPS. Defenders should watch for unexpected cloudflared and trycloudflare.com traffic.

  • CloudNativeSecurityCon 2023: Seattle
    summary

    TL;DR: The CNCF YouTube playlist of recorded talks from CloudNativeSecurityCon 2023 in Seattle, the first standalone CNCF security conference. It has 88 videos.

    • Size: 88 videos, most 30-40 minutes, plus a few tutorials over an hour.
    • Hands-on: “Hands-on Hacking Kubernetes and Ways to Prevent It” tutorial by Eric Smalling (Snyk).
    • Supply chain: Talks on SLSA and GUAC (Ian Lewis, Google), running your own Sigstore (Hayden Blauzvern, Google), and supply chain at scale (Yahoo).
    • Identity: Zero trust with SPIFFE/SPIRE (Frederick Kautz) and workload identity in Kubernetes (Michael Peters, Red Hat).
    • CI/GitOps: Securing self-hosted GitHub Actions with actions-runner-controller; GitOps with Argo CD, Helm and OPA.
    • Keynotes: Priyanka Sharma (CNCF) opening; Brandon Lum (Google) on next steps in supply chain security.

    Takeaway: A focused catalog for Kubernetes and supply chain security. Start with the hacking tutorial and the Sigstore and SLSA talks.

  • Cloud Native Security Talks
    summary

    TL;DR: Cloud Native Security Talks is a searchable index of container and Kubernetes security talks from KubeCon, CloudNativeSecurityCon and Cloud Native Security Day, each with its abstract and recording link.

    • Scope (current page): 471 talks across 27 events, from 2016 to KubeCon Europe 2026.
    • Series filters: KC-EU, KC-NA, CNSC, CNSD and KC-CN, plus a year filter.
    • Search: Matches titles, speakers and full abstracts; there is also an RSS feed.
    • Examples: Talks range from “How Symlinks Pwned Kubernetes” (2018) and Shopify’s $25k bug report to 2026 talks on kcp’s first CVE and LLMs and Kubernetes security.
    • Current state: The index is kept up to date, so it now goes well past the 2023 talks it had when bookmarked.

    Takeaway: Use it as the first stop when looking for conference material on a Kubernetes security topic. It is faster than searching YouTube playlists.

  • managed-kubernetes-auditing-toolkit: Auditing Toolkit for Security Issues in Managed Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: MKAT (Managed Kubernetes Auditing Toolkit), from Datadog, is a CLI for finding common security issues in managed Kubernetes. It currently focuses on Amazon EKS.

    • Role mapping: mkat eks find-role-relationships matches K8s service accounts to AWS IAM roles via IRSA and EKS Pod Identity, shown as a table or graph.
    • Secrets: Finds hardcoded AWS credentials in Pods, ConfigMaps and Secrets; only alerts when an access key ID and secret key appear in the same resource.
    • IMDS: mkat eks test-imds-access starts two temporary pods to test IMDSv1 and IMDSv2 reachability, then deletes them.
    • Install: brew tap datadog/mkat ... then brew install datadog/mkat/managed-kubernetes-auditing-toolkit, or use release binaries.
    • Auth: Uses current AWS and kubectl contexts (aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <cluster>, AWS_REGION, AWS_PROFILE).
    • Updates: Pod Identity support was added after the November 2023 AWS release.

    Takeaway: A quick EKS audit for pod-to-cloud pivot paths. Run test-imds-access on every cluster, since node IMDS access from pods is the classic escalation.

  • Attacking and Securing Cloud Identities in Managed Kubernetes Part 1: Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog Security Labs post by Christophe Tafani-Dereeper (May 16, 2023, updated through February 2024) on how IAM works in Amazon EKS and how attackers pivot from a cluster into the AWS account. It also introduces MKAT.

    • API auth: Covers aws eks update-kubeconfig, aws-iam-authenticator, the deprecated aws-auth ConfigMap and the newer EKS cluster access management.
    • SSRF: SSRF in a pod can reach the node IMDS and steal worker node credentials.
    • Mitigations: Block pod IMDS access cluster-wide with a GlobalNetworkPolicy; enforce IMDSv2 with response hop limit 1.
    • Workload identity: Explains IRSA (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) and EKS Pod Identity, and how stolen node credentials or service account tokens give access to pod roles.
    • Operators: Warns about broad AWS permissions on bridging operators like External Secrets or Crossplane.
    • Tooling: MKAT audits role relationships, hardcoded keys and IMDS access; part 2 covers GKE.

    Takeaway: For EKS, block IMDS from pods and use IRSA or Pod Identity with tight roles. Treat any SSRF in a pod as a possible path to the AWS account.

  • chathub: Use Different Chatbots in One App
    summary

    TL;DR: ChatHub is a Chromium browser extension that puts several chatbots in one app and lets you query them side by side to compare answers.

    • Bots (current README): ChatGPT (web app or API), Gemini, Claude (web app or API), Grok, DeepSeek, Qianwen, Llama and others; earlier versions listed Bing Chat, Bard, Vicuna and ChatGLM.
    • Features: Simultaneous multi-bot chat, prompt library, local conversation history, export/import, share to Markdown, dark mode, web access, global shortcut.
    • Install: Chrome Web Store, or build: corepack enable, yarn install, yarn build, then load dist in developer mode.
    • Sponsor: Stream (getstream.io).
    • Change since 2023: The supported-bot list has been updated as 2023 products like Bing Chat and Bard were renamed or retired.

    Takeaway: Handy for comparing model answers. It holds your sessions and API keys, so check the extension’s permissions and source before installing.

  • prompt-engineering: Tips and Tricks for Working with Large Language Models Like GPT-4
    summary

    TL;DR: Brex’s internal prompt engineering guide, made public in 2023. It covers LLM history, what prompts and tokens are, and strategies, guidelines and safety advice for building production systems on models like GPT-4.

    • Basics: LLMs as next-token prediction engines; hidden prompts, tokens and token limits.
    • Prompt hacking: Jailbreaks and prompt leaks.
    • Patterns: Semantic search (“give a bot a fish”) versus tool use via command grammars and ReAct (“teach a bot to fish”); GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5.
    • Embedding data: Simple lists, Markdown tables, JSON, freeform and nested data.
    • Techniques: Citations, programmatic consumption of output, chain of thought, averaging, interpreting code, delimiters.
    • Fine tuning: When to use it and its downsides.
    • Caveat: Examples come from a non-deterministic model and may give different results; it is described as a living document.

    Takeaway: A practical 2023 primer for engineers starting with LLM features. The data-formatting and delimiter advice still applies; model-specific comparisons are dated.

  • The AI Attack Surface Map v1.0
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Miessler’s May 15, 2023 framework and diagram for thinking about attacks on AI-powered systems as a whole, not just models. It argues natural language is the main attack vector against LLM systems.

    • Components: AI Assistants, Agents, Tools, Models and Storage, borrowing Langchain’s breakdown; prompts are treated as the attack path.
    • Assistants: High-impact targets because they hold deep personal data and can act as the user (payments, posts, messages).
    • Methods: Prompt injection (bypass system prompt, run code, pivot to backends) and training data poisoning.
    • Per-component attacks: Alter agent routing; arbitrary command execution through tools; extract or tamper with embedding databases; bypass model protections, extract other users’ data, access unpublished models.
    • Outlook: Expects a flood of insecure AI-built stacks and a big need for AI security automation.

    Takeaway: A useful mental model for threat-modelling LLM apps. Map each tool and data store an agent can reach, because injection travels through all of them.

  • Building a Kubernetes Purple Teaming Lab
    summary

    TL;DR: Sumo Logic Threat Labs post by Anton Ovrutsky (May 11, 2023) on building a Kubernetes purple teaming home lab: run attacks, check what telemetry catches them, and track results.

    • Stack: Ubuntu 20.04 VM, Docker as Minikube driver, Minikube cluster, free Sumo Logic account for monitoring.
    • Host telemetry: auditd with Florian Roth’s audit rules, plus Laurel to convert audit logs to JSON.
    • Tracking: Vectr, running on the same VM, records purple team test cases and outcomes.
    • Example: kubectl exec into a pod left no trace in Kubernetes logs; adding -w /usr/local/bin/minikube -p x -k minikube to audit rules captured it at host level.
    • Purple teaming: Defined as collaborative attack, check results, track metrics, iterate.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to build and test Kubernetes detections without touching production. The exec example shows why host-level audit data matters alongside K8s audit logs.

  • Fun with Container Images: Bypassing Vulnerability Scanners
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune (raesene), following the KubeCon EU 2023 talk “Malicious Compliance” with Ian Coldwater, Brad Geesaman and Duffie Cooley, shows a simple way to hide an image’s contents from static vulnerability scanners: unpack the filesystem only at runtime.

    • Technique: A static Go binary extracts a tarball of a real container filesystem and runs a command from it, so the image holds only the binary and a tar.
    • Build: CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w", pack with upx, tarball from docker export.
    • Image: FROM scratch, COPY image.tar /, COPY main /, ENTRYPOINT ["/main","image.tar"]; run as docker run --rm obfuscator ls.
    • Result: Trivy, Grype, Docker Scan and Docker Scout all reported clean on a deliberately vulnerable base.
    • Caveat: Marked as a proof of concept only; code is on GitHub.

    Takeaway: If you do not trust who built an image, scanner output tells you little. Scanners are a hygiene check against honest builders, not a defence against malicious ones.

  • smokescreen: Simple HTTP Proxy That Fogs over Naughty URLs
    summary

    TL;DR: Smokescreen is Stripe’s HTTP CONNECT egress proxy. It sends most of Stripe’s outbound traffic (such as webhooks) and only allows approved destinations, blocking SSRF-style access to internal networks.

    • Hostname ACLs: Per-client allowlists of destination hostnames.
    • IP checks: Resolves each name and refuses private or internal IPs; extra allow or deny ranges are configurable.
    • Client identity: Clients usually connect over mTLS; certificates are checked against configured CAs and CRLs, and the CN identifies the client by default (the function is replaceable).
    • Stable egress: Centralizes egress so partners can allowlist fixed Stripe IPs.
    • Build: Go modules, a custom fork of goproxy, Prometheus on by default; -tags=smokescreen_no_prometheus removes it.
    • Support: Targets the two most recent Go versions.

    Takeaway: A proven pattern for webhook senders and any service fetching user-supplied URLs. Route that traffic through an allowlisting proxy that blocks internal IPs.

  • github-oidc-checker: Check for Misconfigured GitHub OIDC Access from AWS Roles and GCP Service Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: github-oidc-checker is a pair of Python 3.11 scripts from Rezonate Labs that scan AWS accounts and GCP projects for misconfigured trust between GitHub Actions OIDC and IAM roles or service accounts.

    • Origin: Released with Rezonate’s 2023 research “From GitHub to Account Takeover”, which found misconfigured GitHub OIDC trust relationships in dozens of public repositories.
    • AWS script: Uses boto3 (pip install boto3) to review IAM roles that trust the GitHub OIDC provider.
    • GCP script: Uses the gcloud CLI to review service accounts and workload identity bindings.
    • Usage: Run as an authenticated user in the target account or project; the README shows example output only as screenshots.
    • Scope: A small single-purpose tool; the README gives no rule list beyond “misconfigured access”.
    • Source caveat: README fetched; research context comes from search snippets of the Rezonate blog post.

    Takeaway: Run it, or check by hand, that every GitHub OIDC trust policy restricts the sub claim to your org and repo. A policy that checks only aud can be assumed from any repository.

  • watchtower: Automate Docker Container Base Image Updates
    summary

    TL;DR: Watchtower is a container that watches the Docker daemon and, when a newer image tag is pushed, pulls it and restarts running containers with their original options. The project is now marked as no longer maintained.

    • Status: The README opens with “This project is no longer maintained” and points to discussion #2135.
    • Run: docker run --detach --name watchtower --volume /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock containrrr/watchtower.
    • Behaviour: Pulls the new image, shuts down the old container gracefully, and restarts it with the same run options.
    • Intended use: Homelabs, media centres and local dev; maintainers advise against commercial or production use and suggest Kubernetes, MicroK8s or k3s.
    • Docs: containrrr.dev/watchtower; Apache-2.0 license.

    Takeaway: Fine for a homelab, but it is unmaintained and has full Docker socket access. Pin images, or move to a maintained fork or a GitOps-style update flow.

  • Best Practices for EKS Cluster Upgrades
    summary

    TL;DR: The Cluster Upgrades chapter of the AWS EKS Best Practices Guide, a checklist for keeping EKS clusters current and upgrading the control plane, add-ons and data plane safely. The guide has since moved into the AWS documentation.

    • Status: The page banner says the EKS Best Practices Guide has moved to AWS Documentation.
    • Before upgrading: Follow the EKS release calendar, check free subnet IPs and the cluster IAM role, migrate to EKS Add-ons, and back up the cluster.
    • Removed APIs: Find them with Cluster Insights, kube-no-trouble (kubent) or pluto; update manifests with kubectl-convert.
    • Order: Control plane first, then data plane in sequence; upgrade add-ons through the Kubernetes API.
    • Availability: Set PodDisruptionBudgets and topologySpreadConstraints; use Managed Node Groups or Karpenter (Drift, ExpireAfter); eksctl for self-managed groups; restart Fargate deployments after the control plane upgrade.
    • Alternatives: Consider blue/green clusters.
    • Removals: Dockershim and PodSecurityPolicy in 1.25, and in-tree storage driver deprecation in 1.23.

    Takeaway: Use it as a pre-upgrade checklist, and run a removed-API scan before every control plane bump. Read the AWS Docs copy for current content.

  • Automate Security and Monitoring with Amazon EKS Blueprints, Terraform, and Sysdig
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Partner Network post by Manuel Boira (Sysdig) and Frank Carta (AWS), May 18, 2023, introducing the Sysdig add-on for EKS and Sysdig EKS Blueprints. These are Terraform blueprints that create EKS clusters already instrumented by Sysdig.

    • Motivation: Cites survey figures: 48% name lack of in-house skills and 29% difficulty training users as Kubernetes adoption obstacles; most containers live under five minutes (Sysdig research).
    • Deploy: Set sysdig_accesskey, sysdig_region, cluster_name, aws_region, then terraform init, plan, apply.
    • Security features: IaC scanning with drift control, image vulnerability scanning (CI, registry, admission, runtime), KSPM, runtime threat detection, forensics, SIEM/SOAR forwarding.
    • Monitoring features: Kubernetes and cloud monitoring, cost advisor, custom metrics.
    • Caveat: EKS Blueprints is open source and does not carry AWS service-level support.

    Takeaway: Mainly vendor content. The useful pattern is shipping security agents as part of the cluster Terraform, so new clusters are never unmonitored.

  • Let’s Debug a Kubernetes Pod Locally
    summary

    TL;DR: Ahmet Enes Bayraktar (May 2022) shows how to debug a service locally while it talks to real dependencies in a dev Kubernetes cluster, using mirrord instead of docker-compose replicas, redeploys or port-forwarding.

    • Problems with alternatives: Local replicas lack resources and data; redeploy loops waste time; port-forward is unstable, does not reconnect on pod restart, and does not help non-HTTP workers.
    • mirrord model: A local layer wraps your process and an agent pod runs in the cluster; incoming requests to the target pod are mirrored to your local process and outgoing calls go through the agent.
    • Protocols: In the author’s tests incoming interception worked for any TCP traffic; UDP was not supported at the time.
    • Stack: Demo is .NET; also works from an IDE debugger.
    • Date: Written in 2022 against an early mirrord version.

    Takeaway: A practical intro to mirrord-style remote-local debugging. Check current mirrord docs, since features have grown since this post.

  • eks-cluster-upgrade: Automated Amazon EKS Cluster Upgrade
    summary

    TL;DR: eksupgrade is an AWS Samples Python utility (on PyPI) that automates Amazon EKS cluster upgrades: control plane, managed node groups and self-managed node groups.

    • Install: python -m pip install eksupgrade; needs AWS IAM permissions (example policy in README) and cluster access.
    • Flow: Request the control plane upgrade (done by AWS), classify nodes as managed or self-managed, update managed node groups, then roll self-managed nodes.
    • Self-managed nodes: Launch upgraded nodes, wait for Ready, cordon old nodes, evict pods; respects PDBs unless --force is given.
    • Change in v0.9.0: Pre/post-flight checks were removed; users are pointed to eksup (clowdhaus) for readiness checks.
    • Status: An aws-samples project, not an official AWS service.

    Takeaway: Useful for clusters with self-managed node groups. Run eksup or a removed-API scan first, because the tool no longer validates readiness itself.

  • devpod: Dev-Environments-as-Code in Any Infra
    summary

    TL;DR: DevPod, from Loft Labs, is an open-source, client-only tool that creates reproducible dev environments from devcontainer.json on any backend: local Docker, Kubernetes, a remote machine over SSH, or a cloud VM.

    • Standard: Reuses the DevContainer spec used by GitHub Codespaces and VS Code Dev Containers.
    • Providers: Pluggable backends; you can write your own provider.
    • Cost claim: README says it is usually 5-10x cheaper than hosted services, because it uses bare VMs and shuts idle ones down automatically.
    • IDEs: VS Code and the JetBrains suite; others connect over SSH.
    • Features: Prebuilds, inactivity shutdown, git and Docker credential sync, desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, plus a CLI.
    • No server: Runs only on the client, with no backend to install.

    Takeaway: An open alternative to Codespaces if you already have devcontainer files. Point it at cheap cloud VMs or a Kubernetes cluster.

  • How to Start a Go Project in 2023
    summary

    TL;DR: Ben Boyter’s May 2023 update of his 2018 guide: a practical checklist for starting a Go project, covering setup, layout, tooling, testing and Docker.

    • Setup: Install from golang.org; ignore $GOPATH in favour of modules; add $(go env GOPATH)/bin to PATH.
    • Editors: VS Code or GoLand, per the Go survey; GoLand can break briefly after new Go releases.
    • Quality: golangci-lint for linting; gitleaks detect / gitleaks protect with a toml config that ignores vendor.
    • Profiling and tests: Built-in profiling, unit and integration testing; multiple main entry points under cmd/.
    • Docker: Sample FROM golang:1.20 Dockerfiles per entry point; readers suggested multi-stage builds.
    • Tools: gow (watch and rerun), hyperfine (benchmarks), dcd (duplicate code), gotestsum, among others.

    Takeaway: A sensible opinionated baseline for new Go repos. Copy the lint, gitleaks and tool list into your template.

  • snips.sh: Passwordless, Anonymous SSH-Powered Pastebin with a TUI and Web UI
    summary

    TL;DR: snips.sh, by Rob Herley, is a pastebin you use over SSH: pipe text to ssh snips.sh to upload, or ssh snips.sh to open a TUI. Snippets get a syntax-highlighted web view, and the only identity is your SSH key.

    • Upload: echo '{ "hello" : "world" }' | ssh snips.sh; no client install needed.
    • Anonymous: No sign-up, login or email; the SSH key is the account.
    • Sharing: Short links, Markdown rendering, and time-limited URLs with optional burn-after-read for sensitive content.
    • Editing: Update a snip in place; each diff is saved as a revision.
    • Extras: ML-based language detection; download and pipe into $PAGER.
    • Self-hosting: Containerized and light on resources; docs cover usage, database, self-hosting, ToS and acceptable use.

    Takeaway: Handy for moving snippets between terminals. For anything sensitive, self-host it rather than trusting the public instance.

  • CureIAM: Clean Accounts over Permissions in GCP Infra at Scale
    summary

    TL;DR: CureIAM, from Gojek, is a Python engine that enforces least privilege on GCP. It pulls GCP IAM Recommender suggestions, scores them, and applies the safe ones automatically every day.

    • Basis: Built on GCP IAM Recommender APIs and the Cloudmarker framework.
    • Scoring: Each recommendation gets safe_to_apply_score, risk_score and over_privilege_score; auto-apply happens only above thresholds set in CureIAM.yaml.
    • Scheduling: Built-in daily scheduler, so no external cron is needed.
    • Audit: Every action is recorded to a file store or Elasticsearch; store plugins are extensible.
    • Design: Config-driven, plugin-based, multiprocess and multithreaded for scale.
    • Setup: Config in /etc/CureIAM.yaml or ~/.CureIAM.yaml plus a service account key file (e.g. cureiamSA.json).

    Takeaway: Automating IAM Recommender cleanup is a good way to cut standing GCP permissions. Start in report-only mode with conservative thresholds, and guard the service account key it needs.

  • Container Security Fundamentals Part 4: Cgroups
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 4 of Rory McCune’s Container Security Fundamentals series on Datadog Security Labs (May 23, 2023). It explains Linux cgroups and how they limit container resources, stop fork bombs and control device access.

    • Versions: cgroup v2 arrived in kernel 4.5 (2016) and is needed for features like rootless containers; check with mount | grep cgroup (Ubuntu 20.04 has both, 22.04 only v2).
    • Inspect: cat /proc/[PID]/cgroup shows a process’s slice and scope.
    • Resource limits: Docker sets cgroup limits on CPU and memory to avoid noisy neighbours.
    • Fork bombs: Containers have no process limit by default; docker run --pids-limit sets the pids cgroup to contain them.
    • Devices: cgroups enforce runc’s allowed-device list; --device /dev/dm-0 adds host devices.
    • Next: Part 5 covers mandatory access control.

    Takeaway: Set PID and memory limits on every workload; Kubernetes pod limits map to these cgroups. Treat --device grants as privileged access.

  • Terraform check{} Block
    summary

    TL;DR: Elif Samedin and Andrei Buzoianu (Unfriendly Grinch, April 10, 2023) demo the Terraform check {} block from the v1.5.0 alpha. It runs assertions on data sources after plan and apply, giving ongoing validation of live infrastructure.

    • Feature: check blocks hold at least one assert with condition and error_message, and may define scoped data sources; failures warn rather than block.
    • Version testing: Uses tfenv install 1.5.0-alpha20230405 and tfenv use, with optional signature verification (trust-tfenv: yes).
    • Azure example 1: An external data source runs ping.py against the VM’s public IP and asserts status == "up".
    • Azure example 2: Asserts the NSG SSH rule is not open to * or 0.0.0.0/0.
    • Demo: Stopping and starting the VM shows the check failing and then passing on the next terraform apply.
    • Use cases: Infrastructure health checks, drift detection, post-apply checks built into modules.

    Takeaway: Use check blocks in modules for cheap post-deploy smoke and security assertions. They do not fail the apply, so alert on the warnings.

  • Terraform AWS Provider 5.0 Adds Updates to Default Tags
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp post by Aurora Chun (May 25, 2023) announcing Terraform AWS Provider 5.0. Its headline is a rework of provider-level default_tags, plus breaking removals.

    • Default tags fixes: Resolves inconsistent final plans with computed tags, duplicate tags in default and resource tags, and perpetual tag diffs.
    • Example: default_tags with environment, department, application, cost_center; a resource can override environment and add its own tags.
    • Enabler: New Terraform plugin SDK and plugin framework features made the fix possible.
    • Breaking: Deprecated attributes now cause an unsupported error, not a warning.
    • EC2-Classic: Support removed after AWS retired EC2-Classic in August 2022.
    • Upgrade: Read the v5 upgrade guide and pin the provider version.
    • Source caveat: curl hit a Vercel bot check; content was fetched with WebFetch.

    Takeaway: If you had worked around default_tags bugs, 5.x lets you drop those workarounds. Pin versions and fix deprecated attributes before upgrading.

  • aws-cloudsaga: Simulate Security Events in AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS CloudSaga, by Joshua McKiddy of AWS, is a CLI that simulates security events seen by the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT). It lets you test whether your controls, alerts and response plans react.

    • CLI: cloudsaga --chapters lists scenarios, --about <scenario> explains one, --scenario <name> runs it.
    • imds-reveal: Simulates SSRF-style IMDSv1 credential exposure (needs ec2:DescribeInstances).
    • mining-bitcoin: Launches instances that mimic crypto-mining abuse.
    • network-changes: Creates VPCs and modifies security groups.
    • iam-credentials: Generates and fetches the IAM credential report.
    • public-resources: Creates and checks public RDS and S3 resources, toggling public access blocks.
    • Where to run: For example AWS CloudShell; the README lists the IAM permissions each scenario needs.

    Takeaway: A simple way to check that GuardDuty, Config rules and alerting fire on common attacker actions. Run it only in a sandbox account, since it creates real and public resources.

  • Finding the Best Go Project Structure: Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Aviv Carmi (HUMAN Security, May 2023) revisits his earlier Go project structure article and explains why his team moved away from the “coupled packages” approach. Part 1 of 2, with an open-source template repository.

    • Goals: Structural coherence (each piece of code in one meaningful package) and separation of business logic from infrastructure, for testability and swappable backends (HTTP and gRPC, adding caches).
    • Single package: Rejected: no private symbols, tight coupling, no guidelines; migrating later is costly.
    • Coupled packages: Shared definition packages; used for years, giving separation and testability.
    • Retro finding: Global variables such as config.Port and config.Token make code unsafe to reuse within a project; a second server with a different token cannot reuse the code.
    • Context: Written for backend services with large scale and real-time decisions; the author says other use cases may differ.
    • Next: Part 2 covers the chosen architecture and directory layout.

    Takeaway: Avoid package-level globals for config and dependencies; pass them in. Read part 2 and the template for the structure they settled on.

  • HardenEKS: Validating Best Practices for Amazon EKS Clusters Programmatically
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post by Doruk Ozturk, Joshua Kurz and Jacob Mevorach (May 26, 2023) introducing HardenEKS. It is an open-source Python CLI that checks an EKS cluster against the EKS Best Practices Guide (EBPG).

    • Coverage: EBPG pillars are Security, Reliability, Autoscaling, Networking, Scalability and Windows Containers; 40+ automated rules at the time.
    • Agentless: Runs externally, so nothing is installed in the cluster.
    • Quick start: pip install hardeneks, then hardeneks --export-html report.html.
    • Report: Lists violated rules with the offending configuration and a link to the relevant best practice.
    • Example: Flags EBS volumes without encryption; setting encrypted in the StorageClass clears the finding.
    • History: First released November 2022; can run on a schedule, e.g. via EventBridge. Repo: aws-samples/hardeneks.

    Takeaway: A cheap periodic EKS posture check mapped to AWS’s own guidance. Use it next to kube-bench or a policy engine, not as a replacement.

  • Securing Cloud Native Microservices with Role-Based Access Control Using Keycloak
    summary

    TL;DR: CNCF Ambassador post by Daniel Oh (Red Hat), May 17, 2023, written after Keycloak joined CNCF as an incubating project. It is a step-by-step tutorial on securing Quarkus microservices with Keycloak RBAC over OpenID Connect.

    • Protocol: Explains the OIDC authorization code flow on top of OAuth 2.0, with ID tokens and SSO.
    • Scaffold: quarkus create secured-apis-keycloak-quarkus with the Quarkus OIDC extension.
    • RBAC: Endpoints annotated @RolesAllowed("admin") (/hello/db) and @RolesAllowed("user") (/hello).
    • Dev Services: Quarkus dev mode starts a Keycloak container (keycloak:21.0.2) automatically, with realm quarkus, client quarkus-app and test users alice and bob.
    • Verification: Calls each endpoint with access tokens issued by Keycloak to confirm role enforcement.
    • Further reading: Keycloak on Kubernetes, secrets in Keycloak, Keycloak CR tuning, Authorization Services.

    Takeaway: A quick hands-on path to role-based auth in Java microservices. Note that the demo endpoint returns DB credentials purely for illustration.

  • Exploring Firecracker MicroVMs for Multi-Tenant Dagger CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: Felipe Cruz (May 25, 2023) tests running Dagger CI/CD pipelines inside Firecracker microVMs, so each tenant’s containers run under their own kernel. He documents the setup and the problems he hit.

    • Host: Firecracker needs KVM; he used a DigitalOcean Debian 11 droplet (2 vCPU, 4 GB, $24/mo) with nested virtualization, and notes a Hetzner bare-metal option.
    • Kernel problem: The stock Firecracker guest kernel lacked modules such as nftables (iptables: Failed to initialize nft), so he built a custom kernel and rootfs.
    • Launch: Firecracker v1.3.2 via a Go launcher using the Firecracker Go SDK, with 1 vCPU, 1024 MB RAM and a static IP in kernel args.
    • Runtime: containerd, runc and CNI plugins in the rootfs; systemctl enable --now containerd on first boot.
    • Dagger engine: registry.dagger.io/engine:v0.5.1 run with nerdctl --privileged, gRPC on tcp://0.0.0.0:1234, cache in /var/lib/dagger.
    • Test: A Go SDK pipeline runs go version in golang:1.19 against the remote engine.

    Takeaway: Shows that microVM isolation for multi-tenant CI is feasible but needs custom kernel work. The Dagger engine still runs privileged inside the VM, so the VM is the security boundary.

  • Understanding Networking in Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Peter Jausovec (Learn Cloud Native, May 31, 2023) explains Kubernetes networking: how CNI wires pods together and how kube-proxy programs iptables to route Service traffic. Examples are traced on a kind cluster.

    • Four problems: Container-to-container (shared network namespace, localhost), pod-to-pod, pod-to-service, and external-to-service.
    • Pod-to-pod: Each node gets a pod CIDR; veth pairs connect pod namespaces to the node.
    • CNI: Kubernetes ships no default CNI plugin; managed offerings preconfigure one.
    • Tracing: iptables -L -t nat inside a kind node: PREROUTING to KUBE-SERVICES to KUBE-SVC-* per Service to KUBE-SEP-* per endpoint.
    • Load balancing: statistic mode random probability rules (0.25, 0.33, 0.5, …) spread traffic evenly across endpoints.
    • Modes: Compares iptables and IPVS mode.

    Takeaway: Dumping the nat table on a node is the fastest way to understand or debug Service routing. Do it once on a test cluster.

  • Amazon Security Lake Is Now Generally Available
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post by Ross Warren, Nisha Amthul and Jonathan Garzon (May 30, 2023) announcing general availability of Amazon Security Lake. It is a security data lake in your own account that normalizes logs to OCSF.

    • Sources: CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 Resolver logs, Security Hub findings (GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer) and 50+ partner sources, plus on-premises and other clouds.
    • Use cases: Investigations, compliance via rollup Regions, multi-year analysis with Athena, OpenSearch or SIEM/XDR tools, and hybrid queries such as CloudTrail joined with Azure audit logs in Athena.
    • Access control: Subscribers get scoped access to specific sources.
    • GA changes: OCSF 1.0 rc2; CloudTrail split into Authentication, Account Change and API Activity classes; automatic IAM role creation; CloudTrail S3 and Lambda data events collected separately.
    • Performance: S3 partitioning changed from hourly to daily.

    Takeaway: Worth considering if you are building a SIEM data layer on AWS. OCSF normalization saves parser work, but check ingestion and storage costs per source.

  • Updated Whitepaper Available: Architecting for PCI DSS Segmentation and Scoping on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog notice by Ted Tanner, Avik Mukherjee and Joseph Okonkwo (June 1, 2023) that AWS republished its whitepaper on PCI DSS scoping and segmentation on AWS, updated for PCI DSS v4.0.

    • Topic: Defining segmentation boundaries between in-scope and out-of-scope resources using AWS services.
    • Audience: Engineers and solution builders, plus QSAs and ISAs who need to understand AWS segmentation controls.
    • Key point: Software-defined networking gives segmentation controls beyond network segmentation, which can shrink the cardholder data environment (CDE).
    • Basis: The PCI Council’s Information Supplement on scoping and network segmentation.
    • Updates: Refreshed AWS best practices and services, and v4.0 requirements.

    Takeaway: Read the whitepaper before designing a CDE on AWS. Account-level and service-level isolation can cut audit scope a lot.

  • Crash Course on Go Generics
    summary

    TL;DR: Jon Calhoun’s short tutorial on Go generics: type parameters, constraint interfaces, common misconceptions, and generic container types.

    • Basic syntax: func Sum[T int | int64 | float64](numbers []T) T replaces one function per type, code generation, or reflection.
    • Constraints: Name the union as type Number interface { int | int64 | float64 } and use [T Number].
    • Misconception 1: Generics do not allow mixed-type slices; []Number{1, 1.10} does not compile.
    • Misconception 2: A function cannot return one type or another at runtime; keep the (int, error) pattern.
    • Containers: Example SortedList[T Number] with AddValue and a copying Values(); marked as inefficient and for illustration only.
    • Playground: Each example links to the Go Playground.

    Takeaway: A clear first read on what Go generics do and do not do. Use them mainly for container types and numeric helpers.

  • flox: Command Line Tool That Helps You Manage Your Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: Flox is a Nix-based environment manager. One manifest declares a project’s tools, environment variables and services, giving reproducible, isolated environments from laptop to CI to production without writing Nix.

    • Quick start: flox init, flox install python3 nodejs, flox activate; the tools disappear again on exit.
    • Model: Declarative, reproducible, and composable (layer per project, team, pipeline).
    • Basis: Built on Nix and Nixpkgs; Nix knowledge is optional.
    • Positioning (current README): Now marketed as a “software environment platform” for teams, with cryptographically pinned environments, supply chain claims, and an AI-agent angle.
    • License: GPL v2.

    Takeaway: A gentler way to get Nix-style reproducible dev shells. Compare it with devbox or plain nix develop before standardizing on it.

  • seaweedfs: Fast Distributed Storage System for Blobs, Objects, Files, and Data Lake
    summary

    TL;DR: SeaweedFS, by Chris Lu, is a distributed storage system designed to store billions of files and serve them fast. A single weed binary provides an S3 object store, a POSIX filer and lakehouse tables over the same data.

    • Design goals: O(1) reads and writes, each blob one disk read away, capacity added by starting another volume server.
    • Quick start: weed mini -dir=./data with AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and S3_BUCKET gives an S3 endpoint on :8333.
    • All-in-one: That process also runs the master, a volume server, the filer, WebDAV, an Iceberg REST catalog and the Admin UI.
    • Features: S3 API compatibility, S3 Tables (Iceberg, Lance), caching or tiering of cloud storage, active-active replication.
    • Deploy: Binary, Docker, Docker Compose, or Helm on Kubernetes.
    • Comparisons: README compares it with HDFS, GlusterFS, Ceph, MooseFS, MinIO and RustFS.

    Takeaway: A strong self-hosted S3 or small-file store, now often named as a MinIO alternative. Turn on Admin auth or mTLS before binding it to a network.

  • How I Use OpenAI’s GPT-4 to Stay in Touch with My Mum More Consistently
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A May 2023 Better Programming (Medium) article by Anna Geller describing a small automation: GPT-4 drafts a short, personal weekly check-in message to the author’s mum, which is then sent by SMS.

    • Generation: A GPT-4 prompt writes the check-in text; an OpenAI API key is required.
    • Delivery: The message is sent as SMS through AWS SNS.
    • Scheduling: Kestra runs the flow on Sundays.
    • Infrastructure: Managed as code with Terraform.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked fetching (403 / Cloudflare). This summary is based only on a search engine summary of the article, so tool details are unverified.

    Takeaway: A toy but complete example of a scheduled LLM workflow: prompt, generate, deliver, all as code. Keep a human review step before anything is sent in your name.

  • EKS with IPv6 Pods
    summary

    TL;DR: An hour-long Containers from the Couch (AWS) livestream, published June 2023, on running Amazon EKS clusters with IPv6 pod networking.

    • Problem: Avoid IPv4 address exhaustion in VPCs as pod counts grow.
    • Topics: How IPv6 EKS clusters work and how pods talk to each other.
    • IPv4 interop: How IPv6 pods still reach IPv4-only endpoints.
    • Getting started: Walkthrough of creating and using an IPv6 cluster.
    • Length: About 60 minutes.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video’s short description and metadata; no transcript was reviewed.

    Takeaway: Worth watching before designing a new EKS VPC where pod IP space is tight. IPv6 mode must be chosen at cluster creation.

  • Optimizing Container Resources with KRR
    summary

    TL;DR: A Containers from the Couch (AWS) live webinar from May 31, 2023, with guest Natan Yellin of Robusta, on right-sizing container CPU and memory requests using KRR.

    • Tool: KRR (Kubernetes Resource Recommender), open source from Robusta at github.com/robusta-dev/krr.
    • Goal: Optimize container resource requests and limits from observed usage.
    • Format: Live webinar, about 60 minutes.
    • Source caveat: Based only on the short video description and metadata; details of the demo were not reviewed.

    Takeaway: If your requests are guesses, KRR is a lightweight way to get Prometheus-based recommendations. Review them before applying, especially for bursty workloads.

  • kubepug: Kubernetes PreUpGrade Checker
    summary

    TL;DR: KubePug (Deprecations), by Ricardo Katz, is a kubectl plugin and standalone CLI that checks a live cluster or manifest files for APIs that are deprecated or removed in a target Kubernetes version. It also tells you the replacement API.

    • Data: Downloads a generated data.json of API deprecations (default https://kubepug.xyz/data/data.json; can be local).
    • Targets: A running cluster via kubeconfig or context, or files via --input-file.
    • Output: Affected objects, the replacement API, and the version where the API was deprecated or deleted.
    • Install: kubectl krew install deprecations, release binaries, or snap.
    • Helm: helm template -f values.yaml . | kubepug --k8s-version v1.22.0 --input-file=-.
    • CI: --error-on-deleted (and the deprecated equivalent) returns exit code 1 so pipelines can fail.
    • Repo: The project now lives under the kubepug GitHub org.

    Takeaway: Add it as a CI gate on rendered manifests before each cluster upgrade, together with pluto or kubent.

  • gitops-playground: Reproducible Infrastructure to Showcase and Evaluate GitOps Operators on Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: GitOps Playground, from Cloudogu, sets up a complete preconfigured GitOps platform on Kubernetes (local, cloud or air-gapped) so you can see GitOps in motion without assembling it yourself.

    • Deployment: Argo CD with a ready-made repository structure and promotion across environments.
    • Monitoring: Prometheus and Grafana, with notifications through an external mail server.
    • Secrets: Vault plus External Secrets Operator.
    • Pipelines: Jenkins with gitops-build-lib and SCM-Manager example apps.
    • Platform: Traefik ingress, cert-manager, and a Content Loader to push your own apps, repos and Argo CD tenants at install time.
    • Origin: Based on Cloudogu’s consulting, its internal developer platform, and its GitOps trainings.
    • Current README: Describes Argo CD as the GitOps operator; the repo title still says it showcases “GitOps operators” in general.

    Takeaway: A fast way to evaluate an Argo CD-based IDP stack end to end. Use it as a reference for repo layout and secrets wiring, not as production configuration.

  • All You Need to Know About Moving to containerd on Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post by Arun Nalpet Ramakrishna, Chance Lee and Gowtham S (June 1, 2023) on moving EKS workloads from Docker Engine to containerd after dockershim was removed in Kubernetes 1.24.

    • Background: EKS AMIs for 1.24+ ship containerd as the only runtime; earlier AMIs defaulted to Docker. The CRI made the dockershim unnecessary.
    • Breaking dependency: Pods that mount /var/run/docker.sock (metrics collectors, security agents, CI builders) stop working, since containerd uses a different API.
    • Detection: kubectl-detector-for-docker-socket (DDS) finds workloads that mount the Docker socket.
    • Image builds: Replace Docker-socket builds with Kaniko or BuildKit pods; docker:dind works but needs elevated privileges.
    • Node tooling: ctr (preinstalled, low-level), nerdctl (docker-like), crictl (CRI debugging); containerd namespaces differ from Kubernetes namespaces (k8s.io).
    • Reference: Links the Kubernetes Docker CLI to crictl mapping.

    Takeaway: Before upgrading past 1.23, run DDS across clusters and move image builds to Kaniko or BuildKit.

  • AWS Fault Injection Simulator Adds New Actions for Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (June 1, 2023) that AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) gained new chaos actions for EKS pods and ECS tasks.

    • Faults: CPU, memory and IO stress, network blackhole, network latency, packet loss, kill process, and delete EKS pod.
    • Targeting: Pods or tasks of a specific application or in a specific Availability Zone.
    • Agents: EKS actions are agentless; ECS actions use the SSM agent.
    • Availability: All Regions where FIS runs, including GovCloud (US).
    • Start: FIS console, plus the EKS and ECS action docs.

    Takeaway: A managed option for AZ-failure and latency game days on containers, without running Chaos Mesh or Litmus yourself. Scope experiments with stop conditions.

  • Amazon ECR Adds registry.k8s.io as a Supported Upstream for Pull Through Cache Repositories
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (June 1, 2023) that Amazon ECR pull through cache now supports registry.k8s.io as an upstream, so Kubernetes project images can be mirrored into private ECR automatically.

    • Context: Starting with Kubernetes 1.25, the project moved to the community-owned registry.k8s.io; from 1.27, releases are published only there, with a redirect from the old registry.
    • Guidance: The Kubernetes project recommends mirroring release images into your own registry where possible.
    • Setup: One pull through cache rule maps the upstream to a namespace in your ECR registry; ECR keeps images in sync.
    • Scope: Only unauthenticated public upstreams; all commercial AWS Regions.

    Takeaway: Mirror registry.k8s.io into ECR for EKS add-ons and core images to avoid upstream rate limits and outages.

  • AWS Introduces Container Image Signing
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (June 6, 2023) of container image signing with AWS Signer and Amazon ECR, so that only approved images get deployed to EKS.

    • Flow: Create a Signer signing profile, then sign images in ECR with client-side tools.
    • Managed parts: Signer manages keys, rotates code-signing certificates, keeps audit logs, and stores signatures next to images.
    • Enforcement: Use admission controllers such as Gatekeeper or Kyverno, or your own tooling, to verify before deploy.
    • Timing: Sign during development or deployment.
    • Cost: No additional charge for Signer.

    Takeaway: A managed alternative to running cosign keys yourself, if you stay in AWS. Signing is only useful once an admission policy enforces verification.

  • Practical Dependency Management for Developers
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Rickard (June 2, 2023) gives short, practical rules for managing software dependencies, based on his work on large projects, CI/CD and build tools.

    • Pin versions: Unpinned packages cause “works locally, fails in CI” bugs and failures when caches expire; for Docker images and git, pin to digest or commit SHA.
    • Separate PRs: Put package file updates in their own pull requests for easier review.
    • Lock files over vendoring: Commit package-lock.json or go.sum; if you must vendor, verify in CI that vendored code matches a reproducible build from the lock file.
    • Add dependencies carefully: “A little copying is often better than a little dependency.”
    • Do not over-modularize: Packages that always change together belong in one repo, to avoid diamond dependencies and cascading releases.
    • Update often: Amortize upgrade cost; pin dependencies inside Dockerfiles too.

    Takeaway: A compact checklist to share with a team. Digest pinning and lock-file verification are the parts that also improve supply chain security.

  • sensitive-data-protection-on-aws: Discover, Protect, and Visualize Sensitive Data Across AWS Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: Sensitive Data Protection on AWS is an AWS Labs solution (CDK, TypeScript) with a self-service web app that catalogs, discovers and visualizes sensitive data such as PII across multiple AWS accounts.

    • Discovery: Regular or on-demand scan jobs using your own data classification templates and identifiers; no manual tagging needed.
    • Metrics: Total sensitive entries, which accounts hold the most, and where the data lives.
    • Architecture: AWS Glue crawls catalogs and runs PII detection jobs in each monitored account; a central admin account holds the combined catalog.
    • App stack: ALB in front of Lambda (container images in ECR) for UI and backend, an identity provider for auth, Step Functions orchestrating jobs in monitored accounts.
    • Deploy: CloudFormation template (about 20 minutes per the README) or build the CDK project; Apache-2.0.

    Takeaway: An open alternative to Macie-style discovery for Glue-catalogued data stores across accounts. Compare its Glue job costs with Macie before adopting.

  • Updated AWS Ramp-Up Guide Available for Security, Identity, and Compliance
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post by Anna McAbee and Conor Colgan (June 6, 2023) on the refreshed AWS Ramp-Up Guide: Security, a learning path from cloud foundations to the AWS Certified Security - Specialty exam.

    • Training focus: Built mainly on AWS Skill Builder digital courses and self-paced labs.
    • Focus areas: Separate tracks for roles such as threat detection and incident response, compliance and data protection; for example, SOC analysts can follow the TD/IR track.
    • Extra resources: Whitepapers, blog posts, re:Invent videos and workshops for each area.
    • Scope of update: Most of the guide was rewritten based on customer feedback and new services.

    Takeaway: A free, structured curriculum for onboarding engineers to AWS security. Pick the track that matches the role instead of going through all of it.

  • Announcing Container Image Signing with AWS Signer and Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post by Jimmy Ray and Jesse Butler (June 6, 2023) walking through signing ECR images with the Notation CLI and AWS Signer, and enforcing signature checks in EKS with Kyverno.

    • Signing: Install the Notation CLI with the AWS Signer plugin and root certificate (Notation 1.0.0-rc.7 at the time); keys and certificates live in Signer signing profiles.
    • Standard: Notation is part of the CNCF Notary project; signatures are stored next to images in ECR.
    • Verification: The kyverno-notation-aws project: install cert-manager, Kyverno, and kyverno-notation-aws, then apply Notation TrustPolicy and TrustStore CRDs.
    • Enforcement: A Kyverno policy calls the Notation verifier at admission and blocks unsigned or untrusted images.
    • Scope: Also works with self-managed Kubernetes on AWS.

    Takeaway: A full recipe for signature enforcement on EKS. Start Kyverno in audit mode, and make sure system images are signed or excluded before you enforce.

19.05.2023

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Playlist
    summary

    TL;DR: The CNCF YouTube playlist of recorded sessions from KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2023 in Amsterdam. It has 314 videos, covering keynotes, project updates and breakout talks.

    • Size: 314 videos.
    • Keynotes: Opening by Priyanka Sharma and Chris Aniszczyk, Taylor Dolezal, an EU end-user panel, sustainable computing keynotes, and Dawn Foster on contributor sustainability.
    • Project updates: CNCF graduated and incubating project updates, Kubernetes project updates.
    • Breakouts in this archive: Kubernetes hacking (OWASP K8s Top 10), buildpacks, edge federation, GitOps at Adobe, SIG Scalability, node resource management, and eBPF versus sidecar meshes.
    • Format: Keynotes of a few minutes up to 30-40 minute sessions.

    Takeaway: Search the playlist by topic instead of browsing it. Pair it with talks.container-security.site for the security sessions.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: The Hacker’s Guide to Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Patrycja Wegrzynowicz (Form3), about 34 minutes. Live demos exploit Kubernetes misconfigurations from the OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 until user accounts in a sample web app are hijacked.

    • Framework: Structured around the OWASP Kubernetes Top 10.
    • Attack surface: Attacks on containers, pods, network, and Kubernetes components.
    • Demo goal: Chain vulnerabilities and misconfigurations up to account takeover in an example application.
    • Defence: Covers common mistakes and hardening best practices for each step.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract and video metadata.

    Takeaway: A good attacker-view session to show developers why pod security and network policies matter. Map each demo to a control you already have.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Customizing Your Buildpacks Build
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Natalie Arellano (VMware) and Aidan Delaney (Bloomberg) on customizing Cloud Native Buildpacks builds beyond the default pack build.

    • For developers: Inline buildpacks and build-time environment variables.
    • For platform operators: Base image extension with Dockerfiles.
    • Governance: How to control how much customization is allowed, to meet security requirements.
    • Audience: Buildpacks users, and teams who thought their workflow ruled buildpacks out.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: If buildpacks seemed too rigid, the Dockerfile-based extension points remove most blockers while keeping a governed base image.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Taming Tactical Cluster Federation at the Edge
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Anna Magdalena Kosek (TNO) and Stefan van Gastel (Dutch Ministry of Defence) on federating Kubernetes clusters at the tactical edge, where clusters move, have unstable links and join or leave at any time.

    • Problem: Federation with unstable networks, varied resources, and stateful apps on clusters that leave.
    • Federation: Liqo for distributed cluster federation.
    • Scheduling: Telemetry Aware Scheduler (TAS) combined with OLSR routing for network-aware placement.
    • Testing: Chaos Mesh to simulate network effects.
    • Concept: A tactical cloud where manned or unmanned vehicles form ad-hoc cloud groups.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: A useful reference if you run Kubernetes on intermittent links. Liqo plus network-aware scheduling is the stack to evaluate.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: GitOps at Adobe
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk “Tips from the Trenches: GitOps at Adobe” by Larisa Andreea Danaila and Ionut-Maxim Margelatu. It covers Adobe’s 2022 move from Spinnaker to Argo-based GitOps deployment pipelines.

    • Migration: Replaced Spinnaker and rebuilt deployment pipelines from scratch on the Argo projects.
    • Challenges: Promoting code across environments, automated rollbacks, deployment validation with functional tests.
    • Scale: Refactored pipelines to serve more apps, with patterns for web, streaming and batch services.
    • Practices: Testing infrastructure changes, removing duplicate manifests, auditing, deployment visibility.
    • Constraint: Had to meet strict organisational CI/CD standards.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: Useful when planning a Spinnaker to Argo migration. Promotion and rollback are the parts to design up front.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Building a Successful Business in Cloud Native
    summary
