    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 panel with Liz Rice (Isovalent), Guillermo Rauch (Vercel), Kelsey Hightower (Google), Sheng Liang (Acorn Labs) and Tom Manville (Kasten by Veeam) on how start-ups and small vendors can succeed in the cloud native ecosystem.

    • Questions covered: How contributing to open source helps a business; making products appeal to an open-source community; how this market differs from traditional ones.
    • Format: Panel of practitioners and founders sharing what worked and what did not.
    • Audience: Founders, vendor staff, and maintainers thinking about commercialisation.
    • Source caveat: Based on the panel abstract.

    Takeaway: Not technical, but useful context for judging vendor-backed open-source projects you depend on.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Intro + Deep Dive: Kubernetes SIG Scalability
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 intro and deep dive on Kubernetes SIG Scalability by Wojciech Tyczynski (Google).

    • Scope: Defining what scalability means for Kubernetes (SLIs and SLOs).
    • Work: Driving performance improvements and maintaining scalability-testing infrastructure.
    • Guardrails: Catching performance regressions before release.
    • Cross-SIG: Many improvements are driven by SIG Scalability but owned by other SIGs.
    • Q&A: Includes community input on the roadmap.
    • Source caveat: Based on the session abstract.

    Takeaway: Watch it to understand where the official Kubernetes scalability limits come from before planning very large clusters.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Archetypes for Reliable Systems
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Steve McGhee and Ameer Abbas (Google) on turning reliability targets into Kubernetes deployment patterns. It is based on the paper “Deployment Archetypes for Cloud Applications” (Berenberg, Calder, 2022).

    • Model: Teams state availability, failure-domain resilience and RTO/RPO needs, and get a matching deployment archetype.
    • Implementation: Multi-tenant, multi-application, multi-cluster Kubernetes setup.
    • Included: CI/CD, micro-segmentation, policy management, traffic routing, SLOs, and app and infrastructure monitoring.
    • Ownership: App teams own their services while infra teams update the platform without interrupting them.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: A useful framework for platform teams: offer a few reliability archetypes, not bespoke designs. Read the paper for the archetype definitions.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Node Resource Management: The Big Picture
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 overview by Sascha Grunert and Swati Sehgal (Red Hat), Alexander Kanevskiy (Intel), Evan Lezar (NVIDIA) and David Porter (Google) of the many proposals for improving Kubernetes node resource management.

    • Scope: Reserving, allocating and isolating CPU, memory, disk, network and accelerators on nodes.
    • Proposals covered: Dynamic Resource Allocation, QoS class resources, CPU management improvements, container lifecycle and stats changes.
    • Runtimes: CRI support for Kata Containers, Firecracker, gVisor and Confidential Containers.
    • Goal: Show how the efforts connect, which problems they solve, and what they mean for users.
    • Community: How to get involved in SIG Node and runtime work.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: Good orientation for anyone running GPU or latency-sensitive workloads, since DRA and CPU manager changes affect how you schedule them.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: How to Blow Up a Kubernetes Cluster
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Felix Hoffmann (iteratec) on how setting resource limits without understanding them broke a whole cluster, and what requests and limits actually do.

    • Story: Adding limits to memory-hungry pods left half the pods crash-looping and the rest stuck in Pending.
    • Basics: Requests are a lower bound used for scheduling; limits are an upper bound enforced at runtime.
    • Scarcity: What happens when demand exceeds supply: how requests affect scheduling and which pods get terminated first.
    • Audience: Kubernetes newcomers handed an existing cluster.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: Set requests from measured usage before adding limits, and understand QoS classes and eviction order first.

  • KubeCon 2023 EU: Life Without Sidecars: Is eBPF’s Promise Too Good to Be True?
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2023 talk by Zahari Dichev (Buoyant, Linkerd) on whether eBPF can really replace sidecar proxies in a service mesh.

    • Question: Can eBPF deliver mesh benefits at a fraction of the performance and operational cost?
    • Exploration: What is and is not possible in an eBPF-powered mesh.
    • Concerns: Whether proxies really go away, and what that means for security, resilience and operational complexity.
    • Perspective: From a sidecar-based mesh vendor, so expect a sceptical view.
    • Source caveat: Based on the talk abstract.

    Takeaway: Useful balance to eBPF mesh marketing. Check where L7 processing and mTLS actually happen in any “sidecarless” design.

  • network-mapper: Map Kubernetes In-Cluster Traffic and Export as Text, Intents, or an Image
    summary

    TL;DR: Otterize network mapper is a zero-config Kubernetes tool that maps pod-to-pod, pod-to-Internet and AWS IAM traffic without a new CNI or service mesh, and exports the map as text, JSON/YAML, intents or an image.

    • Install: helm install network-mapper otterize/network-mapper -n otterize-system --create-namespace.
    • CLI: otterize network-mapper list, visualize, export to JSON/YAML, and reset.
    • Components: A per-cluster mapper; a node sniffer DaemonSet that captures DNS responses and inspects open TCP connections like netstat/ss; a Kafka watcher; an Istio watcher for HTTP paths.
    • Long-lived connections: Handled by polling open TCP connections, since DNS only shows new ones.
    • Limitation: The Istio watcher reports all HTTP traffic since the sidecar started, regardless of when it was seen.
    • Integration: Can feed Otterize Cloud’s access graph and Otterize intents-based access control.

    Takeaway: A quick way to find out what talks to what before writing NetworkPolicies. Use the exported map as the starting point for default-deny rules.

  • pwru: eBPF-Based Linux Kernel Networking Debugger
    summary

    TL;DR: pwru (“packet, where are you?”) is an eBPF-based tool from the Cilium project that traces network packets through Linux kernel functions, with pcap-style filtering, to show where packets get dropped or altered.

    • Use case: The README demo shows where a curl request’s packets are dropped after an iptables rule is added.
    • Kernel requirements: Kernel >= 5.3; --output-skb needs >= 5.9 and --backend=kprobe-multi needs >= 5.18. Needs CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF, CONFIG_KPROBES, CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL and related options; check with zgrep $OPTION /proc/config.gz.
    • Filtering: Takes a pcap-filter expression plus flags such as --filter-func (RE2 on kernel function names), --filter-netns, --filter-mark, and --filter-track-skb to keep tracing a packet after NAT or tunnel decapsulation.
    • Extra tracing: Can trace TC and XDP BPF programs (--filter-trace-tc, --filter-trace-xdp), BPF helpers, and VXLAN/Geneve inner packets.
    • Output: Options such as --output-caller, --output-skb, and --output-file with 100 MB rotation by default.
    • Distribution: Statically linked x86_64 and arm64 binaries on the release page; debugfs at /sys/kernel/debug is optional.

    Takeaway: When a packet vanishes between interface and socket, pwru shows the exact kernel function where it died, which is faster than guessing at iptables, routing or eBPF policy.

  • Kubernetes Removals and Major Changes in v1.27
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post by Harshita Sao (March 2023) listing the planned deprecations and removals for v1.27, plus the move of all image traffic from k8s.gcr.io to registry.k8s.io.

    • Registry redirect: From March 20, traffic to the old k8s.gcr.io registry is redirected to registry.k8s.io. v1.27 is not published to the old registry, and from April neither are patch releases for v1.24-v1.26.
    • API removal: storage.k8s.io/v1beta1 for CSIStorageCapacity is no longer served. Use storage.k8s.io/v1, available since v1.24.
    • Seccomp annotations: The alpha annotations seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod and container.seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io are removed. Use securityContext.seccompProfile.
    • Feature gates: GA volume-expansion gates such as ExpandCSIVolumes and ExpandInUsePersistentVolumes are removed and must not appear in --feature-gates.
    • Policy recap: GA APIs cannot be removed within a major version, beta APIs get 3 releases after deprecation, alpha APIs can go at any time.
    • Page status: The page now carries a banner saying it is more than one year old and may be outdated.

    Takeaway: Before upgrading to 1.27, grep manifests and Helm charts for k8s.gcr.io, seccomp annotations and removed feature gates.

  • DevOps Threat Matrix
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft Defender for Cloud researchers published a MITRE ATT&CK-style threat matrix for DevOps environments (SCM, CI/CD, registries), mapping attacker tactics to techniques specific to pipelines.

    • Motivation: Cites SolarWinds Orion (malware pushed to possibly over 17,000 customers), the Codecov breach, and dependency confusion attacks on PyPI and npm.
    • Initial access: SCM authentication (PATs, SSH keys), CI/CD service authentication, public repositories with CI triggers on PRs, endpoint compromise, and configured webhooks reaching internal networks.
    • Execution: Poisoned pipeline execution in direct, indirect and public variants. Also dependency tampering (public dependency confusion, package hijack or “repo-jacking”, typosquatting), DevOps resource compromise, and control of a common registry.
    • Scope: Further tactics cover persistence, privilege escalation, credential access, lateral movement, defense evasion and impact, interpreted from a pipeline rather than an OS view.
    • Intended use: Categorize attacks and defenses, and work with red teams to test the assumptions.

    Takeaway: Use the matrix as a checklist to threat-model your own GitHub, Azure DevOps or GitLab setup, especially PR-triggered pipelines and how PATs are handled.

  • Spoofy: Check If Domains Can Be Spoofed Based on SPF and DMARC Records
    summary

    TL;DR: Spoofy is a Python tool by Matt Keeley that checks whether domains can be email-spoofed based on their SPF and DMARC records, using a manually tested spoofability table rather than guesswork.

    • Install: Needs Python 3.9+. Run pip3 install spoofy, then spoofy -d example.com, or spoofy -iL domains.txt -o xls for bulk checks.
    • Standards: RFC 7208 SPF evaluation and an RFC 9989 DMARC tree walk, including the sp/np tags for subdomains.
    • Lookups: A caching resolver with failover across 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 and 9.9.9.9. Counts SPF DNS and void lookups and flags unregistered SPF include domains.
    • Verdict codes: Codes 0-9 range from “Spoofing possible” through mailbox-dependent and subdomain-only cases to “Spoofing is not possible” (8) and “DNS lookup failed” (9).
    • Options: Output to stdout, xls or json; -t sets threads (default 4); --dkim enumerates DKIM selectors through an API.
    • Repo status: The README now describes newer features than in 2023 (PyPI package, RFC 9989), so the project has kept evolving.

    Takeaway: Useful for pentest recon or for auditing your own domain portfolio. Run it against every domain you own, including parked ones, and fix p=none or missing sp.

  • automated-security-helper-pipeline: Automated Security Helper Pipeline Template
    summary

    TL;DR: An aws-samples CDK template that builds a CodePipeline/CodeCommit/CodeBuild pipeline to run AWS’s Automated Security Helper (ASH) scanner on every new commit.

    • Flow: New commits pushed to CodeCommit are scanned by ASH, the report goes to an S3 bucket, and a Security Hub alert fires if the scan fails.
    • Prerequisites: Security Hub configured and the AWS CDK installed.
    • Deploy: pip install -r requirements.txt, cdk bootstrap, then cdk deploy or cdk deploy --context repo_name=<name>.
    • License: Apache 2.0, copyright 2022.
    • Scope: A small sample; the scanning logic lives in the separate ASH project.

    Takeaway: A quick way to see ASH in CI on AWS-native tooling. Note that AWS has since closed CodeCommit to new customers, so the source stage may need adapting.

  • amazon-ec2-cloudwatch-alarms-sls: Centralized API for EC2 CloudWatch Alarms in Multi-Account AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: An aws-samples Serverless Framework project that exposes a central API to create and delete CloudWatch alarms for EC2 instances across accounts in an AWS Organization.

    • Metrics covered: CPUUtilization and StatusCheckFailed (AWS/EC2), plus custom metrics such as MemoryUtilization, SwapUtilization, DiskSpaceUtilization (System/Linux) and PartitionUtilization (System/Windows).
    • Notifications: Alarms publish to a per-account SNS topic. Per the README, these topics are created by “VPCx automation” and forward to an SQS queue in a central account.
    • Stack: Python Lambdas deployed with serverless deploy -s dev, using serverless-python-requirements and serverless-deployment-bucket.
    • Auth: An optional MS Active Directory OAuth module (utils.auth), configured in config/config.dev.json.
    • Tests: pytest unit tests and behave BDD integration tests.
    • Age: Instructions target Python 3.6 and Node >= 14, both old now.

    Takeaway: A reference pattern for centralizing alarm management in multi-account setups. Expect to update runtimes and adapt the VPCx-specific SNS assumptions.

  • kube-iptables-tailer: Better Network Visibility for Your Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: kube-iptables-tailer from Box runs in the cluster, watches the host’s iptables log for dropped packets, and reports them as Kubernetes events on the affected pods.

    • Mechanism: Tails the iptables log file (or a journald directory) mounted from the host and parses lines that carry a configured --log-prefix.
    • Attribution: Maps source and destination IPs to running pods, and falls back to DNS lookup for IPs outside the cluster.
    • Visibility: Drops show up as PacketDrop warning events in kubectl describe pods, e.g. “Packet dropped when receiving traffic from …”.
    • Setup: Add a LOG rule such as iptables -A CHAIN_NAME -j LOG --log-prefix "EXAMPLE_LOG_PREFIX: ". Run as a DaemonSet and mount the log’s parent directory so log rotation is handled.
    • Requirements: Go 1.13+, Docker 17.05+, Kubernetes 1.11+. You build the container from source with make container.

    Takeaway: If NetworkPolicy or host firewall drops are invisible to app teams, this pushes them to where developers already look. Check maintenance status, since the listed requirements are dated.

  • Privilege Escalation in AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service
    summary

    TL;DR: Calif researchers show that any pod on a default EKS node can steal the node’s IAM credentials from IMDS, exchange them for a system:node Kubernetes token, and mint service account tokens for other pods on the same node, up to cluster-admin.

    • Step 1: From a low-privilege pod, get the EC2 instance role credentials from the metadata service, then run aws eks get-token --cluster-name=... to get a system:node identity.
    • Step 2: NodeRestriction still lets a node act on pods bound to it. kubectl create token -n ns1 sa-priv --bound-object-kind=Pod --bound-object-name=... --bound-object-uid=... returns a token for a privileged pod’s service account.
    • Test setup: EKS v1.25.7, one node, an alpine pod plus a pod using a cluster-admin service account.
    • Persistence: With admin rights, adding a record to the aws-auth ConfigMap keeps access even after the EC2 role’s permissions are revoked.
    • Mitigations: IMDSv2 with http_put_response_hop_limit set to 1, or iptables rules blocking IMDS. Isolate untrusted workloads on separate nodes and restrict public access to the API endpoint.
    • Update (Nov 2023): cert-manager’s service account has full pod permissions, which opens another escalation path.

    Takeaway: On EKS, treat every pod as having its node’s privileges until IMDS is blocked. Keep privileged service accounts off nodes that run untrusted workloads.

  • Introducing AWS Lambda Response Streaming
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Compute Blog launch post for Lambda response streaming, which lets functions send partial responses to clients as data becomes available, to cut time to first byte and allow larger payloads.

    • Payload size: Streams responses beyond Lambda’s 6 MB buffered limit, up to a soft limit of 20 MB.
    • Runtimes: Node.js 14.x and later managed runtimes, plus custom runtimes.
    • Handler: Wrap the handler with awslambda.streamifyResponse(async (event, responseStream, context) => ...). Use pipeline() rather than write(), and call responseStream.end() when using write().
    • Invocation: Through Lambda function URLs (including as a CloudFront origin), or the new InvokeWithResponseStream API in the SDK.
    • Limits: API Gateway and ALB do not support chunked transfer, so no TTFB gain through them. API Gateway can still return larger payloads, up to 10 MB, via HTTP_PROXY.

    Takeaway: Use function URLs with streaming for SSR, LLM-style token streams or large exports. Do not expect a streaming benefit behind API Gateway or ALB.

  • Announcing Updates to the AWS Well-Architected Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Architecture Blog announcement of a 2023 Well-Architected Framework update touching all six pillars, with more prescriptive best practices and a new Application Security area.

    • Scale: 113 best practices updated and 14 new ones; 78% of the 127 new or updated practices now include explicit implementation steps.
    • Security pillar: A new Application Security (AppSec) area with eight best practices covering development, testing and release.
    • Other pillars: Operational Excellence adds support plans and outage communication plans. Reliability adds design for availability targets and SLAs, plus the resilience shared responsibility model. Cost Optimization adds automation and data-retention enforcement. Sustainability adds a Region selection process.
    • Service coverage: Expanded coverage of Elastic Disaster Recovery, Trusted Advisor, Resilience Hub, Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, Organizations, Control Tower, Compute Optimizer, Budgets, CodeWhisperer and CodeGuru.
    • Context: Combined with 51 practices improved in 2022, more than 50% of the framework’s best practices had been recently updated. Available in 11 languages.

    Takeaway: If your last Well-Architected review predates 2023, re-run the Security pillar at least, since the AppSec questions are new.

  • Investigate Security Events by Using AWS CloudTrail Lake Advanced Queries
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog walkthrough of using CloudTrail Lake SQL queries across an AWS Organization to investigate incidents, starting from a GuardDuty finding about a leaked access key.

    • Prerequisites: An organization-level CloudTrail Lake event data store with management and data events, a delegated administrator account so queries do not run from the management account, and GuardDuty.
    • Scenario 1: A compromised access key. Nine example queries follow step 12 of the “Compromised IAM Credentials” incident response playbook.
    • Example query: SELECT eventSource,eventName,sourceIPAddress,eventTime,errorCode FROM <event-data-store> WHERE userIdentity.accessKeyId = '...' AND eventTime > ..., bounded by GuardDuty’s EventFirstSeen and EventLastSeen.
    • Pivoting: Follow-up queries find which role was assumed via AssumeRole, what that role did, and which IPs are indicators of compromise.
    • Second scenario: The post covers a further incident scenario using the same method.

    Takeaway: Save these queries as an IR runbook before you need them. CloudTrail Lake only helps if the org-wide event data store already exists.

  • Unlock Any CLI Using Biometrics with 1Password Shell Plugins
    summary

    TL;DR: 1Password announced Shell Plugins, which keep CLI API keys in encrypted 1Password vaults instead of plaintext config files and unlock them per terminal session with Touch ID or other biometrics.

    • Problem: CLIs such as GitLab, AWS or Stripe usually store long-lived keys in plaintext config files that any local process can read.
    • Launch plugins: GitLab, CircleCI, AWS, Sentry, Stripe, Twilio and GitHub, among others.
    • Setup: Install 1Password CLI, then for example op plugin init glab. Existing credentials can be imported, then removed from disk.
    • MFA: Where the service supports it, 1Password fills in MFA codes automatically.
    • Extensibility: An open-source plugin SDK, in beta at the time, for adding any CLI.
    • CI/CD: New integrations reference 1Password secrets from CircleCI, Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

    Takeaway: A low-effort way to get static cloud and SaaS keys out of ~/.aws/credentials-style files on developer laptops. Short-lived credentials such as SSO are still better where the service offers them.

  • Intro to Forensics in the Cloud: A Container Was Compromised. What’s Next?
    summary

    TL;DR: A Wiz blog introduction to cloud DFIR covering how it differs from endpoint forensics, a cheat sheet of log sources and tools to set up in advance, and a walkthrough of investigating a compromised container.

    • Guiding questions: Initial access point, lateral spread, persistence, impact, and prevention.
    • Cloud vs endpoint: Cloud architecture (VMs, containers, serverless, identities) differs, and attacker goals differ too. Cloud attacks are mostly resource hijacking (e.g. mass EC2 creation) or access to sensitive data.
    • Five sources: Cloud provider audit logs (CloudTrail, GCP Cloud Audit Logs, Azure sign-in, audit, activity and resource logs), VPC flow logs, orchestration logs (Kubernetes audit), workload image snapshots, and runtime events.
    • Gotcha: Traffic to IMDS appears in provider logs, not in VPC flow logs.
    • Preparation: Logs and tooling must exist before the attack, or the investigation has blind spots.

    Takeaway: Check now that CloudTrail, flow logs and Kubernetes audit logs are on and kept long enough, and that you can snapshot a running container’s disk.

  • Rule Writing for CodeQL and Semgrep
    summary

    TL;DR: Eugene Lim (spaceraccoon) compares writing custom rules in CodeQL and Semgrep after a year with both, arguing that the syntax gap reflects deeper differences in how each tool models code.

    • CodeQL: QL looks like SQL but is Datalog-based and object-oriented. Writing it well means knowing the standard library classes and predicates, e.g. DataFlow::PropWrite.
    • Semgrep: Pattern-oriented YAML rules that look like the target code, shown with an Electron allowRunningInsecureContent rule from njsscan.
    • Code model: Semgrep turns code into a generic AST, then an intermediate language. That makes adding languages easier but loses data flow and control flow detail.
    • Taint tracking: CodeQL does global taint tracking out of the box. In 2023 Semgrep offered it only in paid Semgrep Pro, without path sensitivity, pointer or shape analysis, or soundness guarantees.
    • Trade-off: Semgrep is quicker to learn and extend; CodeQL catches more complex data-flow bugs.

    Takeaway: Use Semgrep for fast pattern and guardrail rules across many languages. Invest in CodeQL when you need interprocedural taint analysis for real vulnerability hunting.

  • Go’s Error Handling Is a Form of Storytelling
    summary

    TL;DR: Preslav Rachev argues that Go’s explicit if err != nil handling pays off when each layer wraps the error with context, so the final message tells the story of what failed.

    • Anti-pattern: Bare return err leads to useless logs like ERROR: not found. Ignoring errors with _ leads to panics, which crash the whole Go app.
    • Wrapping: fmt.Errorf("obtaining result for id %s: %w", id, err) adds context, and %w keeps the original error for errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows).
    • Message style: Keep messages short and describe what was being attempted. Avoid “failed”, “cannot” and “error while”.
    • Result: Wrapped chains read like tracking parcel location: fetching order status: connecting to the DB.
    • Code as docs: Error context also documents intent in the code, much as comments would.

    Takeaway: Make wrapping with %w and a short verb phrase the team convention. It costs little and makes logs readable without stack traces.

  • The Tao of Go
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting) uses the Taoist “three treasures” of kindness, simplicity and humility as a frame for idiomatic Go: work with the grain of the language rather than against it.

    • Kindness: Write for humans. Use descriptive package names, good docs and generous licenses, require minimal configuration and dependencies, give helpful error messages, and be gentle in code reviews.
    • Continuous refactoring: Make small improvements every time you touch the codebase, since full rewrites rarely happen.
    • Simplicity: Be explicit and avoid magic. Do not use concurrency where it does not help. Keep packages decoupled and stop types leaking across boundaries. Process data as a stream.
    • Interfaces: “Accept interfaces, return structs”, and do not pass contexts where they are not needed.
    • Performance: Do not obsess. Go is fast enough that simplicity should win.
    • Humility: Do not be clever, use the standard library, and accept that you make mistakes, which Go’s tooling such as unused-import errors helps catch.

    Takeaway: A short philosophy piece, good for onboarding new Go developers or as a code review reference when debating “clever” designs.

  • How Go Fixed Everything That Was Wrong with Programming
    summary

    TL;DR: An opinion piece by Jan Kammerath (April 2023) arguing that Go is the “Goldene Mitte”, a pragmatic middle ground between C’s performance and the developer ergonomics of JavaScript, Python, Java and C#.

    • Performance: Compiled with garbage collection. The author says it trails C because of GC but beats interpreted (JS, Python) and VM-based (Java, C#) languages.
    • No inheritance: Structs and interfaces with composition instead of class inheritance, which the author frames as enforced simplicity.
    • Static typing: Credited with better maintainability and with avoiding the need to bolt types on later, as TypeScript did for JavaScript.
    • Errors: Explicit err != nil returns instead of exceptions, with examples of handling, panicking, or discarding with _.
    • Weak spots: The author does not recommend Go yet for mobile apps, embedded software or GPU-accelerated code.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching, so this is based on a Wayback Machine copy of the article.

    Takeaway: An opinion essay rather than a technical deep dive. Useful as a framing for choosing Go for server-side and serverless work, not as evidence.

  • Exploiting and Securing Jenkins Instances at Scale with GroovyWaiter
    summary

    TL;DR: Dylan Makowski of NVIDIA’s red team introduces GroovyWaiter, a Python script that checks a list of Jenkins URLs for an unauthenticated Script Console and runs a command on any that are exposed.

    • Target: The Jenkins Script Console at /script runs arbitrary Groovy. It is normally gated by the Overall/Read permission, but lax access control can leave it open to anyone.
    • Tool behavior: For each URL it tries the console and runs id on Linux or whoami.exe on Windows, then prints a results table.
    • Impact: From an open console an attacker can dump all stored secrets, run any system command, and decrypt previously found secrets with Groovy functions.
    • Context: The post cites over 300,000 Jenkins installations. Jenkins is a ransomware and supply-chain target because it holds secrets and source code.
    • Approach: Focuses on abusing intended Jenkins features rather than CVEs.
    • Defense: Apply proper authentication and access control as described in the Jenkins security documentation.

    Takeaway: Scan your own estate for Jenkins instances with an anonymously reachable /script. An exposed Script Console means full compromise of the server and its credentials.

  • Container Security Fundamentals Part 3: Capabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 3 of Datadog Security Labs’ container security series explains Linux capabilities, how Docker restricts them by default, and how to drop the ones containers do not need.

    • Demo: Even as root in a container, date +%T -s "08:08:08" fails with “Operation not permitted” because CAP_SYS_TIME is not granted.
    • Background: Capabilities split root into 41 privileges, from narrow ones (CAP_AUDIT_READ) to broad ones (CAP_SYS_ADMIN).
    • Tooling: pscap and filecap (libcap-ng-utils) show process and file capabilities, setcap adds CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to a binary, and amicontained shows effective rights from inside a container.
    • NET_RAW: Usually not needed for ping, because ping_group_range is set in Docker network namespaces (since 2020) and is a Kubernetes “safe” sysctl since 1.18.
    • NET_BIND_SERVICE: Docker sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0 in containers, so binding low ports often works without it.
    • Method: Run with --cap-drop=ALL, run the test suite, and add back only what fails.

    Takeaway: Default Docker capabilities are more than most apps need. Start from drop: ["ALL"] in pod security contexts and add capabilities back explicitly.

  • Managing Kubernetes Secrets Like a Pro
    summary

    TL;DR: Tanat Lokejaroenlarb (Adevinta) explains when native Kubernetes Secrets fall short and how Adevinta uses Sealed Secrets for secrets kept in Git and External Secrets Operator for secrets synced from a secrets manager.

    • Problem: Native Secrets are only Base64-encoded. Anyone with namespace RBAC read access can decode them, and they cannot be committed to Git next to manifests.
    • Sealed Secrets: Encrypt with kubeseal --cert <public-key> --namespace <ns> secret.json. Only the in-cluster controller, which holds the private key, can decrypt a SealedSecret back into a native Secret.
    • Limitation: Hard to keep aligned with a source-of-truth store such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, especially with credentials that rotate every seven days.
    • External Secrets: A SecretStore defines how to connect (e.g. AWS Secrets Manager in eu-west-1 with access key refs), and an ExternalSecret defines what to sync into a Kubernetes Secret.
    • App impact: Both approaches end in native Secrets, so applications do not change.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching, so this is based on a Wayback Machine copy that was partly truncated.

    Takeaway: Use Sealed Secrets for GitOps-only setups. Use External Secrets when a central secrets manager is the source of truth or secrets rotate.

  • How to Yubikey: A Configuration Cheatsheet
    summary

    TL;DR: A practical cheatsheet by kmille (debugging.works) for configuring a YubiKey 5 on Linux with ykman, covering TOTP, U2F/FIDO2 and other applications, with backup advice.

    • Inspect: ykman list and ykman info show the firmware and enabled applications (OTP, FIDO2, OATH, OpenPGP, PIV). Toggle them with ykman config nfc --disable PIV or ykman config usb --enable-all.
    • TOTP: ykman oath accounts add test --touch, then ykman oath accounts code. A YubiKey 5 NFC holds 32 TOTP secrets; Yubico Authenticator offers a GUI.
    • TOTP backup: Keep the base32 secret elsewhere (e.g. KeePassXC in a separate database, or pyotp), since TOTP secrets are not exportable from the key.
    • U2F/WebAuthn: Phishing-resistant because the challenge-response is bound to the origin. It needs libfido2 on Arch, and Firejail users must set browser-disable-u2f no.
    • U2F backup: Private keys cannot be copied, so register multiple keys per account.
    • Tooling note: Written against ykman 4.0.9. Some features depend on firmware version.

    Takeaway: Keep this as a reference for (re)provisioning keys. Always enroll a second YubiKey for FIDO2 accounts, and back up TOTP seeds before loading them.

  • How to Implement a Centralized Immutable Backup Solution with AWS Backup
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Storage Blog walkthrough for copying backups from workload accounts into a separate central backup account in AWS Organizations, protected by layered guardrails to make them immutable and resistant to ransomware.

    • Data-level guardrails: AWS Backup Vault Lock plus a vault access policy on the central vault.
    • Account-level guardrails: An Organizations SCP that blocks everyone except the authorized admin from changing or managing the central vault.
    • Detection: An EventBridge rule that alerts if anyone other than the admin performs changes or management operations on the vault.
    • Encryption: A KMS customer managed key created in the central backup account encrypts the vault.
    • Delivery: A CloudFormation template, including a custom resource that creates the SCP from the management account and uses StackSets.
    • Prerequisites: All accounts in Organizations with all features and SCPs enabled, plus a delegated administrator.

    Takeaway: Ransomware-resistant AWS backups need a separate account, Vault Lock and an SCP together. Any one of them alone can be bypassed by an admin in the source account.

  • Cloud Red Teaming: AWS Initial Access & Privilege Escalation
    summary

    TL;DR: A slide deck by TweekFawkes from BSidesTampa (April 1, 2023) on getting from zero to cloud admin in AWS, aimed at both red and blue teams.

    • Initial access: Stealing SSO tokens and browser cookies, plus what the abstract calls a unique cloud-native technique for initial access to AWS.
    • Privilege escalation: Using graph databases such as Neo4j to find escalation paths.
    • Detection: Cloud provider logging services and the suspicious events defenders should watch.
    • Audience: Covers cloud basics first, so cloud expertise is not required.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the Speaker Deck abstract; individual slide contents were not reviewed.

    Takeaway: Worth skimming for the SSO token theft and graph-based path-finding ideas. Pair it with checks that your CloudTrail alerts cover these events.

  • How to Troubleshoot Memory Leaks in Go with Grafana Pyroscope
    summary

    TL;DR: A Grafana Labs post on finding Go memory leaks, mainly leaked goroutines, with Grafana Pyroscope continuous profiling.

    • Typical leak: An HTTP handler starts go longRunningTask(responses) but never reads the channel. The goroutine blocks forever and keeps its 100 KB buffer alive.
    • Prevention: Signal exit through channels, use context cancellation, and wait with sync.WaitGroup.
    • Step 1: Find the affected service and time window from logs, metrics or traces (restarts, memory alerts, SLO breaches).
    • Step 2: Add github.com/pyroscope-io/client/pyroscope and call pyroscope.Start(...). CPU, alloc and inuse profiles are on by default; goroutine, mutex and block profiles are optional.
    • Step 3: Look at goroutine counts over time first, then memory flame graphs. Goroutine stacks show where each one is blocked.
    • Caveat: Memory profiles show who allocated memory, not who is still holding it.

    Takeaway: For slow memory growth in Go services, graph goroutine counts before anything else. Continuous profiling makes the leaking call site obvious.

  • Go Integration Testing with Courage and Coverage
    summary

    TL;DR: Vladimir Dementyev (Evil Martians) shows how he raised AnyCable-Go’s reported coverage from about 50% to 76% without writing new Go tests, by measuring coverage of black-box integration tests with Go 1.20’s go build -cover.

    • Starting point: Unit test coverage reported through Coveralls (coverallsapp/github-action@v2) was 54%, even though bug reports were rare.
    • Black-box tests: Rails Action Cable conformance tests (the anyt gem) and per-commit benchmark tests written in a Ruby DSL.
    • Leak test: Launch the server, run websocket-bench twice, read goroutine counts with gops, and fail above 200 or on more than 10% growth.
    • Key feature: Go 1.20 go build -cover produces instrumented binaries, so coverage from external integration runs can be collected and merged.
    • Lesson: Unit-only coverage numbers can understate how well a project is actually tested.

    Takeaway: If your Go service is mainly tested end to end, build it with -cover in CI and merge those profiles, so coverage reflects reality.

  • cw-logs-insights-gpt: Chrome Extension That Generates CloudWatch Logs Insights Queries from ChatGPT Prompts
    summary

    TL;DR: A small Chrome extension by Lars Jacobsson that turns plain-English prompts typed in the CloudWatch Logs Insights console into Logs Insights queries using the OpenAI API.

    • Usage: Type a prompt inside double quotes in the query editor, then click the “Convert to query” button that appears.
    • Setup: Create an OpenAI API key and put it in src/apiKey.js as export const apiKey = '...'.
    • Build: npm install && npm run build, then load build/ as an unpacked extension in Chrome developer mode.
    • Scaffold: Bootstrapped with Chrome Extension CLI.
    • Caveat: The API key is compiled into the extension bundle, and log context goes to OpenAI.

    Takeaway: A 2023-era proof of concept. AWS now offers natural-language query generation in CloudWatch, which avoids sending data to a third party.

  • Google Authenticator Now Backs Up Your 2FA Codes to the Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer reports (April 2023) that Google Authenticator 6.0 for iOS and Android can sync 2FA one-time password secrets to the user’s Google Account, adding backup and multi-device support.

    • Problem solved: Codes were stored on one device only, so losing the phone meant losing every 2FA setup.
    • Flow: After updating, the app prompts you to sign in to a Google Account and sync codes.
    • Requirement: Google requires 2-step verification on that Google Account for cloud backup.
    • Rollout: Available on iOS at publication and rolling out gradually on Android.
    • Scale: The app had over 100 million installs.

    Takeaway: Sync trades the loss risk for account-takeover risk. If you enable it, harden the Google Account itself, ideally with a security key.

  • Using Nix with Dockerfiles
    summary

    TL;DR: Mitchell Hashimoto shows how to build Docker images with a normal Dockerfile that uses Nix in a builder stage and copies only the Nix store closure into a FROM scratch image, so dev, CI and production share one definition.

    • Argument: Without Nix, local dev, CI YAML and the Dockerfile each describe the environment separately and drift apart. With Nix, one flake is the single source of truth.
    • Example: A Flask app packaged with a flake using poetry2nix.mkPoetryApplication, plus a devShell with Python and Poetry. nix build produces result/bin/app.
    • Builder stage: FROM nixos/nix:latest, then nix --extra-experimental-features "nix-command flakes" --option filter-syscalls false build.
    • Closure copy: cp -R $(nix-store -qR result/) /tmp/nix-store-closure, then copy it into FROM scratch.
    • Result: A minimal image holding only the app’s runtime dependencies.
    • Honest trade-off: The author says Nix plus Docker is harder than Docker alone in isolation, and pays off once the same config also drives dev and CI.

    Takeaway: If you already use Nix flakes for dev shells, this pattern gives small, reproducible images without learning dockerTools.

  • Argo CD End User Threat Model: Security Considerations for Hardening Declarative GitOps CD on Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: A short CNCF community post by Andres Vega (ControlPlane) and Michael Crenshaw (Argo CD) announcing ControlPlane’s threat model report for a typical production Argo CD deployment.

    • Scope: A threat-modeling analysis of a representative production Argo CD setup, with security recommendations.
    • Attack trees: Visualizations of the threat landscape, meant to help explain to non-technical stakeholders why controls are needed.
    • Reproducibility: Includes the deployment architecture and code to reproduce it.
    • Format: The blog post is only an announcement. The substance is in the linked full report.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the short CNCF post; the linked report itself was not reviewed.

    Takeaway: Read the full report before exposing Argo CD in production. Its attack trees work well to justify hardening work to management.

  • dexter: Ensure All Your Images Are Pinned by Digest for Better Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Dexter, by ChaosInTheCRD, is a Go CLI meant for CI that finds container image references in a repository and rewrites them from mutable tags to immutable @sha256 digests.

    • Why: Anyone with registry write access can repoint a tag (e.g. grafana/grafana:4.2.0). Pinning to a digest blocks tag hijacking and supply-chain swaps such as injected crypto-miners.
    • Output: References become e.g. index.docker.io/grafana/grafana@sha256:7ff7f9....
    • Parsers: Kubernetes manifests (Pod, Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob) and Dockerfiles.
    • Usage: go run . manipulate --directory <repo>.
    • Config: A YAML file selects parsers and lists files or references to ignore. The README calls the config very basic.
    • URL note: The repo now resolves to github.com/ChaosInTheCRD/Dexter.

    Takeaway: A simple way to enforce digest pinning. Pair it with Renovate or Dependabot so pinned digests still get updated.

  • AWS Announces Three New Amazon GuardDuty Capabilities to Protect Container, Database, and Serverless Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS press release (April 2023) announcing three Amazon GuardDuty extensions: EKS Runtime Monitoring, RDS Protection for Aurora, and Lambda Protection.

    • EKS Runtime Monitoring: Threat detection based on runtime behavior inside containerized workloads.
    • RDS Protection: Detects threats to data in Amazon Aurora databases.
    • Lambda Protection: Detects threats to serverless applications.
    • Scale claims: Tens of thousands of customers, protecting more than half a billion EC2 instances and millions of S3 buckets. Over 100 detection capabilities added since the 2017 launch.
    • Threat intel: AWS feeds plus third parties including CrowdStrike, Proofpoint and Bitdefender.
    • Named customers: Arctic Wolf, Best Buy, GE Digital, Siemens and Wiz.

    Takeaway: A press release, short on detail. Check the GuardDuty docs for the agent requirements and per-feature pricing before enabling these across an organization.

  • Mitigating DDoS with Data Science Using AWS Shield Advanced and AWS WAF
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Architecture Blog case study on how payments company Razorpay layers AWS Shield Advanced, AWS WAF and ML-driven rate limits at its API edge to tell DDoS traffic from legitimate B2B merchant traffic.

    • Baseline: WAF rate limiting on CloudFront for static sites and on ALB for dynamic sites. APIs that carry merchant context need multilayered defenses.
    • Response phases: An automated, risk-ranked inventory of exposed APIs, grouping assets (authenticated or not), then simulated attack traffic for testing.
    • Shield Advanced: Custom alarms, real-time visibility of top client IPs, countries, user agents and routes, and Shield Response Team support for writing WAF rules.
    • WAF: Blocking rules and per-IP rate limiting with scope-down statements.
    • ML loop: Request events go into a time-series database. Models produce malicious-confidence scores and pattern-based rate limits from weekly and monthly patterns.
    • Edge flow: High confidence means block in WAF, low confidence means CAPTCHA, plus rate limits before and after auth. Insights go to Kafka outside the request path.

    Takeaway: Static WAF rate limits are not enough for multi-tenant APIs. Per-consumer, history-based limits fed back to the edge are the reusable idea.

  • Writing an OS in Go: The Bootloader
    summary

    TL;DR: The first post in TotallyGamerJet’s series on writing an operating system in Go using only the standard Go toolchain, covering BIOS and UEFI and how to boot a Go binary.

    • BIOS vs UEFI: The author wants to support both, UEFI for modern machines and BIOS to keep old hardware out of e-waste.
    • UEFI note: UEFI executables are PE files, which the Go toolchain can produce with GOOS=windows.
    • Bootloaders: Looks at Limine and BOOTBOOT, which load ELF kernels using a linker script.
    • GCCGO problem: The existing BOOTBOOT Go example uses GCCGO and dirty hacks. The author rejects it because the goal is a self-hosting OS with no C.
    • Entry point: Go binaries start in per-platform _rt0_GOOS_GOARCH assembly. The author tries the linker -E flag to set a pure-Go _start, then runs into linker-script requirements.

    Takeaway: An educational read on Go runtime start-up and linking internals, not a production technique.

  • Random Testing in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel’s post on random and property-based testing in Go: use many generated inputs and check invariants instead of picking a few examples by hand.

    • Round-trip test: Encode a random value, then decode it, and expect the original back.
    • Determinism: Seed a dedicated generator, e.g. rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2)), to avoid flaky tests.
    • Permutation: rand.Perm(100) covers every value once in random order.
    • Property-based testing: Assert invariants (e.g. a square is never negative) rather than exact outputs.
    • Next step: Promote failing random inputs to example tests, or let Go fuzz testing do it automatically (covered in the next post).
    • Page status: The live page is titled “Random and property-based testing in Go” and uses math/rand/v2, so it was updated after 2023.

    Takeaway: Add one property-based round-trip test to any encode/decode or parse/serialize pair. It is cheap and finds edge cases.

  • Coolify: Open-Source and Self-Hostable Heroku / Netlify Alternative
    summary

    TL;DR: Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable PaaS (a Heroku, Netlify or Vercel alternative) that deploys apps, databases and one-click services to any server you can reach over SSH.

    • Targets: Your own servers, VPS, Raspberry Pi, EC2, DigitalOcean, Linode, Hetzner and others. One or many servers.
    • Builds: Nixpacks, Railpack, Dockerfile, Docker Compose, static sites or prebuilt images.
    • Databases: One-click PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis, KeyDB, Dragonfly and ClickHouse.
    • Features: Git push-to-deploy (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea), PR preview deployments, automatic Let’s Encrypt, webhooks, API, browser terminal, scheduled tasks, team permissions.
    • Model: Free self-hosting with no paywalled features, funded by sponsors, plus a paid Cloud option. The site claims 360+ one-click services.
    • Page status: The current page also advertises an MCP server for AI agents, which is newer than the 2023 link.

    Takeaway: A solid option for small teams that want Heroku-style workflows on cheap VMs. You take on patching and backing up the Coolify host yourself.

  • netchecks: Tool to Validate Assumptions About the Kubernetes Network
    summary

    TL;DR: Netchecks (hardbyte) is a set of tools for asserting that network conditions are as expected: a Kubernetes operator that runs checks and reports results as PolicyReport resources, and a netcheck CLI and Python library.

    • Operator: Written in Rust with kube-rs. Checks are declared as NetworkAssertion resources, and results are reported as PolicyReport objects. Installs via a Helm chart on ArtifactHub.
    • CLI checks: DNS, HTTP, TCP and PostgreSQL connectivity, e.g. netcheck dns --server 1.1.1.1 --host hardbyte.nz --should-pass.
    • Validation rules: CEL-style expressions such as --validation-rule "data.body.contains('GitHub lives!') && data['status-code'] in [200, 201]".
    • Install: pip install netcheck, or docker run -it ghcr.io/hardbyte/netchecks:main.
    • Output: JSON with the spec, response data, timestamps and a pass or fail status.
    • Use case: Continuously confirm that NetworkPolicies or firewalls allow or block what you expect. Full docs are at netchecks.io.

    Takeaway: Turn “this namespace cannot reach the internet” into a test that runs continuously, so policy regressions show up in reports instead of incidents.

  • Use Amazon CodeWhisperer for Your AWS Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Sena Yakut (AWS Community Builder) shows how to use Amazon CodeWhisperer, free Individual tier, generally available April 13, 2023, to generate CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark check functions and to run its security scan in VS Code.

    • Setup: Install the AWS Toolkit in VS Code and sign in with a free AWS Builder ID, which needs no AWS account. Also works in JetBrains, Cloud9 and Lambda.
    • CIS checks generated: MFA for all IAM users, access keys older than 45 days, root MFA, AWS Config enabled in all regions, and CloudTrail logs encrypted with KMS CMKs (CIS v1.5.0).
    • Prompting: The author turns benchmark control text into sentences or comments and lets CodeWhisperer write the code.
    • Security scan: CodeWhisperer found an OS command injection in a SonarQube sample, shown in the Problems panel.
    • Languages: Python, Java, JS/TS, C#, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Scala, Ruby, PHP, SQL, C/C++ and Shell.
    • Source caveat: The site blocked direct fetching, so this is based on a Wayback Machine copy. CodeWhisperer has since been folded into Amazon Q Developer.

    Takeaway: AI-generated CIS checks are a quick start, but review them against the benchmark. Mature tools such as Prowler or Security Hub CIS standards cover this already.

24.04.2023

  • The Adapter Pattern in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting, from “The Power of Go: Tests”) explains the adapter pattern in Go: put all code for one external dependency, such as a database or API, behind a small interface so business logic can be tested without that dependency.

    • Core idea: An adapter, or “ambassador”, holds everything specific to one external system and translates in both directions.
    • Starting point: A Create(db *sql.DB, w Widget) function that mixes SQL details with widget logic and is hard to test.
    • Refactor: Define a Store interface. Business logic depends on the interface, and tests use a simple in-memory mapStore.
    • Production: PostgresStore with a *sql.DB implements the same Store method, with what the author calls about 1.3 million lines of code behind it.
    • Testing the adapter: Split the adapter’s behavior into chunks, inbound and outbound, as in the author’s earlier API client article, so most of it can be tested without a live server.
    • Principle: Quotes Michael Feathers: untestable code points to a design problem.

    Takeaway: If a Go test needs Postgres or a live API just to check business rules, add an interface boundary there and give the real dependency its own small, focused tests.

  • gotraceui: Go Execution Trace Frontend
    summary

    TL;DR: Gotraceui, by Dominik Honnef (dominikh), is a native GUI for visualizing and analyzing Go execution traces, meant to be a faster and more capable alternative to go tool trace.

    • Why: Unlike go tool trace, it does not use deprecated browser APIs or a browser at all, and its UI is tuned to the characteristics of Go traces.
    • Install: A Nix flake is provided. Otherwise you build honnef.co/go/gotraceui/cmd/gotraceui yourself; no distro packages yet.
    • Docs: Manuals for the latest release and the development version at gotraceui.dev.
    • Tech: Built with Gio. Packagers should pass -X gioui.org/app.ID=co.honnef.Gotraceui.
    • License: MIT for code and CC BY-SA 4.0 for the manual.
    • Known issue: Out-of-order timestamps in runtime/trace (golang/go#16755).

    Takeaway: When you need to study goroutine scheduling, GC pauses or blocking in a Go trace, try this before fighting the browser-based go tool trace UI.

  • tint: slog.Handler That Writes Tinted Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: tint, by lmittmann, is a zero-dependency slog.Handler that writes colorized logs, with output inspired by zerolog.ConsoleWriter and slog.TextHandler.

    • Install: go get github.com/lmittmann/tint.
    • Usage: slog.New(tint.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr, &tint.Options{Level: slog.LevelDebug, TimeFormat: time.Kitchen})).
    • Options: tint.Options is a drop-in replacement for slog.HandlerOptions, including ReplaceAttr.
    • Customization: Add a custom TRACE level, drop the time attribute, or color errors with tint.Attr(9, a).
    • Terminal detection: Colors are on by default. Set NoColor: !isatty.IsTerminal(w.Fd()) using go-isatty.
    • Windows: The README has a section on enabling color support on Windows.

    Takeaway: A simple way to get readable, colored dev logs from log/slog while keeping JSON or text handlers for production.

  • AWS KMS Threat Model
    summary

    TL;DR: Costas Kourmpoglou (Airwalk Reply) builds a threat model for AWS KMS symmetric keys, using attack trees and trust boundaries to compare AWS owned, AWS managed and customer managed keys, BYOK, CloudHSM and HYOK.

    • Key types: AWS owned keys are invisible to you. AWS managed keys are visible, but you cannot edit their policy and CloudTrail does not show their use. Customer managed keys (CMKs) give you policy control and CloudTrail visibility.
    • Hierarchy: A Domain Key stays in the HSM and encrypts the HSM Backed Key (HBK). The HBK derives data keys via GenerateDataKey, which returns a plaintext and an encrypted data key for envelope encryption.
    • Responsibility ladder: AWS shared HSM (standard KMS), then a dedicated HSM (CloudHSM), then your own HSM (HYOK). Customer responsibility grows at each step.
    • Attack tree: Covers threats from physical disk theft to an AWS Region outage. Made with deciduous.app, with diagrams in a public repo.
    • Trust boundaries: Modeled on a Lambda in a VPC encrypting data stored in another AWS service. BYOK moves responsibility for the key material and its availability to the customer.
    • Page title: The page <title> reads “AWS Threat Model”, but the article is specifically the KMS threat model.

    Takeaway: For most workloads, a CMK in standard KMS gives the useful controls (key policy, CloudTrail, revocation). BYOK and HYOK add availability risk that you must own.

  • Zero Trust Access to Private Webapps on AWS ECS with Cloudflare Tunnel
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lancini shows how to reach an admin Flask app running in a private subnet on ECS Fargate through Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare Access, with no public exposure and no VPN, all in Terraform.

    • Motivation: AWS lacks a simple equivalent of GCP Identity-Aware Proxy, and Cognito is less streamlined. The author says the post is not sponsored.
    • Components: Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared opens an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare’s edge) plus Cloudflare Access applications that enforce authentication.
    • Terraform: cloudflare_zero_trust_tunnel_cloudflared with a random_password secret, cloudflare_zero_trust_tunnel_cloudflared_config ingress rules, and a proxied CNAME to <tunnel-UUID>.cfargotunnel.com.
    • Automation gotcha: Cloudflare’s docs focus on manual setup. Per a GitHub issue, the tunnel can run with only the JSON credentials file, which avoids the non-rotatable PEM certificate.
    • AWS side: The tunnel token goes in SSM Parameter Store, images in ECR, and a cloudflared sidecar container runs next to Flask in the ECS task.
    • Code: Published in marco-lancini/utils on GitHub.

    Takeaway: A reusable pattern for exposing internal tools on AWS behind SSO without an ALB or VPN. Check the Terraform resource names against the current Cloudflare provider version.

  • The Old Faithful: Why SSM Parameter Store Still Reigns over Secrets Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: Yan Cui (theburningmonk) argues that SSM Parameter Store is still the better default for most app config and secrets than Secrets Manager, on cost and simplicity, and lists when Secrets Manager is worth it.

    • Cost: Secrets Manager charges $0.40 per secret per month (plus $0.40 per replica) and $0.05 per 10,000 API calls. Standard Parameter Store parameters are free: up to 10,000 per Region, 4 KB each, 40 ops/s.
    • Throughput: Higher Throughput mode raises Parameter Store to 3,000 ops/s at $0.05 per 10,000 calls. Values should be cached, since $5 per million calls adds up.
    • Rotation: Secrets Manager rotation still needs your own Lambda and a four-step process. The author calls that overkill outside RDS, DocumentDB or Redshift credentials.
    • Bundling risk: Per-secret pricing pushes teams to group secrets together, which weakens security.
    • When to use Secrets Manager: Cross-region replication, secrets larger than 8 KB (up to 64 KB), and cross-account sharing through resource policies.
    • Portability: Middleware such as Middy makes it easy to switch later.

    Takeaway: Default to Parameter Store SecureString with caching. Move individual secrets to Secrets Manager only when you need replication, large values or cross-account access.

  • Vault Secrets Operator: A New Method for Kubernetes Integration
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: HashiCorp announced the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO), released as beta alongside Vault 1.13. It is a Kubernetes operator that syncs Vault secrets into native Kubernetes Secrets and can trigger actions such as rolling Deployment restarts when secrets rotate.

    • CRDs: A secret resource defines what to sync and references a VaultAuth. VaultAuth holds the login method, mount, role and ServiceAccount, and points to a VaultConnection.
    • Secret types: Static, dynamic and PKI-based secrets.
    • Auth during beta: Only the Kubernetes auth method. The operator needs read and create access to the referenced ServiceAccount to mint short-lived tokens.
    • Positioning: Unlike the agent injector (vault-k8s sidecar) or vault-csi-provider, apps consume native Secrets with no code changes.
    • Observability: A Prometheus metrics endpoint, with a Grafana dashboard planned for GA.
    • Source caveat: A Vercel browser check blocked curl. The summary is from WebFetch’s extracted text, which still worked, so details may be incomplete.

    Takeaway: VSO is HashiCorp’s answer to External Secrets for Vault-only shops. Confirm it is now GA and check its supported auth methods before choosing it.

  • ToBeReviewedBot: GitHub App to Watch for PRs Merged Without a Reviewer Approving
    summary

    TL;DR: ToBeReviewedBot was Tailscale’s GitHub App that opened an audit-trail issue whenever a PR was merged without approval, supporting a SOC 2 control that allowed emergency merges with review afterwards. It is now retired and archived.

    • Original workflow: Branch protection required PRs but not approvals. Within minutes of an unapproved merge, the bot filed an issue with a distinctive title that required follow-up review.
    • Approval heuristics: Merging someone else’s PR counted as approval, and so did an “LGTM” comment.
    • Why retired: Tailscale says growth across timezones made “nobody available to review” unlikely. Unilateral changes were a security risk, and the exception was never used for the night-time on-call case it was built for.
    • Other costs: False positives from accidental early merges, and friction in annual audits because the control was unusual.
    • Outcome: Tailscale rewrote its change control to always require approval before merge.
    • Repo status: Archived April 29, 2026, with a “no longer being developed” warning.

    Takeaway: The README is a useful case study: break-glass merge exceptions often cost more in audit and security risk than they save. Prefer required reviews with a fast emergency reviewer rotation.

  • How to Use Amazon GuardDuty and AWS WAF v2 to Automatically Block Suspicious Hosts
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog pattern that sends GuardDuty findings through EventBridge to a Lambda function, which adds the suspicious host’s IP to AWS WAF v2 IP sets and VPC network ACL deny entries, then emails an alert.

    • Flow: GuardDuty finding, then an EventBridge rule, then a Lambda function that updates the WAF web ACL IP sets and subnet NACLs, then an SNS email.
    • Deployment: A CloudFormation template (guarddutytoacl.template), plus Lambda zips guardduty_to_acl_lambda_wafv2.zip and prune_old_entries_wafv2.zip, from the amazon-guardduty-waf-acl GitHub repo, uploaded to a private S3 bucket.
    • Cleanup: A separate prune function removes old block entries.
    • Testing: Use the gd2acl_test_event.json test event, then confirm the NACL entry, WAF IP set entry and SNS email.
    • Region limit: The example only works in us-east-1 because it uses CloudFront and web ACLs.
    • Framing: Ties into the directive, preventive, detective and responsive controls of the AWS Security Incident Response Guide.

    Takeaway: A simple automated response loop. Remember NACLs have low rule limits and IP blocking is easy to evade, so treat it as a speed bump while you investigate.

  • AWS Cost Anomaly Detection Now Automatically Configured for All New Cost Explorer Users
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (March 27, 2023): new Cost Explorer users automatically get Cost Anomaly Detection with a default service monitor and a daily email summary.

    • Default setup: An AWS services monitor plus a daily email subscription to the account’s primary email.
    • Alert threshold: Fires when actual spend is over $100 and more than 40% above expected spend.
    • Scope: Standalone accounts and management accounts that enable Cost Explorer on or after March 27, 2023.
    • Opt-out: Through the console or API.
    • Availability: All commercial Regions except GovCloud, at no extra cost.

    Takeaway: Existing accounts did not get this automatically. Check that a monitor exists and route alerts to a team channel, not just the root email.

  • AWS Resilience Hub Adds Support for Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (March 23, 2023): AWS Resilience Hub can now assess Amazon EKS clusters and recommend resilience improvements.

    • Onboarding: Add clusters directly or through CloudFormation, Terraform, Resource Groups or Service Catalog AppRegistry.
    • Scope: One or more clusters across Regions, with one or more namespaces each, for single-Region and cross-Region assessments.
    • What it inspects: Deployments, replicas, ReplicationControllers and pods. Supports stateless EKS workloads.
    • Also added: Assessment of EFS replication and AZ configuration, S3 Multi-Region Access Points, S3 Replication Time Control, and AWS Backup point-in-time recovery for S3.

    Takeaway: A quick way to get a second opinion on EKS workload redundancy. It only covers stateless workloads, so stateful sets still need your own review.

  • Managing etcd Database Size on Amazon EKS Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog post on why EKS clusters can hit etcd’s 8 GB database limit, how to monitor it, and how to find and clean up what is filling it. The post has been updated since 2023.

    • Limit: EKS provisions 8 GB. Enforcement uses etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_use_in_bytes, not the physical file size metric (apiserver_storage_size_bytes since EKS 1.28).
    • Failure mode: When the limit is exceeded, etcd raises a no-space alarm and the cluster becomes read-only, rejecting creates and scaling.
    • Why it grows: MVCC keeps a full copy of each object for every revision, so frequent patches (e.g. scheduler status updates on pending pods) inflate it.
    • Detection: Search EKS audit logs with Logs Insights: filter @logStream like /kube-apiserver-audit/ | filter @message like /mvcc: database space exceeded/.
    • Find culprits: kubectl get --raw=/metrics | grep apiserver_storage_objects | awk '$2>100' | sort -g -k 2 (use etcd_object_count before 1.22).
    • Updates: An October 2023 update says EKS now runs automatic compaction and defragmentation recovery. Too many live objects still needs cleanup or EKS Provisioned Control Plane.

    Takeaway: Alert on the in-use etcd metric and on object counts by type. Runaway CRDs, Events or Secrets from controllers are the usual cause.

  • Simplify Service-to-Service Connectivity, Security, and Monitoring with Amazon VPC Lattice: Now Generally Available
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS News Blog GA announcement (signed by Danilo) for Amazon VPC Lattice, an application-layer service network that connects, secures and monitors service-to-service traffic across VPCs and accounts.

    • New at GA: Custom domain names with matching TLS certificates, ALB and NLB as target types, IPv6 for IP targets, and the AWS Gateway API Controller for Kubernetes.
    • Demo app: An Order service (Lambda) calls Inventory (ECS behind an NLB in a dual-stack VPC), Delivery (ECS behind an ALB) and Payment (EC2), across accounts and overlapping CIDRs.
    • Auth policies: IAM-style policies on vpc-lattice-svcs:Invoke, scoped by path and conditioned on vpc-lattice-svcs:RequestMethod, e.g. GET-only on /stock.
    • Health checks: Lattice does not add its own health checks for ALB targets; it relies on the ALB’s.
    • Regions at GA: Ohio, N. Virginia, Oregon, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo and Ireland.
    • Pricing: Per provisioned service-hour, per GB processed, and per request, with the first 300,000 requests each hour free.

    Takeaway: Consider Lattice when cross-account service calls and overlapping CIDRs make Transit Gateway plus PrivateLink painful. Model its pricing for chatty services first.

  • Scaling Kubernetes to 2,500 Nodes
    summary

    TL;DR: OpenAI’s 2018 engineering post on the problems hit while growing a Kubernetes cluster on Azure past 2,500 nodes for deep learning research, and the fixes for each.

    • etcd latency: At about 500 nodes, etcd on network SSDs used only about 10% of its IOPS because of 2 ms write latency. Moving etcd to local temp SSD cut latency to 200 us.
    • API load: Past 1,000 nodes, Fluentd and Datadog agents polling the apiservers caused more than 500 MB/s of etcd reads. They reduced polling and moved Events to a separate etcd via --etcd-servers-overrides.
    • etcd quota: Hitting the 2 GB default caused cascading node failures, and the autoscaler tried to terminate all workers. They raised --quota-backend-bytes and added an autoscaler check against terminating more than 50% of the cluster.
    • Scheduling: A bin-packing policy (MostRequestedPriority) put 10+ KubeDNS pods on some nodes and exceeded Azure’s ~200 QPS per-VM DNS limit. Fixed with pod anti-affinity.
    • Image pulls: --serialize-image-pulls=false (which needed overlay2), Docker root on local SSD, --image-pull-progress-deadline of 30 minutes, max-concurrent-downloads of 10, and preloading the gcr.io pause image to avoid per-IP quota.
    • Networking: Flannel pods maxed out at about 2 Gbit/s against 10-15 Gbit/s host to host. The post covers ways around this and also ARP cache issues.
    • Source caveat: openai.com returned 403 to direct fetches. This is based on a Wayback Machine copy. The post dates from January 2018, not 2023.

    Takeaway: Many of these lessons still apply: put etcd on low-latency disk, isolate Events, watch agents that poll the apiserver, and cap autoscaler blast radius.

  • helmify: Create Helm Charts from Kubernetes YAML
    summary

    TL;DR: Helmify, by arttor, is a Go CLI that converts Kubernetes YAML manifests or kustomize output into a Helm chart. It was designed mainly for packaging Kubernetes operators but works more generally.

    • Pipe input: cat my-app.yaml | helmify mychart creates a mychart/ chart directory.
    • File input: helmify -f /my_directory mychart, with -r for recursive scans and multiple -f flags allowed.
    • Kustomize: kustomize build | helmify mychart.
    • Operator projects: Add a helm target to an Operator-SDK or Kubebuilder Makefile that pipes $(KUSTOMIZE) build config/default | $(HELMIFY), then run make helm.
    • Compatibility: Supports Helm >= v3.6.0, and only a listed set of supported Kubernetes object kinds.

    Takeaway: Handy for a first chart from existing manifests, especially for operators. Expect to clean up the generated values.yaml and templates by hand.

  • You Broke Reddit: The Pi-Day Outage
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Reddit’s engineering postmortem of its March 14, 2023 (“Pi Day”) outage, caused by a Kubernetes 1.23 to 1.24 upgrade on one of its oldest production clusters, which broke pod networking.

    • Trigger: Kubernetes 1.24 removed the node-role.kubernetes.io/master label in favor of node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.
    • Root cause: Calico route reflectors were selected with the old master label. After the upgrade the selector matched no nodes, route distribution failed, and pods across the cluster could no longer reach each other.
    • Snowflake config: Secondary summaries say the Calico setup was hand-configured and unique to that cluster, so testing on other clusters missed it.
    • Recovery: Kubernetes downgrades are not supported, so the team restored the cluster from backup. The cause was only found hours after the restore.
    • Duration: Secondary sources put it at about 314 minutes, roughly five hours.
    • Source caveat: Reddit blocked all fetch attempts, so this summary is based on secondary summaries (an iximiuz Labs course page and search results), not the original post.

    Takeaway: Grep every selector, policy and addon config for platform-owned labels before a Kubernetes upgrade, and rehearse full-cluster restores, not just backups.

  • copacetic: CLI Tool for Directly Patching Container Images Using Vulnerability Scanner Reports
    summary

    TL;DR: Copacetic (copa) is a Go CLI built on BuildKit that patches OS-package vulnerabilities directly in existing container images, optionally driven by a Trivy scan report, without a full rebuild.

    • How: Adds a single patch layer of updated OS packages to the image instead of rebuilding from the Dockerfile.
    • Why: Vulnerabilities inherited deep in base images, or in third-party images you do not maintain, often cannot wait for upstream releases to meet your security SLAs.
    • Benefits: Lets people other than the image publisher, such as DevSecOps engineers, patch images. It keeps existing layer hashes and caching and cuts storage and transfer costs.
    • Report-driven: Takes vulnerability scanner output such as Trivy’s to target specific packages, or updates all packages.
    • Newer support: The current README covers Ubuntu Chiseled images (/var/lib/chisel/manifest.wall, --chisel-release) and was verified with Trivy v0.69.3 in July 2026. This is far newer than the 2023 link.

    Takeaway: A useful break-glass tool for patching third-party or legacy images quickly. It only fixes OS packages, so app dependencies still need a real rebuild.

  • k8sgpt: Scan Kubernetes Clusters, Diagnose and Triage Issues in Simple English with AI
    summary

    TL;DR: K8sGPT scans Kubernetes clusters with built-in analyzers based on SRE experience, then uses an LLM to explain and triage the problems it finds in plain English. It is now a CNCF Sandbox project.

    • Analyzers: Codified checks for common workload problems. They are tested on CNCF-conformant clusters up to N-2 Kubernetes releases.
    • AI backends: OpenAI by default. The README now lists Azure, Cohere, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini and local models such as LocalAI.
    • CLI flow: brew install k8sgpt, k8sgpt generate (opens the OpenAI API key page), k8sgpt auth add, k8sgpt filters, then analyze.
    • Operator: k8sgpt-operator for continuous in-cluster monitoring, integrating with Prometheus and Alertmanager.
    • Security: Can connect to scanners such as Trivy to triage CVEs.
    • Source caveat: The homepage is mostly JavaScript, so details come from a Wayback Machine copy of the homepage and the GitHub README (k8sgpt-ai/k8sgpt, v0.4.41 at the time of fetching).

    Takeaway: Good for quick triage on unfamiliar clusters. Run it against a local model if sending cluster state to a hosted LLM is a concern.

  • kubectl-ai: kubectl Plugin to Generate and Apply Kubernetes Manifests Using OpenAI GPT
    summary

    TL;DR: kubectl-ai, by sozercan, is a kubectl plugin that generates Kubernetes manifests from a natural-language prompt using OpenAI GPT and, after confirmation, applies them to the cluster.

    • Motivation: The author wanted to stop hunting for random manifests while doing dev and test work.
    • Install: Homebrew (brew tap sozercan/kubectl-ai ...), Krew (kubectl krew install kubectl-ai/kubectl-ai), or a release binary.
    • Backends: OpenAI API key, Azure OpenAI (with AZURE_OPENAI_MAP for deployment names), or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as AIKit or LocalAI.
    • Config: OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME, OPENAI_ENDPOINT.
    • Local example: docker run -d --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/sozercan/llama3.1:8b as a CPU-only local endpoint.
    • Safety: --require-confirmation (or REQUIRE_CONFIRMATION) controls whether you are prompted before applying.

    Takeaway: Fine for scaffolding throwaway test manifests. Always review the output before applying it, and never point it at production with confirmation turned off.

  • Announcing the GitHub Actions Extension for VS Code
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub announced the official GitHub Actions extension for VS Code (March 2023). It grew from a community project and is now maintained by GitHub, adding workflow authoring help and run management in the editor.

    • Run management: Monitor, cancel, re-run and manually trigger workflows. Drill down from runs to jobs, steps and logs. A Current Branch view shows results for the checked-out branch.
    • Secrets and variables: List them at org, repo and environment level, and edit repo and environment ones with the right permissions.
    • Authoring: Uses the official Actions schema and a new expressions parser, with syntax highlighting, inline docs, validation and completion.
    • Smart validation: Catches bad job and step references, and knows the event payload shape for each trigger (e.g. a pull_request payload).
    • Referenced actions: Parses inputs and outputs of referenced actions and reusable workflows for completion and validation.
    • Upgrade: Existing community extension installs upgrade automatically.

    Takeaway: Install it to catch broken needs, outputs and expression typos before you push, which cuts down on trial-and-error CI commits.

  • aiac: Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure-as-Code Generator
    summary

    TL;DR: aiac, from Firefly, is a CLI and Go library that asks an LLM to generate IaC templates, config files, CI pipelines, policies, scripts and queries from a short prompt.

    • Providers: OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock and Ollama, with multiple named backends in a config file.
    • IaC examples: aiac terraform for a highly available eks, aiac pulumi golang for an s3 with sns notification, aiac cloudformation for a neptundb.
    • Other outputs: Dockerfiles, Kubernetes manifests, Jenkins and GitHub Actions pipelines, OPA policies (aiac opa policy that enforces readiness probe at k8s deployments), and bash or python utilities.
    • Builders: CLI one-liners (aiac kubectl that gets ExternalIPs of all nodes) and Mongo, Elastic or SQL queries.
    • Usage: Saves output to a file and/or prints it. Runs via Docker or as a library.
    • Repo status: The README covers an upgrade from v4 to v5 with configuration changes, so the 2023 CLI syntax has changed.

    Takeaway: Useful for scaffolding boilerplate. Treat generated Terraform and policies as drafts to review and scan with tools like tfsec or checkov.

  • Automate IAM Credential Reports for Large AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Infrastructure & Automation blog solution that generates IAM credential reports in parallel across every account in a large AWS Organization and collects them into one S3 bucket for auditing.

    • Report contents: All IAM users and the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA devices.
    • Orchestration: An EventBridge rule starts a Step Functions state machine. One Lambda lists account IDs from Organizations, and another assumes a role in each account and generates the report.
    • Cost trick: Step Functions waits 1 minute between status checks instead of keeping a Lambda running, up to 45 cycles, then sends an SNS email on timeout.
    • Cross-account role: Deployed into all member accounts with a CloudFormation StackSet.
    • Deploy: AWS SAM from aws-samples/automating-iam-credential-reports-for-large-aws-organizations, using the root ID (aws organizations list-roots) and org ID (aws organizations describe-organization).
    • Effort: About 15 minutes and about $1, per the post. An alternative deployment stores reports in a separate security account.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to find stale IAM users and keys across many accounts. Prefer the variant that writes to a security or logging account rather than the management account.

  • Exploring Amazon VPC Lattice
    summary

    TL;DR: A One Cloud Please blog post that takes a hands-on look at Amazon VPC Lattice at GA, explaining how it works at the network level and building a Lambda-to-Lambda example in CloudFormation.

    • Mechanism: Unlike PrivateLink, which puts ENIs in your subnets, Lattice exposes services on link-local addresses in 169.254.171.0/24 (plus an IPv6 equivalent).
    • Other link-local endpoints: IMDS at 169.254.169.254, the Route 53 Resolver at .253, ECS task metadata at 169.254.170.2, and Time Sync at .123.
    • Gotcha: Unlike those, Lattice traffic must be allowed by security groups and NACLs. Use the managed prefix list rather than the raw range, since the range may change.
    • Targets: EC2 instances, IPv4 and IPv6 IPs, Lambda functions and ALBs. An EKS target type was in private beta.
    • CloudFormation: Uses AWS::VpcLattice::ServiceNetwork, ServiceNetworkVpcAssociation, Service, Listener (HTTPS 443) and TargetGroup (type LAMBDA). The target group adds the Lambda permission automatically.
    • Routing: Associating the VPC with the service network adds route table entries for the Lattice range.

    Takeaway: Read this before troubleshooting Lattice connectivity. Most “it times out” problems come from security groups not allowing the Lattice prefix list.

  • Welcome to the Jungle: Pentesting AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: A slide deck by Mike Felch (@ustayready, BHIS red team) on a methodology for pentesting AWS in depth and at scale, from scoping and initial access through privilege escalation and data exfiltration.

    • Recon and scanning: ScoutSuite, aws_list_all and the AWS CLI. Verify ScoutSuite findings by hand, since policies can produce false positives.
    • External surface: Elastic IPs, load balancers, RDS endpoints, API Gateway and Beanstalk, scanned with Nmap, GoWitness and Ffuf/Dirbuster. IAM users can be brute-forced because IAM has no lockout.
