    • Lateral movement: Credentials in EC2 user data, Lambda environment variables, CloudFormation parameters, CodeBuild variables and SSM Parameter Store.
    • Privilege escalation: CreatePolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy, PutRolePolicy, SetDefaultPolicyVersion, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, PassRole, plus IMDSv1 abuse and Cognito identity pools.
    • Exfiltration and scale: Public AMIs and EBS snapshots, S3 discovery, ScoutSuite looped over hundreds of accounts with jq, and the author’s Outpost and CloudGPT tools.
    • Source caveat: SlideShare blocked curl. Content is from WebFetch’s text extraction of the slides.

    Takeaway: A compact checklist for AWS assessments. On the defense side, it says block 169.254.169.254 from web apps, avoid PassRole on *, and avoid NotAction with Allow.

  • We Put GPT-4 in Semgrep to Point Out False Positives & Fix Code
    summary

    TL;DR: Bence Nagy (Semgrep, April 2023) describes adding GPT-4 to Semgrep’s cloud service to triage findings as likely false positives before notifying developers, and to suggest autofixes.

    • Problem: SAST false positive rates across vendors are cited at 10-50%, and junior developers struggle to triage alerts.
    • Triage approach: About 3,000 tokens of context (code, rule, PR) go to GPT-4, which explains why a finding is safe, e.g. an obvious placeholder password or an over-broad custom rule.
    • Autofix results: On internal projects, AI fixes were accepted as-is about 40% of the time and were a good starting point another 40%. The goal is 90%+ directly committable.
    • Model chaining: Pairing GPT-4 with code-davinci-edit-001 caused unrelated edits or wrong assumptions, so they settled on GPT-4 alone.
    • Where AI helps: Fixes that depend on local context, and convention rules such as log message formats, which declarative autofix patterns cannot express.
    • Status: Private beta invites were planned from April 6, 2023.

    Takeaway: LLM triage is most useful for noisy custom rules. Keep deterministic rule-based autofixes where they exist, and review AI fixes like any other PR.

  • 69 Ways to Fuck Up Your Deploy
    summary

    TL;DR: Kelly Shortridge and Ryan Petrich wrote a long, deliberately profane list of 69 ways deployments go wrong, grouped into 10 themes plus manual deploys, covering both immediate breakage and traps for later.

    • Themes: Identity Crisis (permissions), Loggers and Monitaurs, Deployment Mismatches, Configuration Tarnation, Statefulness is Hard, Net-not-working, Rolls and Reboots, Disorganized Organization, Business Illogic, The Audacity of Spacetime, and Manual Deploys.
    • #1 Allow all access: allow * hides which services and data an app really uses and widens the blast radius.
    • #2-3 Keys: Plaintext keys, or keys in a KMS that every engineer can read anyway.
    • #4 No authorization on production builds: GitOps setups where any branch push can turn into an accidental production release.
    • Framing: Each item explains the shortcut’s appeal, then the later cost, for both reliability and security.

    Takeaway: Use it as a pre-mortem checklist for your pipeline. Read the themes that match your last incident and see which items you still do.

  • Intro to Forensics in the Cloud: A Container Was Compromised. What’s Next?
    summary

    TL;DR: A Wiz blog introduction to cloud DFIR covering how it differs from endpoint forensics, a cheat sheet of log sources and tools to set up in advance, and a walkthrough of investigating a compromised container.

    • Guiding questions: Initial access point, lateral spread, persistence, impact, and prevention.
    • Cloud vs endpoint: Cloud architecture (VMs, containers, serverless, identities) differs, and attacker goals differ too. Cloud attacks are mostly resource hijacking (e.g. mass EC2 creation) or access to sensitive data.
    • Five sources: Cloud provider audit logs (CloudTrail, GCP Cloud Audit Logs, Azure sign-in, audit, activity and resource logs), VPC flow logs, orchestration logs (Kubernetes audit), workload image snapshots, and runtime events.
    • Gotcha: Traffic to IMDS appears in provider logs, not in VPC flow logs.
    • Preparation: Logs and tooling must exist before the attack, or the investigation has blind spots.

    Takeaway: Check now that CloudTrail, flow logs and Kubernetes audit logs are on and kept long enough, and that you can snapshot a running container’s disk.

  • auth: GitHub Action for Authenticating to Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: google-github-actions/auth is the GitHub Action for authenticating workflows to Google Cloud. Workload Identity Federation (WIF) through GitHub OIDC is preferred over service account key JSON.

    • Three modes: Direct WIF (preferred), WIF through service account impersonation, or a service account key JSON.
    • Usage: Set job permissions: id-token: write (plus contents: read), run checkout first, then google-github-actions/auth@v3 with workload_identity_provider: projects/<num>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool>/providers/<provider>.
    • Gotchas: Add gha-creds-*.json to .gitignore and .dockerignore. gsutil does not use the exported credentials, so use gcloud storage.
    • Token lifetime: GitHub OIDC tokens expire in 5 minutes, so derived credentials do too, per the README at time of writing.
    • Limits: WIF is not supported by the Firebase Admin SDK. The README says this is not an officially supported Google product.
    • Repo status: Now at @v3 on Node 24, newer than the 2023 link.

    Takeaway: Drop exported service account keys from GitHub secrets and switch to direct WIF, scoping the provider’s attribute condition to specific repos and branches.

  • Create a Dry-Run Organization Policy
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud documentation for running organization policies in dry-run mode, where violations are audit-logged but not denied, so you can see the impact of a constraint before enforcing it.

    • Behavior: A dry-run policy is created like a normal one and violations are logged, but the actions go through.
    • Supported constraints: Only custom constraints, managed constraints, and some legacy managed ones (restrict service usage, endpoint usage, TLS versions, TLS cipher suites).
    • Roles: roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin, plus roles/logging.configWriter for aggregated log sinks. Billing must be enabled.
    • Example: Dry-run compute.managed.restrictProtocolForwardingCreationForTypes with value EXTERNAL in the console Dry run tab, or with gcloud org-policies set-policy and a dryRunSpec.
    • Related: The Policy Simulator (“Test changes”) can preview impact too.
    • Page status: The URL now leads to a page titled “Test organization policies”, so the doc has been reorganized since 2023.

    Takeaway: Roll out every new org constraint in dry-run first, and watch the audit logs for a week or so before switching to enforcement.

  • New: Self-Service Provisioning of Terraform Open-Source Configurations with AWS Service Catalog
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS News Blog launch post: AWS Service Catalog can now offer Terraform configurations as products alongside CloudFormation, so end users can self-provision approved Terraform stacks with central governance.

    • Setup: Install the AWS-provided Terraform Reference Engine once in the Service Catalog management account, e.g. ./deploy-tre.sh -r us-east-1.
    • Example product: A main.tf creating a Graviton t4g.large EC2 instance on Amazon Linux 2023, uploaded as a product version.
    • Governance: Hub-and-spoke portfolio sharing from one management account to up to thousands of user accounts, with least-privilege provisioning and tag governance.
    • User experience: End users provision CloudFormation or Terraform products the same way, in a single action.
    • Post update: The post now notes that Terraform moved to the Business Source License (now “Terraform Community”), and the “Terraform open source” product type is now called “External”.

    Takeaway: Useful if platform teams already have Terraform modules and want a self-service catalog without rewriting them in CloudFormation. Use the “External” product type now.

  • Announcing Policy Validations During Synthesis Time with AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK)
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS What’s New post (April 3, 2023): AWS CDK can run policy-as-code validation plugins automatically after synthesis, starting with a CloudFormation Guard plugin.

    • Plugin: CfnGuardValidator runs AWS CloudFormation Guard rules against the synthesized templates.
    • Built-in rules: Ships with a predefined set of AWS Control Tower proactive controls.
    • Report: An allow or deny summary, with misconfiguration details, root-cause analysis and mitigation suggestions for each violation.
    • Extensible: You can write plugins for other tools, with KICS, OPA and Checkov named as examples.
    • Benefit: Feedback during development rather than at deploy time, so fewer failed deployments.

    Takeaway: Add the Guard validator to CDK apps so policy violations fail cdk synth locally and in CI, before CloudFormation or Control Tower hooks reject them.

  • The Smallest Go Binary (5KB)
    summary

    TL;DR: TotallyGamerJet describes shrinking a macOS arm64 Go binary from hundreds of KB to 5 KB, first with the Go assembler and linker directly and then by stripping the Go runtime with go build -overlay.

    • Baseline: Usual size flags only get an empty main down to 863 KB.
    • Assembly attempt: A hello world in Go assembler. GLOBL needs the RODATA flag (8), and assembling needs -p main. Linking alone with go tool link -E _start fails with “not package main”.
    • Runtime replacement: Uses an -overlay JSON file to swap the Go 1.20.1 runtime source files for empty ones.
    • Obstacle: Removing everything triggers linker errors such as “unreachable sym in relocation”. Compiler and linker share metadata (moduledata), so parts must stay.
    • Scope: All examples are macOS arm64 only. The motivation was writing a C compiler in Go.

    Takeaway: A fun deep dive into how tightly Go’s compiler, linker and runtime are coupled. It is not a practical size-optimization recipe for production binaries.

  • coder: Provision Remote Development Environments via Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Coder is a self-hosted platform for cloud development environments, defined as Terraform templates (VMs, Kubernetes pods or Docker containers), connected over a WireGuard tunnel and shut down automatically when idle.

    • Templates: Workspaces are written in Terraform and can target EC2, Kubernetes, Docker and more.
    • Cost control: Idle workspaces shut down automatically.
    • Quickstart: curl -fsSL https://coder.com/install.sh | sh, then coder server and open http://localhost:3000.
    • Production: coder server --postgres-url <url> --access-url <url> with PostgreSQL 13+. Without these flags it uses a built-in DB and a *.try.coder.app URL.
    • Repo status: The README now also promotes “Coder Agents” and an AI Gateway: AI coding agents running on your own infrastructure, with no LLM keys in workspaces and central audit and cost tracking. This is newer than the 2023 link.
    • Licensing: Some features sit in a Premium tier.

    Takeaway: Good fit when you want reproducible, ephemeral dev environments using the Terraform skills the team already has. Budget for running Postgres and the control plane yourself.

31.03.2023

  • Kali Purple: Leveling the Playing Field
    summary

    TL;DR: The Kali Purple wiki home page describes Kali Purple as the Kali team’s effort to make defensive, SOC-grade security tooling as accessible as Kali Linux made offensive tooling.

    • Tooling: Over 100 defensive tools, including Arkime, CyberChef, Elasticsearch SIEM, GVM, TheHive, Malcolm, Suricata and Zeek, plus the usual Kali tools.
    • ISOs: Kali Purple, plus Malcolm and Hedgehog builds based on Kali.
    • Menu structure: Organized by the NIST CSF functions Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
    • SOC-in-a-box: A reference architecture for learning, SOC analysis and threat-hunting practice, control testing, and blue, red or purple team exercises.
    • Kali Autopilot: An attack script builder for automated attacks used in blue-team exercises.
    • Community: A Kali Purple Hub for sharing practice pcaps and Autopilot scripts, plus Discord channels.
    • Source caveat: The GitLab page needs JavaScript, so content was read through the GitLab wiki API.

    Takeaway: A fast way to stand up a home lab SIEM and IDS stack for purple-team practice. It is a learning platform, not a hardened production SOC.

  • BlueHat 2023
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The YouTube playlist of session recordings from Microsoft’s BlueHat 2023 security conference, run by MSRC in Redmond, WA on February 8-9, 2023.

    • Publisher: Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC). The playlist description reads “BlueHat 2023 Conference, Feb 8-9 2023, Redmond WA”.
    • Size: A third-party blog (kurtsh.com, March 2023) says the playlist has 21 session recordings.
    • Speakers: MSRC’s announcement lists 27 security thought leaders, with keynotes by Charlie Bell, Mark Russinovich and Aanchal Gupta. Not every session appears in the playlist.
    • Not to confuse: MSRC also ran a separate BlueHat in October 2023.
    • Source caveat: YouTube served only the playlist title and description to scripted requests, so individual video titles could not be listed. Details come from search results (the MSRC blog and kurtsh.com).

    Takeaway: Worth browsing for Microsoft-ecosystem security research. Pick talks from MSRC’s BlueHat 2023 blog post, since the playlist itself has no agenda.

  • DevSecOps: Collection and Roadmap for Everyone Who Wants DevSecOps
    summary

    TL;DR: hahwul/DevSecOps is a community-maintained roadmap and curated link collection for learning and putting DevSecOps into practice, organized by SDLC phase.

    • Structure: A visual roadmap image, a Tools section (SAST, DAST, secret management, threat modeling and more), and Resources by phase: Overview, Design, Develop, Build, Test, Deploy, Operate and Monitor.
    • Test phase examples: ZAP with GitHub Actions, GitLab DAST, Nuclei as a GitHub Action, and OWASP DevSecOps Verification Standard DAST levels.
    • Deploy phase examples: CIS Benchmarks and Kubernetes DevSecOps guidance.
    • Extras: A dedicated “Security of CICD” section, plus awesome lists and other roadmaps.
    • Usage guidance: The README says you can jump to any section rather than reading it front to back. Contributions are welcome.

    Takeaway: A good starting index for building a DevSecOps learning plan or picking tools per pipeline stage. Check link freshness, since curated lists go stale.

  • noseyparker: Find Secrets and Sensitive Information in Textual Data and Git History
    summary

    TL;DR: Nosey Parker is Praetorian’s Rust CLI for finding secrets in files, directories, GitHub and Git history. It is now officially retired and replaced by Praetorian’s Titus, and the repo is archived.

    • Rules: 188 high-precision regex rules tuned with feedback from security engineers.
    • Noise reduction: Deduplicates matches of the same secret, cutting review work by 10-1000x or more, per the README.
    • Performance: Scans at GB/s on multicore systems and has handled inputs up to 20 TB in engagements.
    • Workflow: scan, then report, then triage. Install with brew install noseyparker or ghcr.io/praetorian-inc/noseyparker.
    • Platforms: Linux and macOS on x86_64 and aarch64. No native Windows build; WSL1 works.
    • Repo status: Archived April 24, 2026. The README points to praetorian-inc/titus as the successor.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt Nosey Parker for new pipelines. Evaluate Titus, or alternatives such as gitleaks or TruffleHog, and keep its dedup-first triage idea.

  • Temporary Policy Exceptions in Kubernetes with Kyverno
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF guest post by Chip Zoller (Nirmata) showing how to make Kyverno 1.9 Policy Exceptions expire automatically by combining them with cleanup policies.

    • Policy Exceptions: New alpha feature in Kyverno 1.9 that decouples exclusions from the policy itself, so a separate team can request an exception without editing the policy.
    • Enabling: Must be turned on with a flag; --exceptionNamespace restricts where exceptions can be created, otherwise they are cluster-wide. Gate creation with RBAC at minimum.
    • Validate the exceptions: Since a PolicyException is a custom resource, Kyverno validate rules can stop overly broad exceptions (e.g. exempting all Pods).
    • Expiry mechanism: A generate rule creates a ClusterCleanupPolicy when an exception appears, scheduled with cron, which deletes the exception after four hours in the example.
    • RBAC: Extra ClusterRoles (via aggregation) let Kyverno create clustercleanuppolicies and let the cleanup controller list and delete policyexceptions.

    Takeaway: Useful pattern for break-glass exceptions, such as a troubleshooting Pod needing host namespaces. Check current Kyverno docs, as these features were alpha in 1.9.

  • Security Certification Roadmap
    summary

    TL;DR: Paul Jerimy’s Security Certification Roadmap is a large chart of security certifications arranged by domain and by level from beginner to expert, often used to plan certification paths.

    • Domains: Columns include Communication and Network Security, IAM, Security Architecture and Engineering, Asset Security, Security and Risk Management, Assessment and Testing, Software Security and Security Operations.
    • Sub-tracks: Cloud/SysOps, *nix, ICS/IoT, GRC, Forensics, Incident Handling, Penetration Testing and Exploitation.
    • Scale: “481 certifications listed | July 2024”, so the page has been updated well past 2023.
    • Range: From entry level (e.g. Security+, eJPT, SC-900) up to expert level (OSEE, CCIE Security, GSE, CISSP concentrations).
    • Project status: The author’s July 2024 update says a JavaScript web app version is in progress. Prints are sold to fund hosting, with an affiliate disclosure.

    Takeaway: Use it to see where a certification sits relative to others in your target domain. Treat the placement as one practitioner’s opinion, not an industry standard.

  • Create a Console Session from IAM Credentials
    summary

    TL;DR: A Hacking The Cloud technique page by Nick Frichette showing how to turn AWS IAM credentials into an AWS Management Console session, mainly with aws-vault.

    • Temporary keys: With ASIA... credentials (for example from an EC2 instance) no extra IAM permissions are needed; run aws-vault login.
    • Long-term keys: With AKIA... credentials you need sts:GetFederationToken or sts:AssumeRole to mint temporary credentials first, e.g. aws sts get-federation-token --name blah.
    • Link only: The -s flag prints the console sign-in URL to stdout instead of opening a browser.
    • Related tools: aws_consoler and Pacu are listed as alternatives.
    • Detection: The page warns this is noisy: a ConsoleLogin CloudTrail event, an odd user-agent (a CI/CD role suddenly using Firefox) and a large volume of CloudTrail logs.
    • In the wild: It cites a CrowdStrike report on an intrusion campaign against telco and BPO companies that used this technique.

    Takeaway: Useful during assessments when the console is faster than the CLI. Defenders should alert on ConsoleLogin events from role sessions that normally only use the API.

  • Vault 1.13 Adds Kubernetes Operator, MFA Improvements, and More
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp’s March 2023 announcement of Vault 1.13 GA, headlined by the Vault Secrets Operator beta for Kubernetes plus MFA, Agent and PKI improvements.

    • Vault Secrets Operator (beta): Syncs Vault secrets natively into Kubernetes Secrets without sidecars or the CSI provider; it was not shipped at GA and was scheduled for late March.
    • Vault Agent: One Agent can fetch secrets from multiple namespaces, read config from multiple files, expose a metrics-only listener role, and run without auth methods (testing only).
    • MFA: Login MFA providers can be referenced by name instead of UUID, and passcode handling is consistent across CLI and API.
    • Auth and secrets engines: Azure auth works from Azure Functions and App Service and gains rotate-root; the Google Cloud secrets engine can use service account impersonation to avoid Google’s 10-key limit.
    • PKI: Cross-cluster CRL and OCSP revocation for shared PKI mounts, and new CLI health checks for CA, CRL validity, roles and unsafe parameters.
    • Crypto: KMIP adds PKCS#11 operations (sign/verify, RNG, MAC); managed Transit keys can offload operations to an HSM or cloud KMS.
    • Alpha/preview: Event-based notifications over a WebSocket API (alpha) and an HCP link for self-managed clusters (private beta).

    Takeaway: The Secrets Operator is the main reason to look at 1.13 if you run Vault with Kubernetes. Check the current operator docs, since it was beta at this release.

  • ssm-helpers: Help Manage AWS Systems Manager with Helpers
    summary

    TL;DR: ssm-helpers is a Go CLI from Disney Streaming that wraps AWS Systems Manager for interactive sessions and fleet-wide command runs.

    • ssm session: Interactive shell on an instance through Session Manager, positioned as an ssh and cssh replacement.
    • ssm run: Runs a command on many instances selected by tags or names, positioned as a replacement for mco and knife.
    • Install: brew install disneystreaming/tap/ssm-helpers, Docker images on the GitHub package registry, or release binaries for Windows, macOS and Linux.
    • Docker tip: The README uses --detach-keys 'ctrl-e,e' so session detach keys do not clash with tmux.
    • Internals: Written in Go with aws-sdk-go and a fork of gomux; the older go-ssmhelpers library was merged in.

    Takeaway: A practical way to drop SSH keys and bastions in favor of SSM while keeping multi-host ergonomics. Check how recently it was maintained before adopting.

  • cloudlist: Tool for Listing Assets from Multiple Cloud Providers
    summary

    TL;DR: cloudlist is a ProjectDiscovery Go tool that lists assets (hosts, IPs, services) from many cloud providers into one inventory for attack surface management.

    • Purpose: Aimed at blue teams to keep a centralized list of assets across clouds with little configuration.
    • Providers: AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare, Fastly, Heroku, Hetzner, Linode, Scaleway, OpenStack, Alibaba, Namecheap, Consul, Nomad, Terraform state and custom sources.
    • Services: Covers things like ec2, eks, ecs, lambda, s3, route53, elb/alb, cloudfront, gke, cloud-run and apigateway.
    • Auth: Keyless support (AWS IRSA and instance profiles, GCP workload identity); -ad auto-discovers providers from environment credentials.
    • Output: -host or -ip only, -json, -o file, -silent for piping into other ProjectDiscovery tools; -ep excludes private IPs.
    • Config: Provider credentials live in ~/.config/cloudlist/provider-config.yaml.

    Takeaway: A cheap starting point for an external asset inventory. Pipe its output into scanners such as httpx or nuclei for continuous checks.

  • What Are AWS Managed Policies?
    summary

    TL;DR: The landing page of the AWS Managed Policy Reference Guide, explaining what AWS managed policies are and how each policy’s reference page is structured.

    • Definition: Standalone policies created and maintained by AWS for common use cases; you cannot edit their permissions.
    • Least privilege caveat: AWS states they may not be least privilege for your case and recommends narrower customer managed policies.
    • Updates: When AWS changes a managed policy, every attached user, group and role is affected; changes usually follow new services or API operations.
    • Policy types: Standard AWS managed, job function, service-linked role (e.g. AmazonRDSPreviewServiceRolePolicy) and service role (e.g. AWSControlTowerServiceRolePolicy) policies.
    • Reference page contents: Attachability, type, creation and edit time, ARN, policy version and the full JSON document.
    • Deprecation: AWS can deprecate managed policies; the guide tracks deprecated ones.

    Takeaway: Use the reference to read the actual JSON before attaching a managed policy. Watch policy versions, because AWS-side changes can silently widen access.

  • Modern Data Protection Architecture on Amazon S3: Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of an AWS Storage Blog series (February 2023) on keeping immutable copies of critical S3 data in an isolated second account using S3 Replication and Object Lock.

    • Replication: Same-Region Replication to a bucket in another account; S3 Batch Replication covers existing objects. Replicate only business-critical data to limit cost.
    • Object Lock: WORM retention; Governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions, Compliance mode cannot be changed even by root. The demo uses Governance for 7 days and recommends Compliance with 7, 15 or 30 days in production.
    • Encryption: SSE-KMS with S3 Bucket Keys and separate customer managed KMS keys per account; the post says Bucket Keys can cut SSE-KMS request costs by up to 99%.
    • Bucket hardening: Versioning on, ACLs disabled, public access blocked; replicas land in S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
    • Automated response: A CloudWatch alarm on abnormal PutRequests triggers EventBridge and a Lambda that stops replication during suspected ransomware.
    • Update: Since November 20, 2023, Object Lock can be enabled on existing buckets.
    • Caveat: Compliance-mode replicas cannot be deleted before retention ends, which adds storage cost.

    Takeaway: A native, low-tooling ransomware defense for S3. Pair it with Part 2’s retrieval process and test restores.

  • Disaster Recovery When Using Crossplane for Infrastructure Provisioning on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Open Source Blog post (March 2023), written with input from Autodesk, DKB, Nike and Upbound, on disaster recovery when AWS infrastructure is managed by Crossplane on EKS, using Velero for backups.

    • Cluster loss: Velero backs up Crossplane composite, sub- and managed resources and restores them into a new cluster, preserving owner references, states and external names.
    • Backup procedure: Scale the AWS provider deployment to zero before backup so it does not reconcile, then scale it back up after restore.
    • Restore pitfalls: Do not overwrite the aws-auth ConfigMap, pause GitOps sync so Git does not clobber restored objects, and back up ProviderConfig objects and their secrets.
    • Provider upgrade failure: Roll back to the previous ProviderRevision; fall back to Velero migration if that fails.
    • Region impairment: Managed resources carry a required region field, so manifests must be rewritten (ideally with a mutating webhook) and stateful data restored from snapshots or replicas.
    • Regional differences: It notes us-west-2 has 4 AZs and us-east-1 has 6, so compositions may need per-region variants.

    Takeaway: A Crossplane control cluster becomes critical infrastructure. Plan and rehearse its backup and restore like any other DR target.

  • 73,000 Pods a Day: Lessons from Misadventures in Multi-Tenant
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF-uploaded KubeCon session (about 37 minutes, published November 2022) by Shane Corbett (AWS) and Wil Reed (Acquia) on lessons from running a large multi-tenant Kubernetes platform.

    • Scale: The title refers to 73,000 pods a day on a multi-tenant application.
    • Research effort: The speakers say they spent over two years studying Linux kernel performance material, tuning obscure control plane settings and building custom monitoring dashboards.
    • Core claim: There is a large gap between CKA-level training and what it takes to run large multi-tenant workloads in production.
    • Best practices questioned: They present evidence that some practices they believed were best practices were what held them back most.
    • Related work: Shane Corbett also wrote the AWS post on CPU limits and throttling in this archive, which covers similar ground.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the YouTube title and description only, not the full talk.

    Takeaway: Worth watching if you run shared clusters at scale. Pair it with the CPU limits post for the concrete metrics.

  • Using Prometheus to Avoid Disasters with Kubernetes CPU Limits
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog post by Shane Corbett (September 2022) explaining that Kubernetes CPU limits are CFS time quotas, not cores, and how to use cAdvisor/Prometheus metrics to size them and spot throttling.

    • Mechanics: A 1000m limit means one CPU-second per second, enforced per 100 ms period; a 500m limit showed a 50 ms cpu.cfs_quota_us.
    • Multi-thread trap: A 1-core limit across four busy threads gives each 25 ms per 100 ms period, so they lose 300 ms per period to throttling.
    • Latency example: A 100 ms single-threaded task with a 400m limit took 220 ms and was throttled in two of three periods.
    • Metrics: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total vs container_cpu_cfs_periods_total, container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total, container_cpu_usage_seconds_total.
    • PromQL: topk(3, max by (pod, container)(rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total{image!=""}[$__rate_interval]))) / 10 gives throttled time per period.
    • Sizing rule: Multiply per-period throttle by 10 to estimate extra limit needed (200 ms becomes 2000m).
    • Caveats: Bursty, latency-sensitive apps are poor candidates for limits; cpu.cfs_burst_us was not yet available in Kubernetes when written.

    Takeaway: Graph throttled seconds before trusting a limit that looks generous. Treat limits as a safety net, not a sizing tool.

  • Why and When Do You Need Argo CD?
    summary

    TL;DR: An mkdev article by Kirill Shirinkin (2023) arguing that Argo CD suits multi-cluster platforms run by strong Kubernetes teams, and is often unnecessary complexity for simple app deployment.

    • Scope: Argo CD only syncs Kubernetes manifests; it is not a job runner like GitHub Actions or Jenkins, so it cannot lint, build or test.
    • Good fit: Many clusters, many operators (monitoring, ingress, secrets) and multi-tenancy with RBAC and SSO.
    • Poor fit: A handful of apps across dev, stage and prod, or small teams where developers also run the cluster.
    • Prerequisites: Working CI that tests, packages and pushes images; teams with a well-understood deploy tool should extend it instead.
    • Image version problem: Code-only changes do not trigger syncs; fixes are writing the image version to Git or using Argo CD Image Updater (pre-1.0 at the time).
    • Repo layout: A separate config repo updated by CI is called best practice for pull-based GitOps, at the cost of more repos and pipeline complexity.
    • Alternatives: Flux CD and Rancher Fleet fit the same reasoning.

    Takeaway: Adopt Argo CD for platform-level fleet management, not because GitOps is fashionable. Settle the image-promotion flow before rollout.

  • Kubernetes PR: In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling Feature
    summary

    TL;DR: The Kubernetes pull request by vinaykul that implements in-place Pod vertical scaling (KEP 1287), opened June 2021 and merged for the v1.27 milestone.

    • Feature: Container resources become mutable for cpu and memory, so a pod can be resized without restart.
    • New fields: Per-container resizePolicy, allocatedResources and resources in container status, and a pod-level resize status (InProgress, Deferred, Infeasible).
    • Scope: API changes, CRI API changes, core kubelet implementation and E2E tests (test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go).
    • Feature gate: Linked issues refer to InPlacePodVerticalScaling.
    • History: The PR sat on hold for long periods with multiple rounds of requested changes before merge.
    • Follow-ups: Linked fixes include renaming ResourcesAllocated to AllocatedResources (#116450), missing ResizePolicy validation (#116854) and flaky CI on low-CPU systems (#116371).

    Takeaway: This is the origin of pod resize without restart. Check the current feature state for your Kubernetes version before relying on it, since it began as alpha behind a feature gate.

  • Terraform on AWS EKS Kubernetes IaC SRE: 50 Real-World Demos
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A paid Udemy course on provisioning and running Amazon EKS with Terraform through a long series of hands-on demos.

    • Networking: Builds a 3-tier VPC as the base for the cluster.
    • Cluster: EKS cluster with public and private node groups.
    • Identity: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) implementation.
    • Add-ons: AWS Load Balancer Controller, Fargate profiles, autoscaling, and EKS monitoring and logging.
    • Level: Course notes say no prior Terraform knowledge is needed; an AWS account is required.
    • Demo count: A Class Central listing states 55 demos, more than the 50 in the title, so the course has likely been revised.
    • Source caveat: Udemy blocked automated access (HTTP 403); summary is based on a Class Central listing and a GitHub mirror of course notes found via search.

    Takeaway: A structured path from Terraform basics to a production-style EKS setup. Expect real AWS charges while following the demos.

  • ouch: Painless Compression and Decompression for Your Terminal
    summary

    TL;DR: ouch (Obvious Unified Compression Helper) is a Rust CLI that compresses, decompresses and lists archives in many formats with one consistent interface.

    • Commands: ouch decompress (d), ouch compress (c) and ouch list (l/ls).
    • Format detection: Infers formats from extensions, e.g. ouch compress one.txt two.txt archive.zip; falls back to file signatures and asks for confirmation when there is no extension.
    • Formats: .tar, .zip, .7z, .gz, .sz, .zst, .xz, .lzma, .lz, .bz2, .bz3, .lz4, .br, plus .rar for decompression and listing only (license limits).
    • Chaining: Stacked extensions like .tar.gz.xz.zst work; gz, sz and zst compression run in parallel.
    • Extras: --dir output directory, stdin input with - and --format, ouch list --tree --show-size, no runtime dependencies, accessibility mode, shell completions.
    • Caveat: zip and 7z cannot be streamed due to format limits.

    Takeaway: Replaces remembering tar, unzip and 7z flags with one command. Build without the unrar feature if you need a fully free build.

  • devdocs: API Documentation Browser
    summary

    TL;DR: DevDocs, created by Thibaut Courouble and run by freeCodeCamp, combines many API documentation sets into one fast web UI with instant search and offline support.

    • Hosted: Recommended use is devdocs.io, which works offline out of the box.
    • Self-host: docker run --name devdocs -d -p 9292:9292 ghcr.io/freecodecamp/devdocs:latest (an -alpine variant exists); images rebuild monthly with fresh docs.
    • Architecture: A Ruby scraper generates documentation and metadata, and a JavaScript app is served by a small Sinatra app.
    • Features: Instant search, mobile version, dark theme and keyboard shortcuts.
    • Maintenance: The README says the project is looking for maintainers.

    Takeaway: Handy for offline or air-gapped work. Run the Docker image locally if you need docs without internet access.

  • crawlee: Web Scraping and Browser Automation Library for Node.js
    summary

    TL;DR: Crawlee is Apify’s open-source Node.js/TypeScript library for building web scrapers and browser automation, with one interface over HTTP and headless browsers.

    • Crawlers: Works with Playwright, Puppeteer, Cheerio, JSDOM and raw HTTP, headful or headless.
    • Quick start: npx crawlee create my-crawler, or npm install crawlee playwright and use PlaywrightCrawler with enqueueLinks() and Dataset.pushData().
    • Core features: Persistent URL queue (breadth or depth first), pluggable storage for tabular data and files, autoscaling to system resources.
    • Anti-blocking: Integrated proxy rotation and session management; the README claims human-like behavior that avoids modern bot protection by default.
    • Storage: Defaults to ./storage in the working directory.
    • Current state: Now requires Node.js 22.13+, and a Python version also exists.

    Takeaway: A batteries-included choice when a scraper needs queues, retries and proxies. Respect target sites’ terms and rate limits.

  • mountpoint-s3: High-Throughput File Client for Mounting an Amazon S3 Bucket as a Local File System
    summary

    TL;DR: Mountpoint for Amazon S3 is an AWS open-source file client (now GA) that mounts an S3 bucket as a local file system and translates file operations into S3 API calls.

    • Best fit: High-throughput reads of large objects, possibly from many clients, and sequential writes of new objects from a single client.
    • Poor fit: Directory renames, symlinks and editing existing files; the README jokes not to run your Git repo or vim on it.
    • POSIX: Not fully POSIX; a separate file system behavior doc lists differences.
    • Install: sudo dnf install mount-s3 on Amazon Linux 2023, or .rpm/.deb packages from the release bucket for x86_64 or arm64.
    • Usage: mount-s3 <bucket> /path/to/mount, using instance role or standard AWS credentials.
    • Kubernetes: A Mountpoint for Amazon S3 CSI driver is available.

    Takeaway: Good for read-heavy analytics and ML data loading without copying data locally. Do not treat it as a general-purpose shared file system.

  • codeql: Libraries and Queries Powering Code Scanning in GitHub Advanced Security
    summary

    TL;DR: The open-source repository of standard CodeQL libraries and queries that power GitHub code scanning and GitHub Advanced Security.

    • Contents: Standard QL libraries and security and quality queries; contributions of new checks are welcome via pull requests.
    • Learning: Points to docs for the CodeQL language, the VS Code extension and the CodeQL CLI.
    • License: Queries and libraries are MIT; the CodeQL CLI and engine live elsewhere under a separate license.
    • Commercial caveat: Analyzing closed-source code with the CLI requires a separate commercial license.
    • Tooling: The CodeQL for VS Code extension adds syntax highlighting, IntelliSense and unit test support for queries.

    Takeaway: Read these queries to understand what code scanning flags. Mind the license if you plan to run CodeQL on private code outside GitHub.

  • cloudlist: Tool for Listing Assets from Multiple Cloud Providers
    summary

    TL;DR: cloudlist is a ProjectDiscovery Go tool that lists assets (hosts, IPs, services) from many cloud providers into one inventory for attack surface management.

    • Purpose: Aimed at blue teams to keep a centralized list of assets across clouds with little configuration.
    • Providers: AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare, Fastly, Heroku, Hetzner, Linode, Scaleway, OpenStack, Alibaba, Namecheap, Consul, Nomad, Terraform state and custom sources.
    • Services: Covers things like ec2, eks, ecs, lambda, s3, route53, elb/alb, cloudfront, gke, cloud-run and apigateway.
    • Auth: Keyless support (AWS IRSA and instance profiles, GCP workload identity); -ad auto-discovers providers from environment credentials.
    • Output: -host or -ip only, -json, -o file, -silent for piping into other ProjectDiscovery tools; -ep excludes private IPs.
    • Config: Provider credentials live in ~/.config/cloudlist/provider-config.yaml.

    Takeaway: A cheap starting point for an external asset inventory. Pipe its output into scanners such as httpx or nuclei for continuous checks.

  • How to Use Policies to Restrict Where EC2 Instance Credentials Can Be Used From
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (March 2023) introducing two global condition keys that let SCPs and policies restrict EC2 instance role credentials to the instance they were issued to.

    • New keys: aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC (instance VPC ID) and aws:EC2InstanceSourcePrivateIPv4 (primary private IP), populated automatically for instance credentials.
    • Comparison: Policies compare them with aws:SourceVpc and aws:VpcSourceIp, which are only set for requests through VPC endpoints.
    • SCP pattern: Two Deny statements (VPC and IP). The VPC check works alone; the IP check should never be used alone since private IPs repeat.
    • Scoping: ec2:SourceInstanceARN with a Null check targets instance roles; aws:ViaAWSService and an aws:ec2-infrastructure exception keep services and EBS/KMS working.
    • Exceptions: A principal tag (exception-to-vpc-ip) or NotAction (e.g. iam:*).
    • Caveats: Requests not made via VPC endpoints are denied; a 2025 update notes actions such as EFS ClientMount do not use VPC endpoints and break.

    Takeaway: A strong control against stolen instance credentials being used elsewhere. Roll it out only after you have VPC endpoints for the services your instances call.

  • From Pod Security Policies to Pod Security Standards: A Migration Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: A Wiz blog guide (March 2023) on migrating from PodSecurityPolicy, removed in Kubernetes 1.25, to Pod Security Admission and the Pod Security Standards.

    • Levels: privileged, baseline and restricted, assigned per namespace via labels.
    • Dry run: kubectl label ns <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level> --dry-run=server lists violating pods as warnings.
    • Two-stage rollout: Apply warn and audit modes first, then switch to enforce with kubectl label --overwrite.
    • Verification: kubectl describe ns <ns> | grep pod-security.
    • Problem workloads: Split namespaces, add exemptions (users, RuntimeClassName, namespaces) or label explicitly as privileged rather than leaving unlabeled.
    • Caveats: Images built to run as root are only caught at container start; completed pods can block labeling; PSP and PSA can coexist only up to 1.24.
    • Research note: Wiz reports PSA adoption lagged earlier PSP usage in environments it saw.

    Takeaway: Label every namespace explicitly and start in warn/audit mode. Do this before any upgrade past 1.24.

  • The One-and-Only, Must-Have, Eternal Go Project Layout
    summary

    TL;DR: Christoph Berger (Applied Go) argues there is no standard Go project layout and that structure should follow the project’s needs, not a template.

    • Moved: The URL now redirects to learn.appliedgo.net/blog/go-project-layout.
    • Directories the toolchain cares about: internal/ (not importable outside the module), testdata/ and names starting with . or _ (ignored), and vendor/ (used by go mod vendor).
    • Naming: Avoid grab-bag packages like util, models, helpers; group by responsibility; skip a src directory.
    • Examples: A small CLI in one root directory; a library with sub-packages; library plus tool with a cmd/ directory.
    • golang-standards/project-layout: Called self-proclaimed and not an official standard.
    • pkg debate: Lists voices for and against; the author suggests skipping pkg for libraries and small projects.
    • Further reading: Ben Johnson’s Standard Package Layout and the Go team’s older Organizing Go code post.

    Takeaway: Start flat and add internal/ and cmd/ only when needed. Do not copy a layout repo wholesale.

  • revive: Fast, Configurable, Extensible Drop-In Replacement for golint
    summary

    TL;DR: revive by Minko Gechev is an MIT-licensed, configurable Go linter and drop-in replacement for golint, with a framework for custom rules.

    • Speed: About 2x faster than golint on the same rules and over 6x with typed rules off. On Kubernetes: golint about 55 s, revive about 8.5 s without type checking, about 26 s with it.
    • Rules: Roughly 105 rules, marked by golint origin and whether they need type info.
    • Config: TOML via -config; enable or disable rules, set severity and arguments, for example [rule.cyclomatic] with arguments = [10].
    • Output: Nine formatters including friendly, stylish, json, ndjson, checkstyle and sarif.
    • Install: go install github.com/mgechev/revive@latest, Homebrew, Docker or binaries.
    • golangci-lint: Available as the revive linter, configured under linters.settings.revive in YAML or JSON.

    Takeaway: If you still run golint (deprecated), revive is the direct replacement. Most teams will use it via golangci-lint and tune rules there.

  • Taskfile v3.22.0: Support for Global Tasks
    summary

    TL;DR: Release notes for Task (go-task) v3.22.0, published March 10, 2023, whose headline change is support for a global Taskfile.

    • Global tasks: New --global / -g flag runs the Taskfile from your $HOME directory, so personal automation works from anywhere (#1029).
    • Output: group output mode gains error_only: true, printing command output only on non-zero exit (#664, #1022).
    • Fix: .task/checksum was not always created when a task also declared status: (#840).
    • Fix: Deadlock with run: once resolved (#715).
    • Refactor: Fingerprinting decoupled from the main executor (#1039).

    Takeaway: task -g makes Task usable as a personal command runner. error_only is a nice way to quiet CI logs.

  • Intro to Kubernetes: Containers at Scale, Illustrated
    summary

    TL;DR: An illustrated beginner introduction to Kubernetes by Kaslin Fields (March 2023), from her Containerized Adventures comics series, built on a cookie-business analogy.

    • Containers: Explained as packaging that bundles an app with its dependencies, isolated with cgroups and namespaces.
    • Control plane: The headquarters: kube-apiserver, etcd as source of truth, kube-scheduler and controller managers.
    • Nodes: Warehouses running kubelet, a container runtime and kube-proxy.
    • Pods: The smallest unit; sidecars share IP and storage.
    • Workload controllers: Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job and CronJob, each with its use case.
    • Scheduling and networking: Labels, nodeSelector, affinity and anti-affinity; ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Services; Ingress noted as being overtaken by the Gateway API.

    Takeaway: A good link to hand to newcomers or non-engineers. It explains the moving parts without assuming prior container knowledge.

  • Building ClickHouse Cloud from Scratch in a Year
    summary

    TL;DR: ClickHouse’s March 2023 engineering write-up on building ClickHouse Cloud, a serverless managed service, in under a year.

    • Timeline: Private Preview in May (over 50 invited users, free), Public Beta in October, GA in December.
    • Storage: Shared-everything design with separated storage and compute; S3-style object storage is primary, local disks only cache.
    • Planes: Control plane and data plane talk only through a bidirectional REST API; events flow via SQS or Google Pub/Sub.
    • Platform: Managed Kubernetes (EKS on AWS), Cilium for networking, and a shared Istio/Envoy ingress replacing per-service NLBs that hit account quotas.
    • Scaling: An idler suspends unused services (modeled on Knative’s activator) and a scaler recomputes allocations every 30 minutes.
    • Availability: Production pods spread across 3 AZs, development across 2; cellular data plane architecture.
    • Billing and lessons: Per-minute compute and 15-minute storage metering via m3ter and Stripe; they found 1 PB of junk from failed multipart uploads, fixed with TTLs.

    Takeaway: A detailed reference architecture for SaaS on Kubernetes. The multipart-upload cleanup lesson applies to any heavy S3 user.

  • Monitoring Kubernetes Clusters on GKE (Google Container Engine)
    summary

    TL;DR: A March 2019 Google Cloud Community article by Ariel Peretz on planning logging and monitoring for GKE clusters with Stackdriver and related tools.

    • Layers: Covers monitoring at the GCP compute, cluster node, pod and application-metric levels.
    • Process: Decide what to monitor (framed with SLIs and SLOs), plan a logging architecture, review clusters to ensure logging is enabled, then implement.
    • Advice: Avoid monitoring everything; monitoring too much is as risky as too little.
    • Tools: Stackdriver as the single pane of glass, Prometheus, kube-state-metrics and OpenCensus.
    • Internals: kubelet’s embedded cAdvisor, Heapster as the cluster metrics repository, prometheus-to-sd-exporter forwarding Prometheus metrics, and metrics-server.
    • Dated content: Stackdriver is now Cloud Monitoring and Heapster is long retired, so the tooling details are historical.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; summarized from a Wayback Machine copy of the article.

    Takeaway: The planning advice (SLO-driven, monitor just enough) still holds. Use current Cloud Monitoring and Managed Prometheus docs for implementation.

  • Kubernetes: Forensic Container Analysis
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post by Adrian Reber (Red Hat, March 2023) showing how to analyze a checkpoint taken with the alpha forensic container checkpointing feature.

    • Creating a checkpoint: curl -X POST https://localhost:10250/checkpoint/<ns>/<pod>/<container> on the node, using kubelet client certs; output lands in /var/lib/kubelet/checkpoints/.
    • Overview: checkpointctl show checkpoint.tar --print-stats shows image, runtime (CRI-O), checkpoint size and CRIU dump stats.
    • Archive layout: rootfs-diff.tar (changed files), checkpoint/ (CRIU images), config.dump, spec.dump, dump.log, stats-dump.
    • Process analysis: crit show checkpoint/pstree.img and core-*.img reveal process tree and names from inside the PID namespace.
    • Memory: grep -ao across checkpoint/pages-*.img found a secret string held in memory.
    • gdb: CRIU’s coredump script converts checkpoints to core files for gdb.
    • Caveat: Anyone with the checkpoint archive can read all process memory, and the feature was alpha.

    Takeaway: Checkpointing gives incident responders a memory and filesystem snapshot without stopping the container. Protect checkpoint archives like secrets.

  • awesome-detection-rules: Collection of Threat Detection Rules and Rules Engines
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated list by jatrost of public threat detection rule repositories and rules engines, grouped by rule language.

    • YARA: Dozens of sources including Elastic protections-artifacts, Neo23x0 signature-base, ESET malware-ioc, Mandiant red team countermeasures, ReversingLabs and Yara-Rules.
    • Sigma: Collections such as the Center for Threat-Informed Defense cloud analytics and LOLDrivers detections.
    • Network and runtime: Sections for Falco, Zeek and Suricata.
    • SIEM and query languages: Splunk, KQL and MQL sections.
    • Other: Nuclei templates and a catch-all section.

    Takeaway: A good starting index when building or benchmarking detection content. Review and test any third-party rule before deploying it.

  • Passwordless Authentication Made Easy with Cognito: A Step-by-Step Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Yan Cui (theburningmonk, March 2023) shows how to build email one-time-code passwordless login on Amazon Cognito, which does not support passwordless out of the box.

    • Triggers: DefineAuthChallenge decides the next step, CreateAuthChallenge generates and emails the code, VerifyAuthChallengeResponse checks it; PreSignUp auto-confirms users.
    • Email: Sent via Amazon SES, which needs a verified domain identity.
    • Code: 6 characters generated in CreateAuthChallenge.
    • Retries: The code is kept in challengeMetadata because privateChallengeParameters is not passed back on retries; remaining attempts are surfaced via publicChallengeParameters.
    • Attempt cap: A MAX_ATTEMPTS constant fails auth after too many wrong answers.
    • Password workaround: The pool still requires a password, so the frontend generates a random 16-character one users never see.
    • Code: Demo plus Serverless Framework backend and Vue 3 frontend repos; the post does not cover code expiry.

    Takeaway: A working blueprint for Cognito custom auth flows. Add expiry and rate limiting before production.

  • Amazon Linux 2023, a Cloud-Optimized Linux Distribution with Long-Term Support
    summary

    TL;DR: Sébastien Stormacq’s AWS News Blog post (March 2023) announcing GA of Amazon Linux 2023, the third generation of Amazon Linux, with a predictable release and support lifecycle.

    • Support: Five years per major version: two years standard plus three years maintenance with security fixes.
    • Cadence: A new major version every two years, with minor updates every three months in the first two years.
    • Base: Starts from Fedora but is not tied to one release; includes components from Fedora 34-36 and some resembling CentOS Stream 9.
    • Packages: dnf replaces yum; /usr/bin/yum symlinks to dnf-3.
    • Versioned repos: Locked to a repository version, so dnf update does not pull new releases; use dnf check-release-update and --releasever or new AMIs.
    • Kernel: Long-term kernel.org releases (6.1 in the example); AMIs for x86_64 and Arm in standard and minimal sizes, gp3 by default.
    • Update note: The page notes Amazon Linux 2 end of life was extended to 2026-06-30.

    Takeaway: Plan AL2 to AL2023 migrations now. Learn the versioned-repo update model, since it differs from AL2.

  • Kubernetes CPU Requests & Limits vs Autoscaling
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sysdig blog post by Jason Umiker (March 2023) arguing that accurate CPU requests plus HPA and Cluster Autoscaler usually beat CPU limits, which can badly hurt performance.

    • Requests: Used by the scheduler’s filter step; a pod stays Pending until a node has enough unrequested CPU.
    • CPU shares: Requests map to cgroup shares; 1,000 of 3,000 total shares means one third of CPU time under contention.
    • Limits: CFS quota over a 100,000 µs (100 ms) period; 10 threads can burn a 1-CPU quota in 10 ms and stay throttled 90% of the period.
    • Defaults and QoS: A limit without a request sets request equal to limit; no request means BestEffort and first eviction.
    • Autoscaling: HPA adds pods; Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when unrequested capacity runs out and drains them on scale-down.
    • Runtime tuning: Match thread counts to CPU: piscina maxThreads for Node.js, -XX:ActiveProcessorCount for Java, GOMAXPROCS or automaxprocs for Go.
    • Caveat: Limits still matter on fixed on-prem capacity to keep tenants fair.

    Takeaway: Invest in correct requests and autoscaling first. If you keep CPU limits, align language runtime thread counts to them.

  • How to Use Kubernetes Events for Effective Alerting and Monitoring
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF guest post by Hrittik Roy (March 2023, also on the Grafana Labs blog) on using Kubernetes events for monitoring, shipping them to Loki with Grafana Agent for retention and alerting.

    • Retention problem: Events are only available for one hour after creation, so they need an external store.
    • Event types covered: Failed (image pull, manifest), Evicted, FailedScheduling, volume (FailedMount, FailedAttachVolume) and node events (NodeNotReady, HostPortConflict).
    • Commands: kubectl get events, kubectl get events -o json, kubectl get events --namespace=<ns>, kubectl describe <kind>/<name>.
    • Troubleshooting: ImagePullBackOff from wrong tags or credentials; taints, labels and tolerations for scheduling and eviction issues.
    • Collection: Grafana Agent eventhandler_config reads events from the API and forwards them to Loki, as a DaemonSet or Deployment; without cache_path, restarts cause duplicates.
    • Alerting: Grafana alerts to Slack or email on evictions, errors and state changes.

    Takeaway: Ship events somewhere durable before you need them in an incident. Any event exporter works; the post uses the Grafana stack.

  • ko: Build and Deploy Go Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: ko is a CNCF Sandbox tool that builds container images for Go applications by running go build locally, with no Docker daemon needed.

    • Best fit: Images that contain a single Go binary with few or no OS dependencies (no cgo, no OS packages).
    • No Docker: Builds and pushes images without Docker installed, which suits lightweight CI.
    • Multi-platform: Makes multi-arch builds easy.
    • SBOMs: Produces SBOMs by default.
    • Kubernetes: Simple YAML templating lets it resolve image references in manifests for Kubernetes deploys.
    • Origin: Based on experience building Docker and Kubernetes support for Bazel.

    Takeaway: For pure Go services, ko removes the Dockerfile and gives small images with SBOMs. Use a regular build when you need cgo or OS packages.

  • Container Security Fundamentals Part 2: Isolation & Namespaces
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 2 of Rory McCune’s container security fundamentals series on Datadog Security Labs (March 2023), covering how Linux namespaces isolate containers.

    • Namespaces: Linux has eight (mount, PID, network, cgroup, IPC, time, UTS, user); Docker uses mnt, uts, ipc, pid and net by default.
    • Inspection: lsns, docker inspect for the PID, then findmnt -N <pid> or nsenter --target <pid> --mount.
    • PID sharing: docker run --pid=container:<name>, Kubernetes shareProcessNamespace: true and kubectl debug --target.
    • Network sharing: docker run --network=container:<name>; ip netns does not work with Docker since its symlinks are missing.
    • Cgroup leakage: Using the host cgroup namespace exposes host service info under /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/.
    • User namespaces: unshare -U -r gives in-namespace root; the post links unprivileged user namespaces to easier exploitation of CVE-2022-0185 and mentions kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone.
    • State at the time: runc was still adding time namespace support, and user namespaces were not yet usable in Kubernetes.

    Takeaway: Knowing which namespaces a container shares tells you what it can see. Treat any host-namespace sharing flag as a security review item.

  • 20 Terraform Best Practices to Improve Your TF Workflow
    summary

    TL;DR: A Spacelift blog article listing Terraform best practices; the archived title says 20, but the page has since been updated (April 2026) to 21 practices.

    • State: Remote backend with locking, no manual state edits, backups and S3 versioning.
    • Modules: Reuse Registry modules, pin versions, and build small reusable modules.
    • Hygiene: terraform fmt and terraform validate in CI or pre-commit; lowercase underscore naming; descriptions on variables and outputs; consistent tags with provider default_tags.
    • Language features: for_each/count, dynamic blocks, lifecycle ignore_changes and create_before_destroy, and variable validation blocks.
    • Secrets and debugging: Keep secrets out of VCS using sensitive = true, TF_VAR_ env vars or Vault/Secrets Manager; TF_LOG=DEBUG and TF_LOG_PATH.
    • Tools: tflint, Checkov, Terratest, pre-commit-terraform, terraform-docs, tfenv, Atlantis and OPA for policy.
    • Changed content: The current version adds safe AI-assistant use and an OpenTofu note; it also promotes Spacelift throughout.

    Takeaway: A solid checklist for reviewing a Terraform repo. The page is vendor content and has been rewritten since it was saved.

  • What the ML Is Up with DevSecOps and AI?
    summary

    TL;DR: A GitLab blog post by Taylor McCaslin (March 2023), first in a series, describing GitLab’s early AI/ML features for DevSecOps and its plans.

    • Suggested Reviewers: Open beta from September 2022; recommends merge request reviewers and had produced tens of thousands of suggestions.
    • Code Suggestions: Closed beta from February 2023 in the GitLab VS Code extension, with plans for the Web IDE and Remote Development.
    • Access: Ultimate customers could request beta access via a form.
    • Data handling: GitLab states customer source code does not leave the instance and is not used to train shared models.
    • Planned: Workflow automation (assigning, labeling, summarizing), intelligent code security for vulnerability remediation, and generative code features.
    • ModelOps: Plans for better Python notebook support, GPU runners and a native Model Registry.
    • Caveat: Forward-looking content carries a disclaimer that it may change.

    Takeaway: A snapshot of GitLab’s AI roadmap at the start of the 2023 AI wave. Check current docs for what actually shipped.

  • A Guide to Delegated Administrator in AWS Organizations and Multi-Account Management
    summary

    TL;DR: A CloudQuery blog guide to delegated administrator in AWS Organizations, letting member accounts manage services org-wide instead of the management account; the page now shows a 2026 rewrite.

    • API method: aws organizations register-delegated-administrator --account-id <id> --service-principal <svc> after enable-aws-service-access.
    • Service-specific APIs: Some services use their own calls, e.g. guardduty:EnableOrganizationAdminAccount or cloudtrail:RegisterOrganizationDelegatedAdmin.
    • Resource-based delegation policy: organizations:PutResourcePolicy is the only way to delegate Organizations policy management, tagging and read access.
    • Limits: IAM Identity Center allows one delegated admin, CloudTrail up to three; regional services (Security Hub, GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Detective) need per-region registration.
    • SCPs: Delegated admin accounts are subject to SCPs, unlike the management account.
    • Coverage: The current page states 37 services support delegation as of early 2026.
    • Source caveat: The live page is a rewritten version dated 2026, not the original 2023 text.

    Takeaway: Move security tooling admin out of the management account. Keep that account for billing and org structure only.

  • aws-cost-cli: Cost Analysis for Your AWS Account with Slack Integration
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-cost-cli is a Node.js CLI by Kamran Ahmed that reports AWS account costs by service and can post them to Slack.

    • Install: npm install -g aws-cost-cli or run with npx; a Dockerfile is included.
    • Default output: aws-cost prints totals with a per-service breakdown.
    • Output modes: --summary, --text (no colors or tables), --json.
    • Credentials: -k/-s/-r flags or an AWS CLI --profile.
    • Slack: --slack-token and --slack-channel post the report, which suits a scheduled job.
    • Moved: The repository now resolves to nilbuild/aws-cost-cli.

    Takeaway: A quick way to send daily spend to Slack without building dashboards. Give it a read-only Cost Explorer role.

  • Use Backups to Recover from Security Incidents
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post by Jason Hurst of the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (March 2023) on using backups to recover from security incidents.

    • Responsibility: Backup configuration is on the customer side; the post states AWS cannot recover a deleted resource.
    • AWS Backup: Centralized, policy-based protection across services, encrypted with KMS keys.
    • Isolation: Cross-account and cross-region copies, org-wide policies via AWS Organizations, and vault resource policies.
    • Governance: Legal hold, retention policies and AWS Backup Audit Manager compliance reports.
    • Service features: Aurora continuous backups with 1 to 35 day retention, DynamoDB point-in-time recovery within 35 days, and EC2 Recycle Bin for deleted EBS snapshots and AMIs.
    • Caveat: S3 buckets that hold backups need their own security configuration.

    Takeaway: Assume attackers will try to delete backups. Copy them to a separate account and confirm you can restore before an incident.

  • awesome-detection-rules: Collection of Threat Detection Rules and Rules Engines
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated list by jatrost of public threat detection rule repositories and rules engines, grouped by rule language.

    • YARA: Dozens of sources including Elastic protections-artifacts, Neo23x0 signature-base, ESET malware-ioc, Mandiant red team countermeasures, ReversingLabs and Yara-Rules.
    • Sigma: Collections such as the Center for Threat-Informed Defense cloud analytics and LOLDrivers detections.
    • Network and runtime: Sections for Falco, Zeek and Suricata.
    • SIEM and query languages: Splunk, KQL and MQL sections.
    • Other: Nuclei templates and a catch-all section.

    Takeaway: A good starting index when building or benchmarking detection content. Review and test any third-party rule before deploying it.

  • Introducing Microsoft Security Copilot
    summary

    TL;DR: The archived link was Microsoft’s March 2023 introduction of Security Copilot; the URL now hosts the current product page for the generally available, agent-based Security Copilot.

    • What it is: A security-focused language model product drawing on Microsoft threat intelligence, which the page says covers more than 100 trillion daily signals.
    • Capabilities: Incident summaries and response guidance, natural-language query generation, malware script analysis and report writing.
    • Agents: Phishing triage, alert triage, vulnerability remediation and Conditional Access optimization agents, plus partner and community agents.
    • Integrations: Defender XDR, Sentinel, Intune, Entra, Purview, Defender for Cloud, Defender EASM and Azure firewalls.
    • Pricing: Usage in Security Compute Units (SCUs); eligible Microsoft 365 E5/E7 customers get 400 SCUs per month per 1,000 licenses, up to 10,000.
    • Vendor claims: Internal studies cite phishing triage up to 550% faster; these are not independently verified.
    • Source caveat: The page no longer shows the original 2023 announcement text.

    Takeaway: Evaluate it on your own incidents and SCU cost. Treat vendor speed-up figures as marketing until you measure them.

  • woodpecker: Community Fork of the Drone CI System
    summary

    TL;DR: Woodpecker is an Apache 2.0, self-hosted CI/CD engine focused on simplicity and plugin extensibility, archived here as a community fork of Drone.

    • Footprint: Uses SQLite by default; about 100 MB RAM for the server and 30 MB for an agent when idle.
    • Extensibility: A plugin catalog combines core-team and community plugins.
    • Adoption: Codeberg uses it as its main CI/CD engine.
    • Docs and i18n: Docs at woodpecker-ci.org and a self-hosted Weblate for translations.
    • Funding: Open Collective and GitHub Sponsors.
    • Source caveat: The current README does not mention the Drone fork history from the archived title.

    Takeaway: A light, fully open option for self-hosted CI. Fits small teams that want Drone-style pipelines without a commercial license.

08.03.2023

  • Privacy Guides: The Guide to Restoring Your Online Privacy
    summary

    TL;DR: Privacy Guides is a non-profit, community-run site offering privacy and security advice and tool recommendations.

    • Positioning: Describes itself as impartial and non-profit, focused on building a privacy advocacy community.
    • Sections: Knowledge Base (guides), Recommendations (tools), Activism, Articles, Videos, News, Forum and Wiki.
    • Independence: States it does not earn money from recommendations, uses no affiliate links, runs no ads and does not partner with listed providers.
    • Funding: Asks readers to become paying members.
    • Homepage content: The homepage names no specific tools; recommendations live under the tools section.

    Takeaway: A good neutral reference to give non-technical people. Use its threat-model guidance first, then pick tools from its recommendations.

  • Hacking Google: Series
    summary

    TL;DR: HACKING GOOGLE is Google’s six-part YouTube documentary series (October 2022) about its internal security teams.

    • Pitch: Five elite security teams and six never-before-told stories, per the playlist description.
    • EP000 Operation Aurora: What happens when a country attacks a company.
    • EP001-EP002: Threat Analysis Group and Detection and Response.
    • EP003 Red Team: The team that hacks Google from the inside.
    • EP004-EP005: Bug Hunters (outside researchers who have made millions hacking Google) and Project Zero (zero-day research).
    • Bonus: A Google Cloud episode hosted by CISO Phil Venables; episodes were first unlocked through the H4CK1NG G00GL3 challenge.
    • Source caveat: Episode list taken from Google’s blog and TheTVDB via search, since the playlist page only exposed the description.

    Takeaway: Easy viewing that explains how a large company organizes threat intel, detection, red teaming and vulnerability research. Useful for team onboarding.

  • tbls: CI-Friendly Tool for Documenting a Database
    summary

    TL;DR: tbls by k1LoW is a single-binary Go tool that documents database schemas, diffs them and lints them, designed to run in CI.

    • Documentation: tbls doc postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db writes GitHub Flavored Markdown docs with ER diagrams.
    • Diff and lint: Compares the database with its committed docs and lints schema rules; also measures document coverage.
    • Databases: Supports many engines (PostgreSQL in the examples) and many output formats.
    • Config: .tbls.yml covers DSN, filters, comments, virtual relations, viewpoints and templates.
    • Install: brew install tbls, deb/rpm packages, go install github.com/k1LoW/tbls@latest, ghcr.io/k1low/tbls image, or the k1low/setup-tbls GitHub Action.

    Takeaway: Keeps schema docs in the repo and fails CI when they drift. Cheap to add next to migrations.

  • Pull Request Merge Queue (Public Beta)
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub’s February 8, 2023 changelog announcing the pull request merge queue public beta for busy branches.

    • How it works: Builds a temporary branch with the latest base, PRs ahead in the queue and the PR itself, then runs CI; required checks must pass before merge.
    • Queuing: Use Merge when ready on the PR page or in GitHub Mobile (beta).
    • Failures: PRs with conflicts or failed required checks are removed automatically when they reach the front, with a notification.
    • Queue page: Shows status, required checks, estimated time to merge and 30-day trends; permitted users can remove PRs or clear the queue.
    • Availability: GitHub Enterprise Cloud repositories and open source organizations at the time.

    Takeaway: Solves the stale-green-build problem on high-traffic main branches. Your CI must also run for merge queue branches before you enable it.

  • OWASP Kubernetes Top 10
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sysdig blog post by Nigel Douglas (February 2023) walking through the OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 with tools and mitigations for each risk.

    • K01 Insecure workload configs: Minimal images and CIS Benchmark audits with kube-bench.
    • K02 Supply chain: Scan images in CI/CD and sign and verify them.
    • K03 Overly permissive RBAC: Audit with RBAC Audit, KubiScan or Krane.
    • K04-K05 Policy and logging: Admission controllers and OPA kube-mgmt; centralize logs and metrics with Prometheus, Grafana and Falco.
    • K06-K07 Auth and network: MFA for humans; NetworkPolicies, Calico or Cilium, or a service mesh like Istio.
    • K08-K09 Secrets and components: Encrypt Secrets at rest with least-privilege RBAC; set kubelet --anonymous-auth=false and audit manifests continuously.
    • K10 Outdated components: Track CVEs, patch, and scan with kubescape or kubeclarity.

    Takeaway: A practical map from each OWASP K8s risk to tools. Use it as a checklist for a cluster review.

  • A Complete Kubernetes Config Review Methodology
    summary

    TL;DR: A Security Cafe article by Stefan Tita (February 2023) laying out a step-by-step methodology for a Kubernetes security configuration review.

    • Images and containers: Trivy and Grype for images; Peirates and kdigger to enumerate privileged pods, host namespaces and tokens from inside a container.
    • CIS Benchmark: Versions, logging, service accounts, security contexts, secrets encryption, anonymous-auth and file permissions; the author prefers manual checks over kube-bench because of false results.
    • RBAC escalation: Risky rights include create pods, list/watch secrets, wildcards, pods/exec, nodes/proxy, rolebindings and impersonation; KubiScan and rbac-tool who-can help find them.
    • Secret exposure: LIST and WATCH return secret values, not just GET, with a jq example.
    • Network: Review Service types and Ingress, NetworkPolicies, and Security Groups for Pods on EKS; no policy means all pod traffic is allowed.
    • Scanning caution: Kube-Hunter active mode can change state, and admission chain fuzzing can create pods.
    • Add-ons: Check add-ons like Prometheus or Argo CD for privilege and public exposure.

    Takeaway: A ready-made scope for a K8s config audit. The LIST/WATCH secrets point is often missed in RBAC reviews.

  • bearer: SAST Tool to Find Security Risks Leading to Sensitive Data Exposure
    summary

    TL;DR: Bearer CLI is an open-source SAST tool that scans code and data flows for security risks and for sensitive data exposure such as PII and PHI.

    • Languages (CLI): Go, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, Python and Ruby.
    • Security rules: Built-in rules mapped to OWASP Top 10 and CWE Top 25, e.g. path traversal, SQL injection, XSS, weak crypto, hard-coded passwords, SSRF and sensitive data in logs.
    • Privacy: Detects sensitive data flows and components that process them, such as databases and third-party APIs.
    • Commercial tier: Bearer Pro is now sold through Cycode, adding cross-file analysis and more languages (C#, Kotlin, Elixir, VB.Net, Rust, Swift).
    • Rules: All rules and code patterns are documented.

    Takeaway: Its focus on sensitive data flow is the differentiator. Run it in CI next to a general SAST tool.

  • Burp-Suite-Certified-Practitioner-Exam-Study: Burp Suite Certified Practitioner Exam Study
    summary

    TL;DR: botesjuan’s study notes, built from over 110 PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs, used to pass the Burp Suite Certified Practitioner (BSCP) exam in 2023.

    • Structure: Follows the exam stages: scanning, foothold (stage 1), privilege escalation (stage 2) and data exfiltration (stage 3).
    • Foothold topics: Content discovery, DOM XSS, XSS, web cache poisoning, host headers, HTTP request smuggling, brute force and authentication.
    • Privesc topics: CSRF account takeover, password reset, SQLi, JWT, prototype pollution, API testing, access control, GraphQL and CORS.
    • Exfiltration topics: XXE, SSRF, SSTI, server-side prototype pollution, path traversal, file uploads, deserialization and OS command injection.
    • Extras: Payloads, word lists, Python scripts, focused scanning tips, and advice to practice the PortSwigger Mystery lab challenge.

    Takeaway: A tight roadmap for BSCP prep. Pair it with the Academy labs rather than reading it alone.

  • Golang Quirks & Intermediate Tricks, Pt 1: Declarations, Control Flow, & Typesystem
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of Efron Licht’s Go quirks series (February 2023) on lesser-known declaration, control flow and type system behavior.

    • Semicolons: Inserted by the lexer, so statements can share a line; gofmt splits them.
    • Method expressions: Call methods as functions, e.g. Point.Add(p, q) or (*big.Float).SetFloat64(&x, 10) for pointer receivers.
    • break in select: Only exits the select, not the loop; use labeled breaks.
    • Composite literals: Element types can be omitted inside arrays, slices and maps, but not for struct fields or function arguments.
    • switch init: switch n, acc := b.Uint64(); acc { and boolean-style switches.
    • goto: Cannot jump into a block or out of a function.
    • Anonymous types: Inline interface{ Flush() error } checks, blank _ struct fields to force keyed initialization, and zero-sized struct{}.

    Takeaway: Good for intermediate Go developers. The break inside select gotcha alone is worth knowing.

  • Rust vs Go in 2023
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting) compares Rust and Go and sums it up as Rust for high stakes, Go for low costs.

    • Moved: The URL now redirects to bitfieldconsulting.com/posts/rust-vs-go.
    • Shared goals: Both aim at memory safety, modern tooling and performance at scale, eliminating buffer overflows, null pointer bugs and data races.
    • Performance: Rust’s compiler produces code as fast as the hardware allows; Go is framed around high-throughput, large-scale operation.
    • Simplicity: Go is small, has few keywords and compiles fast; Rust is described as powerful, rich and rewarding.
    • Safety and control: Rust catches many bugs at compile time with static analysis and offers low-level control plus C/C++ interop.
    • Stability: Go emphasizes backward compatibility and adds features rarely.
    • When to pick: Go for fast onboarding, prototyping and low development cost; Rust for reliability, high performance and efficient resource use.

    Takeaway: Choose based on cost of failure and team ramp-up time, not benchmarks. Both are reasonable general-purpose picks.

  • Under-Documented Kubernetes Security Tips
    summary

    TL;DR: A September 2022 post on Mac Chaffee’s blog arguing that standard Kubernetes hardening guides miss organizational and API-level risks.

    • Organization first: Policies (e.g. security review for public Ingresses), segregation of duties, no unaudited shared cluster-admin token, training, periodic access reviews and an incident plan.
    • Undocumented verbs: There is no complete list of verbs and subresources, so * in Roles has undefined effects; avoid wildcards.
    • escalate verb: Lets a user create Roles beyond their own rights, which effectively grants admin.
    • pods/ephemeralcontainers: Could bypass validating webhooks that block privileged pods; the post says Gatekeeper, Kyverno and OpenShift SCCs were once affected.
    • API as RCE: Use a real identity provider via OIDC (ServiceAccount tokens are not enough), consider 2FA, and run intrusion detection such as Falco.
    • Blast radius: Multiple clusters limit impact, if the extra tooling does not add attack surface.

    Takeaway: Audit for escalate, wildcard rules and ephemeral container access. Read new Kubernetes release notes for new verbs and subresources.

  • Kubernetes Security Checklist
    summary

    TL;DR: The official Kubernetes documentation checklist of baseline cluster security controls, with links to deeper docs; it states it is neither exhaustive nor sufficient alone.

    • Sections: Authentication and authorization, network security, pod security, logs and auditing, pod placement, secrets, images and admission controllers.
    • system:masters: Use only as break-glass after bootstrap; run kube-controller-manager with --use-service-account-credentials.
    • Certificates and reviews: Certificates expire within 3 years, the root CA is protected, and access reviews happen at least every 24 months.
    • Network: CNI supports NetworkPolicies, default-deny per namespace, and the API server, kubelet and etcd not exposed publicly; etcd uses mTLS with its own CA.
    • Metadata and services: Block pod access to 169.254.169.254 if not needed; restrict LoadBalancer and ExternalIPs (CVE-2020-8554, DenyServiceExternalIPs).
    • Pod security: Enforce Pod Security Standards in all namespaces, grant workload create/update rights sparingly, set memory limit no higher than request, and enable Seccomp.

    Takeaway: A vendor-neutral baseline to audit clusters against. Use it as a minimum and layer CIS or OWASP guidance on top.

  • aws-break-glass-role: AWS Break Glass Role
    summary
