    TL;DR: An AWS Labs CDK construct (npm aws-break-glass-role) that creates an emergency break glass role for production accounts with login alerts and action logging built in.

    • Use case: Production accounts with no standing write access, where on-call staff need a controlled emergency path.
    • Basic use: new BreakGlassRole(stack, id, { usernames: [...] }); trust is the account root with an aws:username condition.
    • Permissions: Defaults to full AdministratorAccess if no policies are given, which the README says is not recommended; pass managedPolicies and policyStatements instead, or an existing role.
    • Login alerts: loginAlertEmails creates an EventBridge rule with an SNS target; recipients must confirm the subscription; messages can be customized.
    • Action logging: logActions (all, or only write) and per-service filters to control cost and volume.
    • Extras: Retention and region settings, and documented deployer permissions.

    Takeaway: A quick way to get an auditable break glass role. Scope its permissions and test the alert path before an incident.

  • centralized-logs: Centralizing AWS CloudWatch Log Forwarding via EventBridge and Step Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: Aidan Steele’s code-less CloudFormation pattern for centralizing CloudWatch Logs subscriptions across AWS accounts and regions with Firehose, EventBridge and Step Functions.

    • Destination: One Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream (example firehose.yml) or Kinesis data stream receives all logs; one is enough, not one per region.
    • Log account: logs-account.yml is deployed in every region you collect from, with OrganizationId (from aws organizations describe-organization) and FirehoseArn parameters.
    • Member accounts: every-account.yml is deployed to all accounts and regions, with CentralBusAccountId pointing at the log account.
    • Automation: EventBridge reports new log group creation, and Step Functions assume roles cross-account and call the AWS SDK to add subscriptions.
    • No code: No Lambda functions to maintain; Step Functions SDK integrations do the work.

    Takeaway: A tidy pattern for org-wide log shipping that picks up new log groups automatically. Deploy it with StackSets to reach every account.

  • aws-scps-with-terraform: Template to Create and Apply AWS Service Control Policies with Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Samples Terraform module for deploying AWS Organizations policies; the repo has been renamed to terraform-aws-organization-policies and now covers SCPs, RCPs and other policy types.

    • Module: source = "aws-samples/organization-policies/aws" (version 3.1.0 in the README) with policy_type, e.g. SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY or RESOURCE_CONTROL_POLICY.
    • Attachment: ou_map maps root or OU IDs to policy names; one module instance per policy type.
    • Policy files: JSON files in a directory named after the policy type (e.g. ./service_control_policy/), overridable with policies_directory.
    • Templates: Accepts .json.tpl files with template_variables such as a management account ID.
    • Scope change: The archived title mentions SCPs only; the current repo name and description reflect the broader scope.

    Takeaway: Keeps org guardrails as reviewable JSON in Git. Test new SCPs on a sandbox OU before attaching them to root.

  • Guidance for Baseline Security Assessment on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Solutions guidance that deploys a CloudFormation stack to run an automated baseline security assessment and present results as an AWS Well-Architected custom lens report.

    • Deployment: A CloudFormation template creates a Lambda function and its IAM role.
    • Mechanism: The Lambda deploys a Well-Architected custom lens, assesses the account and answers the lens questions automatically.
    • Checks: Secrets Manager use, Systems Manager Patch Manager, CloudFront for static content, VPC configuration, CloudTrail, billing alarms, Cost Anomaly Detection and S3 public access blocking.
    • Output: View and download the report in the Well-Architected Tool console, with remediation steps.
    • Permissions: The Lambda uses least-privilege, read-only access.

    Takeaway: A low-effort first pass for a new or inherited account. Follow it with Security Hub or Prowler for deeper coverage.

  • Dashbird: Agentless Observability for Serverless Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: Dashbird is a commercial, agentless monitoring and error detection SaaS for AWS serverless applications.

    • Setup: Deploy a CloudFormation template granting read-only permissions; no code instrumentation or Lambda layers. The site says setup takes two minutes.
    • Coverage: Lambda, API Gateway, SQS, ECS, RDS, AppSync, DynamoDB, Kinesis, SNS, OpenSearch, Step Functions, S3 and EventBridge.
    • Features: Cloud inventory, tracing, log analytics, custom dashboards, error tracking, alarms and insights.
    • Best-practice checks: The site lists 148 failure checks, 238 insights and 17 integrations.
    • Pricing model: Charges by invocations, with no seat fee.
    • Vendor claims: Marketing figures such as 85% reduced downtime are the vendor’s own and not independently verified.

    Takeaway: Worth a trial for teams that run many Lambda-based services without a full observability stack. Compare cost with CloudWatch-native options.

  • tokei: Count Your Code, Quickly
    summary

    TL;DR: Tokei is a fast Rust CLI that counts files, lines, code, comments and blanks per language in a codebase.

    • Speed: Counts millions of lines in seconds, per the README.
    • Accuracy: Handles multi-line and nested comments and ignores comment markers inside strings.
    • Languages: Over 150 languages and their extensions, including embedded code in Markdown.
    • Output: CBOR, JSON and YAML, which can be stored and combined with later runs.
    • Platforms: macOS, Linux and Windows.

    Takeaway: A quick way to size a repo before an audit or migration. JSON output works well in CI dashboards.

  • rtx: Runtime Executor (asdf Rust Clone)
    summary

    TL;DR: rtx, a Rust asdf alternative by jdx, has since been renamed mise (mise-en-place) and now manages dev tools, environment variables and tasks from one mise.toml.

    • Rename: The URL now resolves to jdx/mise; rtx is the old name.
    • Tools: Installs tools such as Node.js, Python and Terraform from a registry of 1,000+, with per-project versions.
    • Env vars: Sets per-project environment variables and loads .env files.
    • Tasks: Runs build and test tasks with the project’s tools and environment.
    • Commands: curl https://mise.run | sh, mise exec node@24 -- node --version, mise use node@24.
    • Bootstrap: Newer mise bootstrap sets up a machine’s packages, dotfiles and services.

    Takeaway: If you saved this as rtx, install mise instead. It can replace asdf, direnv and simple Makefiles.

  • moon: Task Runner and Repo Management Tool for the Web Ecosystem, Written in Rust
    summary

    TL;DR: moon is a Rust-based repository management, orchestration and build tool for web-ecosystem monorepos, inspired by Bazel.

    • Toolchain: Downloads and pins explicit tool versions (e.g. Node.js) across the workspace or per project.
    • Builds: Smart hashing for deterministic builds and remote caching shared between developers and CI.
    • Graphs: Project and dependency graphs drive a parallel action pipeline; actions can be distributed across machines.
    • Automation: Can install node_modules, sync package dependencies and TypeScript project references.
    • Ownership: Declares owners and generates CODEOWNERS; includes code generation for scaffolding.
    • Adoption: Designed for incremental, project-by-project migration.

    Takeaway: A lighter alternative to Bazel or Nx for JS/TS monorepos. The remote cache is where CI time savings come from.

  • katana: Next-Generation Crawling and Spidering Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: katana is ProjectDiscovery’s Go web crawler and spider for security reconnaissance, with standard and headless browser modes.

    • Modes: Standard HTTP crawling and headless Chrome (-headless, -system-chrome).
    • JavaScript: Parses and crawls JavaScript for endpoints.
    • Forms: Customizable automatic form filling.
    • Scope: Preconfigured field or regex scope control.
    • Classification: A machine-learning knowledge base classifies page and form types (model downloaded automatically).
    • I/O: Input from stdin, URL or list; output to stdout, file or JSON.
    • Install: CGO_ENABLED=1 go install github.com/projectdiscovery/katana/cmd/katana@latest or docker pull projectdiscovery/katana.

    Takeaway: Feeds endpoint lists into scanners such as nuclei. Only crawl targets you are authorized to test.

  • firefly: Black Box Fuzzer for Web Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: firefly by Brum3ns is a Go black-box fuzzer for web applications that compares responses against verified baseline behavior to find anomalies.

    • Basic use: firefly -u 'http://example.com/?query=FUZZ', with -m GET,POST,PUT and -p https,http,ws.
    • Raw requests: -r takes a raw HTTP request and auto-detects GET and POST parameters to fuzz.
    • Request verifier: Baseline requests teach the tool the target’s normal behavior; the README stresses quality over quantity here.
    • Payloads: Built-in payloads mixed with SecLists wordlists, plus tampering and encoding.
    • Filtering: Filters and verification to cut junk results.
    • Install: go install -v github.com/Brum3ns/firefly/cmd/firefly@latest.

    Takeaway: Useful for parameter fuzzing in bug bounty or pentest work. Only use it against authorized targets.

  • goreplay: Capture and Replay Live HTTP Traffic into a Test Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: GoReplay captures live HTTP traffic from a network interface and replays it to test environments for shadowing, load testing and analysis; the repo now lives at probelabs/goreplay.

    • Approach: Listens passively on interfaces instead of acting as a proxy, so it is not in the request path.
    • Basic capture: sudo ./gor --input-raw :8000 --output-stdout works like tcpdump.
    • Replay: sudo ./gor --input-raw :8000 --output-http http://staging.env mirrors traffic to staging.
    • Uses: Increases confidence in code, config and infrastructure changes using real traffic.
    • Install: Release binaries or build from source.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to test changes with real traffic patterns. Scrub sensitive data and avoid replaying non-idempotent writes against shared systems.

  • earthly: Simple CI/CD Framework with Repeatable Builds That Run Anywhere
    summary

    TL;DR: Earthly is a containerized build framework with Dockerfile-plus-Makefile-style syntax for repeatable builds; it is no longer actively maintained.

    • Status: Earthly Technologies ended active maintenance and shut down Earthly Cloud (including Satellites) on July 16, 2025; the source stays available.
    • Fork: A community-maintained fork is available as EarthBuild.
    • Model: Runs every build step in containers, so the same Earthfile works on laptops and in any CI.
    • Features: Build caching and parallel execution, reusable targets, and support for monorepos and polyrepos.
    • Compatibility: Wraps existing language build tools rather than replacing them.

    Takeaway: Do not start new projects on upstream Earthly. Evaluate EarthBuild or alternatives such as Dagger if you like the model.

  • How to Achieve Application & Cloud Security Resilience
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A February 2023 better appsec article by James Chiappetta, with contributions from Dor Zusman, on building a resilient AppSec and cloud security program through automation and data.

    • Scanning tools: Overview of the types of automated security scanning tools.
    • Scan strategy: When to run comprehensive scans versus targeted scans.
    • Detections: How to build a high-quality detection set.
    • Triage: Root cause analysis, deduplication and attribution of findings.
    • Metrics: Measures for quantifying AppSec program resiliency.
    • Source caveat: The article is a Medium member-only story and the live page blocked access; summary is based on the archived intro and a tl;dr sec newsletter description.

    Takeaway: Useful framing for maturing a scanning program beyond tool sprawl. Read the full piece for the specific metrics.

  • Under-Documented Kubernetes Security Tips
    summary

    TL;DR: A September 2022 post on Mac Chaffee’s blog arguing that standard Kubernetes hardening guides miss organizational and API-level risks.

    • Organization first: Policies (e.g. security review for public Ingresses), segregation of duties, no unaudited shared cluster-admin token, training, periodic access reviews and an incident plan.
    • Undocumented verbs: There is no complete list of verbs and subresources, so * in Roles has undefined effects; avoid wildcards.
    • escalate verb: Lets a user create Roles beyond their own rights, which effectively grants admin.
    • pods/ephemeralcontainers: Could bypass validating webhooks that block privileged pods; the post says Gatekeeper, Kyverno and OpenShift SCCs were once affected.
    • API as RCE: Use a real identity provider via OIDC (ServiceAccount tokens are not enough), consider 2FA, and run intrusion detection such as Falco.
    • Blast radius: Multiple clusters limit impact, if the extra tooling does not add attack surface.

    Takeaway: Audit for escalate, wildcard rules and ephemeral container access. Read new Kubernetes release notes for new verbs and subresources.

  • My CI/CD Pipeline Is My Release Captain
    summary

    TL;DR: An Amazon Builders’ Library article by Clare Liguori (December 2022) on how Amazon’s CI/CD pipelines took over the release captain role, automating release coordination and rollback.

    • Moved: The URL now redirects to the AWS Builder Center.
    • Trunk-based: Merged, reviewed changes on main go to production; release branches are kept for rare urgent fixes.
    • Stages: Each stage deploys in parallel then runs approvals (integration tests, alarm monitoring); failed stages do not promote.
    • Small blast radius: Production split by region, then AZ, with one-box environments as small as one VM or container.
    • Waves: A sample pipeline deploys to 26 regions in five waves of increasing size.
    • Inflight releases: Several releases move through at once; a newer approved release supersedes older waiting ones.
    • Rollback: Immutable artifacts per push; alarms trigger automatic rollback, and manual rollback picks the last approved release while freezing promotions.

    Takeaway: The one-box and wave model is the main idea to copy. Wire alarms to automatic rollback before adding more stages.

  • Down the Cloudflare / Stripe / OWASP Rabbit Hole: A Tale of 6 Rabbits Deep
    summary

    TL;DR: Troy Hunt’s February 2023 account of Stripe webhooks to Have I Been Pwned being intermittently blocked by Cloudflare’s WAF, and the six-step investigation.

    • Symptom: A paid upgrade failed because the invoice.paid webhook got HTTP 403; a single-digit percentage of callbacks failed.
    • Logs: Cloudflare Enterprise logs showed a managed challenge from the Inbound Anomaly Score Exceeded rule.
    • OWASP scoring: A score of 26 from six rules exceeded the threshold of 25; Cloudflare had upgraded the OWASP ruleset to 3.3.4 shortly before.
    • Payload logging: Encrypted payload logs showed no malicious patterns; blocked and passing payloads differed only in dates and IDs.
    • Rollback attempt: Cloudflare rolled back a suspected ruleset change, but blocks continued; Stripe reported no relevant change.
    • Fix: A custom WAF exception scoped to the webhook path, placed first in rule order, plus exceptions for specific OWASP rules.
    • Open question: The root cause was never confirmed.

    Takeaway: Exempt trusted webhook paths from anomaly-scoring WAF rules and alert on webhook failures. Managed WAF rule updates can break integrations silently.

  • Lateral Movement Risks in the Cloud, Part 3: From Compromised Cloud Resource to Kubernetes Cluster Takeover
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 3 of Wiz Research’s lateral movement series by Lior Sonntag (February 2023), on moving from a compromised cloud resource into managed Kubernetes clusters on EKS, GKE and AKS.

    • EKS: The IAM identity that created a cluster gets system:masters automatically; other identities need entries in the aws-auth ConfigMap.
    • Exposed keys: About 15% of environments with managed Kubernetes had a workload storing a cleartext long-term cloud key tied to a highly privileged K8s identity.
    • AKS: About 87% use local accounts; the client certificate with CN masterclient maps to cluster-admin; AAD kubeconfig refresh tokens last 90 days by default.
    • GKE: Project-level IAM admin rights can grant full cluster admin unless RBAC restricts them.
    • Registries: Push access to a compromised registry lets attackers overwrite images that new pods will pull.
    • Mitigations: Workload identities and IMDS temporary credentials instead of static keys, private API endpoints, registry controls (ECR tag immutability, ACR private endpoints, GAR per-repo IAM), and no kubeconfigs on exposed hosts.

    Takeaway: Cloud IAM and cluster RBAC are one attack surface. Audit who can reach cluster admin through cloud permissions.

  • Understanding and Cost Optimizing Amazon EKS Control Plane Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog post (September 2022) explaining EKS control plane log types and how to control their CloudWatch cost.

    • Log types: API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager and scheduler, enabled per cluster.
    • Volume: Audit logs usually have the highest volume.
    • Location: CloudWatch log groups under the /aws/eks prefix, one stream set per component.
    • Retention: Default CloudWatch retention is never expire, so set retention per log group.
    • Archival: Export to S3 (one-time or scheduled with Lambda and EventBridge), apply lifecycle rules or Intelligent-Tiering, and query with Athena since Logs Insights no longer applies.
    • Recommendations: Enable log types selectively outside production; in production enable all and manage retention.
    • GuardDuty: Reads EKS audit logs directly and does not need control plane logging enabled.

    Takeaway: Set retention on /aws/eks log groups today. Consider GuardDuty for audit-based threat detection.

  • Cloud IAM: Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: A July 2022 Google Cloud blog post by Priyanka Vergadia explaining Cloud IAM fundamentals.

    • Model: An IAM policy is a set of bindings tying a principal, a role and a resource or hierarchy node.
    • Principals: Domains, Workspace or Cloud Identity users and groups, and service accounts.
    • Roles: Basic (broad, e.g. owner), predefined (per service, safer) and custom (most precise but costly to maintain).
    • Conditions: Limit bindings by time, resource name prefix (e.g. webapp-frontend-), network or secure tags.
    • Service accounts: User-managed (no roles by default), service default (editor at creation) and Google-managed service agents.
    • Keys: Google-managed keys auto-rotate; user-managed keys must be rotated by you; prefer short-lived credentials.
    • Practices: Grant to groups, use app-specific service accounts instead of defaults, and use VPC Service Controls.

    Takeaway: A clear primer for GCP newcomers. Replace default service accounts’ editor role early.

  • How Attackers Can Exploit GCP’s Multicloud Workload Solution
    summary

    TL;DR: A research post by Liv Matan and Noam Dahan (February 2023) showing how misconfigured Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation lets attackers reach GCP service accounts from AWS, Azure or OIDC identities.

    • Moved: The Ermetic URL now redirects to the Tenable blog.
    • Flows: Azure uses an IMDS-issued token exchanged at GCP STS; AWS sends a presigned sts:GetCallerIdentity, visible in CloudTrail with user agent Google-Identity-Federation.
    • Vector 1: Granting a service account to the whole pool lets any provider in the pool (AWS, Azure, GitHub Actions) impersonate it.
    • Vector 2: Attribute conditions are empty by default, so any role in the attached AWS account, or any identity from the OIDC issuer, can federate.
    • Vector 3: iam.workloadIdentityPoolProviders.update (and .create) can let an attacker attach their own AWS account to a victim pool.
    • Mitigations: Least privilege on attached service accounts, custom attribute mappings and conditions (e.g. on sub), Azure app role assignments, and tight control of provider permissions.

    Takeaway: WIF removes static keys but moves the risk into pool configuration. Always set attribute conditions and bind service accounts to specific principals.

  • AWS EC2 IMDS: What You Need to Know
    summary

    TL;DR: A technical review of the AWS EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) by Liv Matan and Lior Zatlavi, comparing IMDSv1 and IMDSv2 and explaining how attackers abuse IMDS to steal instance-role credentials.

    • Source move: The Ermetic URL now redirects to the Tenable blog (Tenable acquired Ermetic); the republished post is dated August 8, 2023.
    • How IMDS works: EC2 assumes the instance-profile role via sts:AssumeRole and exposes temporary credentials on the link-local address 169.254.169.254.
    • IMDSv1 weakness: A plain HTTP GET with no headers to /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<ROLE_NAME> returns credentials, so any SSRF that can issue a simple GET can steal them.
    • IMDSv2: Adds session-token based, layered (“belt and suspenders”) protections; the post explains why to prefer it and how to migrate machines off IMDSv1 responsibly.
    • Residual risk: It walks through a scenario where an instance with IMDSv2 can still be attacked through a vulnerability, so other controls are still needed.

    Takeaway: Enforce IMDSv2 on EC2 and treat SSRF in instance-hosted software as a credential-theft path. Scope instance-role permissions tightly regardless.

  • Introducing KWOK: Kubernetes WithOut Kubelet
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post (March 1, 2023, by Shiming Zhang, Wei Huang and Yibo Zhuang) introducing KWOK, a toolkit that simulates thousands of fake nodes and pods without running kubelets.

    • Components: kwok simulates the lifecycle of fake nodes, pods and other API resources; kwokctl is a CLI to create and manage simulated clusters.
    • Benefits claimed: Near-instant cluster and node creation, works with any Kubernetes API client (kubectl, helm), runs from pre-built images with Docker or Nerdctl, low CPU and memory use.
    • Configurable: Node types, labels, taints, capacities and conditions, plus pod behaviour and status, to test edge cases.
    • Use cases: Learning, developing controllers without a real cluster, scale testing, simulating node failures or network partitions by changing node conditions.
    • Limits: It is not a kubelet; pod lifecycle, volume mounting and device plugins differ, performance is only approximated, and it enforces no security on simulated nodes.

    Takeaway: Use KWOK to scale-test controllers, schedulers and tooling against large fake clusters cheaply. Do not use it to measure real workload performance.

  • Temporary Policy Exceptions in Kubernetes with Kyverno
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF guest post by Chip Zoller (Nirmata) showing how to make Kyverno 1.9 Policy Exceptions expire automatically by combining them with cleanup policies.

    • Policy Exceptions: New alpha feature in Kyverno 1.9 that decouples exclusions from the policy itself, so a separate team can request an exception without editing the policy.
    • Enabling: Must be turned on with a flag; --exceptionNamespace restricts where exceptions can be created, otherwise they are cluster-wide. Gate creation with RBAC at minimum.
    • Validate the exceptions: Since a PolicyException is a custom resource, Kyverno validate rules can stop overly broad exceptions (e.g. exempting all Pods).
    • Expiry mechanism: A generate rule creates a ClusterCleanupPolicy when an exception appears, scheduled with cron, which deletes the exception after four hours in the example.
    • RBAC: Extra ClusterRoles (via aggregation) let Kyverno create clustercleanuppolicies and let the cleanup controller list and delete policyexceptions.

    Takeaway: Useful pattern for break-glass exceptions, such as a troubleshooting Pod needing host namespaces. Check current Kyverno docs, as these features were alpha in 1.9.

  • staticwebsite-cli: Static Website CLI for AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Labs CLI, written in Rust, that deploys a static website to AWS in one command: it hosts the files, sets up CloudFront, DNS and an SSL certificate.

    • Prerequisite: An existing Route 53 hosted zone matching --domain-zone; the repo notes this has cost implications.
    • Usage: staticwebsite_cli --domain-zone demo.com --domain-name rustacean --deploy sample; omitting --domain-name deploys at the zone apex.
    • Under the hood: Creates a CloudFormation stack, uploads to an S3 bucket and invalidates the CloudFront distribution.
    • Credentials: Uses standard AWS CLI profiles or AWS_ACCESS_KEY/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; a minimum policy.json is provided.
    • Distribution: Release builds for Windows, Mac and Linux, or cargo build from source. Updates are done by re-running the command.

    Takeaway: Quick way to put a static site on S3 plus CloudFront with TLS when you already use Route 53. Review the provided IAM policy before use.

  • Considerations for the Security Operations Center in the Cloud: Deployment Using AWS Security Services
    summary

    TL;DR: Second part of an AWS Security Blog series showing how to deploy AWS Security Hub for centralized, decentralized and hybrid Security Operations Center (SOC) operating models.

    • Security Hub role: Cloud security posture management that aggregates findings from AWS services, partner integrations or custom sources in AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF).
    • Centralized model: A dedicated security tooling account acts as delegated administrator via AWS Organizations, with cross-Region aggregation into one Region.
    • AWS SRA: The AWS Security Reference Architecture provides deployable templates for the Security Hub organization setup.
    • Decentralized and hybrid: A separate org root account governs with service control policies, and each OU gets its own Security Hub administration account using the invite model.
    • Example flow: Amazon GuardDuty findings flow into Security Hub so each OU manages its own findings while the organization keeps overall visibility.

    Takeaway: Pick the SOC model to fit your org (skills, compliance, budget) and map Security Hub administration accounts to it. Start from AWS SRA templates.

  • Three Ways to Boost Your Email Security and Brand Reputation with AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post showing how to deploy BIMI, MTA-STS and SMTP TLS reporting for a domain using Route 53, S3, CloudFront and ACM, on top of SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

    • BIMI: Associates a logo with your mail domain; needs a Verified Mark Certificate from a BIMI-qualified CA, stored in S3.
    • MTA-STS: Makes sending servers use TLS with certificate validation when delivering to your domain.
    • TLS reporting: Receives reports on your domain’s TLS posture; SES or WorkMail is suggested only for receiving these reports (April 2023 clarification).
    • Architecture: DNS records in Route 53 point to policy files and logos served from S3 through CloudFront with an ACM certificate; deployed with AWS CDK, whose custom-resource Lambda runtimes will need updating over time.
    • Warnings: Email is brittle; a typo in DNS can silently stop delivery, and DNS caching can delay effects by hours or more than a day.

    Takeaway: Once SPF, DKIM and DMARC are in place, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT are low-cost hardening steps. Roll out carefully and watch for missing mail.

  • Why You Should Migrate to Network Firewall Policies from VPC Firewall Rules
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog post (March 1, 2023) recommending migration from legacy VPC firewall rules to network firewall policies, and introducing a migration tool.

    • Why: Network firewall policies use IAM-governed Tags instead of ungoverned network tags, fit the hierarchical control model, and all new Cloud Firewall features will only ship for policies.
    • Capabilities: Batch editing of rules in one policy, a single resource per VPC, separate IAM permissions for create, update and associate, and sharing across VPCs in a project.
    • Scope: Global or regional network firewall policies; part of the Cloud Firewall Essentials tier at no extra charge.
    • Migration tool: gcloud beta compute firewall-rules migrate --source-network=SOURCE_VPC_NETWORK --target-firewall-policy=TARGET_NETWORK_FIREWALL_POLICY; the target policy must not already exist and logging settings are preserved.
    • Cutover: Swap evaluation order so the new policy is evaluated first, then use firewall logs and hit counts to confirm old rules are shadowed before deleting them.

    Takeaway: Plan the move to network firewall policies, since legacy rules will not get new features. Verify with logging before removing old rules.

  • Submarine Cable Map 2023: View Internet Cables Around Earth
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: TeleGeography’s interactive 2023 edition of its Submarine Cable Map, showing the undersea fibre cables that carry most international internet traffic.

    • Publisher: TeleGeography, a telecom research firm that also maintains the ongoing map at submarinecablemap.com.
    • Format: A JavaScript-rendered interactive map; the fetched page returned only the title “Submarine Cable Map 2023”.
    • Content: The title indicates a world map of submarine internet cables for 2023.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the page title and URL only; the map content itself could not be extracted.

    Takeaway: Handy visual reference for how internet connectivity between continents depends on a limited set of physical cables.

  • Best Practices for Securing Your Home Network
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NSA Cybersecurity Information Sheet “Best Practices for Securing Your Home Network”, published February 22, 2023 and aimed at teleworkers.

    • Devices: Upgrade and update all equipment and software regularly, including routers; use a modern, up-to-date operating system.
    • Wireless: Use WPA3 or WPA2 and segment the wireless network.
    • Accounts: Protect passwords and limit use of the administrator account.
    • Behaviour: Follow email best practices, such as not opening attachments or links in unsolicited email, and use strong authentication.
    • Telework: Covers confidentiality during telework and securing routing devices.
    • Source caveat: The PDF returned HTTP 403; summary is based on the NSA press release and third-party summaries found by web search.

    Takeaway: A short, shareable checklist for staff working from home. Read the full PDF for exact wording.

  • Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy to the Built-In PodSecurity Admission Controller
    summary

    TL;DR: Official Kubernetes task guide for migrating from PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) to the built-in Pod Security Admission controller, using dry-run, audit and warn modes to avoid outages and security gaps.

    • Requirement: Kubernetes v1.22 or later.
    • What PSA lacks vs PSP: It is non-mutating (no default security settings), offers only 3 standard levels, and cannot bind policies per service account or user within a namespace; use mutating or validating webhooks or a third-party tool for those.
    • Namespace labels are the control: Anyone who can create, update or patch a namespace can change its Pod Security level, so restrict those permissions first.
    • Migration steps: Decide fit, review namespace permissions, simplify and standardize PSPs, pick a Pod Security level per namespace, verify it, enforce it, bypass PSP, review namespace creation, then disable PSP.
    • Exemptions: PSA supports static exemptions for specific users or RuntimeClasses only.

    Takeaway: Follow this sequence, especially the dry-run and audit stages, before PSP removal in 1.25. Plan a webhook policy engine if you relied on mutating PSPs.

  • Pod Security Policy (PSP) Removal FAQ
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: AWS EKS user guide FAQ on the removal of PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) in Kubernetes 1.25 and what EKS users need to do before upgrading.

    • Page status: The URL now redirects to the EKS user guide home page; the FAQ appears to have been removed.
    • Default policy: EKS clusters on Kubernetes 1.13 to 1.24 ship a default PSP named eks.privileged, which is no longer relevant from 1.25.
    • Do not delete early: Removing eks.privileged or its ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding before 1.25 stops Pods from starting.
    • Custom PSPs: Any PSPs you created beyond the default must be migrated before upgrading to 1.25.
    • Replacement: Pod Security Admission is stable and enabled by default in EKS 1.25; policy-as-code tools are the alternative.
    • Source caveat: Based on an AWS re:Post answer, AWS EKS best-practices docs and the AWS EKS 1.25 announcement found by web search, not the original FAQ.

    Takeaway: Inventory custom PSPs and move them to Pod Security Admission or a policy engine before upgrading EKS to 1.25.

  • Using Azure Active Directory to Authenticate to Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog walkthrough for letting users log in to Amazon EKS clusters with Azure Active Directory credentials using EKS OIDC identity provider authentication.

    • Two options: AWS IAM Identity Center (if Azure AD already syncs users to it) or direct EKS OIDC authentication; the post covers OIDC.
    • No IAM users: Azure AD authenticates; authorization is native Kubernetes RBAC, so no IAM users or roles are needed.
    • Azure side: Register an app (e.g. eks-auth), record the Application (client) id and Directory (tenant) id, and create users and groups for it.
    • EKS side: Associate Azure AD as the OIDC provider on the cluster, then bind Azure AD groups to Kubernetes Roles and RoleBindings.
    • Client: Users authenticate with kubelogin, a kubectl plugin maintained by Microsoft.

    Takeaway: If your workforce identity lives in Azure AD, this gives corporate SSO to EKS with RBAC tied to AD groups, without managing IAM principals.

  • Lessons Learned While Scaling a Kubernetes Cluster to 1000 Pods in AWS EKS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Medium post (devopslearning, November 2022) on problems encountered when scaling an Amazon EKS cluster to 1000 pods.

    • Topics: AWS resource limits, IP address exhaustion, packet drops and control plane performance.
    • Sizing: Works through a workload estimate for 1000 pods and recommends a /21 subnet for IP capacity.
    • Format: About a 10-minute read.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned HTTP 403 and the archive copy could not be read; summary is based on the search-result snippet only, so details are limited.

    Takeaway: Before scaling EKS, plan subnet size for VPC CNI pod IPs and check AWS service quotas early.

  • Kubernetes Infrastructure at Medium
    summary

    TL;DR: Medium Engineering post by Eduardo (February 2023) giving a high-level view of how Medium runs its micro-services on Kubernetes.

    • Topology: Production runs in four separate Kubernetes clusters, one per availability zone, so traffic can be shifted between AZs with in-house tooling.
    • Safe rollouts: Infrastructure changes are tested by shifting most traffic to the other three clusters while one cluster is changed.
    • Stack: Istio service mesh with in-house controllers for ingress and egress gateways; Terraform plus an in-house templating and apply tool for cluster configuration.
    • Over-provisioning: cluster-overprovisioner pods sized slightly above the burst service’s pods, 50 replicas per cluster (200 pods’ worth across four), are preempted by real pods and trigger cluster-autoscaler scale-up.
    • Results: Node count peaks fell from 800 to 900 nodes to around 400, rarely above 600, after over-provisioning and right-sizing requests.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetch; read from an archive.org copy.

    Takeaway: Priority-based placeholder pods plus right-sized requests are a cheap way to absorb traffic bursts while node scale-up catches up.

  • Flux Subsystem for Argo
    summary

    TL;DR: Flamingo, the Flux Subsystem for Argo (FSA), is an Argo CD image that can also visualize and manage Flux workloads, combining Flux automation with the Argo CD UI.

    • Drop-in: The container image replaces the equivalent Argo CD version; upstream Argo CD CVEs are backported.
    • Extra features: Flux Helm support, Flux OCIRepository, Weave GitOps Terraform Controller, Weave Policy Engine, and Argo CD ApplicationSet for Flux-managed resources.
    • Install: brew install fluxcd/tap/flux and brew install flux-subsystem-argo/tap/flamingo, then flux install and flamingo install --version=v2.8.6.
    • Apps: flamingo generate-app --app-name=podinfo-ks -n podinfo-kustomize ks/podinfo creates an Argo CD app from a Flux Kustomization.
    • Login: flamingo show-init-password, user admin, then port-forward svc/argocd-server.

    Takeaway: Worth a look if teams want the Argo CD UI but you reconcile with Flux. Check the project’s current status and version before adopting.

16.02.2023

  • Securing Lambda Function URLs Using Amazon Cognito, Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Compute Blog post by Madhu Singh and Krupanidhi Jay showing how to protect a Lambda function URL with auth type NONE using Cognito-based checks in code, plus CloudFront, AWS WAF and Shield.

    • Auth modes: Function URLs support IAM or NONE; this pattern uses NONE with custom authorization logic in the function.
    • Cognito: A user pool with the hosted UI handles sign-in; the returned authorization code is stored in a cookie named code and validated by the function.
    • Edge protection: CloudFront in front of the function URL caches content, and AWS WAF web ACLs plus AWS Shield help against application and network DDoS.
    • Demo app: A React site on AWS Amplify works in authenticated and guest modes.
    • Limit: Function URLs are not a replacement for API Gateway, which adds request validation and throttling.

    Takeaway: If you use function URLs publicly, front them with CloudFront and WAF and enforce auth in code. Choose API Gateway when you need throttling or validation.

  • Haekka: Cybersecurity Awareness Training on Slack!
    summary

    TL;DR: Haekka is a commercial microlearning platform that delivers employee training, including security awareness, directly inside Slack.

    • Delivery: Assignments, reminders and full courses (including video) are taken inside Slack without leaving it.
    • Content: Customizable courses for security awareness, HIPAA, privacy, GDPR, PCI, SOC 2, harassment and more; content import from other platforms.
    • Assignment: To individuals, groups, workspaces or channels, plus HRIS, LMS and IAM provisioning options.
    • Reporting: Dashboards and an API for completion and compliance evidence.
    • Current site: Now marketed more broadly (sales enablement, onboarding, “Haekka One”, “Streams”), not only security training.

    Takeaway: An option for teams that live in Slack and need trackable compliance training. Evaluate pricing and content quality with a demo.

  • Improve GitHub Actions OIDC Security Posture with Custom Issuer
    summary

    TL;DR: Aidan Steele explains how GitHub Enterprise Cloud’s unique OIDC token URL puts the enterprise slug in the issuer. An AWS IAM OIDC provider can then trust only your enterprise, not all of GitHub.com.

    • Feature: Tokens carry iss: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<enterprise-slug>. GitHub announced this in August 2022.
    • AWS setup: Create AWS::IAM::OIDCProvider with that URL and ClientIdList: [sts.amazonaws.com]. Roles then trust oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<slug>.
    • Blast radius: A role trust policy missing its sub condition now exposes only repositories in your enterprise, not every GitHub repository.
    • Delegation: This makes it safer to let developers call iam:CreateRole.
    • Still missing: The author still wants more IAM OIDC controls, and full JWT claims in CloudTrail.

    Takeaway: GitHub Enterprise Cloud users should switch to the enterprise-specific issuer. Keep the sub conditions on role trust policies.

  • Hunting for Amazon Cognito Security Misconfigurations
    summary

    TL;DR: Yassine Aboukir’s NahamCon EU 2022 talk, posted December 27, 2022, on common Amazon Cognito security misconfigurations and how to test for them.

    • Format: The blog post embeds the conference video (YouTube) rather than a written article.
    • Scope: Outlines several common misconfigurations in Cognito implementations and techniques to test against them.
    • Speaker: Bug bounty hunter and application security consultant.
    • Audience: Bug bounty hunters and appsec testers assessing apps that use Cognito.
    • Source caveat: The page text is only a short abstract; the specific misconfigurations are in the video, which was not transcribed here.

    Takeaway: Watch the talk before testing or deploying Cognito user pools and identity pools, and check your own configuration against it.

  • Palantir Passwordless Authentication Series
    summary

    TL;DR: A three-part Palantir Blog series (November 2022 to January 2023) on how Palantir rolled out passwordless authentication across the company.

    • Part 1, Hardware Selection and Logistics (Nov 18, 2022): Choosing and distributing authenticator hardware.
    • Part 2, Technical Controls, Rollout & Edge Cases (Dec 1, 2022): The controls used and how the rollout handled exceptions.
    • Part 3, New Hires, Lost Keys & Lessons Learned (Jan 17, 2023): Onboarding, lost-key recovery and lessons from the programme.
    • Format: A Medium tag page listing the three posts.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned HTTP 403; only the tag listing (titles and dates) was read from an archive.org copy, not the article bodies.

    Takeaway: A practical case study to read before planning a hardware-key or passwordless rollout, especially the lost-key and onboarding parts.

  • Leaking Secrets from GitHub Actions: Reading Files and Environment Variables, Intercepting Network/Process Communication, Dumping Memory
    summary

    TL;DR: Karim Rahal (January 5, 2023) shows how a command injection in a GitHub Actions workflow can leak secrets even when they are not exposed in environment variables, by examining the Actions runner internals.

    • Root bug: ${{ github.event.comment.body }} inside run: is not escaped, so a comment like ; whoami executes on the runner.
    • Runner internals: Runner.Listener receives encrypted job messages and launches Runner.Worker; self-hosted runners store an RSA private key in .credentials_rsaparams, which decrypts the AES key for jobs. Decrypted job messages contain all secrets and the job’s GitHub token in the variables field.
    • File reading: Shell steps are rendered with secrets expanded into .sh files under /home/runner/work/_temp, which can be read or continuously exfiltrated for later steps.
    • Other techniques: JavaScript actions receive inputs as environment variables of the Node.js process; the post also covers intercepting network and process communication and dumping memory.
    • Method: Analysis done by proxying a self-hosted runner through Burp Suite and writing a decryption script based on the runner source.

    Takeaway: Any injection in a job exposes every secret that job can reach, not just those in env. Pass untrusted input via environment variables, never ${{ }} in run:, and scope secrets per job.

  • terraform-google-modules: Terraform Modules for Google Cloud by Google
    summary

    TL;DR: The terraform-google-modules GitHub organization (“Google Cloud and HashiCorp”) hosts the Cloud Foundation Toolkit (CFT) Terraform modules for Google Cloud.

    • Size: 65 repositories at fetch time, mostly HCL, Apache-2.0 licensed, and still actively updated.
    • Popular modules: terraform-google-kubernetes-engine (opinionated GKE clusters), terraform-google-project-factory (projects with Shared VPC, IAM and APIs), terraform-google-network, terraform-google-sql-db, terraform-google-vm.
    • Reference foundation: terraform-example-foundation shows how to compose CFT modules into a secure cloud foundation.
    • Other modules: IAM, service accounts, HTTP load balancer, BigQuery, Cloud Logging and Monitoring, event and scheduled Cloud Functions.
    • Docs samples: terraform-docs-samples and docs-examples hold samples used on cloud.google.com and in Google provider docs.

    Takeaway: Start GCP Terraform work from these maintained modules, and use the example foundation as a reference landing zone design.

  • Setting Up a Secure CI/CD Pipeline in a Private Amazon VPC with No Public Internet Access
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS DevOps Blog walkthrough of a CI/CD pipeline that runs inside a private VPC with no internet access, using CodeCommit, CodePipeline, CodeBuild, CodeArtifact and S3.

    • Package source: AWS CodeArtifact serves dependencies for Maven, Gradle, npm, yarn, pip, twine and NuGet, so builds never reach public registries.
    • VPC endpoints: CloudWatch Logs (for CodeBuild logs), CodeArtifact, AWS STS and Amazon S3.
    • Flow: Push to CodeCommit triggers CodePipeline; CodeBuild in private subnets pulls packages through endpoints.
    • Buildspec: Sets AWS_STS_REGIONAL_ENDPOINTS=regional and runs aws codeartifact login --tool npm with Node.js 16.
    • Flexibility: CodePipeline is used, but Jenkins or other CI tools can integrate with CodeArtifact the same way.

    Takeaway: For isolated build environments, route all package and AWS API traffic through VPC endpoints and CodeArtifact. The pattern also works with other CI tools.

  • How to Revoke Federated Users’ Active AWS Sessions
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post on revoking a federated user’s already-issued AWS role sessions, which stay valid after the user is disabled in the identity provider.

    • Problem: Role sessions last 1 hour by default and up to 12 hours, so a user revoked in the IdP keeps access until the session expires.
    • Avoid: Denying all on the role or deleting it disrupts every user of that role.
    • Identifiers: Use principalId (e.g. AROA...:JohnDoe@example.com) or sourceIdentity, both visible in CloudTrail userIdentity records.
    • SCP approach: A deny-all SCP with conditions on aws:userid and aws:SourceIdentity blocks named users across member accounts regardless of session duration.
    • IAM approach: Similar deny statements in IAM policies, plus the option to revoke session tokens; a February 2023 update adds that trust policies can enforce required sourceIdentity values.

    Takeaway: Set sourceIdentity from your IdP and keep session durations short. Keep a ready-made SCP for emergency revocation of a specific user.

  • monokle: Unified Visual Tool for Authoring, Validating and Deploying Kubernetes Manifests
    summary

    TL;DR: Monokle, from Kubeshop, is a desktop tool for authoring, validating and deploying Kubernetes manifests, combining a YAML editor, policy validation and live cluster views.

    • Maintenance status: The README now says Kubeshop is not able to maintain or evolve Monokle, linking issue #4265.
    • Editing: Single IDE for manifests, form-based resource creation, templating system for multi-step forms, refactoring with name and reference integrity.
    • Validation: Real-time checks against YAML formatting and Kubernetes schemas (including installed CRDs), plus OPA policy rules.
    • Cluster: Connects to clusters for real-time state, compares resources with the cluster, and applies changes directly or through pull requests.
    • Templating tools: Previews and debugs Kustomize and Helm output; Git integration for configuration lifecycle.
    • Platforms: Windows, macOS and Linux builds.

    Takeaway: Interesting ideas for visual manifest management, but the project is unmaintained, so do not adopt it for new work.

  • Top 15 kubectl Plugins for Security Engineers
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sysdig list of kubectl plugins useful for Kubernetes security work. The URL now serves a 2025 edition (June 11, 2025) with maintenance status for each plugin.

    • RBAC: access-matrix (formerly rakkess) for a permissions matrix, rolesum for role summaries, rbac-tool for access analysis.
    • Tracing and capture: kubectl-trace (bpftrace), kubectl-capture (Sysdig syscall captures), ksniff (tcpdump and Wireshark), inspektor-gadget (eBPF).
    • Network: np-viewer for network policy visualization, kubectl-cilium.
    • Secrets and auth: kubectl-whisper-secret, kubectl-ssm-secret, kubelogin, cert-manager plugin.
    • Other: kube-policy-advisor for least-privilege policies, stern for multi-pod log tailing.
    • Staleness flagged: Several are marked partially maintained, e.g. kubectl-trace last released 2021, ksniff 2020, kubectl-ssm-secret 2019.
    • Content changed: The page now shows the 2025 edition, not the original 2023 article.

    Takeaway: access-matrix, rolesum and np-viewer are quick wins for audits. Check maintenance and the access you give any plugin before installing it.

  • Canarytokens: Breach Detection Honeypot Tokens, Including Credit Cards
    summary

    TL;DR: Canarytokens, a free service from Thinkst, generates tripwire tokens that alert you when an attacker opens or uses them.

    • Concept: “Motion sensors” for networks, computers and clouds, designed to look attractive to attackers so they get touched.
    • Token types: Includes AWS API keys, Azure login certificate, credit card, kubeconfig, MS Word and Excel, PDF, DNS, HTTP and web image, cloned website, SQL Server, MySQL dump, QR code, WireGuard, Windows directory, Log4Shell and MCP configuration tokens.
    • Footprint: No software to install and no background processes.
    • Relation: A distilled, free version of Thinkst’s commercial Canary product.
    • Source caveat: The /generate page is a JavaScript app; details come from the Canarytokens documentation site.

    Takeaway: Cheap, high-signal breach detection. Plant fake AWS keys or kubeconfigs where an intruder would look, such as CI variables, laptops and repos.

  • git-sim: Visually Simulate Git Operations in Your Own Repos with a Single Terminal Command
    summary

    TL;DR: git-sim, from Initial Commit, visually simulates Git commands on your own repo before you run them, by prefixing the command with git-sim instead of git.

    • Usage: pip install git-sim, then e.g. git-sim merge dev, git-sim reset --hard HEAD^, git-sim rebase main.
    • Output: Now a web-first, shareable interactive graph by default; animated video with --animate needs Manim.
    • Requirements: Python 3.10 to 3.14 and Git; minimal Linux needs libEGL, libGL and fontconfig.
    • Newer features: VS Code extension, Jupyter integration, a GitHub Action describing PR merges, live recording of repo operations, and a preflight check for risky Git commands from AI agents.
    • Content changed: The README has grown well beyond the 2023 Manim-based image and video simulator.

    Takeaway: Useful for teaching Git or checking what a rebase or reset will do before running it.

  • Caido: Lightweight Web Security Auditing Toolkit, Alternative to Burp/ZAP
    summary

    TL;DR: Caido is a web security auditing toolkit and intercepting proxy, positioned as an alternative to Burp Suite and ZAP, for bug bounty hunters, pentesters and security engineers.

    • Querying: HTTPQL syntax to search and filter requests and responses.
    • Automation: Node-based workflows built ad hoc; headless, API-first proxy for security engineers.
    • AI (current site): “Bring your own model” plugins with Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and others via OpenRouter, plus a Client SDK for AI agents.
    • Community figures (site claim): 7,000+ active hackers, 58+ community plugins, 4,500+ Discord members.
    • Content changed: The homepage now emphasises AI and team features, unlike its 2023 “lightweight” positioning.

    Takeaway: Worth trialling as a faster, scriptable Burp alternative. Compare feature tiers on the pricing page before switching.

  • Security Drone: Scaling Continuous Security at Revolut
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Revolut’s Application Security Team describes Security Drone, an internal tool built to keep security checks scalable in a fast-moving CI/CD environment.

    • Context: Every new feature is checked, using automated scans in CI/CD pipelines.
    • Scale: Nearly 39,000 commits from over 900 authors in July 2022.
    • Problem: Scanners produced many false positives that security staff had to review by hand.
    • Goal: Security Drone was built to keep a high security bar despite fast deployments.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned HTTP 403; based on an FF News summary (January 2023) found by search, which does not describe how the tool works.

    Takeaway: At high commit volume, the bottleneck is triaging scanner output, so invest in automating that, not only in adding more scanners.

  • AWS Service Control Policies
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A post in the Cloud Security publication on Medium about AWS Service Control Policies (SCPs), the AWS Organizations guardrails that cap what accounts can do.

    • What SCPs are: Organization-level policies that set the maximum permissions for users, roles and root users in member accounts; they do not grant permissions.
    • Scope: Applied to the organization root, OUs or accounts.
    • Risk: Overly strict denials can disrupt development work.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned HTTP 403 and no copy was found; these bullets are based on the title and general SCP guides found by search, not on the article itself.

    Takeaway: Read the original if you can reach it. In general, use SCPs for a few broad deny guardrails and test them on a sandbox OU first.

  • security-response-automation: Take Automated Actions Against Threats and Vulnerabilities in Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: Security Response Automation, from Google Cloud Platform, runs automated remediation of Security Command Center findings with Cloud Functions. The repository is archived and no longer maintained.

    • Pipeline: Findings from SCC (or legacy Cloud Logging) go to Pub/Sub, then a Filter function, then a YAML-configured Router, then remediation functions.
    • False positives: The Filter can apply Rego (Open Policy Agent) policies to mark expected findings as false positives and set them INACTIVE.
    • Automations: CloseBucket, CloseCloudSQL, ClosePublicDataset, CloudSQLRequireSSL, DisableDashboard, EnableAuditLogs, EnableBucketOnlyPolicy, IAMRevoke, OpenFirewall, RemovePublicIP, SnapshotDisk, UpdatePassword.
    • Controls: Least-privilege service account, per-project enforcement, all actions logged to Cloud Logging, and a monitor-only mode.
    • Notifications: Can notify PagerDuty, Slack or email.

    Takeaway: Use it as a reference design for SCC auto-remediation, not as a dependency, since it is archived.

  • containerdbg: All-in-One CLI to Debug Kubernetes Containers with Common Issues
    summary

    TL;DR: containerdbg, from Google, is a CLI and DaemonSet that finds common problems when legacy applications are moved into Kubernetes containers. It is archived (snapshot of May 13, 2025).

    • Missing files: Tracks failed file opens to find files left out of the image, with special handling for *.so, *.py and *.rb.
    • EXDEV moves: Detects move or rename failures caused by overlay filesystem copy-and-delete on base-image files.
    • Network: Logs failed connections and failed DNS queries for services missing from the deployment.
    • Static IPs: Warns about connections not preceded by a DNS lookup, which suggest hard-coded IPs.
    • Install: Pre-built v0.0.9 binaries for Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64.

    Takeaway: The checks are a good checklist for lift-and-shift containerization. Do not rely on the tool itself, as it is archived.

  • security-guard: Runtime Security Plug to Protect User Containers
    summary

    TL;DR: Security-Guard is a Knative project that protects microservices and serverless containers by detecting and blocking exploits sent to services, and by detecting and restarting compromised pods.

    • Repo move: The URL now redirects to knative-extensions/security-guard.
    • guard-gate: Usually a sidecar in front of each service that monitors and can block requests and responses.
    • Guardian: A per-service CRD or ConfigMap of micro-rules for fine-grained filtering of each value sent to or from the service.
    • Learning: guard-service auto-learns micro-rules; guard-ui helps configure them by hand.
    • Indicators: Alerts on out-of-pattern requests and responses, unusually long service times, and the list of external IPs a pod contacts.
    • Platforms: Integrated into Knative and also usable on plain Kubernetes.

    Takeaway: An interesting learned-behaviour approach to runtime protection for HTTP services. Evaluate maturity and overhead before production use.

  • Slack bot which promotes Defense in Depth/Zero Trust security practicesAA
  • imaginAIry: Pythonic Generation of Stable Diffusion Images
    summary

    TL;DR: imaginAIry is an MIT-licensed Python library and CLI by Bryce Drennan for generating Stable Diffusion images, and now also videos, with a “just works” install on Linux and macOS (M1).

    • Install and run: pip install imaginairy, then imagine "a scenic landscape" "a photo of a dog"; on macOS install Rust first.
    • Python: README says use Python 3.10; 3.11 was not supported at the time of writing.
    • Video: aimg videogen --start-image rocket.png uses Stable Video Diffusion models (svd, svd_xt and decoders); Nvidia GPUs only, not Mac or CPU.
    • Video options: --num-frames, --fps, --motion-amount (0 to 255), --seed and others.
    • Platform caveat: Windows works “sometimes” and needs torch 2.0 installed first.
    • Content changed: The README now leads with video generation, added after the 2023 link date.

    Takeaway: A simple way to script local image generation from Python or the shell. Check the current model support and Python version before installing.

  • 10 Things I Hate About Go
    summary

    TL;DR: A video from the Boldly Go channel in which a Go fan lists ten things about the language he dislikes.

    • Error handling: Go’s error handling (0:00 intro, 1:12).
    • Stdlib design: Exported variables in the standard library, and http.Handler not returning an error.
    • Language quirks: No pointers to literals, loop variable semantics, naked returns, relative imports.
    • Tooling: gofmt’s format and comment directives.
    • Terminology and style: Array vs slice terminology, and pure functions.
    • Reference: Links Dave Cheney’s post on constant errors.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video description and chapter list, not a transcript.

    Takeaway: A useful list of Go gotchas for people new to the language. Check each point against the current Go release, as some may have changed since 2023.

  • Enhancing Kubernetes Security with User Namespaces
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz Research examines Linux user namespaces (alpha in Kubernetes v1.25), how they limit container escapes, where they add risk, and which workloads can use them.

    • UID remapping: Each pod gets 64K host UIDs, so UID 0 in the container maps to a non-zero host UID (e.g. 65536); an escaped root process cannot read /etc, /dev, root’s home or the kubelet kubeconfig.
    • Examples: Would have broken the Azurescape exploit chain; lets workloads needing SYS_ADMIN (gcsfuse mounts) or NET_ADMIN (OpenVPN) avoid host-level privilege.
    • Other benefits: Better separation between pods on a node and separate UID-bound limits, such as filesystem notifications shared by many UID 1000 pods.
    • Risk: Userns grants namespaced CAP_SYS_ADMIN, opening kernel code paths such as CVE-2022-0185; block unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) with seccomp (default seccomp profile went beta in 1.25).
    • Compatibility data: In environments Wiz studied, over 30% of pods use host-shared namespaces, 44% mount problematic volumes, 24.4% are privileged and 1.8% allow privilege escalation.
    • Testing: Done on GKE alpha clusters, the only managed option at the time.

    Takeaway: User namespaces are a strong mitigation for container escape where workloads are compatible. Pair them with a seccomp profile and use the post’s decision tree to pick candidates.

  • A Guide to Running Sigstore Locally
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sigstore blog guide by Felix Wolff and Andrew Block (January 24, 2023) to running a private Sigstore deployment on Kubernetes (minikube) for organisations that cannot use the public instance.

    • Why private: The public Rekor transparency log is permanent and public; for example, GitHub OIDC provenance baked into certificates is visible to anyone.
    • Monitoring: The authors stress that a private log without monitoring delivers no value.
    • Deployment: Components installed via the Sigstore project’s Helm charts, using the scaffold chart.
    • Clients: cosign, or a Kyverno policy controller that checks Rekor before admitting an image.
    • Tool versions used: minikube 1.28.0, helm 3.10.0, kubectl 1.25.2, cosign 1.13.1, ko 0.12.0, Go 1.19.1 on macOS Intel.

    Takeaway: Consider a private Sigstore when signing internal artifacts would leak repo or workflow names. Budget for operating and monitoring it.

  • Provisioning Kubernetes Clusters on GCP with Terraform and GKE
    summary

    TL;DR: A Learnk8s tutorial by Kristijan Mitevski (January 2023), part 3 of 4 in a series, on creating GKE clusters with the gcloud CLI and with Terraform, ending with automated dev, staging and prod clusters.

    • Site move: The URL now redirects to learnkube.com.
    • GKE basics: Google manages API servers, etcd, control-plane scaling, upgrades and certificate rotation for USD 0.10 per hour per cluster.
    • Ingress: The GKE Ingress controller is enabled by default; load balancers add extra charges.
    • Approaches compared: Web console (discouraged as not repeatable), gcloud, and Terraform, with pros and cons.
    • Outcome: Terraform modules build three environments with GKE Ingress “in a single click”; also covers a Hello World deployment and kubeconfig tricks.

    Takeaway: A clear step-by-step path from first GKE cluster to module-based multi-environment Terraform. Check provider and GKE versions against current docs.

  • dynamodb-shell: ddbsh, a Simple CLI for DynamoDB Modeled on isql and the MySQL CLIs
    summary

    TL;DR: ddbsh, from AWS Labs, is a command-line shell for DynamoDB modelled on isql and the MySQL CLI, accepting SQL-like DDL and DML commands.

    • Interface: Interactive prompt where SQL-like commands run against DynamoDB and results print in the same window.
    • Warning: Provided as-is, not supported for production; drops and deletes are irreversible, and scans or queries consume capacity and can cost a lot.
    • Safety advice: Restrict APIs with DynamoDB fine-grained access control and try DynamoDB Local first.
    • Rewrite in progress: Being reimplemented as a C++23 library (libddbsh) plus thin CLI, version 0.9.19 at fetch time; global tables are the remaining unsupported family.
    • Build: Needs a C++23 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, flex, bison, readline, zlib and the AWS SDK for C++.

    Takeaway: Handy for exploring tables with familiar SQL-style syntax in development. Keep it away from production credentials.

  • Accessing Cloud SQL Using Private Service Connect
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog post (January 24, 2023) describing a workaround to reach Cloud SQL through Private Service Connect (PSC) across VPCs and projects, now marked deprecated for Cloud SQL.

    • Deprecation note: Since April 18, 2024, Cloud SQL supports PSC natively (GA), and this approach is deprecated for Cloud SQL.
    • Problem: Consumers in other VPCs or projects cannot rely on VPC peering because Cloud SQL does not support transitive peering, and peering needs IP range planning.
    • Design: The database team exposes the database via a service attachment; app teams use PSC endpoints in their own VPC (e.g. 172.168.32.2:3306); many-to-many consumers and producers are possible.
    • Wider use: The workaround also applies to other PSA-dependent services without native PSC, such as Memorystore and AlloyDB.

    Takeaway: For Cloud SQL, use native PSC now. The pattern may still help for managed services that only support Private Service Access.

  • Recommendations to Mitigate OWASP API Security Top 10 Threats Using Azure API Management
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft Learn article giving Azure API Management recommendations for each OWASP API Security Top 10 risk, now updated to the 2023 list.

    • Scope: Applies to all API Management tiers.
    • Complementary services: Defender for APIs, Azure API Center, Front Door, Application Gateway and WAF, DDoS Protection, Monitor and Log Analytics, Key Vault and Microsoft Entra.
    • Example risk: Broken object level authorization, where weak or iterable object identifiers allow data leaks or manipulation.
    • Structure: One section per OWASP API risk with matching API Management controls.
    • Content changed: Updated from the 2019 list to the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023.

    Takeaway: Use it as a checklist when hardening APIs behind Azure API Management. Remember that object-level authorization must still be enforced in the backend.

  • automated-security-helper: ASH, the Automated Security Helper
    summary

    TL;DR: ASH (Automated Security Helper) is an AWS tool that runs several open-source scanners over code, infrastructure-as-code and IAM configuration early in development.

    • Repo move: The URL now redirects to awslabs/automated-security-helper.
    • Scanners: Bundles open-source tools such as Bandit, Checkov and Semgrep, isolated via UV.
    • ASH v3: Rewritten in Python; runs in local, container or precommit mode; YAML or JSON config with CLI overrides.
    • Reports: SARIF, JSON, HTML, Markdown and CSV; pluggable scanners and reporters.
    • AI integration (newer): An MCP server and plugins for AI coding agents.
    • Positioning: Not a replacement for human review or security standards.

    Takeaway: A quick way to run a curated set of free scanners locally or in CI with one command. Tune findings before gating builds on them.

  • capital: Built-to-Be-Vulnerable API Application Based on the OWASP Top 10 API Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: c{api}tal, by the Checkmarx research team, is an intentionally vulnerable blogging API with 10 challenges mapped to the OWASP API Security Top 10, for training and CTFs.

    • Stack: FastAPI backend and React frontend, with a Medium-style blogging UI.
    • Run: docker-compose up -d; backend on http://localhost:8000/, frontend on http://localhost:4100/, API docs at /docs.
    • Tooling: OpenAPI 3 spec importable as a Postman collection; use Postman or Burp against /api.
    • Auth: JWT token authentication with adjustable lifetime.
    • License: AGPL v3; educational purpose.

    Takeaway: Good hands-on practice for API testing skills or an internal CTF. Run it only in an isolated environment.

  • caretta: Instant K8s Service Dependency Map, Right to Your Grafana
    summary

    TL;DR: Caretta, from groundcover, is an Apache 2.0 tool that builds a live service dependency map of a Kubernetes cluster using eBPF and shows it in Grafana.

    • How it works: An eBPF agent maps all service network interactions; Grafana queries and visualizes the data, with no cluster changes needed.
    • Install: helm repo add groundcover https://helm.groundcover.com/ then helm install caretta --namespace caretta --create-namespace groundcover/caretta.
    • Config values: tolerations so the agent runs on all nodes, victoria-metrics-single.server.persistentVolume.enabled for persistent metrics (default false), and pollIntervalSeconds.
    • Footprint: Described as lightweight and standalone; install in its own namespace.
    • Background: groundcover’s blog post explains how it is built.

    Takeaway: A quick way to see who talks to whom in a cluster, useful for drafting network policies or onboarding to an unknown system.

  • How Adversaries Can Persist with AWS User Federation
    summary

    TL;DR: CrowdStrike Services (Vaishnav Murthy and Joel Eng, January 30, 2023) describe attackers using sts:GetFederationToken to create federated sessions that survive deactivation of the compromised IAM user’s access keys.

    • Technique: With valid IAM user keys and STS and IAM permissions, the attacker calls sts:GetFederationToken; the federated session inherits the user’s permissions.
    • Why containment fails: Temporary STS credentials are independent of the long-term keys, so deactivating keys does not revoke the session; it lasts until the token expires.
    • What works: Attach an explicit deny-all IAM policy to the compromised user, since reducing that user’s policies also reduces the session’s rights.
    • Deleting the user: It revokes privileges, but CrowdStrike does not recommend it, for reasons given in the post.
    • Root keys: If a root API key is compromised, containment is much harder and may not be possible; AWS discourages root access keys.
    • Escalation: Attackers can use the technique to persist and escalate if the base user had escalation privileges.

    Takeaway: Add “attach deny-all policy” to your AWS incident runbooks, not just key deactivation. Alert on GetFederationToken calls.

  • CloudGPT: Use ChatGPT to Analyze AWS Policies for Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudGPT is a short Python gist by ustayready (January 16, 2023) that pulls IAM role policies with boto3 and asks OpenAI whether each has security vulnerabilities.

    • Collection: Paginates list_roles and list_attached_role_policies, then fetches the default version via get_policy and get_policy_version.
    • Analysis: Sends each policy to OpenAI text-davinci-003 with the prompt “Does this AWS policy have any security vulnerabilities” (temperature 0.5, 500 max tokens).
    • Output: Prints role name, policy ARN, the policy document and the model’s answer.
    • Setup: requirements.txt with boto3 and openai; API key hard-coded in the script.
    • Limits: Only managed policies attached to roles; the text-davinci-003 model and old openai.Completion API it calls are dated. A commenter asks how it compares to IAM Access Analyzer.

    Takeaway: A proof of concept, not a scanner. Use IAM Access Analyzer or policy linters for real checks, and consider what policy data you send to a third-party API.

  • gato: GitHub Self-Hosted Runner Enumeration and Attack Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: Gato (GitHub Attack TOolkit), from Praetorian, enumerates and attacks GitHub Actions pipeline weaknesses, especially self-hosted runners. The repo is archived and superseded by Praetorian’s Trajan.

    • Status: Deprecated; no further updates or security patches. Trajan combines Gato (GitHub Actions) and Glato (GitLab) in one maintained tool.
    • Enumeration: Workflow file and run-log analysis to find repos with vulnerable self-hosted runner setups at scale.
    • Post-exploitation: Uses a compromised personal access token to explore an organization’s public and private repos.
    • Poisoned pipelines: Identifies poisoned pipeline execution vulnerabilities.
    • Artifacts scanner (v1.7): Downloads and extracts workflow artifacts and scans them for secrets with NoseyParker.
    • Requirements: Python 3.7+; NoseyParker on $PATH for the artifact scanner.

    Takeaway: Run Trajan, or Gato’s ideas, against your own org to find exposed self-hosted runners and leaky artifacts. Keep self-hosted runners off public repos.

  • production-readiness-checklist: Gorrion Production Readiness Checklist
    summary

    TL;DR: A production readiness checklist from software house Gorrion, as a table of items with severity level, scope and a linked doc for each.

    • Security: Meet OWASP ASVS level 1, at least a “B” grade on securityheaders.com, JWT secret only on the server, CORS limited to client domains, no stack traces in client errors.
    • TLS and domains: Frontend and backend on the client’s domain with TLS, HTTP redirected to HTTPS, apex redirected to www.
    • Operations: Error, uptime and logging systems, backups, auto-scaling, production-grade hosting for app and database.
    • Process: Deploy via CI, run tests and audits in CI/CD, quick hotfix path, one source of truth for cron jobs, versioning and changelog.
    • Governance: Share passwords only via a password manager, and keep a written risk management and disaster recovery plan.

    Takeaway: A compact go-live checklist for web apps that you can copy and adapt into a release template.

  • envless: Open-Source, Frictionless and Secure Way to Share and Manage App Secrets Across Teams
    summary

    TL;DR: Envless was an open-source tool for sharing and managing application secrets across teams. The repo is archived and the maintainers recommend Dotenv instead.

    • Status: Archived; README says it is not actively maintained and may be picked up again later.
    • Purpose: Store and share API keys, passwords and certificates among authorized team members.
    • Claims: Encryption and access control so only authorized members can read secrets.
    • Targets: Containers, serverless functions and traditional servers, with support for many languages.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt it for new work. Look at maintained secret managers instead.

  • Kubestroyer: Exploit Kubernetes Cluster Misconfigurations, the Swiss Army Knife of Kubernetes Pentests
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubestroyer is an MIT-licensed Go tool by Rolix44 that scans for exposed Kubernetes ports and exploits common misconfigurations, for use in pentests.

    • Install: Pre-built binaries, go install github.com/Rolix44/Kubestroyer@latest, or build from source (Go 1.19).
    • Targets: -t accepts IPs, domains or a file, e.g. -t localhost,127.0.0.1.
    • Scanning: Known Kubernetes ports with descriptions; --node-scan covers NodePorts 30000 to 32767.
    • Kubelet RCE: --anon-rce uses anonymous kubelet API auth; -x sets the command (defaults to printing the service account token).
    • etcd: --etcd reads objects when anonymous etcd access is enabled.

    Takeaway: Use it to check that kubelet anonymous auth and etcd are not exposed. Only run it against clusters you are authorised to test.

  • exploitation-course: Offensive Security & Reverse Engineering (OSRE) Course
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub user ashemery’s free Offensive Security and Reverse Engineering (OSRE) course, originally taught at Champlain College in Spring 2020/21, with labs and YouTube recordings.

    • Materials: Slides largely shared via the HTID course on OpenSecurityTraining; labs written by the author.
    • Vulnerable software: From Exploit-DB and Stephen Bradshaw’s VulnServer.
    • Tools: Immunity Debugger, Kali Linux, CFF Explorer, PE-bear, Ghidra, IDA Free, x64dbg, Sysinternals, FLARE capa, NetCat.
    • Target VM: A Windows 10 VM from Microsoft (version 1809 build 17763.1339).
    • Scope note: Not all modules were covered due to time; the full course is under course/2021.

    Takeaway: A free, structured route into Windows exploitation and reverse engineering with hands-on labs.

  • computer-science: Path to a Free Self-Taught Education in Computer Science!
    summary

    TL;DR: Open Source Society University’s free, self-taught computer science curriculum built from online courses, often from Harvard, Princeton and MIT.

    • Course criteria: Open for enrollment, run regularly (ideally self-paced), high quality, and aligned with the CS 2013 curriculum guidelines; a book fills gaps.
    • Structure: Intro CS, Core CS (roughly the first three years of a degree), Advanced CS electives, and a peer-reviewed Final Project.
    • Duration: About 2 years at roughly 20 hours per week; a spreadsheet helps estimate an end date.
    • Scope: Undergraduate CS major requirements, minus general education.
    • Extras: High-quality material outside the core goes in extras/courses and extras/readings.

    Takeaway: A good reference to fill gaps in CS fundamentals, even if you only take selected courses.

  • Go: Profile-Guided Optimization Preview
    summary

    TL;DR: Go blog post by Michael Pratt (February 8, 2023) introducing profile-guided optimization (PGO) as a preview in Go 1.20.

    • Idea: Feed a CPU profile from production to the compiler so it can optimise hot functions more aggressively; Go 1.20 uses it for inlining.
    • Usage: go build -pgo=<profile> or -pgo=auto to use default.pgo in the main package; commit default.pgo to the repo.
    • Default: In 1.20 the default is -pgo=off; the post expects a future version to default to auto.
    • Example: A Markdown-to-HTML service profiled via net/http/pprof; benchstat shows 393.8µs vs 383.6µs per op, about 2.6% faster.
    • Typical gain: 2% to 4% CPU improvement in Go 1.20 workloads.
    • Caveat: Described as having rough edges that may prevent production use at the time.

    Takeaway: PGO is a cheap win: collect a representative profile, commit it as default.pgo and rebuild. Re-collect profiles as code changes.

  • New: Visualize Your VPC Resources from Amazon VPC Creation Experience
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS News Blog announcement of the Amazon VPC resource map, which shows an existing VPC’s resources and routing as a diagram in the console.

    • Where: VPC console, select a VPC, then the Resource map tab.
    • Shows: Subnets, which subnets use the public route table, which route tables route to a NAT gateway, and links to each resource.
    • Interaction: Hovering highlights related resources and connections; clicking shows details.
    • Background: Extends the March 2022 VPC creation experience, which removed more than 90 percent of manual steps but only showed the diagram during creation.

    Takeaway: Use the resource map for a quick sanity check of routing and subnet layout when reviewing or troubleshooting a VPC.

  • GitHub Actions: Updating the Default GITHUB_TOKEN Permissions to Read-Only
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub changelog (February 2, 2023): the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission for GitHub Actions changes from read/write to read-only for new enterprises, organizations and repositories.

    • Reason: Read/write by default was too permissive.
    • Existing setups: Not affected; existing enterprises, orgs and repos keep their current setting.
    • New defaults: New enterprises, non-enterprise orgs and personal-account repos get read-only; new orgs and repos inherit from their parent enterprise or org.
    • Override: You can still switch to read/write.

    Takeaway: Check older orgs and repos, which keep read/write, and set the default to read-only. Grant extra scopes per workflow with permissions:.
