  • Kubernetes Hands-On Introduction (2023): Amazon EKS Workshop
    summary

    TL;DR: A “Containers from the Couch” livestream in which Justin Garrison and Sai Vennam walk through the redesigned Amazon EKS Workshop hands-on.

    • Workshop: eksworkshop.com, with source at github.com/aws-samples/eks-workshop-v2.
    • Setup: Creating the workshop environment with Terraform (9:00).
    • Managed node groups: Adding nodes, then affinities and anti-affinities (18:17, 29:20).
    • Fargate: Running pods on Fargate (45:35).
    • Networking: Exposing applications with the AWS Load Balancer Controller (59:20).
    • Storage: Amazon EBS and EFS (1:16:52).
    • Source caveat: Based on the video description and chapter list, not a transcript.

    Takeaway: A guided video companion to the EKS Workshop, useful if you prefer following along to reading the labs.

  • How to Rapidly Scale Your Application with ALB on EKS (Without Losing Traffic)
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog post showing how to remove 50x errors during scale-down of an app behind an ALB on EKS, by combining a health endpoint, readiness probe and PreStop hook.

    • Test setup: A Django logistics app with the AWS Load Balancer Controller and Cluster Autoscaler; at peak 623 simulation pods on 30 t4g.xlarge nodes.
    • Health endpoint: A separate /logistics/health set via alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path, with healthcheck-interval-seconds: '3' and success-codes: '200-301'.
    • Readiness probe: Same path, periodSeconds: 3.
    • PreStop hook: Makes the health endpoint fail and then sleep 120, so the ALB removes the target before the container gets SIGTERM.
    • Results: 504 errors during scale-down went from an average of 340 to zero; 502 errors from 200 to 30, and those 30 were seen by kubelet, not end users.
    • Code: Full deployment artifacts in an aws-samples repository.

    Takeaway: For any ALB-fronted EKS service, align ALB health checks with readiness and add a PreStop delay so pods drain before termination.

  • Amazon Detective Adds Amazon VPC Flow Logs Visualizations for Amazon EKS Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (January 23, 2023) that Amazon Detective now visualizes VPC Flow Logs for Amazon EKS workloads, aggregated by pod.

    • Questions answered: Which ports and services EKS workloads used, whether there were large data transfers, and which IPs connected.
    • Data source: Detective collects VPC flow logs automatically; previously flow log views covered only EC2 instances.
    • Requirement: Enable EKS audit logs as a data source in the Detective behavior graph.
    • Cost: First 30 days of EKS audit logs as a data source are free for existing accounts; new accounts get it in the 30-day trial, with an estimated post-trial cost shown in the console.
    • Where: Network visualizations appear in the profile panel for EKS pods; available in all Detective Regions, including GovCloud (US).

    Takeaway: If you use Detective, enable the EKS data source to speed up investigations of suspicious pod network activity. Check the cost estimate after the trial.

  • Introducing the Amazon EKS Workshop
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announces the fully redesigned Amazon EKS Workshop, replacing the old one (now at archive.eksworkshop.com).

    • Modules: Networking, Security, Cost Optimization, DevOps Automation and more, each split into standalone labs (e.g. Karpenter in Cost Optimization).
    • Tenets: Modular, one consistent sample app (AWS Containers Retail Sample), EKS-focused, and continuously tested.
    • Infrastructure: Prerequisites deployed with Terraform (v1.3.x at launch), chosen because many EKS customers already use it.
    • Audience: Users with a basic understanding of containers and Kubernetes; the “Learn Kubernetes and EKS” playlist on Containers from the Couch is the suggested primer.
    • Requirements: An AWS account with administrative permissions.

    Takeaway: A good structured way to learn EKS features hands-on. Run it in a sandbox account and tear it down afterwards.

  • Optimizing Your Kubernetes Compute Costs with Karpenter Consolidation
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers Blog post demonstrating Karpenter’s workload consolidation, which repacks pods onto fewer, cheaper nodes to cut compute cost.

    • Change: Earlier Karpenter only removed nodes with no non-DaemonSet pods; consolidation also removes or downsizes underutilized nodes.
    • Enable: consolidation: enabled: true in the karpenter.sh/v1alpha5 Provisioner; it is mutually exclusive with ttlSecondsAfterEmpty.
    • Requirement: Set CPU and memory requests on pods so consolidation works well; scheduling constraints such as topology spread are honoured.
    • Demo: 20 replicas at 1 CPU each led to 3 Spot nodes (2 x t3.2xlarge, 1 x c6a.2xlarge) across eu-west-1a/b/c; scaling to 10 replicas removed one node.
    • Tools: EKS Blueprints for Terraform for setup, eks-node-viewer for live cost, and kubecost suggested for production cost monitoring.

    Takeaway: Turn on consolidation with accurate requests for easy savings. The post uses the alpha v1alpha5 Provisioner API, so check current Karpenter docs for the syntax.

  • Scale from 100 to 10,000 Pods on Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: OLX Autos engineers (with AWS) describe scaling the single EKS cluster behind their internal developer platform ORION from 100 to over 10,000 pods, running 100+ non-prod environments on 100% Spot instances.

    • DNS ndots: With EKS’s default ndots of 5, a lookup for amazon.com produced 7 DNS questions; CoreDNS crashed under load.
    • Fix: Appending a trailing dot (amazon.com.) in endpoint environment variables cut questions from 7 to 2 with 0 NXDOMAIN, over 70% fewer CoreDNS queries; NodeLocal DNSCache improved it further.
    • CPU limits: Limits caused throttling that worsened DNS latency, so they rolled CPU limits back to defaults.
    • IP starvation: VPC CNI defaults reserved 58 IPs per c5.9xlarge node, exhausting the VPC; tuning MINIMUM_IP_TARGET, WARM_IP_TARGET and WARM_ENI_TARGET helped.
    • Trade-off: WARM_IP_TARGET=1 fixed starvation but caused IP allocation races and pod start delays when many pods were scheduled at once.
    • Debug: kubectl exec <aws-node-pod> -c aws-node -- curl localhost:61679/v1/enis shows assigned and available IPs.

    Takeaway: At high pod density, check ndots and DNS caching, CPU limits and VPC CNI warm-IP settings first. Read the full post for the final CNI settings they chose.

  • On Amazon EKS and Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Dirk Michel (January 2023) surveys how AWS-native security services help protect Amazon EKS clusters and their surrounding AWS resources.

    • Grouping: Identity and access management, data protection, logging and detective services, infrastructure security, and incident response.
    • Identity: IAM authenticates to the EKS API and Kubernetes RBAC authorizes; workforce users federated via IAM Identity Center (e.g. AD with ADFS via AD Connector and SAML2); workloads use IRSA; IAM roles map to RBAC through aws-auth.
    • Data at rest: KMS customer-managed keys for EBS, EFS, RDS and Backup Vaults, with key policy conditions like viaService.
    • Secrets: EKS can envelope-encrypt Kubernetes Secrets in etcd with a KMS key if set at cluster creation; otherwise they are only base64-encoded. Secrets Manager plus the Secrets Store CSI Driver for external secrets.
    • In transit: ACM certificates on ALB and NLB provisioned through the AWS Load Balancer Controller.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetch; read from an archive.org copy, partially.

    Takeaway: A useful map of which AWS service covers which EKS security concern. Use it to spot gaps such as missing Secrets envelope encryption.

  • EKS Security Best Practices: Practical Enforcement Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: A Datree guide that turns the AWS EKS Best Practices Guide for Security into 14 policy rules and shows how to check and enforce them with Datree’s admission webhook.

    • Site status: The datree.io URL no longer responds; read from an archive.org copy.
    • Rules: Include read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, no service account token auto-mounting, limited capabilities, equal memory request and limit, replicas on different nodes, read-only hostPath mounts, and SELinux and Windows privilege limits.
    • Install: helm install -n datree datree-webhook datree-webhook/datree-admission-webhook --set datree.policy=EKS with a Datree token, in monitor mode first.
    • Posture score: Example dashboard shows 48% of resources failing 6 rules.
    • Remediation example: Fix privilege escalation by setting allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in the securityContext.
    • Enforcement: Then switch to blocking misconfigured resources at admission.

    Takeaway: The rule list is a handy checklist. Since Datree appears to be gone, implement the same rules in Kyverno, Gatekeeper or Pod Security Admission.

  • werf CI/CD Tool Becomes a CNCF Project!
    summary

    TL;DR: Dmitry Shurupov announces (February 2023) that werf, the CI/CD CLI originally created at Flant, has become a CNCF Sandbox project.

    • What werf does: CLI for delivery to Kubernetes that assumes Git, builds images with Buildah, embeds and extends Helm, and works with any CI, with built-in GitLab CI/CD and GitHub Actions integrations.
    • Practices: Advanced build caching, “Giterminism” (Git as single source of truth for reproducibility), content-based tagging, better Helm resource tracking, and cleanup of unused images.
    • History: Open source since its start seven years earlier; began as a Docker image build tool at Flant.
    • CNCF effect: CNCF owns the project with open governance; the same core maintainers continue.
    • Audience: Teams replacing DIY build-and-deploy scripts, and beginners wanting a ready path to Kubernetes delivery.
    • Source caveat: Medium-hosted blog blocked direct fetch; read from an archive.org copy.

    Takeaway: Consider werf if you want an opinionated Helm-based pipeline with reproducible builds and image cleanup built in.

  • The Efficient Way to Publish Multi-Arch Containers from GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Ellis (February 1, 2023) explains how to build and publish multi-arch (Intel and Arm) container images from GitHub Actions with buildx, using the inlets-operator as the example.

    • Site move: Now served from actuated.com.
    • Manifests: A multi-arch image is a manifest list with one entry per platform; inspect it with crane manifest.
    • Dockerfile changes: FROM --platform=${BUILDPLATFORM:-linux/amd64}, plus ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH, and GOOS=${TARGETOS} GOARCH=${TARGETARCH} go build so Go cross-compiles instead of emulating.
    • Workflow: docker/setup-qemu-action@v2, docker/setup-buildx-action@v2, then docker/build-push-action@v4 with platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm/v6,linux/arm64.
    • Registry auth: Push to GHCR with GITHUB_TOKEN, which needs permissions: packages: write.
    • Without Actions: The same can be done with docker buildx create --use and the Docker CLI.

    Takeaway: Cross-compile in the builder stage rather than relying on QEMU for the whole build; it is much faster for Go and similar languages.

  • Manage Multi-Cloud Resources with Crossplane: Rise Above the Clouds
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: An Upbound video, “Manage Multi-Cloud Resources With Crossplane - Rise Above The Clouds”, on using Crossplane and Upbound to manage resources across multiple clouds.

    • Channel: Upbound, the company behind Crossplane.
    • Question posed: How to manage resources spread across multiple clouds, and “rise above clouds” with Crossplane and Upbound.
    • Tools named: Crossplane and Upbound’s offering are the two products covered, per the title and description.
    • Source caveat: Only the one-line video description was available; no transcript or chapters, so specifics of the demo are unknown.

    Takeaway: Watch it if you are evaluating Crossplane as a Kubernetes-native alternative to Terraform for multi-cloud provisioning.

19.01.2023

  • Cloud Native Landscape
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s interactive Cloud Native Landscape, a categorized map of cloud native projects and products.

    • Publisher: CNCF.
    • Format: A JavaScript-rendered interactive page; the fetch returned only the title “CNCF Landscape”.
    • Use: Browsing cloud native tools by category when surveying options in an area.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the page title and URL only; the categories and entries could not be extracted.

    Takeaway: A starting point for finding candidate tools in a category. Check each project’s maturity and activity separately.

  • hardeneks: Harden EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: hardeneks, from AWS Samples, is a Python CLI that checks a running EKS cluster against the EKS Best Practices Guide.

    • Install: pip install hardeneks in a virtualenv, then run hardeneks.
    • Targeting: --region, --context, --cluster, --namespace, plus --insecure-skip-tls-verify.
    • Reports: --export-txt, --export-csv, --export-html, --export-json, and --export-security-hub to send failed checks to AWS Security Hub.
    • Config: --config file selects rules and ignores namespaces such as kube-system or karpenter.
    • Example checks: check_endpoint_public_access, restrict_wildcard_for_cluster_roles, check_default_deny_policy_exists, use_encryption_with_ebs, deploy_workers_onto_private_subnets, ensure_namespace_psa_exist, use_immutable_tags_with_ecr, plus reliability checks.

    Takeaway: A quick way to audit an EKS cluster against AWS’s own guidance and push the findings into Security Hub.

  • lnav: Log File Navigator
    summary

    TL;DR: lnav (Logfile Navigator) by tstack is a terminal log viewer that auto-detects formats, merges files by time and lets you query logs with SQLite.

    • Ingest: Decompresses files, detects format, merges multiple files into one time-ordered view, tails and follows renames, and finds new files in directories.
    • Navigation: e/E jump to next or previous error, / regex search, :highlight, and P to pretty-print structured text.
    • Analysis: Filter with regex or SQLite expressions, i for a histogram over time, ; for SQL queries.
    • JSON: Pretty-prints JSON-lines logs.
    • Try it: ssh playground@demo.lnav.org or ssh tutorial1@demo.lnav.org before installing.
    • Why not tail, grep, less: They do not order multiple files by time, return full multi-line messages or handle compressed files.

    Takeaway: Worth installing on any box where you read logs. The SQL interface makes ad hoc incident analysis much faster than grep.

  • Learning by Auditing Kubernetes Manifests
    summary

    TL;DR: The author of blog.frankel.ch ran Checkov over the Kubernetes manifests of his demos and writes up the rules he broke and what each taught him.

    • Command: checkov -d infrastructure/kube/ --quiet --compact | grep CKV | sort --unique lists unique failed rules.
    • Digests: CKV_K8S_43 prefers image digests to tags, because tags are mutable pointers.
    • Privilege escalation: CKV_K8S_20; by default a child process can gain more privileges than its parent, so set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.
    • securityContext: CKV_K8S_30 (low severity, but he considers it essential), covering runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, seccompProfile, fsGroup and more.
    • Other rules: CKV_K8S_23 (avoid root containers), CKV_K8S_40 (high UID to avoid host conflict), CKV_K8S_31 (seccomp RuntimeDefault).
    • Context: Some rules, such as requests and limits, he chose to ignore for demos.

    Takeaway: Running a scanner like Checkov over your manifests is a fast way to learn Kubernetes hardening defaults. Fix the privilege-escalation and securityContext findings first.

  • Cloud Penetration Testing: Not Your Typical Internal Penetration Test
    summary

    TL;DR: The sethsec blog author (December 15, 2022) describes, in nine playful “levels”, how an experienced internal pentester learns that assumed-breach cloud testing is very different.

    • Levels 1 to 3: From running nmap against a VPC /16, to using IAM credentials and the AWS API to enumerate EC2 IPs, to finding more attack surface via Route 53 records (EKS, ECS, API Gateway, ELB).
    • Level 4, IAM privesc: e.g. ec2:RunInstances plus iam:PassRole, or a service role that can assume other roles; cites Spencer Gietzen and IAM Vulnerable.
    • Level 5, secrets: Secrets in S3 objects, Kubernetes secrets, Lambda environment variables or EC2 user data.
    • Levels 6 and 7: Thinking in attack graphs and cross-account role trusts; CI/CD tooling without RBAC often holds production admin credentials.
    • Levels 8 and 9: Big differences between cloud providers, and accepting that attack surface depends on each org’s specific services.

    Takeaway: For cloud pentests, start from the cloud API and IAM, not the network. Always review CI/CD tooling access and secrets.

  • Kubernetes 1.26: Introducing Validating Admission Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post by Joe Betz and Cici Huang (December 20, 2022) introducing alpha validating admission policies in 1.26, which use CEL expressions as an in-process alternative to validating webhooks.

    • Problem with webhooks: Each needs a binary to build, deploy, monitor and upgrade, and an unavailable webhook can make the control plane unavailable.
    • Policy: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1alpha1) with matchConstraints and CEL validations, e.g. object.spec.replicas <= 5 for Deployments.
    • Binding: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding scopes the policy, e.g. to namespaces labelled environment: test.
    • Parameters: paramKind lets policies read configurable values from a custom resource.
    • Rationale: The authors found most production webhooks perform simple checks that CEL can express.

    Takeaway: For simple validation rules, CEL policies remove a whole webhook deployment. Check the current API version, since this was alpha in 1.26.

  • Kubernetes v1.26: GA Support for Kubelet Credential Providers
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubernetes blog post by Andrew Sy Kim and Dixita Narang (December 22, 2022): kubelet credential provider plugins are GA in v1.26, letting kubelet fetch image registry credentials dynamically through exec plugins.

    • Before: Until v1.20, dynamic credentials were compiled into kubelet and only for ECR, ACR and GCR; other registries needed kubelet code changes.
    • Timeline: Alpha in v1.20, GA in v1.26.
    • Protocol: kubelet runs the plugin binary, sends a CredentialProviderRequest on stdin and reads a CredentialProviderResponse on stdout as JSON.
    • Caching: The plugin can set cacheDuration (e.g. 6h) and cacheKeyType (e.g. Image) to control reuse of credentials.
    • Ecosystem: Any cloud provider or vendor can publish a plugin for their registry.

    Takeaway: Use credential provider plugins instead of long-lived imagePullSecrets for private registries where a plugin exists.

  • confidant: Open Source Secret Management Service from Lyft
    summary

    TL;DR: Confidant, from Lyft, is a secret management service that stores secrets in DynamoDB, encrypted at rest. The repository was archived on February 14, 2025.

    • Status: Read-only; no new pull requests, issues, features or updates, though existing releases stay downloadable.
    • Storage: Secrets kept in DynamoDB, encrypted at rest.
    • Docs: Installation, configuration and usage guides at lyft.github.io/confidant.
    • Security reports: Sent to security@lyft.com.

    Takeaway: Of historical interest as an AWS-native secret store design. For new work, use a maintained secrets manager.

  • kube-exec-controller: Admission Controller and kubectl Plugin to Handle Container Drift in K8s Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: kube-exec-controller, from Box, is a validating admission webhook. It detects container drift caused by kubectl exec, attach, cp and similar interactive requests, then evicts the touched Pods after a set interval.

    • Deployment: It runs as a Deployment and is wired in through a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. A demo is in demo/, deployed with make deploy.
    • Labeling: Interacted Pods get labels such as box.com/podInteractorUsername and box.com/podTTLDuration, plus Kubernetes events.
    • kubectl plugin: kubectl-pi (pod-interaction) lists interacted Pods and can extend their eviction time.
    • Requirements: Docker 17.05+ and Kubernetes 1.16+. Kind is used for local development.
    • Goal: Pods that someone changed by hand are replaced, so running state goes back to the declared image.

    Takeaway: This gives you an audit trail and automatic cleanup for break-glass shell access. It fits clusters where exec is allowed but drift is not.

  • Architecting Your Security Model in AWS for Legacy Application Migrations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Architecture Blog post with guidelines for giving phased legacy and mainframe migrations secure access to both on-premises and AWS resources, by turning mainframe-style authority into a role-based IAM model.

    • Problem: Migrations run in phases over years, so apps need access to databases, file storage and shared services on both sides at once.
    • Legacy model: Mainframe control facilities identify users and grant authority through privileges tied to a unique identifier. In AWS this becomes an IAM role the application assumes.
    • Federation: An on-premises IdP (the post names Okta and Ping) federates to AWS with SAML 2.0 or OIDC, so on-premises apps get IAM role credentials.
    • Credential options: SAML federation fits per-user or service-account access. IAM Roles Anywhere exchanges X.509 certificates for temporary credentials for service accounts.
    • No long-term keys: The post advises against IAM user access keys because they stay valid until removed.
    • Principles: Zero Trust concepts, central identity control, guardrails and fine-grained access for workforce and applications.

    Takeaway: Map each legacy surrogate identity to an IAM role, and get temporary credentials through SAML federation or IAM Roles Anywhere instead of static keys during the hybrid period.

  • AWS CIRT Announces the Release of Five Publicly Available Workshops
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) released five free workshops that simulate the security events it handles most often, and teach the tools and steps it uses to detect and investigate them.

    • Unauthorized IAM credential use: A script run in AWS CloudShell performs reconnaissance and privilege escalation. You then hunt for the evidence.
    • Ransomware on S3: CloudFormation builds IAM users and five S3 buckets. A bash script then simulates exfiltration and deletion.
    • Cryptominer events: Three EC2 instances make DNS requests to known cryptomining domains.
    • SSRF on IMDSv1: A vulnerable web app on EC2 leaks instance credentials through server-side request forgery.
    • CIRT toolkit: Hands-on use of the tools CIRT uses daily to find misconfigurations and respond to events.
    • Services covered: GuardDuty, CloudTrail, CloudWatch, Athena, AWS WAF, plus open source CIRT tools. You only need an AWS account.

    Takeaway: These are a cheap way to rehearse AWS incident response. Run them in a sandbox account before you need the skills in a real incident.

  • Kubernetes v1.26: Advancements in Kubernetes Traffic Engineering
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post by Andrew Sy Kim (Google) on three v1.26 traffic features: Service internal traffic policy (GA), EndpointSlice terminating conditions (GA), and proxy terminating endpoints (beta).

    • Problem fixed: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, load balancers could drop traffic during rolling updates when a node held only terminating Pods.
    • ProxyTerminatingEndpoints: Now on by default in kube-proxy. It routes to terminating Pods based on readiness when nothing else is left on the node.
    • Health check change: kube-proxy fails the health check NodePort when only terminating Pods remain. The load balancer stops sending new connections, and existing ones drain.
    • EndpointSlice conditions: New serving and terminating conditions. serving acts like ready but can stay true while a Pod terminates.
    • Internal traffic policy: internalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps in-cluster traffic on node-local endpoints.
    • Caveat: The page flags the article as more than one year old.

    Takeaway: On 1.26 or later, Services that use externalTrafficPolicy: Local should lose far less traffic during rollouts. Check that your load balancer health check interval is short.

  • kamaji: Build and Operate Kubernetes at Scale with a Fraction of Operational Burden
    summary

    TL;DR: Kamaji, from CLASTIX, is a Kubernetes Control Plane Manager. It runs tenant control planes as Pods in a management cluster (hosted control planes), not on dedicated machines.

    • APIs: Two CRDs. TenantControlPlane (tcp, namespaced) defines a control plane. Datastore (cluster-scoped) holds state for one or more clusters.
    • Speed claims: The README says Tenant Control Planes are ready in 16 seconds, and version rollouts take 10 seconds with Blue/Green deployment.
    • Resources: Decoupling the datastore removes the need for odd-numbered RAFT instances. The README claims up to 60% hardware savings.
    • Automation: Certificates come from kubeadm and rotate automatically. It also manages kube-proxy, CoreDNS and konnectivity, and remediates them if deleted.
    • Datastores: Several control planes can share one datastore. Through kine, backends other than etcd can be used.
    • Exposure: Control planes can be exposed as ClusterIP, LoadBalancer or NodePort, with normal Pod scheduling options.

    Takeaway: Consider Kamaji if you run many clusters and want control planes managed as cheap, reconciled workloads. Test datastore sharing and upgrades before production use.

  • pgwatch2: PostgreSQL Metrics Monitor and Dashboard
    summary

    TL;DR: pgwatch2, from CYBERTEC, is a self-contained PostgreSQL metrics monitoring and dashboard tool built on Grafana. It is now archived in favour of the newer pgwatch repository.

    • Status: The README says pgwatch2 is in archived mode and points to github.com/cybertec-postgresql/pgwatch.
    • Coverage: Monitors PostgreSQL 9.0 to 16 out of the box. Base functionality needs no extensions or superuser rights.
    • Quick start: docker run ... -p 3000:3000 -p 8080:8080 cybertec/pgwatch2-postgres:latest exposes Grafana on 3000 and an admin UI on 8080.
    • Metrics: Metrics are defined in plain SQL. Many dashboards come preconfigured for Statistics Collector data.
    • Storage backends: PostgreSQL (with or without TimescaleDB), InfluxDB, Graphite and Prometheus.
    • Integrations: PgBouncer, Pgpool-II, AWS RDS and Patroni. A Helm chart and Kubernetes/OpenShift templates are included.

    Takeaway: pgwatch2’s ideas still apply, such as SQL-defined metrics and non-superuser monitoring. New deployments should use its successor, pgwatch.

  • State of Azure IAM 2022
    summary

    TL;DR: David Okeyode’s own December 2022 analysis of Azure IAM over the year. His main points are that permissions grow fast, new features open new persistence paths, and built-in roles remain heavily over-privileged.

    • Growth: 2,710 permissions were added in the year, for 16,210 in total. 60 built-in roles were added, about 5 a month, for 377 in total.
    • Risky new permissions: Microsoft.ContainerService/fleets/listCredentials/action (AKS Fleet Manager) could expose credentials for many clusters. Microsoft.Network/bastionHosts/createShareableLinks/action could backdoor VMs.
    • Feature churn: 389 Azure updates, 193 preview and 196 GA. SFTP for Blob Storage and RBAC for Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) both allow data-plane local accounts, which could be used for persistence.
    • Built-in roles dominate: 87% of assignments use built-in roles. These hold almost twice as many permissions as custom roles, and they gain new permissions without review.
    • Over-privilege: The most used roles are Contributor, Owner, Storage Blob Data Contributor, Billing Reader and Virtual Machine Contributor. Only 0.83% of permissions granted through built-in role assignments were used in the last 60 days.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy of the article.

    Takeaway: Prefer scoped custom roles over broad built-in ones. Review new GA features for data-plane identities that could become persistence paths.

  • kube-exec-controller: Admission Controller and kubectl Plugin to Handle Container Drift in K8s Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: kube-exec-controller, from Box, is a validating admission webhook. It detects container drift caused by kubectl exec, attach, cp and similar interactive requests, then evicts the touched Pods after a set interval.

    • Deployment: It runs as a Deployment and is wired in through a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. A demo is in demo/, deployed with make deploy.
    • Labeling: Interacted Pods get labels such as box.com/podInteractorUsername and box.com/podTTLDuration, plus Kubernetes events.
    • kubectl plugin: kubectl-pi (pod-interaction) lists interacted Pods and can extend their eviction time.
    • Requirements: Docker 17.05+ and Kubernetes 1.16+. Kind is used for local development.
    • Goal: Pods that someone changed by hand are replaced, so running state goes back to the declared image.

    Takeaway: This gives you an audit trail and automatic cleanup for break-glass shell access. It fits clusters where exec is allowed but drift is not.

  • Awesome ChatGPT Prompts
    summary

    TL;DR: prompts.chat began as “Awesome ChatGPT Prompts”, a community list of ChatGPT prompts by Fatih Kadir Akın (github.com/f/prompts.chat), released on December 5, 2022. The site has since grown into a much broader prompt platform.

    • Origin: The site calls itself the first prompts library, released December 5, 2022. Greg Brockman and Wojciech Zaremba of OpenAI praised it in December 2022.
    • Now: The page markets itself as a free, open source “social platform for AI agents” with prompts, skills, workflows and bots. It can be self-hosted.
    • Scale: The site claims about 175k GitHub stars. It also claims to be the most liked dataset on Hugging Face and to have 40+ academic citations.
    • Clients: A command-line client, an App Store app and a Raycast extension are offered.
    • Content changed: The current page shows newer content, such as a 2026 email security guardrails prompt, not the original 2022 list.

    Takeaway: It is useful as a large, searchable prompt catalogue. Treat community prompts as starting points to review, not trusted instructions.

  • Scott Piper on the Challenges of Rolling Out YubiKeys in Practice
    summary

    TL;DR: An October 2022 thread by Scott Piper. He argues that moving a company to FIDO2/YubiKey enforcement is mostly planning work, not “buy yubikeys”, and that neither Yubico nor Okta help with that planning.

    • Context: A reply to Panther’s post about rolling out FIDO2 with Okta.
    • Vendor gap: He asked Yubico for migration help on a 10,000-key purchase and got none. Okta support helped only with Okta configuration.
    • Device questions: Which laptops support FIDO2 (MacBook TouchID, Chromebook Titan)? What about phones, people with several laptops, or replaced devices?
    • Recovery questions: What happens with a lost laptop, a lost key, or a laptop forgotten at home? How do onboarding and time-limited exceptions work?
    • Coverage gaps: Some apps and VPNs do not support FIDO2. Virtual desktops such as Amazon WorkSpaces break the flow. Some apps need SSO onboarding or pricier licenses.
    • Policy questions: Is the key company property or the employee’s? Does TouchID differ from a YubiKey or a cheap FIDO2 key? Expect privacy objections to fingerprints.
    • Follow-up: Eric Rubin linked a GitLab blog post that answers many of these questions.

    Takeaway: Use the thread as a checklist before a phishing-resistant MFA rollout. Recovery and exception processes are the real work.

  • AWS Phishing: Four Ways
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy collects AWS-specific phishing vectors beyond generic credential theft, with prevention and detection ideas for each. A fifth vector, SES phishing, was added in October 2023.

    • Credential phishing: Fake AWS sign-in pages, some of which capture TOTP or SMS MFA, plus hijacked search ads. Mitigation: WebAuthn everywhere and email provider protections.
    • Device code phishing: AWS SSO OIDC device authorization lets an attacker get an SSO token valid for 8 hours. Hardware MFA does not stop it.
    • Device code detection: Block device.sso.{region}.amazonaws.com links at the mail gateway. Alert on sso-oidc:CreateToken from different IPs, or unusual sso:ListAccountRoles volume. The post notes PKCE support changed the signals.
    • CloudFormation stack phishing: Launch Stack URLs prefill a malicious template. Mitigate by disabling CloudFormation with an SCP if unused, or restricting cloudformation:TemplateUrl.
    • ACM email validation phishing: ACM sends domain validation mail to WHOIS contacts and to addresses such as admin@ and webmaster@. Attackers can abuse that approval flow.
    • Further reading: Each section links research from Expel, Rhino Security Labs, Cado and others.

    Takeaway: Add device code and Launch Stack phishing to your threat model. Use DNS validation for ACM, and restrict template sources.

  • SES-pionage: Detecting SES Abuse
    summary

    TL;DR: Permiso (Nathan Eades, January 2023) reports that leaked long-lived AWS keys are often used first against SES, not IAM. The post describes how attackers check SES and which CloudTrail events to alert on.

    • Trigger case: An October 2022 investigation traced an AKIA key leaked on public GitHub. It was followed by SES calls GetAccount, ListServiceQuotas and ListIdentities.
    • Why SES: Attackers get free bulk mail from a trusted sender, and the victim pays the bill.
    • Sandbox limits: A sandboxed account can send only to verified addresses, at most 200 messages per 24 hours and 1 per second. Attackers check for this first.
    • Recon calls: GetSendQuota, GetAccount and ListServiceQuotas reveal sandbox status. ListIdentities plus GetIdentityVerificationAttributes find verified senders.
    • Enablement calls: UpdateAccountSendingEnabled and GetAccountSendingEnabled check whether the account can send.
    • Detection: Alert when long-term (AKIA) keys make these SES calls. The post lists Permiso’s own alert IDs and an appendix on SES email defense.

    Takeaway: Add CloudTrail alerts for SES recon calls from long-lived keys. A leaked key will likely touch SES early.

  • Detecting Anomalous AWS Sessions from Temporary Credentials, Part 1 of 2
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of a two-part Uptycs series (Andre Rall, December 2022). It explains AWS temporary credentials, how to recognise them in CloudTrail, and how STS issues them, as groundwork for detecting compromised sessions.

    • Key prefixes: Long-term access key IDs start with AKIA and never expire. Temporary ones start with ASIA and include a sessionToken in CloudTrail.
    • Lifetime: Temporary credentials usually last 15 minutes to 12 hours.
    • STS APIs: GetSessionToken, AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AssumeRoleWithSAML and GetFederationToken.
    • GetSessionToken: Needs no IAM permission, and no policy can block it. Its credentials can call only AssumeRole and GetCallerIdentity among STS APIs. It is typically used for MFA-protected calls.
    • AssumeRole: Credentials take the role’s permissions and cannot call GetFederationToken or GetSessionToken. The example is an EC2 instance profile.
    • Framing: The post cites a Gartner estimate that 75% of security failures will stem from poor identity management by 2023. Part 2 covers Uptycs’ ITDR product.

    Takeaway: This is a solid primer on which STS call produced a session. That knowledge is a prerequisite for spotting stolen ASIA credentials in CloudTrail.

  • Cedar: A New Policy Language from AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: A One Cloud Please post (January 2023) introduces Cedar, the AWS policy language behind Amazon Verified Permissions and AWS Verified Access. It covers why AWS built it, its syntax, and how it evaluates policies.

    • Why new: IAM policies depend on AWS constructs such as ARNs. Cedar is general purpose, so it can authorise non-AWS applications.
    • Design: Built by the Amazon automated reasoning team in Rust. It evaluates in milliseconds and is designed so tools can prove two policies equivalent.
    • Syntax: permit(principal == User::"John", action == Action::"view", resource) when { ... };. The effect is permit or forbid, with optional when or unless conditions.
    • Entities: Written as Type::"id" and can be namespaced. Actions must use the Action keyword.
    • Evaluation: Any matching forbid denies the request. Otherwise at least one permit must match, or the default is deny.
    • Availability then: At the time of writing, Cedar was not open source or downloadable, only offered in a playground and the two services.
    • Name: It follows IAM’s internal policy language, “Balsa”.

    Takeaway: This is a good primer if you are weighing Cedar for application authorisation. Check its current open source status, since the post predates any release.

  • Improve GitHub Actions OIDC Security Posture with Custom Issuer
    summary

    TL;DR: Aidan Steele explains how GitHub Enterprise Cloud’s unique OIDC token URL puts the enterprise slug in the issuer. An AWS IAM OIDC provider can then trust only your enterprise, not all of GitHub.com.

    • Feature: Tokens carry iss: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<enterprise-slug>. GitHub announced this in August 2022.
    • AWS setup: Create AWS::IAM::OIDCProvider with that URL and ClientIdList: [sts.amazonaws.com]. Roles then trust oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<slug>.
    • Blast radius: A role trust policy missing its sub condition now exposes only repositories in your enterprise, not every GitHub repository.
    • Delegation: This makes it safer to let developers call iam:CreateRole.
    • Still missing: The author still wants more IAM OIDC controls, and full JWT claims in CloudTrail.

    Takeaway: GitHub Enterprise Cloud users should switch to the enterprise-specific issuer. Keep the sub conditions on role trust policies.

  • Responding to an Attack in AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of a three-part case study by Cado Security and Invictus Incident Response (January 2023). They investigate an unknown AWS super-user account with CloudTrail, jq and Splunk.

    • Trigger: An account audit found an unrecognised new admin user, DevOps3.
    • Acquisition: The open source Invictus-AWS script lists the logging that is enabled and pulls every available log (CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, S3 access logs) into an S3 bucket.
    • Processing: jq -r '.Events[].CloudTrailEvent' extracts the events. They load into Splunk with sourcetype cloudtrail_json and a props.conf that has INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS = json and TIMESTAMP_FIELDS = eventTime.
    • Findings: DevOps1-bpvbp created the account through the console on 26-10-2022 at 21:29:03, from 185.195.232.111. A ConsoleLogin six minutes earlier showed that user had no MFA.
    • Pivot: DevOps3 did nothing after its creation, which suggests it was meant for persistence. The creating user ran an SSM StartSession in the same minute.
    • Method: Follows the incident handling phases, with this part focused on acquisition, processing and analysis.
    • Source caveat: The page blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy.

    Takeaway: This is a practical walk-through of CloudTrail triage. Pivot from the suspicious identity to its creator, then to that creator’s other activity.

  • Cloud Native and Kubernetes Security Predictions 2023
    summary

    TL;DR: Andrew Martin of ControlPlane lists security predictions for cloud native and Kubernetes in 2023, from supply chain CVEs to eBPF, VEX, Rust in the kernel and the legal exposure of CISOs.

    • Supply chain: CVE counts and supply chain attacks keep rising. The post cites the PyTorch attack at Christmas 2022 and typosquatting on PyPI and NPM.
    • Reachability: Tools such as Semgrep Supply Chain, Snyk Priority Score and CodeQL judge whether a vulnerable code path is reachable.
    • Kubernetes complexity: CRDs and RBAC complexity keep growing. Platform engineering adds secure-by-default guardrails on top.
    • Identity: Credential theft continues while zero trust adoption is slow. Attackers will use AI and ML better than defenders.
    • Tech trends: eBPF powers new networking, security and observability projects. SBOM demands grow, VEX sees early adoption, and confidential computing gets tested.
    • Other calls: The first Rust module in the Linux kernel, server-side WebAssembly after Docker’s alpha driver, insurers descoping ransomware, and CISOs carrying legal responsibility.

    Takeaway: This is a 2023 snapshot of where cloud native security attention was heading. Supply chain reachability and VEX are the parts to act on.

  • How to Connect to Kubernetes Clusters Using HashiCorp Boundary
    summary

    TL;DR: A HashiCorp blog post (Van Phan and Ravi Panchal, January 2023) on giving remote users identity-based access to Kubernetes through HCP Boundary. Vault issues short-lived service account tokens on demand, so none sit on laptops.

    • Prerequisites: An HCP Boundary cluster, Vault (self-managed or HCP), and a Kubernetes cluster such as EKS or AKS.
    • Cluster prep: A vault namespace with a service account, ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding. Uses kubectl create token vault -n vault on Kubernetes 1.24+.
    • Vault: vault secrets enable kubernetes plus kv-v2. The cluster CA is stored at secret/k8s-cluster. Role auto-managed-sa-and-role has a 10-minute token TTL.
    • Boundary token: A boundary-controller policy and vault token create -orphan -period=20m.
    • Credential store: A Vault credential store with two libraries, kubernetes/creds/auto-managed-sa-and-role (POST) and secret/data/k8s-cluster (GET), attached to a TCP target on port 443.
    • Connect and verify: kubectl get pod --tls-server-name kubernetes --server=https://127.0.0.1:$PORT through the Boundary session. The test account could list pods but not nodes.

    Takeaway: Brokering kubectl through Boundary with Vault-minted tokens removes long-lived kubeconfigs. The pattern carries over to other managed clusters.

  • azure-security-survival-kit: Azure Security Survival Kit
    summary

    TL;DR: Azure Security Survival Kit, from O3 Cyber, is a Bicep template that centralises Azure logs and deploys a minimum set of threat detections. It was inspired by Victor Grenu’s AWS Security Survival Kit.

    • Log sources: Management Group activity, Azure Activity, and Azure AD sign-in and audit logs. Exporting AD logs requires an Azure AD P1 or P2 license.
    • Alerts: Azure Monitor Scheduled Query Rules, one per detection.
    • Detections: ConditionalAccessModified, RunCommandInvoked, VMDiskSnapshotGenerated, VMPasswordResetInvoked, BastionShareableLinkCreated and ElevatedAccessToggleInvoked.
    • Scope: Deploys at Management Group level, so management group operations such as Elevated Access Toggle are logged too.
    • Deploy: Edit main.parameters.json (location, resource group, subscription, management group, notification email), then run az deployment mg create --template-file ./main.bicep ....
    • Limits: The authors say this is a bare minimum. For comprehensive detection they recommend Sentinel and a more rigid process.

    Takeaway: This is a quick baseline for small Azure estates without Sentinel. The six detections also make a good list of Azure persistence and abuse techniques to watch.

  • Amazon RDS Announces Integration with AWS Secrets Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS announcement (December 22, 2022): Amazon RDS can now fully manage the master user password in AWS Secrets Manager, including automatic rotation.

    • What changes: RDS creates and stores the master password in Secrets Manager when instances are created, modified or restored.
    • Rotation: Regular automatic rotation is built in, so you no longer need custom Lambda rotation functions.
    • Exposure: Administrators do not see the password in plaintext during database creation.
    • Encryption: Use your own KMS key or the one Secrets Manager provides.
    • Scope: Covers RDS and Aurora. Supported engines, versions and Regions are listed in the user guides.

    Takeaway: Turn on managed master passwords for new RDS and Aurora instances. Drop custom rotation Lambdas where the managed option covers your engine.

  • Updated Whitepaper Available: AWS Security Incident Response Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post announcing a major update of the AWS Security Incident Response Guide whitepaper. The guide now explains more clearly what to do before, during and after a security event.

    • New intro: A “Key differences of incident response on AWS” section lists six core differences from on-premises incident response.
    • Standards alignment: Restructured to follow NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2.
    • Operations section: Detection, analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, with a summary table of response techniques.
    • Preparation table: A checklist of actions to take before an event, to assess your current state.
    • Post-incident: A framework and a list of questions for learning from incidents.
    • Suggested use: Read the whole guide, check off preparation items you already have, then plan short-term and long-term roadmaps for the gaps.

    Takeaway: Use the preparation table as a gap assessment for your AWS incident response program, and revisit it as services change.

  • Eliminate Kubernetes Node Scaling Lag with Pod Priority and Over-Provisioning
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog walkthrough that hides the 1 to 2 minute node provisioning lag on EKS. It keeps low-priority dummy pause pods as spare capacity, which real workloads preempt.

    • Mechanism: Dummy pods run a pause container at the lowest priority. When a higher-priority pod is pending, kube-scheduler evicts a dummy pod and places the real one at once.
    • Autoscaling: Evicted dummy pods go pending, so Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds a node in the background.
    • Sizing: A static replica count does not scale with large clusters. The post uses cluster-proportional-autoscaler to size the dummy deployment by node and vCPU count.
    • Demo: A high-priority Nginx service with HPA plus a low-priority dummy service.
    • Scope: Applies to EKS on EC2, not Fargate. Estimated cost is about $40 in us-west-2, at level 400.
    • Trade-off: You pay for idle capacity in exchange for faster scaling.

    Takeaway: Use priority-based over-provisioning for latency-sensitive or spiky workloads. Size the headroom to your scale-up rate, not to a fixed count.

  • Authenticate to Amazon EKS Using Google Workspace
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog walkthrough for signing in to Amazon EKS with Google Workspace identities. It uses Dex as the OIDC provider, because Google’s OIDC ID token does not include group claims.

    • Why Dex: Dex’s Google connector pulls group membership from the Google Directory API through a service account.
    • Prerequisites: An EKS cluster, a DNS domain with ACM certificates for dex.example.com and login.example.com, Google Workspace admin access, eksctl and helm.
    • Google setup: An internal OAuth consent screen with email, profile and openid scopes. A web OAuth client with redirect https://dex.example.com/callback.
    • Service account: Domain-wide delegation with only the admin.directory.group.readonly scope. The post says other scopes break group lookups.
    • Example groups: admins@example.com and readonlygroup@example.com, mapped to Kubernetes RBAC.
    • IAM still used: Cluster components such as kubelet keep authenticating through AWS IAM.

    Takeaway: If your company runs on Google Workspace, this gives group-based kubectl access without IAM users. Dex becomes another critical component to run and secure.

  • On Amazon EKS and Cost Optimisation
    summary

    TL;DR: Michel Dirk’s long Medium post (December 2022) on seven levers for cutting Amazon EKS costs. It argues that cost optimisation is continuous FinOps work, not a one-time task.

    • 1. Purchase options: On-Demand, Spot, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans. Compute Savings Plans suit dynamic fleets better than RIs, because nodes from autoscalers fall out of RI coverage.
    • 2. Flexible compute: A node autoscaler is needed unless everything fits on Fargate. The post favours Karpenter.
    • 3. Right sizing: Managed Node Groups make right-sizing nodes hard.
    • 4. Consolidation: Karpenter consolidation removes or replaces nodes using pricing and bin-packing data. It disrupts Pods, so plan for availability.
    • 5. Graviton: Arm-based Graviton instances, including Graviton3, for better price-performance.
    • 6. Storage and 7. Applications: Cloud-native storage options, plus calibrating resource requests and workload autoscaling.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy.

    Takeaway: Start with Savings Plans sized from the recommendation engine, plus Karpenter with consolidation. Then fix requests, the lever applications control.

  • kubernetes-chatgpt-bot: A ChatGPT Bot for Kubernetes Issues
    summary

    TL;DR: A Robusta.dev playbook that adds an “Ask ChatGPT” button to Prometheus alerts in Slack, so OpenAI suggests fixes. The README says it is being deprecated in favour of HolmesGPT.

    • Status: The README banner says the project will be deprecated and replaced by robusta-dev/holmesgpt.
    • Flow: Prometheus sends alerts to Robusta by webhook. The bot asks OpenAI how to fix the alert and posts the answer to Slack.
    • Install: Install Robusta with Helm, then add playbookRepos.chatgpt_robusta_actions and a customPlaybooks entry with on_prometheus_alert and chat_gpt_enricher.
    • Config: Put chat_gpt_token in globalConfig in generated_values.yaml, then run helm upgrade robusta robusta/robusta ....
    • Requirements: A Slack workspace and an OpenAI API key.

    Takeaway: This was an early experiment in LLM alert enrichment. Look at HolmesGPT instead, and consider what alert data you send to a third-party API.

20.12.2022

  • hishtory: Sync Shell History Between Computers
    summary

    TL;DR: hiSHtory, by ddworken, records shell history together with its context. It syncs the history end-to-end encrypted across machines, and you query it from a CLI or a Control+R interface.

    • Context captured: Working directory, exit code, duration, hostname and user for each command, stored locally.
    • Shells: bash, zsh and fish. Install with curl https://hishtory.dev/install.py | python3 -.
    • Multi-machine: Run hishtory status to get the secret, then hishtory init $YOUR_HISHTORY_SECRET on other hosts.
    • Query syntax: Filters such as hostname:my-server, user:root, exit_code:127, before:2022-02-01 and after:.... Power users can query the SQLite database directly at ~/.hishtory/.hishtory.db.
    • Self-hosting: The sync backend can be self-hosted. It is a Go binary (backend/server/server.go) using SQLite or Postgres. The default hosted backend cannot read the encrypted data.
    • Extras: Prefix a query with ? to ask ChatGPT for a command. Commands can be disabled, enabled and deleted.

    Takeaway: Useful if you work across many hosts and want searchable history with exit codes and context. Self-host the backend if you do not want history leaving your infrastructure, even encrypted.

  • awesome-cybersecurity-conferences: Cybersecurity Conference Links and Videos
    summary

    TL;DR: A community-maintained Markdown catalogue of cybersecurity conferences by Tal Eliyahu, with links to slides, videos, social accounts, locations, languages and schedules. It also feeds a searchable website.

    • Format: Tables per year with month, conference, slides, video, hashtag, location, language and schedule.
    • Coverage now: The repo is still maintained. It lists 2025 and 2026 events, such as Black Hat Europe 2025, BSides TLV and Lisbon 2025, and AlligatorCon Europe 2026.
    • Website: awesomecybersecurityconferences.com offers search and filters by year, country, language and series.
    • Extra views: Upcoming conferences, call-for-papers deadlines, country guides and browsing by year.

    Takeaway: A good single place to find recorded security talks or CFP deadlines. Check the website for the filtered view.

  • legitify: Detect and Remediate Misconfigurations and Security Risks Across Your GitHub Assets
    summary

    TL;DR: Legitify, from Legit Security, is an open source Go CLI that detects and helps fix security misconfigurations across GitHub (and now GitLab) organisations, repositories and members.

    • Install: brew install legitify, release binaries that bundle the built-in policies, from source, or as a GitHub CLI extension with gh extension install legit-labs/gh-legitify.
    • Run: SCM_TOKEN=<token> legitify analyze --org org1,org2 --namespace organization,member. It needs a classic PAT. Fine-grained tokens are not supported.
    • Scoping: --namespace (resource types), --org, --repo, and --scm github|gitlab. GitLab Server needs SERVER_URL.
    • GitLab limits: Some policies, such as branch protection, are skipped on non-premium GitLab accounts.
    • CI: A custom GitHub Action runs legitify in pipelines, with ignore-policies support.
    • Extra: A gpt-analysis subcommand sends repository configuration to OpenAI for review (needs OPENAI_TOKEN).

    Takeaway: Run legitify against your GitHub org to find quick wins in branch protection, member settings and repository settings. Then wire it into CI.

  • terraform-aws-clickops-notifier: Get Notified on Manual Actions in the AWS Console
    summary

    TL;DR: A Terraform module from cloudandthings that sends notifications when people make changes by hand in the AWS Console (“ClickOps”). It works by watching CloudTrail.

    • Where to deploy: Tested in the AWS Control Tower Log Archive account. Control Tower is not required.
    • Modes: Organizational mode uses centralised CloudTrail with S3 bucket notifications through SNS. standalone mode works in one account with CloudTrail sent to a CloudWatch Log Group and a subscription filter.
    • Noise control: Actions that are normal or console-only are excluded by default. Tune this with excluded_scoped_actions and excluded_scoped_actions_effect.
    • Delivery: A Lambda function posts to configured webhooks. The inputs include Microsoft Teams webhooks, and SNS topic and KMS options.
    • Extensibility: additional_iam_policy_statements lets you add to the Lambda role.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to enforce “everything through IaC” culture. Alert on console write actions, then decide case by case what to codify.

  • A Visual Guide to SSH Tunnels: Local and Remote Port Forwarding
    summary

    TL;DR: Ivan Velichko (iximiuz) explains SSH local and remote port forwarding visually, with cheat-sheet diagrams. The page has since become an interactive iximiuz Labs tutorial titled “A Practical Guide to SSH Tunnels”.

    • Page changed: The current version was last updated in July 2026. It runs labs on a playground with four hosts across home, public and VPC networks.
    • Use cases: Reach internal VPC endpoints through a public EC2 bastion, open a remote VM’s localhost port in your browser, and expose a local server from a private network.
    • Local forwarding: ssh -L [local_addr:]local_port:remote_addr:remote_port [user@]sshd_addr. The client listens locally and forwards through the SSH server.
    • Bind address: Whether the local listener binds only to localhost depends on the GatewayPorts setting.
    • Background tip: ssh -f -N -L ... runs the tunnel without a shell, in the background.
    • Remote forwarding: Covered with diagrams and the sshd settings it may need. A visual cheat sheet helps you remember which flag does what.

    Takeaway: Keep the cheat sheet handy. Local forwarding reaches into a network, and remote forwarding exposes something from your side.

  • Multi-Cluster Management for Kubernetes with Cluster API and Argo CD
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog walkthrough that pairs Cluster API (with the AWS provider, CAPA) and Argo CD. Both self-managed EC2 clusters and EKS clusters are declared in Git and managed from one management cluster.

    • Cluster API: A declarative Kubernetes API for creating, configuring and upgrading clusters. CNCF declared v1.0 production-ready in October 2021.
    • CAPA for EKS: Provisions and upgrades EKS, plus machine pools, managed machine pools, EKS add-ons, Fargate profiles and aws-iam-authenticator config.
    • Bootstrap: A Kind cluster becomes the management cluster through clusterctl. The post notes Kind is for demos only and recommends EKS in production.
    • GitOps: Argo CD on the management cluster syncs workload cluster definitions from Git. New clusters are registered with Argo CD to receive a sample app.
    • Tooling: kubectl, kind, clusterctl, clusterawsadm, argocd, aws CLI, jq and docker. Sample repo: aws-samples/eks-ec2-clusterapi-gitops.

    Takeaway: A reference pattern for running a fleet of clusters as Git-managed resources. Run the management cluster with proper backups, not Kind.

  • Amazon Simple Email Service Announces Virtual Deliverability Manager to Help Enhance Email Delivery Success Rate
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS announcement (November 2, 2022) of Amazon SES Virtual Deliverability Manager, a feature that monitors and improves email delivery success rates.

    • Purpose: Lower the chance that mailbox providers such as Gmail or Yahoo mark SES mail as spam.
    • Reports: At-a-glance views of bounce rate, opens and clicks in the SES console.
    • Recommendations: Optimisation advice and concrete steps to improve deliverability.
    • Automation: Some changes are applied automatically, such as choosing which sending IP address to use.
    • Availability: All Regions where SES is available.

    Takeaway: Worth enabling if you send transactional or bulk mail through SES. Better bounce and complaint visibility also helps spot account abuse.

  • kubetunnel: Develop Microservices Locally While Connected to Your Kubernetes Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeTunnel, by Dcode.tech, lets you run one service locally in your IDE while the rest of your microservices stay in Kubernetes. Traffic flows both ways through a secure tunnel.

    • How it works: You pick a Kubernetes service and a local process. KubeTunnel starts a pod in your namespace, repoints the service to it, and the pod forwards traffic to your machine.
    • Reverse path: The CLI forwards every service in the namespace to localhost, so your local process can call them.
    • Benefits: No build, push and deploy loop. You keep local debuggers, and can work on apps too large to run locally.
    • Install: brew tap we-dcode/tap && brew install kubetunnel, or release binaries (including Windows).
    • Requirements: cluster-admin for the initial operator install. NetworkPolicies that allow operator traffic. Local admin rights, because it edits your hosts file.
    • Warning: For development environments only, since all services in the namespace connect to you.

    Takeaway: An alternative to Telepresence-style workflows for shared dev namespaces. Never point it at a shared or production namespace.

  • alt-tab-macos: Windows Alt-Tab on macOS
    summary

    TL;DR: AltTab, by lwouis, brings Windows-style Alt-Tab window switching to macOS, with a list of every window rather than every app, and window previews.

    • Core: Switch between individual windows, including several windows of the same app. Badges mark minimized, hidden and other-Space windows.
    • Previews: Shows the selected window at full size before switching. Shortcuts can be customised.
    • License: Free and open source under GPL-3.0, with no tracking or telemetry, according to the project site.
    • AltTab Pro: A newer paid tier for signed binaries adds search by title or app, more switcher styles and more shortcuts. Pro has a 14-day trial.
    • Requirements and scale: macOS 12+, Apple silicon and Intel. The site claims 9.4M downloads and 16K GitHub stars.
    • Source caveat: The GitHub README now shows only banners, so details come from the project site, alt-tab.app.

    Takeaway: One of the best fixes for macOS app-level Cmd-Tab if you think in windows. The free core still covers the basics.

  • How We Use Terraform at Slack
    summary

    TL;DR: Archie Gunasekara of Slack’s Cloud Foundations team (October 2022) describes how Slack runs Terraform across AWS, DigitalOcean, NS1 and GCP. Topics include state layout, pipelines, versioning and developer sandboxes.

    • Why Terraform: One tool and syntax across providers, rather than CloudFormation for AWS alone.
    • State evolution: Slack started with one state per region in one account. Tens of thousands of EC2 instances and rate limits led to child accounts. Now about 1,400 state files are owned by service teams.
    • Layout: One state per region per child account, plus one global state (IAM, CloudFront). Large services get isolated states so the blast radius stays small.
    • Backend: An S3 backend with object versioning for rollback, and DynamoDB locking.
    • Pipelines: Jenkins workers with IAM roles. Plan and apply stages are chained sandbox, then dev, then prod.
    • Ops boxes: Self-service instances with the same tooling but read-only AWS access, so engineers can plan but not apply. Idle boxes are terminated automatically.
    • Upgrades: The 0.11 to 0.12 upgrade took a quarter. For 0.13 and AWS provider 3.74.1 to 4.x, Slack built a per-state version config so multiple binaries and plugins can coexist.

    Takeaway: Small, team-owned states, versioned remote state and per-state Terraform version pinning are the parts worth copying. Plan major upgrades as long projects.

  • get-secretmanager-secrets: GitHub Action for Accessing Secrets from Google Secret Manager as Outputs
    summary

    TL;DR: A GitHub Action from the google-github-actions org. It reads secrets from Google Cloud Secret Manager and exposes them as step outputs, so Secret Manager stays the source of truth for CI secrets.

    • Usage: Authenticate with google-github-actions/auth@v3 (Workload Identity Federation in the example), then run get-secretmanager-secrets@v3 with secrets: token:my-project/docker-registry-token.
    • Consumption: Later steps read values as ${{ steps.secrets.outputs.token }}.
    • Masking: Fetched values are added to the build log mask, to reduce accidental printing.
    • Permissions: The job needs id-token: write for OIDC auth, plus credentials allowed to access the requested secrets.
    • Runtime: Runs on Node 20. Self-hosted runners must support it.
    • Support: The README says it is not an officially supported Google product and is not covered by Google Cloud support.

    Takeaway: Pair it with keyless Workload Identity Federation, so no static GCP key sits in GitHub secrets. Only the secrets the workflow needs flow into the job.

  • kubediff: Show Differences Between Running State and Version-Controlled Kubernetes Configuration
    summary

    TL;DR: Kubediff, from Weaveworks, compares the Kubernetes YAML in version control with what is running in the cluster and prints the differences. The repository is deprecated and archived.

    • Status: The README title reads “DEPRECATED: Kubediff”, and GitHub marks the repo as archived.
    • CLI: ./kubediff [--kubeconfig] [--context] [--namespace] [--json] [--no-error-on-diff] paths.... It exits with code 2 when a diff exists.
    • Output: Per-object field diffs, for example .spec.template.spec.containers[0].args[0]: 'a' != 'b'.
    • Mechanics: Shells out to kubectl, so it depends on the kubeconfig context. Python dependencies install with pip install -r requirements.txt.
    • Service mode: It could also run in-cluster, periodically pulling the latest config from Git and reporting drift.

    Takeaway: This is historical. Today kubectl diff or GitOps controllers such as Argo CD and Flux provide drift detection.

  • Implementing Pod Security Standards in Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog guide to replacing the removed PodSecurityPolicy with Pod Security Admission (PSA) and the Pod Security Standards (PSS) on Amazon EKS. It covers namespace labels and a migration approach.

    • Why: PSP was deprecated in 1.21 and removed in 1.25. It confused users, lacked dry-run and audit modes, and could not be on by default.
    • Availability: PSA and PSS went beta in Kubernetes 1.23 and are enabled by default in EKS 1.23.
    • Levels: privileged, baseline and restricted. Modes are enforce (reject), audit (annotate the audit log) and warn (warn the user).
    • EKS defaults: All modes are set to privileged at latest, with no exemptions. Namespaces must opt in to stricter levels.
    • Labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL>, with an optional pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>-version: v1.24 to pin a version.
    • Migration: PSA or policy-as-code tools can run alongside PSP. A kubectl get pod -A -o jsonpath=... snippet finds pods annotated with kubernetes.io/psp.

    Takeaway: Start with warn and audit set to restricted on each namespace, fix the violations, then turn on enforce. Use policy-as-code where PSS is too coarse.

  • Crossplane on Kubernetes Explained
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A “Containers from the Couch” video (October 25, 2022) in which Sai Vennam explains Crossplane, and how platform teams use it to manage cloud infrastructure and managed services on AWS from Kubernetes.

    • Topic: What Crossplane is, and how it uses the Kubernetes control loop to reconcile cloud resources.
    • Example: The description says Sai Vennam shows how to deploy and manage a production-ready Amazon EKS setup with Crossplane.
    • Chapter: One visible chapter is “The Kubernetes Control Loop”.
    • Reach: About 44K views on a channel with about 38K subscribers.
    • Promo: The description links a free hands-on Amazon EKS Workshop.
    • Source caveat: YouTube served only the title, description and chapter list, with no transcript. This summary is based on those.

    Takeaway: A short conceptual introduction for teams weighing Crossplane against Terraform for Kubernetes-native infrastructure management.

  • Grafana Faro: Highly Configurable Web SDK for Real User Monitoring (RUM)
    summary

    TL;DR: Grafana Faro is Grafana Labs’ open source frontend observability project. Its configurable JavaScript Web SDK does real user monitoring (RUM) in browsers.

    • Signals: Collects performance metrics, logs, exceptions, events and traces from web apps.
    • Correlation: Frontend data can be correlated with backend and infrastructure data in the LGTM stack (Loki, Grafana, Tempo, Mimir).
    • Origin: Started at Grafana Labs and announced in 2022. Grafana leads development and builds Faro support into Grafana.
    • Goals: Monitor web performance, find frontend errors and track user behaviour, to speed up failure resolution.
    • Page now: The current page also carries GrafanaCON 2026 and ObservabilityCON promotions around the same project overview.

    Takeaway: An open source RUM option if you already run the Grafana stack. It joins browser traces to backend traces.

  • A Dive into Web Application Authentication
    summary

    TL;DR: A Better Appsec primer by James Chiappetta, with contributions from Jeremy Shulman (October 2022), on how web application authentication works and how it has evolved, for both consumers and businesses.

    • AuthN vs AuthZ: Authentication verifies an identity’s credentials. Authorization then decides which resources that identity can access.
    • Passwords: Humans reuse passwords and store them badly, which is why a second factor became standard.
    • Topics covered: Why MFA matters, how “Sign in with” works on OAuth 2.0 and whether to use it, SSO, passwordless authentication, API authentication, and deep links as a bonus.
    • Framing: Looks at how authentication matured over the past ten years and where it may go next.
    • Disclaimer: The authors state that the opinions are their own and the products mentioned are not endorsements.
    • Source caveat: The page blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy of the opening sections.

    Takeaway: Good onboarding material for engineers new to authentication concepts. It does not cover implementation depth.

  • AWS Security Assessment: What Scanners Are Missing and How Threat Modeling May Help You?
    summary

    TL;DR: An October 2022 Towards AWS post arguing that automated AWS scanners such as Prowler and ScoutSuite cannot replace a human assessor. It says threat modeling the environment first finds the issues that matter.

    • No context: Scanners accept SSE-S3 encrypted, non-public PII buckets. They miss that AmazonS3FullAccess with "Resource": "*" lets many principals read the data.
    • Noise: Un-tuned scanners report hundreds of findings, such as password policy alerts in accounts with no IAM users. Real issues get stuck in the backlog.
    • Coverage gaps: Hardcoded credentials in EC2 user data or ECS task definition environment variables usually go undetected.
    • Threat modeling: Before assessing, identify critical assets, data flows and attack vectors with the team, using its real architecture diagrams.
    • Checklist: Points to Marco Lancini’s spreadsheet “What to look for when reviewing a company’s infrastructure”.
    • Source caveat: The page blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy.

    Takeaway: Run the scanners, but scope the assessment with a threat model, so findings are prioritised by the data and paths that matter.

  • ShadowClone: Distribute Long-Running Tasks Across Thousands of Serverless Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: ShadowClone, by fyoorer, splits long-running CLI tasks (typically recon tools) across up to 1,000 parallel serverless function invocations, and collects the results in seconds instead of hours.

    • Usage: python shadowclone.py -i INPUT -s SPLITNUM -c COMMAND [-o OUTPUT]. --no-split passes a file through unsplit.
    • Mechanics: Setup builds a container image registered as a function runtime. At run time the input is chunked, for example 10,000 lines at 100 per chunk gives 100 parallel instances.
    • Clouds: Cloud agnostic across AWS, GCP and Azure, and designed to fit within free tiers.
    • Comparison: Inspired by Axiom and Fleex, but uses serverless functions and containers instead of a fleet of VPSes.
    • Output: Results can be piped to other tools.
    • Setup: Installation and configuration are documented in the repo wiki.

    Takeaway: Handy for bursty, embarrassingly parallel scanning jobs. Check the cloud provider’s acceptable-use rules before pointing it at targets.

  • paralus: All-in-One Kubernetes Access Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: Paralus is a free, open source CNCF Sandbox project for controlled, audited access to Kubernetes clusters. It offers user-level credentials, RBAC, SSO and audit logs through a GUI, API and CLI.

    • Identity: Integrates with existing RBAC and with SSO or OIDC identity providers.
    • Just-in-time access: Creates service accounts on demand and manages fine-grained user credentials.
    • Controls: Custom roles, users and groups, plus preconfigured roles across clusters, namespaces and projects.
    • Revocation: Permissions can be changed and revoked dynamically and immediately.
    • Auditing: Real-time audit logs to help spot and respond to threats.
    • Project: Written in Go, Apache 2.0, with a Helm chart and an OpenSSF Best Practices badge.
    • Note: The archive lists this repo twice, under two title variants with the same URL.

    Takeaway: Consider Paralus for centrally brokered, revocable kubectl access across many clusters without distributing static kubeconfigs.

  • paralus: All-in-One Kubernetes Access Manager with User-Level Credentials, RBAC, SSO, and Audit Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: Paralus is a free, open source CNCF Sandbox project for controlled, audited access to Kubernetes clusters. It offers user-level credentials, RBAC, SSO and audit logs through a GUI, API and CLI.

    • Identity: Integrates with existing RBAC and with SSO or OIDC identity providers.
    • Just-in-time access: Creates service accounts on demand and manages fine-grained user credentials.
    • Controls: Custom roles, users and groups, plus preconfigured roles across clusters, namespaces and projects.
    • Revocation: Permissions can be changed and revoked dynamically and immediately.
    • Auditing: Real-time audit logs to help spot and respond to threats.
    • Project: Written in Go, Apache 2.0, with a Helm chart and an OpenSSF Best Practices badge.
    • Note: The archive lists this repo twice, under two title variants with the same URL.

    Takeaway: Consider Paralus for centrally brokered, revocable kubectl access across many clusters without distributing static kubeconfigs.

  • Monorepo.tools: Everything You Need to Know About Monorepos and the Tools to Build Them
    summary

    TL;DR: Monorepo.tools is an explainer site made by the Nx team. It covers what monorepos are, why to use them, and which features to look for in monorepo tooling.

    • Definition: “A single repository containing multiple distinct projects, with well-defined relationships”. Code colocation alone, or one big undivided app, does not count.
    • Not a monolith: The site argues a good monorepo is the opposite of monolithic.
    • Polyrepo tax: Shared code needs separate repos, CI and publishing. Shared code gets duplicated, cross-repo changes need sequenced PRs, and conventions drift.
    • Monorepo benefits: Sharing without publishing, a single source of truth, atomic commits across projects, and conventions enforced in one place.
    • Page changed: The current version adds sections on AI agents (“Monorepos Amplify AI Agents”) and “Synthetic Monorepos”.
    • Tooling: A comparison of what a best-in-class tool provides. The page is written from the Nx perspective.

    Takeaway: A useful framing doc for a monorepo decision. Remember that a tool vendor wrote it, and compare tools on the capabilities it lists.

  • Hacking Your Offensive Security Career
    summary

    TL;DR: Lawrence Munro (November 2022) gives career advice for offensive security people who feel overlooked. The theme is to “engineer” your career ethically, after putting hard work and skill-building first.

    • Premise: Capability comes before career engineering. Spend more time on skills than on your Twitter presence.
    • Own your learning: Avoid the “teacher-student mind-set”. Certs, degrees and experience are all valid, and neither certifications nor tenure prove proficiency.
    • Mentors: Find a coach, sponsor or cheerleader through rapport, not by asking the company star on week one. The best technical performer is often not the best mentor.
    • Community: Reach out to creators who share your interests. The author says most are happy to help.
    • Training budget: Build a business case around company benefit. Treat blockers like a hacking challenge.
    • What fails: “I haven’t had training in X months” sounds like a moan. Comparing yourself to colleagues sounds immature.

    Takeaway: Practical soft-skills advice for pentesters. Frame requests around business outcomes, and build relationships before asking for sponsorship.

  • A Case for Go Code Generation: testify
    summary

    TL;DR: A November 2022 post that walks through how Go’s stretchr/testify uses code generation and templates to produce its many assertion variants from one canonical implementation.

    • Combinatorics: Each assertion exists in assert and require, as suite methods, and as *f formatted variants. That makes eight versions of each function.
    • Canonical impl: assert.Equal holds the logic (built on ObjectsAreEqual) and returns a bool.
    • require wrapper: require.X calls assert.X and runs t.FailNow() on false.
    • Templates: Go text/template bodies such as func {{.DocInfo.Name}}(t TestingT, {{.Params}}) { ... } generate the boilerplate for every assertion.
    • Helper calls: Generated functions call h.Helper() when available, so failure lines point at the caller.
    • Source caveat: The page blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a reader-proxy copy.

    Takeaway: A good real-world pattern for generating repetitive Go API surfaces from one implementation, instead of copying code by hand.

  • notify: Dead Simple Go Library for Sending Notifications to Various Messaging Services
    summary

    TL;DR: Notify, by nikoksr, is a “dead simple” Go library that sends one notification to many messaging services through a single interface.

    • Install: go get -u github.com/nikoksr/notify.
    • Model: Create a service such as Telegram, add receivers, register it with notify, then call send once to fan out.
    • Services: The README table lists about 30 services, including Amazon SES, Amazon SNS, Bark, DingTalk, Discord, email and Firebase Cloud Messaging.
    • Dependencies: Each service wraps an upstream client library, such as aws-sdk-go-v2 or discordgo.
    • Caveat: The authors say not to rely on it in critical scenarios, because it depends on external services and their client libraries.
    • Warning: Spamming through it may get accounts permanently banned on most platforms.

    Takeaway: Handy for adding multi-channel alerts to small Go tools and bots. Use a proper alerting pipeline for anything critical.

  • Substrate: Command-Line Tools for Managing Secure, Compliant Infrastructure in Many AWS Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: Substrate, from Source & Binary, is a commercial tool for running AWS as many isolated accounts. It provides account creation, role management, short-lived credentials and Terraform bootstrapping behind one CLI and dashboard.

    • Isolation model: Separates development from production, services from each other, analytics from the critical path, and customers from each other, each in narrowly scoped accounts.
    • Credentials: Authenticates through your existing identity provider. It issues time-limited, least-privilege credentials (twelve-hour access in daily use) and stores none on disk.
    • Developer experience: Human-readable account names, simpler CLI parameters, environment switching and a dashboard.
    • Terraform: It “speaks native AWS and Terraform” for provisioning.
    • Networking: Shared VPCs for cross-account communication “without CIDR math”.
    • Compliance: Marketed as easing SOC 2 change management and segmentation evidence.
