    Takeaway: Worth a look if you want a multi-account AWS layout with an opinionated access layer and do not want to build it yourself. It is a vendor product, so compare it with Control Tower and with in-house setups.

  • An AWS Account Just for Getting into Other AWS Accounts
    summary

    TL;DR: A Source & Binary (Substrate) post arguing that a multi-account AWS organization needs a dedicated “administrative access” account. People sign in there, and that account is the only path into every other account.

    • Supporting accounts: The management account for Organizations, an audit log account and a network or shared VPC account. The admin access account joins these and is called “the most important account” in the organization.
    • Contents: Only the minimum resources for authentication, authorization and cross-account actions. No customer-facing services and no customer data.
    • Getting in: IAM users (password plus MFA), IAM Identity Center (time-bound keys, no long-lived keys) or an external IdP over OIDC or SAML. The author prefers an external IdP, and noted Identity Center lacked Google and OIDC support at the time.
    • Moving across: sts:AssumeRole, higher-level tools, and service-specific cross-account access.
    • Rejected alternatives: Overloading the management account, or using IAM users in every account, which adds offboarding burden and keys that never expire.
    • Moved page: The original URL now redirects to src-bin.com/substrate/blog/an-aws-account-just-for-getting-into-other-aws-accounts/.

    Takeaway: Keep human entry in one hardened account backed by your IdP, and reach everything else by role assumption. Never sign in through the management account.

  • Get Certified for GitOps with Argo
    summary

    TL;DR: The Codefresh GitOps certification portal for Argo, now branded under Octopus Deploy. It offers GitOps certification courses that teach GitOps theory and hands-on practice with the Argo project family.

    • Rebrand: The page now reads “GitOps Certification | Octopus Deploy”, reflecting the Codefresh link moving under Octopus.
    • Content: Courses teach GitOps principles and how to apply them to your own application using Argo CD and Argo Rollouts.
    • Labs: Learner quotes praise rolling deployment and migration scenarios and well-structured labs.
    • Bundle: All three GitOps certifications together cost 23% less. An Octopus Deploy fundamentals certification is also listed.
    • Instructors: Kostis Kapelonis (Argo team member, focused on Argo CD and Rollouts), Steve Fenton and Matt Allford of Octopus Deploy.

    Takeaway: A structured, lab-based route to learning Argo CD and Rollouts. Check the current course list and any fees, since the portal changed ownership.

  • AWS Network Firewall Workshop
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: An AWS Workshop Studio hands-on workshop for AWS Network Firewall, the managed stateful network firewall and IPS for VPCs.

    • Platform: Hosted on AWS Workshop Studio (catalog.us-east-1.prod.workshops.aws). The page renders only with JavaScript.
    • Subject: AWS Network Firewall, whose stateful rule groups use Suricata-compatible IPS rules, according to AWS documentation.
    • Rule options (AWS docs): Write Suricata rule strings, use the simpler AWS rule specification, or use domain lists, which AWS converts to Suricata.
    • Flow caveat (AWS docs): Rules that use flow: established need stateless rules that forward both directions to the stateful engine.
    • Source caveat: The workshop content could not be retrieved, and search did not index this workshop ID. Only the title and AWS Network Firewall documentation were available, so the workshop’s modules are unknown.

    Takeaway: Open it in a browser and run it in a sandbox account to learn Network Firewall deployment and rule writing. Tear down afterwards, because firewall endpoints bill hourly.

  • aws-sso-reporter: AWS SSO Reporter
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS SSO Reporter, by onemorepereira, is a pair of Python scripts that export AWS SSO (IAM Identity Center) assignments and permission sets to CSV, to answer “who has access to what”.

    • Problem: The console cannot easily answer questions such as which accounts John Doe can reach, or who can access App-Prod-Account.
    • Scripts: sso-account-permission-assignment-report.py handles account assignments. sso-permission-set-report.py handles permission set details.
    • Views: Users and groups per account with their permission set, accounts per user or group, and accounts and principals per permission set.
    • Policy detail: Managed and inline policies attached to each permission set.
    • Run: Use credentials in the SSO management account that can read Organizations and SSO. Set the region, for example aws configure set default.region eu-west-1, then run the scripts.
    • Scale: A small repo with 12 commits.

    Takeaway: A quick way to produce access review evidence for IAM Identity Center. Load the CSVs into a spreadsheet for periodic recertification.

  • alternat: High Availability Implementation of AWS NAT Instances
    summary

    TL;DR: alterNAT, from Chime Engineering, is a Terraform module for highly available NAT instances on AWS. It avoids the NAT Gateway $0.045/GB processing fee and keeps a standby NAT Gateway for failover.

    • Moved repo: The URL now resolves to chime/terraform-aws-alternat.
    • Cost case: The README says 10TB a month (5TB in, 5TB out) costs about $954 through NAT Gateway versus about $526 on a c6gn.large NAT instance, roughly 45% less. It puts 1PB through NAT Gateway at $75,604.
    • Architecture: One single-instance Auto Scaling Group per AZ, each with a standby NAT Gateway.
    • Patching: The maximum instance lifetime (14 days by default) replaces instances regularly. A Terminating:Wait lifecycle hook fires through SNS.
    • Failover: The replace-route Lambda points the private route table to the standby NAT Gateway. The new instance then reclaims its Elastic IP and the route.
    • Health check: A CloudWatch Events rule also invokes the Lambda once a minute for every private subnet, as a health check.

    Takeaway: Consider it if NAT Gateway data processing is a large part of your bill. You take on operating EC2 NAT instances in exchange.

  • Introducing AWS Resource Explorer: Quickly Find Resources in Your AWS Account
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS News Blog launch post for AWS Resource Explorer. It searches resources across Regions in an account by name, tag and ID, from the console, CLI or SDKs.

    • Indexes: Local indexes per Region, plus an aggregator index in one Region for cross-Region search.
    • Views: Control what is searchable, such as ARNs without tags, and which resources a view includes.
    • Setup: Quick setup indexes all Regions and creates a default view. Advanced setup lets you choose Regions and skip replication for governance reasons.
    • Query syntax: tag.value:MyApp, tag:Project=MyApp, region:eu-west-1 and service:ecs.
    • Navigation: Results link straight to the right service console and Region.
    • Price: No additional charge.

    Takeaway: Enable it in every account. It is free, and it speeds up “where is that resource” questions and incident triage across Regions.

  • kcp: Kubernetes-Like Control Plane for Workloads on Many Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: kcp is a Kubernetes-like control plane for many isolated logical clusters, called workspaces. It lets API providers offer APIs centrally through multi-tenant operators. The multi-cluster workload scheduling in the original description has since been removed.

    • Focus now: A control plane for many isolated workspaces, central API offering with multi-tenant operators, and easy API consumption.
    • Use case: A building block for SaaS providers and enterprise IT that need massively multi-tenant, Kubernetes-native APIs.
    • Restructure: In May 2023, the syncer and transparent multi-cluster (TMC) code were removed for lack of interest and maintainers. They remain on the main-pre-tmc-removal branch.
    • Try it: go run ./cmd/kcp start, then export KUBECONFIG=.kcp/admin.kubeconfig && kubectl get workspaces.
    • Project: Apache 2.0, with an OpenSSF Best Practices badge. Docs are at docs.kcp.io.

    Takeaway: Read kcp today as a multi-tenant API control plane, not as the “workloads on many clusters” scheduler in the archive’s title.

  • Running Resilient Workloads in EKS Using Spot Instances
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A member-only ITNEXT post (November 2022) on running production workloads on EKS with EC2 Spot Instances. It argues Spot works for production if applications are configured to handle interruptions.

    • Spot basics: Uses spare EC2 capacity, up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand, but AWS can interrupt it.
    • Interruption causes: The Spot price exceeds your maximum, EC2 needs the capacity back (including for host maintenance), or group constraints such as launch groups can no longer be met.
    • Tools mentioned: The Spot Instance Advisor shows historical interruption rates per instance type. CloudTrail shows whether EC2 interrupted an instance.
    • Visible extras: A rolling-update tip, and a conclusion that well-configured apps can run production on Spot.
    • Source caveat: The article is paywalled. Only the opening overview and search-result excerpts were available, so the later sections, such as interruption handling, are not covered here.

    Takeaway: Read it as a Spot primer. For the resilience details, see AWS guidance on Node Termination Handler or Karpenter interruption handling, plus PodDisruptionBudgets.

  • Blazing Fast CI with MicroVMs
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Ellis introduces actuated, then in pilot. It runs GitHub Actions jobs in ephemeral Firecracker microVMs, fixing the limits of hosted runners and the security and drift problems of self-hosted ones.

    • Hosted runner limits: 2 cores and 7GB RAM, too little for KinD or E2E tests. Disk runs out, there are no ARM runners, 20 concurrent runners on the free plan, and private repos are billed per minute.
    • ARM example: Parca’s ARM64 build fell from 33m5s under QEMU to 1m26s on an actuated ARM64 microVM, about 22x faster.
    • Self-hosted problems: Packages are hard to keep in line with hosted images. Mutable hosts cause caching bugs, there is one job per machine, and Docker as root can take over the host.
    • Public repos: GitHub advises against self-hosted runners on public repos, because forks can run code. The GitHub team told him ephemeral VMs with immutable images solve this.
    • ARC criticism: Actions Runner Controller is non-trivial and needs a GitHub App or PAT. It uses reusable Pods, not one-shot ones.
    • Firecracker: The post says microVMs complement containers rather than replace them, where hard isolation is needed.

    Takeaway: For heavy or ARM CI, use one-shot isolated VMs per job. Whether you buy actuated or build it yourself, that is the safe pattern for self-hosted runners.

  • gke-policy-automation: Review GKE Clusters Against Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: GKE Policy Automation, from Google (not an officially supported product), is a tool plus policy library that checks GKE clusters against configuration best practices and scalability limits.

    • Install: Container image ghcr.io/google/gke-policy-automation, the Krew plugin kubectl krew install gke-policy, release binaries, or a build from Go source.
    • Run: kubectl gke-policy check --discovery -p my-project, or ./gke-policy check -c config.yaml.
    • Discovery: Finds clusters across projects, folders or a whole organization through Cloud Asset Inventory.
    • Checks: A best-practices policy library (gke-policies-v2) plus a separate scalability limits check.
    • Outputs: JSON file, Pub/Sub topic, Cloud Storage bucket or Security Command Center.
    • Ops: Supports serverless execution for scheduled runs.

    Takeaway: Run it organization-wide with Security Command Center output for a continuous GKE posture baseline at no licence cost.

  • octodns: Tools for Managing DNS Across Multiple Providers
    summary

    TL;DR: octoDNS, originally built at GitHub by Ross McFarland and Joe Williams, is an MIT-licensed “DNS as code” toolset. You manage records across multiple DNS providers from config kept in a repository.

    • Model: DNS config lives in Git and is deployed like other code, with review and a clear history.
    • Multi-provider: Built to manage records across several DNS providers from one source.
    • Pluggable: Adding a provider usually means one class and a couple hundred lines, mostly translating between the provider’s schema and octoDNS’s.
    • Docs: Usage and extension guides are at octodns.readthedocs.io.
    • Org: It now lives in its own octodns GitHub organisation. GitHub keeps its logo trademarks.

    Takeaway: Use it to put DNS under code review and to run several providers for resilience, without vendor-specific tooling.

  • devenv: Fast, Declarative, Reproducible, and Composable Developer Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: devenv, from Cachix, builds fast, declarative and reproducible developer environments on Nix. A devenv.nix file defines the packages, languages, services and processes for a project.

    • Start: devenv init generates devenv.nix with settings such as env, packages = [ pkgs.git ] and languages.*.
    • Coverage: 50+ languages with tooling, 100,000+ Nixpkgs packages on Linux and macOS (x64 and ARM64, including WSL2), and 40+ services such as PostgreSQL, Redis and MySQL.
    • Processes: A native Rust process manager with dependency ordering, readiness probes and automatic port allocation. Tasks run as a DAG with caching.
    • Speed: Incremental Nix evaluation caching, under 100ms when nothing changed. Version 2.0 (March 2026) added a terminal UI and native shell reloading.
    • Packaging: OCI containers built without Docker, profiles (--profile backend), imports for composition, and polyrepo references.
    • Integrations: direnv, git hooks, devenv test, SecretSpec secrets (keyring, 1Password, dotenv) and an MCP server.

    Takeaway: A friendlier interface to Nix for “clone and get a working environment”. It is well suited to onboarding and to keeping CI and laptops identical.

  • vscode-neovim: Vim Mode for VS Code Using Embedded Neovim
    summary

    TL;DR: vscode-neovim is a VS Code extension that embeds a real Neovim instance as the editing backend, instead of emulating Vim. VS Code handles insert mode and its own features.

    • Approach: Full Neovim backend, so normal and visual modes behave like real Vim. The exceptions are insert mode and some Nvim UI plugins.
    • Config: Supports a custom init.lua and most Neovim plugins.
    • Insert mode: Handled natively by VS Code for lag-free typing.
    • Integration: Works with VS Code LSP, autocompletion, snippets and multi-cursor.
    • Docs cover: Composite escape keys, the jumplist, multiple cursors, remote development, performance and troubleshooting.
    • API: Lua functions vscode.action(name, opts) and vscode.call(name, opts, timeout) call VS Code commands from Neovim config.

    Takeaway: The closest thing to real Vim inside VS Code. Reuse your Neovim keymaps, but expect some UI plugins not to work.

  • images: Public Chainguard Images, Secure Distroless Images
    summary

    TL;DR: The public build configuration for Chainguard Images. These are minimal, hardened OCI images built with apko and published at cgr.dev/chainguard/<image>, with SBOMs and cosign attestations.

    • Usage: docker pull cgr.dev/chainguard/static:latest or .../nginx:latest. The catalog is at images.chainguard.dev.
    • Reproducible builds: Each images/<name>/locked_config.json pins exact package versions, accounts, entrypoint and environment per architecture.
    • Release flow: The release.yaml workflow runs on changes or daily. It calls Terraform with the apko provider to build, publish and tag images.
    • Supply chain: SBOMs and Sigstore cosign attestations are published alongside the images.
    • Local builds: Reproduce with apko and the lock file, as described in BUILDING.md.
    • Repo now: The README describes the current lock-file layout, so the repo has changed since the 2022 public catalogue.

    Takeaway: A good source of low-CVE base images with signed provenance. Check which tags are free and which need a subscription before standardising on them.

  • finch: Open Source Client for Container Development
    summary

    TL;DR: Finch, from AWS, is an open source client for container development. It bundles nerdctl, containerd and BuildKit inside a Lima-managed VM, behind one simple installer and CLI.

    • Components: The finch CLI wraps nerdctl for build, run, push and pull. containerd manages containers, BuildKit builds OCI images and Lima runs the VM.
    • Philosophy: An opinionated distribution that promotes existing projects, rather than adding more options to reason about.
    • macOS: Install with brew install --cask finch or a package. Requires macOS Catalina (10.15)+. Run finch vm init once, which takes about a minute.
    • Windows: Supported on Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041)+ on AMD64.
    • Commands: Most common nerdctl commands work, though not 100% of upstream. The nerdctl reference serves as docs.
    • Security note: The README says the VM does not create a security boundary, and exists only to run Linux containers.

    Takeaway: A free, open source alternative to Docker Desktop for local builds. Do not treat its VM as isolation for untrusted workloads.

  • kubectl-foreach: Run kubectl Commands in All or Some Contexts in Parallel
    summary

    TL;DR: kubectl-foreach, by ahmetb, runs a kubectl command across many kubeconfig contexts in parallel, like GNU parallel or xargs for cluster fleets.

    • Syntax: kubectl foreach [OPTIONS] [PATTERN]... -- [KUBECTL_ARGS...].
    • Matching: Empty matches all contexts. Use an exact name, /regex/, or prefix ^ to exclude.
    • Options: -c NUM caps parallelism, -I VAL substitutes the context name into arguments, and -q skips confirmation prompts ($KUBECTL_FOREACH_DISABLE_PROMPTS).
    • Output: Each line is prefixed with the context name. Example: kubectl foreach /-prod/ minikube -- get pods -n kube-system ....
    • Install: kubectl krew install foreach, or go install (without update notifications).

    Takeaway: Handy for fleet-wide queries. Keep the confirmation prompt on for write commands, and use -c to avoid overloading API servers.

  • gh-actions-importer: Plan and Automate Migration of CI Pipelines to GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub Actions Importer is GitHub’s tool for planning, testing and automating CI migrations to GitHub Actions from Azure DevOps, Bamboo, Bitbucket, CircleCI, GitLab, Jenkins and Travis CI.

    • Distribution: A Docker container driven by a GitHub CLI extension. Install with gh extension install github/gh-actions-importer.
    • Prerequisites: Docker running, the gh CLI, and credentials for GitHub Container Registry.
    • Updates: gh actions-importer update pulls the latest version, which is released regularly.
    • Credentials: gh actions-importer configure prompts for values such as GITHUB_ACCESS_TOKEN, stored in environment variables or .env.local.
    • Registry: GitHub recommends pulling the image from the official GitHub Container Registry. Custom registries are supported.
    • Support: Through GitHub Support tickets.

    Takeaway: Use it to inventory and convert existing pipelines in bulk. Review the generated workflows by hand, especially secrets and runner choices.

  • Three Recurring Security Hub Usage Patterns and How to Deploy Them
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Solutions Architects describe the three most common ways customers deploy AWS Security Hub, with stakeholders, value and setup steps for each.

    • Background: Security Hub aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Firewall Manager, AWS Health and partners, normalised to the AWS Security Findings Format (ASFF). It also integrates with AWS Organizations.
    • Pattern 1, app owner dashboard: Read-only visibility for workload owners, through a role with the AWS managed AWSSecurityHubReadOnlyAccess policy. Optional custom insights.
    • Pattern 2, single pane of glass: Security teams view, triage and act on findings across accounts and Regions, using standards-based automated checks.
    • Automation: EventBridge-driven responses filtered on ASFF attributes, to improve MTTD and MTTR.
    • Pattern 3, SIEM routing: Security Hub as the aggregation point that forwards normalised findings to an existing SIEM or log tool, common in hybrid environments.
    • Trade-off: Pattern 2 gives central visibility without the cost and complexity of running a SIEM.

    Takeaway: Pick a pattern by audience. Most organisations combine them: read-only for app teams, a central view for security, and export to a SIEM where one exists.

  • nx: Next Generation Build System with First-Class Monorepo Support
    summary

    TL;DR: Nx, from Nrwl, is a build system and monorepo tool for TypeScript and polyglot codebases. It is written in Rust and extensible in TypeScript. It caches unchanged work and runs only the projects a change affects.

    • Adoption: npx nx init in any npm, pnpm or yarn workspace picks up existing package.json scripts and caches their outputs, with no setup changes.
    • Affected runs: Executes only tasks affected by a change, with local and remote caching.
    • Plugins: Optional plugins discover tasks, configure cache inputs and outputs, and scaffold code. They cover Vite, Webpack, Jest, Vitest, ESLint, Gradle, Maven, .NET, Go and more.
    • CI: Integrates with GitHub Actions, GitLab, Azure and others for remote caching, distribution across machines and automatic e2e test splitting.
    • Repo now: The README now pitches Nx as “AI-native” and describes a “self-healing CI” agent that proposes and verifies fixes, with MCP integration. That is newer than the 2022 listing.
    • Team: Core team includes Victor Savkin, Jason Jean, Benjamin Cabanes and Jack Hsu.

    Takeaway: Start with nx init on an existing workspace to get caching and affected-only CI. Adopt plugins and paid CI features only where they pay off.

  • tea: The Unified Package Manager (brew2)
    summary

    TL;DR: tea was a “brew2” unified package manager. The repo now resolves to pkgxdev/pkgx: pkgx, a 4 MiB standalone binary that runs any tool, at any version, without installing it system-wide.

    • Renamed: github.com/teaxyz/cli redirects to pkgxdev/pkgx. The tea CLI became pkgx.
    • Install: brew install pkgx || curl https://pkgx.sh | sh. On Windows 10+, irm https://pkgx.sh | iex, with limited packages.
    • Run without installing: pkgx deno runs Deno, while deno alone is still “command not found”. Your wider system is untouched.
    • Any version: pkgx node@14 --version and pkgx python@2 --version.
    • Platforms: macOS 11+ (Intel and Apple Silicon), Linux with glibc 2.28+ and libgcc (x86_64 and arm64), WSL2, and experimental native Windows.
    • Elsewhere: The pkgxdev/pkgx Docker image, the pkgxdev/setup@v4 GitHub Action, and shebangs such as #!/usr/bin/env -S pkgx +git python@3.12.

    Takeaway: Useful for ephemeral, pinned tool versions in scripts and CI. The “unified package manager” pitch from 2022 now lives on as pkgx.

  • infisical: Open-Source, End-to-End Encrypted Tool to Sync Environment Variables
    summary

    TL;DR: Infisical started as an open source, end-to-end encrypted tool for syncing environment variables. Its MIT-licensed repo now describes a broader security platform for secrets, certificates, privileged access and AI agent access.

    • Secrets: A dashboard per project and environment, versioning with point-in-time recovery, and rotation for PostgreSQL, MySQL and AWS IAM. Dynamic ephemeral secrets and expiring share links.
    • Delivery: Secret Syncs to GitHub, Vercel and AWS, plus Terraform and Ansible integrations. A Kubernetes Operator with auto-reload and an agent for injection without code changes.
    • Detection: Honey tokens that alert on use. Repository scanning for GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket history, and a CLI pre-commit hook that blocks secrets.
    • Certificates: Internal CA, external CAs (Let’s Encrypt, DigiCert, Microsoft AD CS), ACME, EST and SCEP enrollment, discovery, syncs to ACM and Azure Key Vault, and code signing.
    • Deployment: Infisical Cloud or self-hosting.
    • Scope change: The project grew from env-var sync (the 2022 title) into a wide security platform.

    Takeaway: A strong open source alternative to Vault or Doppler for app secrets. Evaluate self-hosting and which features need paid tiers.

  • registry.k8s.io: Faster, Cheaper and Generally Available (GA)
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post by Adolfo Garcia Veytia (Chainguard) and Bob Killen (Google), November 28, 2022. It announces that registry.k8s.io replaces k8s.gcr.io as the project’s image registry, spreading load across cloud providers like a CDN.

    • Cutover: Images for Kubernetes 1.25 and later go only to registry.k8s.io. December 2022 patch releases backported the new default to 1.22, 1.23 and 1.24.
    • Why: Less reliance on one vendor and faster downloads. Google renewed a $3 million infrastructure donation, and Amazon matched it at KubeCon NA 2022.
    • Mechanism: A secure blob redirector that sends clients to the closest backend. Load is split between Google and Amazon, with more providers to come.
    • Restricted networks: No stable list of domains or IPs is published. Allowlists for k8s.gcr.io break, so mirror images to a private registry.
    • Caveat: The page notes the article is more than one year old.

    Takeaway: Update manifests, allowlists and mirrors to registry.k8s.io. In locked-down environments, mirror release images instead of chasing backend IPs.

  • Attacker Persistence in Kubernetes Using the TokenRequest API: Overview, Detection, and Prevention
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune at Datadog Security Labs shows how attackers can abuse the Kubernetes TokenRequest API (kubectl create token, added in 1.24) for long-lived, hard-to-detect persistence. He also covers detection in audit logs and prevention.

    • No revocation: You cannot revoke issued tokens directly. The only way is to delete the bound object (service account, pod or secret), which is impractical for system accounts.
    • Long lifetimes: --duration accepts any value by default, for example one year. EKS caps tokens at 24 hours.
    • No inventory: The API keeps no record of issued tokens. Audit logs of creation events are the only trail.
    • Prevention: Restrict RBAC on the serviceaccounts/token subresource, and be careful with wildcard roles such as admin and cluster-admin.
    • Detection signals: The requesting user and IP, the target object (for example clusterrole-aggregation-controller, which has effective cluster-admin), and the kubectl user-agent, which attackers can spoof.
    • Audit level: expirationSeconds appears only at Request audit level or higher on 1.22+. The Metadata default on EKS and AKS hides it.

    Takeaway: Alert on TokenRequest calls against privileged service accounts, and lock down who can create tokens. Ask your provider about audit levels on managed clusters.

  • kubectl-plugins: Collection of Plugins for kubectl Integration
    summary

    TL;DR: A collection of Bash kubectl plugins by Jordan Wilson for kubectl 1.12+, some also on krew. Includes ssh, switch, prompt, image, ip and uptime.

    • kubectl ssh: Like exec, but with -u to run as root or any user. It works by mounting the Docker socket as a volume. Example: kubectl ssh -n default -u root -c prometheus <pod> -- bash.
    • Other plugins: switch (context and namespace), prompt (a shell prompt with cluster context), image, ip (needs jq) and uptime.
    • Install: git clone ..., ./install-plugins.sh, then source ~/.bash_profile. Uninstall steps use ex to clean the profile.
    • Compatibility: Works with BSD and GNU tools and requires Bash. Use the 1.11.0 branch for older kubectl.

    Takeaway: Convenient helpers, but kubectl ssh depends on Docker socket access to run as root. It will not work on containerd-only nodes, and it is a privilege red flag in hardened clusters.

  • Announcing Delegated Administrator for AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS announcement (November 27, 2022): AWS Organizations now supports delegated administrators for policy management. Member accounts can manage selected policy types without access to the management account.

    • Policy types: Backup policies, service control policies (SCPs), tag policies and AI services opt-out policies.
    • Granularity: You specify which actions the delegated account may perform.
    • Experience: Delegated users manage, and create, the policies they are permitted to in the Organizations console.
    • Goal: Decentralise policy administration to lines of business while limiting access to the highly privileged management account.
    • Availability: GA in all commercial AWS Regions.

    Takeaway: Move day-to-day SCP and tag policy work out of the management account into a delegated security or governance account. Scope its permissions tightly.

  • kubecolor: Colorizes kubectl Output
    summary

    TL;DR: kubecolor, by hidetatz, wraps kubectl and colourises its output, and does nothing else. This repository is archived.

    • Status: GitHub marks hidetatz/kubecolor as archived.
    • Usage: alias kubectl="kubecolor". A safer version is command -v kubecolor >/dev/null 2>&1 && alias kubectl="kubecolor", for synced dotfiles.
    • Behaviour: Calls kubectl internally. Unsupported subcommands still pass through uncoloured, and errors are highlighted.
    • Themes: --light-background for light terminals.
    • Coverage: Not all subcommands are colourised yet, according to the README.

    Takeaway: The idea is good, but this repo is archived. Look for a maintained fork before adopting it.

  • Black Hat USA 2022
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A YouTube playlist of recorded talks from Black Hat USA 2022, the security conference held in Las Vegas and online in August 2022.

    • Event: Black Hat USA 2022 ran as a hybrid event with more than 90 technical Briefings, per Black Hat’s press material.
    • Keynotes: Chris Krebs (“Black Hat at 25: Where Do We Go from Here?”) and journalist Kim Zetter gave the keynotes.
    • Format: A playlist of session recordings, so content covers many unrelated research talks rather than one topic.
    • Source caveat: The playlist page returned only its title; the track list could not be read. Summary based on the title and Black Hat 2022 press coverage found via search.

    Takeaway: Use it to browse Black Hat 2022 research talks by title and pick those relevant to your stack. Check the conference archive for matching slides and white papers.

  • AWS re:Invent 2022: Security Track
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The link opens the re:Invent 2022 session SEC203, “Revitalize your security with the AWS Security Reference Architecture”, inside AWS’s re:Invent 2022 security track playlist.

    • Speakers: Sarah Currey (AWS Professional Services) and Johnny Ray (Amazon Managed Services); a 200-level breakout.
    • Topic: The AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA), a multi-account guide for deploying the full set of AWS security services.
    • Uses shown: Bootstrapping a security architecture and defining a target security state.
    • Living document: The SRA is described as continuously updated as customer needs change.
    • Playlist: The list= parameter points to the wider re:Invent 2022 security track, so other sessions follow in the same playlist.
    • Source caveat: Video page gave only the title; details come from the AWS re:Invent session catalog blog and a Classmethod session report found via search.

    Takeaway: Watch it if you are designing a multi-account AWS security baseline. Pair it with the AWS SRA prescriptive guidance docs and the SRA code examples on GitHub.

  • Sigstore the Easy Way
    summary

    TL;DR: Sigstore The Easy Way is a hands-on guide by Rewanth Tammana to signing and verifying container images with the Sigstore toolset.

    • Cosign: Sign and verify images with a key and keyless; attach, attest and verify artifacts; download artifacts.
    • Rekor: Upload artifacts to the public and to a private Rekor transparency log, query the log, compare registry signatures with log entries.
    • Fulcio: Analyze the short-lived code-signing certificates used for keyless signing.
    • SBOM: Use cases, formats and generation of software bills of materials.
    • Scope: Works on container images and pulls in non-Sigstore tools where needed.
    • Format: MkDocs site backed by the rewanthtammana/sigstore-the-easy-way GitHub repo, created November 2022.

    Takeaway: A good lab path for learning cosign signing, keyless flows and transparency logs before adding image signing to a CI pipeline.

  • Ian Mckay’s Top 10 Favorite / Most Impactful re:Invent Announcements
    summary

    TL;DR: A December 2022 thread by AWS Community Hero Ian Mckay ranking his top 10 re:Invent 2022 announcements.

    • #10-#8: Amazon Inspector scanning Lambda packages (Java, Node, Python); AWS Verified Access, an identity-aware ZTNA proxy; delegated admin accounts for Organizations and AWS Backup.
    • #7: KMS external key stores for CMK key material, with a note that AWS warns of the risks.
    • #6-#5: Zero-ETL style feeds into Redshift from S3, RDS, Kinesis and MSK; EventBridge Pipes for service-to-service data pipelines with filtering and enrichment.
    • #4: Amazon Verified Permissions, an authorization engine using the new Cedar policy language.
    • #3-#2: Step Functions Distributed Map (up to 10k concurrent child executions); Lambda SnapStart for Java cold starts.
    • #1: VPC Lattice, likened to PrivateLink via a link-local address, with IAM auth and cross-account routing.

    Takeaway: A fast, security-leaning digest of re:Invent 2022. Verified Access, Verified Permissions and Lattice are the items most relevant to access control design.

  • Introducing VPC Lattice: Simplify Networking for Service-to-Service Communication (Preview)
    summary

    TL;DR: Danilo Poccia’s AWS News Blog post (29 Nov 2022) announcing the preview of Amazon VPC Lattice, an application-layer service network for service-to-service traffic.

    • Status: A note at the top says VPC Lattice became generally available on 31 March 2023.
    • Service network: A logical boundary across VPCs and accounts that provides discovery via DNS, connectivity and shared access and observability policies.
    • Protocols: Listeners support HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and gRPC, including HTTPS.
    • Targets: EC2 instances, IP addresses, Lambda functions, and Kubernetes services and pods via the AWS Gateway Controller.
    • Security: Access policies are IAM resource policies on the service network or service; sharing uses AWS RAM.
    • Routing: Rule-based and weighted routing for blue/green and canary deployments; handles IPv4/IPv6 and overlapping IPs.

    Takeaway: Lattice is an AWS-managed alternative to a service mesh or PrivateLink sprawl for cross-VPC service calls. Check the GA docs, as preview details changed.

  • New in Go 1.20: Wrapping Multiple Errors
    summary

    TL;DR: Lukáš Zapletal explains Go error wrapping and the Go 1.20 change that lets one error wrap several others.

    • Recap: Since Go 1.13, fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error; errors.Is and errors.As walk the chain.
    • errors.Join: New in 1.20, joins a variadic list of errors; output is newline-separated, which can surprise log tooling.
    • Multiple %w: fmt.Errorf("%w + %w", err1, err2) is now valid.
    • Unwrap() []error: A type can implement this instead of Unwrap() error, but not both.
    • Traversal: Wrapped errors become a tree; errors.Is/As do a pre-order, depth-first walk.
    • Use case: Collecting errors from goroutines when the count is unknown in advance.

    Takeaway: On Go 1.20+, use errors.Join or multiple %w instead of third-party multierror packages. Watch for newlines in joined messages.

  • Visualizing Multi-Cloud IAM Concepts
    summary

    TL;DR: Julian Wiegmann’s November 2022 post sharing hand-drawn mind maps of IAM concepts and terminology for AWS, Azure and GCP.

    • Content: One diagram per cloud, drawn in Miro, with links to JPG and vector PDF versions hosted on Google Cloud Storage.
    • Motivation: The author moved from security operations to cloud security and found the three clouds’ IAM terms and GCP’s lack of visuals confusing.
    • Caveats: Not a complete picture; federation and service-specific IAM (such as database admins) are not all shown, and accuracy is not guaranteed.
    • Printing: Best printed at A3.
    • Positioning: The author says it is not exam study material; read the provider docs and test in each cloud.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Useful as a side-by-side map when you work across clouds and need to translate IAM terms. Verify details against provider docs.

  • pike: Determine the Permissions or Policy Required for IaC Code
    summary

    TL;DR: Pike, by James Woolfenden, statically scans Terraform/OpenTofu code to determine the minimum IAM permissions needed to deploy it.

    • Providers: AWS (most resources), GCP and Azure (newest).
    • Usage: pike scan -d ./path/to/your/terraform outputs the required permissions or a policy.
    • Install: brew install jameswoolfenden/tap/pike, Scoop on Windows, or go install github.com/jameswoolfenden/pike@latest.
    • Newer features: JSON module support, GCP compare against a deployed role, S3 and GCP backend detection.
    • Caveat: Output has no conditions and partial resources are wild-carded; some GCP org-level entries are placeholders without validated permissions.
    • Short-lived creds: Can generate short-lived credentials for builds (AWS so far).

    Takeaway: Use Pike as a starting point for least-privilege CI deploy roles, then tighten the generated policy by hand.

  • How to Detect Security Issues in Amazon EKS Clusters Using Amazon GuardDuty: Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of an AWS Security Blog series (22 Nov 2022) walking through a real-world EKS compromise and how Amazon GuardDuty detects each step.

    • Prerequisites: GuardDuty with Kubernetes Protection and Malware Protection enabled.
    • Root cause: A developer granted RBAC access to system:anonymous to reach the public cluster endpoint without VPN.
    • Phases: Misconfiguration, Discovery, Initial Access (reading Kubernetes secrets), Persistence and Impact, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.
    • Defaults noted: EKS endpoints are public by default; the cluster creator gets system:masters.
    • Findings: Shows which GuardDuty findings fire at each phase.
    • Part 2: Covers Amazon Detective investigation, remediation and preventive controls.

    Takeaway: Enable GuardDuty EKS protection and never bind system:anonymous. Use the phases as a tabletop scenario for EKS incident response.

  • kubie: A More Powerful Alternative to kubectx and kubens
    summary

    TL;DR: kubie is a Rust CLI alternative to kubectx, kubens and prompt scripts, isolating Kubernetes context and namespace per shell.

    • Per-shell context: Each shell has its own context and namespace, so switching in one terminal does not affect others.
    • Split configs: Loads contexts from multiple kubeconfig files in configurable paths.
    • Commands: kubie exec runs a command in a context and namespace without spawning a shell; kubie lint checks kubeconfig files.
    • Install: brew install kubie, cargo install kubie, MacPorts, Nix, Arch pacman -S kubie, or release binaries.
    • Status: README points to issue #385 about the future of kubie development.

    Takeaway: Good fit if you juggle many clusters in parallel terminals and want to avoid running commands in the wrong context. Check issue #385 before adopting.

  • Managing Pod Security on Amazon EKS with Kyverno
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post (Jimmy Ray, with Nirmata’s Jim Bugwadia, 30 Nov 2022) on using Kyverno alongside Kubernetes Pod Security Admission on EKS.

    • PSA/PSS: Pod Security Standards define 17 controls in three levels (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted); PSA modes are enforce, audit and warn.
    • EKS default: From EKS 1.23, PSA is on but set to privileged for all pods, so nothing is enforced unless namespaces opt in.
    • Labels: Opt in with pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL> and optional version pinning.
    • Limitation: EKS does not allow custom PSA static config, and PSA applies per namespace with no per-pod exceptions.
    • Kyverno: Adds granular exceptions and extra behaviors on top of PSA/PSS.

    Takeaway: Label namespaces with PSA levels on EKS, and use Kyverno where you need per-workload exceptions or stricter rules.

  • wtf: The Personal Information Dashboard for Your Terminal
    summary

    TL;DR: WTF (wtfutil) is an open-source Go terminal dashboard showing at-a-glance stats and data from many sources.

    • Purpose: A personal information dashboard for your terminal, built from configurable modules.
    • License: MPL-2.0.
    • Install: Homebrew, go install, MacPorts or a release binary.
    • Rename: README says the project is being renamed to Tessera and moving to github.com/linodians/tessera ahead of v1.0.
    • Funding: Supported via GitHub Sponsors.

    Takeaway: Handy for a terminal status board of services you check rarely. Track the Tessera repo for future releases.

  • Google Cloud Infrastructure Reliability Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud’s Architecture Center guide to designing reliable infrastructure on GCP, covering building blocks, requirements, design and operations.

    • Parts: Building blocks (zones, regions, location-scoped resources), assessing reliability requirements, designing infrastructure, managing traffic and load, and managing and monitoring.
    • Availability math: 99.99% allows at most 8.64 seconds of downtime per 24 hours, or 10 failures per 100,000 requests.
    • Indicators: Availability, latency, throughput, durability and data correctness, by workload type.
    • Factors: App design, dependencies, infrastructure, capacity and DevOps processes all affect reliability.
    • DR: Points to a separate disaster recovery planning guide.
    • Updates: Page shows last review in 2026 with release notes, so content has changed since 2022.

    Takeaway: Read it before choosing zonal, regional or multi-regional deployments on GCP. Set availability targets first, then map them to resource scope.

  • YaraHunter: Malware Scanner for Cloud-Native, in CI/CD and at Runtime
    summary

    TL;DR: YaraHunter from Deepfence scans container images, running Docker containers and filesystems for malware using YARA rules.

    • Modes: CI/CD build scanning, images at rest, running containers, and local filesystems.
    • Rules: Uses the deepfence/yara-rules ruleset to match known malware signatures.
    • Form factor: Runs as a Docker container (quay.io/deepfenceio/deepfence_malware_scanner_ce) with JSON output for automation.
    • Example: Scanning the metal3d/xmrig image to find the XMRig cryptominer.
    • Status: Described as work in progress and integrated into the ThreatMapper platform.

    Takeaway: A simple way to add malware signature checks to image pipelines, complementing CVE scanners that do not look for malware.

  • A Roadmap to Zero Trust Architecture
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A vendor-agnostic Zero Trust reference architecture and implementation roadmap, launched in 2022 by Cloudflare with a group of security practitioners.

    • Structure: Four implementation phases with an example timeline, aimed at organizations starting their Zero Trust work.
    • Topics: Global DNS filtering, corporate identity, an inventory of corporate applications, enforced MFA, and finding misconfigured or publicly shared SaaS data.
    • Timeline: A full program is said to take about 2 to 3 years and stay ongoing.
    • Steps: Cloudflare’s related download lists 28 steps with dependencies and time estimates.
    • Source caveat: The site now sits behind a Cloudflare Access login. Summary based on a Cloud Security Alliance article and Cloudflare landing pages found via search.

    Takeaway: Use the phased roadmap to sequence Zero Trust work, starting with identity, MFA and app inventory. Get it now from Cloudflare’s roadmap page.

  • GCPGoat: A Damn Vulnerable GCP Infrastructure
    summary

    TL;DR: GCPGoat from INE is a deliberately vulnerable GCP environment, deployed with Terraform, for practicing cloud attack and defense.

    • Vulnerabilities: XSS, IDOR, SSRF on Cloud Functions, sensitive data exposure and password reset, Storage bucket misconfigurations, IAM privilege escalation.
    • Basis: OWASP Top 10 2021 plus misconfigurations in IAM, Storage, Cloud Functions and Compute Engine.
    • Stack: GCP, React, Python 3 and Terraform; black-box approach with multiple escalation paths.
    • Use: Cloud pentesting and red teaming, IaC auditing, secure coding, detection and mitigation.
    • Prerequisite: A GCP account with admin privileges; manual install needs Linux with bash.
    • Presented: Black Hat Asia 2023 Arsenal.

    Takeaway: Deploy it in an isolated throwaway project to practice GCP privilege escalation, then tear it down. Do not run it in a shared org.

27.10.2022

  • Istio: Introducing Ambient Mesh
    summary

    TL;DR: The September 2022 Istio blog post by Google and Solo.io engineers introducing ambient mesh, a sidecar-less Istio data plane mode.

    • Sidecar problems: Injection requires pod restarts, per-pod proxies are sized for worst case and waste resources, and HTTP processing can break non-conformant apps.
    • Two layers: A secure L4 overlay for routing and zero trust, plus optional L7 processing when needed.
    • ztunnel: A shared per-node agent that redirects workload traffic and provides mTLS, telemetry, authentication and L4 authorization, with no L7 processing.
    • Incremental adoption: Move per namespace from no mesh to secure overlay to full L7, and mix with sidecar workloads.
    • Status: Launched as a preview; a banner on the page now says ambient mode is generally available.

    Takeaway: Ambient mode lowers the cost of getting mTLS across a cluster. Start with the L4 overlay and add L7 only for namespaces that need it.

  • The Complete Guide to AWS KMS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Noga Yam Amitai’s September 2022 Lightspin blog guide to AWS KMS key types and access control.

    • Key types: Customer managed keys (you control access, rotation, policy), AWS managed keys (aws/service-name, rotated yearly, not editable) and AWS owned keys (not visible or auditable).
    • Inspect: aws kms describe-key --key-id KEY-ID --region REGION shows KeyManager as CUSTOMER or AWS.
    • Choosing: Neither type is more secure by default; AWS managed keys leave less room for misconfiguration, customer managed keys give more control and allow imported key material.
    • Access control: Key policies, IAM policies and grants; access needs an explicit allow in at least one and no deny (grants cannot deny).
    • Key policy: Each KMS key has exactly one key policy, the primary access control.
    • Source caveat: The live page is behind a Cloudflare challenge; summary based on the first part of a 2022 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Audit KMS key policies and grants together, since either can grant access. Use customer managed keys where you need tight cross-account control.

  • matano: Open-Source Security Lake Platform for AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: Matano is an open-source, serverless security data lake for AWS, written in Rust, from Matano Labs.

    • Ingest: 50+ managed log sources (such as CloudTrail and Route53) plus custom sources.
    • Transform: VRL (Vector Remap Language) scripts parse, enrich and normalize logs on ingest.
    • Storage: Apache Iceberg tables with the Elastic Common Schema (ECS), queryable from Athena, Snowflake, Spark or Trino.
    • Detection-as-code: Realtime Python detections, with import of Sigma rules.
    • Use cases: Reduce SIEM costs, add context to an existing SIEM, or replace an ELK/Elastic Security stack.
    • Commercial: The README notes Matano now also offers a managed commercial Cloud SIEM.

    Takeaway: Worth a look if SIEM ingest costs hurt and you want security logs in open formats in your own AWS account.

  • aws-security-assessment-solution: AWS Self-Service Security Assessment Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Labs solution that deploys an inexpensive, self-service security assessment of AWS accounts, built on the open-source Prowler scanner.

    • Engine: Runs Prowler point-in-time checks against AWS best practices and produces a report.
    • Version: README describes v2.0, installing a pinned Prowler release (5.41.0 at time of reading) via pip in a CodeBuild template.
    • Upgrade: Change the pip3 install prowler== line in 2-sat2-codebuild-prowler.yaml.
    • Continuous option: AWS recommends Security Hub’s Foundational Security Best Practices standard for ongoing checks.
    • Caveat: Prowler is not AWS-owned; review it before running.
    • Guide: Step-by-step instructions in module 2 of the SHIP Workshop.

    Takeaway: A fast way to baseline an account with no security tooling. Move to Security Hub for continuous monitoring afterwards.

  • plumber: Swiss Army Knife CLI for Interacting with Kafka, RabbitMQ and Other Messaging Systems
    summary

    TL;DR: plumber is a Go CLI, “like curl for messaging systems”, for reading, writing and relaying data in Kafka, RabbitMQ, GCP Pub/Sub and other brokers.

    • Features: View stream contents, write plain or encoded messages, route data between systems.
    • Decoding: Realtime protobuf, Avro, Thrift and JSON decoding, including google.protobuf.Any fields.
    • Example: plumber write kafka --topics test --input foo.
    • Install: brew tap streamdal/public then brew install plumber, or a single binary per OS.
    • Ownership: The repo now redirects to streamdal/plumber, and the tool relays data to the Streamdal platform.

    Takeaway: Saves writing throwaway consumers when debugging event-driven systems. Use it to peek into topics and queues.

  • Understanding Basic Networking in GKE: Networking Basics
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud blog post (August 2022, Ammett Williams and Abdel Sghiouar) explaining IP addressing and networking components in GKE.

    • Components: Containers, Pods, Nodes, ClusterIP services, load balancers and Ingress for HTTP(S).
    • Host formula: Google Cloud subnets give 2^n - 4 usable hosts, not the on-premises 2^n - 2.
    • Node IPs: Come from the cluster’s VPC; internal load balancer IPs default to the node IPv4 block.
    • Pod ranges: Default max is 110 Pods per node; doubled to 220 and rounded to a /24 per node, configurable at creation.
    • Service IPs: ClusterIPs come from a separate reserved range in VPC-native clusters.

    Takeaway: Size node, Pod and Service ranges before you create a VPC-native cluster. The /24-per-node default consumes address space fast.

  • Scaling Cross-Account AWS KMS-Encrypted Amazon S3 Bucket Access Using ABAC
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post (September 2022, Jorg Huser and Ravi Sankar Prasad Kadiri) on sharing KMS-encrypted S3 data lake buckets across many accounts using attribute-based access control.

    • Scenario: One central data lake account sharing to many tenant accounts, for services not using Lake Formation.
    • Org restriction: aws:PrincipalOrgID in trust and resource policies limits access to your AWS Organization, even with Principal: *.
    • ABAC: Session tags on the assumed role are matched with S3 object tags, so fewer roles and policies are needed.
    • Identity source: A SAML IdP can pass employee attributes as session tags via STS.
    • Cross-account needs: Bucket policy, KMS key policy and the caller’s IAM policy must all grant access.

    Takeaway: For multi-tenant data sharing, tag-based policies scale better than per-account statements. Combine them with aws:PrincipalOrgID as a guardrail.

  • jqp: A TUI Playground to Experiment with jq
    summary

    TL;DR: jqp by Noah Gorstein is a terminal UI playground for running jq queries interactively, built on the Go gojq implementation.

    • Input: JSON or NDJSON from a file (-f) or stdin; stdin takes precedence.
    • Example: curl https://api.github.com/repos/jqlang/jq/issues | jqp '.[] | {"title": .title, "url": .url}'.
    • Keys: tab to cycle sections, ctrl-y copies the query, ctrl-s saves output.
    • Config: $HOME/.jqp.yaml, with themes via -t.
    • Install: brew install jqp, MacPorts, AUR jqp-bin, Snap, or releases.

    Takeaway: Use it to build and debug jq filters against real API output before pasting them into scripts.

  • OpenTelemetry in Various Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: The 10 October 2022 edition of the o11y news newsletter, a link roundup on OpenTelemetry and observability.

    • Rust: Peterpaul Klein Haneveld’s hands-on OpenTelemetry context propagation article.
    • Profiling: InfoQ article and podcast with Frederic Branczyk on continuous profiling with eBPF.
    • IoT: HiveMQ’s distributed tracing extension with OpenTelemetry support for its MQTT broker.
    • AWS: Lumigo’s Michele Mancioppi on OpenTelemetry on AWS and resource attributes.
    • Demo and events: Honeycomb’s Pierre Tessier showing the OpenTelemetry community demo; OpenTelemetry talks at KubeCon NA 2022 compiled by Alolita Sharma.

    Takeaway: A short reading list for OpenTelemetry in different runtimes. The AWS resource attributes talk and the community demo are the most practical picks.

  • Stop Messing with Kubernetes Finalizers
    summary

    TL;DR: The URL now shows Martin Heinz’s “Stop Messing with Kubernetes Finalizers”, which argues against force-deleting stuck resources, not the archived title about Python automation.

    • Title mismatch: The link was saved as “Automate All the Boring Kubernetes Operations with Python”, but /blog/74 serves the finalizers article.
    • Finalizers: Metadata keys like kubernetes.io/pvc-protection that block deletion until a controller cleans up; deletionTimestamp makes the object read-only.
    • Force delete risks: Removing finalizers can leave cloud storage or load balancers dangling and still billed.
    • Pods: kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force removes the Pod from etcd but it may keep running on the node.
    • StatefulSets: Force deletion can create two Pods with the same identity accessing the same storage, risking data corruption.
    • Namespaces: Use .spec.finalizers (kubernetes) rather than .metadata.finalizers.

    Takeaway: When deletion hangs, find which controller or resource holds the finalizer and fix that. Do not strip finalizers.

  • On Amazon EKS and FIS (Chaos Engineering)
    summary

    TL;DR: Dirk Michel’s September 2022 article on using AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) to coordinate chaos experiments across AWS resources and Kubernetes workloads on EKS.

    • Problem: AWS-level faults and Kubernetes-level faults (LitmusChaos, Chaos Mesh) usually run with separate tools.
    • FIS templates: Experiments are defined as Action Sets, Targets, Stop Conditions and Log Destinations.
    • IAM: FIS ties into IAM to authorize defining and running experiments, in CI/CD or by humans.
    • Cross-layer: Coordinates faults across AWS services, Kubernetes and apps, including those using AWS Controllers for Kubernetes.
    • GitOps: Fits experiment definitions into a GitOps flow for review, audit and authorization.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Use FIS as the single orchestrator if you want guarded, auditable chaos experiments on EKS that span cloud and cluster faults.

  • K8s Troubleshooting: Namespace Stuck in Terminating State
    summary

    TL;DR: A short September 2022 Dev Genius troubleshooting post on fixing a Kubernetes namespace stuck in Terminating.

    • Step 1: Run kubectl get ns <name> -oyaml and read status.conditions, such as NamespaceDeletionDiscoveryFailure from an unavailable metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 API.
    • Step 2: List leftover resources with kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n 1 kubectl get --show-kind --ignore-not-found -n <ns>.
    • Broken APIService: Inspect with kubectl get APIService <version>.<group> and kubectl describe it.
    • Step 3: As a last resort, dump the namespace to JSON, remove spec.finalizers, and submit it to the finalize endpoint.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Most stuck namespaces come from a broken aggregated API or leftover resources. Fix those before force-removing the finalizer.

  • VS Code Draw.io Integration
    summary

    TL;DR: An unofficial VS Code extension by Henning Dieterichs that embeds the Draw.io (diagrams.net) editor in VS Code.

    • Formats: Edit .drawio, .dio, .drawio.svg and .drawio.png; the SVG/PNG variants are valid images with the diagram embedded.
    • Git-friendly: .drawio files are plain XML and diff cleanly; the page recommends them over .drawio.png for review.
    • Offline: Uses an offline Draw.io by default, with several themes.
    • Collaboration: VS Code Live Share support for co-editing and presenting.
    • Code links: Nodes and edges can link to code spans.
    • Adoption: Over 4.2 million installs at time of reading.

    Takeaway: Keep architecture diagrams as .drawio.svg next to code so they render in READMEs and change in the same pull request.

  • Wails v2 Released: Rich Frontends for Go Programs
    summary

    TL;DR: Lea Anthony’s 22 September 2022 announcement of Wails v2, a lightweight Go alternative to Electron for building desktop apps with web frontends.

    • Windows: WebView2 component, no CGO requirement, dark/light and custom themes.
    • Templates: Svelte, Vue, React, Preact, Lit and vanilla, with Vite hot reload in dev mode.
    • Native features: Menus, dialogs, translucency with Mica and Acrylic backdrops.
    • Tooling: NSIS installer generation, garble obfuscation, UPX compression, automatic TypeScript generation for Go structs.
    • Deployment: No extra libraries or DLLs to ship, and no separate frontend asset bundle.
    • Effort: About 2.2K commits by 89 contributors since the first alpha.
    • Source caveat: The live site showed a Cloudflare challenge; read from a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: A good option for small cross-platform desktop tools in Go without Electron’s footprint.

  • Test Scripts in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting), in an excerpt from “The Power of Go: Tests”, shows how to test Go CLI binaries with the testscript package.

    • Package: github.com/rogpeppe/go-internal/testscript.
    • Script language: Shell-like files, for example exec echo 'hello world' followed by stdout 'hello world\n'.
    • Runner: testscript.Run(t, testscript.Params{Dir: "testdata/script"}) runs each script as a parallel subtest.
    • Problem solved: Avoids hand-written tests that build the binary, run it, and parse exit codes and output.
    • Layout: Scripts live in testdata/script next to the Go source.

    Takeaway: Use testscript for end-to-end CLI tests in Go. Scripts are easier to read and extend than hand-rolled os/exec tests.

  • AWS Ramp-Up Guide: Security
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Training and Certification’s five-page Ramp-Up Guide for security, a curated list of AWS courses, docs and workshops for building cloud security skills.

    • Fundamentals and IAM: AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials, AWS Security Essentials, Introduction to IAM, plus Control Tower and STS.
    • Detection: Getting Started with Amazon GuardDuty and with AWS Security Hub; also Security Lake, CloudTrail, Detective, Inspector, Macie and KMS.
    • Governance and audit: Security Governance at Scale, Cloud Audit Academy, AWS Config and Audit Manager.
    • Incident response: Guides for compromised IAM credentials, ransomware and cryptomining, plus threat modeling and hands-on workshops.
    • Certification: Points to AWS Certified Security - Specialty exam readiness and the SCS-C02 practice question set.
    • Version: PDF metadata shows it was updated in June 2024, so the content is newer than the 2022 link date.
    • Source caveat: Text was extracted with limited fidelity; structure was inferred from the PDF’s headings and link targets.

    Takeaway: Use it as a structured study plan for AWS security or the Security Specialty exam. Work through it in order, from IAM to detection to incident response.

  • eraser: Cleaning Up Images from Kubernetes Nodes
    summary

    TL;DR: Eraser, originally from Azure, removes a list of non-running container images from all nodes in a Kubernetes cluster.

    • Purpose: Clean up unused and often vulnerable images left on nodes.
    • Location: The repo now lives at eraser-dev/eraser, with docs at eraser-dev.github.io/eraser.
    • Governance: Follows the CNCF Code of Conduct; has OpenSSF Best Practices and Scorecard badges.
    • Community: #eraser channel on Kubernetes Slack, a mailing list and biweekly meetings.
    • Docs: A quick start guide and development setup in the project documentation.

    Takeaway: Useful for clusters with long-lived nodes, where stale images pile up and show up in node vulnerability scans.

  • AWS Security Hub Launches a New Security Best Practice Control
    summary

    TL;DR: An 8 September 2022 AWS What’s New item: Security Hub added one control to its Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) standard.

    • New control: [AutoScaling.9] Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups should use EC2 launch templates.
    • Total: Security Hub supported 224 security controls at that point.
    • Auto-enable: Enabled automatically if you use FSBP with automatic enabling of new controls.
    • Integrations: Aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Config, Inspector, Macie, Firewall Manager, IAM Access Analyzer and over 65 partner tools.
    • Standards: FSBP, CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and PCI DSS.
    • Trial: 30-day free trial.

    Takeaway: If Auto Scaling groups still use launch configurations, expect this finding and migrate them to launch templates.

  • requests-ip-rotator: Use AWS API Gateway’s Large IP Pool as a Proxy for Pseudo-Infinite IPs
    summary

    TL;DR: requests-ip-rotator is a Python library that routes requests traffic through AWS API Gateway so each request leaves from a different AWS IP, defeating IP-based rate limits.

    • Mechanism: API Gateway sends requests from its large IP pool; the library randomizes X-Forwarded-For so the real client IP is not passed on.
    • Usage: ApiGateway("https://site.com"), start(), session.mount(...), then shutdown(), or a with block.
    • Install: pip3 install requests-ip-rotator.
    • Cost: API Gateway’s free tier covers the first million requests per region; then about $3 per million, plus $0.09 per GB data transfer.
    • Detectable: Requests carry AWS headers such as X-Amzn-Trace-Id, so they can be identified and blocked.
    • Warning: Gateways not shut down can keep incurring charges.

    Takeaway: Relevant to defenders as much as testers: IP-based rate limiting alone does not stop brute forcing. Consider blocking or flagging API Gateway traffic patterns.

  • merloc: Live AWS Lambda Function Development and Debugging Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: MerLoc from Thundra runs an AWS Lambda function locally while it stays part of the live cloud flow, for live development and debugging.

    • Runtimes: Java, Go, Python, Node.js and .NET; works with Serverless Framework and AWS SAM.
    • Real events: The local function receives real requests from the Lambda environment while other functions run in AWS.
    • Debugging: IDE breakpoints and hot reload, with no build, package and deploy cycle.
    • IAM: Propagates the real Lambda’s IAM credentials to the local function, so permission issues can be tested locally.
    • Hosting: Free with Thundra APM, or self-host the MerLoc broker.

    Takeaway: Speeds up debugging event-driven Lambda flows. Check that the project is still maintained before relying on it.

  • A Guide to Improving Security Through Infrastructure-as-Code
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Viktor Gazdag’s September 2022 NCC Group guide to building security into infrastructure-as-code workflows, focused on free and open-source tools.

    • Threat modeling: STRIDE, Draw.io, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, attack trees, CIS Benchmarks and MITRE ATT&CK.
    • Static analysis: TFLint, tfsec, Checkov, Regula, Semgrep, tfscan and KICS in IDEs and CI/CD.
    • Policy as code: OPA, Regula, cfn_nag, CloudFormation Guard, Azure Policy, plus GCP Organization Policy and AWS SCPs.
    • IAM analysis: Policy Sentry, Cloudsplaining, PMapper, AWSPX, Pacu, IAM Zero and GCP-focused tools.
    • Pipelines: Signed commits, pair review, branch protection with status checks, small traceable changes.
    • Drift: driftctl, InSpec, Serverspec and Terratest; OpenCSPM and magpie for mature setups.
    • Source caveat: The original research.nccgroup.com URL now redirects to the research index; content read from the article’s current location at nccgroup.com/research.

    Takeaway: A good checklist of where to put security gates in an IaC pipeline. Pick one scanner and one policy engine and enforce them in CI.

  • Terraform 1.3 Improves Extensibility and Maintainability of Terraform Modules
    summary

    TL;DR: Kyle Ruddy’s 21 September 2022 HashiCorp post on Terraform 1.3, which improves module design and refactoring.

    • Optional attributes: Optional object type attributes with defaults are now stable (experimental since 0.14), for example protocol = optional(string, "tcp").
    • Behavior: Missing optional attributes without a default become null.
    • Moved blocks: moved (added in 1.1) now works across module sources, including Registry and private registry modules.
    • Example: Moving aws_instance.hashiapp into module.web-server-aws.aws_instance.hashiapp.
    • Benefit: Replaces error-prone manual terraform state mv runs.
    • Source caveat: curl hit a Vercel browser check; content read via WebFetch.

    Takeaway: On Terraform 1.3+, use optional() defaults to simplify module inputs and moved blocks to refactor into shared modules without state surgery.

  • dexter: Kubernetes OIDC Helper with as Much Automation as Possible
    summary

    TL;DR: dexter from Gini is a Go OIDC helper that logs you in to Kubernetes through Google or Azure and updates your kubeconfig automatically.

    • Status: Archived; the notice says it is no longer maintained as of 2025-05-15 and suggests int128/kubelogin.
    • Providers: Google and Microsoft Azure, both complete.
    • Flow: Opens a browser to the IdP; after login, kubeconfig is updated with the tokens.
    • Setup: OAuth client with redirect URI http://127.0.0.1:64464/callback.
    • Auto pilot: Extracts OIDC settings from an existing kubectl context.
    • Build: Release binaries or goreleaser release --snapshot --clean.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt it for new setups. Use kubelogin for OIDC logins to Kubernetes.

  • Supply Chain Security on Amazon EKS Using AWS KMS, Kyverno, and Cosign
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Open Source Blog post (Imtranur Rahman, 21 Sep 2022) on signing container images with Cosign and an AWS KMS key, then enforcing signatures on EKS with Kyverno.

    • Framework: Uses the four principles of the CNCF Security TAG supply chain paper: verification, automation, authorization in controlled environments, secure authentication.
    • Signing: Cosign generates and uses a key pair backed by AWS KMS.
    • Enforcement: A Kyverno ImageVerify policy only admits images signed against the KMS public key.
    • Kyverno: A Kubernetes-native policy engine where policies are Kubernetes resources, no new language required.
    • Scope: Applies across source repos, dependencies, build pipelines, artifact registries and deployments.

    Takeaway: A practical pattern for admitting only signed images on EKS without managing private keys on build machines.

  • Use AWS Network Firewall to Filter Outbound HTTPS Traffic from Applications on Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post (Kirankumar Chandrashekar, 12 Sep 2022) on restricting EKS egress HTTPS to an allow list of hostnames, using SNI in AWS Network Firewall.

    • SNI: The TLS extension that carries the destination hostname unencrypted, so a firewall can filter HTTPS by name, not by IP.
    • Architecture: Per AZ, public subnets hold firewall endpoints, private subnets hold EKS nodes, protected subnets hold NAT gateways.
    • Flow: Pod to NAT gateway, to Network Firewall endpoint, to internet gateway; rules allow or drop by SNI hostname.
    • Logging: Also shows how to collect the hostnames your apps access.
    • Update: The architecture diagram was revised on 13 Oct 2022.

    Takeaway: Use SNI allow lists for EKS egress control when destinations change IPs. Log first to build the list, then enforce.

  • Integrating Kubecost with Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Cloud Operations blog post (September 2022, with Kubecost) on running Kubecost for EKS cost insight backed by Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus.

    • Problem: Cost and Usage Reports show control plane and EC2 costs, but not costs by namespace, pod or label.
    • Kubecost: Built on OpenCost, a CNCF Sandbox project; breaks down costs by pods, nodes, namespaces and labels against the real AWS bill.
    • Backend: Uses an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace instead of a self-managed Prometheus.
    • Scope: Covers a single EKS cluster setup.
    • AMP: Prometheus-compatible service that scales ingestion, storage, alerting and querying automatically.

    Takeaway: A way to get per-team Kubernetes cost reports without running Prometheus storage yourself.

  • nginxpwner: Look for Common Nginx Misconfigurations and Vulnerabilities
    summary

    TL;DR: Nginxpwner is a Python tool that checks a target for common Nginx misconfigurations and known vulnerabilities.

    • Usage: python3 nginxpwner.py https://example.com /tmp/pathlist, with paths taken from Burp or unfurl.
    • Version check: Finds the Nginx version and looks up exploits with searchsploit.
    • Checks: CRLF via $uri in redirects, external PURGE, variable leakage, path traversal via merge_slashes off or a misconfigured alias (using Kyubi).
    • Bypasses: Hop-by-hop header tests and 401/403 bypass via X-Accel-Redirect.
    • CVE: Tests the range filter integer overflow CVE-2017-7529.
    • Limits: Relies on the Server header (a separate script exists without it); does not test cache poisoning or request smuggling.

    Takeaway: A quick first pass when testing Nginx fronted apps. Use it against your own configs to catch alias and $uri mistakes.

  • aws-security-survival-kit: Bare Minimum AWS Security Alerting
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Survival Kit (ASSK) from zoph.io is a minimal AWS account alerting setup: two CloudFormation stacks, about 30 EventBridge rules and an SNS topic.

    • Alerts: Root logins, CloudTrail tampering, IAM user and MFA changes, AdministratorAccess attachments, SSH opened to 0.0.0.0/0, shared snapshots or AMIs, AccessDenied bursts.
    • Delivery: Email, or Slack and Teams via AWS Chatbot.
    • Deploy: Set variables in the Makefile, run make deploy; make tear-down removes it.
    • Hardening: Deploy also enables S3 Block Public Access, EBS encryption, IMDSv2 by default and public AMI/snapshot blocks in every region.
    • Positioning: Complements GuardDuty; not a SIEM or SOAR.
    • Cost: Described as free or near-free, with no agents or SaaS.

    Takeaway: A sensible baseline for small or personal AWS accounts that have no alerting today.

  • Serverless Ad Blocking with Cloudflare Gateway
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lancini shows how to replicate a Pi-hole with no hardware, using Cloudflare Gateway DNS policies managed through Terraform.

    • Gateway: Cloudflare’s Secure Web Gateway inspects DNS, network (TCP/UDP/GRE) and HTTP traffic; the post focuses on DNS policies.
    • Plan: The free Cloudflare for Teams (Zero Trust) plan is enough.
    • Terraform: cloudflare_zero_trust_gateway_settings configures the block page, antivirus, TCP/UDP proxy and logging.
    • Devices: Install the Cloudflare root certificate and the WARP client to route DNS through Gateway.
    • Policies: One to block security risks, one for ad blocking from domain lists that Terraform splits into chunks.
    • Updates: GitHub Actions keep the blocklist current; a reusable Terraform module was released in January 2023.

    Takeaway: A cheap, maintenance-free way to get network-wide ad and malware blocking for a home office, kept as code.

  • Tool Release: Project Kubescout, Adding Kubernetes Support to Scout Suite
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Liyun Li’s September 2022 NCC Group post announcing Kubescout, Kubernetes cluster auditing added to the open-source Scout Suite cloud scanner.

    • Run: pip3 install ScoutSuite then scout kubernetes, using the local kubeconfig; options include --config-file, --context and --do-not-persist-config.
    • Providers: EKS, GKE and AKS via -c/--cluster-provider, adding provider data such as control plane logging settings.
    • Data handling: Downloads cluster resources and redacts Secret values before writing to disk; supports custom resources.
    • Rules: A base set including CIS Benchmark rules, for example hard-coded secrets in ConfigMaps and over-privileged subjects.
    • Limits: Feature preview, basic RBAC review, no pagination yet; output is a static HTML report.
    • Source caveat: The original research.nccgroup.com URL now redirects to the research index; content read from the article’s current nccgroup.com/research location.

    Takeaway: If you already use Scout Suite for cloud accounts, scout kubernetes adds a quick cluster misconfiguration review in the same report format.

  • xg2xg: By Ex-Googlers, for Ex-Googlers, a Lookup Table of Similar Tech and Services
    summary

    TL;DR: xg2xg is a community lookup table mapping Google-internal technologies to their public Google and open-source equivalents, for ex-Googlers.

    • Format: Three columns: Google Internal, Google External, Open Source / Real-World.
    • Examples: MapReduce to Hadoop and Spark; Flume to Dataflow and Apache Beam; Stubby to gRPC; Chubby to ZooKeeper, etcd and Consul; Goops/PubSub to Cloud Pub/Sub and Kafka.
    • Serialization: Protocol Buffers alongside Cap’n Proto, Thrift, Avro, Amazon Ion and CBOR.
    • Related links: System Design Primer, Hadoop Ecosystem Table, the AWS-to-GCP service map, Database of Databases.
    • Rule: Pull requests welcome, but no confidential projects.

    Takeaway: Handy for anyone reading Google papers or talks who wants the open-source equivalent of a named internal system.

  • How Kubefirst Builds Kubernetes Platforms in 8 Steps
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A September 2022 Kubefirst blog post listing eight building blocks of a GitOps Kubernetes platform that the open-source kubefirst CLI automates.

    • Steps 1-2: Choose a Git provider (GitHub or self-hosted GitLab); automate IaC with Terraform plus Atlantis, Pulumi or Crossplane, avoiding cloud-proprietary tools.
    • Steps 3-4: Pick a GitOps driver guided by OpenGitOps principles; commit to a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault).
    • Steps 5-6: Set up an artifact repository (Harbor, Artifactory, Nexus or Git provider registries); build CI with Tekton, Argo Workflows or self-hosted runners.
    • Steps 7-8: Connect identity, cloud and cluster roles through OIDC managed by Terraform; add observability (Datadog early, or Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger).
    • Claim: The kubefirst CLI sets this up in your cloud in under 25 minutes, with replaceable components.
    • Source caveat: kubefirst.io now redirects to Civo’s Konstruct product page; summary based on the DEV Community repost of the article.

    Takeaway: Use the eight steps as a checklist for an internal developer platform, whether or not you use Kubefirst.

  • Internet.nl: Test Your Email Server, Website, and Connection
    summary

    TL;DR: Internet.nl is a free Dutch test site that checks whether a website, email domain or your own connection uses modern Internet standards.

    • Website test: IPv6, DNSSEC, HTTPS/TLS configuration, security headers including CSP and security.txt, and RPKI route authorization.
    • Email test: IPv6, anti-phishing (DMARC, DKIM, SPF), STARTTLS and DANE secure transport, and RPKI.
    • Connection test: IPv6 reachability and DNSSEC validation by your resolver.
    • Hall of Fame: Lists domains scoring 100% on both web and mail tests.
    • Self-hosting: Available as a ready-to-go Docker package.
    • Updates: Recent news mentions a fully updated TLS test and a new CAA test.

    Takeaway: Run your domains through both tests after DNS or mail changes. It quickly flags missing DMARC, DNSSEC or weak TLS.

  • maigret: Collect a Dossier on a Person by Username from Thousands of Sites
    summary

    TL;DR: Maigret is a Python OSINT tool that builds a dossier on a person from a username, checking thousands of sites with no API keys.

    • Coverage: About 5,900 sites; a default run checks the top 500 by traffic, -a checks all, --tags filters by category or country.
    • Install: pip install maigret then maigret YOUR_USERNAME (Python 3.10+).
    • Extraction: Pulls profile data and linked accounts, then searches recursively on new usernames and IDs.
    • Evasion: Detects and partly bypasses blocks, censorship and CAPTCHA; supports Tor and I2P sites.
    • Outputs: Web interface with a graph view and report downloads; optional --ai summary via an OpenAI-compatible API.
    • Database: Site list auto-updates from GitHub once per 24 hours.

    Takeaway: Useful for authorized OSINT and for checking your own or your staff’s username exposure. Handle results under privacy rules.

  • 26 AWS Security Best Practices to Adopt in Production
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sysdig blog post listing 26 AWS security best practices grouped by service, now shown as updated by Alejandro Villanueva in November 2024.

    • IAM: No * admin policies, policies on groups and roles, rotate keys every 90 days or less, no root access keys, MFA for console users, hardware MFA for root, remove credentials unused for 90+ days.
    • S3: Account-level and bucket-level Block Public Access, server-side encryption.
    • Logging: A multi-Region CloudTrail trail with encryption and log file validation; AWS Config in all Regions.
    • EC2/VPC: EBS encryption by default, VPC flow logs everywhere, default security group with no rules.
    • Other services: No public DMS replication instances or EBS snapshots, OpenSearch encryption at rest, SageMaker notebooks without direct internet, supported Lambda runtimes.
