    • KMS and GuardDuty: Watch for unintended key deletion; enable GuardDuty in all supported Regions.
    • Version note: The page now carries a 2024 date, so its content may differ from the 2022 version linked.

    Takeaway: A compact production checklist, largely aligned with CIS AWS benchmarks. Automate it with Security Hub or a CSPM rather than checking by hand.

  • Our Application Security Journey (Part 1)
    summary

    TL;DR: Cristiano Corrado’s September 2022 post on how Wise’s Application Security team built automated container vulnerability management with clear ownership.

    • Problem: Split ownership between platform-maintained base images and product teams’ code, plus assigning findings to the right owners.
    • Scanner: Trivy for OS packages and application libraries in container images.
    • Ownership: An internal service catalogue with tiering and team mappings, plus the deployment service API to find images running in production.
    • Vulnerability management: DefectDojo for de-duplication, custom parsers, APIs, product tags, ownership and SLA counters.
    • Dashboards: Data goes to Looker on Snowflake, which engineers already used, instead of adding another UI.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Ownership mapping matters more than the scanner. Route findings to teams through tools they already use.

  • Kubernetes: Multi-Tenancy
    summary

    TL;DR: The official Kubernetes docs page on cluster multi-tenancy: use cases, isolation options and best practices for sharing clusters.

    • Use cases: Multiple teams in one organization, and multiple customers (SaaS or “multi-customer tenancy”).
    • Trade-off: Sharing saves cost and admin work but raises security, fairness and noisy-neighbor issues.
    • No tenant object: Kubernetes has no first-class tenant concept and relies on several features instead.
    • Controls: Namespaces, RBAC, resource quotas and network policies as the baseline for team tenancy.
    • Data plane isolation: Network and storage isolation, sandboxed containers and node isolation.
    • Other topics: API Priority and Fairness, QoS, DNS, operators, and two implementation models: namespace per tenant or a virtual control plane per tenant.

    Takeaway: Decide your tenancy model first. Then layer namespaces, RBAC, quotas and network policies, and add node or cluster isolation for untrusted tenants.

  • Run a Tailscale VPN Relay on ECS/Fargate
    summary

    TL;DR: David Norton of Platformers (February 2022) describes running a Tailscale subnet relay on ECS Fargate to give staff access to private VPC resources.

    • Why: Move databases to private subnets without the overhead of a bastion host and SSH keys; AWS Client VPN looked too expensive.
    • Tailscale: WireGuard-based VPN; free personal tier, business plans from $5 per user per month at the time.
    • Downsides noted: No official Terraform provider, and OIDC login only on Enterprise plans at the time.
    • Setup: A one-off, ephemeral auth key; Fargate task in relay mode with userspace networking, so no elevated container permissions.
    • Image: A custom Docker image with a bootstrap script that runs tailscale up, or a Terraform null_resource alternative.

    Takeaway: A low-cost VPN pattern for small AWS teams. Recheck current Tailscale pricing and features before adopting.

  • Chainguard Images: Container Images Designed for Minimalism and Security
    summary

    TL;DR: The Chainguard Images GitHub org hosts minimal, mostly distroless container images built for security and nightly rebuilds.

    • Distroless: Many images contain only the app and its runtime dependencies, with no shell or package manager.
    • Build tools: melange builds APKs from declarative YAML; apko assembles APKs into OCI images.
    • Base: Built on the Wolfi un-distro, except a few Alpine/musl images such as cgr.dev/chainguard/static and busybox.
    • Supply chain: SBOMs and signatures on images for provenance.
    • Freshness: Aim to rebuild from latest sources every night to address vulnerabilities quickly.
    • Registry: Images are served from cgr.dev/chainguard.

    Takeaway: Minimal, nightly-rebuilt, signed base images reduce attack surface and CVE noise. Test for missing shells or tools before switching.

  • La Terminal: iOS Terminal
    summary

    TL;DR: La Terminal is a native SSH client app for iPhone and iPad (and now Vision Pro); xibbon.com now redirects to la-terminal.net.

    • Native UI: Built for touch, unlike HTML-based terminal emulators; based on the open-source SwiftTerm library.
    • Author: From the creator of Midnight Commander.
    • Security: Private keys are stored in the Secure Enclave.
    • Features: Command search over history, a workflow gallery, resource and network monitors, inline images and a file manager.
    • AI: “El Copiloto” helps write shell commands from plain English.
    • Distribution: Apple App Store.

    Takeaway: A good option for on-call SSH from an iPad or phone, with hardware-backed key storage.

  • CasaOS: Your Home Cloud OS
    summary

    TL;DR: CasaOS is an open-source (Apache 2.0) personal cloud system built around Docker; the site now points users to its successor, ZimaOS.

    • Install: curl -fsSL https://get.casaos.io | sudo bash.
    • Apps: 20+ preinstalled Docker-based apps and 50+ community-verified self-hosted apps.
    • Hardware: ZimaBoard, Intel NUC and Raspberry Pi; amd64, armv7 and arm64.
    • OS: Ubuntu, Debian, Raspberry Pi OS and CentOS.
    • Features: Dashboard, file manager, file sharing, remote access and a CLI.
    • Status: The page says CasaOS has been upgraded to ZimaOS, a NAS OS.

    Takeaway: An easy home-lab front end for Docker apps. Review the install script before piping it to sudo bash, and check ZimaOS for new setups.

  • Eraser: Diagrams as Code
    summary

    TL;DR: The Eraser docs page of example architecture diagrams written in Eraser’s diagram-as-code syntax.

    • Examples: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Kubernetes architecture diagrams, each with an “Open in Eraser” link to duplicate.
    • Syntax: Nodes with icons, such as Lambda [icon: aws-lambda]; groups in braces, such as VPC Subnet { ... }.
    • Connections: Arrows like API gateway > Lambda > Server > Data, with fan-out such as Queue > Worker1, Worker2, Worker3.
    • Icons: Provider icon sets for AWS (aws-ec2, aws-rds), GCP (gcp-pubsub, gcp-bigquery), Azure and Kubernetes.
    • Styling: Per-node attributes such as color: grey.

    Takeaway: Copy one of the examples as a starting template for versionable architecture diagrams instead of drawing boxes by hand.

  • Encryption in AWS and Multi-Account Access
    summary

    TL;DR: Jason Kao’s September 2022 CloudQuery post on choosing KMS key types for encryption in multi-account AWS environments.

    • Services: AWS KMS and CloudHSM for symmetric encryption; KMS now also supports asymmetric and HMAC keys.
    • Expanded table: Compares customer managed keys with external key material, with a CloudHSM custom key store, and with AWS-provided material, plus AWS managed and AWS owned keys.
    • Key difference: Only customer managed keys allow multi-account access; AWS managed keys do not.
    • Rotation: Automatic rotation is optional for customer managed keys with AWS material, unavailable for imported or custom store keys, required for AWS managed keys.
    • Example: An IAM role in a compute account reading an encrypted S3 bucket in a data account, using a customer managed key.

    Takeaway: If data will be shared across accounts, encrypt it with a customer managed key from the start. AWS managed keys block cross-account access.

  • Unofficial List of Free Resources to Learn AWS for Absolute Beginners
    summary

    TL;DR: A community-maintained Google Doc listing free resources for absolute beginners learning AWS, with a Netherlands focus.

    • Programs: AWS re/Start (via TechGrounds and Refugee Talent Hub in NL), IT Skills 4U for Ukrainians with free exam vouchers, AWS CloudUp for Her, AWS Cloud Women Mentoring Program EMEA.
    • Self-study: Learn to Cloud, the free 12-week Cloud Project Bootcamp, Serverless Land, FooBar Serverless on YouTube.
    • AWS Educate: Free hands-on labs and self-paced resources.
    • Tip: A prepaid Visa, Mastercard or American Express debit card can open an AWS account without a credit card.
    • Updates: Entries reference 2024 programs, so the list has been maintained since 2022.
    • Source caveat: Read via the document’s plain-text export, as the editor view needs JavaScript.

    Takeaway: A good list to share with career changers. Check program dates, as many run in cohorts.

  • Diving Deeply into IAM Policy Evaluation: Highlights from AWS re:Inforce IAM433
    summary

    TL;DR: Noam Dahan’s September 2022 Ermetic (now Tenable) write-up of AWS re:Inforce session IAM433 on IAM policy evaluation internals and edge cases.

    • Speakers: Matt Luttrell and Dan Peebles of AWS; slides are featured in the post.
    • Outcomes: Implicit deny, explicit deny and explicit allow; there is no implicit allow.
    • Principals: Role sessions, not roles, make requests; also IAM users, federated users from sts:GetFederationToken, anonymous and root.
    • Authorization context: Policy evaluation matches statements against a property bag such as aws:PrincipalTag/project and aws:PrincipalOrgId.
    • Gotcha: ForAllValues:StringEquals on a missing key evaluates to true; use ForAllValues/ForAnyValue only on multi-valued keys like aws:TagKeys.
    • Boundaries: The session explains how resource policies can bypass permissions boundaries.
    • Domain: The ermetic.com URL now serves the article under Tenable branding.

    Takeaway: Required reading before writing condition-heavy IAM policies. Audit existing policies for ForAllValues on single-valued keys.

  • State of AWS Security: A Look into Real-World AWS Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog’s State of AWS Security report (published October 2022) presents IAM and exposure statistics from real customer AWS environments.

    • IAM users: 40% of IAM users had not used credentials in 90 days; 75% with active keys had a key older than 90 days.
    • MFA: 40% of organizations had at least one console IAM user without MFA.
    • Root: About 10% of organizations had an active root access key, some up to 13 years old; 25% used root credentials in the prior 30 days.
    • Exposure: 18% of SQS users and 15% of SNS users had a public queue or topic; 36% of S3 users had a public bucket.
    • Context: Cites a GitGuardian finding of 84 leaked AWS keys per 10,000 commits.
    • Remediation: Use IAM Identity Center for humans and instance or execution roles for workloads; tools like Repokid and Policy Sentry help with least privilege.

    Takeaway: Use these numbers to argue for removing IAM users and root keys. Check your own accounts for public SQS, SNS and S3 policies.

  • Cyber Security Career Pathways
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lancini’s October 2022 post with a first-draft mind map of cyber security career pathways, part of his book “The CloudSec Engineer”.

    • Problem: The industry has no standard map of security specializations, and most lists serve certification vendors.
    • Sources: Draws on company security org structures (such as GitLab) and the UK Cyber Security Council.
    • Output: A mind map grouping roles into macro-functions common in tech companies.
    • Caveat: The author calls it a possible oversimplification and asks for feedback.
    • Context: A preview for the book’s introduction, placing cloud security in the wider field.

    Takeaway: Useful for mentoring or planning a move between security domains, as a map of where roles sit.

  • AWS Secrets Manager GitHub Action
    summary

    TL;DR: The official, verified aws-actions/aws-secretsmanager-get-secrets GitHub Action loads AWS Secrets Manager secrets into a workflow as masked environment variables.

    • Usage: uses: aws-actions/aws-secretsmanager-get-secrets@v3 with a secret-ids list; v3.0.2 at time of reading.
    • Auth: Configure credentials first with configure-aws-credentials, ideally assuming a role via GitHub OIDC.
    • IAM: Needs GetSecretValue on the secrets, ListSecrets on all secrets, and kms:Decrypt for customer managed keys.
    • JSON parsing: JSON secrets can be split into one environment variable per key; binary values are converted to strings.
    • Scope: Retrieved secrets are available to all later steps in the job.

    Takeaway: Pair it with OIDC role assumption so no long-lived AWS keys sit in GitHub. Scope the role to only the secrets the job needs.

  • AWS Announces Updated Support Plans Console with New IAM Controls
    summary

    TL;DR: A 30 September 2022 AWS What’s New item: a redesigned Support Plans Console, and IAM control over who can change support plans.

    • Console: Shows your current Support plan, its features and a comparison with other plans.
    • IAM: Support plans can now be managed by IAM identities, not only the root user.
    • Managed policies: New AWS managed policies grant support plan permissions.
    • Examples: A read-only policy to view the plan, and a read-write policy to upgrade or downgrade it.

    Takeaway: One more task removed from root user duty. Grant it through IAM and keep root credentials locked away.

  • k2tf: Kubernetes YAML to Terraform HCL Converter
    summary

    TL;DR: k2tf converts Kubernetes YAML manifests into Terraform HCL for the Terraform Kubernetes provider.

    • Single file: k2tf -f test-fixtures/service.yaml, or add -o service.tf to write to a file.
    • Directory: k2tf -f test-fixtures/ converts all manifests in a folder.
    • From cluster: kubectl get deployments -o yaml | k2tf -o deployments.tf.
    • Install: brew install k2tf, the asdf plugin, or release binaries.
    • Build: Go modules; make build and make test.

    Takeaway: Speeds up moving hand-applied Kubernetes resources into Terraform. Review the output, as generated HCL usually needs cleanup.

  • konf-go: Lightweight kubeconfig Manager for Using Different kubeconfigs at the Same Time
    summary

    TL;DR: konf is a lightweight Go kubeconfig manager that lets each shell use a different kubeconfig without spawning subshells.

    • Speed: Runs directly in the current shell, unlike kubie, so switching is fast.
    • Per-shell: Different kubeconfigs can be active in different shells at the same time.
    • Install: Release binaries, Nix nix-env -iA nixpkgs.konf, or go install github.com/simontheleg/konf-go@latest.
    • Shell wrapper: Add source <(konf-go shellwrapper zsh) (zsh/bash) or konf-go shellwrapper fish | source.
    • License: Apache-2.0.

    Takeaway: A fast option for working on several clusters in parallel terminals. Call the konf wrapper, not the binary.

  • Kubernetes Guide: Graceful Shutdown with Lifecycle preStop Hook
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A September 2022 Datree guide arguing that Kubernetes pods need a preStop lifecycle hook, not just SIGTERM handling, to shut down without dropping traffic.

    • Hook types: preStop can be an httpGet call or an exec command, and runs before SIGTERM is sent.
    • Race condition: A pod can finish draining and exit before the ingress controller deregisters it, so traffic hits a dead pod.
    • Mistake 1: Exposing the HTTP shutdown endpoint publicly.
    • Mistake 2: Using a bare sleep; instead start deregistration and verify it completed.
    • Mistake 3: Keeping the default terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which must cover both the hook and SIGTERM handling.
    • Mistake 4: Putting deregistration logic in the app instead of the hook.
    • Source caveat: The datree.io page now returns an empty response; summary based on a 2022 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Add a preStop hook and size the grace period to cover deregistration, especially behind cloud load balancers.

  • Do Not Use ‘git checkout’ Anymore
    summary

    TL;DR: A short August 2022 post by TheDevStory explaining that Git 2.23 split git checkout into git switch and git restore.

    • Switch branches: git switch develop replaces git checkout develop.
    • New branch: git switch -c new-branch replaces git checkout -b new-branch.
    • Restore files: git restore README.md replaces git checkout -- README.md.
    • Unstage: git restore --staged README.md replaces git reset HEAD README.md.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Use switch and restore for clearer intent and fewer accidental file overwrites. checkout still works.

  • Introducing Wolfi: The First Linux (Un)distro Designed for Securing the Software Supply Chain
    summary

    TL;DR: Dan Lorenc’s 22 September 2022 announcement of Wolfi, Chainguard’s community Linux “(un)distro” built for container images and supply chain security.

    • Problem: Container images lag upstream, carry extra software, lack provenance and rarely meet standards like SLSA.
    • SBOMs: Every package ships a build-time SBOM.
    • Packaging: Granular, independent APK packages for minimal images, with glibc support.
    • Builds: Fully declarative and reproducible; images are rebuilt rather than upgraded in place.
    • Goal: Images with zero known vulnerabilities.
    • Also announced: New Chainguard Images for static binaries, nginx, and Go and C toolchains.

    Takeaway: Wolfi is the base of Chainguard Images. Consider it when you need glibc compatibility with distroless-style minimal images.

  • lima: Linux Virtual Machines on macOS for Running containerd
    summary

    TL;DR: Lima launches Linux VMs with automatic file sharing and port forwarding, like WSL2 for macOS, originally to bring containerd and nerdctl to Mac users.

    • Start: brew install lima, limactl start, then lima uname -a.
    • containerd: lima nerdctl run --rm hello-world.
    • Docker: limactl start template:docker and point DOCKER_HOST at the VM socket.
    • Kubernetes: limactl start template:k8s and use the copied kubeconfig.
    • Scope: Also supports Podman, non-container workloads, and Linux and NetBSD hosts.
    • Supply chain: Releases include CycloneDX SBOMs since v2.3; OpenSSF Best Practices badge.

    Takeaway: A free, scriptable way to run containerd, Docker or Kubernetes on macOS without Docker Desktop.

28.09.2022

  • Cloud DNS Security: How to Protect DNS in the Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: Brett Wolmarans’ August 2022 Sysdig post on DNS threats and how to protect DNS in cloud environments.

    • Threats: DDoS (such as the 2016 Dyn/Mirai attack), tunneling and exfiltration, cache poisoning, hijacking (Sea Turtle), typosquatting and subdomain takeover.
    • Providers: Compares Google Cloud DNS and AWS Route 53 on RPZ, DoH, DoT, DNSSEC, logging and DNS firewalls.
    • Hardening: Patch DNS software, use MFA on DNS admin accounts, enable DNSSEC where appropriate, add DDoS protection and a DNS firewall.
    • Visibility: Inventory all domains and zones, monitor DNS separately, send DNS logs to a SIEM, log API calls with CloudTrail.
    • Resilience: Use multiple DNS providers to survive one outage or attack.
    • Tools: dig, dnstwist, dnsperf, Terraform for DNS as code, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and GuardDuty.
    • Source caveat: curl returned only a search template; content read via WebFetch.

    Takeaway: Treat DNS as critical infrastructure. Lock down registrar and DNS console access, and log resolver queries to catch tunneling.

  • Exploring Kubernetes Operator Pattern
    summary

    TL;DR: An illustrated iximiuz.com deep dive (2021, updated November 2023) into the Kubernetes Operator pattern and the API mechanics behind it.

    • Objects vs controllers: Objects are records of intent; controllers are loops that move current state toward desired state.
    • API design: RESTful, declarative HTTP API; list resources with kubectl api-resources; API groups and versioning.
    • Custom resources: How to create CRDs, and CRDs compared with custom API servers.
    • Operators: Custom resources plus a custom controller that feel native to Kubernetes.
    • Example: Walks through a concrete operator example.
    • Series: Part of the author’s “Writing Kubernetes Controllers/Operators” learning series.

    Takeaway: Read it before writing your first operator. It explains why operators behave like built-in resources.

  • Why You Should Avoid Sealed Secrets in Your GitOps Deployment
    summary

    TL;DR: Denilson Nastacio’s February 2022 article arguing against Sealed Secrets in GitOps repos in favor of a managed key service.

    • Reason 1: Per-environment keys lead to sprawl of encrypted Secret files across folders and namespaces.
    • Reason 2: Encrypted secrets still sit in the repo, in the hands of anyone with read access.
    • Reason 3: The decryption key protecting everything is itself just another key to manage.
    • Reason 4: Git has no key rotation, secret references, usage audit or tiered admin access.
    • GitOps tools: Argo CD is “un-opinionated” about secrets; Flux can decrypt with KMS but still stores encrypted secrets in Git.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct access; content read through the Freedium mirror.

    Takeaway: Start GitOps with a managed key or secrets service rather than encrypted secrets in Git, since migrating away later means paying twice.

  • terralist: A Private Terraform Registry
    summary

    TL;DR: Terralist is a self-hosted private registry for Terraform and OpenTofu modules and providers, implementing the official registry protocols.

    • Features: Upload, version and distribute modules and providers, with a web dashboard for docs and API keys.
    • Auth: OAuth via GitHub, GitLab, BitBucket or any OIDC provider.
    • RBAC: Built-in admin, readonly and anonymous roles plus Casbin custom policies; scoped API keys for CI/CD.
    • Storage: AWS S3, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage, local filesystem or proxy mode.
    • Ops: Prometheus metrics; a single Go binary with no external dependencies.
    • Repo: Now lives under the terralist/terralist organization; MPL 2.0.

    Takeaway: A lightweight option when you want a private module registry without Terraform Cloud or Enterprise.

  • Cloud Audit Academy
    summary

    TL;DR: Cloud Audit Academy is AWS’s free learning path for auditors and risk and compliance professionals assessing regulated workloads in the cloud.

    • Level 1: New to Cloud, a cloud-agnostic course on how cloud auditing differs from on-premises.
    • Level 2: Auditing in AWS, assessing customer-configured AWS controls with real-world risk examples and control objectives.
    • Level 3: Industry-specific courses for PCI DSS and NIST SP 800/CMMC, with console walkthroughs and evidence sources.
    • Approach: Risk-based, applying cloud-specific verification techniques to control frameworks written for on-premises.
    • Format: Structured curriculum with instructor-led options and subject matter experts.

    Takeaway: Point your auditors here before an AWS-focused audit. It reduces back-and-forth over where evidence lives.

  • How to Hack Web Applications in 2022: Part 1
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of a web application hacking guide by Luke “Hakluke” Stephens on Detectify Labs (May 2022). It sets up an intercepting proxy and walks through the main injection-class bugs with working payloads.

    • Setup: Burp Suite Community Edition as the interception proxy, using its built-in Chromium browser so no manual proxy configuration is needed.
    • Framework: Uses the OWASP Top 10 (2021) as the map of risk classes, from Broken Access Control to SSRF.
    • Command and code injection: A PHP ping script exploited by appending ; whoami; unsanitised input passed to PHP eval().
    • SQL injection: Manual payloads such as 1 OR 1=1 and UNION SELECT, then SQLMap automation (--dbms=sqlite -T users --dump).
    • XXE and deserialization: An external entity reading file:///etc/passwd; tampering with serialized object fields (e.g. an isAdmin flag) and gadget-chain RCE with ysoserial.
    • XSS: Reflected XSS, cookie theft (blocked by HttpOnly), and a payload that creates a WordPress admin user.
    • Part 2 scope: SSRF, business logic bugs, IDOR, authentication, CSRF, directory traversal, LFI/RFI and cache poisoning.

    Takeaway: A practical starter path for web testing: get Burp running, then learn each injection class with a concrete payload. It is a sequel to the same author’s “How to Hack APIs in 2021”.

  • Error Handling with Go Tooling
    summary

    TL;DR: Eli Bendersky shows how Go tools built on golang.org/x/tools/go/packages find out about parse and type errors in the code they analyse, instead of quietly working on a broken AST.

    • Surprise: A tool run on code with errors still dumps an AST without complaint. The parser recovers and drops bad parts, e.g. util(5 6) keeps only the first argument.
    • Why recovery exists: IDE tooling parses code while you type, so it must keep going past errors to offer highlighting and jump-to-definition.
    • Error reporting: packages.Package.Errors holds the errors. Each packages.Error has a Kind: ListError, ParseError or TypeError.
    • Example output: Three errors are reported for the sample: missing , in an argument list, cannot use 5.5 ... as string value, and s declared but not used.
    • IllTyped: The IllTyped field marks a package or its dependencies as broken. It is set only when packages.NeedTypes is requested.
    • Code: The full sample tool is on GitHub.

    Takeaway: If your analysis tool assumes valid code, check len(pkg.Errors) > 0 and stop early so you do not report false results. Tools meant for half-written code can keep going on purpose.

  • GitOps: A Simple Approach to Using AWS Secrets Manager with Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lau (Ops Sorry, Aug 2022) gives a minimal Terraform setup that maps each Kubernetes namespace to an AWS Secrets Manager path, read through the Secrets Store CSI driver.

    • Cluster: terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws v18.23.0 with enable_irsa = true, which creates the OIDC provider for IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
    • Driver: Helm chart csi-secrets-store-provider-aws v0.0.3 from aws.github.io/eks-charts, installed in kube-system.
    • IAM: One policy per namespace, created with for_each, allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and DescribeSecret on <cluster>/<namespace>/*. Roles come from the iam-role-for-service-accounts-eks module v5.1.0.
    • Service account: The namespace’s default service account gets the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation.
    • Consumption: A SecretProviderClass (provider aws) mounted as a CSI volume. No Kubernetes Secret object is created.
    • Test: A pod in one namespace trying to read another namespace’s secret fails with AccessDeniedException.
    • Caveat: The author warns this breaks least privilege: any app in a namespace can read every secret in it.

    Takeaway: A good-enough first step when per-app IAM wiring is too much. Plan to move to per-app service accounts and paths later.

  • Kubernetes Removals and Major Changes in 1.25
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post (Kat Cosgrove, Frederico Muñoz, Debabrata Panigrahi, Aug 2022) that lists what v1.25 removes or changes, chiefly the removal of PodSecurityPolicy.

    • PodSecurityPolicy: Removed in v1.25 after deprecation in v1.21. It is replaced by Pod Security Admission, which goes GA in the same release.
    • CSI migration: The core CSI Migration feature goes GA, moving in-tree volume plugins toward out-of-tree CSI drivers.
    • Storage plugins: GlusterFS and Portworx in-tree plugins are deprecated. Flocker, Quobyte and StorageOS in-tree plugins are removed.
    • vSphere: The in-tree vSphere volume driver no longer supports vSphere releases before 7.0u2.
    • iptables: The kubelet starts to stop creating the KUBE-MARK-DROP, KUBE-MARK-MASQ and KUBE-POSTROUTING nat chains, behind the IPTablesCleanup feature gate.
    • Next up (1.26): flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta1 and autoscaling/v2beta2 HPA are scheduled for removal.
    • Policy recap: Beta APIs stay supported for 3 releases after deprecation. GA APIs cannot be removed within a major version.

    Takeaway: Before going to 1.25, migrate any PSP use to Pod Security Admission and check for removed storage plugins. Do not depend on kube-proxy’s internal iptables chains.

  • Write Your Kubernetes Infrastructure as Go Code: Extend cdk8s with Custom Constructs
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Abhishek Gupta (Better Programming, Aug 2022) shows how to package a whole WordPress deployment as a reusable cdk8s construct written in Go.

    • cdk8s: A CNCF open-source framework that defines Kubernetes apps in ordinary programming languages instead of YAML. Constructs are its basic building blocks.
    • cdk8s-plus: Cuts boilerplate. A Deployment, its container and a LoadBalancer Service take three calls: NewDeployment, AddContainer, ExposeViaService.
    • Custom construct: NewWordpressStack(chart, ..., &WordpressProps{...}) creates a full WordPress install in one line, configured through a props struct.
    • Wiring: The construct goes into a cdk8s.Chart, which goes into a cdk8s.App, and app.Synth() produces the manifests.
    • Ecosystem: Ready-made constructs from the community and AWS are listed at constructs.dev.
    • Source caveat: The live Medium page blocked fetching. This summary is based on the Aug 2022 Wayback Machine copy, first part of the article only.

    Takeaway: Wrapping repeated Kubernetes patterns in typed constructs pays off most for teams and organisations, less for one-off apps.

  • Tips for Saving AWS EKS Cost
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Jeewan Sooriyaarachchi (Medium, Jul 2022) lists practical ways to cut Amazon EKS cost without losing high availability.

    • Budget alerts: Tag every cluster resource (load balancers, CloudFront and so on) and set AWS Budgets alerts by tag. Examples he caught: idle GPU instances off-peak, and an app bug that drove up S3 GetObject/ListObjects charges.
    • Right-size and autoscale: Measure usage, set requests and limits, and use HPA (min 2 pods in production) with cluster-autoscaler.
    • Spot: He gives t3.xlarge as about $0.2112/h on-demand versus about $0.0634/h spot. Pair spot and on-demand node groups with the same label, and have the autoscaler try spot first.
    • Non-AWS costs: Datadog charged per node, so many small t3.medium spot nodes cost more in Datadog. He moved to fewer, larger instances.
    • Off-hours shutdown: ASGs with min 0. A CronJob runs kubectl scale --replicas=0 on deployments and statefulsets, using an IRSA-trusted role plus a namespaced RBAC role on deployments/scale and statefulsets/scale.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a May 2025 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Tagging and budgets come first, then spot and off-hours scale-to-zero for non-production. Count per-node SaaS agent fees when choosing node size.

  • Intro to eBPF
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Short’s short introduction to eBPF (Aug 2022, adapted from DevOps’ish 278): what it is, how it hooks into the kernel, and which projects use it.

    • Definition: eBPF runs sandboxed programs in privileged kernel context without changing kernel source or loading kernel modules.
    • Execution model: Programs are event-driven and attach to hooks: syscalls, function entry/exit, tracepoints and network events.
    • Projects cited: Cilium/Isovalent, Pixie, Calico, bpftrace, Falco’s eBPF probe, Tracee, SysmonForLinux, Katran (Facebook’s load balancer) and ebpf-for-windows.
    • References: ebpf.io (run by Daniel Borkmann), ebpf.foundation (Linux Foundation), the BPF and XDP Reference Guide, awesome-ebpf, and Liz Rice’s GOTO 2021 talk.
    • Safety: Presented as generally safer than kernel modules, and no modprobe or reboot is needed.
    • Verdict: The author says it is worth the hype, calling it “a rubber mallet”: it cannot fix everything but can help find almost anything.

    Takeaway: A link-rich starting page. Use it to pick a project (bpftrace for ad-hoc tracing, Cilium for networking) rather than to learn how to write eBPF programs.

  • GitOps: A Simple Approach to Using AWS Secrets Manager with Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Marco Lau (Ops Sorry, Aug 2022) gives a minimal Terraform setup that maps each Kubernetes namespace to an AWS Secrets Manager path, read through the Secrets Store CSI driver.

    • Cluster: terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws v18.23.0 with enable_irsa = true, which creates the OIDC provider for IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
    • Driver: Helm chart csi-secrets-store-provider-aws v0.0.3 from aws.github.io/eks-charts, installed in kube-system.
    • IAM: One policy per namespace, created with for_each, allowing secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and DescribeSecret on <cluster>/<namespace>/*. Roles come from the iam-role-for-service-accounts-eks module v5.1.0.
    • Service account: The namespace’s default service account gets the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation.
    • Consumption: A SecretProviderClass (provider aws) mounted as a CSI volume. No Kubernetes Secret object is created.
    • Test: A pod in one namespace trying to read another namespace’s secret fails with AccessDeniedException.
    • Caveat: The author warns this breaks least privilege: any app in a namespace can read every secret in it.

    Takeaway: A good-enough first step when per-app IAM wiring is too much. Plan to move to per-app service accounts and paths later.

  • Scaling Kubernetes to Thousands of CRDs
    summary

    TL;DR: Nic Cope (Upbound, Aug 2022) explains which Kubernetes limits Crossplane hit when installing thousands of CRDs, and the upstream fixes Upbound helped land.

    • Scale: Full-coverage AWS, Azure and GCP providers mean about 2,000 managed-resource kinds across about 300 API group/versions, so discovery takes about 300 requests.
    • kubectl throttling: “client-side throttling” waits for minutes. The discovery burst limit went from 100 to 300 (v1.22) and the cache TTL from 10 minutes to 6 hours.
    • Disk cache: fsync on about 300 cache files made discovery take about 20 s on macOS. Switching to checksums in v1.25 made it about 25x faster.
    • OpenAPI: Lazy schema computation cut CPU spikes after CRD creation (v1.23.0, backported to 1.20.13, 1.21.7 and 1.22.4).
    • Memory: About 4 MiB of API server RSS per CRD. Sharing one Zap logger across etcd clients cut memory by about 20% (v1.25).
    • Hosted control planes: GKE, EKS and AKS saw API server unavailability from seconds to about an hour.
    • Future work: Aggregated discovery with ETags (alpha targeted for 1.26), one etcd client per transport, and GC tuning (a naive test cut peak RSS by 25%).

    Takeaway: If you run Crossplane or many operators, use recent kubectl and Kubernetes versions. Install only the provider CRDs you need.

  • eks-multi-cluster-gitops: Build Multi-Cluster GitOps Using Amazon EKS, Flux CD, and Crossplane
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Samples reference implementation of hub-and-spoke multi-cluster GitOps on Amazon EKS. Flux CD and Crossplane manage both the clusters and the AWS resources apps depend on.

    • Model: A management EKS cluster is created by hand with eksctl and bootstrapped. It then creates and bootstraps workload clusters through GitOps.
    • Self-service: App teams request a cluster with a pull request. The PR is either auto-merged after checks or approved by the platform team, then provisioned to org standards.
    • Tooling: FluxCD for GitOps, Crossplane as the infrastructure controller, and Sealed Secrets plus External Secrets Operator for secrets.
    • Cloud resources: Extends GitOps to stateful AWS services such as Amazon RDS, DynamoDB and SQS, alongside native Kubernetes resources.
    • Lifecycle: Covers provisioning, bootstrapping, upgrading and deleting clusters through Git.
    • Status: The repository is not archived.

    Takeaway: A full blueprint for a platform team that wants PR-driven cluster vending on EKS. Expect to adapt the repo layout and secrets handling to your own organisation.

  • AWSGoat: A Damn Vulnerable AWS Infrastructure
    summary

    TL;DR: AWSGoat, from INE, is an AWS environment built to be vulnerable for practising cloud pentesting. It is deployed into your own account with Terraform.

    • Coverage: OWASP Top 10 (2021) web bugs plus misconfigurations in IAM, S3, API Gateway, Lambda, EC2 and ECS.
    • Vulnerabilities listed: XSS, SQL injection, IDOR, SSRF on the Lambda environment, sensitive data exposure and password reset, S3 misconfigurations, IAM privilege escalation and ECS container breakout.
    • Module 1: A serverless blog app (Lambda, S3, API Gateway, DynamoDB).
    • Module 2: An internal HR payroll app on ECS. Both have documented escalation paths.
    • Deploy: Fork the repo, add AWS_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as GitHub secrets, and run the Terraform Apply action. A minimum-permission policy.json is provided.
    • Cost: After free tier, about $0.0125/h for Module 1 and $0.0505/h for Module 2 in US-East.
    • Presented at: Black Hat USA 2022 Arsenal, DEF CON 30 Demo Labs, Rootcon 16 and Black Hat Asia 2023.

    Takeaway: A good hands-on lab for AWS attack paths. Run it in an isolated sandbox account and tear it down after use.

  • monkey365: Office 365, AD, and Azure Security Review
    summary

    TL;DR: Monkey365, by silverhack, is a PowerShell module that assesses the security configuration of Microsoft 365, Microsoft Entra ID and Azure, and reports findings with remediation guidance.

    • Scope: Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Teams, Purview and Fabric, plus Entra ID and Azure subscriptions.
    • Self-contained: Bundles its dependencies, so it does not need Azure CLI, Az PowerShell, ExchangeOnlineManagement or the Graph SDK.
    • Auth: Interactive sign-in, service principals, certificates or a direct access token.
    • Rules: Declarative JSON rules and rulesets mapped to best practices and compliance standards.
    • Output: HTML, JSON and CSV reports. Supports Azure Public, China and Government clouds.
    • Install: Install-Module -Name monkey365 -Scope CurrentUser, then run with an options hashtable such as Instance = 'Microsoft365' and IncludeEntraID = $true.
    • License: Apache 2.0. Actively maintained and published to the PowerShell Gallery.

    Takeaway: A free alternative to commercial M365 and Azure posture scanners. Good for consultants and for periodic tenant reviews.

  • Codify Your Best Practices Using Service Control Policies: Part 2
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 2 of Som Chatterjee’s AWS series (Feb 2022) maps AWS Well-Architected pillars to concrete service control policy (SCP) examples attached to the organisation root or to OUs.

    • Operational excellence: Deny changes to admin-issued CloudWatch alarms and dashboards (Admin-issued-*) except for Admin-role-*. Deny logs:PutRetentionPolicy and logs:DeleteLogGroup. Deny stopping or deleting AWS Config recorders and rules.
    • Security, org: Deny organizations:LeaveOrganization. Deny * in a Suspended OU.
    • Security, IAM: In the Sandbox OU, deny IAM role, user and policy actions plus sts:AssumeRole, except for an admin role.
    • Region lock: Deny when aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-central-1 or eu-west-1, using NotAction to exempt global services.
    • Secrets and detection: Protect an admin secret in Secrets Manager. Deny GuardDuty UpdateDetector/DeleteDetector and disassociation.
    • Cost: Deny budgets:ModifyBudget and DeleteBudgetAction.
    • Caveats: One example’s title (“Deny ability to pass IAM roles”) does not match its Secrets Manager content. The budget SCP’s exemption matches all roles, which weakens it.

    Takeaway: A copy-ready set of guardrail SCPs. Review the condition keys and exemptions before you attach them; some examples need tightening.

  • A Lightweight Approach to Implement Secure Software Development Lifecycle (Secure SDLC)
    summary

    TL;DR: Anshuman Bhartiya (Aug 2022) sets out a phased, lightweight Secure SDLC plan for a founding product security engineer: crawl, walk, run.

    • Crawl: Rapid Risk Assessment (RRA), tech design/architecture review with a data-flow diagram, threat modeling (STRIDE, conversational), and SAST with Semgrep (also used for IaC and policy-as-code).
    • Walk: Third-party dependency scanning on every PR (Dependabot), DAST against staging, and time-boxed pentests focused on threat-model areas.
    • Run: Pre-commit secret scanning and a bug bounty programme.
    • RRA scoring: Data classification plus exposure, authentication and availability needs, and confidentiality/integrity/availability impact (each 1-3), give a rating from Negligible to Critical.
    • Required follow-up: Moderate needs a design review. High adds threat modeling. Critical adds a pentest or manual assessment.
    • Automation: An RRA form for engineering managers that auto-scores, adds to a risk register and creates backlog tickets. Skip it for cosmetic or static frontend changes.
    • Moved: The URL now redirects to anshuman.ai.

    Takeaway: A useful template for rationing scarce AppSec time: score risk first, then require heavier reviews only for high-risk changes.

  • Hacking APIs: Workshop
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Microsoft Sway presentation titled “Hacking APIs: Workshop”. Only the title loads; the content is rendered by JavaScript, or it is restricted.

    • What loads: The page returns only the title “Hacking APIs: Workshop” and the Microsoft Sway frame. The URL now redirects to sway.cloud.microsoft.
    • Author: Not identifiable from the page. Web searches for this Sway ID found nothing.
    • Possible context: “Hacking APIs” is also the title of Corey Ball’s 2022 No Starch Press book on web API security testing. Nothing links this Sway to him.
    • Access: Sway decks can be limited to an organisation’s sign-in, which may be why the content does not load.
    • Source caveat: Based on the page title and general search results only. Nothing about the workshop content could be checked.

    Takeaway: Treat this as a dead or private link. For API hacking practice, look for a maintained workshop or book instead.

  • Why Leaving Pods in CrashLoopBackOff Can Have a Bigger Impact Than You Might Think
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Paul Dally (Medium, Aug 2022) argues that pods left in CrashLoopBackOff harm the node and the cluster, not only their own workload.

    • Backoff math: Restart delay starts at 10s and doubles up to a 5-minute cap, then resets after 10 minutes of successful running. A broken container can still restart 300 or more times a day.
    • cgroup leaks: On some runtimes and kernels, each restart can leak cgroups. New containers on the node then fail with cannot allocate memory when cgroups are applied.
    • Mitigations named: Reboot (temporary), a newer kernel, or the cgroup.memory=nokmem kernel parameter (needs a reboot and has its own side effects).
    • Startup cost: Startup is often the most CPU-intensive phase (his example is Spring Boot). Constant restarts burn node resources and can trigger scaling cost.
    • Stalled rollouts: If the first new pod never becomes ready, a Deployment rollout stalls and old pods keep running.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching. This summary is based on a Jan 2025 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Alert on container restart counts and CrashLoopBackOff, including in pre-production. Do not leave crashing deployments running.

  • Kubernetes Security Compliance Frameworks
    summary

    TL;DR: An ARMO blog post that compares the main Kubernetes security and compliance frameworks and says when to use each. It ends with a pitch for ARMO’s open-source Kubescape.

    • CIS Kubernetes Benchmark: Hardening checks in Level 1 (baseline) and Level 2 (stricter) tiers, with EKS and AKS variants. Criticised as rigid and slow to update.
    • MITRE ATT&CK for Kubernetes: A tactic matrix from initial access to impact, e.g. privileged containers, exposed dashboards and listing secrets. Deep but large and sometimes ambiguous.
    • PCI DSS: Mapping cardholder-data connections, network restriction, configuration standards, key distribution, environment separation and change detection.
    • NIST container security guide: Risks grouped by image, registry, orchestrator, container and host OS.
    • NSA-CISA hardening guide: Pod security, network separation, authentication and authorisation, audit logging and patching. It gives no lifecycle guidance.
    • When to use: CIS and NSA-CISA for pre-production, MITRE for production, NIST for testing and scanning, PCI DSS throughout.
    • Page changed: The current page shows author Jonathan Kaftzan and a date of Aug 2023, later than when it was bookmarked.

    Takeaway: A quick comparison for picking a baseline. Most teams start with CIS or NSA-CISA scans (Kubescape runs both) and use MITRE for threat modeling.

  • Use TouchID to Authenticate sudo on macOS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Digitaino IT how-to for approving sudo in the macOS Terminal with Touch ID, by adding one PAM line.

    • Change: Edit /etc/pam.d/sudo (the post uses sudo pico) and add auth sufficient pam_tid.so below the pam_smartcard.so line.
    • Effect: New Terminal windows prompt for Touch ID on sudo. If Apple Watch unlock is enabled, a double-click of the watch side button also approves.
    • Caveat: macOS overwrites the file on OS updates, so the line must be added again after each update. A commenter suggests a check after each restart.
    • Reported issue: A commenter says it does not work in clamshell mode.
    • Source caveat: The live site returns an HTTP 522 error. This summary is based on a Feb 2024 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: A handy convenience tweak. Expect to redo it after macOS updates and keep the password fallback.

  • devbox: Instant, Easy, Predictable Shells and Containers
    summary

    TL;DR: Devbox is a CLI from Jetify (formerly jetpack.io) that creates isolated, reproducible development shells from a devbox.json package list, using Nix underneath.

    • Model: Works like yarn, but for OS-level packages. It can install from over 400,000 package versions in the Nix registry.
    • Commands: devbox shell for an interactive environment and devbox run for one-off commands.
    • Team consistency: Everyone who runs devbox shell gets the same tool versions.
    • Isolation: Try tools without polluting the laptop, and with no VM layer slowing file access.
    • Containers: The same definition can be turned into an equivalent container when you ship.
    • Install: curl -fsSL https://get.jetify.com/devbox | bash.
    • Moved: The repository now lives at jetify-com/devbox after the company renamed itself.

    Takeaway: An easy way to get Nix-level reproducibility without learning Nix. A good fit for onboarding and for CI parity.

  • AWS and Kubecost Collaborate to Deliver Cost Monitoring for EKS Customers
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post (Aug 2022, Mike Stefaniak, Vipin Mohan and Kubecost) announcing a free, EKS-optimised Kubecost bundle for cost monitoring. Kubecost is built on the CNCF OpenCost project.

    • What you get: Cost broken down by pod, node, namespace and label, cost allocation and chargeback, and single-cluster optimisation recommendations, at no charge with Kubecost support.
    • Install: helm upgrade -i kubecost oci://public.ecr.aws/kubecost/cost-analyzer --version 1.99.0 --namespace kubecost --create-namespace -f values-eks-cost-monitoring.yaml.
    • Prerequisites: Helm 3.9+, kubectl, and the EBS CSI driver on Kubernetes 1.23+.
    • Access: kubectl port-forward deployment/kubecost-cost-analyzer 9090. For lasting access, Nginx ingress with basic auth or an ALB with Cognito.
    • Architecture: Bundles Prometheus and kube-state-metrics, which can be skipped if already present. Pricing comes from the AWS Price List API, with optional CUR integration for RIs, Savings Plans and spot.
    • Limits: Cost allocation views cover up to the last 15 days. Multi-cluster support is listed as future work.

    Takeaway: A low-effort way to get per-namespace EKS cost visibility. Connect CUR if you want numbers that reflect your actual discounts.

  • Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide for Networking
    summary

    TL;DR: The networking chapter of AWS’s EKS Best Practices Guide, covering the VPC CNI, IP address planning and pod networking options. The guide has since moved into AWS documentation.

    • VPC CNI: The default add-on. Pods get real VPC IPs, managed by ipamd through ENIs and a warm IP pool.
    • IP exhaustion: Pods take IPs from node subnets. Use subnets in at least two AZs and check free IPs before scaling.
    • Prefix mode: Recommended over the default secondary-IP mode when pod density per node is limited by ENI/IP counts.
    • Custom networking: Places pods in other CIDRs such as 100.64.0.0/10 or 198.19.0.0/16 to save RFC1918 space, at the cost of extra operational overhead.
    • IPv6: Preferred over custom networking once IPv4 runs out.
    • Security groups for pods: Per-pod network rules instead of inheriting the node’s ENI security group. A subnet calculator models WARM_IP_TARGET/WARM_ENI_TARGET.
    • Moved: This page is now a legacy copy. Current content is at docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/networking.html.

    Takeaway: Plan pod IP space before building EKS clusters. Prefix mode or IPv6 avoid most IP-exhaustion problems.

  • AWS Support Launches Support for Managing Cases in Slack
    summary

    TL;DR: An Aug 24, 2022 AWS announcement of the AWS Support App for Slack, for working on support cases inside Slack channels.

    • Actions: Create, update, search and resolve support cases from Slack channels.
    • Live chat: Start a live chat with AWS support agents that teammates can join.
    • Knowledge sharing: Search past cases and share earlier fixes with the team.
    • Eligibility: Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise Support plans.
    • Cost and scope: No additional cost. Available in the standard AWS partition.
    • Setup: Not covered on the page. It points to the AWS Support App section of the AWS Support User Guide.

    Takeaway: Useful if your incident response already happens in Slack and you have a paid support plan. It keeps case history visible to the whole channel.

  • botkube: Monitor and Debug Your Kubernetes Cluster from Chat
    summary

    TL;DR: Botkube, from Kubeshop, is a ChatOps bot that sends Kubernetes events and alerts to chat platforms and lets you run cluster commands from there.

    • Platforms: Slack, Discord and Mattermost.
    • Monitoring: Watches Kubernetes events and other sources such as Prometheus alerts, with filtering and consolidation.
    • Actions: Run kubectl, helm and other commands from the chat workspace, plus automated actions triggered by plugins.
    • Extensibility: A plugin system, with support for custom plugins.
    • Audience: Lets developers troubleshoot without direct cluster access or deep Kubernetes knowledge.
    • License: MIT. Docs are at docs.botkube.io.

    Takeaway: Useful for getting cluster events into the team channel quickly. Scope the RBAC for in-chat command execution carefully.

  • AWS IAM Interview Questions
    summary

    TL;DR: A k9 Security guide of AWS IAM interview questions with sample answers, graded from basic to advanced, for hiring cloud, DevOps, SRE and security staff.

    • Basic (Q1-5): What IAM does, policy statement elements, principal types, explicit Deny wins, and roles versus users.
    • Intermediate (Q6-8): Policy types (including SCPs as guardrails that can only restrict), policy evaluation order, and federating directory identities such as AD to roles.
    • Advanced (Q9-13): Condition keys (MFA, org scoping), least privilege, scaling permissions across an organisation, CI/CD auth via OIDC federation instead of static keys, and just-in-time access.
    • Evaluation logic: Covers how permission boundaries and session policies fit into the decision.
    • Vendor content: The page also promotes k9 Security products and an IAM eBook.
    • Page changed: The current page shows a 2026 copyright and no author or date, so it may have been revised since it was bookmarked.

    Takeaway: A good checklist for self-assessment or for interviewing. If a candidate can explain policy evaluation order and OIDC for CI, they understand IAM beyond the basics.

  • Incident Response in AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris’s AWS incident response guide (Aug 2022, updated Mar 2023): how to prepare, detect, investigate and contain incidents in API-driven AWS environments.

    • Preparation: Org-wide CloudTrail (enable S3, DynamoDB and Lambda data events separately) and GuardDuty via delegated admin. Add a security account with read-only IR roles, an inventory with business context (Steampipe suggested), and security alternate contacts on every account.
    • Detections: StopLogging, DeleteTrail, DeleteDetector. Recon via GetCallerIdentity (which cannot be denied), ListBuckets and DescribeInstances. CreateUser persistence. Lateral movement via AssumeRole, SendCommand and SendSSHPublicKey.
    • Investigation: Pivot from a suspicious resource to its creator identity and source IPs. Query CloudTrail in S3 with Athena and map event names to MITRE TTPs.
    • Containment: Disable (do not delete) leaked access keys. Revoke role sessions issued before a timestamp. Apply a deny-all or NotAction deny, or restrict with aws:SourceIp.
    • AWS automation: Publicly exposed keys often get a quarantine policy from AWS within minutes.
    • Breach scoping: ListBuckets alone does not prove exfiltration. You need S3 data events.
    • Help: The AWS CIRT assists customers regardless of support plan.

    Takeaway: Most of the work is done before the incident. Turn on org-wide logging, set up IR roles and contacts now, and keep the containment policies ready.

  • Learn Istio: How to Manage, Monitor, and Secure Microservices
    summary

    TL;DR: A long freeCodeCamp handbook by Rinor Maloku (May 2022) that teaches Istio hands-on with a sample microservices app on a local kind cluster.

    • Setup: kind with Kubernetes 1.23.1, Istio 1.13.2 via istioctl install --set profile=demo, and sidecar injection via the istio-injection=enabled label.
    • Architecture: Data plane of Envoy sidecars and the control plane, explained before the hands-on parts.
    • Ingress: Gateway and VirtualService routing through the ingress gateway, port-forwarded to localhost:8080.
    • Observability: Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger and Kiali via istioctl dashboard <name>, plus access logs.
    • Traffic management: Canary releases with a DestinationRule and weighted VirtualService routes.
    • Security: Automatic mTLS, PeerAuthentication in STRICT mode, RequestAuthentication with Keycloak JWTs, and AuthorizationPolicy.
    • Demo app: A “Sentiment Analysis” app (SA-Frontend, SA-WebApp, SA-Logic, SA-Feedback). The author says it takes a few hours.

    Takeaway: A thorough free walkthrough of Istio’s core features. The versions are 2022, so check current Istio install steps and APIs.

  • AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) for RDS, Lambda, Step Functions, Managed Prometheus, and KMS Now GA
    summary

    TL;DR: A Sep 6, 2022 AWS announcement that five more AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) reached general availability.

    • Newly GA: Amazon RDS, AWS Lambda, AWS Step Functions, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and AWS KMS controllers.
    • Totals: 12 ACK controllers GA, with 13 more in preview.
    • What ACK does: Defines and manages AWS service resources directly from Kubernetes manifests, so apps can use managed services without separate IaC or running databases in-cluster.
    • Resources: Docs at aws-controllers-k8s.github.io, plus AWS blog walkthroughs for RDS and Lambda.
    • Install: Not described on the page. It points to the ACK documentation.

    Takeaway: ACK is the AWS-native option for managing cloud resources from Kubernetes (compare Crossplane). Check controller maturity per service before relying on it.

  • Understanding and Cost Optimizing Amazon EKS Control Plane Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers Blog post (September 2022) explaining EKS control plane log types and how to control their CloudWatch cost.

    • Log types: API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager and scheduler, enabled per cluster.
    • Volume: Audit logs usually have the highest volume.
    • Location: CloudWatch log groups under the /aws/eks prefix, one stream set per component.
    • Retention: Default CloudWatch retention is never expire, so set retention per log group.
    • Archival: Export to S3 (one-time or scheduled with Lambda and EventBridge), apply lifecycle rules or Intelligent-Tiering, and query with Athena since Logs Insights no longer applies.
    • Recommendations: Enable log types selectively outside production; in production enable all and manage retention.
    • GuardDuty: Reads EKS audit logs directly and does not need control plane logging enabled.

    Takeaway: Set retention on /aws/eks log groups today. Consider GuardDuty for audit-based threat detection.

  • How to Apply GitOps to Everything Using Amazon EKS, Crossplane, and Flux
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Open Source blog post (Sep 2022, Paul Roberts, Mo Ahmed, Viktor Farcic) that uses Flux and Crossplane on a management EKS cluster to provision clusters, apps and databases from Git.

    • Management cluster: Created with eksctl in us-east-1. It runs Flux (flux bootstrap github) and Crossplane (Helm chart 1.6.4) with AWS credentials stored as a Kubernetes secret.
    • Cluster as a claim: A single ClusterClaim named production, committed to Git, builds a new EKS cluster with its VPC and subnets in about 20-30 minutes.
    • App and DB claims: AppClaim and SQLClaim deploy an app plus either in-cluster PostgreSQL or Amazon RDS PostgreSQL to dev and prod.
    • Compositions: AWS provider config comes from vfarcic/devops-toolkit-crossplane.
    • Security note: The provider-helm service account is given cluster-admin, which is broader than needed.
    • Teardown: Delete the manifests from Git; Flux prunes them and Crossplane deletes the cloud resources.

    Takeaway: Shows the “everything as a claim” pattern end to end. Replace the static credentials secret and the cluster-admin binding before using it for real.

  • k8s-pod-restart-info-collector: Automatically Collect Kubernetes Pod Restart Reasons, Logs, and Events
    summary

    TL;DR: A small Kubernetes controller from Airwallex’s DevOps team. When a pod restarts, it collects the restart reason, logs and events and posts them to Slack.

    • What it sends: A brief alert, expandable to the reason, pod status, pod events, node status and events, and pod logs from before the restart.
    • Install: helm upgrade --install k8s-pod-restart-info-collector ./helm --set slackWebhookUrl=... --set clusterName=... --set slackChannel=....
    • Local dev: export SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL=... then go run ..
    • Verify: Run a short-lived debug-pod (e.g. kubectl run debug-pod --image=alpine -- date;sleep 30) and watch for the Slack message.
    • Background: Explained in the Medium post “Automated Troubleshooting of Kubernetes (K8s) Pods Issues”.
    • Status: Not archived. The README says Airwallex actively uses and maintains it.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to capture the logs from before a crash, which are often gone by the time someone looks. Pair it with restart-count alerting.

25.08.2022

  • Using CDK to Perform Continuous Deployments in Multi-Region Kubernetes Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post (Jul 2022, Elamaran Shanmugam and Re Alvarez-Parmar) that defines two regional EKS clusters, their workloads and a CI/CD pipeline in one TypeScript CDK codebase.

    • Topology: Primary EKS cluster in us-east-2 and secondary in eu-west-2 (Kubernetes 1.21, r5.2xlarge and m5.2xlarge nodes).
    • Stacks: Five CDK stacks: ClusterStack-<region> and ContainerStack-<region> for each region, plus CicdStack.
    • Pipeline: CodeCommit, CodePipeline and CodeBuild, plus ECR in each region. It builds the image, deploys to the primary, then waits for manual approval before the secondary.
    • Steps: cdk bootstrap aws://$ACCOUNT_ID/<region> per region, cdk diff, cdk deploy "*", then git push codecommit master for the sample app.
    • Prerequisites: AWS CDK 2.19.0+, Node 17.8.0+, kubectl, Docker and jq.
    • Not included: Traffic routing across regions. The post suggests Global Accelerator or DNS. ArgoCD is mentioned only as GitOps background.
    • Repo: aws-samples/containers-blog-maelstrom, path aws-cdk-eks-multi-region-skeleton.

    Takeaway: A usable skeleton for a CDK-first team running EKS in several regions. Add cdk-nag and traffic routing before treating it as production-ready.

  • Amazon Detective Supports Kubernetes Workloads on Amazon EKS for Security Investigations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS News Blog post by Channy Yun (Jul 2022) announcing that Amazon Detective ingests EKS audit logs for security investigations.

    • Data: Reads EKS audit logs and correlates them with CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs. You do not enable or store the logs yourself.
    • Retention: Keeps about 12 months of activity in its behaviour graph.
    • Views: Cluster details, containers with pod, image and security context, and Kubernetes API activity by subject, source IP and outcome (success, failure, unauthorized, forbidden).
    • Anomalies: Highlights newly seen API calls and subjects whose call volume went up.
    • GuardDuty link: GuardDuty EKS Protection findings can be investigated in Detective. GuardDuty is a prerequisite.
    • Enable: Settings, General, Optional source packages, “EKS audit logs”. It is on by default for new customers. No cluster changes are needed.
    • Pricing: Based on audit log volume, with a 30-day free trial.

    Takeaway: If you already run GuardDuty, this adds Kubernetes context to investigations with no agents. Watch the cost on busy clusters.

  • kubernetes-event-exporter: Export Kubernetes Events to Multiple Destinations with Routing and Filtering
    summary

    TL;DR: kubernetes-event-exporter is an actively maintained fork of Opsgenie’s tool (unmaintained since Nov 2021). It ships Kubernetes events to many destinations with tree-based routing and filtering.

    • Purpose: Kubernetes events are easy to miss and short-lived. This exports them for observability and alerting.
    • Routing: A YAML config (a ConfigMap in-cluster) defines a route tree with match and drop rules on namespace, labels, reason and so on.
    • Receivers: For example, critical events to Opsgenie, all events to Elasticsearch, and pod events to owners via Slack.
    • Deploy: Apply the deploy/ YAMLs in order after editing 01-config.yaml, or use Kustomize from a Git ref. For Helm, the README recommends the Bitnami chart.
    • History: Originally presented at KubeCon 2019 San Diego. Fork development was sponsored by Resmo.
    • Moved: The URL now resolves to mustafaakin/kubernetes-event-exporter.

    Takeaway: A simple way to keep event history and alert on warnings such as FailedScheduling or BackOff. Check that the fork is still maintained before adopting it.

  • Best Practices for AWS Organizations Service Control Policies in a Multi-Account Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS for Industries post (Feb 2022, Rajeswari Malladi and Jim Kozlowski) proposing an OU structure and starter SCPs for financial services multi-account setups.

    • Mechanics: SCPs set the maximum permissions, including for root, in member accounts. Effective permissions are the intersection of inherited SCPs and IAM policies.
    • Layering: Broad policies go high in the hierarchy and stricter ones lower down. A top-level “Corporate” OU under the root holds org-wide SCPs.
    • Deny vs allow lists: Deny-lists block leaving the org, unapproved regions and disabling security tools. The workloads OU sample is an allow-list built with NotAction.
    • Exemptions: Use ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalARN so that only approved roles bypass a policy.
    • Protections: Keep GuardDuty, Config and CloudTrail running, deny admin IAM actions except for approved roles, block root user access, lock S3 Block Public Access, and require encryption, tags and MFA delete.
    • Network: Deny VPC peering except for approved roles, to limit exfiltration paths.
    • OU design: Separate public-facing and internal production OUs. SDLC OUs mirror the production structure.

    Takeaway: A sensible baseline SCP set and OU layout for regulated organisations. Test policies in a non-production OU first, because a wrong deny can lock everyone out.

  • What Is eBPF, Anyway, and Why Should Kubernetes Admins Care?
    summary

    TL;DR: A groundcover blog explainer on what eBPF is, how programs are verified and run in the kernel, and why it matters for Kubernetes observability.

    • Lifecycle: Programs are written in restricted C, compiled with Clang, loaded through the bpf() syscall, checked by the verifier and JIT-compiled.
    • Verifier: Rejects unsafe programs, e.g. out-of-bounds access, often without a clear reason. A program can pass on one kernel and fail on another.
    • Maps and helpers: Maps pass data between the kernel and user space. Helpers cover tasks such as memory copies, PIDs and timestamps.
    • Kubernetes uses: Network visibility without a service mesh, per-process performance monitoring, profiling and security auditing. Tools are usually deployed as a DaemonSet.
    • Tooling named: BCC, bpftrace, bpftool, libbpf, cilium/ebpf (Go) and redbpf (Rust), plus groundcover’s own agent.
    • Caveats: Steep learning curve, limited stack space, and portability gaps across distributions and kernels. Check uname -r on nodes.
    • Page changed: The current page is dated Mar 2024 (author Aviv Zohari), so it has been rewritten since it was bookmarked in 2022.

    Takeaway: A good conceptual primer. Check node kernel versions before adopting eBPF-based tools, because features depend heavily on the kernel.

  • pixie: Instant Kubernetes-Native Application Observability
    summary

    TL;DR: Pixie is an open-source observability tool for Kubernetes applications. It uses eBPF to collect telemetry automatically, without code changes.

    • Auto-telemetry: eBPF captures full-body requests, resource and network metrics, and application profiles.
    • In-cluster: Data is collected, stored and queried inside the cluster. The README says it uses under 5% of cluster CPU, usually under 2%.
    • PxL: A Pythonic query language used across the UI, CLI and client APIs.
    • Network: Traffic flow, DNS requests and responses, and maps of TCP drops and retransmits.
    • Infra and services: Resource use per pod, node and namespace, CPU flame graphs, per-endpoint latency, and samples of the slowest requests.
    • Status: Not archived.

    Takeaway: Good for instant service maps and request inspection when you have no tracing set up. Treat captured request bodies as sensitive data.

  • CDK for Terraform Is Now Generally Available
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: HashiCorp’s announcement that CDK for Terraform (CDKTF) reached general availability with version 0.12, about two years after the community preview built with the AWS CDK team.

    • What it is: Write Terraform configurations in TypeScript, Python, C#, Java or Go while using the full ecosystem of Terraform providers and modules.
    • Constructs: Custom abstraction layers to reuse resource configuration and cut duplication.
    • Interop: CDKTF synthesizes JSON that Terraform deploys directly, so teams can choose HCL or CDKTF project by project.
    • 0.12 highlights: Full Go support (after JSII added Go support), unit-testing utilities for all supported languages, and Terraform iterator support.
    • CI/CD: A new GitHub Action for running CDKTF with Terraform Cloud or Enterprise, plus Deployment Patterns docs.
    • Source caveat: The live page shows a Vercel bot check. This summary is based on a Jan 2025 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: CDKTF suits teams that want loops, types and tests in a general-purpose language on top of Terraform. Check its current support status before starting new projects on it.

  • A Guide to the Go Garbage Collector
    summary

    TL;DR: The official Go guide to the garbage collector, written for Go 1.19. It covers the cost model, GOGC, the memory limit, latency and how to cut heap allocations.

    • Design: Tracing, non-moving, concurrent mark-sweep. Escape analysis decides between stack and heap.
    • GOGC: Target heap = live heap + (live heap + GC roots) x GOGC/100. Doubling GOGC roughly doubles heap overhead and halves GC CPU.
    • Memory limit: GOMEMLIMIT or debug.SetMemoryLimit (Go 1.19+) is a soft limit. GC CPU is capped at about 50% to avoid thrashing.
    • Limit guidance: Good for containers you control, with 5-10% headroom. Avoid it for CLI or desktop tools with unknown inputs.
    • Latency: Mostly brief stop-the-world transitions, the 25% background mark CPU, and allocation assists. Allocating less helps both throughput and latency.
    • Diagnostics: GODEBUG=gctrace=1, CPU profiles (runtime.mallocgc over 15% means heavy allocation), heap profiles with alloc_space, and go build -gcflags=-m=3 for escape analysis.
    • Updated: The living document now also covers later changes: THP settings for Go 1.21+, and runtime.AddCleanup and weak pointers in Go 1.24+.

    Takeaway: The reference for tuning Go services in containers. Set GOMEMLIMIT just under the container limit and profile allocations before changing GOGC.

  • What’s New in Go 1.19?
    summary

    TL;DR: Carl Johnson’s (now Carlana) tour of Go 1.19 (Jul 2022), focused on smaller standard library additions, several of which he took part in.

    • url.JoinPath: A new function and method for joining URL paths. He was interested because of his HTTP request library.
    • time.Duration.Abs(): Handles the asymmetric negative extreme of Duration by saturating. He says Russ Cox helped find the fix.
    • http.MaxBytesError: Lets callers detect MaxBytesReader overflow with errors.As instead of matching strings.
    • atomic.Pointer[T]: The first generics-based standard library API, alongside the revised memory model.
    • Soft memory limit: GOMEMLIMIT or debug.SetMemoryLimit, which he says makes “memory ballast” tricks obsolete.
    • Others: fmt.Append/Appendf/Appendln, flag.TextVar, sort.Find, pattern-defeating quicksort in sort.Sort, and doc comment links and formatting fixed by go fmt.
    • Moved: The blog now redirects to blog.carlana.net.

    Takeaway: A readable complement to the official release notes. GOMEMLIMIT and http.MaxBytesError are the most useful for production code.

  • Kubernetes Cluster Upgrade: The Blue-Green Deployment Strategy
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post (Jul 2022) by AWS and TheFork on upgrading EKS by building a new cluster and moving traffic, instead of upgrading in place.

    • Why: Going from EKS 1.15 to 1.18 and Istio 1.4 to 1.8 meant seven sequential upgrades per cluster across seven clusters, 49 in total, which they called high risk.
    • Rule: Rolling in-place upgrades for non-breaking changes, blue-green for breaking ones. Blue-green took 1-2 months versus 2-4 weeks.
    • Pre-checks: Changelogs, kubent (kube-no-trouble), istioctl analyse and istioctl experimental precheck.
    • Setup: Terraform-managed clusters named aws-environment-{spoon,knife} in eu-west-3. Jenkins and Helmfile deploy to both clusters in parallel.
    • Cutover: ALB target group weights move from 25% through 33%, 50%, 66% and 75% to 100%, one ingress at a time, so HPA has time (its 5-minute window) to scale.
    • Stateful caveat: EBS volumes attach to one node, so each StatefulSet needs its own migration plan. The Elasticsearch example stops Logstash, disables shard allocation and moves.

    Takeaway: Blue-green is worth it when you need to jump several versions. Plan stateful workloads first; they are the hard part.

  • Scaling Kubernetes with Karpenter: Advanced Scheduling with Pod Affinity and Volume Topology Awareness
    summary

    TL;DR: A 25-minute video by Lukonde Mwila (Jul 2022) showing Karpenter autoscaling an Amazon EKS cluster for workloads with pod affinity, anti-affinity and volume topology requirements.

    • Topic: Automatically scaling EKS compute with Karpenter while meeting advanced scheduling rules.
    • Concepts covered: Pod affinity and anti-affinity rules, cluster topology, and use cases for both (per the chapter timestamps).
    • Demo 1: Scaling the cluster with Karpenter for workloads that have pod affinity rules (from 03:11).
    • Demo 2: Scaling with dynamic volume provisioning and volume topology awareness (from 11:31).
    • Companion links: karpenter.sh, the matching AWS Containers blog post, the Karpenter launch post, terraform-aws-eks-blueprints and the EKS best-practices Karpenter page.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the YouTube title, description and timestamps. The video itself was not watched.

    Takeaway: Useful if you need Karpenter to provision nodes in the right zone for EBS-backed pods. Check today’s Karpenter APIs, which have changed since 2022.

  • The Art of Mac Malware
    summary

    TL;DR: The site for Patrick Wardle’s “The Art of Mac Malware” book series from the Objective-See Foundation, with chapters readable online as PDFs.

    • Volume I, Analysis: Infection vectors, persistence and capabilities, then nonbinary analysis, binary triage, disassembly and decompilation, dynamic analysis tools, debugging and anti-analysis.
    • Case study: Two chapters on the EvilQuest malware: infection, triage and deobfuscation, then persistence and core functionality.
    • Volume II, Detection: Programmatic detection of malicious code with behavioural heuristics, for building macOS defensive tools.
    • Access: Each chapter has a “Read Chapter” PDF link, and print copies can be ordered.
    • Author: Wardle created Objective-See and the “Objective by the Sea” conference, and previously worked at NASA and the NSA.
    • Changed since bookmarked: The site now covers two volumes. Volume II on detection was added after the original 2022 bookmark.

    Takeaway: The standard free reference for macOS malware analysis. Start with Volume I if you triage Mac incidents.

  • How to Reverse Mac Malware Without Getting Infected
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: “How to Reverse Malware on macOS Without Getting Infected”, a sponsored SentinelOne ebook by Phil Stokes with a foreword by Patrick Wardle. It teaches safe macOS malware analysis from lab setup to dynamic analysis.

    • Part One, lab: Setting up a safe environment, isolating macOS guest VMs, tools for testing malware, and where to find macOS malware samples.
    • File triage: First steps of file analysis, checking code signatures, application bundle structure, and gathering file metadata.
    • Part Two, Mach-O: What a Mach-O binary is, exploring segments and sections, pulling strings, using otool to examine binaries, and compiling indicators of compromise.
    • Part Three, dynamic analysis: Running malware in a controlled way to observe its behaviour.
    • Origin: Matches SentinelOne’s three-part blog series of the same name by Phil Stokes.
    • Source caveat: The PDF (over 10 MB) could not be parsed in full. The outline was recovered from its table of contents and confirmed with search results.

    Takeaway: A practical first manual for Mac malware triage in a VM. Pair it with Wardle’s “The Art of Mac Malware” for depth.

  • brev-cli: Cloud Coding Workspaces
    summary

    TL;DR: brev-cli was bookmarked as a CLI for cloud coding workspaces. The repository is now the NVIDIA Brev CLI, for creating and connecting to NVIDIA GPU instances on cloud platforms.

    • Changed scope: The README now describes NVIDIA Brev: streamlined access to GPU instances, automatic environment setup and flexible deployment. The original “cloud dev workspaces” framing is gone.
    • Install: brew install brevdev/homebrew-brev/brev on macOS, an install script on Linux and WSL, or pixi global install brev from conda-forge.
    • Usage: brev login, brev create <name> and brev ls.
    • Platforms: macOS, Linux, and Windows via WSL (Ubuntu 22.04 or newer).
    • Extras: The README mentions a bundled skill for AI coding agents.
    • Docs: docs.nvidia.com/brev/latest/.

    Takeaway: Useful now mainly for getting GPU dev boxes quickly. It is no longer a general replacement for remote development workspaces.

  • kubefire: Create and Manage Kubernetes Clusters Using Firecracker MicroVMs
    summary

    TL;DR: KubeFire creates and manages Kubernetes clusters that run on Firecracker microVMs, through weaveworks/ignite.

    • Images: Uses rootfs and kernel from OCI images rather than qcow2 or vhd VM images, and containerd manages the Firecracker processes.
    • Bootstrappers: kubeadm, K3s, RKE2 and k0s.
    • Architectures: x86_64 and ARM64 (ARM for K3s, RKE2 and k0s).
    • Quickstart: kubefire install (as root, installs runc, containerd, CNI plugins and Ignite), then kubefire cluster create demo.
    • Minimum versions: runc 1.1.3, containerd 1.6.6, CNI 1.1.1 and Ignite 0.10.0.
    • Install: A curl install script or huber install kubefire. Clusters can also be defined in a declarative config file.

    Takeaway: A lightweight way to get VM-isolated local multi-node clusters on Linux hosts with KVM. Check that the Ignite dependency is still maintained before you rely on it.

  • aws-auto-cleanup: Delete AWS Resources Based on an Allowlist and TTL Settings
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Auto Cleanup deletes unneeded AWS resources using user-defined allowlists and time-to-live (TTL) policies, to keep accounts tidy and cut cost.

    • Approach: Resources not on an allowlist and older than their TTL are deleted.
    • Components: Three modules, APP, API and WEB, each with its own deployment steps.
    • Use case: Sandbox and development accounts where forgotten resources pile up cost.
    • Moved: The repository now resolves to mlevit/aws-auto-cleanup.
    • Archived: The owner archived the repository on Aug 15, 2024, so it is read-only and unmaintained.
    • Source caveat: The current README is minimal. Details per module are in sub-READMEs that were not reviewed.

    Takeaway: The allowlist-plus-TTL pattern is still sound for sandbox accounts. Since this tool is archived, consider maintained alternatives such as aws-nuke.

  • vscode-gitops-tools: VS Code GitOps Extension
    summary

    TL;DR: Weaveworks’ GitOps Tools extension for VS Code shows, configures and debugs Flux objects in a Kubernetes cluster from the editor.

    • Built on: Flux (CNCF). Manages sources such as GitRepository and workloads such as Kustomization and HelmRelease.
    • Workflow: Create a GitRepository source that tracks manifests, add a Kustomization that reconciles them, and manage changes through Git.
