    • Requirements: kubectl with a selected cluster context (kind or Docker Desktop is enough). The flux CLI can be installed from the extension.
    • Extras: Extra dependencies for Weave GitOps Enterprise and Azure users.
    • Stability: The README says the extension is under active development with rolling beta releases and possible breaking changes.
    • Status: The repository is not archived.

    Takeaway: Handy for seeing Flux reconcile state without CLI round-trips. Check recent commit activity and Flux version compatibility before you depend on it.

  • awesome-cloudnative-trainings: Awesome Cloud Native Trainings
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated list of free cloud-native and Kubernetes trainings that come with certificates or badges. It started as a Medium post by joseadanof.

    • Claim: More than 50 certificates or badges are available through the listed courses, and the repo has over 1.7k stars.
    • Providers: Chainguard, Akuity (Argo CD), AWS, Isovalent, Arrikto, ScyllaDB, ArangoDB, Redis University, O11y Academy, Cockroach Labs, IBM, Harness, Ambassador Labs, Nirmata, Tetrate, Codefresh, Kasten and solo.io.
    • Examples: Chainguard “Painless Vulnerability Management”, Akuity “Introduction to Continuous Delivery and GitOps using Argo CD”, and AWS Skill Builder storage learning plans.
    • Audience: People studying for Kubernetes certifications, and DevOps, platform, cloud and SRE roles.
    • Status: Not archived. New entries such as AI/ML supply-chain courses show it has kept being updated.

    Takeaway: A good free study map. Check each link before you plan around it, because vendor course URLs change often.

  • Exploiting Authentication in AWS IAM Authenticator for Kubernetes
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Gafnit Amiga’s research for Lightspin (Jul 2022) on three flaws in AWS IAM Authenticator for Kubernetes, the component that maps IAM identities to EKS users. All three came from the same line of code. Tracked as CVE-2022-2385.

    • Mechanism: kubectl sends a presigned STS GetCallerIdentity URL as the token. The authenticator checks the host, path and allowlisted query parameters, then calls STS.
    • Root cause: Query parameters were validated in an unordered loop that did not reject duplicate names. Repeating a parameter could override the checked value.
    • Impacts: Bypassing the replay protection (unsigned cluster ID header), changing the STS action, and impersonating other identities through the AccessKeyID-based username mapping.
    • Age: Two flaws existed since the first commit (Oct 12, 2017). Impersonation was possible from v0.5.2 (Sep 2, 2020).
    • Fix: EKS added validation that rejects duplicate parameter names. AWS patched all EKS clusters and published a security bulletin.
    • Timeline: Reported May 25, 2022. Fix validated on Jun 10, 2022.
    • Source caveat: The live page is behind a Cloudflare challenge. This summary is based on a Sep 2023 Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Managed EKS was patched by AWS. Self-managed users and EKS Anywhere users of aws-iam-authenticator must upgrade.

  • How Attackers Use Exposed Prometheus Server to Exploit Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Miguel Hernández of Sysdig (Jul 2022, from a KubeCon EU 2022 talk) shows how much an exposed Prometheus server reveals about a Kubernetes cluster and how attackers could use it.

    • Exposure: Search engines list 31,679 (Shodan), 61,854 (Censys) and 161,274 (Fofa) exposed Prometheus servers. The tests used only a demo environment.
    • Infra leaks: node_dmi_info (cloud vendor and instance type), node_network_info (IPs, AZ, VPC ID) and kube_node_info (OS image and kernel, to match against CVEs).
    • Workload leaks: kube_ingress_path, kube_pod_labels, kube_pod_container_info (images and digests) and kubernetes_build_info.
    • Secrets: kube_secret_info exposes secret names. Old kubectl last-applied annotations could expose secret contents.
    • No audit trail: Prometheus query logging is off by default.
    • Scenarios: Supply-chain attacks via lookalike image names, cryptomining via Log4Shell, and ransomware via Spring Cloud CVE-2022-22963 followed by etcd access.

    Takeaway: Never expose Prometheus or metrics endpoints without authentication. Treat metric labels as sensitive data.

  • Cloud Design Patterns
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft’s Azure Architecture Center catalog of technology-agnostic cloud design patterns. Each pattern is mapped to the Well-Architected Framework pillars it supports.

    • Catalog: About 44 patterns, each with the problem, considerations and an Azure-based example.
    • Resilience: Retry, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Health Endpoint Monitoring, Rate Limiting, Throttling and Leader Election.
    • Messaging: Queue-Based Load Leveling, Competing Consumers, Publisher-Subscriber, Claim Check, Priority Queue, Sequential Convoy and Idempotent Consumer.
    • Data: Cache-Aside, CQRS, Event Sourcing, Materialized View, Sharding, Index Table, Saga and Compensating Transaction.
    • Edge and gateways: Ambassador, Sidecar, Gatekeeper, Gateway Routing/Aggregation/Offloading, Backends for Frontends, Valet Key, Strangler Fig and Anti-Corruption Layer.
    • Guidance: Choose patterns by problem, not technology. It lists combinations such as Retry with Circuit Breaker, and Saga built on Compensating Transaction.
    • Moved and updated: The URL now redirects to learn.microsoft.com. The page has a newer section linking to AI agent orchestration patterns.

    Takeaway: A good vocabulary for design reviews on any cloud. Read the trade-offs section of each pattern before adopting it.

  • Vantage: Save on Cloud Costs
    summary

    TL;DR: Vantage is a commercial multi-cloud cost management platform. It now describes itself as the system of record for allocating and optimising cloud, SaaS and AI costs.

    • Reporting: Cost reports, virtual tagging, budgets, unit costs, network cost views and asset inventory.
    • Optimisation: Waste detection, cost recommendations, and Autopilot for buying AWS Savings Plans.
    • Kubernetes: An agent that breaks cost down by namespace and label, flags idle and pod waste, and suggests rightsizing.
    • Integrations: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Cloudflare, SaaS such as Datadog and New Relic, and data platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks.
    • AI features: LLM token cost allocation, a FinOps agent, and an MCP server for querying costs from AI assistants.
    • Ops: Anomaly and budget alerts to Slack, Teams, Jira or email, and a Terraform provider.
    • Changed since bookmarked: The 2022 bookmark predates the AI and MCP features. No pricing tiers are shown on the homepage.

    Takeaway: Worth a look if native cost tools are too fragmented across clouds and SaaS. Compare it with free options such as OpenCost before paying.

  • API-Security-Checklist: API Security Checklist
    summary

    TL;DR: Shieldfy’s API Security Checklist lists the main security countermeasures for designing, testing and releasing APIs, with translations into many languages.

    • Authentication: No Basic Auth. Use standard token and password-storage schemes. Use max-retry and jail on login.
    • Access: Rate limiting, TLS 1.2+ with Host matching SNI, HSTS, no directory listings, and IP allowlists for private APIs.
    • Input: Correct HTTP methods (405 otherwise), Accept/content-type validation (406), and no secrets in URLs.
    • Processing: Authentication on every endpoint, /me/orders instead of user IDs, UUIDs instead of auto-increment IDs, and XML entity parsing off to avoid XXE.
    • Other sections: Authorization, Output, CI and CD, and Monitoring, plus an advanced best-practices section.
    • Format: Markdown checkboxes, easy to copy into a review template.

    Takeaway: A fast pre-release review list for any HTTP API. Pair it with the OWASP API Security Top 10 for threat context.

  • How to Build Multi-Arch Docker Images
    summary

    TL;DR: Kush Mansingh (Speedscale, Jul 2022) shows how to build one image tag for both amd64 and arm64 with Docker Buildx, using either emulation or cross-compilation.

    • Setup: docker buildx create --use.
    • Build: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t <image> --push . Multi-arch results need --push, because --load cannot export manifest lists.
    • Emulation: docker run --rm --privileged multiarch/qemu-user-static --reset -p yes lets steps such as apt-get run for foreign architectures.
    • Cross-compile: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM with GOOS/GOARCH set from the TARGETOS/TARGETARCH build args.
    • Timing: About 9 s emulated versus about 7 s cross-compiled for a trivial Go app. The author expects the gap to grow with project size.
    • cgo caveat: Needs a C cross-toolchain such as gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu.

    Takeaway: Cross-compile in the build stage and keep the runtime stage on an architecture-specific base. That gives fast builds for Graviton and Apple Silicon.

  • Attesting Image Scans with Kyverno
    summary

    TL;DR: Chip Zoller (Jul 2022) shows how to scan images on a schedule, attach the results as signed Cosign attestations, and have Kyverno block pods whose scans are too old.

    • Pipeline: A daily GitHub Actions workflow with scan and attest jobs. Trivy v0.31.2 (format: cosign-vuln, ignore-unfixed: true). A SHA-256 check of scan.json between jobs.
    • Attest: cosign attest --replace --predicate scan.json --type vuln <image> with keyless signing (Cosign v1.10.0, which the author says fixed --replace).
    • Predicate: cosign.sigstore.dev/attestation/vuln/v1.
    • Policy: Kyverno 1.7.2 verifyImages with validationFailureAction: enforce and failurePolicy: Fail, checking the keyless GitHub Actions subject and issuer.
    • Freshness rule: time_since on metadata.scanFinishedOn must be LessThanOrEquals 168h. Lowering it to 10h denies the pod.
    • Not covered: Filtering by CVE severity or allow-lists is left for a later post.

    Takeaway: Admission control on scan freshness is a cheap supply-chain gate. Add severity rules before relying on it to block real vulnerabilities.

  • The Kubernetes Networking Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: The Kubernetes Networking Guide (TKNG) is a free site that explains exactly how Kubernetes networking components work, aimed at people designing, running and troubleshooting cluster networks.

    • Audience: Not a beginner resource. It assumes you know pods, deployments and services, and it is written for people with a network engineering background.
    • Sections: The network model, CNI, Services, Ingress and Egress, Network Policies, IPv6 and DNS.
    • Structure: Follows how Kubernetes SIG Network is organised into interest groups. Parts can be read independently.
    • Labs: Most topics include a hands-on lab that runs locally in minutes. Setup is on the Lab Setup page.
    • Source: The content is on GitHub (networkop/k8s-networking-guide), and contributions go through pull requests with a matching lab.

    Takeaway: The best deep dive when you need to know what kube-proxy or a CNI actually programs on the node. Use the labs to reproduce problems.

  • User and Workload Identities in Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: A LearnKube article (Part 1 of 4) on how the Kubernetes API server authenticates human users and workloads, and how workload tokens extend to cloud IAM.

    • Users: Kubernetes stores no user objects. The options are static token files (--token-auth-file), X.509 client certs (--client-ca-file), OIDC JWTs, webhook token auth and authenticating proxies.
    • Multiple authenticators: Any one of them accepting a request is enough. Unauthenticated requests become system:anonymous.
    • Service accounts: Tokens from the TokenRequest API are mounted through projected volumes at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount, refreshed by the kubelet, and bound to the pod.
    • Manual token: kubectl create token <sa> --duration=10m. JWT claims are sub, aud, iss, exp and pod/node binding.
    • Legacy tokens: Secret-based tokens never expire and are not recommended.
    • Cloud identity: IRSA and EKS Pod Identity. The projected token with audience sts.amazonaws.com is checked by STS against the cluster’s OIDC discovery and JWKS (kubectl get --raw /openid/v1/jwks). TokenReview validates tokens in-cluster.
    • Moved and updated: The URL now redirects to learnkube.com. The current version is dated May 2026 (Gulcan Topcu, Arthur Chiao).

    Takeaway: Prefer OIDC or a proxy for humans, and short-lived, audience-scoped bound tokens for workloads. Remove any remaining Secret-based service account tokens.

  • Minimal Container Images: Towards a More Secure Future
    summary

    TL;DR: Adrian Mouat (Chainguard, Jul 2022) argues that the number of components in an image, more than its size, drives risk. He traces slim, scratch and distroless images to Chainguard’s apk-based approach.

    • Slim bases: Debian 11 slim is about 74 MB versus 118 MB for the full image. Alpine is about 5 MB but uses musl, which matters if an app needs glibc.
    • Scratch: Static binaries can be tiny: a Rust CLI at 15.9 MB, Go hello-world at 2.07 MB, and a C program at 452 bytes.
    • Distroless: Only certs, libc, the runtime and basic files, with no shell or package manager. Google’s images are built with Bazel and hard to extend.
    • Debugging: Use Kubernetes ephemeral containers (still beta at the time).
    • Chainguard tooling: apko builds images from a YAML list of apk packages. melange builds apk packages reproducibly.
    • Moved: The old blog URL now redirects to Chainguard’s blog index. The article lives at chainguard.dev/unchained/minimal-container-images-towards-a-more-secure-future.

    Takeaway: Fewer packages mean fewer CVEs to triage. Move production images to distroless-style bases and keep debugging tools out of the image.

  • fwd:cloudsec
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The YouTube playlist of talk recordings from fwd:cloudsec 2022, a community-run cloud security conference.

    • Event: fwd:cloudsec 2022 was its third year. A search-result recap describes a one-day event at District Hall, Boston, on July 25, 2022, just before AWS re:Inforce.
    • Known talks: Recaps mention Zack Allen’s “Cloudy with a chance of IOCs” on modernising detection writing. Speakers also included Darwin Salazar and Orca researchers Tzah Pahima and Yanir Tsarimi.
    • Format: Recorded sessions on the conference’s YouTube channel (“fwd:cloudsec”).
    • Source caveat: YouTube returned only the playlist title, with no video list. Event details come from Datadog Security Labs and Orca Security recap pages found by web search.

    Takeaway: fwd:cloudsec talks are vendor-light, practitioner cloud security research. Browse the playlist for AWS and Azure attack and detection topics.

  • Kubernetes Removals and Major Changes in 1.25
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes blog post (Kat Cosgrove, Frederico Muñoz, Debabrata Panigrahi, Aug 2022) that lists what v1.25 removes or changes, chiefly the removal of PodSecurityPolicy.

    • PodSecurityPolicy: Removed in v1.25 after deprecation in v1.21. It is replaced by Pod Security Admission, which goes GA in the same release.
    • CSI migration: The core CSI Migration feature goes GA, moving in-tree volume plugins toward out-of-tree CSI drivers.
    • Storage plugins: GlusterFS and Portworx in-tree plugins are deprecated. Flocker, Quobyte and StorageOS in-tree plugins are removed.
    • vSphere: The in-tree vSphere volume driver no longer supports vSphere releases before 7.0u2.
    • iptables: The kubelet starts to stop creating the KUBE-MARK-DROP, KUBE-MARK-MASQ and KUBE-POSTROUTING nat chains, behind the IPTablesCleanup feature gate.
    • Next up (1.26): flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta1 and autoscaling/v2beta2 HPA are scheduled for removal.
    • Policy recap: Beta APIs stay supported for 3 releases after deprecation. GA APIs cannot be removed within a major version.

    Takeaway: Before going to 1.25, migrate any PSP use to Pod Security Admission and check for removed storage plugins. Do not depend on kube-proxy’s internal iptables chains.

  • Go 1.19 Release Notes
    summary

    TL;DR: The official Go 1.19 release notes. The release came five months after 1.18 and centres on a revised memory model, a soft memory limit and doc comment tooling.

    • Memory model: Revised to align with C, C++, Java, JavaScript, Rust and Swift. Go provides only sequentially consistent atomics.
    • Runtime: Soft memory limit via GOMEMLIMIT or debug.SetMemoryLimit (works even with GOGC=off), with GC CPU capped at about 50% near the limit. On Unix, programs that import os raise the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE to the hard limit.
    • Types: sync/atomic adds Int64, Bool, Pointer[T] and others.
    • Breaking change: os/exec no longer resolves PATH lookups relative to the current directory. Use ./prog explicitly.
    • Tools: gofmt reformats doc comments (go/doc/comment), a unix build constraint, and -trimpath recorded in build info.
    • Compiler: Jump tables for large switch statements, up to about 20% faster on amd64 and arm64.
    • Library: url.JoinPath, sort.Find, pdqsort, fmt.Append*, flag.TextVar and http.MaxBytesError. Ports: linux/loong64 added, and riscv64 now passes arguments in registers.

    Takeaway: If you upgrade old code, check os/exec callers. For containers, start setting GOMEMLIMIT.

09.08.2022

  • btop: Monitor of Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: btop is a terminal resource monitor by aristocratos, showing CPU, memory, disks, network and processes. It is the C++ successor to bashtop and bpytop.

    • UI: A game-style menu system, full mouse support, and selectable graph symbols and themes.
    • Processes: Detailed stats per process, filtering, tree view, switchable sorting, a pause option, and sending any signal to the selected process.
    • I/O: Disk I/O activity and speeds, auto-scaling network graphs, and a battery meter.
    • Platforms: Builds documented for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD. A snap is available and GPU monitoring is supported.
    • Config: Every config option can be changed from a UI menu.
    • Maintenance: Active. The README news (2025-2026) adds rules requiring PRs with AI-generated code to be labelled.

    Takeaway: A nicer drop-in for top or htop on workstations and servers. Install it from your package manager.

  • data-diff: Efficiently Diff Rows Across Two Different Databases
    summary

    TL;DR: data-diff, from Datafold, compared tables within or across SQL databases quickly. Datafold stopped supporting and developing the open-source version on May 17, 2024.

    • Purpose: Fast row-level comparison of datasets, within one database or across two different ones.
    • Sunset: The README says Datafold no longer supports or develops open-source data-diff and links a blog post explaining why.
    • Archived: The owner archived the repository on May 17, 2024.
    • License: MIT.
    • Source caveat: The current README is reduced to the sunset notice. Details of features and how it worked were not available from it.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt it for new work. The diffing approach is still useful, but look for a maintained tool for migration validation.

  • Whist: The First Cloud-Hybrid Browser
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Whist was a startup’s “cloud-hybrid” Chrome-based browser that ran web pages on remote servers and streamed them to the device. The company shut down in December 2022.

    • Pitch (2022 site): Like remote desktop, but for web apps. It streamed draw commands rather than pixels to cut latency and bandwidth.
    • Compatibility: A modified Chrome supporting Chrome extensions, with import of settings and passwords, and a built-in ad and tracker blocker.
    • Pivot: The later marketing aimed at enterprises: isolating company data, turning endpoints into thin clients, and admin controls such as blocking screen sharing.
    • Shutdown: The founder’s note says Whist shut down on 12/10/2022. The founders went on to start ParadeDB.
    • Source caveat: The live domain returns an empty page. This summary is based on a 2022 Wayback Machine copy and search results.

    Takeaway: A dead product. Keep the link only as a reference for the browser-isolation and remote-rendering approach.

  • EKS Anywhere on Bare Metal
    summary

    TL;DR: Amazon EKS Anywhere lets you create and operate EKS-style Kubernetes clusters on your own infrastructure. It was bookmarked when bare-metal support was announced.

    • Purpose: Run clusters on premises with default component configurations and automated cluster management tooling, consistent with EKS in the cloud.
    • Hybrid: Unify how apps run across cloud and on-premises environments.
    • Data sovereignty: Keep large datasets on premises to meet data-location rules.
    • AI workloads: The current page also pitches on-prem LLM training and inference on GPUs.
    • Next steps: Links to the installer, pricing and FAQs.
    • Page changed: The current product page has no bare-metal-specific content. Details on infrastructure providers and subscriptions are in the linked docs and pricing pages, which were not reviewed.

    Takeaway: Consider it when you need EKS-consistent tooling on premises. Read the linked pricing and FAQ pages for supported infrastructure and support terms.

  • Awesome Go: Over 2400 Resources!
    summary

    TL;DR: Awesome Go is the long-running curated directory of Go frameworks, libraries and software, inspired by awesome-python and maintained at avelino/awesome-go.

    • Scope: Categorised links with one-line descriptions. The bookmark title cites over 2,400 resources; the current page gives no total.
    • Categories: Examples include Actor Model, Artificial Intelligence, Authentication and Authorization, Command Line, Configuration, Database and Database Drivers, Networking, Testing, Text Processing and Web Frameworks.
    • Format: Each entry is a linked project name and a short description.
    • Curation: Contributions go through pull requests following CONTRIBUTING.md. Unmaintained projects are removed or replaced.
    • Site: awesome-go.com renders the GitHub list as a website.

    Takeaway: A good first stop when choosing a Go library. Still check stars, last commit and license yourself, because listing is not a quality guarantee.

  • Custom GitHub Action with Go
    summary

    TL;DR: A TheDeveloperCafe tutorial on writing a custom GitHub Action in Go, packaged as a Docker container action.

    • Program: A small main.go that prints its os.Args[1:], tested with go run main.go hello world.
    • Dockerfile: golang:1.18.3-alpine3.16, go build -o /bin/app main.go, ENTRYPOINT ["app"].
    • action.yml: runs: using: docker, image: Dockerfile, a required message input, and args: ["${{ inputs.message }}"].
    • Publish: Push to a repository, tag v1 and create a release. Consume it with uses: <owner>/<repo>@v1 and with: message: ..., or uses: ./ locally.
    • Internals: Shows the full docker run command the runner uses, with --workdir /github/workspace, environment variables and the /var/run/docker.sock mount.
    • Not covered: INPUT_* environment variables and writing outputs via GITHUB_OUTPUT.

    Takeaway: A minimal template for Go-based actions. Docker actions run only on Linux runners and add image build time; a prebuilt image or a JavaScript wrapper avoids that.

  • Debugging containerd
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Zendesk Engineering Medium post titled “Debugging containerd”. The content could not be retrieved, so only the topic is known.

    • Topic: Investigating a problem in containerd, the container runtime under Kubernetes nodes, from Zendesk’s engineering team.
    • Publication: The Zendesk Engineering blog on Medium (zendesk.engineering), bookmarked in Aug 2022.
    • Access: Medium blocked direct fetching, no Wayback Machine snapshot was found, and web searches did not turn up the article or a mirror.
    • Source caveat: This summary is based only on the title and URL. No technical claims from the article could be checked.

    Takeaway: Treat it as an unread link. Open it in a browser if you need Zendesk’s specific containerd findings.

  • op-vscode: 1Password for VS Code
    summary

    TL;DR: 1Password’s official VS Code extension. It ties editor workflows to 1Password through the 1Password CLI.

    • Requirement: 1Password CLI v2.4.0 or newer installed.
    • Unlock: Biometric unlock must be enabled. Without a biometric device you can use the device user password.
    • Install: From the VS Code Marketplace (1Password.op-vscode) or GitHub releases. Then pick an account and vault when prompted.
    • Docs: Features are documented on the 1Password developer portal.
    • License: MIT. Use of the 1Password APIs falls under the 1Password API Terms of Service.

    Takeaway: Useful for keeping secrets out of source files by referencing 1Password items from the editor. It requires the CLI and biometric unlock.

  • Kubernetes Security Scanning with Trivy CLI and Trivy Operator
    summary

    TL;DR: A 17-minute video by Anais Urlichs (Jun 2022) on scanning a Kubernetes cluster for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, first with the Trivy CLI and then with the Trivy Operator.

    • Scope: Cluster scanning for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
    • Trivy CLI: One-off scans from the command line (segment from 04:43).
    • Trivy Operator: In-cluster, continuous scanning that writes results as Kubernetes resources (segment from 08:24).
    • Comparison: A section on how the CLI and Operator approaches differ (from 11:23).
    • Resources: Demo repo AnaisUrlichs/trivy-demo, the Trivy docs and repo, and an earlier Trivy CLI video.
    • Source caveat: Summary based on the YouTube title, description and timestamps. The video itself was not watched.

    Takeaway: Use the CLI for CI and ad-hoc checks and the Operator for continuous in-cluster reports. The commands have changed since 2022, so follow the current Trivy docs.

  • Code-Server, Caddy, Tailscale, and Hugo = My Ultimate Dev Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Short (Jul 2022) describes his browser-based dev setup: code-server behind Caddy with DNS-challenge TLS, reachable only over Tailscale, with Hugo live preview.

    • Host: An Ubuntu VM (6 cores, 24 GB RAM). Later a home server, an 11th Gen Intel NUC i5 with 32 GB and 2 TB NVMe.
    • code-server: Installed with the official script, listening on 127.0.0.1:8080.
    • Caddy: A custom build with a DNS provider module. reverse_proxy for coder.example.com, a tls block using DNS validation, run as a caddy user with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE under systemd.
    • Tailscale: The DNS record points at the host’s Tailscale IP, so only tailnet members can reach it.
    • Hugo: A localHugo script runs hugo server with drafts and future posts, bound to the Tailscale IP on port 1313.
    • Caveats: Keep systemd units holding the DNS API token at root-owned 0600. Early public exposure drew heavy probing, which is why he made it private.

    Takeaway: Private-network-only access plus real TLS is a clean pattern for self-hosted dev tools. Do not expose code-server to the public internet.

  • Remote Development at Slack
    summary

    TL;DR: Sylvestor George (Slack Engineering, Jun 2022) describes moving Slack’s webapp development from laptops to on-demand EC2 environments accessed through VS Code Remote SSH.

    • Problem: A fresh clone of the Hack/HHVM backend took nearly 30 minutes. Local HHVM was heavy and fragile, and the webapp accounts for 60% of code changes.
    • Warm pool: An Auto Scaling Group keeps ready environments synced with master. Reserving one detaches it and saves about 12 minutes of bootstrap.
    • Workflow: slack remote-dev -b <branch> creates the branch, reserves a box, installs dependencies and opens VS Code. Dotfiles live in ~/.remote-dev-home.
    • Lifecycle: Short-lived. Environments terminate on detach or when the branch merges. A new instance is ready in under 90 seconds.
    • Sizing: Moved from c5.2xlarge to c5.4xlarge, which doubled cost but was a single config change.
    • Adoption: Beta in Aug 2021 (about 30% switched), GA in Oct 2021, and over 90% of engineers by end of Jan 2022. New-hire setup dropped from about an hour to minutes.

    Takeaway: For heavy monorepos, a pre-warmed pool of ephemeral cloud dev boxes beats laptop setup. Allow personal customisation to drive adoption.

  • Best Linux Commands for Advanced Hardware and System Info
    summary

    TL;DR: A Nix Sanctuary cheat sheet (Jun 2022) of Linux commands for inspecting hardware and system details.

    • Overview tools: lshw (--short, --sanitize, --html), hwinfo --short and inxi (-F full, -z to hide sensitive data).
    • Firmware: dmidecode -t bios|system|memory|processor (needs sudo) for SMBIOS data.
    • Buses: lspci -vvv, lsusb (-t tree, -d vendor:product) and lsscsi.
    • CPU and kernel: lscpu (-e, -p), uname -a/-m, and /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/version.
    • Storage: lsblk -a, blkid, fdisk -l, gdisk, parted, df -H, mount | column -t and hdparm -tT for a read benchmark.
    • Events: dmesg for hardware attach and detach messages.

    Takeaway: Handy for quick inventory or support tickets. Use lshw --sanitize or inxi -z before you share output.

  • Ripgrep-all Command in Linux: One grep to Rule Them All
    summary

    TL;DR: An It’s FOSS article (Jun 2022, Pratham Patel) introducing ripgrep-all (rga), a ripgrep wrapper that searches inside PDFs, office documents, archives, databases and media.

    • File types: PDF, epub, docx and odt, ipynb, zip/tar/gz/xz/zst archives, SQLite databases, video subtitles (mkv, mp4) and OCR on jpg and png.
    • Dependencies: ripgrep, pandoc, poppler-utils and ffmpeg.
    • Install: pacman -S ripgrep-all, brew install ripgrep-all or Nix. On Debian/Ubuntu, a musl release binary (rga plus rga-preproc) placed in ~/.local/bin.
    • Usage: ripgrep flags such as -i, -s, -v, -A/-B/-C and -j threads.
    • Cache: Extracted text is cached in ~/.cache/rga on Linux and ~/Library/Caches/rga on macOS. --rga-no-cache turns it off.
    • Naming: The project is ripgrep-all; the command is rga.

    Takeaway: Useful for searching document dumps or evidence folders. The cache makes repeat searches fast.

  • terratag: Maintain Tags Across All Terraform Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: Terratag, from env0, is a CLI that adds tags or labels to every AWS, GCP and Azure resource across a set of Terraform or OpenTofu files.

    • Why: Tagging by hand across a whole codebase is error-prone. Terratag adds tags retroactively to existing IaC.
    • Prerequisites: OpenTofu 1.x or Terraform 0.12 through 1.x. Run terraform init or tofu init first to get provider schemas and child modules.
    • Install: brew install env0/terratag/terratag or a release binary.
    • Usage: terratag -dir=foo/bar -tags={"environment_id": "prod"} or -tags="environment_id=prod,some-tag=value".
    • Output: Rewrites the .tf files so taggable resources merge in the tags, shown with before and after examples.
    • Status: Not archived. It has been updated to support OpenTofu.

    Takeaway: A quick fix for adding cost-allocation tags to a large legacy codebase. For new code, provider default_tags may be enough on AWS.

  • viddy: A Modern watch Command
    summary

    TL;DR: Viddy, by sachaos, is a modern replacement for watch. It runs a command periodically and adds history you can rewind.

    • Basics: Runs a command at an interval with colour output and diff highlighting.
    • Time machine: Rewind through earlier outputs “like video”. History can be saved and loaded.
    • Navigation: Output in a pager, Vim-like keymaps, text search, and suspend or restart of execution.
    • Customisation: Keymaps and colours. Supports shell aliases.
    • Install: cargo install viddy, brew install viddy, release tarballs, and community packages (APT via pkg.haus, MacPorts, Scoop, AUR).
    • Status: Not archived. The current README gives a Cargo install, which shows the tool is now distributed as a Rust crate.

    Takeaway: Drop it in wherever you use watch, e.g. viddy kubectl get pods. Rewinding means you can still see a short-lived state after it has passed.

  • Things You Should Know About Databases
    summary

    TL;DR: An Architecture Notes explainer by Mahdi Yusuf (June 2022) on the two RDBMS internals the author considers most important: indexes and transactions. The page is now titled “Relational Databases Explained”.

    • Scope: Covers relational databases in general (MySQL and PostgreSQL as examples) without database-specific quirks, with an infographic summary.
    • Index trade-off: Indexes cut lookup time but cost storage, memory and slower writes, because every write must keep the index up to date.
    • Data structures: Explains why sorting the table itself does not scale and walks through B+ trees, where intermediate nodes hold no data and point to leaf ranges.
    • Storage: Short aside on SSD vs HDD access latency and why it matters for random row placement.
    • Transactions: Covers ACID and the isolation levels READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, and the anomalies (dirty and non-repeatable reads) each prevents.
    • Title change: The archived title differs from the current page title; the content matches the original topic.

    Takeaway: A good refresher before tuning indexes or picking an isolation level. Know which isolation level your database uses by default and set it deliberately.

  • Advanced Features of Kubernetes’ Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
    summary

    TL;DR: Martin Heinz walks through Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler features beyond CPU and memory: custom and external metrics plus the alpha/beta gates for scale-to-zero, container metrics and logarithmic scale-down.

    • Lab setup: A KinD cluster (kindest/node:v1.23.6, 1 control plane, 3 workers) with feature gates HPAScaleToZero, HPAContainerMetrics and LogarithmicScaleDown, and the e2e resource-consumer image to simulate CPU, memory and metrics.
    • Metrics stack: metrics-server (patched with --kubelet-insecure-tls on KinD), Prometheus Operator with ServiceMonitors, and a Prometheus adapter to serve custom and external metrics APIs.
    • Custom metrics: autoscaling/v2 HPAs using type: Pods or type: Object (e.g. a Service), with AverageValue vs Value targets; discover metrics via kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/...".
    • External metrics: Scaling on a queue depth metric (external_queue_messages_ready) served from external.metrics.k8s.io.
    • Scale to zero: With the gate on, minReplicas: 0 works, but only for External or Object metrics.
    • Container metrics: type: ContainerResource scales on one container’s usage, ignoring sidecars.
    • Logarithmic scale-down: Picks pods to delete semi-randomly instead of newest-first, to keep replica distribution balanced (KEP-2189).

    Takeaway: Use ContainerResource metrics when sidecars distort pod CPU, and check the HPA status.conditions to confirm a metric is recognized. The alpha gates may have changed status since 2022.

  • Managing Kubernetes Without Losing Your Cool
    summary

    TL;DR: Marcus Noble (Giant Swarm) turns a webinar into a post of 11 numbered tips for working with many Kubernetes clusters every day, from shell aliases up to writing operators.

    • Basics: Learn your shell and dotfiles, alias k='kubectl', and use kubectl explain pods.spec.containers to look up fields offline.
    • Many kubeconfigs: Compares kubectx/kubens, kubeswitch and kubie; the author prefers kubeswitch for loading one kubeconfig file per cluster, and shows a KUBECONFIG merge hack.
    • Tooling: k9s as a terminal UI and kubectl plugins (via krew) for extra commands.
    • Node access: kshell / kubectl debug and kube-ssh style tricks for getting a shell on nodes; a later update adds an nsenter example from Ian Coldwater.
    • Advanced: Admission webhooks, talking to the Kubernetes API directly, and custom resources and operators for automation.
    • Tip #0: Tongue-in-cheek suggestion to pay someone else (a managed provider) to run clusters.

    Takeaway: Pick a kubeconfig switcher and a few aliases first; they prevent most wrong-cluster mistakes. The later tips suit people who already script against the API.

  • TryHackMe: Kubernetes
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A TryHackMe room titled “Kubernetes for Everyone” (slug kubernetesforyouly), a medium-rated Kubernetes hacking challenge aimed at DevOps/SRE people.

    • Format: Listed as about 60 minutes, medium difficulty, as a capture-the-flag style challenge.
    • Initial access: Find the cluster and credentials, with Nmap suggested to find open ports and a vulnerable service for a foothold.
    • Tasks: Questions ask for a username, a password and a secret, then a flag found by enumerating storage shared by pods.
    • Final task: A scenario about a “FANG interview” asks you to find a secret left behind in the cluster.
    • Source caveat: TryHackMe returned HTTP 429; summary is based on search result listings of the room, whose task wording varies between versions.

    Takeaway: A short hands-on exercise in finding secrets and shared volumes in a misconfigured cluster. Useful practice before a Kubernetes pentest or CKS-style study.

  • paralus: All-in-One Kubernetes Access Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: Paralus is a free, open source CNCF Sandbox project for controlled, audited access to Kubernetes clusters. It offers user-level credentials, RBAC, SSO and audit logs through a GUI, API and CLI.

    • Identity: Integrates with existing RBAC and with SSO or OIDC identity providers.
    • Just-in-time access: Creates service accounts on demand and manages fine-grained user credentials.
    • Controls: Custom roles, users and groups, plus preconfigured roles across clusters, namespaces and projects.
    • Revocation: Permissions can be changed and revoked dynamically and immediately.
    • Auditing: Real-time audit logs to help spot and respond to threats.
    • Project: Written in Go, Apache 2.0, with a Helm chart and an OpenSSF Best Practices badge.
    • Note: The archive lists this repo twice, under two title variants with the same URL.

    Takeaway: Consider Paralus for centrally brokered, revocable kubectl access across many clusters without distributing static kubeconfigs.

  • Understanding Data Transfer Costs for AWS Container Services
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post that maps common ECR, ECS and EKS deployment patterns to the data transfer charges each one incurs. Service charges are out of scope.

    • ECR private: Inbound transfer is free and same-Region transfer to other services is free; cross-Region pulls are charged at internet rates on both sides, and replication at cross-Region rates.
    • ECR Public: Authenticated users pay after 5 TB/month out to non-AWS destinations; anonymous pulls are capped at 500 GB/month, after which anonymous transfer stops.
    • ECS: Compares clusters with internet access (IGW, NAT gateway or Transit Gateway), private clusters with PrivateLink endpoints, and ECS Anywhere (free over internet; standard Data Transfer Out over VPN or Direct Connect).
    • Fargate note: Fargate in private ECS clusters does not need the ECS PrivateLink endpoints, but still needs ECR endpoints to pull images.
    • EKS: Charges accrue for cross-AZ pod-to-pod and pod-to-database traffic and for ALB egress; same-AZ traffic and same-Region ECR pulls are free.
    • NAT cost: Public EKS endpoints from private subnets go through a NAT gateway, which adds a per-GB processing fee.

    Takeaway: Cross-AZ traffic and NAT gateway processing are the usual hidden container costs. Keep chatty services AZ-local and use VPC endpoints for ECR.

  • Run an Active-Active Multi-Region Kubernetes Application with AppMesh and EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS tutorial for running the same application active-active in two Regions with one EKS cluster each, AWS App Mesh ingress gateways, and Route 53 latency-based records with health checks for failover.

    • Deprecated: An October 2024 notice says the post no longer reflects best guidance and its examples no longer work; AWS points to Amazon VPC Lattice instead.
    • Architecture: Two isolated EKS clusters (clusterA in us-east-2, clusterB in us-west-2) built with eksctl.
    • Mesh: App Mesh handles east-west traffic and a single ingress (virtual) gateway per cluster exposes multiple apps north-south.
    • Routing: Route 53 latency records send users to the lowest-latency Region; health checks fail traffic over when a Region is unhealthy.
    • Alternative: The authors note the same result is possible with a plain Ingress controller instead of App Mesh, since Route 53 provides the active-active behaviour.

    Takeaway: The durable idea is Route 53 latency plus health-check routing over independent regional clusters. Do not follow the App Mesh steps for new work.

  • Infrastructure Self-Service with Crossplane
    summary

    TL;DR: Sascha Selzer (INNOQ) explains how Crossplane lets platform teams offer cloud infrastructure as Kubernetes resources, so developers can self-serve databases and similar resources without cloud credentials.

    • Problem: Even with Kubernetes, external resources such as databases still go through the platform team, a different cloud API, separate identity management and wide developer credentials.
    • Operator pattern: Crossplane follows the Kubernetes operator pattern and moves infrastructure management into the cluster.
    • Providers: Provider packages give access to external APIs (e.g. AWS) and are configured with credentials held in the cluster.
    • Abstractions: Platform teams define composite resources (XRDs) and Compositions that bundle best-practice settings behind a simple developer-facing API.
    • Distribution: Shows how to package and distribute your own resource definitions as Crossplane packages.

    Takeaway: Crossplane suits teams that want one Kubernetes API and RBAC model for both apps and their cloud dependencies. Plan the XRD interfaces carefully, since they become your platform contract.

  • Extend AWS IAM Roles to Workloads Outside of AWS with IAM Roles Anywhere
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security blog introduction to IAM Roles Anywhere, which lets servers, containers and apps outside AWS swap X.509 certificates for temporary IAM role credentials instead of using long-term access keys.

    • Trust: You register a certificate authority as a trust anchor; it can be your existing PKI or an ACM Private CA.
    • Flow: The workload sends its certificate and a signature made with its private key, names the role, and IAM Roles Anywhere validates both before creating a role session via STS.
    • Profiles: Profiles define which roles can be assumed and can limit permissions further.
    • Client: The aws_signing_helper tool plugs into the AWS CLI and SDKs through credential_process in the AWS config file.
    • Use cases: On-premises servers, hybrid containers and other compute platforms that today rely on static access keys.

    Takeaway: If you have long-lived access keys on non-AWS hosts and already run a PKI, this replaces them with short-lived credentials. Protect the private keys and scope trust policies to certificate attributes.

  • What GKE Users Need to Know About Kubernetes’ New Service Account Tokens
    summary

    TL;DR: A Google Cloud blog post explaining how Kubernetes 1.21 replaced legacy service account tokens with bound tokens by default, and what GKE users must change.

    • Legacy tokens: Up to 1.20, an admission controller mounted a Secret with ca.crt, namespace and a JWT token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount; these tokens did not expire.
    • Bound tokens: From 1.21 the default token is time-limited, has an audience, and is only valid while the pod is still running.
    • Client libraries: Official Kubernetes clients and GKE Workload Identity need no changes beyond up-to-date libraries that reload the token from disk.
    • Vault: Vault checks the issuer and expects the legacy kubernetes/serviceaccount; you must configure the GKE issuer https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT/locations/LOCATION/clusters/NAME.
    • External services: Should agree on a unique audience (DNS name or UUID) and migrate TokenReview calls to validate it in phases, so stolen tokens only work for that service.

    Takeaway: Check that apps reload tokens from disk and that Vault’s Kubernetes auth has the new issuer. Use dedicated projected tokens with a unique audience for anything outside the cluster.

28.06.2022

  • New for AWS DataSync: Move Data Between AWS and Other Public Locations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS News Blog launch post (2022) showing AWS DataSync moving data between AWS storage and Google Cloud Storage or Azure Files, using a DataSync agent on EC2.

    • Targets: AWS side supports S3, EFS and FSx; external side is Google Cloud Storage (as “Object storage” at storage.googleapis.com) or Azure Files (as SMB).
    • Agent: Deployed on EC2 from the AMI ID in Parameter Store: aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/datasync/ami.
    • Networking: The instance needs access to source and destination and must accept HTTP from DataSync for activation; VPC endpoints are recommended.
    • Security: End-to-end encryption and integrity validation; logging and monitoring via CloudWatch and CloudTrail.
    • Update: A May 2025 note says DataSync Enhanced mode now supports cross-cloud transfers without an agent and with higher performance.

    Takeaway: For GCS or Azure Files migrations into AWS, DataSync is the managed option. Check Enhanced mode first, since the agent steps in the post are now optional.

  • devtron: Tool Integration Platform for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Devtron is an open-source (Apache 2.0, Go) Kubernetes management platform by Devtron Labs. It was linked as a tool integration platform and now presents itself as an “AI-Native Kubernetes Management Platform” built around a Kubernetes dashboard.

    • Dashboard: Helm app management with rollback, a resource browser for nodes, pods, ConfigMaps and CRDs, and one view of Helm, Argo CD and Flux CD apps across clusters.
    • Drift: Compares and reconciles configuration drift across environments.
    • Access: Built-in SSO and fine-grained RBAC for dashboard and cluster resources.
    • Platform mode: A separate “Devtron Platform” section covers the CI/CD capabilities.
    • Install: helm repo add devtron https://helm.devtron.ai then helm install devtron devtron/devtron-operator --create-namespace --namespace devtroncd; the admin password is in the devtron-secret Secret.
    • Repositioning: The README was restructured since 2022 and now leads with AI features; the CI/CD platform is no longer the headline.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted option for a multi-cluster Helm and GitOps dashboard with RBAC. Evaluate the current scope, since the product focus has shifted since this link was saved.

  • HashiCorp Vault 1.11 Adds Kubernetes Secrets Engine, PKI Updates, and More
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp’s release post for Vault 1.11 (GA June 22, 2022), headlined by a new Kubernetes secrets engine plus PKI, Transit and Enterprise storage changes.

    • Kubernetes secrets engine: Dynamically creates service account tokens, service accounts, role bindings and roles, with leases (the example uses 10m0s).
    • PKI: New /keys and /issuers endpoints allow non-disruptive root and intermediate rotation; CPS URLs in custom policy identifiers are supported.
    • Transit: Can import externally generated keys, such as keys from an HSM.
    • Enterprise: Integrated storage autopilot adds automated upgrades and redundancy zones; KMIP and Transform engines gain new operations.
    • Other: UI login MFA (TOTP, Duo, Okta, PingIdentity), KV v2 -mount and -output-policy CLI flags, Vault CSI provider GA, usage metrics export in tech preview.
    • Removals: Mount filters, stored licenses with sys/license endpoints (Enterprise), and legacy MFA.
    • Source caveat: curl returned only a stub; summary based on WebFetch’s extraction of the post.

    Takeaway: The Kubernetes secrets engine gives short-lived, Vault-issued cluster credentials instead of static kubeconfigs. Check the removal list before upgrading from 1.10.

  • Terraform Cloud Adds Drift Detection for Infrastructure Management
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp’s June 2022 announcement of drift detection in Terraform Cloud, which continuously compares real infrastructure against Terraform state and alerts when they diverge.

    • Detection: Runs continuously against workspace state to find resources changed outside Terraform.
    • UI: The workspace list shows drift status with a filter; a Drift tab lists drifted resources, changed attributes and when the last check ran.
    • Alerts: Configurable notifications to email, Slack or a webhook.
    • Remediation: Accept the change with a refresh-only plan, or update the configuration to match, both from the Drift tab.
    • Availability: Public beta for Terraform Cloud Business at announcement; no GA date or pricing given.
    • Source caveat: curl returned only a stub; summary based on WebFetch’s extraction of the post.

    Takeaway: Drift detection catches console hot-fixes before the next apply reverts them. Without that tier, a scheduled terraform plan -detailed-exitcode in CI covers the basic case.

  • How to Manage Kubernetes Secrets with GitOps?
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Hoang (Akuity, June 2022) summarizes a 40-minute webinar comparing six ways to handle Kubernetes secrets with GitOps and Argo CD, and recommends External Secrets.

    • Sealed Secrets: Encrypt locally with kubeseal; a controller decrypts SealedSecret resources in the cluster. Needs no secrets manager but each secret is encrypted by hand; suited to few clusters or a quick start.
    • Argo CD Vault Plugin: Replaces placeholders in Git manifests at sync time; no CRDs, but only one backend per Argo CD and a hard refresh is needed when a secret changes.
    • SOPS: Manual encryption with keys from a keystore and a SOPS plugin for Argo CD; the author’s “when to use” is “In 2018”.
    • Vault Agent: Sidecar per pod that renders files from Vault; no Kubernetes Secret, but 1000 pods means 1000 agents and apps fail to start if Vault is down.
    • Secrets Store CSI Driver: DaemonSet that mounts secrets from multiple managers at pod start; does not update mounted files.
    • External Secrets: ExternalSecret plus namespace or cluster SecretStore creates Kubernetes Secrets from many backends, with templates and versioned immutable secrets.
    • Cloud auth: Use cloud IAM, or workload identity federation when the cluster and secrets manager are in different clouds.

    Takeaway: For most teams, External Secrets Operator is the Kubernetes-native, backend-agnostic default. Pick the others only for a specific constraint.

  • Introducing Tailscale SSH
    summary

    TL;DR: Tailscale’s announcement of Tailscale SSH (beta, in all plans), which uses Tailscale node identity and ACLs to authorize SSH between devices so you no longer manage SSH keys.

    • How it works: With it enabled, Tailscale claims port 22 for traffic arriving on the device’s Tailscale IP and hands it to an SSH server inside the Tailscale daemon.
    • Auth: The connection is already authenticated by WireGuard node keys, so the server knows the remote party and asks the client for no further proof.
    • Policy: An "ssh" section in the tailnet ACL file defines who may connect to which hosts as which users.
    • Check mode: For high-risk access such as root, requires recent re-authentication with your SSO before the session starts.
    • Enable: tailscale up --ssh on the target device.
    • Scope: Only traffic over Tailscale is affected; the normal SSH server still handles other interfaces.

    Takeaway: Tailscale SSH removes key distribution and ties SSH access to SSO and ACLs. Use check mode for privileged users, and keep a non-Tailscale break-glass path.

  • Quamina: Optimizing Go Code for Speed
    summary

    TL;DR: Tim Bray’s Quamina diary entry on making his Go event-pattern-matching library faster, using a profiler, unit tests and a repeatable benchmark.

    • Method: Test, benchmark, refactor, iterate, with a profiler always at hand; he calls Go’s built-in profiler far better than what he used for Java and Ruby.
    • Benchmark data: The San Francisco Parcels JSON file, a couple of hundred thousand objects (~190 MB), with large arrays of 19-digit floats as a worst case.
    • Bottleneck: The JSON flattener used up to 90% of runtime, mostly in memory allocation, when built on Go’s json package.
    • Fix: A custom, non-general JSON tokenizer flattenJSON (about 750 lines of Go) built from state-machine mini-parsers that work on the input []byte without allocating.
    • Profiling: Uses go tool pprof -pdf -show_from flattenJSON cpu.prof (and mem.prof) to focus the call graph.
    • Open issue: storeArrayElementField stays expensive because it copies the array trail per field; he weighs segmented trails or pointer arrays against complexity and memory locality.

    Takeaway: In hot Go paths, allocation is often the cost; profile memory as well as CPU. Write a benchmark on realistic worst-case data before optimizing.

  • talos: Modern Linux Distribution Built for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Talos Linux by Sidero Labs is an open-source, minimal and immutable Linux distribution made only to run Kubernetes, managed entirely through an API.

    • No shell: There is no SSH, shell or interactive console; all system management goes through an API.
    • Security: Minimal, hardened and immutable, with all API access secured by mutual TLS.
    • Predictability: Immutable infrastructure removes configuration drift, and updates are atomic.
    • Currency: Aims to always ship current stable Kubernetes and Linux versions.
    • Support: Production-ready per the README, with commercial support from Sidero Labs, GitHub Discussions, Slack and monthly office hours.

    Takeaway: Talos suits teams who want cluster nodes they never log into and can rebuild from config. Plan for API-only debugging (talosctl) before migrating.

  • resoto: Cloud Inventory with Deep Visibility That Reacts to Infrastructure Changes
    summary

    TL;DR: Resoto from Some Engineering has been renamed Fix Inventory; the repo now redirects to someengineering/fixinventory. It is an open-source, agentless cloud inventory and security tool that stores resources in a graph.

    • Rename: The linked “resoto” cloud inventory project now presents itself as Fix Inventory, an open-source alternative to Orca, Prisma Cloud or Wiz.
    • Coverage: Over 300 cloud services across AWS, GCP, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Kubernetes and GitHub, plus an example collector for custom sources.
    • Pipeline: Collects metadata from cloud APIs, normalizes it into a graph schema (40+ “base kinds” such as database, ip_address), then scans it against compliance frameworks.
    • Graph queries: Dependency and access graph answers questions like blast radius of a public resource or paths to privileged roles.
    • History: Hourly snapshots by default, with a timeline and diff of configuration changes per resource.
    • Use cases: CSPM, compliance, CIEM, asset inventory, Kubernetes security and data export; SaaS or self-hosted.

    Takeaway: Useful for a free multi-cloud asset graph and posture checks. Note the rename when searching for docs, and check project activity before adopting.

  • aws-cost-saver: CLI Tool to Save Costs in Development Environments While You Sleep
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-cost-saver is a small Node.js CLI by Aram Alipoor that cuts AWS costs in development accounts by stopping or shrinking resources overnight (conserve) and putting them back later (restore).

    • Install and run: npm install -g aws-cost-saver, then aws-cost-saver conserve and aws-cost-saver restore; --dry-run, --no-state-file and --only-summary let you preview.
    • Targeting: --tag Team=Tacos (repeatable) limits actions to tagged resources.
    • Tricks: 10 actions, including shutting down EC2, stopping Fargate ECS services and RDS instances and clusters, removing NAT gateways, snapshot-and-remove ElastiCache, lowering DynamoDB RCU/WCU and Kinesis shards, and scaling down or suspending Auto Scaling groups.
    • State file: Original settings are saved to S3 or the local file system so restore can rebuild them.
    • Credentials: Uses the AWS SDK credential chain (env vars, then ~/.aws/credentials).
    • Warning: The README says it is meant only for development environments where stopping and removing resources is not risky.

    Takeaway: A quick way to stop paying for idle dev resources overnight. Run it with --dry-run first, and keep the state file safe or restore cannot rebuild removed NAT gateways and caches.

  • httploot: Crawl Sites, Fill Forms and Loot Secrets from Client-Facing Code
    summary

    TL;DR: HTTPLoot by RedHunt Labs is a Go tool (MIT, v0.1) that crawls many sites at once, fills and submits forms to trigger error and debug pages, and extracts secrets from client-facing code.

    • Inputs: A list of domains via -input-file, plus lootdb.json and regexes.json with the detection patterns; results go to CSV (httploot-results.csv).
    • Concurrency: -concurrency (sites at once, default 100) and -parallelism (URLs per site, default 15).
    • Crawling: -depth (default 3); -wildcard-crawl follows off-domain links and the README warns it can crawl forever.
    • Debug pages: -submit-forms auto-submits forms with -form-string or random values once a tech stack is identified, to provoke stack traces.
    • Network: -timeout, -user-agent and -verify-ssl flags.
    • Background: Based on RedHunt Labs research published as “The HTTP Facet” blog post.

    Takeaway: Useful in recon for finding keys leaked in JavaScript and debug pages across many hosts. Only run form submission against targets you are authorized to test.

  • socless: Serverless Security Orchestration, Automation and Response
    summary

    TL;DR: SOCless from Twilio Labs is a serverless framework for security teams to automate incident response and SOC workflows on AWS Step Functions and Lambda.

    • Playbooks: Workflows are JSON definitions triggered by real-time alerts or schedules.
    • Integrations: Existing security tools are orchestrated through Lambda functions in Python 3, packaged as reusable plugins.
    • Human in the loop: Workflows can ask people questions and adapt to their answers.
    • Networking: Provides a static IP address that can be allowlisted on internal resources.
    • Deployment: Infrastructure and playbooks deploy as code with the Serverless Framework; docs built with MkDocs.
    • Cost model: Serverless design for low cost and low operational overhead, per the README.

    Takeaway: A lightweight, code-first SOAR option for AWS-heavy teams. Check repository activity before building on it.

  • mirrord: Run Your Local Service in the Context of Its Cloud Environment by Mirroring Traffic
    summary

    TL;DR: mirrord, by MetalBear, runs a local process as if it were inside a live Kubernetes pod: traffic, file access and environment variables are routed through a chosen target pod, so you can test against real cluster services without deploying.

    • Interfaces: VS Code extension, IntelliJ plugin and CLI (mirrord exec ... --target pod/my-pod); uses your default kubeconfig.
    • Mechanism: Starts an agent pod on the target’s node that mirrors incoming traffic to your process and routes outgoing traffic, file reads/writes and env vars through the target.
    • Capabilities needed: CAP_NET_ADMIN (iptables redirection), CAP_SYS_PTRACE (access via /proc), CAP_SYS_ADMIN (join the network namespace); can be reduced with agent.disabled_capabilities.
    • Non-disruptive: Mirrors rather than steals traffic by default, so others using the cluster are not affected.
    • Current README: Now also pitches use by AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) and lists adopters such as monday.com and SurveyMonkey.
    • License: MIT.

    Takeaway: Shortens the dev loop for services that depend on many in-cluster dependencies. The agent needs privileged capabilities, so limit it to dev or staging clusters.

  • raspberry-pi-os: Learning Operating System Development Using Linux Kernel and Raspberry Pi
    summary

    TL;DR: A step-by-step course by GitHub user s-matyukevich on writing a simple OS kernel (RPi OS) from scratch for the Raspberry Pi, with each lesson comparing the feature to how the Linux kernel does it.

    • Approach: Each lesson first implements a feature in RPi OS, whose code is largely based on Linux, then walks through the matching Linux kernel code, followed by exercises.
    • Lessons 1-3: Kernel initialization (bare-metal “Hello, world”, Linux project structure, build system, startup), processor initialization, interrupt handling (exceptions, interrupt controllers, timers).
    • Lessons 4-6: Process scheduler, user processes and system calls, virtual memory management.
    • Unfinished: Lessons 7-11 (signals, file systems, ELF, drivers, networking) are still marked “To be done”.
    • Status: The README says the project is still under active development and invites contributions.

    Takeaway: A hands-on route into kernel internals that ties toy code to real Linux sources. Expect to stop at virtual memory, since later lessons were never written.

  • furiko: Cloud-Native, Enterprise-Level Cron Job Platform for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Furiko is an Apache 2.0, Kubernetes-native operator for scheduled (cron) and ad hoc jobs and workflows, aimed at enterprise use in self-hosted private clusters.

    • Scope: A general-purpose job platform covering cron jobs, batch jobs and ad hoc runs.
    • Design: Built as an operator for managing, scheduling and executing jobs, supporting many users across a large organization.
    • Docs: The README defers features and install steps to furiko.io.
    • Website gone: furiko.io now shows a parked “domain may be for sale” page, so the linked docs are unavailable.
    • Source caveat: The README is minimal; the feature list could not be read because the docs site is dead.

    Takeaway: Treat Furiko as likely unmaintained given the lapsed domain. For new cron platforms, check activity first or stay with native CronJobs or Argo Workflows.

  • robusta: Open Source Kubernetes Troubleshooting and Automation Platform
    summary

    TL;DR: Robusta (now “Robusta Classic”) is an open-source, rule-based Prometheus alert enrichment and automation engine for Kubernetes; AI root-cause analysis has moved to the separate HolmesGPT project.

    • Prometheus integration: Receives alerts by webhook; works with kube-prometheus-stack and Prometheus Operator, or without Prometheus.
    • Enrichment: Attaches pod logs and other context to alerts, and groups notifications into Slack threads.
    • Self-healing: Auto-remediation rules for alerts.
    • Detection without PromQL: Native alerts for OOMKills, failing Jobs and similar events, plus change tracking to correlate alerts with rollouts.
    • Routing and sinks: Route by team or namespace to Slack, MS Teams, Jira and dozens of others; can auto-resolve external tickets.
    • Change since 2022: The README now separates Classic from HolmesGPT and offers optional AI investigation.

    Takeaway: Useful for turning bare Prometheus alerts into actionable Slack messages with logs attached. Start with enrichment before enabling automatic remediation.

  • dashy: Self-Hostable Personal Dashboard
    summary

    TL;DR: Dashy by Alicia Sykes (Lissy93) is a self-hosted personal dashboard for homelab and self-hosted services, configured in YAML with a built-in UI editor.

    • Status checks: Real-time status monitoring for each app, link or host.
    • Widgets: Show live data from self-hosted services.
    • Navigation: Multiple pages, instant search by name, domain or tag, and custom hotkeys.
    • Look: Many themes, a color editor, custom CSS and icon sources (Font Awesome, homelab icons, favicons, images, emoji).
    • Auth: Optional multi-user authentication with privileges and SSO.
    • Extras: 30+ human-translated languages and optional encrypted off-site backup and sync.
    • Quick start: docker run -p 8080:8080 lissy93/dashy.

    Takeaway: A feature-rich start page for a homelab. Turn on authentication before exposing it, since it lists your internal services.

  • Debugging Kubernetes Pods: Deep Dive
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Better Programming (Medium) article from May 2022, about a 6-minute read, on debugging running pods with Kubernetes ephemeral containers.

    • Problem with exec: The app image may lack debugging tools, adding privileges can force pod restarts, and baking tools into the main image adds security risk.
    • Ephemeral containers: Attach to a running pod without a restart, sharing its network and process namespaces, volumes and node access.
    • Demo: Uses a kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.23 or later, where the feature was beta.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned a Cloudflare block; summary based on search-result descriptions of the article. Author name and exact commands were not confirmed.

    Takeaway: Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug) let you keep app images minimal and still debug them. Keep RBAC on the pods/ephemeralcontainers subresource tight.

  • ACK: AWS Controllers for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) is an open-source AWS project that lets you define and manage AWS service resources, such as databases and queues, as Kubernetes custom resources.

    • Model: A set of CRDs and custom controllers, one per AWS service API, so app dependencies live next to the app in the cluster.
    • Repos: The community repo is the hub; code is split into a common runtime, a code generator, test infrastructure and per-service controllers.
    • Maturity: Controllers go through maintenance phases; those in Preview are not recommended for production and fall under AWS beta service terms.
    • Purpose: Avoids defining resources outside the cluster or running stateful backing services inside it.

    Takeaway: ACK is the AWS-native alternative to Crossplane for managing AWS resources from Kubernetes. Check each controller’s maintenance phase before relying on it.

  • A Quick Path to Amazon EKS Single Sign-On Using AWS SSO
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog walkthrough for giving users single sign-on to EKS by combining AWS SSO (now IAM Identity Center) with Kubernetes RBAC through the aws-auth ConfigMap.

    • Prerequisites: AWS CLI v2 with admin credentials, eksctl, kubectl and jq.
    • What you build: An Organizations root and member account, AWS SSO with Twilio Authy for MFA, and an EKS cluster with a two-node managed node group.
    • Identities: A matrix of roles used during setup: admin IAM user, OrganizationAccountAccessRole, an EKSClusterCreator role, an EKSClusterAdminAccess SSO permission set and a Kubernetes ClusterAdmin role.
    • Mapping: eksctl create iamidentitymapping maps the SSO role to a Kubernetes group in aws-auth.
    • Usage: Users run aws sso login with a named profile and then use kubectl normally.
    • Benefit: Disabling one IdP account removes all cluster access, which simplifies offboarding and audits.

    Takeaway: Map SSO permission-set roles, not individual IAM users, into cluster RBAC. On current EKS, consider access entries instead of editing aws-auth.

  • Harden Amazon EKS in Minutes with Styra DAS Free and OPA
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers partner post showing how Styra DAS Free, a control plane for Open Policy Agent, installs OPA on EKS as validating and mutating admission control with ready-made policy packs.

    • Positioning: Presents policy-as-code as the next step after custom code, Pod Security Policies and OPA Gatekeeper, with more flexibility than built-in pod security admission.
    • Install: A couple of commands deploy OPA as both validating and mutating admission controller, so non-compliant workloads can be blocked or fixed.
    • Policy library: Over 100 built-in policies, including all 16 control aspects of a pod.
    • Packs: Prebuilt packs for MITRE ATT&CK, CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, PCI DSS 3.2 and PSP equivalents.
    • Workflow: GUI and CLI to validate existing clusters, test policies against local manifests and preview impact before enforcing; the post claims setup in about 15 minutes.
    • Trade-off: Acknowledges policy-as-code needs new skills such as Rego, which DAS aims to hide.

    Takeaway: A fast way to get baseline admission policies on EKS without writing Rego. Run new policies in monitor mode before enforcing them.

  • cdk-github-runners: CDK Constructs for Self-Hosted GitHub Actions Runners
    summary

    TL;DR: cdk-github-runners from CloudSnorkel is an AWS CDK construct that creates ephemeral, on-demand self-hosted GitHub Actions runners inside your own AWS account.

    • Providers: EC2, CodeBuild, Fargate, ECS and Lambda; each job gets a fresh runner started on demand, so you pay only while jobs run.
    • Limits by provider: Lambda caps jobs at 15 minutes and has no Docker or sudo; CodeBuild allows up to 36 hours (default 1 hour); EC2, ECS and Fargate have no time limit; Fargate has no Docker.
    • Options: x86_64 and ARM64 everywhere, GPU on EC2, CodeBuild and ECS, spot pricing on EC2, Fargate and ECS, Linux and Windows except Lambda.
    • Selection: Multiple runner configurations chosen by job labels, plus composite providers, custom provider selection and warm runners.
    • Setup: A web-based interface handles the GitHub app integration; a status Lambda (aws lambda invoke --function-name ...status...) helps troubleshooting.
    • Use cases: Access to internal resources, pre-installed software, basic AWS API access, and GitHub Enterprise Server.

    Takeaway: A good fit when Actions jobs need VPC access and you already use CDK. Pick the provider per label based on job length and Docker needs.

  • The CloudSec Engineer Book
    summary

    TL;DR: The CloudSec Engineer is a career book by Marco Lancini (CloudSecList author) on entering and progressing in cloud security engineering.

    • Part I: Choosing infosec and cloud security as a career, and career levels.
    • Parts II-IV: Skills, learning tips and expectations for entering the field, establishing yourself as a senior engineer, and thriving toward Staff+.
    • Part V: Choosing companies, finding jobs, interview preparation and managing offers.
    • Bonus: Templates for side projects, a brag document, reverse interview questions and offer tracking.
    • Format: DRM-free PDF and EPUB, 250+ pages, 1,100+ links, lifetime updates; no print edition.
    • Price: $18 book only, $26 complete package (discount codes listed on the page).

    Takeaway: Aimed at people planning a cloud security career path or preparing for interviews; the free newsletter gives a taste of the author’s style.

  • awesome-ios-security: Awesome iOS Security
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated awesome-list of iOS application security and penetration testing resources: tools, jailbreak tweaks, Frida scripts, courses, books, articles, labs and CTFs.

    • Reverse engineering: Hopper, Ghidra, Radare2, Cutter, and IPA decryptors such as frida-ios-dump, bagbak, flexdecrypt, bfdecrypt and r2flutch.
    • Analysis tools: Separate sections for static and dynamic analysis tools.
    • Tweaks: Reverse-engineering tweaks plus jailbreak-detection and SSL-pinning bypass tweaks.
    • Frida scripts: A dedicated section of ready-made scripts.
    • Learning: Courses, books, talks and workshops, articles on pentesting, RE, jailbreak and pinning bypass, checklists and cheatsheets.
    • Practice: Labs, CTFs and writeups.

    Takeaway: A starting index when preparing an iOS app assessment. Check tool compatibility, since many entries target specific older iOS and jailbreak versions.

  • sake: Task Runner for Local and Remote Hosts
    summary

    TL;DR: sake (by GitHub user alajmo) is an MIT-licensed task runner for local and remote hosts: you define servers and tasks in sake.yaml and run tasks across them over SSH.

    • Config: Servers, tags and tasks live in sake.yaml, and configs can import other sake.yaml files.
    • Run: sake run <task>, with --output table for a compact per-host table.
    • Access: sake ssh <server> into servers or Docker containers.
    • Discovery: sake list servers|tasks and shell auto-completion for tasks, servers and tags.
    • Editing: sake edit task <task> opens the definition in your editor.
    • Install: Linux and macOS via release binaries, install script, Homebrew (brew tap alajmo/sake) or MacPorts.

    Takeaway: A lighter alternative to Ansible ad-hoc commands for running the same scripts on a fleet. Good for ops runbooks that do not need full config management.

  • UTM: Free Virtual Machines for iOS and macOS, Works on M1
    summary

    TL;DR: UTM is a QEMU-based system emulator and virtual machine host for macOS, iOS and visionOS, used to run Windows, Linux and other systems on Macs including Apple Silicon.

    • Emulation: Full system emulation with QEMU, 30+ CPU architectures including x86_64, ARM64 and RISC-V, with JIT acceleration via QEMU TCG.
    • macOS virtualization: Hardware-accelerated virtualization via Hypervisor.framework, and macOS guests via Virtualization.framework.
    • Display and devices: SPICE/QXL VGA graphics, a text terminal mode and USB device passthrough.
    • iOS: JIT needs a jailbreak or version-specific workarounds; UTM SE (“slow edition”) uses a threaded interpreter instead, limited to ARM, PPC, RISC-V and x86.
    • Frontend: Native UI built for macOS 12+ and iOS 15+.

    Takeaway: On Apple Silicon, UTM is a free way to run ARM64 Linux or Windows VMs at near-native speed. x86 guests work but are fully emulated and slow.

  • Get More Out of Service Control Policies in a Multi-Account Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security blog post giving five techniques for working within AWS Organizations service control policy (SCP) limits in a multi-account setup.

    • Evaluation: An explicit Deny in any policy wins, and SCPs need an Allow before evaluation continues; SCPs set the maximum permissions for accounts.
    • Policies per entity: Spread SCPs across the hierarchy; OUs can nest up to five levels deep with different policies at each level.
    • Inheritance: Put broad guardrails high in the tree and specific ones lower.
    • Segment by workload: Group accounts with similar workloads into OUs that share guardrails.
    • Combine and compact: Merge statements; each SCP is limited to 5,120 bytes and, unlike IAM policies, whitespace counts, so remove it (the console does this automatically) or script it.
    • Wildcards: Use prefixes such as Disable* to combine actions, but the post warns new actions matching the wildcard will be denied automatically.

    Takeaway: Design your OU tree around SCP inheritance before you hit the size limit. Minify SCP JSON in your IaC pipeline and review wildcard denies when AWS adds actions.

  • kubectl-tree: kubectl Plugin to Browse Kubernetes Object Hierarchies as a Tree
    summary

    TL;DR: kubectl-tree by Ahmet Alp Balkan (ahmetb) is a kubectl plugin that shows ownership relationships between Kubernetes objects as a tree, based on ownerReferences.

    • Install: kubectl krew install tree, then e.g. kubectl tree deployment <name>.
    • Examples: Shows Deployment to ReplicaSet to Pod chains, and works with CRD-based objects such as Knative Services and Agones Fleets.
    • Scope: By default searches only the object’s namespace; -A searches all namespaces and cluster-scoped objects.
    • Filtering: -l label selectors (equality, set-based, existence) reduce load on large clusters.
    • Status: --condition-types sets which conditions to show (default Ready).
    • Alternative: The README points to kubectl lineage, which also understands logical relationships without ownerReferences.

    Takeaway: Handy for seeing what an operator or Helm release actually created and which child is not Ready. Install it alongside other krew plugins.

  • ggshield: Detect Secrets in Source Code and Prevent API Key Leaks
    summary

    TL;DR: ggshield is GitGuardian’s CLI for detecting 500+ types of hardcoded secrets locally or in CI, using the GitGuardian API.

    • Scan modes: ggshield secret scan path, repo, docker, pypi and pre-commit, among others.
    • Integration: Runs as a pre-commit hook, a GitHub Action or a CI step; the README now also covers AI coding assistant integrations.
    • API: Scans go through GitGuardian’s public API via py-gitguardian, so you need an account and API key (ggshield auth login).
    • Privacy: Only metadata such as call time, request size and scan mode is stored; files and secrets are not stored, per the README.
    • Install: Install script, Homebrew, .pkg, deb/rpm, Chocolatey, MSI, pipx or pip.
    • Note: A current README warning says upgrading to 1.54.0 on macOS triggers a Keychain prompt for a second binary, ggshield-py.

    Takeaway: A pre-commit hook is the cheapest place to stop secret leaks. Note that content is sent to GitGuardian’s API for scanning, which may matter for your policy.

  • Enumeration and Lateral Movement in GCP Environments
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: An InfoSec Write-ups pentest write-up about compromising a hybrid infrastructure hosted on Google Cloud, using native GCP tools for situational awareness and lateral movement.

    • Approach: Relies on built-in GCP tooling (such as gcloud) after an initial foothold, rather than custom malware.
    • Focus: Enumerating the GCP environment and moving laterally between resources.
    • Credits: Builds on earlier public work from GitLab’s red team and a Medium post by Tomasz W.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; summary based only on search-result descriptions. Specific commands and findings were not verified.

    Takeaway: Read alongside GitLab’s GCP red-team notes. Defensively, limit service account scopes on VMs and watch for unusual gcloud enumeration from workloads.

  • Awesome-Azure-Pentest: Awesome Azure Penetration Testing
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated awesome-list of tools and resources for penetration testing and securing Microsoft Azure, Azure AD (Entra ID) and Microsoft 365.

    • Structure: Tools split into enumeration, information gathering, lateral movement and exploitation (including credential attacks), then articles, labs, talks, books and tips.
    • Enumeration examples: o365creeper, cloud_enum, CloudBrute, BlobHunter, ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudFox, Monkey365, ROADtools, PowerZure, MicroBurst.
    • Azure AD graphing: Stormspotter, AzureADLateralMovement and SkyArk for privileged entities and attack paths.
    • Defensive tools: CISA’s Sparrow and ScubaGear, Hawk, and Microsoft’s Azure AD Assessment.
    • Practice: Includes lab exercises and talks.

    Takeaway: A good checklist of tools for an Azure or M365 engagement. Defenders can run the same enumeration tools against their own tenant first.
