  • Enabling AWS IAM Group Access to an EKS Cluster Using RBAC
    summary

    TL;DR: A Grip Security engineering post on giving an AWS IAM group access to EKS, which aws-auth cannot map directly, by mapping an assumable IAM role and assuming it on the fly only for kubectl.

    • Limitation: aws-auth supports mapAccounts, mapUsers and mapRoles, but not IAM groups; Grip wrote their own aws-auth format specification by reading the aws-iam-authenticator source.
    • Pattern: Create dev.eks-access.role with EKS permissions, map its ARN in mapRoles, and give the R&D group a policy allowing it to assume that role.
    • Friction removed: Instead of switching profiles, add --role-arn to the kubeconfig exec command (aws eks get-token --cluster-name ... --role-arn ..., also supported by update-kubeconfig).
    • Effect: Kubernetes calls use the assumed role while other AWS CLI calls keep the user’s own identity.
    • Background: Covers RBAC Roles, ClusterRoles and bindings and how aws-iam-authenticator maps IAM identities to Kubernetes users and groups.
    • Caveat: The authors suggest a stricter permission model for production.

    Takeaway: Use aws eks update-kubeconfig --role-arn so group membership controls cluster access. On current EKS, access entries are another way to manage this mapping.

  • DNS Toys: Useful Utilities and Toys over DNS
    summary

    TL;DR: dns.toys is a public DNS server that returns handy utilities as DNS answers, queried with dig.

    • Time and weather: dig mumbai.time @dns.toys, timezone conversion, and dig mumbai.weather @dns.toys.
    • Conversions: Units (dig 42km-mi.unit @dns.toys, 70+ units), currency at daily rates (100USD-INR.fx), number bases and Unix epochs.
    • Network helpers: IP echo (dig -4 ip @dns.toys) and CIDR first and last usable IP (dig 10.0.0.0/24.cidr @dns.toys).
    • Generators: UUIDs, NanoIDs, random numbers, dice, coin tosses, Pi digits.
    • Extras added since 2022: Dictionary, Sudoku solver, developer excuses, ISS location, Indian IFSC and DIGIPIN lookups.
    • Shortcut: alias dy="dig +short @dns.toys" in bash or zsh.

    Takeaway: A fun terminal shortcut, and ip and cidr are useful on boxes with only dig. Do not send anything sensitive in queries, since they go to a third-party server.

  • litmus: Practice Chaos Engineering the Cloud-Native Way
    summary

    TL;DR: LitmusChaos is a 100% open-source CNCF chaos engineering platform that defines faults, targets and steady-state checks as Kubernetes custom resources, managed from a central ChaosCenter.

    • Control plane: ChaosCenter builds, schedules and visualizes chaos workflows.
    • Execution plane: A chaos agent and operators run and monitor experiments in the target Kubernetes environment.
    • ChaosExperiment: Installable template describing a fault, its required permissions and defaults; supports bring-your-own-chaos.
    • ChaosEngine: Links a workload, node or infrastructure component to a fault, with tunables and “probes” for steady-state validation; reconciled by the Chaos-Operator.
    • ChaosResult: Holds the verdict, probe outcomes and revert status; the chaos-exporter publishes results as Prometheus metrics.
    • ChaosHub: Shared experiments are published at hub.litmuschaos.io; experiments can be chained in Workflows.

    Takeaway: Litmus fits teams that want chaos tests defined in Git next to their manifests. Start with pod-delete experiments in staging, with probes that encode your SLOs.

  • opencost: Cross-Cloud Cost Allocation Models for Kubernetes Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: OpenCost is an Apache 2.0 specification and Go implementation for monitoring Kubernetes and cloud costs, originally built and open-sourced by Kubecost. The repo now lives at opencost/opencost.

    • Allocation: Real-time cost by cluster, node, namespace, controller, service or pod, covering CPU, GPU, memory and persistent volumes.
    • Pricing: On-demand asset pricing via AWS, Azure and GCP billing APIs; on-prem clusters use custom CSV pricing.
    • Cloud costs: Multi-cloud monitoring of all cloud services, plus external costs such as Datadog through plugins.
    • Export: Prometheus /metrics endpoint for pricing data.
    • Newer features: Carbon costs, MCP support, and AI inference cost tracking for vLLM-based deployments (cost per million tokens).
    • Install: Helm only: helm repo add opencost https://opencost.github.io/opencost-helm-chart then helm install opencost opencost/opencost on Kubernetes 1.20+.

    Takeaway: A free baseline for showback per namespace or team. Label workloads consistently first, or the allocation will not map to owners.

  • security-study-plan: Complete Practical Study Plan to Become a Cybersecurity Engineer
    summary

    TL;DR: A GitHub repo by jassics with role-based study plans for becoming a cybersecurity engineer, each listing free and paid resources, tools and concepts.

    • Cloud: Separate plans for AWS, GCP and Azure security.
    • AppSec: Web pentesting, application security testing, API security, secure code review and secure SDLC.
    • Platform: DevSecOps, Docker, Kubernetes and software supply chain security.
    • Foundations: Common skills, network security, cryptography, threat modeling, GRC and security architecture.
    • Newer additions: GenAI security, product security, IAM, and blue team detection and response plans.
    • Status: 20 plans are marked done, with additional plans listed separately.

    Takeaway: Useful for building a learning path for a specific security role. Pick one plan and follow it end to end rather than sampling them all.

  • ifto: Simple Debugging Module for AWS Lambda Timeouts
    summary

    TL;DR: IFTO (“If Timeout”) is a small TypeScript module by rpgeeganage that buffers debug logs in AWS Lambda and flushes them only when the function is about to time out.

    • Problem: Task timed out after 2.00 seconds gives no clue where the time went; raising the timeout or always-on debug logging are poor fixes.
    • Mechanism: Watches context.getRemainingTimeInMillis() and flushes buffered logs to stdout when remaining time drops below a threshold.
    • Config: IFTO_START=true enables monitoring; IFTO_FLUSH_WHEN sets the threshold in milliseconds (default 50).
    • Usage: import 'Ifto' in the entry file creates a global logger that other files use without passing an object.
    • Docs: TypeScript API docs are published on GitHub Pages.

    Takeaway: A cheap trick for chasing intermittent Lambda timeouts without noisy logs on every run. Remove it once the slow call is found.

  • Trunk Check: Code Quality Checking
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Trunk Check was Trunk.io’s code quality tool that runs many linters and formatters through one CLI, IDE extension and CI integration. The product URL now redirects to Trunk’s home page, which promotes Merge Queue and flaky test tools.

    • Hold the line: Lints only new or changed lines by comparing your branch against upstream and reporting only issues introduced by the diff.
    • Mechanism: Runs linters on both versions (often cached) and diffs results at line level, so custom linters work without special support.
    • Override: Enabled by default for most linters, can be disabled per linter; trunk check --all scans the whole codebase.
    • CI: On pull requests, only new issues are flagged, using the same engine as the CLI and VS Code extension.
    • Current page: Shows merge queue, flaky test quarantine and CI acceleration, not Check; Trunk docs now cover it under “code quality”.
    • Source caveat: Based on Trunk docs and blog pages found by search, since the original product page no longer exists.

    Takeaway: The “hold the line” idea is the useful part: adopt linters on legacy code without fixing every old warning first. Check whether Trunk still offers the product before adopting.

  • Monitoring and Alerting Break-Glass Access in an AWS Organization
    summary

    TL;DR: A syndicated copy of an AWS Architecture blog post by Haresh Nandwani describing how Nationwide Building Society alerts on break-glass access across an AWS Organization using AWS SSO (now IAM Identity Center) and CloudTrail.

    • Context: A Control Tower landing zone with AWS SSO for workforce access in a regulated environment, where privileged access must be reported to operators and audit.
    • Option 1: Decentralized CloudFormation StackSets deploying EventBridge rules and Lambdas in each account, forwarding to an audit account and Slack.
    • Option 2 (chosen): The organization trail in the management account sent to CloudWatch Logs, with Lambda posting to Slack via webhooks (built with a public Terraform module).
    • Option 3 (rejected): Control Tower centralized logs, because they arrive as .gz JSON objects that must be expanded repeatedly.
    • Events watched: Console path Authenticate, ListApplications, ListApplicationProfiles, Federate; CLI path CreateToken, ListAccounts, ListAccountRoles, GetRoleCredentials.
    • Gotcha: EventBridge only triggers on events with readOnly false, so they used a CloudWatch Logs filter such as {($.eventSource = sso.amazonaws.com) && ($.eventName = Federate||$.eventName = GetRoleCredentials)}, later moving parsing into Lambda.
    • Token caveat: SSO tokens last 1 hour by default; GetRoleCredentials only fires when a token is first used against the target account.

    Takeaway: Alert on Federate and GetRoleCredentials for break-glass roles from the organization trail. Do not rely on EventBridge for read-only SSO events.

  • Securing Cloud Services Against Squatting Attacks
    summary

    TL;DR: Eric Pauley and Patrick McDaniel (May 2022) explain “cloud squatting” for IT practitioners: reused cloud IP addresses still referenced by old configuration let a new tenant receive another organization’s traffic and data.

    • Root cause: Public IPs released back to the provider are reassigned while latent configuration (DNS records, other services, hard-coded mobile app addresses) still points at them.
    • Research findings: Over 5,400 domains were vulnerable; they received real-time location data, PII and browsing data; leaks came via AWS SNS, Route 53, CloudFront and API Gateway, with SNS the most sensitive.
    • Opportunistic attack: Attackers do not need a target; they lease IPs, collect traffic and identify victims afterwards, bypassing perimeter monitoring.
    • Prevent IP reuse: Use private IPs inside the cloud, Bring Your Own IP, and IPv6 where possible.
    • Prevent latent config: Keep one authoritative source (DNS), audit zones regularly to confirm referenced IPs are still yours, and remove records when decommissioning.
    • Control trust: Authenticate services before sending data, and restrict certificate issuance with CAA records, since DNS-validated CAs will issue certificates to a squatter.
    • Provider table: Links AWS, GCP and Azure docs for private IPs, BYOIP and IPv6.

    Takeaway: Make DNS cleanup part of every decommission, and alert on records pointing at IPs you no longer own. Avoid public IPs for internal service-to-service traffic.

  • dockerfile: Dockerfile Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: A Hexops repository by @slimsag with a commented, production-ready Dockerfile template and the reasoning behind each practice, drawn from personal projects and work at Sourcegraph.

    • Moved: The repo now redirects to the hexops-graveyard organization, which suggests it is no longer maintained.
    • Non-root: Run as a non-root user to reduce container-to-host escalation risk.
    • UIDs: Use a static UID and GID, and not below 10,000, so an escape does not map onto a privileged host user.
    • Tags: Pin major.minor tags rather than latest; SHA pinning is reproducible but hides security fixes unless you automate updates (docker-lock suggested).
    • Init: Use tini as the ENTRYPOINT and keep only arguments in CMD.
    • DNS: Install bind-tools for DNS resolution on some older Docker versions.

    Takeaway: The non-root, high static UID and tini practices still hold. Copy the template as a checklist, but expect no updates.

  • The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Pod Security
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Pod Security”, a conference talk by Lachlan Evenson (Microsoft) on Kubernetes Pod Security admission, the built-in successor to PodSecurityPolicy.

    • Topic: Pod Security admission, beta as of Kubernetes v1.23, which checks pods against the predefined Pod Security Standards before admitting them.
    • Background: PodSecurityPolicy was deprecated in v1.21 and scheduled for removal in v1.25.
    • Levels: Three standards: Privileged, Baseline and Restricted.
    • Event: Listed in a Sysdig recap of KubeCon EU 2022; another listing mentions KubeCon NA 2022, so the exact event is unconfirmed.
    • Source caveat: The YouTube page returned only the title and speaker; details come from search results about the talk and Pod Security admission.

    Takeaway: Useful viewing for migrating off PSP. Label namespaces with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce, starting in warn or audit mode.

  • Terraform as Part of the Software Supply Chain, Part 1: Modules and Providers
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 1 of a GitLab security series by Joern Schneeweisz (June 2022) on Terraform supply chain risk, covering how providers and modules can be tampered with and how to defend.

    • Providers: They are executable binaries, so a malicious provider can do whatever the host allows; Terraform checks signatures on install.
    • Lock file hashes: .terraform.lock.hcl holds zh: (SHA256 of the provider zip) and h1: (a “dirhash” of the unpacked directory); multiple unrelated hashes per provider are allowed, which an attacker can abuse to accept a modified provider.
    • Lesson: Commit the lock file and review every change to it.
    • Modules: Unsigned; Registry modules resolve to Git tags with no content guarantee. Pinning a commit SHA helps, but some Git hosts let a branch be named like a commit hash.
    • Malicious module impact: local-exec runs commands on the Terraform host, and ANSI escape codes can hide its output in the terminal.
    • Other vector: References xssfox’s research on abusing provider source declarations such as an unqualified http = {}.

    Takeaway: Treat terraform init on untrusted modules as running untrusted code. Commit and review the lock file, and host vetted modules in a location you control.

  • batnoter: Open Source, Markdown-Based, Self-Hosted Note Taking Webapp
    summary

    TL;DR: BatNoter is an open-source, markdown-based note-taking web app that stores notes as files in your own GitHub repository. This repo is the React (TypeScript) frontend.

    • Login: Sign in with GitHub.
    • Storage: All notes are stored in the user’s GitHub repository, at the root or in nested folders, and cached to reduce API calls.
    • Editing: Markdown with links, tables, headings, code blocks and quotes, live preview, and copy-to-clipboard for code.
    • Navigation: Explore a whole directory with one click; note URLs can be bookmarked.
    • UI: Dark and light modes; built with React, Redux Toolkit and MUI.
    • Dev setup: Node.js 18+, npm install then npm start on localhost:3000.

    Takeaway: A simple way to keep notes in Git with a web UI. Check that a backend and project activity still exist before self-hosting.

  • How to Store an SSH Key on a Yubikey
    summary

    TL;DR: A short 2022 post by Xe Iaso showing how to keep an SSH private key on a YubiKey using OpenSSH 8.2+ FIDO keys, so the key cannot be copied off disk.

    • Requirement: OpenSSH 8.2 or later (February 2020) supports FIDO security key types.
    • Check the key: Install yubikey-manager and run ykman list; set a FIDO PIN first if none exists.
    • Generate: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident; fall back to ecdsa-sk if the hardware key cannot store the key.
    • Use: Load the resident key with ssh-add -K, list with ssh-add -L, and upload the public key to GitHub or servers.
    • Cleanup: Delete the local stub ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk so only the YubiKey holds the key.
    • Other keys: Should work with other FIDO keys such as Google Titan, but the author did not test them.

    Takeaway: Hardware-backed -sk keys are an easy upgrade from on-disk SSH keys. Register a second hardware key as a backup before relying on one.

  • ugit: Undo Git Commands, Your Damage Control Git Buddy
    summary

    TL;DR: ugit (also git-undo) by Bhupesh Varshney is a Bash script with an fzf menu that walks you through undoing 20+ common Git mistakes.

    • Supported undos: git commit, add, push, branch -D, pull, reset, tag -d, tag, merge, cherry-pick, and stash apply/pop/drop/clear.
    • File recovery: Restore a file deleted after a commit, or restore a file to a previous version.
    • Not yet: git rebase and git worktree remove are listed as work in progress.
    • Requirements: Bash 4.x or later and fzf 0.21.0 or later.
    • Purpose: Saves searching “how to undo …” and keeps focus on the task.

    Takeaway: Handy as a guided safety net, especially for less frequent Git users. Learn the reflog behind it for cases the menu does not cover.

  • Malcolm: Network Traffic Analysis Tool Suite for PCAP Files and Zeek Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: Malcolm, from CISA and Idaho National Laboratory (Battelle Energy Alliance), is an Apache 2.0 suite for analysing network traffic from PCAP files, Zeek logs and Suricata alerts.

    • Inputs: Upload artifacts through a browser interface or forward them passively from sensors.
    • Analysis UIs: OpenSearch Dashboards with dozens of prebuilt dashboards, and Arkime for finding and inspecting network sessions.
    • Deployment: Runs as a cluster of containers with a few setup scripts.
    • Security: UI and remote log forwarder traffic is encrypted.
    • ICS focus: Aims to give extra visibility into industrial control system protocols.
    • Licensing: Built from widely used open-source tools, as a free alternative to paid NSM products.

    Takeaway: A ready-made Zeek plus Suricata plus Arkime stack for incident response or OT monitoring. Plan for significant RAM and disk, since it runs OpenSearch.

  • Tailscale Tricks for Security Testers
    summary

    TL;DR: Pulse Security (May 2022) describes two Tailscale behaviours found during a client review that matter in security testing: bypassing inbound ACLs from a device you control, and leaking environment variables via the peer API.

    • Inbound-only ACLs: Tailscale ACLs and device filters apply only to inbound traffic, enforced on each node.
    • Reverse shell trick: On a compromised workstation, patch net/tstun/wrap.go to skip the inbound filter, rebuild tailscaled, and receive a reverse shell (e.g. via socat) from a server that the ACL only allowed you to reach.
    • Peer API: Each tailscaled runs a small HTTP API exempt from filtering; /v0/env returns the daemon’s environment to any node logged in as the same user.
    • Container risk: In Docker or Kubernetes, the daemon inherits container env vars, so secrets passed by env (example pulse_api_key) leak to same-user nodes.
    • Tailscale response: Recommends endpoint monitoring for modified clients and ACL tags for non-personal devices; tagged devices get a different user ID and are denied peer API access.
    • Status: Pulse says these are design consequences rather than new vulnerabilities, discussed with Tailscale before publishing.

    Takeaway: Tag servers and containers instead of logging them in as a person, and do not rely on Tailscale ACLs to block outbound connections from a device an attacker controls.

  • sshnoports: SSH to a Remote Linux Device Without Any Open Ports
    summary

    TL;DR: SSH No Ports from the Atsign Foundation, now branded NoPorts (repo atsign-foundation/noports), lets you SSH or tunnel to a device with no external listening ports, relaying through Atsign’s atPlatform.

    • Rename: The repo redirects to noports, with a product site at noports.com and docs at docs.noports.com.
    • Binaries: Dart CLI tools sshnp (client), sshnpd (device daemon), npt (port tunnel) and srvd (relay).
    • Implementations: Dart (core library noports_core), a C implementation, and a deprecated Python version (C recommended instead).
    • Desktop: NoPorts Desktop, a Flutter app (npt_flutter).
    • Open source: The README points auditors to the packages/ directory for the source.
    • Source caveat: The current README is mostly a code map; usage details are on the docs site, which was not fetched.

    Takeaway: An option for reaching IoT or home devices behind NAT without opening inbound ports. Review its trust model, since connections depend on the relay and atSign identities.

  • dragonfly: Modern Replacement for Redis and Memcached
    summary

    TL;DR: Dragonfly is an in-memory data store compatible with the Redis and Memcached APIs, built with a multi-threaded, shared-nothing design to use all cores of modern cloud machines.

    • Compatibility: Drop-in for Redis and Memcached clients with no code changes, per the README; it lists support for most Redis commands (to the Redis 5.0 API level) and Memcached commands.
    • Claims: Up to 25X more throughput than Redis and up to 80% fewer resources for the same workload, according to the project.
    • Benchmarks: On an m5.large, SET throughput is similar (Redis 159K vs Dragonfly 173K QPS); on c6gn.16xlarge Dragonfly passes 3.8M QPS, 25X a single Redis process. Tests use memtier_benchmark.
    • Design: Shared-nothing architecture partitions the keyspace across threads; the Dashtable data structure improves memory efficiency.
    • Source caveat: Benchmarks are vendor-run.

    Takeaway: Worth testing when a single Redis instance is CPU-bound and you want to scale up rather than cluster. Run your own benchmark with your access patterns and check its license terms first.

31.05.2022

  • Tailscale Authentication for NGINX
    summary

    TL;DR: A Tailscale blog post introducing nginx-auth, which uses NGINX’s HTTP subrequest (auth_request) protocol to authenticate requests to internal services by Tailscale identity.

    • Why: Earlier Grafana and Minecraft proxy tricks needed a new tailnet node per service; this reuses an existing NGINX setup for everything.
    • Install: sudo apt-get install tailscale-nginx-auth from Tailscale’s repos (x86_64 Debian/Ubuntu at the time), then sudo systemctl enable --now tailscale.nginx-auth.socket using socket activation.
    • NGINX config: An internal /auth location proxies to unix:/run/tailscale.nginx-auth.sock; service locations add auth_request /auth;.
    • Identity headers: auth_request_set captures Tailscale-User, -Name, -Login, -Tailnet and -Profile-Picture and forwards them, e.g. as X-Webauth-User for Grafana.
    • Scope: Configured per server block, so services on Tailscale and on the internet can use different auth.

    Takeaway: A simple way to put SSO-like identity in front of internal web apps without an extra login. Make sure the backend only trusts these headers from NGINX.

  • kube-no-trouble: Easily Check Your Clusters for Use of Deprecated APIs
    summary

    TL;DR: Kube No Trouble (kubent) by DoiT International scans a cluster and its manifests for deprecated or removed Kubernetes API versions, so you can fix workloads before a cluster upgrade.

    • Sources: Local YAML or JSON files, the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation, and Helm v3 release data stored in Secrets or ConfigMaps.
    • Target version: -t, --target-version sets the Kubernetes version to check against (autodetected by default).
    • CI use: -e, --exit-error returns non-zero when issues are found; JSON output allows checks like kubent -o json | jq -e 'length == 0'.
    • Install: sh -c "$(curl -sSL https://git.io/install-kubent)", or download a release binary; the README warns to read the script first.
    • Limit: It needs the original manifest stored somewhere, since the API server returns objects in the current version.
    • Origin: Created when Kubernetes 1.16 introduced major API deprecations.

    Takeaway: Run kubent against the target version before every minor cluster upgrade, and add it to CI for Helm charts.

  • How to Control Access to AWS Resources Based on AWS Account, OU, or Organization
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security blog post introducing the IAM condition keys aws:ResourceOrgID, aws:ResourceOrgPaths and aws:ResourceAccount, which restrict principals to resources inside your organization, OU or account.

    • New keys: aws:ResourceOrgID (single value, the resource’s organization ID), aws:ResourceOrgPaths (multi-value, the OU path) and aws:ResourceAccount (the owning account).
    • Main example: Deny S3 actions unless aws:ResourceOrgID matches your organization ID, so principals cannot write objects to buckets outside your organization.
    • Scope: Attach to individual IAM principals or apply broadly through SCPs; the rule holds regardless of other IAM or bucket policies.
    • Perimeter: Complements principal-side keys like aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:PrincipalOrgPaths to build data perimeters in both directions.
    • Caution: SCPs apply to whole accounts, so the post warns to plan exceptions some AWS services need to work.

    Takeaway: A resource-org SCP is a strong guard against data exfiltration to attacker-owned buckets. Test it in one OU first, since some AWS-owned resources are outside your organization.

  • Using AWS Load Balancer Controller for Blue/Green Deployment, Canary Deployment and A/B Testing
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers post showing how to do blue/green, canary and A/B testing on EKS with only the AWS Load Balancer Controller and ALB features, set through Kubernetes Ingress annotations.

    • Weighted target groups: Since November 2019, ALB listener rules can forward to several target groups with weights; weights of 8 and 2 split traffic 80/20.
    • Advanced routing: Rules can match HTTP headers and methods, path, query string and source IP, removing the need for a routing proxy fleet.
    • Blue/green and canary: An alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/actions.blue-green annotation with forwardConfig.targetGroups sets weights across hello-kubernetes-v1 and v2 Services.
    • A/B testing: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/conditions.ab-testing routes requests carrying a header such as HeaderName: HeaderValue1 to the new version.
    • Verification: Curl loops against the ALB hostname show the traffic split.
    • Alternative to: Flagger, service meshes or CI/CD-driven traffic shifting.

    Takeaway: For simple weighted rollouts on EKS you may not need a mesh. Pair the annotations with Argo Rollouts or Flagger if you want automated, metric-gated promotion.

  • Experience Report: 6 Months of Go
    summary

    TL;DR: The author of typesanitizer.com writes up six months of server-side Go at Sourcegraph, from a background in C++, Rust, Haskell and Swift. It is mostly critical of the language, tooling and ecosystem as a whole.

    • Positives: Very fast compile times, the built-in pprof profiler, a debugger that inspects variables reliably, GoLand, and the Playground with runnable examples.
    • Flow complaints: Compile errors for unused code interrupt work while experimenting.
    • Type system gaps: No sum types with exhaustive matching, no operator overloading for common operations, no standard set type, and no anonymous interface composition (with a later correction).
    • Naming: Short or misleading names in the standard library.
    • Tooling: go get behaviour and module tooling are confusing to him.
    • Framing: Disclaims negativity bias; a 2026 edit by the author says the 2022 wording was unnecessarily unkind but leaves the content unchanged.

    Takeaway: A detailed list of Go’s sharp edges from a type-system-focused developer. Useful for teams new to Go, and to weigh against Go’s fast builds and simple tooling.

  • Introducing SWIFT on Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: A 2022 Google Cloud blog post announcing reference implementations for running SWIFT components on Google Cloud, timed with SWIFT’s Alliance Connect Virtual for connecting to the SWIFT network from public cloud.

    • Context: SWIFT carries payment messages for banks, corporates and others in over 200 countries; traditionally it needs on-prem or co-location hardware or a third-party service bureau.
    • Alliance Connect Virtual: SWIFT’s product that turns its hardware VPN connectivity into virtual appliances in public cloud, with a phased launch through 2022.
    • Connectivity: The SWIFT VPN virtual appliance runs on Compute Engine with Cloud KMS as the trusted key store for FIPS 140-2 Level 2.
    • Data and HSM: Bare Metal Solution hosts the Alliance Message Hub (AMH) Oracle database; Hosted Private HSM meets SWIFT HSM requirements.
    • Timeline: Reference implementations expected GA later in 2022, alongside SWIFT’s GA.
    • Compliance: Aims to help customers meet SWIFT security requirements and attest CSP compliance.

    Takeaway: Relevant mainly to banks planning to move SWIFT connectivity off-premises. Check current GA status and SWIFT CSP control mappings before designing on it.

  • Disabling Security Hub Controls in a Multi-Account Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security blog post with a script and a scheduled alternative for disabling or enabling selected Security Hub controls across many accounts and Regions at once.

    • Superseded: A February 2024 note says Security Hub central configuration now covers many of these scenarios, reducing or removing the need for the scripts.
    • Why disable: Controls for unused services, controls on global resources (e.g. IAM.1 to IAM.7 in Regions other than where AWS Config records global resources), and controls with compensating controls.
    • Check types: Periodic checks run every 12 hours; change-triggered checks do not run without in-scope resources, so they need no disabling.
    • Ad hoc script: Assumes a cross-account role with securityhub:UpdateStandardsControl to update a --control-id-list across accounts and Regions; rerun for new accounts.
    • Scheduled option: Keeps member accounts in line with the Security Hub administrator account; needs an administrator setup and per-Region deployment.
    • Deployment: Execution role deployed org-wide with CloudFormation StackSets.

    Takeaway: Use Security Hub central configuration today. The list of reasons to disable controls is still a useful guide for noise reduction.

  • ChopChop: CLI to Scan Endpoints for Exposed Sensitive Services, Files and Folders
    summary

    TL;DR: ChopChop (gochopchop) is a Go CLI from the Michelin CERT for dynamic security testing of web apps: it scans many endpoints for exposed services, files and folders under the webroot.

    • Signatures: Checks are defined in a configurable YAML file (chopchop.yml by default), meant to be extended by developers.
    • Inputs: Scan one URL or a list via -u, --url-file; --threads sets concurrency.
    • CI gate: -b, --max-severity fails the pipeline when findings reach a given severity; --severity-filter and --plugin-filters (e.g. Git,Zimbra,Jenkins) narrow checks.
    • Output: --export=csv,json with --export-filename; plugins --severity High lists checks.
    • Build and run: go build ., or docker run ghcr.io/michelin/gochopchop scan https://foobar.com.
    • History: Started as a Python tool and was rewritten in Go.

    Takeaway: A lightweight CI check for exposed .git folders, admin panels and debug files on your own endpoints. Add signatures for your stack’s sensitive paths.

  • RFC 9116: A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure (security.txt)
    summary

    TL;DR: RFC 9116 (Informational, IETF, 2022) by E. Foudil and Y. Shafranovich defines security.txt, a machine-parsable file where organizations publish how researchers should report vulnerabilities.

    • Location: Served at /.well-known/security.txt over HTTPS.
    • Required fields: Contact (mailto, tel or https URI, e.g. Contact: mailto:security@example.com) and Expires.
    • Expiry: The RFC recommends Expires be less than a year in the future to avoid stale data.
    • Optional fields: Encryption, Acknowledgments, Preferred-Languages, Canonical, Policy and Hiring.
    • Signing: The file can be signed with an OpenPGP cleartext signature.
    • Motivation: Researchers often find vulnerabilities but lack a reporting channel, so issues go unreported.

    Takeaway: Publishing a security.txt takes minutes and gives researchers a clear path to you. Put the Expires renewal in a calendar or automation.

  • The Bug Hunter’s Methodology: Application Hacking v1
    summary

    TL;DR: Jason Haddix’s “The Bug Hunter’s Methodology: Application Hacking v1” slide deck (2022), which covers where to look for web bugs after recon: automation, content discovery and application analysis.

    • Getting started: Recommends practice labs (OWASP’s vulnerable apps directory with 180+ apps, Vulnhub with 400+) and a list of hacking content creators.
    • Pre-manual testing: Tech profiling (browser extensions, webanalyze), Nuclei for known CVEs and misconfigs (3,428 templates listed), plus other scanners such as Jaeles, Sn1per, Intrigue Core, Vulners and retire.js.
    • Content discovery: Technology-specific wordlists (wordlists.assetnote.io), historical URL lists (gau), endpoints from mobile apps (apkleaks), and monitoring targets for changes.
    • “Big 7” questions: How the app passes data, how it references users, multi-tenancy and roles, unique threat model, past vulnerabilities, and how it handles XSS, CSRF and injection.
    • Spidering and JS: Burp and ZAP spiders, GoSpider and hakrawler, xnLinkFinder and the GAP Burp extension for parameters and paths.
    • Heat mapping and parameters: Focus on risky features (uploads, exports, integrations, APIs) and statistically vulnerable parameter names via gf patterns, e.g. cat urls.txt | gf sqli.

    Takeaway: A practical checklist for web app testing beyond automated scanners. Use the Big 7 questions to plan manual testing time on each target.

  • poro: Scan Publicly Accessible Assets in Your AWS Cloud Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: poro is a small Python (boto3) script that finds publicly accessible assets in an AWS account and can check whether they carry a required tag.

    • Services covered: ELB, API Gateway, S3 buckets, RDS, EC2 and Redshift.
    • Tag check: --tag-key and --tag-value flag public resources that lack an expected tag (for example, an approved-public marker).
    • Usage: pip install -r requirements.txt, then python poro.py --profile PROFILE --export FILE_NAME --verbose.
    • Permissions: Needs only read-only access to the listed services.
    • Requirements: Python 3 with requests, boto3, botocore and enlighten.

    Takeaway: A quick way to list internet-facing resources across an account. Pair it with a tag convention so intentionally public assets are easy to tell apart.

  • Bidirectionally Integrate AWS Security Hub with Jira Software
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Prescriptive Guidance pattern by Joaquin Rinaudo for two-way sync between Security Hub (now “Security Hub CSPM”) findings and Jira tickets.

    • Automatic tickets: Choose which controls create or update Jira tickets; custom actions in the Security Hub console allow manual escalation.
    • Assignment: Tickets are assigned from a SecurityContactID tag on accounts in AWS Organizations, or a default assignee.
    • Sync back: Findings marked false positive or accepted risk in Jira are suppressed; archived findings close tickets; recurring findings reopen them.
    • Mechanics: A CloudWatch (EventBridge) event triggers a Lambda that checks the finding’s GeneratorId against its config and uses Jira credentials from Secrets Manager.
    • Workflow: A custom Jira workflow derived from Dinis Cruz’s SecDevOps Risk Workflow; the pattern suggests only security team members can change status.
    • Jira versions: Works with Jira Data Center and Jira Cloud, but Cloud cannot import XML workflows, so you re-create it by hand and use an API token.

    Takeaway: Route findings to the teams that own the accounts, and let accepted-risk decisions flow back to Security Hub. Restrict who can mark tickets as accepted risk.

  • Security Reference Architecture for a Serverless Application
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Anunay Bhatt describes security controls for a serverless app on AWS, using a demo vulnerability-management application, with a companion GitHub repo anunay-bhatt/secure-serverless-reference-architecture.

    • Demo app: REST APIs via API Gateway and Lambda, with data in DynamoDB and S3.
    • First control: Mutual TLS on API Gateway, with a root CA configured to validate client certificates, suited to clients in other clouds or on-premises.
    • Portability: The author says the same concepts apply to other public clouds.
    • Context: References common serverless patterns from the AWS Well-Architected Serverless Applications Lens (RESTful microservices, mobile backends, stream processing, web apps).
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; summary based on search-result descriptions. Controls beyond mTLS were not verified.

    Takeaway: Read with the companion repo for working examples. mTLS on API Gateway is a good option for machine-to-machine APIs from outside AWS.

  • AWS Security Maturity Model
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS Security Maturity Model (now v2) is a matrix of AWS security practices arranged by AWS CAF security capability and four phases: Quick Wins, Foundational, Efficient and Optimized.

    • Quick wins: Security contacts, region restriction, MFA, root account protection, detecting common threats, auditing API calls, billing alarms, block public access, WAF with managed rules, no secrets in code.
    • Foundational: Identity federation, SCP/RCP guardrails, temporary credentials, IMDSv2, CSPM, VPC segmentation, multi-account management, encryption at rest, backups, incident response playbooks.
    • Efficient: Least-privilege reviews, data perimeters, DevSecOps pipeline security, image pipelines, threat modeling, automated evidence gathering, VPC Flow Logs analysis.
    • Optimized: Temporary elevated access, custom threat detection (Security Lake or SIEM), red and blue teams, zero trust access, advanced automation.
    • Capabilities: Governance, assurance, IAM, threat detection, vulnerability management, infrastructure, data and application protection, incident response.
    • Format: Interactive web pages with an Excel export; newer items such as GenAI data protection appear in v2.

    Takeaway: Use it as a prioritized backlog: finish the Quick Wins column across all capabilities before starting the advanced items.

  • Securing AWS Lambda Function URLs
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz blog post on the attack surface created by AWS Lambda function URLs, the dedicated HTTPS endpoints AWS launched in 2022, and how misconfigured ones can be abused.

    • Feature context: Function URLs expose a Lambda directly without API Gateway or a load balancer, so they must be secured on their own; the post compares them to GCP HTTP functions and Azure HTTP triggers.
    • Attack preconditions: An attacker must find the URL, find it unauthenticated, and work out what arguments the function accepts; verbose error messages help them guess.
    • Impact: Data read or tampering, privilege escalation if the function does admin work, RCE in vulnerable code (cryptomining until the up-to-15-minute timeout), plus denial of service and denial of wallet.
    • DoS detail: Repeated invocation can fill the regional unreserved concurrency pool and block all of the account’s other functions in that region.
    • Discovery: URLs could be enumerated through passive DNS for *.lambda-url.*.on.aws; certificate transparency does not help because Lambda uses one wildcard certificate per region.
    • Related threat: Cites Denonia, malware built to run cryptominers in Lambda.

    Takeaway: Treat every function URL as an internet-facing endpoint. Require IAM auth unless it truly must be public, and inventory which functions have URLs enabled.

  • ssc-reading-list: Software Supply-Chain Security Reading List
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated, somewhat academic reading list on software supply-chain security from Chainguard.

    • Status: The repository was archived on Mar 22, 2024 and is read-only.
    • Policy section: NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF), NIST 800-161r1, Executive Order 14028, the September 2022 OMB memo, and NSA/CISA/ODNI developer guidance from August 2022.
    • Incidents and threats: Historical cases starting with kik, left-pad and npm.
    • Related lists: Points to chughes757/SecureSoftwareSupplyChain, bureado/awesome-software-supply-chain-security and meta-fun/awesome-software-supply-chain-security for wider coverage.
    • Focus: Leans toward papers and policy over tools, as the README says.

    Takeaway: A good starting bibliography for SSDF and SBOM background. Since it is frozen, use the linked awesome lists for anything after early 2024.

  • aztfy: Bring Existing Azure Resources Under Terraform’s Management
    summary

    TL;DR: Microsoft’s tool for bringing existing Azure resources under Terraform management. It is now called Azure Export for Terraform (aztfexport).

    • Rename: The Azure/aztfy URL now redirects to Azure/aztfexport.
    • Goal: Exports supported resources into Terraform state and generates matching configuration so that terraform plan shows no diff.
    • Providers: Supports both the AzureRM and AzAPI Terraform providers.
    • Non-goal: The generated configuration is not meant to be complete and does not guarantee the infrastructure can be fully rebuilt from it.
    • Install: Release binaries, a Windows MSI, or go install github.com/Azure/aztfexport@latest.

    Takeaway: Useful for adopting click-ops Azure estates into Terraform. Review and refactor the generated code before treating it as your source of truth.

  • korb: Move Kubernetes PVCs Between Storage Classes and Namespaces
    summary

    TL;DR: Korb is a CLI by Jens Langhammer (BeryJu) that moves data between Kubernetes PVCs, for example to change a StorageClass, namespace or name.

    • Install: brew tap beryju/tap && brew install korb, or a release binary.
    • Usage: korb [pvc [pvc]] [flags] with --new-pvc-storage-class, --new-pvc-namespace, --new-pvc-name, --new-pvc-size and --new-pvc-access-mode.
    • Mechanism: Runs mover jobs using the image ghcr.io/beryju/korb-mover:v2, configurable with --container-image.
    • Defaults: Empty options reuse the source PVC’s values, such as size, access mode and name.
    • Safety: Validation warnings stop the run unless you pass --force.

    Takeaway: Handy when a PVC needs to move to a new storage backend, which Kubernetes cannot change in place. Scale the workload down and back up the data first.

  • Administer AWS Single Sign-On from a Delegated Member Account in Your Organization
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (May 12, 2022) that AWS SSO, now IAM Identity Center, can be administered from a delegated member account instead of the Organizations management account.

    • What changed: Centralized administration and API access for all member accounts from an Organizations delegated administrator account.
    • Setup: Enable AWS SSO in the management account, then designate a member account in the AWS SSO console.
    • Delegated tasks: Admins in that account assign users and groups to applications and to member accounts.
    • No per-account work: No extra setup is needed in individual member accounts.
    • Rationale: Follows the AWS best practice of keeping day-to-day work out of the management account.

    Takeaway: Move identity administration to a dedicated security or identity account so fewer people need management-account access.

  • How to Use New Amazon GuardDuty EKS Protection Findings
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog walkthrough of GuardDuty EKS Protection, which analyzes Kubernetes audit logs to find threats in EKS clusters, and of how to read and respond to its findings.

    • Data source: GuardDuty pulls EKS audit logs itself, with no need to turn on EKS control plane logging, and needs no agents.
    • Detections: Access from known malicious IPs or Tor nodes, API calls by anonymous users, misconfigurations allowing unauthorized access, and ML-flagged privilege escalation such as a container launched with root access to the host.
    • Root-cause groups: Compromised images, configuration issues, Kubernetes user compromise, pod compromise and node compromise.
    • Finding details: Pod ID, container image ID and cluster tags, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics.
    • Rollout: Delegated administrators can enable it for existing and new member accounts; it is included in the 30-day GuardDuty trial.

    Takeaway: If you run EKS and GuardDuty, turn this on. Prepare runbooks for the anonymous-access and privileged-container findings first.

  • Building a Data Perimeter on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS whitepaper on building always-on permission guardrails, a “data perimeter”, around identities, resources and networks in an AWS Organization.

    • Core rule: Allow access only when the identity is trusted, the resource is trusted and the network is expected; otherwise deny.
    • Scope: Uses AWS Organizations as the boundary of “my AWS”, plus the on-premises networks that reach into it.
    • Purpose: Prevents unintended access and configuration errors, especially to data, as part of the customer’s side of the Shared Responsibility Model.
    • Versioning: The current page shows a publication date of June 13, 2023, so it has been revised since it was first linked in 2022.
    • Structure: Overview first, then perimeter objectives and the controls that enforce them.

    Takeaway: Use it as the design reference when writing SCPs, resource policies and VPC endpoint policies that keep data inside your organization.

  • ratchet: Secure CI/CD Workflows with Version Pinning
    summary

    TL;DR: Ratchet, by Seth Vargo, pins and unpins upstream versions in CI/CD workflow files to checksummed references, like a lockfile tool for pipelines.

    • Problem: CI references like actions/checkout@v4 or ubuntu:24.04 use mutable tags, which the README calls “one layer of indirection away from curl | sudo bash”.
    • Fix: Rewrites references to commit SHAs or image digests, such as ubuntu@sha256:..., and manages the update lifecycle.
    • Supported systems: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Google Cloud Build, Harness Drone and Tekton.
    • Distribution: Go CLI, Dockerfile and a GitHub Action (action.yml).
    • Caveat: The README tracks the main branch and may describe unreleased features.

    Takeaway: Run ratchet over your workflow files so third-party actions and images are immutable, then let it handle upgrades instead of editing SHAs by hand.

  • kubectl-ice: View Kubernetes Information About Multi-Container Pods and Sidecars
    summary

    TL;DR: kubectl-ice is a kubectl plugin that shows container-level configuration and metrics inside pods, which helps when debugging multi-container pods and sidecars.

    • Views: Volumes, images, ports, commands, securityContext and POSIX capabilities per container, including init and ephemeral containers.
    • Metrics: Current CPU and memory per container (requires metrics-server).
    • Tree view: Container to pod to ReplicaSet or StatefulSet, up to the node.
    • Safety: Uses only read permissions; standard kubectl selectors work.
    • Install: kubectl krew install ice, then run kubectl ice status, kubectl ice capabilities and so on.

    Takeaway: A quick way to see which sidecar in a pod is misconfigured or using resources, without reading raw YAML.

  • Announcing Policy Guardrails for Terraform on Google Cloud CLI Preview
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud announcement (May 19, 2022) of gcloud beta terraform vet, a free client-side tool that checks Terraform plans against organization policies before deployment.

    • Origin: Successor to the GitHub Terraform Validator, with migration instructions for existing users.
    • New capability: Policies can now target any resource in the google and google-beta providers, not only CAI-based constraints.
    • Policy format: Gatekeeper-style constraint templates and constraints, for example GCPIAMAllowedPolicyMemberDomainsConstraintV2 to restrict IAM members to gserviceaccount.com.
    • Workflow: Clone the policy library, add constraints under policies/constraints, generate a Terraform plan as JSON, then run the vet step.
    • Use cases: Platform teams gate CI between plan and apply, developers check locally, and security teams keep one central policy library.

    Takeaway: Put the vet step between terraform plan and apply in GCP pipelines so policy violations fail early with a clear message.

  • Flux from End-to-End
    summary

    TL;DR: Flux documentation that follows a commit through every Flux component in order, written partly as a starting point for security auditors.

    • Components: Source, Kustomize, Helm and Notification controllers, plus Image Reflector and Image Automation controllers.
    • Approach: Assumes a full installation with all optional features and describes each point where Flux talks to the cluster, Git, registries or external systems.
    • Terminology: Defines cluster, commit, resource, custom resource (GitRepository, Kustomization, HelmRelease and others), agent and service.
    • Updated: The page now says it was updated for Flux v2.7 and covers ArtifactGenerator for monorepo decomposition and composing Helm charts from multiple sources.
    • Limits: Not a full operational guide; it links out to feature docs.

    Takeaway: Read it to understand Flux’s data flow and trust boundaries before a security review or when debugging why a commit has not reconciled.

  • forgit: Utility Tool Powered by fzf for Using Git Interactively
    summary

    TL;DR: forgit is a shell plugin by wfxr that wraps common git commands in interactive fzf pickers.

    • Core commands: ga for interactive add, glo for the log viewer, gd for the diff viewer and gi for a .gitignore generator.
    • More commands: grh (reset HEAD file), gcf/gcb/gsw (checkout file or branch, switch), gbd (delete branch), gss/gsp (stash), grc (revert), gcp (cherry-pick) and others.
    • Shells: Plugin files for bash/zsh (forgit.plugin.sh, forgit.plugin.zsh), with a fish setup in conf.d.
    • Dependency: Requires junegunn/fzf.

    Takeaway: A low-friction upgrade to daily git use if you already have fzf, especially for staging hunks and browsing logs.

  • grype: Vulnerability Scanner for Container Images and Filesystems
    summary

    TL;DR: Grype, from Anchore, is an Apache-2.0 vulnerability scanner for container images, filesystems and SBOMs.

    • Targets: Docker, OCI and Singularity images, directories, and SBOMs such as grype sbom:./sbom.json or input piped from Syft.
    • Ecosystems: OS packages (Alpine, Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux) and language packages (Ruby, Java, JavaScript, Python, .NET, Go, PHP, Rust).
    • Prioritization: EPSS, KEV and risk scoring; OpenVEX support for filtering results.
    • Usage: grype alpine:latest, grype ./my-project, or grype --from containers-storage ... on Linux for Podman or Buildah images.
    • Install: curl -sSfL https://get.anchore.io/grype | sudo sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin, or Homebrew, Docker and others.

    Takeaway: Pair it with Syft: generate an SBOM once in CI, then rescan the SBOM quickly as new CVEs appear.

  • Cloud Native Maturity Model 2.0
    summary

    TL;DR: CNCF post (May 18, 2022) by Danielle Cook and Simon Forster announcing version 2.0 of the Cartografos Working Group’s Cloud Native Maturity Model.

    • Model shape: Five maturity levels, each covering people, process, policy and technology, broken out by theme.
    • New section: Business outcomes for CEOs, CFOs and boards, such as “scale to 1 million users”, “deliver exceptional customer experience” and “get features to market faster”.
    • Process: Six months of review with new contributors and with CNCF TAGs, to keep the model current.
    • History: The model was first launched at KubeCon NA 2021, alongside the book “Admiral Bash’s Island Adventure”.

    Takeaway: Use the model to place your organization on the five levels and to explain cloud-native work to business leadership in outcome terms.

  • tetragon: eBPF-Based Security Observability and Runtime Enforcement
    summary

    TL;DR: Tetragon is the Cilium project’s eBPF-based tool for security observability and runtime enforcement on Linux hosts and Kubernetes.

    • Events: Process execution and exit (process_exec, process_exit by default), system call activity, and file and network I/O.
    • Kubernetes-aware: Events are enriched with namespace and pod identity, so detection can be scoped per workload.
    • Generic tracing: process_kprobe, process_tracepoint and process_uprobe events, configured through TracingPolicy resources.
    • Use cases: Network observability, filename access, credential monitoring and privileged execution.
    • Tooling: Install guides for Kubernetes and plain Linux (Docker), plus the tetra CLI. Docs live at tetragon.io.
    • License: Apache 2.0 for user space, with BSD/GPL for eBPF code.

    Takeaway: Worth evaluating as a Falco-style runtime sensor if you already run Cilium. Start with process lifecycle events, then add TracingPolicies for sensitive files.

  • Track Costs with Detailed Billing Reports for Amazon EKS on AWS Fargate
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog walkthrough on using AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) to get pod-, namespace- and cluster-level costs for EKS on Fargate.

    • Problem: The billing dashboard only shows total GB-hours and vCPU-hours across all EKS Fargate clusters in a Region.
    • Step 1: Create a Cost and Usage Report that includes resource IDs.
    • Step 2: Store the reports in an S3 bucket, then query them to extract pod-level usage.
    • Use cases: Analyzing rollouts and peak-hour traffic, and allocating cost between teams.
    • Alternative: Mentions third-party tools such as Kubecost as the earlier common approach.

    Takeaway: If you run EKS on Fargate, turn on CUR with resource IDs early, because the native dashboard cannot attribute spend to teams.

  • Automate All the Boring Kubernetes Operations with Python
    summary

    TL;DR: Martin Heinz’s tutorial on automating Kubernetes tasks with the official Kubernetes Python client instead of bash and kubectl.

    • Playground: A KinD cluster with one control-plane node and three workers (kindest/node:v1.23.5).
    • Auth: A long-lived ServiceAccount token, plus a ClusterRole and RoleBinding to grant pod permissions.
    • Under the hood: kubectl get pods -v 10 reveals the raw curl calls, which are then replayed with a Bearer token.
    • Client library: pip install kubernetes, then the same operations through the Python API.
    • Least privilege: Recommends narrow roles and uses cluster-admin only inside the KinD playground.

    Takeaway: When a shell script of kubectl calls grows unwieldy, move it to the Python client. The -v 10 trick shows the exact API calls to reproduce.

  • The Differences Between Docker, containerd, CRI-O and runc
    summary

    TL;DR: Tutorial Works explainer that untangles Docker, containerd, CRI-O, runc, OCI and CRI and shows how they stack.

    • Standards: OCI defines the image format, runtime and distribution; CRI is the Kubernetes API for plugging in container runtimes.
    • Docker stack: The docker CLI talks to dockerd, which calls containerd, which uses runc.
    • runc: The low-level OCI runtime that uses Linux features to create containers; it includes libcontainer.
    • containerd and CRI-O: High-level runtimes that handle images, storage and networking; Kubernetes can use either directly.
    • Context: Prompted by the confusion around the Kubernetes dockershim deprecation; quotes Joe Beda on “so many things called docker”.

    Takeaway: Docker is one developer tool on top of shared standards. Removing dockershim does not break OCI images, which still run on containerd or CRI-O.

  • Announcing the HCL Extension for Visual Studio Code 0.1
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp announcement (May 23, 2022) that it adopted the community HCL extension for VS Code, first written by William Holroyd in 2016, and released it as an official project.

    • Features: HCL v2 syntax highlighting, including grammar for expressions and type constraints; files ending in .hcl are highlighted automatically.
    • Audience: Users of HCL-based products such as Packer and Nomad, alongside Terraform.
    • Relation to Terraform extension: Separate from the Terraform extension and language server; both share TextMate grammars in hashicorp/syntax.
    • Upgrade: Users of the original author’s extension get the HashiCorp version automatically.
    • Source caveat: Direct curl was blocked by a bot check; summary is based on WebFetch of the page.

    Takeaway: Install it if you edit Packer or Nomad HCL in VS Code. It is a highlighter, not a language server.

  • Terraform Best Practices for Better Infrastructure Management
    summary

    TL;DR: Spacelift article (May 15, 2022) by Ioannis Moustakis listing Terraform practices for structuring and running infrastructure code well.

    • State: Use a remote backend with locking, never edit state by hand, and keep backups such as S3 versioning.
    • Reuse: Prefer Terraform Registry and community modules, and import resources that were created by hand.
    • Hygiene: No hard-coded values (use variables or data sources like aws_caller_identity), run terraform fmt and terraform validate in CI or pre-commit, and use consistent naming.
    • Tags and policy: Tag resources consistently (with provider default_tags where available) and enforce rules with policy as code.
    • Secrets: Never commit plaintext; use TF_VAR_ env vars with sensitive = true, or Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.
    • Testing and tools: Use plan, static analysis and integration tests; debug with TF_LOG=DEBUG; tools mentioned include tflint, tfenv, checkov, terratest, terraform-docs and atlantis.
    • Source caveat: medium.com blocked direct fetch; summary is based on a Freedium mirror of the Medium copy, which links to the full post on spacelift.io.

    Takeaway: A solid checklist for reviewing a Terraform repo. Remote state with locking and fmt/validate in CI are the first two to fix.

  • Secure Your Docker Images with Cosign (and OPA Gatekeeper)
    summary

    TL;DR: Justin Polidori’s walkthrough of signing container images with Cosign in a Tekton pipeline and verifying them at admission time with OPA Gatekeeper.

    • Keys: cosign generate-key-pair.
    • Sign: cosign sign --key cosign.key my-registry/my-image:1.0.0; add annotations such as build time or user with -a.
    • Verify: cosign verify --key cosign.pub ... checks claims and signatures against the public key.
    • CI integration: A Tekton ClusterTask that uses gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign:v1.4.1 to sign the image just before Argo CD deploys it.
    • Enforcement: Gatekeeper blocks pods whose images have a missing or wrong signature.

    Takeaway: Shows the full sign-in-CI, verify-at-admission loop. Check the pinned Cosign version (v1.4.1), since Cosign’s CLI has changed a lot since then.

07.05.2022

  • gh-dash: GitHub CLI Extension to Display a Dashboard of PRs and Issues
    summary

    TL;DR: gh-dash (DASH) is a GitHub CLI extension by Dolev Hadar that gives you a terminal UI dashboard for PRs and issues.

    • Sections: User-defined PR and issue sections, which can be set per repository.
    • Actions: Diff, comment, checkout, push and update from the TUI, plus custom actions.
    • Config: One YAML file controls everything; vim-style hotkeys can be overridden.
    • Stack: Bubble Tea, Lip Gloss, Glamour and Cobra, with gh for GitHub calls and delta for diffs.
    • Adoption: MIT-licensed, about 12.7k stars at the time of fetching; docs at gh-dash.dev.

    Takeaway: A good fit for reviewing many repos from the terminal. Define sections like “needs my review” to replace GitHub notification triage.

  • GitOps Article Series from Giant Swarm
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The GitOps topic page of Giant Swarm’s blog, which collects the company’s articles on GitOps for Kubernetes platforms.

    • Current content: The page now shows recent posts, such as a June 2026 series on configuration management at Giant Swarm, edge infrastructure, and Grafana persistence with PostgreSQL.
    • 2022 series: The GitOps article series this link pointed to in 2022 is no longer on the first page.
    • Context: Giant Swarm runs managed Kubernetes platforms; its blog topics include Cluster API, platform engineering and observability.
    • Source caveat: Fetched the live topic index only; the 2022 series it was saved for could not be identified on it.

    Takeaway: Browse the archive for Giant Swarm’s GitOps posts. The configuration-management history series is the most relevant current entry.

  • dagger: Portable Devkit for CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: Dagger is a programmable engine for building, testing and shipping code that runs the same way locally, in CI or in the cloud.

    • Model: Tools run in containers, orchestrated by sandboxed functions; the only host dependency is a container runtime.
    • SDKs: Eight languages: Go, Python, TypeScript, PHP, Java, .NET, Elixir and Rust, all generated from one API schema.
    • Caching: Every operation is keyed by its inputs, so only affected steps re-run; caching is content-addressed across local and CI runs.
    • Observability: Each operation emits an OpenTelemetry trace that can be viewed in the terminal or a web UI.
    • Changed scope: Linked in 2022 as a “portable devkit for CI/CD”; the current README describes a broader platform with reusable modules and an interactive REPL.
    • Install: brew install dagger/tap/dagger.

    Takeaway: Consider it when CI YAML has become untestable. Pipeline logic in real code that runs locally makes debugging much faster.

  • Automated Dependency Updates for Flux Using Renovate
    summary

    TL;DR: Renovate documentation for its Flux manager, which opens automated PRs to update Flux components and Helm charts referenced in Flux manifests.

    • Default file match: /(?:^|/)gotk-components\.ya?ml$/; extend managerFilePatterns to cover HelmRelease and source files.
    • Datasources: bitbucket-tags, docker, git-refs, git-tags, github-releases, github-tags, gitlab-tags and helm.
    • Dep type: HelmChart from HelmRelease or HelmChart resources, or an OCIRepository that selects a chart layer.
    • Parsing: Reads Flux YAML resources such as HelmRelease and their referenced sources.
    • Page state: The live page also carries notices about Renovate 44’s version numbering.

    Takeaway: Add the Flux manager with file patterns for your HelmRelease directories so chart bumps arrive as reviewable PRs instead of drifting.

  • Terraform: Up & Running, 3rd Edition Early Release Is Now Available
    summary

    TL;DR: Yevgeniy Brikman (Gruntwork) announces the early release of Terraform: Up & Running, 3rd edition (April 7, 2022) and previews the Terraform problems fixed since the 2nd edition.

    • Scale of changes: Six Terraform releases since 2019 (0.13 to 1.2) and AWS provider versions 2.0 to 4.0; about 100 new pages, including two new chapters.
    • Part 1 topics: Multiple regions, accounts and clouds; provider versioning with required_providers and the lock file; secrets management (Vault, KMS and others).
    • More topics: CI/CD security using OIDC and isolated workers, and module iteration with count and for_each on module blocks.
    • Update: A note at the top says the final 3rd edition was published September 28, 2022.
    • Format: The first of a two-part series covering 10 problems in total.

    Takeaway: A useful changelog of Terraform best practices from 2019 to 2022. Get the final 3rd edition rather than the early release.

  • flamingo: Visualize Flux with Argo CD
    summary

    TL;DR: Flamingo, the Flux Subsystem for Argo (FSA), is a drop-in Argo CD image that lets the Argo CD UI show and manage Flux workloads.

    • Mechanism: “Loopback Reconciliation”: with the FluxSubsystem feature enabled, Flamingo converts Argo CD Applications into Flux Kustomization or HelmRelease objects plus sources.
    • Benefits claimed: Flux’s Helm and OCIRepository support and Weave GitOps tools inside the Argo CD UI, plus Argo CD ApplicationSets for Flux-managed resources.
    • Security: Says upstream Argo CD CVEs are backported quickly.
    • CLI: A new Flamingo CLI is announced.
    • Status: The README says the project is looking for sponsorship to continue.

    Takeaway: Useful if your team wants Argo CD’s UI but Flux’s reconciliation. Check its maintenance status before relying on it in production.

  • Announcing AWS Lambda Function URLs: Built-in HTTPS Endpoints for Single-Function Microservices
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS News Blog launch post (2022) for Lambda Function URLs, built-in HTTPS endpoints for single functions that need no API Gateway or ALB.

    • Use cases: Webhook handlers, form validators and other single-function services.
    • Mapping: Each URL is globally unique and points at an alias or the unqualified ARN, which invokes $LATEST.
    • Recommendation: Map URLs to an alias so you can test new versions, shift traffic gradually and deploy safely.
    • CORS: Optional CORS header configuration.
    • Tooling: Available in the console, SDKs, CloudFormation, SAM and other IaC tools.

    Takeaway: Fine for simple endpoints, but read the Wiz post alongside it: choose IAM auth or explicit public access on purpose, and bind URLs to aliases.

  • Cado Discovers Denonia: The First Malware Specifically Targeting Lambda
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Cado Security’s April 2022 report on Denonia, described as the first malware built specifically to run in AWS Lambda.

    • Sample: A 64-bit Go ELF named “python”, uploaded to VirusTotal on February 25, 2022; a January sample was also reported.
    • Payload: A customized XMRig Monero miner that runs from memory and uses /tmp, the only writable path in Lambda, and connects to a pool on port 3333.
    • Evasion: Resolves its C2 domain over DNS-over-HTTPS through Google, which avoids plain DNS monitoring.
    • Environment check: Looks for Lambda environment variables but can also run on ordinary Linux.
    • Access vector: Unknown; Cado suspected stolen AWS access keys. AWS said the malware exploits no weakness in Lambda.
    • Source caveat: The URL now redirects to a Darktrace forensics page (Cado was acquired); summary is based on coverage in The Hacker News and TechRepublic found by web search.

    Takeaway: Serverless does not mean safe from malware. Protect Lambda deploy permissions and keys, and watch for unusual DoH or mining traffic.

  • Incident Report: From CLI to Console, Chasing an Attacker in AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: Expel SOC incident report (April 5, 2022) on an attacker who used a leaked long-term access key to escalate through IAM in a customer’s AWS account and was stopped before going further.

    • Initial lead: A CloudTrail-based alert for a console login by an IAM user from Indonesia, an unusual location, without MFA.
    • Escalation: The same IP called CreateUser, CreateAccessKey and AttachUserPolicy to set up persistent admin access, creating two new users with keys.
    • Pivot: The attacker first ran ListUsers from the aws-cli as a different IAM user, showing a second compromised identity.
    • Tooling: Expel’s bot “Ruxie” listed non-read API calls (not Get/List/Describe/Head) and the user’s usual login regions.
    • Telemetry: CloudTrail only; GuardDuty was not enabled.
    • Tip: Console sessions get temporary ASIA... keys, unlike long-term AKIA... keys.

    Takeaway: Alert on IAM user creation, access key creation and policy attachment. Remove long-term access keys and require MFA.

  • container.training: Slides and Code Samples for Docker, Containers and Kubernetes Workshops
    summary

    TL;DR: Jérôme Petazzoni’s repository of slides, scripts and demo apps for Docker, Swarm and Kubernetes workshops, published at container.training.

    • Courses: Introduction to Docker and Containers, Container Orchestration with Docker Swarm, and Container Orchestration with Kubernetes.
    • Design: Assumes little prior knowledge, works in a classroom or self-paced, and is hands-on with progressive chapters.
    • Tooling: Markdown slides built to HTML, a semi-automated test harness for exercises, and scripts to start training VMs in bulk.
    • Hosting: Continuously deployed through Netlify to container.training.
    • History: Formerly “orchestration-workshop”; the Swarm workshop started in June 2015.

    Takeaway: One of the best free, hands-on Kubernetes courses. Use the slides directly, or fork the repo to run your own training.

  • git-credential-manager: Secure, Cross-Platform Git Credential Storage
    summary

    TL;DR: Git Credential Manager (GCM) is a cross-platform .NET Git credential helper that adds secure storage and MFA-capable sign-in for major Git hosts.

    • Hosts: Azure DevOps and Azure DevOps Server, Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center, GitHub and GHES, and GitLab.
    • Versus built-ins: wincred, osxkeychain and libsecret handle only username and password; GCM adds OAuth, Entra with broker support, and Windows Integrated Auth.
    • Platforms: Windows, macOS and Linux on x64 and ARM64; HTTPS remotes only, not SSH.
    • Lineage: Replaces the .NET Framework GCM for Windows and the Java GCM for Mac and Linux.
    • Caveat: Intel Mac support is best effort.

    Takeaway: Use it on HTTPS remotes to avoid storing plain personal access tokens and to get browser-based SSO and MFA.

  • cicd-goat: Deliberately Vulnerable CI/CD Environment for Learning CI/CD Security
    summary

    TL;DR: CI/CD Goat, by Cider Security (later acquired by Palo Alto Networks), is a deliberately vulnerable CI/CD lab with 11 capture-the-flag challenges.

    • Coverage: Maps to the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks, such as insufficient flow control, poisoned pipeline execution (PPE), dependency chain abuse and pipeline-based access controls.
    • Stack: Docker containers for Gitea, Jenkins and an agent, GitLab and a runner, LocalStack, a Prod container (Docker-in-Docker with Lighttpd) and CTFd.
    • Run: Download docker-compose.yaml, then docker compose up -d; Windows needs bridge replaced with nat.
    • Theme: Each challenge is an Alice in Wonderland character; flags look like flag2.
    • Spoilers: The repo files contain solutions, so the README warns against browsing them.

    Takeaway: A practical way to teach engineers how pipeline attacks like PPE work. Run it locally in a team workshop.

  • Introducing AWS Blueprints for Crossplane
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Open Source Blog post introducing AWS Blueprints for Crossplane, reference Compositions for provisioning AWS infrastructure from Kubernetes in a GitOps style.

    • Crossplane: CNCF, Apache-2.0 project that extends the Kubernetes API to provision and manage cloud resources.
    • Compositions: Opinionated templates that enforce organization rules, such as required tags on every AWS resource or specific KMS keys for S3 buckets.
    • Pattern: Git is the source of truth and controllers reconcile the resources it describes.
    • Related: Mentions AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) as another way to manage AWS resources from Kubernetes.
    • Audience: Platform teams offering self-service infrastructure APIs to application teams.

    Takeaway: Start from these blueprints if you plan Crossplane on AWS, and add your guardrails to the Compositions rather than to each claim.

  • Migrating from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter
    summary

    TL;DR: Karpenter’s official guide to replacing the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler with Karpenter on an existing EKS cluster.

    • Assumptions: Existing EKS cluster, VPC, subnets, security groups and node groups; PDBs in place; an OIDC provider for service accounts.
    • Variables: Gathers the cluster name, Region, OIDC endpoint, account ID, Kubernetes version and AL2023 AMI alias with aws CLI calls.
    • IAM: Creates a Karpenter node role and a controller role with an inline policy and trust relationship.
    • Goal: Switch automatic node provisioning from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter while reusing existing networking.
    • Versioning: The preview URL tracks current Karpenter docs (now AL2023-based), not the 2022 version.

    Takeaway: Follow it step by step for a CAS-to-Karpenter switch. Pin the doc version that matches your Karpenter release.

  • Argo CD Best Practices You Should Know
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Datree article (2022) listing Argo best practices to prevent misconfigurations across Argo Workflows, Argo CD and Argo Rollouts.

    • Workflows retries: Reject an empty retryStrategy, which can retry a container until it runs out of memory.
    • Service accounts: Do not run Workflow pods under the default service account, which gives a compromised container access to the Kubernetes API.
    • Scope: About ten items in total; it was republished on opensource.com as “10 Argo CD best practices I follow” and mirrored on learncloudnative.com.
    • Context: Datree was a Kubernetes policy-check tool, and the article ties these checks to its policies.
    • Source caveat: The datree.io page returned no content (the page body is empty now); summary is based on web-search snippets of the article and its republished copies.

    Takeaway: Read the opensource.com copy for the full list, and enforce the rules with any admission or policy tool.

  • Security List: Curated Tools, Tips and Resources for Digital Security and Privacy
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Security List is Lissy93’s curated site of tools, tips and resources for personal digital security and privacy.

    • Current state: The page only shows “New version available! digital-defense.io”, so the project has moved.
    • Successor: digital-defense.io hosts the Personal Security Checklist, with lists you can filter by threat model and tick off.
    • Related repo: github.com/Lissy93/personal-security-checklist, which offers the data as YAML, a website, a Docker image and a free API.
    • Source caveat: The old site is a client-side app with a redirect notice; summary is based on that notice and the successor repo’s README.

    Takeaway: Update the bookmark to digital-defense.io and use its threat-model filter rather than reading every list.

  • Android App Hacking Workshop from Google
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Google Bug Hunters’ hands-on Android app hacking workshop: slides, materials and a custom vulnerable app with CTF challenges.

    • Origin: Run by Google with HackerOne and PayPal for researchers and students, in person and virtually; announced on the Google Security Blog on Dec 14, 2021.
    • Materials: Slide deck, workshop materials and source code for a custom Android app with capture-the-flag challenges; solutions are available as hints.
    • Later edition: A 240-minute version, “Android App Hacking - Hacking for Good!”, ran at DEF CON 31 (Aug 2023) for beginner-to-intermediate learners and ended with a reverse-engineering CTF.
    • Page note: The page description points to a separate Android learning page for more resources.
    • Source caveat: The page renders client-side and only its meta description was retrievable; details come from the Google Security Blog and DEF CON listings found by web search.

    Takeaway: A good free entry point into Android bug bounty work. Do the CTF app before moving on to real Play Store targets.

  • docker-slim: Generate Smaller Container Images
    summary

    TL;DR: DockerSlim, now renamed SlimToolkit (“Slim”) and a CNCF Sandbox project, makes container images smaller and more secure without changing your Dockerfile.

    • Rename: The docker-slim/docker-slim URL now redirects to slimtoolkit/slim.
    • Claim: Minifies images by up to 30x by analyzing what the application actually uses.
    • Commands: xray, lint, build, debug, run, images, merge, registry and vulnerability.
    • Security profiles: Generates Seccomp and AppArmor profiles automatically.
    • Backing: Created by Kyle Quest; supported by Root.io (formerly Slim.AI), which the README promotes for vulnerability remediation.

    Takeaway: Try slim build on a large image and compare. Test the minified image well, since dynamically loaded files can be stripped out.

  • parca: Continuous Profiling for Analysis of CPU and Memory Usage
    summary

    TL;DR: Parca is an open-source continuous profiler for CPU and memory usage over time, down to the line number, built on an eBPF agent and pprof.

    • eBPF profiler: One agent finds targets from Kubernetes or systemd automatically, needs no instrumentation and has low overhead; supports C, C++, Rust, Go and more.
    • Open formats: Produces and ingests pprof profiles.
    • Storage and query: Keeps raw data, with label-based search to slice and compare profiles by deploy, version or region.
    • Rationale: The README says many organizations waste 20-30% of resources on easily optimized code paths.
    • Use cases: Cost savings, hot-path optimization, and debugging memory leaks or CPU and I/O spikes.

    Takeaway: Run the Parca agent cluster-wide to find your most expensive code paths without changing any application code.

  • How to Get Started with OrgFormation: Managing AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: Michael Bahr’s guide (Feb 7, 2022) to managing AWS Organizations as code with OrgFormation, presented as a lighter alternative to Control Tower for small setups.

    • Model: Accounts, OUs, budgets, SCPs and SSO defined in YAML (organization.yml plus numbered task folders) and applied by CodePipeline on push.
    • Bootstrap: npm install -g aws-organization-formation, then org-formation init-pipeline --region <region>, which creates a CodeCommit repo and pipeline.
    • Patterns: Account tags such as budget-alarm-threshold drive budget alerts; OrgFormation custom CloudFormation types assign SSO groups.
    • Caveats: Account deletion is slow (7 days before suspension, then about 90 days), Cost Explorer must be launched first, budgets are USD only, and root emails must be unique.
    • Manual steps: Enabling SSO and creating its users and groups stay manual; request an account limit above the default 10 early.
    • URL note: The original URL now shows the blog index; the article lives at /articles/2022-02-07-org-formation.

    Takeaway: A practical path to Organizations as code for small teams. Rehearse in a throwaway organization, because account mistakes are slow to undo.

  • When to Use Generics in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Ian Lance Taylor’s Go blog post (April 12, 2022) with guidelines on when to use type parameters in Go 1.18, and when not to.

    • First rule: Write Go by writing code, not by defining types. Start with functions and add type parameters later if needed.
