    • Good fits: Functions over the built-in container types (slices, maps, channels) that make no assumptions about element types, such as MapKeys[Key comparable, Val any].
    • More good fits: General-purpose data structures, and cases where the same method implementation works for every type.
    • Avoid: Using type parameters when an interface type or a plain method call works, or when implementations differ per type.
    • Basis: Blog version of talks given at Google Open Source Live and GopherCon 2021.

    Takeaway: Reach for generics when you notice yourself writing the same code for several types, not as the first design step.

  • A Deep Dive into Golang for OpenFaaS Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Ellis’s April 13, 2022 OpenFaaS post comparing the three Go function templates and showing how Go 1.18 improves local development in VS Code.

    • Templates: The classic go template (STDIN/STDOUT plus the Classic Watchdog, kept for historical reasons) and two newer HTTP-based templates he recommends instead.
    • History: The first OpenFaaS, called faas, had no templates: you built a binary and added the watchdog, reachable on port 8080.
    • Go 1.18: The post shows a Go 1.18 feature that improves the VS Code and IDE experience when developing functions locally.
    • Background: Links his GopherCon keynote “Zero to OpenFaaS in 60 months” and the “Dude, where’s my coldstart?” post.

    Takeaway: For new Go functions on OpenFaaS, use one of the HTTP templates rather than the classic go template.

  • Security Overview of AWS Fargate
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: AWS whitepaper giving a security overview of AWS Fargate, the serverless compute engine for ECS and EKS containers.

    • Isolation: AWS says Fargate tasks moved from a dedicated EC2 VM per task to Firecracker microVMs, keeping kernel-level isolation between tasks.
    • Firecracker: An open-source virtual machine monitor that runs lightweight microVMs with hardware-virtualization isolation and a minimal device model.
    • Topic: Per the title, the paper covers Fargate’s security architecture; its section contents could not be checked.
    • Source caveat: The PDF URL returns an XML error (removed from the CDN) and the whitepaper was not found by search; summary is based on the title and the AWS Open Source Blog post on Firecracker.

    Takeaway: Look for the current Fargate security material in AWS documentation. The key point is that each task gets its own VM-level boundary, unlike shared-node Kubernetes.

  • Where’s My Stuff on GCP?
    summary

    TL;DR: Short post (Feb 28, 2022) by Nick Brandaleone on finding every resource across a GCP organization with Cloud Asset Inventory.

    • Problem: Untracked resources cost money, and in AWS finding them means looping over every region.
    • Tool: Cloud Asset Inventory (released 2018) searches resources globally.
    • Command: gcloud asset search-all-resources --asset-types='storage.googleapis.com/Bucket' --limit 2.
    • Output fields: assetType, createTime, location, project and parent resource.
    • Scale: For large projects, export results to a storage bucket or BigQuery instead of printing everything.
    • Source caveat: medium.com blocked direct fetch; summary is based on a Freedium mirror of the post.

    Takeaway: Run gcloud asset search-all-resources regularly to find forgotten resources, and export the results to BigQuery for real audits.

  • warpgate: Smart SSH Bastion That Works with Any SSH Client
    summary

    TL;DR: Warpgate is a Rust bastion host for SSH, HTTPS, Kubernetes, MySQL, PostgreSQL, RDP and VNC that works with standard clients and records every session.

    • Transparent: Not a jump host; it forwards connections straight to the target and needs no client app or SSH wrapper.
    • Access model: Precise 1:1 assignment of users to hosts and URLs, set up in the DMZ.
    • Auth: Built-in TOTP 2FA, OpenID Connect SSO, temporary access tickets, and brute-force protection with IP blocking and user lockout.
    • Audit: Session recording with live view and replay in the admin web UI; browser-based SSH, RDP and VNC.
    • Packaging: Single binary with no dependencies, written in safe Rust; the README compares it with jump hosts, VPNs and Teleport.

    Takeaway: A lightweight, self-hosted alternative to Teleport when you need recorded, per-user access to a few internal services.

  • Bootstrapping Clusters with EKS Blueprints
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS launch post for EKS Blueprints, open-source IaC modules that build consistent, add-on-ready EKS clusters across accounts and regions.

    • Frameworks: Available for Terraform and for AWS CDK.
    • Add-ons: EKS add-ons plus open-source ones such as Prometheus, Karpenter, NGINX, Traefik, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Fluent Bit, KEDA and Argo CD.
    • Multi-team: Security controls for running several teams’ workloads in one cluster, including network policies and access to the cluster and to AWS resources.
    • Motivation: Assembling a tailored EKS cluster from many tools takes a long time and deep expertise; standardizing a fleet is hard.

    Takeaway: Use Blueprints as a reference for cluster add-ons and team onboarding.

  • Go, Generics, and Concurrency
    summary

    TL;DR: Jon Bodner, author of Learning Go, uses Go 1.18 generics to build a type-safe, reusable async/await-style concurrency helper (post dated April 25, 2022).

    • Problem: Goroutines, channels and select need boilerplate; his example calls two services in parallel and passes their results to a third within 50 ms.
    • Func type: A generic function type taking context.Context and one input and returning one value plus an error; closures adapt other signatures to it.
    • Promise: A generic Promise struct with unexported value and error fields and a done channel; Run launches a function and returns *Promise at once.
    • Tools built: Run any function asynchronously, wait for several to finish, add context cancellation, and chain outputs into inputs.
    • Source caveat: medium.com blocked direct fetch; summary is based on a Freedium mirror of the post.

    Takeaway: A good example of generics simplifying algorithms rather than just containers. Copy the pattern for fan-out/fan-in calls with timeouts.

  • The Go Programming Language and Environment
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Communications of the ACM article (May 2022, vol. 65 no. 5, pp. 70-78) by Go’s creators and core team on the history and design of the Go language and its environment.

    • Authors: Russ Cox, Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, Ian Lance Taylor and Ken Thompson.
    • Timeline: Design work began in late 2007; Go was released as open source in November 2009.
    • Access: DOI 10.1145/3488716; OpenAlex lists it as open access under CC-BY.
    • Source caveat: cacm.acm.org blocked the fetch with a Cloudflare check; summary is based on bibliographic data and mailing-list mentions found by web search, not the article text.

    Takeaway: Worth reading for why Go is shaped as it is. Get it through the DOI if the CACM site blocks you.

12.04.2022

  • Digital Forensics & Incident Response on Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Sysdig’s practical guide (March 29, 2022, Alberto Pellitteri) to digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) on Kubernetes, with a worked scenario on a compromised pod.

    • Challenge: Ephemeral containers make traditional forensics and post-mortems hard.
    • IR plan phases: Identification, coordination, resolution and improvement.
    • Detection tools: A SIEM (e.g. Elasticsearch), Falco for runtime alerts, Falcosidekick to fan events out, and Prometheus.
    • Forensic tools: Docker Explorer for offline analysis of snapshotted volumes, kube-forensics to save pod artifacts to AWS buckets, and Cloud Forensics Utils.
    • Offensive tooling: Also lists kubesploit for simulating attacks.
    • Scenario: Walks through the events affecting a Kubernetes pod and the response steps.

    Takeaway: Set up evidence capture (Falco alerts to a SIEM, plus a way to snapshot pods) before an incident. Afterwards is too late with ephemeral workloads.

  • difftastic: Diff That Understands Syntax
    summary

    TL;DR: Difftastic, by Wilfred, is a structural diff tool that compares files by their syntax tree instead of line by line.

    • Smarter diffs: Highlights only the syntax that changed, knows when whitespace matters, and handles code reformatted across lines.
    • Languages: Over 30 supported; unknown files fall back to a line diff with word highlighting, as do files with parse errors.
    • Git integration: Works as a git difftool or external diff, and with Mercurial; difftastic.el and a magit setup exist for Emacs.
    • Known issues: Slow and memory-hungry on files with many changes; the side-by-side view can be confusing.
    • Non-goals: Does not produce applicable patches and does not merge (it points to mergiraf for AST merging).

    Takeaway: Configure it as git’s external diff for reviewing refactors and reformat-heavy changes. Keep normal diff for patches.

  • Compose with Markdown in Google Docs on Web
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Workspace update (March 29, 2022): Google Docs on the web can auto-convert Markdown syntax as you type.

    • Enable: Tools > Preferences > “Automatically detect Markdown”; off by default for each user.
    • Already supported: * or - for bullets, numbered lists, and [] for checkboxes.
    • New: Headings, italic, bold, bold italic, strikethrough and links.
    • Admin: There is no admin control for the feature.
    • Rollout: Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains.

    Takeaway: Turn it on if you write Markdown by habit. It saves learning Docs keyboard shortcuts.

  • Managing Pod Scheduling Constraints and Groupless Node Upgrades with Karpenter in Amazon EKS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Containers blog post on Karpenter’s group-less autoscaling: how pod scheduling constraints drive node provisioning, and how to upgrade nodes without node groups.

    • Updated: A note says the post was updated in Feb 2024 for Karpenter v0.33.1 and the v1beta1 API, so it is not the 2022 original.
    • How Karpenter works: Watches the total resource requests of unschedulable pods, then launches right-sized nodes and binds pods to them for efficient bin-packing.
    • Versus Cluster Autoscaler: CAS relies on node groups and the kube-scheduler, which can mean minutes of pod scheduling latency.
    • Group-less: Capacity is managed without predefined node groups.
    • Topics: Pod scheduling constraints (node selectors, affinity and similar) and rolling node upgrades.

    Takeaway: Read it with the current Karpenter v1 docs, since the API has changed again after v1beta1.

  • kubectl-detector-for-docker-socket: kubectl Plugin for Detecting Dockershim Usage
    summary

    TL;DR: Detector for Docker Socket (DDS), from AWS, is a kubectl plugin that finds workloads mounting docker.sock, which matters for the dockershim removal.

    • Status: The repository is archived and AWS no longer supports or recommends using it.
    • Install: kubectl krew install dds.
    • How it works: Inspects Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs, checking volumes for paths matching *docker.sock.
    • Usage: kubectl dds scans every namespace you can access; --namespace limits the scope.
    • Context: Links the Kubernetes dockershim deprecation FAQ at k8s.io/dockershim.

    Takeaway: The migration it was built for is over. A quick kubectl get pods -A -o yaml | grep docker.sock does the same check today.

  • Kubernetes Infrastructure the GitOps Way
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: CNCF on-demand webinar (about 64 minutes, published Mar 31, 2022) by Michal Vančo of Kubermatic on applying GitOps to the Kubernetes infrastructure layer as well as to apps.

    • Toolchain: Flux, Helm, Grafana and Prometheus combined into an end-to-end pipeline.
    • Demo: Delivering the Kubermatic Kubernetes Platform through a simple web wizard (start.kubermatic).
    • Scope: From choosing a Git provider down to detailed stack configuration, including secrets management.
    • Channel: CNCF YouTube channel.
    • Source caveat: The YouTube description is empty; details come from the CNCF online-programs listing and a Kubermatic resource page found by web search.

    Takeaway: Watch it for a worked example of bootstrapping a whole platform stack with Flux and Helm from Git.

  • Charm: Tools to Make the Command Line Glamorous
    summary

    TL;DR: Charm builds open-source Go libraries and CLI tools that make terminal apps look good.

    • Libraries: Bubble Tea (TUI framework), Bubbles (components), Lip Gloss (styling and layout), Huh (forms), Glamour (Markdown rendering), Wish (SSH apps), Log and Harmonica (animation).
    • Tools: Gum (styled shell-script prompts without Go), Glow (Markdown reader), Skate (key-value store) and Mods (an LLM CLI).
    • Reach: The site says Charm technology is used in over 25,000 applications.
    • Current focus: The homepage now leads with Crush, an AI coding agent for the terminal, which was not on the site in 2022.

    Takeaway: Use Gum to make shell scripts interactive in minutes, and Bubble Tea when you need a full Go TUI.

  • kaar: Kubernetes Application Archive
    summary

    TL;DR: kaar (Kubernetes Application Archive), by Kris Nóva, bundles a Kubernetes app’s manifests and all its referenced container images into one OCI artifact.

    • Process: Recursively finds valid Kubernetes YAML, collects every referenced image (local first, then remote) and archives the images with the YAML.
    • Output: An OCI-compliant image that can be pushed to any registry.
    • CLI: tar-like flags: kaar -cf myapp.kaar ./app to create and kaar -xf myapp.kaar ./app to extract, with -z for compression.
    • Internals: A .kaar directory holds raw image data and metadata.
    • Status: The README says “Active Development”; the repo has about 152 stars and now lives under krisnova/kaar.

    Takeaway: An interesting idea for air-gapped or offline delivery. For production, check maintained tools that do the same job.

  • sa-hunter: Correlate Service Accounts, Pods and Nodes to Their RBAC Permissions
    summary

    TL;DR: sa-hunter, from Twistlock (Palo Alto Networks), maps Kubernetes service accounts and their pods and nodes to the RBAC permissions bound to them.

    • Status: Deprecated in favor of rbac-police.
    • Output: JSON listing each service account, the nodes and pods using it, and its roles and clusterroles with their rules.
    • Cloud IAM: Detects eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn and iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account annotations, which link service accounts to cloud identities.
    • Usage: Python 3; pip3 install -r requirements.txt, then ./sa_hunter.py with -a (all SAs), -o (output file) and -l (loud).
    • Purpose: Shows which nodes host powerful credentials, which matters for container escape scenarios.

    Takeaway: Use rbac-police now. The idea of mapping privileged service accounts to the nodes that run them is still worth checking in any cluster.

  • personal-security-checklist: 300+ Tips for Protecting Digital Security and Privacy
    summary

    TL;DR: Lissy93’s Personal Security Checklist is a curated list of 300+ tips for securing your digital life, also published as the website digital-defense.io.

    • Formats: CHECKLIST.md, raw data in personal-security-checklist.yml, a website and a free API.
    • Website: Filter by threat model, tick items off and track progress with charts.
    • Self-hosting: Built with Qwik and TypeScript; deploy as a static site or with the lissy93/personal-security-checklist Docker image (about 11 MB, non-root, nginx on port 8080).
    • Adoption: About 22.6k GitHub stars at the time of fetching.

    Takeaway: A good list to hand to non-security colleagues. Filter it by threat model rather than trying to do all 300 items.

  • stackrox: Kubernetes Security Platform with Risk Analysis, Visibility and Runtime Alerts
    summary

    TL;DR: StackRox is an open-source Kubernetes security platform that does risk analysis, visibility, runtime alerts and hardening advice.

    • Lifecycle coverage: Integrates at build, deploy and runtime.
    • Install: The operator is the supported method from release 4.10; Helm and script installs are marked deprecated.
    • Platforms: EKS, AKS, GKE, OpenShift, and Docker Desktop, Colima or minikube for local testing.
    • History: Built on the product formerly known as Prevent, and before that Mitigate and Apollo.
    • Community: Slack #stackrox and stackrox.io.

    Takeaway: A full open-source alternative to commercial Kubernetes security suites. Install with the operator, and budget for its resource footprint.

  • TruffleHog v3: Improved Secrets Detection
    summary

    TL;DR: TruffleHog, from Truffle Security, finds leaked credentials and checks whether they are still live. v3 was a rewrite focused on detection and verification.

    • Discovery: Scans Git, chats, wikis, logs, API testing platforms, object stores and filesystems.
    • Classification: Recognizes more than 800 secret types and maps each to its provider.
    • Validation: Tries to log in with each secret to confirm it is live.
    • Analysis: For about 20 common credential types, finds out who owns the secret and what it can access.
    • Run: docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/pwd" trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --org=....
    • Enterprise: A paid version adds continuous monitoring of Jira, Slack, Confluence, Teams and SharePoint.

    Takeaway: Run it in CI and against your GitHub org history. Treat verified-live findings as incidents and rotate those keys first.

  • Pixsy: Find and Fight Image Theft
    summary

    TL;DR: Pixsy is a commercial service that finds where your images are used online and pursues compensation for unlicensed use.

    • Import: Sync from image platforms, upload in bulk or use sFTP; the site says over 150,000,000 images are monitored daily.
    • Monitoring: Scans the public web and groups matches with AI filters; it reports over 350,000,000 matches found.
    • Enforcement: In-house copyright experts and partner law firms handle infringement cases on a no-win, no-fee basis; over 250,000 cases managed.
    • Alerts: Notifies you of new matches automatically.

    Takeaway: Useful for photographers or brands with valuable images. Check the commission terms before handing over cases.

  • PacketStreamer: Distributed tcpdump for Cloud Native Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: PacketStreamer, from Deepfence, is a distributed tcpdump: lightweight sensors capture packets on many hosts and stream them to one central pcap receiver.

    • Status: The repository was archived on Feb 11, 2026.
    • Sensors: Run on bare metal, Docker hosts, Kubernetes nodes and AWS Fargate, on Linux and Windows; packets are selected with BPF filters.
    • Transport: Streams can be compressed and encrypted with TLS.
    • Receiver: Writes one combined pcap, or feeds live traffic to Zeek, Wireshark, Suricata or ML models.
    • Build: Needs Go and libpcap-dev; build with make.
    • Origin: Used by Deepfence’s ThreatStryker to collect traffic for forensic analysis.

    Takeaway: The design is a neat way to do multi-host capture, but the project is archived, so fork it or use maintained alternatives.

  • Kubernetes Native Testing with Testkube
    summary

    TL;DR: “Containers from the Couch” video (about 46 minutes, April 6, 2022) looking at Testkube, a Kubernetes-native test framework.

    • Concept: Brings the flexibility of Kubernetes CRDs and the power of controllers to testing.
    • Executors: Different executors run the tests, and test status is stored directly in Kubernetes.
    • Project: github.com/kubeshop/testkube.
    • Channel: Containers from the Couch, tagged #aws #kubernetes #cloud.
    • Source caveat: Based on the video’s metadata and description only; the video itself was not watched.

    Takeaway: Worth a look if you want tests to run inside the cluster as Kubernetes objects instead of from an external CI runner.

06.04.2022

  • asdf: Extendable Version Manager for Ruby, Node.js, Elixir, Erlang and More
    summary

    TL;DR: asdf is a plugin-based CLI that manages several language runtime versions per project, replacing separate tools like nvm, rbenv, pyenv and gvm.

    • Config: One .tool-versions file per project, plus one global config.
    • Migration: Reads legacy files such as .node-version, .nvmrc and .ruby-version.
    • Switching: Changes runtime versions automatically as you move between directories.
    • Extensibility: A simple plugin system and an asdf-plugin-template; shell completion for Bash, Zsh, Fish and Elvish.
    • Adoption: About 25.6k GitHub stars at the time of fetching.

    Takeaway: Commit a .tool-versions file so the whole team and CI use the same toolchain versions.

  • Learn Anything: Learn Anything with Mind Maps
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Learn Anything is a free site for discovering learning resources on any topic, originally organized as interactive mind maps.

    • Current page: Shows little more than an “I want to learn” search prompt; content loads client-side.
    • Description: Its meta description says it connects you to the best resources for every subject.
    • Mind maps: The 2022 link described mind maps; the current page does not mention them.
    • Source caveat: Only the title, meta description and search box could be read; features could not be confirmed.

    Takeaway: Try it as a starting point for a new topic, but check that the linked resources are current.

  • lazygit: Simple Terminal UI for Git Commands
    summary

    TL;DR: lazygit, by Jesse Duffield, is a terminal UI for git that makes interactive rebases, partial staging and similar tasks quick.

    • Staging: Stage individual hunks or lines without editing patch files.
    • History editing: Interactive rebase, amend an old commit, cherry-pick, custom patches, and rebase from a marked base commit.
    • Other features: Bisect, worktrees, a commit graph, comparing two commits, filtering, custom commands, “nuke the working tree” and undo.
    • Install: Homebrew, MacPorts, Scoop and many Linux distro packages, or a release binary.
    • Pitch: The README’s rant targets git’s power being painful in daily use.

    Takeaway: If you avoid interactive rebase or git add -p, lazygit makes them routine. Learn its undo before experimenting.

  • Hacking the Cloud: CI/CDon’t CTF Walkthrough (GitLab, AWS)
    summary

    TL;DR: CI/CDon’t, by Nick Frichette on Hacking The Cloud, is a low-difficulty AWS and GitLab CI/CD capture-the-flag you deploy into your own AWS account with Terraform.

    • Deploy: git clone https://github.com/Hacking-the-Cloud/htc-ctfs.git, cd htc-ctfs/aws/cicdont, then terraform init and terraform apply.
    • Warning: It deploys intentionally vulnerable infrastructure, so use an account with no sensitive data.
    • Mitigations: The vulnerable EC2 instance is only reachable from your public IP and needs a randomly generated password.
    • Cost: The author reports three hours of running cost nothing on the bill, but longer runs may add up.
    • Content: The page covers the storyline, objective and a full walkthrough.

    Takeaway: A quick, cheap exercise in CI/CD-to-AWS attack paths. Run terraform destroy as soon as you finish.

  • How to Burp Good
    summary

    TL;DR: n00py’s 2017 blog post of practical Burp Suite tips for web application penetration tests, especially using Intruder for login attacks.

    • Brute force: Send the login POST to Intruder, clear auto-selected positions, mark the password field, use “Sniper” with a simple-list payload, then sort results by response length.
    • Response analysis: Use Grep - Match or Grep - Extract to flag keywords in responses.
    • Password spraying: Mark both username and password and switch to “Cluster bomb” with two payload sets.
    • Rationale: Tuning these attacks in Burp is easier than with tools like Hydra, the author says.
    • Age: Written in 2017, so Burp’s UI labels may have changed.

    Takeaway: A handy refresher on Intruder attack types. Respect lockout policies and the test scope when spraying.

  • Network Infrastructure Security Guidance by NSA
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NSA’s March 2022 Network Infrastructure Security Guidance, a technical report for network administrators on securing network architecture, devices and remote administration.

    • Document: A 58-page technical report, PP-22-0266, version 1.0.
    • Principles: Built on zero trust, defense in depth, segmentation and least-privilege access, according to coverage of the report.
    • Architecture: Reported recommendations include layered next-generation firewalls and placing public-facing systems in DMZ subnets.
    • Caveat in the source: NSA notes the guidance may need changes as owners adopt more mature zero trust designs.
    • Related: A separate NSA paper on zero trust maturity for the network pillar covers data flow mapping, macro- and micro-segmentation and SDN.
    • Source caveat: media.defense.gov returned 403 to automated fetches; summary is based on secondary coverage (eSecurity Planet, a mirrored copy listing) found by web search.

    Takeaway: Download the PDF in a browser and use it as a checklist for router, switch and firewall hardening and for admin access paths.

  • Magic Eraser: Remove Unwanted Things from Images in Seconds
    summary

    TL;DR: Magic Eraser, by Magic Studio, is a free web tool that removes unwanted objects, people or text from photos with AI.

    • Workflow: Upload, brush over the area, click erase and download.
    • Formats: JPG, PNG, AVIF and WEBP (the help also lists HEIC and TIFF); the site says there is no resolution limit.
    • Bulk: A Pro bulk mode edits 50 pictures at once.
    • Tips: Include the object’s shadow in the brush stroke, erase again instead of undoing, and erase long thin objects in short sections.
    • Pricing: Free with no signup; the site also upsells AI headshots.

    Takeaway: Fine for quick cleanups of screenshots or photos. Do not upload sensitive images to a third-party service.

  • aws-automated-incident-response-and-forensics: Automated Incident Response and Forensics Framework
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Labs framework that automates incident response and forensics steps across many AWS accounts with Lambda functions, following the AWS Incident Response whitepaper.

    • Origin: Built for an automotive-industry customer with many accounts, where IR was manual, slow, error-prone and hard for untrained staff.
    • Phases: Containment, acquisition, examination and analysis.
    • Trigger: Environment owners start the process with tags, so little knowledge is needed.
    • Isolation: Separate accounts for the automation, for artifact storage and for forensic environments; several analysis environments can run in parallel.
    • Evidence types: Static (memory and disk images) and live but segregated systems.
    • Limitation: Not meant to produce evidence admissible in court.

    Takeaway: A good reference design for tag-triggered isolation and evidence capture on EC2. Adapt the account split to your own landing zone.

  • BotKube: Messaging Bot for Monitoring and Debugging Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Botkube is a chat-based Kubernetes monitoring and troubleshooting tool. In 2022 it was an open-source ChatOps bot; it is now marketed as an AI assistant.

    • Alerts: Kubernetes alerts sent to your chat platform, with custom rules to cut noise and route alerts to the right developers.
    • Investigation: The Botkube Assistant uses your tools and docs to suggest root causes and generate commands.
    • Remediation: Suggests fixes, generates manifests and runbooks, and drafts post-mortem or RCA reports.
    • Access model: Lets developers troubleshoot from chat without direct CLI access to clusters.
    • Shift: The current site is a commercial, AI-led product page, unlike the open-source bot that was linked in 2022.

    Takeaway: Chat-based cluster access needs tight RBAC on the bot’s service account. Review what commands it is allowed to run.

  • AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK): Define and Use AWS Service Resources Directly from Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Overview page for AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK), which lets you define and manage AWS service resources as Kubernetes objects.

    • Deprecated site: The page says this documentation site is deprecated and has moved to a new site.
    • Purpose: Use AWS managed services, such as databases or queues, from Kubernetes without defining them outside the cluster or running them inside it.
    • Packaging: One controller image per AWS service in the ECR Public Gallery, at gallery.ecr.aws/aws-controllers-k8s/$SERVICENAME-controller, for example s3-controller.
    • Versioning: No :latest tags; you must always pin a release version.
    • Requirements: Any Kubernetes cluster works; EKS is not required.

    Takeaway: Install only the service controllers you need, pin their versions, and scope each controller’s IAM role tightly.

  • Kubernetes Security Through GitOps Best Practices: Argo CD and Starboard
    summary

    TL;DR: A roughly 24-minute tutorial by Anais Urlichs that adds Aqua’s Starboard to an Argo CD GitOps workflow so Kubernetes workloads are continuously scanned for vulnerabilities.

    • Argo CD setup: Deploys Argo CD and manages Helm charts declaratively through it.
    • Starboard install: Installs the Starboard operator via Helm, then deploys an app and inspects the generated vulnerability reports and other scan results.
    • What Starboard does: Open source tool that wraps other scanners and exposes their reports through the Kubernetes API as custom resources.
    • Observability: Deploys Prometheus through Argo CD and reads Starboard metrics via a Starboard exporter.
    • Companion material: A blog post at anaisurl.com/gitops-argocd-starboard accompanies the video.
    • Status note: Starboard has since been discontinued and folded into Trivy (trivy kubernetes and Trivy Operator).

    Takeaway: The pattern of managing a security scanner as just another GitOps-deployed app, with results queryable as Kubernetes objects and Prometheus metrics, still applies. Today you would do it with Trivy Operator instead of Starboard.

  • Your Pocket-Sized Cloud with a Raspberry Pi
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Ellis shows how to turn a spare Raspberry Pi into a small API-driven “cloud” using faasd (OpenFaaS without Kubernetes) to run functions, cron jobs, webhook receivers and web pages.

    • Scaled-down definition: Targets under 1GB of RAM, containers for packaging and a REST API for deployment; accepts a single point of failure but recommends an NVMe SSD over an SD card.
    • Why not Kubernetes: Kubernetes has a non-trivial cost on a Pi; faasd runs containers directly on containerd, with few moving parts and simple upgrades (replace the binary).
    • Components: OpenFaaS gateway with REST management API, built-in Prometheus monitoring and a NATS-based queue for async invocations.
    • Public access: Optional inlets HTTPS tunnel to expose the OpenFaaS API and custom function domains.
    • Triggers and CI: Covers cron-scheduled functions via cron-function, asynchronous invocation, and deploying from GitHub Actions.
    • Real use: The author runs 7 applications 24/7 on a Raspberry Pi 3.

    Takeaway: If you have an idle Pi, faasd gives you a low-maintenance place to run small automations and webhooks without operating a Kubernetes cluster.

  • 10 Must-Have Kubernetes Tools
    summary

    TL;DR: Viktor Farcic (DevOps Toolkit channel) walks through the Kubernetes tools he uses almost daily, grouped by job, in about 16 minutes.

    • Local dev: Rancher Desktop.
    • Operate: kubectl, kubectx and kubens; k9s as a terminal UI.
    • Packaging: Helm for third-party applications.
    • GitOps: Argo CD or Flux for synchronization.
    • Certificates and infra: cert-manager for TLS; Crossplane for infrastructure; Crossplane or KubeVela for application definitions.
    • Observability: Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, Loki and Promtail for logs.
    • Policy: Admission control with Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper. A gist with the commands is linked in the description.

    Takeaway: A reasonable reference stack for a 2022-era cluster. Treat it as a checklist of categories (GitOps, certs, policy, observability) rather than as fixed tool picks.

  • How We Discovered Vulnerabilities in CI/CD Pipelines of Popular Open-Source Projects
    summary

    TL;DR: Cycode researchers found script-injection flaws in GitHub Actions workflows of popular open-source projects, where unsanitized issue and comment input could run code in builds and steal privileged tokens.

    • Affected projects: Liquibase, Dynamo BIM, FaunaDB, Wire, Astro, Kogito and Ombi, among dozens reported; all were fixed after disclosure, with no sign of prior exploitation.
    • Root cause: Workflows interpolated attacker-controlled values such as ${{github.event.issue.title}} directly into run steps.
    • Token abuse: GITHUB_TOKEN has read/write rights by default for non-fork events; a job-level env var can be read with env | grep GITHUB_TOKEN.
    • Runner internals: With code execution an attacker controls later steps and can capture secrets from process environments, network traffic or Runner.Worker memory, including secrets not referenced in the workflow.
    • Mitigations: Prefer maintained actions over inline run scripts, pass untrusted input through env: variables, set permissions: read-all or tighter, scope PATs and org secrets, and require approval for all outside collaborators.
    • Scope: These are workflow misconfigurations, not GitHub platform bugs, and can exist in private repos too.

    Takeaway: Grep your workflows for ${{ github.event. inside run: blocks and move those values into env:. Also set explicit minimal permissions: on every workflow.

  • Fantastic AWS Hacks and Where to Find Them
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper (Datadog) gives a primer on how companies actually get breached on AWS and how to prevent the most common causes. The deck is also titled “A Primer on Cloud Security and How Companies Get Hacked on AWS” and has a SANS New2Cyber video.

    • Framing: Cloud APIs are Internet-exposed with no internal network for the control plane, so identity is the perimeter. Quotes Scott Piper: the responsibility model is “split”, not shared.
    • Cause 1, stolen long-lived credentials: IAM user keys never expire and leak via build logs, app logs, source code, Docker images and laptops. Use AWS SSO or another IdP for humans and instance roles or cross-account roles for apps.
    • Cause 2, public S3 buckets: Driven by insecure defaults, confusing terms like “Authenticated users”, and bucket policy/ACL complexity. Use S3 Block Public Access.
    • Cause 3, SSRF to instance metadata: Exploiting 169.254.169.254 (Capital One case); enforce IMDSv2.
    • Tooling appendix: Prowler, ScoutSuite, Cloudsplaining, IAM Access Analyzer; IaC scanners tfsec, checkov, terrascan, regula, KICS; offensive Pacu, enumerate-iam; emulation Stratus Red Team, Leonidas.
    • Learning resources: flaws.cloud, flaws2.cloud, CloudGoat, hackingthecloud, permissions.cloud, tl;dr sec and CloudSecList newsletters.

    Takeaway: Three fixes cover most of the disclosed incidents in the deck: no IAM users with static keys, S3 Block Public Access, and IMDSv2 enforcement. Start there before buying tools.

  • access-undenied-aws: Explain AWS AccessDenied CloudTrail Events and Suggest Remediation
    summary

    TL;DR: Access Undenied, by Ermetic (author noamdahan), is a Python CLI that parses AWS CloudTrail AccessDenied events, works out why access was denied, and suggests least-privilege fixes.

    • Problem solved: Many services (S3, SSO, EFS, EKS, GuardDuty, Batch, SQS and others) return AccessDenied without detail, and explicit denies are hard to trace across policies.
    • SCP support: Can evaluate service control policies in the management account, which otherwise must be hunted down manually.
    • Install and run: pip install access-undenied-aws, then access-undenied-aws analyze --events-file cloudtrail_events.json.
    • Output: An AccessDeniedReason plus details such as PoliciesToAdd and ExplicitDenyPolicies.
    • Deployment options: Same-account mode with default permissions, or cross-account roles for multi-account and SCP analysis; can also run as a Lambda.
    • Repo moved: The URL now redirects to tenable/access-undenied-aws after Tenable acquired Ermetic.

    Takeaway: Useful for debugging permission errors in multi-account AWS Organizations with SCPs. Feed it the CloudTrail event instead of guessing which policy layer blocked the call.

22.03.2022

  • 10 Real World Stories of How We’ve Compromised CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NCC Group consultants (Aaron Haymore, Iain Smart, Viktor Gazdag, Divya Natesan, Jennifer Fernick) describe ten CI/CD pipeline compromises from real assessments, arguing that pipelines are highly privileged “execution engines”.

    • Jenkins #1: S3 bucket with directory listing exposed a script holding a Git credential. That credential also worked on Jenkins, which led to admin access, where Groovy in the script console dumped about 200 credentials (AWS keys, SSH certs, SAST/DAST tokens).
    • Jenkins #2-3: A “least-privilege” builder role still had Build/Replay, which allows arbitrary Groovy. The GitHub OAuth plugin option “Grant READ permissions to all Authenticated Users” let any GitHub account in.
    • GitLab #4-8: Shared, non-isolated runners using --privileged, secrets in plain environment variables, missing protected branches, and the host Docker socket mounted into jobs, allowing container escape and cross-job compromise.
    • #9-10: Kube2IAM abuse and the developer laptop as an entry point.
    • Recommendations given: Remove hardcoded credentials, keep Jenkins off the Internet, add audit plugins, enforce MFA for admins, use isolated and protected runners, and avoid exposing the Docker socket.
    • Source caveat: The original URL now redirects to NCC Group’s research landing page. This summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy from 2022.

    Takeaway: Audit who can trigger code execution in your CI (replay rights, unprotected branches, shared runners) as carefully as who has admin. In these stories, an execution path was enough to reach every secret.

  • threat-matrix-cicd: Threat Matrix for CI/CD Pipelines
    summary

    TL;DR: An ATT&CK-style threat matrix for CI/CD pipelines, created by the Mercari Security Team (author rung) and published alongside the CODE BLUE 2021 talk “Attacking and Securing CI/CD Pipeline”.

    • Tactics covered: Initial Access, Execution, Execution (Production), Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration and Impact, each with techniques and mitigations.
    • Component model: Developer device, Git repository service (GitHub, GitLab), CI and CD services (CircleCI, Cloud Build, CodeBuild, GitHub Actions, Spinnaker, Argo CD), secret management (AWS/GCP Secret Manager, Vault) and production (cloud, registries, Kubernetes).
    • Key argument: Supply-chain attacks are not the only CI/CD risk; the pipeline’s access to production and secrets is a target in itself.
    • Format: A matrix image plus per-tactic tables in the README; reviewed by Mercari’s Platform Team.
    • Current status: A June 2026 note says the author is now building cicd-sensor, a pre-release open-source runtime security sensor for CI/CD pipelines.

    Takeaway: Use the matrix as a checklist when threat-modelling your own pipeline. Walk each tactic against your CI, CD and secret store and note which mitigations you lack.

  • AWS ClickOps: Notify on Manual Actions by Monitoring CloudTrail
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Paul Zietsman (cloudandthings.io) built ClickOops, a Lambda that scans CloudTrail logs for manual AWS console actions and posts them to Slack so teams can bring IaC back in sync.

    • Motivation: Read-only console access for everyone is too strict, but console changes (“ClickOps”) cause drift; the aim is to alert and investigate, not block.
    • Detection: Filters CloudTrail events to identify human console actions, building on Arkadiy Tetelman’s analysis of which CloudTrail events indicate manual actions.
    • Deployment: Fits AWS Control Tower, running in the Log Archive account that receives all org CloudTrail logs. Can also run single-account if S3 keys match */{{account_id}}/CloudTrail/*/*.json.gz.
    • Notifications: Slack app incoming webhook, with the URL stored in SSM Parameter Store. Messages include the IAM action, the identity and the full event.
    • Terraform module: A March 2022 update points to cloudandthings/terraform-aws-clickops-notifier.
    • Source caveat: Medium blocked direct fetching; this summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy of the post.

    Takeaway: A cheap drift-detection control for teams that allow console write access. Deploy the Terraform module in your central logging account and route alerts to a dedicated channel.

  • x509-certificate-exporter: Monitor Kubernetes x509 Certificates with Prometheus
    summary

    TL;DR: A Prometheus exporter from Enix that watches X.509 certificates in and around Kubernetes and turns expiration dates into metrics and alerts.

    • Sources watched: TLS Secrets of any type, ConfigMaps, kubeconfigs, PKCS#12 and JKS/JCEKS stores, on-disk PEM files via glob patterns, and admission webhook/APIService/CRD caBundle fields.
    • Chains: Every certificate in a PEM bundle becomes its own series, so intermediate and root CAs are tracked too.
    • CRLs: Tracks Certificate Revocation List freshness in a dedicated x509_crl_* metric family.
    • Deployment: In-cluster (Helm chart on Artifact Hub), as a node-level DaemonSet for on-disk PKI, or as a standalone binary.
    • v4 changes: Full rewrite around a YAML config, memory-safe watches (README claims about 10x lower limits on Secret-heavy clusters), and multi-cluster fan-in from one instance.
    • Supply chain: SLSA Build L3 provenance, cosign-signed binaries, images and chart, and SBOM attestations.

    Takeaway: Install it with the Helm chart and alert on days-to-expiry. It catches certificates cert-manager does not manage, such as kubeadm, kubelet and webhook CA certificates.

  • How to Set Up Federated Single Sign-On to AWS Using Google Workspace
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog guide to federating Google Workspace into AWS through IAM SAML federation, so Workspace users can open the AWS console without separate credentials. The post is now titled “How to set up IAM federation using Google Workspace”.

    • Title change: Retitled in March 2022, and updated in August 2022 for the rename of AWS SSO to IAM Identity Center. The post now points readers to Identity Center as the simpler, central option.
    • Mechanism: Create a SAML identity provider in IAM per account. Google Workspace sends SAML 2.0 assertions that map users to IAM roles.
    • Required attributes: https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/Role and https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/RoleSessionName; optionally SessionDuration.
    • User flow: The user starts from the Google apps menu (myaccount.google.com), picks the custom AWS app, and lands in the console with the selected role’s permissions.
    • Limitation: Per-account IAM federation has to be configured in every AWS account, which is why the post now steers to Identity Center.

    Takeaway: For multi-account setups, use IAM Identity Center with Google Workspace as the external IdP. Keep per-account IAM SAML for single accounts or special cases.

  • starboard: Kubernetes-Native Security Toolkit
    summary

    TL;DR: Starboard was Aqua Security’s Kubernetes-native security toolkit that ran scanners and stored their results as CRDs. It has been discontinued and merged into Trivy.

    • Status: The README says Starboard is discontinued with no new features, PRs or issues accepted. The CLI became trivy kubernetes and the operator became Trivy Operator.
    • Idea: Integrate heterogeneous security tools by writing their outputs into Kubernetes custom resources readable through the Kubernetes API.
    • Vulnerability scanning: Automated scanning of workload images.
    • Config audit: Checks Kubernetes resources against predefined rules or custom OPA policies.
    • Compliance: CIS Benchmark infrastructure checks and NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening compliance reports.

    Takeaway: Do not adopt Starboard now. Use Trivy Operator, which keeps the reports-as-CRDs model.

  • wireguard-operator: Provision WireGuard VPN in a Kubernetes Cluster
    summary

    TL;DR: A Kubernetes operator that deploys a WireGuard VPN server and peers from custom resources. This repo is archived; the project is now maintained by Namecheap at nccloud/wireguard-operator.

    • Status: The README states the repo is archived; continue at github.com/nccloud/wireguard-operator.
    • CRDs: A Wireguard resource creates the server, and WireguardPeer resources (with wireguardRef) create peers. Get a client config with kubectl get wireguardpeer peer1 --template={{.status.config}} | bash.
    • Features: Automatic key generation and IP allocation; keys stored as Kubernetes Secrets, so no persistence is needed; falls back to wireguard-go if the kernel module is missing.
    • Metrics: Exposes Prometheus metrics via prometheus_wireguard_exporter.
    • Tested platforms: IBM Cloud, Gcore, GKE (needs mtu: "1380", no Autopilot or COS-containerd images) and DigitalOcean (needs serviceType: "NodePort", since its load balancer lacks UDP). EKS and AKS are unchecked.

    Takeaway: A simple way to get VPN access into a cluster’s network. Use the nccloud fork and verify support on your provider first, since EKS and AKS were untested.

  • container-security-checklist: Container Security Checklist
    summary

    TL;DR: A curated checklist by krol3 covering container security from image build to running workload, with links to tools and further reading.

    • Threat model: Insecure host, misconfigured containers, vulnerable apps, supply chain attacks, exposed secrets, insecure networking, image integrity and container escapes.
    • Supply chain: Image signing with Notary (TUF) and Sigstore Cosign, plus material on Sigstore with SPIFFE/SPIRE.
    • Image hardening: Minimal or container-optimized OS images, multi-stage builds, official base images, non-root dedicated users, minimal capabilities, --read-only, no host path mounts, and fixed tags.
    • Runtime profiles: SELinux, AppArmor and Seccomp, plus avoiding privileged containers.
    • Scanning: CVE and secret scanning of images, Dockerfile linting and dynamic analysis for runtime behaviour.
    • Wider scope: Later sections cover the infrastructure and workload (Kubernetes) side.

    Takeaway: A good review list for a Dockerfile or platform baseline. Tick through the image-hardening items in a PR template or a CI policy.

  • PurplePanda: Identify Privilege Escalation Paths Within and Across Clouds
    summary

    TL;DR: PurplePanda, by Carlos Polop (HackTricks/PEASS author), enumerates cloud and SaaS permissions into Neo4j to find privilege escalation paths and dangerous permissions, for both red and blue teams.

    • Supported platforms: The README lists Google Cloud (GCP), GitHub and Kubernetes. Docker examples also show Concourse and CircleCI discovery variables; AWS and Azure are not listed.
    • Backend: Requires a Neo4j database set through PURPLEPANDA_NEO4J_URL and PURPLEPANDA_PWD. An optional SHODAN_KEY enriches discovered public IPs.
    • Usage: python3 main.py -e -p google,github,k8s --github-only-org --k8s-get-secret-values --gcp-get-secret-values.
    • Cross-platform paths: Links identities across platforms, for example a GitHub or Kubernetes credential that leads into GCP.
    • Red-team mode: Can ingest API keys and tokens found by PEASS tools, since attackers rarely have read access to whole configurations.
    • Docs: Each /intel module has its own README, and the main README links HackTricks pages on abusing each platform.

    Takeaway: Worth running against a GCP plus GitHub plus GKE estate to find cross-platform escalation paths. For AWS you need a different tool, despite the title’s “across clouds”.

  • awesome-security-hardening: Security Hardening Guides, Tools and Resources
    summary

    TL;DR: An awesome-list by decalage2 collecting security hardening guides, best practices and audit tools across operating systems, network gear, services and cloud.

    • OS guides: RHEL, CentOS, SUSE, Ubuntu, Windows and macOS.
    • Network and virtualization: Switches, routers, IPv6, firewalls and VMware.
    • Containers: Docker and Kubernetes hardening references.
    • Services: SSH, TLS/SSL, Apache, Tomcat, Jetty, IIS, mail, FTP, databases, Active Directory, ADFS, Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, NTP, NFS and CUPS.
    • Other areas: Authentication and passwords; hardware, CPU, BIOS and UEFI; cloud.
    • Audit tools: Lynis, testssl.sh, ssh-audit, CHIPSEC, ANSSI chipsec-check and Docker Bench for Security, among others.

    Takeaway: A starting index when you need the authoritative hardening guide (CIS, ANSSI, vendor) for a specific system. Pair the guide with the matching audit tool listed there.

17.02.2022

Free Labs To Learn Cloud Pentesting:

  • flaws.cloud: AWS Security Challenges
    summary

    TL;DR: flaws.cloud is Scott Piper’s (Summit Route) free browser-based challenge that teaches common AWS mistakes and gotchas through a series of levels.

    • Focus: AWS-specific issues only; the site says there is no SQL injection, XSS, buffer overflows or similar.
    • Structure: Everything runs from a single AWS account, and each challenge is a sub-domain of flaws.cloud. Level 1 is a hint about S3 “buckets”.
    • Hints: A series of hints teaches how to find the needed information. You can follow the hints alone to reach the next level without running commands.
    • Defensive angle: Each level opens by explaining how to avoid the problem from the previous level.
    • Credits: Thanks Andres Riancho, Ken Johnson, Nicolas Gregoire and others for ideas; feedback goes to scott@summitroute.com.
    • Sequel: flaws2.cloud adds attacker and defender paths.

    Takeaway: A short, free way to build intuition for how AWS misconfigurations are found. It works well as onboarding for anyone new to cloud security.

  • flaws2.cloud: AWS Security Challenges for Attackers and Defenders
    summary

    TL;DR: flaws2.cloud is Scott Piper’s follow-up to flaws.cloud. It teaches AWS security through two paths: an Attacker path and a Defender path that investigates the same attack.

    • Attacker path: Exploit misconfigurations in serverless (Lambda) and containers (ECS Fargate).
    • Defender path: Work as an incident responder for the same app, using logs of a previous successful attack.
    • Skills taught: Analysing logs with jq, and instructions for setting up Athena in your own environment.
    • Hands-on optional: As with the original, you can click through hints instead of playing.
    • Suggested order: The author recommends playing the Attacker side first, then the Defender side.
    • Scope: AWS-specific issues only, with no XSS or buffer overflows.

    Takeaway: The Defender path is the rarer part. Use it to practise reconstructing an AWS incident from logs, not just exploitation.

  • Serverless-Goat: OWASP Deliberately Vulnerable Serverless Application
    summary

    TL;DR: OWASP ServerlessGoat is a deliberately vulnerable AWS Lambda app, a .doc-to-text converter, that demonstrates the weaknesses in PureSec’s Serverless Security Top 10 (SAS-01 to SAS-10).

    • App: Takes a URL to an MS-Word .doc file and returns its text, which serves as the attack surface.
    • Deployment: One-click from the AWS Serverless Application Repository; the CloudFormation stack output WebsiteURL gives the app address.
    • Injection (SAS-01): Event-data injection leading to OS command injection.
    • Config and permissions (SAS-03/04): Publicly open S3 bucket discoverable from the URL, and over-privileged function roles that leak a DynamoDB table and allow S3 tampering.
    • Other weaknesses: Poor monitoring and logging (SAS-05), vulnerable dependencies (SAS-06), application-layer DoS (SAS-08) and verbose errors (SAS-10).
    • Walkthrough: LESSONS.md holds the lesson walkthrough, marked as under development.

    Takeaway: A quick lab to show developers that Lambda apps still get classic injection plus cloud-specific IAM over-permissioning. Deploy it only in a throwaway account.

  • AWS S3 CTF Challenge
    summary

    TL;DR: The author (n0j) shares solutions and setup instructions for four short AWS S3 misconfiguration challenges written for the AppSec USA 2017 and CactusCon 2017 CTFs.

    • Challenge 1: Public object in a named bucket; solve by understanding S3 URL styles or with aws s3 ls s3://<bucket>.
    • Challenge 2: Object readable by “any authenticated AWS user” via a canned ACL; any valid AWS credentials in awscli retrieve it.
    • Challenge 3: Bucket policy that allows public s3:ListBucket but restricts object reads to EC2 IP ranges in us-west-2, so you must fetch it from an EC2 instance there.
    • Challenge 4: Pre-signed URLs; rebuild the URL from bucket, object, access key, signature and expiry in Unix time. Setup uses aws s3 presign --expires-in.
    • Format: Each prompt is a fake email, followed by the solution and the setup steps.
    • Policy note: Recommends checking AWS’s Acceptable Use Policy for penetration testing before running similar events.

    Takeaway: A compact lesson in S3’s access layers (ACLs, bucket policies, IP conditions, pre-signed URLs). The setup steps are reusable if you want to run the same challenges internally.

  • AWS-Vulnerable-Lambda: Vulnerable AWS Lambda Application
    summary

    TL;DR: A small, deliberately vulnerable Flask application deployed to AWS Lambda with Zappa, for exploring Lambda-specific attack ideas.

    • Vulnerability: Command injection via a query parameter, used as https://url/dev/?ping=ls.
    • Deployment: pip install -r requirements.txt in a virtualenv, set a unique S3 bucket and region in zappa_settings, then bash deploy.sh.
    • Prerequisites: An IAM user with Lambda, S3 and API Gateway permissions in ~/.aws/credentials.
    • Context covered: How Lambda sandboxes work, warm containers, and the idea of escalating from function code into wider AWS resources.
    • Further reading: Links Rich Jones’ 33C3 talk “Gone in 60 milliseconds” and the Black Hat 2017 talk on hacking serverless runtimes.

    Takeaway: Useful as a minimal demo of command injection on Lambda and container reuse. It is a small, older project, so use it for a quick lab rather than a full course.

  • lambhack: Vulnerable Serverless Lambda Application
    summary

    TL;DR: lambhack, by wickett, is a vulnerable serverless Lambda application written in Go. Its first release only demonstrates arbitrary OS command execution through the query string.

    • Exploit example: curl "https://XXXX.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/lambhack/c?args=uname+-a;+sleep+1".
    • Container reuse: Shows files written to /tmp persisting between invocations, which demonstrates warm container reuse.
    • Setup: go get github.com/wickett/lambhack, with AWS credentials in a limited-permission profile (suggested name sparta).
    • Background: Accompanies the author’s Velocity talk “Serverless Security: Are You Ready for the Future?”.
    • Known gaps: The README lists no UI, no XSS, injection or auth attacks yet, and asks for contributions.

    Takeaway: A tiny demo showing that Lambda does not remove classic RCE and that /tmp state survives between calls. For broader labs, DVSA or ServerlessGoat cover more ground.

  • iam-vulnerable: Vulnerable-by-Design AWS IAM Privilege Escalation Playground
    summary

    TL;DR: IAM Vulnerable, by Bishop Fox, uses Terraform to deploy a vulnerable-by-design AWS IAM privilege escalation playground with 31 supported privesc paths.

    • Scale: Deploys over 250 IAM resources into an AWS account you choose; use a dedicated account with no production data.
    • Cost: The default configuration costs nothing. Optional non-free modules add resources such as those needed for ssm:StartSession paths, and can be toggled on demand.
    • Learning path: Read Spencer Gietzen’s 21 original privesc methods (Rhino), practise using Gerben Kleijn’s Bishop Fox guide, then run tools against it.
    • Tool testing: Suggested targets for Cloudsplaining, AWSPX, Principal Mapper and similar scanners.
    • Successor: The README points to CloudFoxable, a gamified CTF-style sandbox by the same author.
    • Deploy: Standard terraform init and terraform apply with your AWS credentials.

    Takeaway: A good way to benchmark IAM analysis tools or train on escalation paths without building the policies yourself. Run terraform destroy when done.

  • cloudgoat: Vulnerable-by-Design AWS Deployment Tool
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudGoat is Rhino Security Labs’ “vulnerable by design” cloud deployment tool that spins up CTF-style scenarios for practising cloud penetration testing.

    • Scenarios: About 30 standalone scenarios graded Easy to Hard, e.g. iam_privesc_by_rollback, cloud_breach_s3, ec2_ssrf, codebuild_secrets, rce_web_app, ecs_takeover, detection_evasion, vulnerable_cognito.
    • Newer content: The current README also lists AI-related scenarios such as bedrock_agent_hijacking and agentcore_identity_confusion, plus Azure support.
    • Install and use: pipx install cloudgoat, cloudgoat config aws, then cloudgoat create <scenario> and destroy.
    • Requirements: Linux or macOS, Python 3.9+, Terraform >= 1.5.0, AWS CLI, Azure CLI and jq.
    • Warnings: Never deploy into production. CloudGoat only removes resources it created, so delete anything you add manually.
    • Design goals: Curated scenarios, good documentation, modular start/reset/shutdown and community expandability.

    Takeaway: Still a maintained standard for hands-on AWS attack practice, and it now covers Azure and AI services. Run it in an isolated account and use the IP whitelist config.

  • attacking-cloudgoat2: Attacking CloudGoat 2 Walkthrough
    summary

    TL;DR: Appsecco’s free, step-by-step walkthrough book for six CloudGoat 2.0 AWS scenarios, written in Markdown for mdBook.

    • Scenarios covered: IAM privesc by rollback, cloud_breach_s3, IAM privesc by attachment, EC2 SSRF, RCE web app and CodeBuild secrets.
    • Audience: Penetration testers learning AWS attacks, and developers, sysadmins and cloud engineers who want to understand the AWS attack surface.
    • Local hosting: cargo install mdbook, then mdbook serve in documentation/ and browse to localhost:3000.
    • License: Book content under CC-BY-SA 4.0; code and commands under MIT.
    • Version caveat: Written for CloudGoat 2.0. Current CloudGoat has many more scenarios, and details may have drifted.

    Takeaway: Use it as a reference when stuck on the original CloudGoat scenarios. Try each scenario yourself first.

  • dvca: Damn Vulnerable Cloud Application
    summary

    TL;DR: Damn Vulnerable Cloud Application is a demo project for AWS privilege escalation, with a write-up on going from SSRF to global account administrator.

    • Scope: AWS-centric. The frontend does not depend on the backend technology, so other backends could be added.
    • Write-up: Usage is explained in the author’s Poka Techblog post “Privilege Escalation in the Cloud: From SSRF to Global Account Administrator”.
    • Prerequisites: An AWS-managed domain, its Route 53 hosted zone ID, and ACM certificates (root and wildcard).
    • Deployment: make all DOMAIN_NAME=... ROOT_CERTIFICATE=... CERTIFICATE=... HOSTED_ZONE=..., or modular targets such as prerequisites, frontend and fargate.
    • Warning: The README says not to deploy it unless you know very well what you are doing.

    Takeaway: Read the linked write-up for the SSRF-to-admin chain. Deploying the lab needs a real domain and certificates, which is more setup than most alternatives.

  • DVSA: Damn Vulnerable Serverless Application
    summary

    TL;DR: OWASP DVSA (Damn Vulnerable Serverless Application) is a deliberately vulnerable AWS serverless app for practising common serverless vulnerabilities and testing security tools.

    • Purpose: Lets security professionals test skills and tools legally, and helps developers understand how serverless apps get attacked.
    • Vulnerabilities: Includes both documented and intentionally undocumented issues.
    • Deployment: From the AWS Serverless Application Repository; the CloudFormation outputs give the DVSA website URL.
    • Local dev: Client build needs Node 8.16.2 and python2. The backend uses AWS SAM CLI, managed with ./dvsa.sh commands such as client-build, client-connect --stack and package-template.
    • Warning: Do not install it in a production account.

    Takeaway: One of the more complete serverless security labs. Deploy it in a sandbox account and use it to test SAST or runtime tools against Lambda-based apps.

  • sadcloud: Stand Up Insecure AWS Infrastructure with Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: sadcloud, from NCC Group, spins up intentionally insecure AWS infrastructure with Terraform: about 84 misconfigurations across 22 services, initially drawn from ScoutSuite’s checks.

    • Use cases: Training, and evaluating AWS security tools, both built-in and third-party.
    • Cost: A 24-hour run cost about $10, mostly Redshift ($6/day) and EKS ($2.40/day).
    • Sample audits: Published reports from ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, CloudSploit and tfsec run against the full corpus.
    • Setup: Generate keys with ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f data/ssh_keys/terraform_rsa, then use Terraform from sadcloud/sadcloud, toggling modules per misconfiguration.
    • Warning: Use a new, dedicated AWS account, never production.

    Takeaway: Handy for comparing CSPM or IaC scanners on a known set of misconfigurations. Disable the Redshift and EKS modules if you want it cheap.

  • Breaking and Pwning Apps and Servers on AWS and Azure: Free Training Courseware and Labs
    summary

    TL;DR: Appsecco open-sourced its complete 3-day hands-on training “Breaking and Pwning Apps and Servers on AWS and Azure”, including courseware and lab setup.

    • Why released: During COVID-19 lockdowns, Appsecco released it to the community rather than let it go out of date.
    • Content: Scenarios from their pentesting, vulnerability assessment and OSINT engagements: discovering, identifying and exploiting weaknesses in AWS and Azure apps and servers.
    • Repo layout: documentation (Markdown course), setup-files (to build a student VM and the cloud labs) and extras.
    • Requirements: An AWS account activated for payments and an Azure account.
    • Style: Attack-focused, with guided walkthroughs and tool coverage; the README notes it is not heavy on documentation.

    Takeaway: A free, structured course for learning cloud pentesting across AWS and Azure. Budget for lab costs and tear the resources down after each module.

Others:

  • gita: Manage Many Git Repositories with Sanity
    summary

    TL;DR: gita, by nosarthur, is a Python CLI that shows the status of many Git repos side by side and runs Git or shell commands across them from any directory.

    • Status view: gita ll lists every registered repo with branch, local/remote sync state (5 colour-coded situations), modifications and last commit message.
    • Registering repos: gita add <paths>, gita add -a <parent> to add recursively, and -b for bare repos.
    • Delegated commands: Predefined commands such as gita fetch and gita remote <repo> (defined in cmds.json); custom commands can be added.
    • Superman mode: gita super [repos|groups] <git-command>, e.g. gita super checkout master across all repos.
    • Shell mode: gita shell [repos|groups] <shell-command> runs arbitrary shell commands per repo.
    • Groups and context: gita group add ... -n <group>, and gita context <group> or gita context auto to scope operations.

    Takeaway: Handy if you juggle many repos, such as microservices or dotfiles plus infra. Group them and use gita ll and gita fetch as a morning check.

  • tf-controller: GitOps Terraform Controller for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Weave TF-Controller is a Flux controller that reconciles Terraform resources the GitOps way. It is now renamed Tofu Controller, lives at flux-iac/tofu-controller, and supports OpenTofu and Terraform.

    • Repo moved: The weaveworks URL now redirects to github.com/flux-iac/tofu-controller; docs are at flux-iac.github.io/tofu-controller.
    • GitOps automation model: Manage resources from provisioning to enforcement, e.g. a whole EKS cluster.
    • Hybrid model: GitOps only parts of existing infrastructure, such as an existing cluster’s node group or security group.
    • State enforcement model: Use GitOps to enforce an existing tfstate without other changes.
    • Drift detection model: Only detect drift against a tfstate and decide later what to do.
    • Incremental adoption: “At your own pace”: you do not need to GitOps-ify everything at once.

    Takeaway: If you already run Flux, this lets Terraform or OpenTofu run as Kubernetes-reconciled objects, with drift detection as a low-risk first step. Point any old references at the flux-iac repo.

  • Aerides: Dynamic IaC Scanning by Deploying Terraform Against LocalStack
    summary

    TL;DR: Aerides, by Erik Steringer (NCC Group), demonstrates “dynamic” IaC scanning: deploy Terraform to LocalStack, then run API-based tools like Scout Suite and Principal Mapper against it before anything reaches real AWS.

    • Problem: Scout Suite and PMapper query AWS APIs and cannot read IaC files directly.
    • Approach: Deploy Terraform HCL for a sample “TKTK Service” (S3 buckets, VPCs and security groups, IAM users, groups and roles) into LocalStack.
    • PMapper: Supports LocalStack natively via graph create --localstack-endpoint.
    • Scout Suite: Pointed at LocalStack through a mitmproxy addon (proxy_aws_to_localstack.py) using HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and AWS_CA_BUNDLE.
    • Tests: Test cases check privilege escalation risks, s3:PutObject limits on low-privilege users, IAM policies using NotAction, and world-open security groups. They run in GitHub Actions on pull requests.
    • Prereqs: Python 3.8+, Terraform, LocalStack, mitmproxy and Scout Suite; tested on Ubuntu 20.04.

    Takeaway: The mitmproxy-to-LocalStack trick lets you reuse any AWS API-based auditor in CI. Use it as a pattern for catching IAM privesc paths that static IaC scanners miss.

  • aws-oidc-ci: Terraform, GitHub and AWS with OIDC
    summary

    TL;DR: A Terraform module from Marco Lancini’s utils repo that sets up OIDC identity federation between AWS and GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, so pipelines get short-lived role credentials instead of stored keys.

    • GitHub usage: allow_github = true, github_org, and github_repos entries such as "<repo>:*" or a branch-scoped "<repo>:ref_type:branch:ref:main".
    • GitLab usage: allow_gitlab = true with gitlab_repos such as "project_path:mygroup/*:ref_type:branch:ref:main".
    • Scoping: Restrict trust to specific repos and branches through the subject claim patterns.
    • Background: Points to CloudSecDocs “CI/CD Providers” for how it works.
    • References: GitHub’s OIDC announcement and hardening docs, the ScaleSec write-up, Google’s keyless auth post, and GitLab’s AWS OIDC docs and Terraform example.

    Takeaway: A small, readable starting point for removing long-lived AWS keys from CI. Always pin the trust to repo and branch rather than *.

  • kubelogin: Access Kubernetes via OIDC, e.g. Keycloak
    summary

    TL;DR: kubelogin, by int128, is a kubectl plugin (kubectl oidc-login) for Kubernetes OpenID Connect authentication. It opens a browser login with your IdP and hands the token to kubectl.

    • Mechanism: Runs as a client-go credential plugin via the kubeconfig exec section with oidc-login get-token --oidc-issuer-url=... --oidc-client-id=....
    • Install: brew install kubelogin, kubectl krew install oidc-login, choco install kubelogin, or a release binary saved as kubectl-oidc_login.
    • Flow: Run kubectl get pods; kubelogin opens the browser, you log in, and the credentials return to kubectl.
    • Setup needed: An OIDC provider (the README shows Google Identity Platform; the title example is Keycloak), an API server OIDC configuration, and a cluster role binding.
    • Docs: A setup guide in docs/setup.md covers the provider, cluster and kubeconfig steps.

    Takeaway: The standard way to give humans SSO-backed, short-lived kubectl access on self-managed clusters. Pair it with RBAC bindings on OIDC groups.

  • Announcing Grafana Incident: Smart Incident Management for Your Teams
    summary

    TL;DR: Mat Ryer (Grafana Labs) announced Grafana Incident, an incident management tool built into Grafana Cloud to cut the coordination, communication and documentation overhead of incidents.

    • Collaboration: Automatically creates online meeting spaces for each incident.
    • Roles: Assign incident roles and quickly message the people holding them.
    • Tracking: Task and TODO tracking, plus an automatically maintained timeline for postmortems.
    • Context: Embed Grafana graphs and queries, attach GitHub issues, PRs and dashboards, and get suggested related dashboards.
    • Chatbot: A command-line-style chatbot interface usable without opening a browser; more third-party integrations were planned.
    • Availability: Launched in preview for free and paid Grafana Cloud users. An update note on the page says it is now generally available at no extra cost to all Grafana Cloud users.

    Takeaway: If you already run on Grafana Cloud, it is a no-extra-cost option for incident coordination tied to your dashboards. Compare it with dedicated tools before standardising.

  • action-validator: Validate GitHub Actions YAML Files
    summary

    TL;DR: action-validator, by mpalmer, is a standalone Rust tool that lints GitHub Actions and workflow YAML against published JSON schemas and checks that paths/paths-ignore globs match real files.

    • Intended use: Git pre-commit hooks and similar local checks.
    • Schema validation: Ensures action and workflow files are well-formed according to the official JSON schemas.
    • Glob check: Flags paths or paths-ignore patterns that match no file in the repo.
    • Install: Prebuilt binaries, cargo install action-validator, asdf or mise plugins, or npm install -g @action-validator/core @action-validator/cli.
    • Node use: The @action-validator/core package can be used inside Node.js apps.
    • Funding: The author is experimenting with a “code fund” model to pay for new features.

    Takeaway: Cheap to add as a pre-commit hook so broken workflow syntax is caught before a push. It checks structure only; it is not a security linter.

  • amazon-ecr-credential-helper: Docker Credential Helper for Amazon ECR
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS’s Docker credential helper for Amazon ECR, which gets registry credentials from your AWS credentials automatically so you never run docker login for ECR.

    • Configure: Put docker-credential-ecr-login on PATH and set "credsStore": "ecr-login" in ~/.docker/config.json, or use credHelpers per registry, including public.ecr.aws.
    • Install: sudo dnf install -y amazon-ecr-credential-helper on AL2023, packages for AL2, macOS, Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, Alpine and Windows, mise, or go install.
    • Credentials: Uses the standard AWS chain: env vars, AWS_PROFILE, shared config and credentials files, and instance or task roles.
    • Caching: Local auth cache in ~/.ecr; control it with AWS_ECR_DISABLE_CACHE and AWS_ECR_CACHE_DIR.
    • Login calls: AWS_ECR_IGNORE_CREDS_STORAGE makes it ignore docker login/logout and report success.
    • Prereqs: Docker 1.11 or later and available AWS credentials.

    Takeaway: Use credHelpers scoped to your ECR registries on CI runners and dev machines. It removes token refresh scripts and avoids storing ECR passwords in Docker config.

  • jless: Command-Line Pager for JSON Data
    summary

    TL;DR: jless, by Paul Julius Martinez, is a Rust command-line JSON viewer meant to replace combinations of less, jq, cat and an editor for reading JSON.

    • Display: Syntax-highlighted output that omits key quotes, closing delimiters and trailing commas.
    • Navigation: Expand and collapse objects and arrays, with vim-inspired movement commands.
    • Search: Full regex-based search.
    • Platforms: macOS and Linux; Windows support is planned.
    • Install: brew install jless, pacman -S jless, cargo install jless, MacPorts, Void, NetBSD and FreeBSD packages, or release binaries.
    • Build note: Building from source on Linux needs X11 (libxcb) libraries for clipboard support.

    Takeaway: Pipe large API responses or kubectl get -o json output into jless when you want to explore structure. Keep jq for transforming the data.

  • dockly: k9s-Style Terminal UI for Docker
    summary

    TL;DR: dockly, by Liran Tal, is a Node.js terminal UI for managing Docker containers, services and images. The README calls it an “immersive terminal interface”.

    • Install: npm install -g dockly, then run dockly.
    • Connection: Connects to the local Docker daemon over the Unix socket by default.
    • Remote daemons: -H/--host, -P/--port and -T/--protocol (http, https or ssh), or -s/--socketPath.
    • Filtering: --containerFilters="name=test&status=running" limits which containers are shown.
    • Recognition: Featured in DevOps Weekly and console.dev.
    • Title note: The “k9s-style” wording is the archive’s description; the README does not reference k9s.

    Takeaway: A quick TUI for inspecting containers on a box without remembering docker flags.

  • simulator: Kubernetes Security Training Platform
    summary

    TL;DR: Simulator, by ControlPlane, creates a Kubernetes cluster in your AWS account and runs scenarios that misconfigure it, so you can practise attacking and then mitigating Kubernetes vulnerabilities.

    • Repo moved: The URL now redirects to controlplaneio/simulator. The README reflects a V2 redesign and links 2023 CNCF CTF walkthroughs.
    • Prereqs: Docker and an AWS account; authenticate with environment variables or the shared credentials file, with required IAM permissions documented.
    • Components: Simulator CLI, container images, AMIs, infrastructure code and scenario definitions.
    • Getting started: The Player Guide covers launching environments and deploying and playing scenarios.
    • Hosted option: A waitlist at kubesim.io for private scenarios and training content.

    Takeaway: A realistic, self-hosted Kubernetes CTF for platform and security teams. Expect AWS costs, and tear environments down after each session.

  • validkube: Ensure Kubernetes YAML Best Practices, Hygiene and Security
    summary

    TL;DR: ValidKube, by Komodor, is an open-source web tool that runs pasted Kubernetes YAML through several open-source checkers for validity, hygiene, security and best practices.

    • Validate: Schema checks with kubeconform.
    • Clean: Removes clutter from manifests with kubectl-neat.
    • Secure: Scans with Trivy and with Kubescape for vulnerabilities and DevOps best practices.
    • Audit: Fairwinds Polaris best-practice checks.
    • Self-hosting: The backend deploys to AWS with the Serverless framework and the frontend to Netlify, via make deploy. It needs Go 1.17+, Yarn and the CLI tools above.

    Takeaway: Handy for one-off checks of a manifest. For CI, run kubeconform, Trivy, Kubescape or Polaris directly. Avoid pasting sensitive manifests into a hosted instance.

  • A Hello World GitOps Example Walkthrough
    summary

    TL;DR: The zwischenzugs blog walks through a trivial “hello world” GitOps setup he uses to demonstrate GitOps principles, built from four GitHub repos with GKE, Terraform, GitHub Actions and FluxCD.

    • Repos: gitops-example, gitops-example-app, gitops-example-deploy and gitops-example-infra under github.com/ianmiell.
    • Separation of concerns: Three actors (Dev owns app code, Ops owns deployment, Infra owns the cluster), mirrored in the repo split. The author notes one repo could also do all of it.
    • Stack: Docker, Kubernetes, GitHub, GitHub Actions, shell, Google Kubernetes Engine and Terraform.
    • Steps: Prerequisites, fork the repos, create infrastructure, set up a Docker registry login secret and a repository access token, install and set up FluxCD, then build and run the app.
    • Prereqs: GitHub, Google Cloud and Docker registry accounts.
    • Background: Links the author’s ebook on GitOps history and a separate post on “GitOps Decisions”.

    Takeaway: Follow it end to end to see how app, deploy and infra repos hand off through CI and Flux. Then decide how much of that repo separation your team actually needs.

  • The Delivery Hero Reliability Manifesto
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Delivery Hero CTO Christian Hardenberg published the company’s Reliability Manifesto (October 2021): a seven-page set of numbered, assertive rules for building reliable systems at roughly 10 million orders a day.

    • Context: Sunday-night peaks, minutes to recover before food gets cold, and growth above 1000% year-on-year in some countries. Run in a decentralized way without a common infrastructure team.
    • Meta and architecture: Rules are not bypassed silently and are reviewed twice a year. Start with a monolith; microservices must not share storage and must avoid synchronous call chains deeper than 2 services. Data mesh, managed services over self-hosted, RFCs and ADRs.
    • Delivery: Deploy every day, track deployments, deploy with a safety net, infrastructure as code, automated tests, never code alone.
    • Resilience: Service tiers, graceful degradation, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks; failure testing, central logging, ongoing load tests, runbooks, chaos, surviving an AZ outage, disaster recovery.
    • Culture, security, cost: Track all incidents, blameless culture, weekly operations review; edge blocking, central access control, secret storage, attack simulation; cost visible per squad, frugal logging.
    • Supporting practices: A published per-service “reliability score”, a weekly operations meeting and quarterly tech-debt tracking.
    • Source caveat: The live page is behind a bot-check challenge. This summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: A strong template for writing your own engineering standards: short, numbered, assertive rules with a built-in review cadence. Borrow the format and the reliability-score idea.

  • The Startup Guide to Sensible Incident Management
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Evans (incident.io, February 2022) gives early-stage startups a lightweight set of incident management defaults, essentially how incident.io ran its own incidents at the time.
