    • Low threshold: Treat any interruption to normal work as an incident, even a single Sentry error or a customer report. This makes ownership clear, shares knowledge and helps prioritisation.
    • Severities: Keep just two, a higher and a lower one (they use Minor and Major); severity matters little when small.
    • Roles and logging: Do not worry about formal roles yet. Log incidents somewhere simple; a Notion DB or Google Sheet linked to a Slack channel works.
    • Running incidents: Open a fresh Slack channel or doc, say clearly whose incident it is, and post logs, errors, graphs and your thinking as you go.
    • Customers: Over-share via a status page, tweets or direct messages, since early customers tend to be forgiving.
    • After incidents: Skip lengthy post-mortems at small scale (they had run none) and read through incidents you were not involved in instead.
    • Vendor note: Explicitly partly a pitch; product details are kept to the end, with pricing of £149/month for Slack workspaces under 25 users at the time.

    Takeaway: Copy the defaults: a low threshold, two severities, a channel per incident, and narrating in the channel. Add formal roles and post-mortems only when headcount and complexity demand them.

  • IaC Security Scanning: Why, Flaws, Etc.
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper’s deck “Scanning Infrastructure-as-Code for security flaws” (OWASP DevSlop; March 2021, updated January 2022) covers why to scan IaC, how the open-source Terraform scanners compare, and why IaC scanning alone is not enough.

    • Baseline first: Start with high-signal checks: network exposure, trivially over-privileged *:* policies, and public resources such as writable buckets, public AMIs and shared RDS snapshots. Ship secure-default Terraform modules.
    • Code vs plan: Plan scanning catches variables, interpolations and child modules but needs AWS credentials and is slower. Per the March 2021 table, checkov and regula do both, terraform-compliance does plan only, and terrascan, tfsec and semgrep do code only.
    • Custom checks: checkov in Python (low complexity), regula and terrascan in Rego (expressive but harder), tfsec in YAML (limited), terraform-compliance as a BDD DSL.
    • CI challenges: Lack of warn vs break-the-build modes; suggests IDE extensions and scanning only git diffs.
    • Drift: terraform plan ignores unmanaged extras such as an added SG ingress rule or an attached policy. Prevent drift with locked-down prod accounts, SCPs and break-glass access; detect it with CloudTrail queries and driftctl scan.
    • Runtime scanning: A last line of defence: ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, Cartography, Cloudsplaining, Steampipe.

    Takeaway: Treat IaC scanning, drift detection and runtime scanning as three layers. Scanning Terraform alone misses console changes and unmanaged resources. The tool comparison dates from 2021.

  • GitOps Model for Provisioning and Bootstrapping Amazon EKS Clusters Using Crossplane and Flux
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 2 of an AWS Containers blog series. It uses Flux on a management EKS cluster to drive Crossplane, which provisions a complete new EKS cluster, then deploys workloads to it, all from Git.

  • watchexec: Run a Command Whenever a Watched Path Changes
    summary

    TL;DR: watchexec is a standalone Rust tool that watches a path and runs a command whenever files change, for running tests, linters or rebuilds automatically.

    • Examples: watchexec -e js,css,html npm run build, and watchexec -r -e py -- python server.py to restart a server.
    • Behaviour: Watches the current directory recursively and coalesces bursts of events, such as editors’ swap files, into one run.
    • Ignores: Honours .gitignore and .ignore.
    • Process handling: Uses process groups to track forking programs; passes changed paths through environment variables or STDIN.
    • Platforms and install: macOS, Linux and Windows; package managers, cargo binstall watchexec-cli, release binaries, or cargo install --locked watchexec-cli.
    • Pairs with: checkexec, just and systemfd; there is also a watchexec library for building custom tools.

    Takeaway: A language-agnostic replacement for ad-hoc entr, nodemon or xargs loops. Use -r for long-running servers and -e to limit triggers.

  • Swimm: Documentation as Code
    summary

  • IAM on EKS Done Right
    summary

    TL;DR: NextLink Labs explains how to give people access to an EKS cluster with AWS IAM: assumable admin and developer roles mapped into Kubernetes through the aws-auth ConfigMap.

    • Creator role tip: Create the cluster with a role others can assume, because EKS maps key permissions to the creating identity.
    • IAM setup (no SSO): aws iam create-role for eks-admin-role and eks-developer-role, assume-role policies, groups eks-admin-group and eks-developer-group via put-group-policy, then add-user-to-group.
    • With SSO: Users assume the same roles through SSO instead of IAM groups.
    • aws-auth mapping: Map role ARNs to Kubernetes groups in aws-auth, with node roles in system:bootstrappers and system:nodes. Configure it through the Terraform EKS module or eksctl.
    • RBAC: Bind the mapped groups with ClusterRole and RoleBinding objects for scoped developer access.

    Takeaway: Use roles, not individual IAM users, in aws-auth, and keep the cluster creator identity break-glass only. On current EKS, evaluate access entries instead of hand-editing the ConfigMap.

  • Comparing Two Methods for Integrating Vault with Kubernetes
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Nico Kabar (HashiCorp, January 2022) compares the two supported ways to get Vault secrets into Kubernetes pods: the Vault Agent sidecar injector and the Vault CSI provider.

    • Sidecar injector: A mutating webhook (vault-k8s) adds a Vault Agent container that renders secrets into a shared in-memory tmpfs volume. It supports all Vault auto-auth methods, plus templating and caching.
    • CSI provider: A DaemonSet on every node uses SecretProviderClass objects and the pod’s service account to mount secrets into an ephemeral CSI volume during container creation. It supports only Kubernetes auth and uses hostPath, which some platforms such as OpenShift disable by default.
    • Projection differences: The post says CSI can render into Kubernetes Secrets and env vars, while the injector cannot create Kubernetes Secrets and reaches env vars only via Agent templating.
    • Shared traits: No app code changes, all secrets engines, the service account token as “secret zero”, Vault roles instead of Kubernetes RBAC, Helm deployable, secrets fetched before pod start, auto-renewal.
    • Design checklist: Secret projection, scope, types, definition, encryption, governance, rotation, caching, auditability.
    • Source caveat: The live page returned a Vercel bot check. This summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy.

    Takeaway: Pick the injector when you need Agent features (templating, caching, non-Kubernetes auth). Pick CSI when you want a lighter per-node driver or synced Kubernetes Secrets, provided hostPath is allowed.

  • GitOps on Kubernetes: Deciding Between Argo CD and Flux
    summary

    TL;DR: Christian Hernandez (Red Hat-sponsored post, December 2021) compares Argo CD and Flux, the two CNCF GitOps projects, covering what they share and where they differ.

    • Status then: Both were CNCF incubating. The post lists 30 public references and about 14 contributing companies for Flux, against 176 references and about 90 companies for Argo CD.
    • Similarities: Secret encryption support, webhook receivers, alerting and notifications, and image update automation (Flux Image Update Automation, Argo CD Image Updater).
    • Bootstrapping: Flux bootstraps itself into a GitHub or GitLab repo and hands off to in-cluster controllers; Argo CD has no native bootstrap.
    • Reconciliation: Flux intervals are set per component; Argo CD uses a global setting (default 3 minutes).
    • Delivery: Flux renders everything through Kustomize and uses the Helm Go library, so helm ls works. Argo CD runs kubectl apply style, with sync waves, and renders Helm templates itself, so helm ls shows nothing.
    • UI and RBAC: Flux has no official UI and relies purely on Kubernetes RBAC. Argo CD has a rich UI plus its own granular ACL RBAC and users, with OIDC or Dex integration.

    Takeaway: Choose Flux if you want Kubernetes-native RBAC and Helm compatibility, and Argo CD if you want a UI and app-level multi-tenant access control. The adoption figures are from 2021.

  • What Happens After Kubernetes Upgrade to 1.24 (Dockershim Removal)
    summary

    TL;DR: Jim Angel tests the Kubernetes v1.24 dockershim removal ahead of release: he builds a kubeadm single-node v1.23 cluster on Docker, upgrades to a v1.24 alpha, watches kubelet fail, and switches to containerd. The page is now titled “Upgrade gotchas for Kubernetes v1.24”.

    • Why 1.24 matters: dockershim lived inside kubelet’s codebase from before CRI existed, and 1.24 removes it.
    • Who is affected: Mainly users of upstream open-source Kubernetes; many cloud providers already used a non-Docker CRI.
    • Baseline: Ubuntu 20.04, kubeadm v1.23.0 and Calico. The first run failed until kubelet and Docker used the systemd cgroup driver, a v1.22+ change.
    • Pre-release testing: Builds Debian packages from kubernetes/release to install v1.24 alphas.
    • Failure seen: failed to run Kubelet: using dockershim is not supported, please consider using a full-fledged CRI implementation.
    • Fix: Configure containerd and point kubelet at --container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock, ending at v1.24.0-alpha.1 Ready. Introduces ctr as the containerd CLI.

    Takeaway: Historical now, but the method still applies: test the next minor release on a throwaway kubeadm node using alpha packages before your upgrade window.

  • Darker Corners of Go
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Rytis Biel’s long guide to Go’s surprising behaviours and traps, aimed at experienced programmers who know Go syntax but not its pitfalls. It is also available as an ebook and a printed book.

    • Formatting and imports: gofmt, opening brace placement, trailing commas, unused, underscore and dot imports, goimports.
    • Variables and operators: Short declarations and variable shadowing, operator precedence, no ternary operator, iota.
    • Slices and strings: Copying slices, append growth, nil slices, make traps, retained backing arrays; immutable strings, string vs []byte, runes and UTF-8 length.
    • Maps and loops: Random iteration order, maps as pointers, non-addressable values, data races and sync.Map; reused for-loop iterator variables, labeled break/continue.
    • Goroutines and interfaces: Running goroutines do not keep main alive, and one panicking goroutine crashes the app. Covers nil interface checks, implicit satisfaction and wrong type assertions.
    • Other topics: Embedding vs redefining types, equality and uncomparable types, pass-by-value vs pointer, logging and time.
    • Source caveat: The live site returned an empty response. This summary is based on a Wayback Machine copy of the post.

    Takeaway: A good reading list for Go code reviewers. The loop-variable section predates Go 1.22, which changed per-iteration loop variable semantics, so check your Go version.

  • On Go Application Structure
    summary

    TL;DR: A Changelog post argues there is no copy-paste Go project layout. Structure should follow your application’s contexts, illustrated with his Go courses web app.

    • Core claim: Good structure isolates work and decouples components; over-complex structure hurts more than it helps.
    • Peter Bourgon quote: Go project structure is idiomatically different from project to project, unlike frameworks in Ruby and similar languages.
    • Contexts first: He splits the app into student and admin packages, each with its own Lesson type. The student view has video URLs and CompletedAt; the admin view has video provider, repo info and permission strings.
    • Other patterns: Discusses a core domain with services implemented by layers, and his experiments with a single flat package.
    • Beginner advice: Using familiar MVC is acceptable when you lack experience. It never gives the clarity of a tailored structure, but it lets you ship and learn.
    • Title note: The page title now reads “Thoughts on how to structure Go code”.

    Takeaway: Start from the bounded contexts of your app and let packages mirror them, rather than importing a generic cmd/pkg/internal template. Refactor as your understanding grows.

  • The Busy Developer’s Guide to Go Profiling, Tracing and Observability
    summary

    TL;DR: Datadog’s (author felixge) “Busy Developer’s Guide to Go Profiling, Tracing and Observability”, a practical, work-in-progress guide to Go’s built-in profilers and the runtime internals behind them.

    • Mental model: Covers the goroutine scheduler, the garbage collector, and stack versus heap allocation as the background needed to read profiles.
    • CPU profiler: The OS sends SIGPROF for every 10ms of CPU time consumed. Covers labels, CPU utilisation, syscalls in profiles and limitations.
    • Memory profiler: Allocs vs heap profiles, sampling via runtime.MemProfileRate (set once, early in main()), and in-use vs RSS. It shows where allocations were made, not what keeps them alive.
    • Block and mutex profilers: Enable with runtime.SetBlockProfileRate, how the two differ, and their limitations.
    • Other profilers: Goroutine and ThreadCreate profiles, plus advanced sections on stack traces and the pprof format.
    • Status: Marked as a work in progress; some sections were planned but not yet written.

    Takeaway: Read the limitations sections before trusting a profile; they explain most misleading pprof results. Bookmark it for setting sampling rates in production services.

  • mizu: API Traffic Viewer for Kubernetes, Think tcpdump for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Mizu was UP9’s API traffic viewer for Kubernetes (“tcpdump for Kubernetes”). The repo now redirects to Kubeshark, its successor, which indexes cluster-wide traffic with eBPF.

    • Repo moved: github.com/up9inc/mizu now resolves to kubeshark/kubeshark, and the README describes Kubeshark, not Mizu.
    • Capture: Indexes cluster-wide network traffic at the kernel level using eBPF and answers queries using network, API and Kubernetes semantics.
    • PCAPs: Retrospective cluster-wide packet captures filtered by node, time, workload and IP, with long-term retention.
    • TLS: Decrypts TLS/mTLS traffic via eBPF without key management or sidecars.
    • Install: helm repo add kubeshark https://helm.kubeshark.com, helm install kubeshark kubeshark/kubeshark, then kubectl port-forward svc/kubeshark-front 8899:80. An ingress is recommended for production.
    • AI integration: Exposes traffic data over MCP, e.g. claude mcp add kubeshark -- kubeshark mcp.

    Takeaway: Use Kubeshark for debugging inter-service API calls in a cluster. Treat its plaintext TLS visibility as sensitive and restrict who can access the dashboard.

  • pleco: Automatically Remove Cloud Managed Services and Kubernetes Resources by TTL Tags
    summary

    TL;DR: Pleco, from Qovery, is a garbage collector that deletes cloud and Kubernetes resources once their ttl tag expires, while a do_not_delete tag protects resources. Qovery uses it in its own production environment.

    • Providers: Kubernetes (namespaces), AWS, Scaleway, DigitalOcean, GCP and Azure.
    • AWS coverage: DocumentDB, ElastiCache, RDS (databases, subnet and parameter groups, snapshots), EBS, ELB, EC2 key pairs, ECR, EKS, IAM users, groups, roles, policies and OIDC providers, CloudWatch logs, KMS keys, VPCs and more.
    • Safety: Runs in dry-run by default. Deletion needs --disable-dry-run/-y; do_not_delete=true, ttl=0, malformed labels and negative TTLs block deletion.
    • Usage: pleco start aws --level debug -i 240 -a eu-west-3 ... -y, with per-resource flags; similar for scaleway and do.
    • Packaging: A Helm chart on Artifact Hub and a Docker image qoveryrd/pleco.

    Takeaway: Useful for cleaning up ephemeral preview and test environments. Start in dry-run mode in a non-production account and tag anything long-lived do_not_delete first.

  • chezmoi: Dotfile Manager
    summary

    TL;DR: chezmoi, by twpayne, manages dotfiles securely across multiple diverse machines from one source repo; documentation is at chezmoi.io.

    • Secrets: Integrates with password managers so secrets stay out of the dotfiles repo.
